trackers.name: Sher Edling LLP (climate & pollution accountability)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the dominant U.S. plaintiff firm in climate-accountability litigation — representing states, counties, cities, tribes and water providers to hold fossil-fuel and chemical companies financially responsible for climate deception and for contamination (PFAS, 1,4-dioxane, PCBs, MTBE), with over $1B recovered. WHO IT SUITS: a government or public entity (not individuals) facing climate-driven damages or drinking-water contamination from corporate polluters. Works nationwide.

trackers.name: Crag Law Center (Pacific Northwest)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: “legal aid for the environment” — a Portland nonprofit providing free and low-cost legal services to community groups, conservation organisations and tribes across the Pacific Northwest, with a strong record stopping freeways, warehouses, mega-dairies, logging and fossil-fuel projects (it helped stop a Nestlé water-bottling plant and defend Portland’s fossil-fuel policy). WHO IT SUITS: a PNW frontline community facing a well-funded developer or polluter.

trackers.name: Environmental Integrity Project
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a national watchdog founded by former EPA enforcement attorneys that both litigates and documents to force enforcement of anti-pollution laws against coal plants, factory farms, refineries and the oil-and-gas industry — and runs data tools like Ashtracker (coal-ash groundwater contamination). WHO IT SUITS: a community near a major industrial polluter where agencies won’t enforce. Also a source of hard evidence for a campaign.

trackers.name: Native American Rights Fund (NARF)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the leading nonprofit Indian-rights law firm (since 1970), using treaties and existing law to hold federal and state governments to their obligations — including landmark environmental and water fights (e.g. representing the Bay Mills Indian Community against the Line 5 pipeline tunnel under the Straits of Mackinac). WHO IT SUITS: a tribe or tribal community facing a project that threatens treaty rights, water or sacred lands.

trackers.name: Advocates for the West
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a nonprofit public-interest environmental LAW FIRM (Boise, ID) that litigates — free to communities and grassroots groups — against harmful grazing, mining, drilling, logging and development across the Western U.S., with a deep record of Clean Water Act, NEPA and ESA wins. WHO IT SUITS: a Western community or group facing an unlawful federal land or water decision. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before deadlines to comment or sue pass.

trackers.name: Public Justice — Environmental Enforcement Project
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a national public-interest litigation team that brings Clean Water Act and other citizen-suit cases against corporate polluters — factory farms, industrial discharges — alongside affected communities, winning enforceable settlements it then monitors. WHO IT SUITS: a community harmed by illegal pollution where the government won't act. Core environmental laws let any affected person sue; this team helps you do it.

trackers.name: National Environmental Law Center (NELC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a nonprofit litigation center (since 1990) that brings citizen-suit lawsuits to enforce anti-pollution laws — Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, hazardous waste, endangered species — working side by side with state and local citizen groups to hold corporate polluters accountable. WHO IT SUITS: a local group needing legal firepower against an illegal polluter.

trackers.name: WildEarth Guardians
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Western conservation organisation with a strong in-house and partnered LITIGATION program protecting wildlife, wild rivers, public lands and climate — a frequent plaintiff on NEPA, ESA and Clean Air/Water cases (from keeping coal in the ground to protecting imperiled species). WHO IT SUITS: a fight over public-lands extraction, wildlife or a polluting facility in the American West.

trackers.name: Western Watersheds Project
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a conservation nonprofit that LITIGATES (with partners like Advocates for the West) to protect Western public lands, watersheds and wildlife from livestock overgrazing and energy development, forcing the BLM and Forest Service to comply with environmental law. WHO IT SUITS: a fight over grazing, habitat degradation or public-lands energy across the interior West.

trackers.name: National Parks Conservation Association — litigation
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the leading national-parks advocacy organisation, which establishes and enforces legal safeguards through the courts — joining and bringing lawsuits to defend parks and surrounding lands from harmful development, pollution and habitat fragmentation. WHO IT SUITS: a project threatening a national park, monument or adjacent landscape.

trackers.name: Global Greengrants Fund
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a grassroots environmental grant fund that makes small, fast grants (typically a few hundred to a few thousand dollars) to community-led and Indigenous groups defending land, water and climate — over 14,000 grants in 168 countries since 1993. WHO IT SUITS: a frontline group that needs quick, flexible money to organise. HOW IT DIFFERS from a crowdfunder: this is grant money from a foundation (no repayment, no public campaign), identified through on-the-ground advisory networks rather than an open application — connect with a local ally or advisor to be put forward.

trackers.name: Patagonia Environmental Grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Patagonia funds small, grassroots activist groups with direct-action agendas and multi-pronged campaigns to protect a specific place — over $140M given to local environmental groups, through retail, corporate and international grant programs. WHO IT SUITS: a scrappy campaign taking on the root cause of a threat with clear, measurable goals. HOW IT DIFFERS: a corporate grantmaker that deliberately backs confrontational, place-based fights larger funders avoid; check its guidelines and deadlines and apply directly.

trackers.name: The Conservation Alliance — grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a business-funded grantmaker awarding grants to grassroots groups working to protect land and water across North America, with a dedicated Confluence program for Indigenous and communities-of-colour led work. WHO IT SUITS: a campaign to permanently protect a specific wild place or waterway. HOW IT DIFFERS: member businesses vote on which conservation projects to fund, so a concrete land/water protection outcome and community backing matter most.

trackers.name: Earth Island Institute — fiscal sponsorship
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (fiscal sponsor): lets a new campaign or project WITHOUT its own nonprofit status receive tax-deductible grants and donations under Earth Island's established 501(c)(3), providing the legal, financial and administrative backbone (for a standard fee on funds raised). WHO IT SUITS: a group too new or small to form its own nonprofit but that needs to accept grant and foundation money now. HOW IT DIFFERS: not a grant — it is the vehicle that lets you legally hold and spend money others give you, so funders and grantmakers will take you seriously.

trackers.name: CrowdJustice — legal crowdfunding
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (for a lawsuit): a crowdfunding platform built specifically to fund legal action — judicial reviews, planning, environmental and community cases — that transfers funds directly to your lawyer's client account (UK and US). WHO IT SUITS: a community that has a lawyer (or is engaging one) and needs to cover the cost of a legal challenge. HOW IT DIFFERS from a grant or general crowdfunder: it is designed around legal cases, handles the compliance, and pays the lawyer directly — the natural tool once you decide to litigate.

trackers.name: GoFundMe — general crowdfunding
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (general): the largest general crowdfunding platform — fast to set up and best for rallying your own community and networks around an urgent, concrete need (a fight fund, an expert study, emergency costs). WHO IT SUITS: a campaign with a story and a network to share it. HOW IT DIFFERS: no vetting and no legal-fund handling (for a lawsuit use a legal-specific platform), and it is donation-based public fundraising rather than grant money — momentum and a clear ask drive success.

trackers.name: OpenCorporates
trackers.desc: The largest open database of companies worldwide, pulled from official registries. You CAN get: a company’s registration, officers, and parent/subsidiary links across jurisdictions. You CAN’T get: hidden beneficial owners where a registry doesn’t require them. For activists: when a nondescript LLC files to build a warehouse or evict a block, OpenCorporates helps trace it up the chain to the real parent company you can actually pressure or boycott.

trackers.name: EPA ECHO
trackers.desc: Enforcement and Compliance History Online — the single most useful environmental tool. You CAN get: for almost any regulated facility, its permits, inspections, violations, pollutant discharges and enforcement actions under the Clean Air/Water Acts and more. You CAN’T get: unregulated or unpermitted sources. For activists fighting an industrial plant or incinerator: ECHO documents its violation history and pollution in black and white — the backbone of a permit challenge or press story.

trackers.name: EPA Envirofacts
trackers.desc: A gateway to EPA’s many environmental databases by location. You CAN get: air, water, waste, toxics and cleanup data tied to a facility or ZIP code. You CAN’T get: data on things EPA doesn’t track. For activists: build a pollution profile of a site or neighborhood for environmental-justice work.

trackers.name: EPA Toxics Release Inventory (TRI)
trackers.desc: A public inventory of toxic chemicals released by industrial facilities. You CAN get: what chemicals a plant releases into air, water and land, and how much, year over year. You CAN’T get: releases below reporting thresholds or from non-covered industries. For activists: map the toxic burden near a community and compare facilities to prove disproportionate impact.

trackers.name: OSHA Establishment Search
trackers.desc: The federal record of workplace-safety inspections. You CAN get: a company’s inspection history, citations, penalties and any fatalities. You CAN’T get: states running their own OSHA plans always show identically (check the state). For activists: expose a bad-actor employer’s safety record when fighting a subsidy or contract.

trackers.name: Internet Archive — Wayback Machine
trackers.desc: A free archive of hundreds of billions of saved web pages. You CAN get: what a company’s or agency’s website said on a past date, even after they edit or delete it. You CAN’T get: pages that were never crawled (save them yourself, now). For activists: prove a broken promise or a quietly-scrubbed claim by pulling the original.

trackers.name: County Property Records (NETR Online)
trackers.desc: A free directory linking to county assessor, recorder and GIS sites nationwide. You CAN get: the route to look up who owns a given parcel, its sale history and tax status — for free or a small fee, county by county. You CAN’T get: a single national search (records are local). For activists: unmask an absentee landlord’s portfolio, trace who really owns a development site, and document displacement patterns.

trackers.name: USGS EarthExplorer
trackers.desc: Free access to decades of satellite and aerial imagery from the U.S. Geological Survey. You CAN get: historical and recent imagery to document land clearing, construction, wetland loss or a growing waste site over time. You CAN’T get: real-time or very-high-resolution commercial shots (those are paid). For activists: build a before/after visual timeline of an industrial or development site.

trackers.name: Google Earth
trackers.desc: Free global satellite imagery with a historical-imagery time slider. You CAN get: zoomable current and past imagery to document change on the ground. You CAN’T get: guaranteed recent dates everywhere. For activists: quickly show a site’s transformation, or pollution visible from above, to a reporter or hearing.

trackers.name: Google Alerts
trackers.desc: A free service that emails you when new web content matches your terms. You CAN get: ongoing monitoring of a company, official, project name or permit. You CAN’T get: content behind logins or paywalls. For activists: get notified the moment your target is mentioned so you can respond fast.

trackers.name: National Archives (NARA)
trackers.desc: The U.S. National Archives and its online Catalog. You CAN get: historical federal records, declassified files and direct FOIA routes to agency archives. You CAN’T get: recent operational records (those go through agency FOIA). For activists: dig up the historical paper trail behind a policy, agency or land decision.

trackers.name: Library of Congress
trackers.desc: The largest library in the world and a deep free reference source. You CAN get: historical newspapers, maps, photos, legal materials (via Congress.gov) and research guides. You CAN’T get: paywalled commercial databases. For activists: ground a campaign in historical record — old maps and news showing what a site or neighborhood used to be.

trackers.name: DocumentCloud
trackers.desc: A public repository where journalists and researchers upload, search and annotate primary-source documents. You CAN get: a searchable trove of government and corporate documents others have already liberated. You CAN’T get: guaranteed coverage of your specific topic. For activists: find primary documents behind a story — and host and annotate your own.

trackers.name: EPA — Report an Environmental Violation
trackers.desc: WHO TO CONTACT to report suspected violations of environmental law. You CAN: report air, water, waste or pesticide violations to the federal regulator that can investigate, fine and force cleanup. You CAN’T: guarantee action, or report purely local nuisances (try state/county). For activists fighting a polluting facility: escalating documented violations to EPA creates an official record and can trigger enforcement that a company can’t ignore.

trackers.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service
trackers.desc: WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and endangered species. You CAN: report wildlife crimes and habitat destruction, and check Endangered Species Act listings and critical-habitat designations. You CAN’T: get them to act on non-listed species quickly. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or wetland on the site can legally stop or reshape the whole project — F&W is who confirms and enforces that.

trackers.name: Sierra Club
trackers.desc: The largest grassroots environmental organization in the U.S. WHO TO ENLIST: local chapters that already organize, lobby and litigate against harmful projects. You CAN: join a ready-made network with campaign experience, volunteers and sometimes legal support. For activists: a force multiplier — you don’t have to fight a development or polluter alone.

trackers.name: Earthjustice
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a nonprofit public-interest environmental law organisation — 'the law firm for the environment' — that represents clients FREE OF CHARGE and has litigated thousands of cases, including the twenty-year Clean Air Act fight that produced the first protections against coal-fired power plants and the first federal rules on toxic coal ash. Also runs an international programme supporting partners such as AIDA in Latin America and CER in South Africa. WHO IT SUITS: do not assume they take every case — they pick high-impact ones with reach beyond a single site. If yours is a purely local fight, a state or regional public-interest firm is the better first call.

trackers.name: The Nature Conservancy
trackers.desc: The largest land-conservation nonprofit. WHO TO CONTACT/ENLIST on protecting land and water. You CAN: connect on conservation science, land deals and easements. You CAN’T: expect them to fight every local development. For activists: a potential partner to protect threatened land through acquisition or stewardship rather than only opposition.

trackers.name: Land Trust Alliance (find a land trust)
trackers.desc: The national network of local land trusts and conservancies. WHO TO CONTACT: find the land trust near you that can hold, buy or accept a conservation easement on threatened land. You CAN: locate a local conservancy and learn how easements work. For activists fighting development: a land trust may permanently protect the parcel you’re trying to save.

trackers.name: Public Citizen
trackers.desc: A national nonprofit that fights corporate and government abuse of power. WHO TO ENLIST on corporate accountability, regulation and money-in-politics. You CAN: draw on their research, campaigns and occasional litigation. For activists: an experienced ally and a body of accountability research to build on.

trackers.name: OSINT Framework
trackers.desc: A free, categorized directory of open-source-intelligence tools and sites. You CAN get: a guided menu pointing you to the right tool for searching people, companies, domains, social media, images and public records. You CAN’T get: the data itself — it routes you to the tool. For activists: a map of where to look when you don’t yet know which tool finds what you need.

trackers.name: Sentinel Hub EO Browser
trackers.desc: A free browser for recent, frequently-updated satellite imagery (ESA Sentinel and more). You CAN get: near-current and historical imagery, including infrared bands that expose vegetation loss, water and heat. You CAN’T get: street-level detail. For activists: document deforestation, construction, flooding or a pollution plume with fresh, citable imagery — often newer than Google Earth.

trackers.name: NASA Worldview
trackers.desc: NASA’s free browser for daily global satellite imagery. You CAN get: near-real-time imagery and layers for fires, smoke, floods, dust and vegetation. You CAN’T get: high-resolution close-ups. For activists: show a wildfire, flood or smoke event hitting a community, day by day, with an authoritative source.

trackers.name: Data.gov
trackers.desc: The U.S. government’s open-data catalog. You CAN get: hundreds of thousands of downloadable federal (and some state/local) datasets — environment, spending, health, demographics. You CAN’T get: records agencies haven’t published (that’s what FOIA is for). For activists: find the raw dataset behind an issue and analyze it yourself instead of taking an agency’s word.

trackers.name: OCCRP Aleph
trackers.desc: A vast free archive of investigative material — company registries, leaks, court records and documents from around the world, searchable in one place. You CAN get: cross-border company and person records that are otherwise scattered or hard to reach. You CAN’T get: guaranteed coverage of every jurisdiction. For activists: search a name or company across many countries’ records and leaked datasets at once.

trackers.name: ADS-B Exchange (flight tracking)
trackers.desc: A community flight-tracking service that — unlike commercial trackers — doesn’t let owners hide their aircraft. You CAN get: real-time and historical flight tracks of private and corporate jets by tail number. You CAN’T get: passenger identities. For activists: document a corporation’s or official’s private-jet use and the emissions and access it implies.

trackers.name: FEMA Flood Map Service Center
trackers.desc: FEMA’s official flood-hazard map portal. You CAN get: the flood-zone designation for any address or parcel, and the maps behind it. You CAN’T get: future climate projections (these are regulatory flood zones). For activists fighting development in risky areas: show that a proposed project sits in a floodplain — a powerful, official argument against approval and insurance.

trackers.name: Global Witness
trackers.desc: An investigative NGO that publishes data and reports on environmental destruction, corruption and the money behind them. You CAN get: datasets and investigations on land, extractives, dark money and threats to land defenders. You CAN’T get: on-demand research for your case. For activists: reusable data and methods linking environmental harm to the companies and finance driving it.

trackers.name: Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
trackers.desc: The federal regulator of nuclear power and materials. You CAN get: plant licensing, inspection reports, event notifications and enforcement actions (much via the ADAMS document system). You CAN’T get: classified security details. For activists near a nuclear facility: its safety record, license renewals and incident history — and how to comment on licensing.

trackers.name: PHMSA (pipeline safety)
trackers.desc: The federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration. You CAN get: pipeline incident data, operator inspection and enforcement records, and mapping of pipeline systems. You CAN’T get: some security-sensitive routing detail. For activists fighting a pipeline: the operator’s spill and violation history and the federal safety record behind it.

trackers.name: Mine Safety & Health Administration (MSHA)
trackers.desc: The federal mine-safety regulator. You CAN get: a mine’s inspection history, violations, penalties and accidents, searchable by operator. You CAN’T get: non-mining worksites (use OSHA). For activists near a mine: document the operator’s safety and violation record when contesting a permit or expansion.

trackers.name: Right-to-Know Network (RTKNet)
trackers.desc: A free portal (OMB Watch legacy / Center for Effective Government) to federal environmental and chemical databases. You CAN get: searchable toxic-release, spill, chemical-storage and enforcement data by facility and community. You CAN’T get: unreported releases. For activists: a community-oriented front end to the federal environmental data behind a local facility.

trackers.name: SkyTruth
trackers.desc: A nonprofit that uses satellite imagery to expose environmental damage. You CAN get: tools and projects mapping oil spills, drilling, fracking, mining and other visible impacts, plus methods you can reuse. You CAN’T get: on-demand imagery of your exact site (pair with Sentinel Hub / USGS). For activists: satellite-based evidence and techniques for documenting environmental harm from above.

trackers.name: EWG Tap Water Database
trackers.desc: The Environmental Working Group’s database of drinking-water quality by utility. You CAN get: the contaminants detected in a local water system and how they compare to health guidelines. You CAN’T get: private-well data. For activists on water-quality fights: a community-specific starting point showing what’s in the tap and which utility is responsible.

trackers.name: National Security Archive
trackers.desc: A nonprofit research institute and library of declassified U.S. government documents obtained through FOIA. You CAN get: primary-source documents and analysis on government secrecy, foreign policy, surveillance and more, plus expert FOIA guidance. You CAN’T get: still-classified records. For activists: a model FOIA operation and a trove of documents proving what agencies did behind closed doors.

trackers.name: FAS — Project on Government Secrecy
trackers.desc: The Federation of American Scientists’ long-running work on government secrecy and classification. You CAN get: analysis, leaked/released documents and tracking of the classification system and intelligence budgets. You CAN’T get: classified material itself. For activists: understand and challenge over-classification and secrecy in the agency you’re fighting.

trackers.name: U.S. Forest Service
trackers.desc: The federal manager of national forests and grasslands. You CAN get: land-management plans, permits, timber sales, project environmental reviews and public-comment opportunities. You CAN’T get: private-land data. For activists fighting logging, mining or development on public forest land: the plans, permits and comment windows are here.

trackers.name: Bureau of Land Management (BLM)
trackers.desc: The federal manager of vast public lands and their resources. You CAN get: land-use plans, oil/gas and grazing leases, mining claims and environmental reviews, plus public-comment opportunities. You CAN’T get: private-land records. For activists: track and contest drilling, mining and grazing leases on public land, and comment on land-use decisions.

trackers.name: National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB)
trackers.desc: The independent federal investigator of major transportation accidents. You CAN get: accident investigation reports, safety recommendations and a searchable accident database (aviation, rail, pipeline, hazmat, marine). You CAN’T get: minor incidents. For activists: authoritative findings on a rail, pipeline or industrial-transport disaster affecting your community.

trackers.name: National Freedom of Information Coalition (NFOIC)
trackers.desc: A network of state open-government coalitions. You CAN get: state-by-state FOI resources, sample request letters, appeal help and connections to local open-government advocates and hotlines. You CAN’T get: the records themselves. For activists: practical, state-specific help getting a records request unstuck — and allies who fight secrecy locally.

trackers.name: CDC (public-health data)
trackers.desc: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. You CAN get: public-health data and tools — environmental health, toxic exposures, disease clusters, injury and mortality statistics by area (e.g., via CDC WONDER and the Environmental Public Health Tracking network). You CAN’T get: individual medical records. For activists: link a suspected environmental hazard to community health outcomes with authoritative data.

trackers.name: Center for Biological Diversity
trackers.desc: A national nonprofit that uses science and the law — especially the Endangered Species Act — to stop harmful projects. WHO TO ENLIST when a development, mine, road or pipeline threatens wildlife or habitat anywhere in the U.S. You CAN: draw on their litigation, petitions and expertise; an ESA-listed species on your site can halt a project. For activists: a relentless national litigator that has blocked countless developments.

trackers.name: Waterkeeper Alliance (find your local Waterkeeper)
trackers.desc: A global network of local ‘Waterkeeper’ groups (Riverkeepers, Baykeepers, Coastkeepers) that patrol and defend specific waterways. WHO TO CONTACT: find the Waterkeeper for your river, bay or coast — a dedicated local organization that monitors polluters and fights harmful projects on your water. For activists: the closest thing to a local environmental watchdog assigned to your watershed.

trackers.name: EPA Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) Database
trackers.desc: EPA’s official database of every Environmental Impact Statement filed for a major federal action. You CAN find: proposed dams, mines, pipelines, highways, drilling and other big projects the moment they enter federal review — with comment deadlines. You CAN’T find: purely local/private projects with no federal nexus. For activists: the single systematic list to catch a major development early, while there’s still a comment window to organize around.

trackers.name: FERC eLibrary
trackers.desc: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s document library. You CAN find: interstate gas pipelines, LNG terminals and hydropower projects — applications, filings and the docket to intervene or comment. You CAN’T find: intrastate or non-FERC projects. For activists fighting a pipeline or LNG terminal: this is where the project lives on paper, and how you formally get involved.

trackers.name: Army Corps of Engineers — Public Notices (Section 404)
trackers.desc: The Army Corps’ program for permits to fill or build in wetlands and waterways (Clean Water Act Section 404). You CAN find: public notices of proposed projects affecting wetlands/streams, with comment periods (notices are posted by district). You CAN’T find: projects that avoid regulated waters. For activists: wetland impacts are a common way to challenge a development — the Corps notice is the opening.

trackers.name: BLM ePlanning (NEPA register)
trackers.desc: The Bureau of Land Management’s planning and NEPA register for public lands. You CAN find: proposed drilling, mining, grazing, rights-of-way and land-use plans on BLM land, with documents and comment opportunities. You CAN’T find: private-land projects. For activists: track and contest extractive and development projects on public land before they’re approved.

trackers.name: Forest Service — Schedule of Proposed Actions (SOPA)
trackers.desc: The U.S. Forest Service’s quarterly schedule of proposed and ongoing projects on each national forest. You CAN find: logging, roads, mining and other proposed actions by forest, with status and contacts, before decisions are final. You CAN’T find: non-Forest-Service land. For activists: an early-warning list for national-forest projects and the comment windows to intervene.

trackers.name: Federal Register — Environmental Notices
trackers.desc: The daily federal journal, filtered to environmental agencies. You CAN find: proposed rules, project notices, permit actions and public-comment deadlines across EPA and related agencies. You CAN’T find: state/local actions. For activists: a catch-all to spot federal environmental actions and never miss a comment window.

trackers.name: Global Energy Monitor
trackers.desc: A research network that tracks fossil-fuel and energy infrastructure worldwide. You CAN find: pipelines, LNG terminals, coal plants, gas fields and mines — mapped, with the companies and financiers behind each project and its status. You CAN’T find: non-energy developments. For activists: the closest thing to a live atlas of energy projects to resist, with the corporate names already attached.

trackers.name: Environmental Justice Atlas (EJAtlas)
trackers.desc: A global, curated map of environmental conflicts — documented from the affected-community and resistance perspective. You CAN find: thousands of specific project conflicts (mines, dams, dumps, plantations), who’s fighting them, the companies involved and outcomes. You CAN’T find: exhaustive coverage of every new project (it’s curated, not automated). For activists: see how communities elsewhere fought the same kind of project — and add your own.

trackers.name: FracTracker Alliance
trackers.desc: A nonprofit that maps the oil-and-gas industry and its impacts. You CAN find: wells, pipelines, compressor stations and related infrastructure mapped, with data tools and mobile apps to document impacts. You CAN’T find: non-oil/gas sectors. For activists in drilling country: locate and monitor the fossil infrastructure around a community.

trackers.name: Land Matrix
trackers.desc: A global initiative tracking large-scale land acquisitions. You CAN find: big land deals — who’s acquiring land, where, how much, and for what (agriculture, forestry, mining). You CAN’T find: small local transactions. For activists: expose land grabs and the investors behind large acquisitions threatening communities and ecosystems.

trackers.name: ConstructConnect (project search)
trackers.desc: A commercial construction-intelligence service with some publicly searchable project data. You CAN find: local commercial and public construction projects in planning and bidding stages (fuller access is paid). You CAN’T find: everything free — the deep data is a paid product. For activists: an early look at local construction projects entering the pipeline; pair with your city/county permit portal for the fuller local picture.

trackers.name: Public Herald
trackers.desc: US nonprofit investigative newsroom exposing environmental harm and public corruption. — Holds to account: officials handling public money & power — find investigations into regulators, industry and public officials.

trackers.name: National Freedom of Information Coalition (NFOIC)
trackers.desc: US coalition of state open-government organisations defending the public's right to government records and meetings and fighting official secrecy. It offers state-by-state FOI resources, appeals help and open-government advocacy. USE IT: find the coalition in your state when a records request stalls.

trackers.name: OpenSecrets
trackers.desc: Money-in-politics leader. Links lobbyists, issues, bills and contacted agencies, built on FEC and Senate lobbying-disclosure data. — Holds to account: US politicians and lobbyists — find federal campaign-finance, lobbying and revolving-door records by politician, donor and industry.

trackers.name: DataDawn / OpenRegs
trackers.desc: Aggregates legislation, floor speeches, lobbying filings, campaign finance and stock trades into one searchable layer. — Holds to account: US politicians — find legislation, floor speeches, lobbying filings, campaign finance and stock trades in one searchable layer.

trackers.name: Senate LDA – Lobbying Disclosure
trackers.desc: The official U.S. Senate Office of Public Records database of federal lobbying registrations and reports. — Holds to account: federal lobbyists — find the Senate's database of lobbying registrations and quarterly activity reports.

trackers.name: House Lobbying Disclosure
trackers.desc: The U.S. House Clerk's database of federal lobbying registrations and quarterly activity reports. — Holds to account: federal lobbyists — find the House Clerk's database of lobbying registrations and quarterly reports.

trackers.name: FOIA.gov
trackers.desc: Central hub for U.S. Freedom of Information Act requests — agency request portals, processing data and FOIA reports. — Holds to account: U.S. federal agencies — find each agency's request portal, government-wide processing data and annual FOIA reports.

trackers.name: National Declassification Center (NARA)
trackers.desc: U.S. records body that reviews and releases formerly classified federal records to the public. — Holds to account: U.S. federal agencies — find declassified federal records released to the public and the declassification review backlog.

trackers.name: CourtListener (Free Law Project)
trackers.desc: Largest free archive of U.S. federal & state opinions, dockets and oral arguments, run by the nonprofit Free Law Project. Also hosts a judges database with biographical data and judicial financial disclosures. · Find here: free U.S. federal and state opinions, oral-argument audio and PACER dockets (via RECAP), plus a searchable judges database (Free Law Project).

trackers.name: RECAP Archive
trackers.desc: Searchable collection of millions of PACER documents and dockets contributed by RECAP browser-extension users, addressing PACER's paywall. · Find here: federal court dockets and filings liberated from PACER by the RECAP project.

trackers.name: PACER
trackers.desc: Official U.S. federal courts portal for case and docket information from appellate, district and bankruptcy courts (paywalled). · Find here: the U.S. federal judiciary's official electronic case dockets and filings (per-page fees apply).

trackers.name: Caselaw Access Project
trackers.desc: Harvard Law School Library Innovation Lab project digitizing all official, book-published U.S. state and federal case law through 2020. · Find here: the digitised full text of U.S. case law from 1658–2020, from the Harvard Law School library (Caselaw Access Project).

trackers.name: Oyez
trackers.desc: Multimedia archive of U.S. Supreme Court oral-argument audio, case summaries and decisions. · Find here: U.S. Supreme Court oral-argument audio, synchronised transcripts and plain-language case summaries.

trackers.name: Legal Information Institute (Cornell)
trackers.desc: Cornell LII: free Supreme Court and federal case law, statutes and legal encyclopedia. · Find here: free U.S. statutes, regulations and Supreme Court opinions with plain-language explanations (Cornell LII).

trackers.name: Legal Services Corporation (LSC)
trackers.desc: Largest U.S. funder of civil legal aid; publishes 'By the Numbers' national and state-level data on legal-aid caseloads and the justice gap. · Find here: the largest U.S. funder of civil legal aid for low-income people (Legal Services Corporation). READ THE RESTRICTIONS BEFORE YOU ASK. LSC-funded offices are bound by 45 CFR Part 1612, and the provision that matters for land campaigns is this: during working hours, while providing legal assistance, or while using recipient resources provided by the Corporation OR BY PRIVATE ENTITIES, no person shall participate in any public demonstration, picketing, boycott or strike. An LSC-funded office cannot join your demonstration, and the restriction reaches privately-provided resources, not only federal money. THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDES WHETHER THEY CAN ACT AT ALL: the rule separates administrative proceedings producing determinations of particular rather than general applicability, affecting only private rights or interests — expressly including the granting or withholding of licences — from adjudicatory proceedings to formulate or modify an agency policy of general applicability and future effect. A single permit affecting you is particular applicability; changing an agency policy is general — and that is where the restrictions bite. Merely communicating with agency staff to obtain information, clarification or interpretation of rules is expressly distinguished from lobbying. So bring LSC-funded offices the particular-applicability work and take policy work elsewhere — this map records environmental law clinics and private land-use firms separately for that reason.

trackers.name: Justice Index (NCAJ)
trackers.desc: National Center for Access to Justice index ranking all U.S. states on attorney access, fines & fees, language access and self-representation support. · Find here: state-by-state rankings of U.S. access-to-justice policies (Justice Index, NCAJ).

trackers.name: National Legal Aid & Defender Association
trackers.desc: Association of civil legal-aid and public-defender programs across the U.S. · Find here: the U.S. association of legal-aid and public-defender providers (NLADA).

trackers.name: Reporters Committee – Open Courts Compendium
trackers.desc: State-by-state guide to public and press rights of access to court proceedings and records. · Find here: a state-by-state guide to court-access rights for the press and public (Reporters Committee).

trackers.name: Office of Government Information Services (OGIS, US FOIA Ombudsman)
trackers.desc: Office of Government Information Services (OGIS, US FOIA Ombudsman) — oversight body for the right of access to public information.

trackers.name: Mongabay (investigative outlet)
trackers.desc: Independent accountability-journalism outlet (GIJN member); Mongabay — environmental accountability & deforestation investigations.

trackers.name: MuckRock (investigative outlet)
trackers.desc: Independent accountability-journalism outlet (GIJN member); MuckRock — US FOI platform liberating public records at scale.

trackers.name: Public.Resource.Org
trackers.desc: Accountability source (records access / aggregator); Public.Resource.Org — Carl Malamud’s nonprofit that liberates primary public-domain records — statutes, court opinions, safety codes, SEC EDGAR filings — winning the Supreme Court ruling that the law itself can’t be copyrighted.

trackers.name: OPRA Machine (New Jersey) — FOI requests (USA)
trackers.desc: Accountability source (FOI request platform); OPRA Machine (New Jersey) — civic Freedom-of-Information request platform (Alaveteli/mySociety network) — lets citizens file public-records requests and publishes the requests and the authorities’ responses in a public archive.

trackers.name: PR Newswire (Cision)
trackers.desc: EXAMPLE (global, usable anywhere) — the heavyweight newswire: distributes your press release to a large network of journalists, outlets and websites worldwide. Higher-budget; for spreading a story at scale.

trackers.name: EIN Presswire
trackers.desc: EXAMPLE (global) — affordable, nonprofit-friendly press-release distribution to journalists and news sites; a low-cost way to push a release out at national or global scale.

trackers.name: Fenton Communications
trackers.desc: EXAMPLE — a public-interest communications firm that runs earned-media and advocacy campaigns for causes, nonprofits and movements (not corporate PR). Illustrates the 'PR firm for your side' category.

trackers.name: M+R
trackers.desc: EXAMPLE — a campaigns-and-communications firm for nonprofits and advocacy groups; the kind of outfit you can hire to help run the visible opposition for the cause side.

trackers.name: BerlinRosen
trackers.desc: EXAMPLE — a strategic-communications and campaigns firm serving nonprofits, advocacy groups and unions. Illustrates the 'run the whole show, transparently' category.

trackers.name: Claude.ai
trackers.desc: AI assistant for explaining a law, summarising a document, or drafting fast — a general research aid for any fight. Always verify its facts and citations.

trackers.name: Google Scholar
trackers.desc: Free search of scholarly literature (and some case law) — for the studies that back up your health, environmental or economic claims.

trackers.name: Trust for Public Land — protect & create public land
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: national nonprofit that buys threatened private land and transfers it to public agencies for parks and public lands, and runs conservation-finance tools (LandVote, the National Conservation Easement Database) to help pass funding for land protection. USE IT: to protect a place by acquiring it for the public, or to fund a local land-protection ballot measure.

trackers.name: Land Trust Alliance — how to conserve your land
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: national umbrella for ~1,000 U.S. land trusts; explains how to permanently protect land through conservation easements (restrict development while keeping ownership), donation or fee-simple sale, and connects you to an accredited local land trust. USE IT: to lock in permanent protection for a place without it becoming fully public.

trackers.name: The Conservation Fund — land acquisition for conservation
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: national nonprofit that buys at-risk land — forests, farms, ranches and working landscapes near growing cities — and holds or transfers it to keep it from development. USE IT: to protect a threatened place by having it acquired and conserved, especially working lands under development pressure.

trackers.name: USDA NRCS — Agricultural Conservation Easement Program (ACEP)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: federal program that funds the purchase of permanent conservation easements on farmland, grassland and wetlands, partnering with land trusts, tribes and state/local governments to keep working land from being developed. USE IT: to permanently protect farm, ranch or wetland acreage in place — land stays privately owned but development is barred.

trackers.name: American Farmland Trust — protect farmland
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: national nonprofit dedicated to protecting farmland from conversion through conservation easements, policy and technical help; runs the Farmland Information Center, a clearinghouse of protection laws and sample documents. USE IT: to protect threatened farm or ranch land, or to find the legal tools and models for doing so.

trackers.name: Grassroots International — funding land, water and territory defence
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a US grantmaker funding movements that defend land, territory, water, food and seeds, and a member of the CLIMA Fund alongside Global Greengrants, Thousand Currents and Urgent Action Fund. WHO IT SUITS: organised movements and community organisations rather than one-off campaigns — they fund long-term partners. HOW IT DIFFERS: movement funding, including urgent protection money for defenders under threat, rather than project grants against a workplan.

trackers.name: CLIMA Fund — grassroots climate and land-defence grantmaking
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pooled fund joining Global Greengrants Fund, Grassroots International, Thousand Currents, Urgent Action Fund for Feminist Activism and the Youth Climate Justice Fund — collectively over 20,000 grants to grassroots groups in 150+ countries. WHO IT SUITS: grassroots movements led by women, youth, Indigenous Peoples and small-scale farmers, anywhere in the world. HOW IT DIFFERS: the single best entry point for a group outside the US, because one approach reaches five grantmakers at once.

trackers.name: Thousand Currents
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (fiscal sponsor): a US grantmaker and fiscal sponsor for grassroots movements in the Global South, and the fiscal sponsor of the CLIMA Fund. WHO IT SUITS: a group WITHOUT its own nonprofit status that needs to receive grants or tax-deductible donations — fiscal sponsorship is often the fastest way to unblock funding. WHAT IS VERIFIED, from the CLIMA Fund's own site: that Thousand Currents is one of five collaborating organisations — with Global Greengrants Fund, Grassroots International, Urgent Action Fund for Feminist Activism and the Youth Climate Justice Fund. Note the fifth member: the Youth Climate Justice Fund is now named, which older descriptions of a four-way collaboration omit. The collaboration reports over 130 years of collective experience and reaching grassroots movements in over 150 countries. BUT UNDERSTAND WHAT CLIMA IS: its stated purpose is to give influential funders a simple and effective way to invest in grassroots movements — it is a route for funders INTO movements, not an application window for groups. A group seeking money approaches one of the five member funds, not CLIMA itself. SOURCING, STATED PLAINLY: this organisation's own domain has not been verified against a canonical source in this map's checks — it is recorded because the CLIMA Fund names it as a member on the Fund's own site. Confirm the domain before sending anything.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund for Feminist Activism
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (rapid response): a rapid-response grantmaker and CLIMA Fund member that funds activists and defenders under threat on very short timescales. WHO IT SUITS: a land or environmental defender facing an immediate security threat who needs money in days, not months. WHAT IS VERIFIED, from the CLIMA Fund's own site: that this fund is one of five collaborating organisations — with Global Greengrants Fund, Grassroots International, Thousand Currents and the Youth Climate Justice Fund — reaching grassroots movements in over 150 countries. Note the fifth member: the Youth Climate Justice Fund is now named, which older four-way descriptions omit. CLIMA IS A DOOR FOR FUNDERS, NOT FOR APPLICANTS — approach a member fund directly. ONE THING TO CHECK RATHER THAN ASSUME: this fund is widely described as operating through independent regional ‘sister funds’, which would mean approaching the one covering your region — but that appears only in directory listings, not on a canonical source, so verify the current structure before applying. SOURCING, STATED PLAINLY: this organisation's own domain has not been verified against a canonical source in this map's checks — it is recorded because the CLIMA Fund names it as a member on the Fund's own site. Confirm the domain before sending anything.

trackers.name: AIDA — Interamerican Association for Environmental Defense
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional organisation of Latin American environmental legal experts providing FREE legal and scientific support to communities and local groups, using international and inter-American human-rights law. Track record includes stopping a large dam in Mexico, halting clear-cutting of native forest in Chile, and the La Oroya smelter ruling in Peru. WHO IT SUITS: communities whose national system has already failed them and whose fight needs to go to an international body. AIDA works across Latin America, so it may be able to act in your country even if it has no office there — ask.

trackers.name: Bureau of Indian Affairs — fee-to-trust land acquisition
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the process by which the United States takes title to land and holds it in trust for a Tribe or individual tribal member, under section 5 of the Indian Reorganization Act 1934 and the regulations at 25 CFR part 151. Over 56 million acres are held this way. USE IT: the protection here is unusually hard — TRUST LAND CANNOT BE ALIENATED OR ENCUMBERED (sold, gifted, leased) WITHOUT THE APPROVAL OF THE SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR, it is exempt from state and local taxation, and it is generally outside state legal authority except where Congress has said otherwise. It also establishes tribal jurisdiction. All federally recognised Tribes and individuals may apply, by written request to the BIA Office of Trust Services; a Tribe may use a tribal resolution. Regional Directors decide non-gaming, off-reservation and fee-to-trust applications. Slow, but close to permanent once done.

trackers.name: Public Participation Project — anti-SLAPP protection by state
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the national organisation working to enact and strengthen anti-SLAPP laws, which also provides legal resources and referrals to people facing a strategic lawsuit against public participation — a suit brought not to win but to drain and silence a critic through cost and delay. WHO IT SUITS: anyone sued, or threatened with suit, for objecting at a hearing, writing, or organising against a project. CHECK YOUR OWN STATE FIRST: coverage is uneven and moving — sources counted 28 states some years ago and 40 plus DC more recently — so verify current status where you are rather than relying on any figure, including this one.

trackers.name: ELAW — Environmental Law Alliance Worldwide
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a global alliance of public-interest environmental lawyers and scientists collaborating across 88 COUNTRIES, founded 1989. It does not take your case — it BACKS THE LAWYER WHO DOES, with legal and scientific expertise most local advocates cannot buy: critiquing environmental impact assessments, supplying expert testimony to courts, building monitoring systems, and recommending cleaner alternatives to a proposed project. Partners call on the network for 400+ projects a year. WHO IT SUITS: your lawyer, more than you. If you have counsel who is out-resourced by the proponent's experts, this is where the technical firepower comes from. It also runs a SECURITY PROGRAMME for environmental lawyers who are targeted for this work, and co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous, and Environmental Defenders. Its published guidebooks on evaluating EIAs, environmental sampling and challenging oil and gas projects are free and usable without any referral.

trackers.name: Land Conservation Assistance Network (LandCAN) — find funding and advisers in your state
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY / WHO TO ENLIST — nationwide: a nonprofit that maintains web tools connecting landowners to the grant, assistance and advisory programmes available in their own state, plus dedicated conservation centres for Arkansas, California, Colorado, Idaho, Louisiana, Maine and Mississippi and a Houston-area resource. It indexes state and federal programmes, conservation districts, land trusts and professional advisers by locality. USE IT: it is the fastest way to find what exists near you in states with no single headline conservation fund — and it lists advisers as well as money, which matters when a landowner needs an appraiser, forester or easement attorney rather than a grant.

trackers.name: The Conservation Fund — Conservation Loans (bridge financing)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (when the seller will not wait) — nationwide: the largest conservation bridge lender in the country, making low-interest loans since 1993 to 501(c)(3) nonprofits and municipal and tribal organisations so they can buy a threatened property before the fundraising is finished. Loans have run roughly $12,000 to $10 million, averaging about half a million, with terms of three months to three years, and repaid money is relent elsewhere. Extensive free technical assistance comes with it — on the transaction, on fundraising strategy, and loan officers will attend your board meeting to explain the process. USE IT: talk to a loan officer BEFORE a property comes up; note the loans cannot cover long-term stewardship costs, so budget those separately.

trackers.name: Open Space Institute — Conservation Capital grants and bridge loans
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to close a land deal fast) — eastern US and Canada: OSI regrants foundation money to local and regional land trusts as capital grants for acquisition and conservation easements, and — unusually — makes SHORT-TERM, LOW-COST BRIDGE LOANS so a land trust can close on a threatened property before its own fundraising is complete. $136 million in grants and loans since 2001 across 13 states and three Canadian provinces, through named funds targeting particular landscapes (Appalachians, Kittatinny, Delaware River watershed, Southern Cumberland, community forests). USE IT: rounds are competitive with annual deadlines and a match is usually expected, so build the relationship before the parcel you care about comes up for sale.

trackers.name: USDA heirs' property programs — farm number and relending
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to clear title to inherited land) — nationwide: heirs' property is family land passed down without a will, jointly owned by every descendant, with no marketable title — and without proof of ownership families have historically been locked out of USDA programmes and exposed to forced partition sales by third parties. The 2018 Farm Bill fixed both ends. Alternative documentation now lets an heirs' property operator get a FARM NUMBER without owner verification, which is the gateway to lending, disaster relief and county committee eligibility. The Heirs' Property Relending Program lends through intermediaries (CDFIs, credit unions, co-ops) to buy out other heirs' fractional interests and pay for closing costs, appraisals, title searches, surveys, mediation and legal services. USE IT: apply directly to a listed intermediary lender, not to USDA.

trackers.name: Indian Land Tenure Foundation — land recovery for Native nations
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST / WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to get land back into tribal hands) — nationwide: a Native-led national foundation whose mission is that land within original reservation boundaries, and other areas where tribes retain aboriginal interests, returns to Indian ownership and management. It grants roughly $10,000–$100,000 for land recovery planning — note it does NOT fund the purchase price itself — and owns the Indian Land Capital Company, a Native CDFI making loans to tribal nations specifically for land acquisition, which is how several tribes have bought back forest and coastal homelands. It also funds free estate planning and will-writing for Indian landowners, the main defence against further fractionation. USE IT: tribal, local and state governments and 501(c)(3)s can apply; leadership support for the project must be evidenced.

trackers.name: Institute for Justice — eminent domain abuse litigation
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (when land is taken for someone else's benefit) — nationwide: a public interest law firm that represents property owners FREE OF CHARGE in constitutional takings cases, particularly where government condemns land and hands it to a private developer or company. It litigated Kelo v. New London and, after losing, took the fight to state courts, legislatures and ballot measures — 47 states have since strengthened protections against eminent domain abuse. It also publishes an Eminent Domain Abuse Survival Guide of tactics that work outside the courtroom, and grades each state's protections. USE IT: strongest where a taking has private benefit behind a public-sounding justification, or where 'blight' has been declared over a whole neighbourhood.

trackers.name: Farmers' Legal Action Group (FLAG) — national family farmer legal hotline
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (if you farm) — nationwide: a nonprofit law centre founded in 1986 out of the farm credit crisis (its first cheque was signed by Willie Nelson via Farm Aid), running a national Family Farmer Legal Assistance Hotline that takes calls from across the country on farmland access, property rights, landlord-tenant disputes, foreclosure, USDA programme appeals, contracts and estate matters. It publishes free plain-language Farmers' Guides — including on wind energy and carbon contracts — and has trained tens of thousands of farmers and advocates in 42 states. USE IT: call before signing anything a developer or energy company puts in front of you; most farmers have no other source of independent legal help.

trackers.name: National Agricultural Law Center — eminent domain and land-law research
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (to understand the law before you hire anyone) — nationwide: created by Congress in 1987 at the University of Arkansas, federally funded and nonpartisan, the only institution of its kind in the country. It publishes free, plain-language research written for non-attorneys as well as lawyers, including an Eminent Domain FAQ for rural landowners and fifty-state compilations of right-to-farm statutes, conservation easement law, recreational use statutes, partition law and farmland ownership restrictions. USE IT: read the compilation for your state before a first meeting with a lawyer — it tells you what your statute actually says, including points landowners routinely miss, such as compensation for lost field and pasture access, and how compensation is split when condemned land is already under a conservation easement.

trackers.name: Lawyer referral services by state (American Bar Association)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (to find a lawyer at all) — nationwide: the ABA's public directory of bar-sponsored lawyer referral and 'find a lawyer' services in every state, plus many county and city bar associations. Unlike commercial attorney directories, non-profit referral services do not rank lawyers by who paid most for advertising — they refer on a rotating basis after grouping attorneys by location and practice area, and ABA-approved services must meet published standards with client satisfaction checks. USE IT: ask specifically for land use, zoning, eminent domain or environmental practice; many services offer a low-cost initial consultation, which is often enough to find out whether you have a case before committing money.

trackers.name: Law school environmental law clinics — directory
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (free representation) — nationwide: a compiled directory of roughly 50 university environmental, natural resource and environmental justice law clinics, from Hawaiʻi to Maine. Clinics represent real clients — community groups, neighbourhood organisations, small non-profits, tribal nations — under faculty supervision, in permit hearings, agency proceedings, citizen suits and appeals, and exist partly to reach people who could not otherwise afford environmental counsel. USE IT: approach the clinic in your region early and out of term-time deadlines, since cases are taken on a semester cycle; a clinic that cannot take your case often knows who can.

trackers.name: Owners' Counsel of America — find an eminent domain lawyer in your state
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (when your land is being taken) — nationwide: an invitation-only network of eminent domain and condemnation attorneys, limited to one primary member per state, who represent PRIVATE PROPERTY OWNERS only — against transportation departments, utilities, energy companies, redevelopment authorities, local and state government and federal agencies. Most lawyers never handle a condemnation case; these do little else, and members share strategy across the network. USE IT: pick your state from the map to find the member firm. Ask early — they act from pre-condemnation planning through negotiation, trial and appeal, and the pre-condemnation stage is where a route or project footprint can still be changed. These are private firms charging fees, not free legal aid.

trackers.name: America the Beautiful Challenge (NFWF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (landscape-scale) — nationwide: a single competitive application that draws on Interior, Agriculture, Defense and private funds at once, established in 2022 to stop applicants having to chase half a dozen separate federal programmes. Awards have run $91–141 million a year for landscape-scale habitat conservation, restoration and connection on public and private land. Demand hugely exceeds supply — one round drew $1.1 billion of requests against about 10% funded — so it suits well-prepared coalitions. USE IT: states, tribal and Native nations and territories can apply in every category; nonprofits, local and municipal governments and universities can apply in the National Forest and Private Forests/Rangeland/Farmland categories. Tribal projects are an explicit priority and cost share is waived for some tribes and territories.

trackers.name: Recreation & Public Purposes Act — acquiring federal land (BLM)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES — nationwide (public-land states): the R&PP Act lets the BLM sell or lease public land to states, tribes, counties, municipalities and qualified nonprofits at far below market value — free for recreation and historic monument purposes for government bodies — for parks, campgrounds, trails and other public uses. About 410,000 acres transferred in over 1,600 patents, plus 630+ active leases. Patents carry a reversionary clause: if the land stops being used for the stated public purpose, title returns to the United States. USE IT: apply to your local BLM field office with a development plan ($100 application fee); nonprofits can take up to 640 acres for recreation. Talk to the district office early — the land must already be identified for disposal in the resource management plan.

trackers.name: National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grants — US Fish & Wildlife Service
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy coastal land) — nationwide: annual grants of up to $1 million to coastal and Great Lakes states and US territories to acquire, restore or enhance coastal wetlands and adjoining uplands — over $530 million awarded since 1992, protecting or restoring some 600,000 acres. Funded by excise taxes on fishing tackle and motorboat fuel, not general revenue, so it survives budget fights that hit other programmes. USE IT: the applicant must be a state agency (or one the Governor designates), but land trusts, counties and tribes routinely partner as the on-the-ground buyer; match is 50% non-federal, dropping to 25% if the state runs its own land conservation programme, and waived for CNMI, American Samoa, Guam and the US Virgin Islands.

trackers.name: Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund (Section 6) — habitat land acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (when a listed species is on the land) — nationwide: under Section 6 of the Endangered Species Act, roughly $50 million a year in competitive grants to states and territories for species and habitat conservation on non-federal land, including two acquisition streams — Recovery Land Acquisition (fee or easement purchase supporting an approved recovery plan) and HCP Land Acquisition (habitat linked to an approved Habitat Conservation Plan). USE IT: only states can hold the grant, but counties, local governments and conservation organisations partner as subgrantees — so approach your state wildlife agency. The parcel must benefit a listed species whose recovery plan names habitat protection as a priority action; non-federal match is 25%, or 10% for joint projects between states.

trackers.name: Community Forest Program (USDA Forest Service)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the forest outright) — nationwide: authorised by the 2008 Farm Bill, the Community Forest and Open Space Conservation Program funds up to 50% of the cost for local governments, tribal governments and Alaska Native corporations, and qualified conservation nonprofits to buy private forest land threatened with conversion — fee simple only, easements are not eligible — and hold it as a community forest. Public access is required, and the land is managed under a community forest plan for recreation, education, clean water and forest-based economic benefit. USE IT: a 50% non-federal match is required and applications go through your State Forester (or tribal equivalent), who can also help write the community forest plan.

trackers.name: FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance — property acquisition for open space
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to retire flood-prone land permanently) — nationwide: under 44 CFR Part 80, FEMA's mitigation grants (HMGP, Flood Mitigation Assistance and the Safeguarding Tomorrow revolving loan fund) pay a local or state government to buy flood-prone property from willing sellers, demolish or relocate the structure, and dedicate the land as open space in perpetuity under a recorded deed restriction — no new building, natural floodplain function restored, pocket parks and river access allowed. USE IT: participation is strictly voluntary and the community must formally commit not to use eminent domain; owners apply through their town or county, which submits the subapplication to the state.

trackers.name: Forest Legacy Program (USDA Forest Service)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to keep a forest a forest) — nationwide: established in 1990 and funded through LWCF, Forest Legacy pays up to 75% of the cost of buying either a conservation easement or the land itself on privately owned forest threatened with conversion, in 53 states and territories, and has protected over 3 million acres. Owners can keep title, keep harvesting timber and keep managing under an approved forest plan while selling only the development rights; the interest acquired must be held by a state agency or other unit of government. USE IT: projects must sit inside a designated Forest Legacy Area and need a 25% non-federal match (donated land value counts) — contact your state's Forest Legacy coordinator, usually in the state forestry agency.

trackers.name: North American Wetlands Conservation Act (NAWCA) grants — US Fish & Wildlife Service
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy a wetland) — nationwide: NAWCA makes competitive matching grants to public-private partnerships for long-term protection, restoration or enhancement of wetlands and associated uplands — acquisition explicitly included. Small Grants run up to $250,000 with a simpler application; Standard Grants run $250,001–$3,000,000. Match must be non-federal and at least 1:1, and every grant and match dollar has to be tied to an acre acquired, restored or enhanced. USE IT: a land trust, local government or coalition can apply for a threatened marsh, bottomland or riparian tract; keeping administrative and overhead costs under 20% of the request makes a proposal more competitive.

trackers.name: Find your local conservation district (NACD directory)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST — nationwide: nearly 3,000 conservation districts cover almost every county in the United States. They are local units of government established under state law, run by roughly 17,000 locally elected or appointed board members, and they deliver soil, water and natural-resource programmes to landowners on private and public land — technical assistance, cost-share, watershed and habitat work. Their board meetings are public and their boards are elected locally, which makes them one of the most accessible bodies of government in rural America. USE IT: find your district in this directory to get technical evidence on soil, erosion, water quality and habitat for a hearing, and to find allies who already work with the landowners around a threatened site.

trackers.name: Land and Water Conservation Fund — State & Local Assistance (NPS)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land) — nationwide: the LWCF State & Local Assistance Program, administered by the National Park Service and funded by offshore oil-and-gas revenue (no taxpayer dollars), sends matching grants of up to 50% to every state, which pass them to state, local and tribal governments to acquire land and develop parks for public outdoor recreation, protected in perpetuity. This is the primary 'buy the property' funding path in states that lack their own conservation fund. USE IT: contact your state's LWCF lead agency (listed on the NPS site); nonprofits typically partner with a local park department to supply the match.

trackers.name: INECE — not where you report, but how you find who enforces
trackers.desc: READ THIS BEFORE YOU WRITE TO THEM: INECE IS NOT A COMPLAINT ROUTE. Its members are inspectors, prosecutors, regulators, parliamentarians and judges — a community cannot report a violation to INECE. It is worth an entry for three other reasons. FIRST, THE REGIONAL NETWORKS ARE A ROUTING DEVICE: INECE names AECEN (Asian Environmental Compliance and Enforcement Network), AELERT (Australasian Environmental Law Enforcement and Regulators network) and RedLaFiCA (Red Latinoamericana de Fiscalización y Cumplimiento Ambiental) as part of the network — if you do not know which body enforces in your country, the regional network is a shorter list to search than the world. SECOND, ITS CITIZEN-SCIENCE POSITION IS LEVERAGE: INECE runs an ongoing webinar series on ‘how can citizen and community science contribute to environmental compliance and enforcement?’ — that the global network of enforcers is itself asking that question is citable when an agency dismisses community-gathered evidence. THIRD, IT SHOWS WHAT KIND OF BODY TO LOOK FOR: its named members include a superintendency, a protection agency, a ministry and a supreme court — which is why searching for ‘EPA’ by name fails outside the US. The Secretariat is the Environmental Law Institute, not a government; it keeps an online library of compliance and enforcement resources and runs training — a recent series on environmental and social impact assessment drew 161 people from 31 countries. Founded 1989, covering administrative, civil, criminal and judicial enforcement, with support from UNEP, the World Bank, the European Commission and the OECD. BE AWARE OF THE MEMBERSHIP WALL: members have exclusive access to INECE materials and capacity-building programmes. IN THIS COUNTRY: US EPA co-founded INECE in 1989, remains a key funder and co-chairs the Executive Planning Committee.

trackers.name: TAG, TASC and TAP — if the TAG is taken, TASC is still open
trackers.desc: THREE SEPARATE ROUTES, AND CHOOSING WRONGLY WASTES THE APPLICATION. TAG (Technical Assistance Grant) gives up to $50,000 for a community group to hire their own technical advisor to interpret technical reports, site conditions and EPA's proposed actions — and to help comment on redevelopment, public health, and site five-year reviews. The five-year review is the overlooked one: a finished cleanup is re-examined every five years, and a funded advisor can be used then, long after most people assume the process is closed. BUT ELIGIBILITY IS NARROW: only groups, whose members live near and are potentially affected, that are representative of the community and non-profit and incorporated — or in the process of becoming incorporated. That last clause is the door: an unincorporated neighbourhood association can begin incorporating and apply. TAG covers only NPL Superfund sites (or proposed-NPL where a response action has begun), and there can be only one TAG at a time per site — so the first question is not ‘are we eligible’ but ‘has someone already taken it’: contact your Regional TAG Coordinator before doing the paperwork. A 20 percent match is required but most groups meet it through in-kind volunteer hours, not cash. IF THE TAG IS TAKEN, TASC IS STILL OPEN — that is the most useful fact here. TASC supplies scientists, engineers and other professionals through a national EPA contract at no cost; it is not a grant, so there is no money to manage. Its eligibility is far wider — any group willing to share the benefit with the affected community, no incorporation required — there is no specific limit on the amount of assistance, it reaches removal actions and RCRA cleanups as well as Superfund, and more than one group can receive TASC at a site, including while another holds the TAG. Ask also about a Technical Assistance Needs Assessment. Brownfields go to the separate TAB programme. AND ASK FOR A TAP DURING SETTLEMENT NEGOTIATIONS: a Technical Assistance Plan is funded by the potentially responsible parties through terms in a negotiated settlement — the polluter pays for your advisor, and like the monitoring-access term recorded in this map's citizen-suit entry, it is rarely requested. CHECK YOUR STATE TOO: California's DTSC runs its own TAG at $40,000 to $150,000 — well above the federal figure — covering sites under DTSC oversight, and its funds can pay for community science projects under the advisor's guidance.

trackers.name: The Wildlands Conservancy
trackers.desc: The Wildlands Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in California. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.
