trackers.name: Georgia Outdoor Stewardship Program (GOSP) — Conserve Georgia grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Georgia's first dedicated conservation funding source, administered by DNR — competitive Conserve Georgia grants and loans to local governments, recreation authorities, state agencies and nonprofit organizations to acquire and protect lands critical to wildlife, clean water and outdoor recreation, and to support parks and trails. USE IT: apply, as a nonprofit or local government, to fund the acquisition or protection of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Land Conservation Acquisition Program — Athens-Clarke County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Athens-Clarke County unified government buys land and easements under a SPLOST-funded programme (a continuation of the 2001 Community Greenspace and 2005 Greenspace Acquisition programmes) with a standing goal of permanently protecting 20% of the county's land base — riparian zones, wetlands, steep slopes, forest and farm land assembled into a countywide green infrastructure network. USE IT: property owners can nominate their own parcel using the programme's downloadable nomination form; nominations are reviewed by the ACC Ecological Resources Administrator, and the county has stacked purchases with Georgia DNR Land Conservation Program money.

trackers.name: Georgia Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Georgia (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Georgia Attorney General
trackers.desc: Georgia’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Georgia. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Turner Environmental Law Clinic — Emory Law, Atlanta
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: since 1998 this clinic has given FREE legal representation to individuals, community groups and nonprofits seeking to protect the natural environment and promote environmental justice — litigation, transactional and policy work, including zoning fights, reservoir proposals, conservation easements and opposition to licence applications. It also publishes the ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE GREENBOOK, an online tool built to put information in the hands of Georgia residents defending their own communities, and co-authored the Georgia Model Solar Zoning Ordinance adopted by several cities and counties. USE IT: clinics take cases on a semester cycle, so approach early.

trackers.name: Gathering Waters (WI land trusts)
trackers.desc: Gathering Waters (WI land trusts) — a leading land trust/conservancy in Wisconsin. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Clean Wisconsin
trackers.desc: Clean Wisconsin — a leading citizen environmental watchdog for Wisconsin. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, extraction, sprawl and pollution. You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC)
trackers.desc: The Midwest’s leading public-interest environmental legal advocacy organization. WHO TO ENLIST against polluting facilities, pipelines, factory farms and dirty-energy projects across the region. You CAN: get legal and policy advocacy to challenge projects and permits. For activists: regional legal muscle and clean-energy expertise to fight harmful development. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Wisconsin Dept. of Natural Resources (DNR)
trackers.desc: Wisconsin’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Wisconsin. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Wisconsin Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Wisconsin’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Wisconsin, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Wisconsin and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: EPA Region 5 (Chicago)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 5, Chicago — the federal environmental regulator covering Wisconsin. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Wisconsin, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Midwest Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Midwest Region, Bloomington MN — the federal wildlife authority covering Wisconsin. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Wisconsin Knowles-Nelson Stewardship Program — DNR grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Wisconsin's primary land-conservation funding program, administered by the DNR — dollar-for-dollar matching grants to local governments and to nonprofit conservation organizations and land trusts to purchase land and conservation easements for parks and nature preserves statewide. USE IT: apply, or partner with a local government or land trust, to fund the purchase or easement of threatened land.

trackers.name: Dane County Conservation Fund Grant Program — Dane County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): the Dane County Conservation Fund, established in 1990, has helped protect more than 22,000 acres; since 2000 its grant program has paid nonprofits and local governments a share of the purchase price (up to 75% of project costs in the 2026 round) for land or land interests identified in the Dane County Parks & Open Space Plan, or in buffer areas adjacent to park land. USE IT: a local land trust or town can apply, typically stacking the county grant with a state Knowles-Nelson Stewardship grant to fund a full purchase.

trackers.name: Planning & Parks — Ozaukee County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ozaukee County's Planning & Parks Department protects priority natural areas identified in its Park and Open Space Plan and Farmland Preservation Plan through fee-simple purchase, land donations and easement acquisition — recent additions include the 134-acre Clay Bluffs Cedar Gorge Nature Preserve (Lake Michigan clay bluffs, coastal gorge, 0.7 miles of shoreline) and floodplain and wetland parcels bought outright. It uses a GIS ecological prioritisation tool to rank habitat and aquatic-connectivity projects and partners with the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District, which holds easements on some parcels. USE IT: the Park and Open Space Plan update runs public open houses — that is where a parcel gets onto the acquisition list.

trackers.name: Greenseams — Milwaukee, Ozaukee, Washington & Waukesha Counties (MMSD)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District runs a flood-management programme that buys undeveloped private land and conservation easements — from willing sellers only — along streams, shorelines and wetlands across a 720-square-mile, six-watershed, four-county area, specifically targeting water-absorbing hydric soils in places expected to see major development. Over 5,000 acres acquired since 2001, with a goal of 10,000 more acres of river buffer; one protected acre can store up to 651,000 gallons. The Conservation Fund runs the transactions. USE IT: a wetland or floodplain parcel facing development is worth putting to MMSD as flood infrastructure, not just habitat.

trackers.name: Midwest Environmental Advocates — Madison
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: on its own account the only nonprofit environmental law centre in Wisconsin providing legal services directly to individuals and grassroots groups — combining litigation with organising rather than treating them separately. Work covers water, nitrate contamination of rural wells, clean energy and open-government enforcement. Record includes a Wisconsin circuit court ordering Enbridge to halt pipeline construction at certain locations while a challenge to state approvals for the Line 5 reroute around the Bad River Reservation proceeds. USE IT: strongest where a state permit was granted without the record the law required.

trackers.name: Lessard-Sams Outdoor Heritage Council — Outdoor Heritage Fund (Minnesota)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the council that recommends annual appropriations from Minnesota's Outdoor Heritage Fund — one of four funds created when voters passed the CLEAN WATER, LAND AND LEGACY AMENDMENT in 2008, so the money is constitutionally dedicated rather than discretionary. Funds land ACQUISITION for wildlife management areas, aquatic management areas, scientific and natural areas and state forests; prairie, wetland, trout stream and forest restoration; and PERMANENT CONSERVATION EASEMENTS. WHO IT SUITS: proposals must fit the Minnesota Conservation and Preservation Plan and address wetlands, prairie, forest or fish and wildlife habitat — and note the statutory framing rewards preventing FOREST FRAGMENTATION and encouraging forest consolidation, which is directly usable language if your site is a parcel that would break up a larger block.

trackers.name: Minnesota Environment & Natural Resources Trust Fund (LCCMR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land, and more): Minnesota's lottery-funded Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund, allocated by the Legislative-Citizen Commission on Minnesota Resources (LCCMR) through a competitive annual RFP (~$100M+/year) open to nonprofits, local governments and others — funding land acquisition, habitat protection, water and other environmental projects. USE IT: submit a proposal, or partner with an eligible applicant, to fund acquisition or protection of a threatened place.

trackers.name: Dakota County Land Conservation Program — Dakota County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: begun in 2003 as the Farmland and Natural Areas Program, Dakota County's Land Conservation Program has completed 156 projects protecting over 12,000 acres — 127 permanent agricultural and natural-area conservation easements bought from willing landowners plus 33 fee acquisitions with partner agencies, leveraging state Outdoor Heritage and ENRTF money against county funds. USE IT: landowners inside a designated Conservation Focus Area can apply in the annual round (donations of land or easements are accepted year-round); the easement pays cash while permanently barring development.

trackers.name: Washington County Land and Water Legacy Program — Washington County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created by a 2006 voter referendum authorising $20 million, the LWLP buys conservation easements and land in the county's “Top Ten” priority conservation areas along the Mississippi and St. Croix rivers — more than 50 completed projects protecting over 1,900 acres, with county money leveraging some $34 million in partner funds from the Minnesota Land Trust, Trust for Public Land and the state Outdoor Heritage Fund. USE IT: landowners inside a priority conservation area can approach county planning staff or the Minnesota Land Trust to start an easement.

trackers.name: Three Rivers Park District — suburban Hennepin, Carver, Dakota, Scott & Ramsey Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an independent special park district created by the Minnesota Legislature in 1957 (as the Hennepin County Park Reserve District) and charged with acquiring, developing and maintaining large park reserves and regional trails — over 27,000 acres, with a standing policy that at least 80% of each park reserve stays in or is restored to a natural state. It bought nearly 21,000 acres of threatened suburban farmland in its first decade and still buys corridor land, often with state Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund money. USE IT: landowners along planned trail corridors are invited to contact the Director of Planning directly about selling.

trackers.name: Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO) — Land Acquisition program
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy land): a competitive grant programme that has helped conserve more than 1.4 million acres in Colorado, funding fee-simple purchases and — where tax credits are insufficient or impractical — conservation easements. WHO IT SUITS: Colorado cities, towns and counties, Title 32 special districts, and LAND CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS — so a land trust can apply, an unincorporated neighbourhood group cannot. HOW IT DIFFERS: eligible fee-simple projects must PROVIDE PUBLIC ACCESS, so a pure no-access habitat purchase is a poor fit for this window; pitch the easement route instead.

trackers.name: Boulder County Parks & Open Space — Boulder County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Boulder County's voter-funded open-space program (a county sales-and-use tax first passed in 1993) has conserved 100,000+ acres — buying land outright and holding conservation easements to keep farms, ranches, wildlife habitat and community buffers from being developed. USE IT: if you own threatened land in Boulder County, contact the Real Estate Division about selling or donating a conservation easement; if you're fighting sprawl, point to the program as the local tool for permanent protection.

trackers.name: Jeffco Parks & Open Space — Jefferson County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 1972 by a half-percent county sales tax — the first sales-tax-funded county open space program in the country — Jeffco Parks & Open Space has preserved more than 58,000 acres, buying land and easements from willing sellers under published Land Acquisition Criteria and its Conservation Greenprint. USE IT: nominate a threatened property to the Open Space Department against those criteria, and take the case to the Open Space Advisory Committee, whose public meetings feed acquisition recommendations to the Board of County Commissioners.

trackers.name: PLAN Jeffco — Jefferson County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the citizen nonprofit that drafted and won the 1972 Open Space Resolution and later the 1998 $160 million open-space bond, and that has since acted as the watchdog on the program — monitoring Open Space Advisory Committee meetings, keeping residents informed, and training citizens in how to advocate for open space against Front Range development. USE IT: bring them a Jefferson County parcel worth protecting or a proposal that would erode the Open Space Program, and use their classes and OSAC presence to get a local campaign heard.

trackers.name: Larimer County Open Lands — Larimer County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by the voter-approved Help Preserve Open Spaces quarter-cent sales tax (1995, extended 1999 and 2014), Larimer County has conserved over 55,000 acres through outright purchase and conservation easements on working ranches and foothills habitat. A 12-member citizen Natural Resources Advisory Board reviews possible acquisitions in monthly public meetings. USE IT: landowners can sell or donate an easement through the Landowner Conservation pages; communities can take a threatened property to the Advisory Board, whose recommendations go to the County Commissioners.

trackers.name: Douglas County Open Space & Natural Resources — Douglas County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a sixth-of-a-cent open space sales and use tax approved by Douglas County voters in 1994 and extended for 15 more years in 2022, the programme has protected roughly 65,000 acres on the fast-developing Front Range — about 70% of it through conservation easements on private land, the rest county-owned — and it leverages $2.92 in partner money for every $1 of county tax. USE IT: bring a threatened ranch or corridor to Open Space staff or to the Douglas Land Conservancy, which co-holds many of the easements; recent deals include the 2,038-acre Sandstone Ranch.

trackers.name: Pitkin County Open Space and Trails — Pitkin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded in 1990 by a voter-approved dedicated property tax — reauthorised three times, most recently through 2040 — Pitkin County OST has conserved nearly 30,000 acres of the Roaring Fork watershed through outright purchase and conservation easements, including the $34 million Snowmass Falls Ranch buy that stopped development on 650 acres ringed by wilderness. USE IT: acquisitions are recommended by the five-member Open Space and Trails Board of Trustees before going to the County Commissioners, so that board is where a case for a threatened property gets made in public.

trackers.name: Eagle County Open Space and Natural Resources — Eagle County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a 1.5-mill property tax approved by Eagle County voters in 2002 and extended to 2040, the programme has helped conserve well over 15,000 acres through fee-simple purchases, conservation easements, and — usefully — by paying the transaction costs of easements that other conservation partners will hold. An Open Space Advisory Committee evaluates and recommends projects. USE IT: if a land trust is close to a deal but stuck on survey, appraisal and legal costs, Eagle County money can close that gap; bring ranch and river-corridor parcels to OSAC.

trackers.name: Summit County Open Space & Trails — Summit County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by open space mill levies Summit County voters approved in 1993, 1999, 2003, 2008 and 2019, the programme has protected nearly 18,000 acres through roughly 400 acquisitions since 1995 — buying land at fair market value, taking donated conservation and access easements, and leveraging each county dollar into about $3 of protected land via Great Outdoors Colorado and town partnerships. Priorities include community buffers, growth limitation, scenic corridors, wetlands and wildlife habitat. USE IT: landowners can sell, donate, or partially donate; the department works from the Open Space and Trails Master Plan's acquisition priorities.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights Program — Routt County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Routt County voters in 1996, amended in 2005 and reauthorised through 2035, the PDR programme uses a 1.5-mill property tax (up to about $1.25 million a year) solely to buy development rights and cover easement costs — nearly 70,000 acres of ranchland, river corridor and wildlife habitat conserved for roughly $32 million, typically paying only part of an easement's value with landowners, Great Outdoors Colorado, land trusts and USDA covering the rest. USE IT: proposals go to the citizen PDR Advisory Board in two tiers (proposal evaluation, then due diligence) before the County Commissioners vote; a land trust such as CCALT usually carries the project.

trackers.name: Open Space & Mountain Parks — City of Boulder
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: in 1967 Boulder voters approved a 0.40-cent sales tax to buy and manage open space — the first time residents of any US city taxed themselves specifically for it, passed by 57%. The programme now holds more than 46,640 acres forming a development buffer around the city, roughly 90% funded by sales and use tax, with a 1971 charter amendment allowing bonds for acquisition and a 1986 charter amendment (77% yes) giving open space permanent protection. USE IT: land comes in by purchase, by joint acquisition with Boulder County, and by dedication during annexation or development — that last route is the one a community can invoke when a project needs city approval.

trackers.name: Natural Areas Department — City of Fort Collins
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a small group of residents put a quarter-cent sales and use tax on the ballot by citizens' initiative in 1992; voters renewed it in 2002 as 'Open Space, Yes!'. Over 55,000 acres conserved and 114 miles of trails, stacked with the separate Larimer County 'Help Preserve Open Space' tax and Great Outdoors Colorado grants. USE IT honestly: the funding has an expiry date, which is why residents keep having to run renewal campaigns, and about 71% of the protected acreage lies outside city limits — a live local argument about whether taxpayers without a car can actually reach what they paid for. The Land Conservation and Stewardship Board advises Council and is the place to raise both points.

Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. trackers.name: Pennsylvania DCNR Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): DCNR's C2P2 program (~$50M/year, funded by the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund and the Environmental Stewardship Fund) makes grants to local governments, nonprofit conservation organizations and pre-qualified land trusts to acquire land and conservation easements for critical habitat, open space, parks and trails (50% match typical). USE IT: apply, as a land trust, nonprofit or municipality, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Lancaster County Agricultural Preserve Board — Lancaster County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 1980 under Pennsylvania's Act 442/Act 43, the Preserve Board runs the county's agricultural conservation easement purchase program — landowners apply to sell their development rights, the Board ranks applications, commissions appraisals and makes formal offers using combined county and state funds, then monitors the perpetual easement recorded on the deed. trackers.name: Chester County Preservation Partnership Program — Chester County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): since 1989 Chester County's Open Lands division has given grants to municipalities and non-profit land conservation organizations for fee-simple purchases and conservation easements — over 20,000 acres preserved through this program alone, with recent awards including 204 acres at Crebilly and 493 acres added to William Penn State Forest. Preference goes to projects that leverage state or federal money. USE IT: an eligible land trust or your township applies in the annual spring grant cycle; a community campaign works by getting one of them to sponsor the parcel.

trackers.name: Bucks County Agricultural Land Preservation — Bucks County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 1989 under Pennsylvania Act 43 and funded by county, state and municipal money, the Bucks County Agricultural Land Preservation Board buys conservation easements that permanently extinguish development rights on productive farmland, ranking farms by soil quality, location, conservation practices and threat of development. A Municipal Partnership Program added in 2025 lets townships put their own money alongside the county's. USE IT: farm owners apply through the county board; townships can top up the county offer to reach full easement value.

trackers.name: Montco Forever Green Open Space Grant Program — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): launched in 2025 as the successor to Montgomery County's 1993 and 2003 open space programmes, Montco Forever Green gives municipalities and qualified non-profit land conservation organisations up to $500,000 per project toward fee-title purchases or conservation easements — any open land in the county, any size, rural to urban, with only a 25% match (down from the old dollar-for-dollar requirement). USE IT: applications are taken on a rolling basis by the County Planning Commission, reviewed by the Open Space Board, then voted by the County Commissioners.

trackers.name: Agricultural Conservation Easement Program — Berks County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Berks ranks second in Pennsylvania and among the leaders nationally for farmland preservation, with over 65,000 acres protected since 1989 — the nine-member county Agricultural Land Preservation Board buys perpetual agricultural conservation easements with combined county and state money, deliberately building large contiguous clusters of preserved farms rather than isolated parcels. Townships can join a purchase alongside the county and state. USE IT: landowners apply free of charge by 31 December each year with no commitment to proceed; applications are scored on the LESA system, which weights soil quality and development pressure.

trackers.name: Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services — Pittsburgh (nonprofit law firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a 501(c)(3) nonprofit law firm founded in 2013 to close the environmental legal services gap in the Appalachian Basin, representing residents, grassroots groups and nonprofits on a PRO BONO or sliding-scale, income-based fee — explicitly so that people can act regardless of means. Practice covers oil and gas, land use and zoning, eminent domain, mine reclamation, landfill regulation, stormwater, land conservation and land trusts, citizen suits under the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts, and nonprofit incorporation. It also runs Community Democracy training on civic engagement and organising. USE IT: they publish free guidance on how municipalities rezone quietly for data centres, warehouses and industrial facilities — ring them BEFORE the rezoning hearing.

trackers.name: Florida Forever — state land acquisition programme
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: one of the largest PUBLIC land-acquisition programmes in the United States, run by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. It buys environmentally significant land outright (fee simple) OR buys a conservation easement over it (less-than-fee, so the owner keeps the land but development is barred). Florida Forever and its predecessor Preservation 2000 have together protected more than 2.6 million acres. USE IT: two hard gates decide whether your site is eligible — there must be a WILLING SELLER, and the project must be on the Florida Forever Priority List, which the ten-member Acquisition and Restoration Council ranks. Anyone can sponsor a project: government agencies, conservation organisations or private citizens. Getting a threatened parcel onto that list is the actual fight. Land trusts often act as the intermediary with the owner.

trackers.name: Florida Forever — how to get a parcel considered (FAQ)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the state's own answers on eligibility, sponsorship and process — how projects get onto the Priority List, who ends up owning and managing acquired land (title vests in the Governor and Cabinet as Board of Trustees, held in trust for the people of Florida), and how a landowner can request REMOVAL of their property from a project boundary. USE IT: read this before pitching a site, and note the removal route — a hostile owner can use it, so speed matters. It also names the companion programmes for smaller or local acquisitions: Florida Communities Trust, the Land and Water Conservation Fund, and the Florida Recreation Development Assistance Program.

trackers.name: Earthjustice — Florida Regional Office
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (environmental lawyers): the Florida regional office of Earthjustice, the nation's premier nonprofit environmental law organization, with attorneys in Tallahassee and Miami providing free legal representation to citizen groups and conservation organizations — it has defended the Everglades and Florida's waters and wetlands for 35+ years and overturned the state's takeover of federal wetlands permitting. USE IT: contact them, or partner with a local group they represent, to challenge a project threatening Florida's land, water or wildlife.

trackers.name: Alachua County Forever — Alachua County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created by a 2000 bond referendum and now funded by the voter-renewed Wild Spaces Public Places half-cent sales tax, Alachua County Forever has protected more than 36,000 acres by buying land outright and by purchasing conservation easements from willing landowners; condemnation is not permitted. USE IT: anyone can nominate a property using the program's one-page nomination form — staff score it on a 25-question matrix (water, habitat, species, social value) and the Land Conservation Board ranks it onto the acquisition list.

trackers.name: Jan K. Platt ELAPP — Hillsborough County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Environmental Lands Acquisition and Protection Program, created by Hillsborough County voters in 1987 and expanded by referendum in 1990 and 2008, has acquired or helped protect roughly 62,000 acres of environmentally sensitive land. It is voluntary and non-regulatory — it buys only from willing sellers — and citizen volunteer committees run every key stage. USE IT: anyone can nominate a site, which triggers a staff assessment and a public ELAPP committee evaluation and ranking; a threatened wetland, scrub or river corridor in Hillsborough belongs in that queue.

trackers.name: Environmentally Endangered Lands (EEL) Program — Miami-Dade County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a property tax Miami-Dade voters approved in 1990, the EEL Program has brought more than 20,700 acres of pineland, hardwood hammock, salt marsh and wetland into public ownership, buying only from willing sellers and stretching its money with matching grants and acquisition partners. USE IT: the program considers newly proposed sites twice a year — staff and the citizen-volunteer Land Acquisition Selection Committee inspect each one and, after a public hearing, recommend sites to the County Commission, so a threatened natural area can be put into that pipeline from outside.

trackers.name: Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program — Sarasota County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Sarasota County voters in 1999 and extended to 2029 in 2005, ESLPP (with the companion Neighborhood Parkland program) has protected more than 42,000 acres by outright purchase and conservation easement — including three easements totalling 8,060 acres on Longino Ranch in the Eastern Ranchlands priority site. Purchases require a willing seller. USE IT: any resident can submit a land nomination form to landnominations@scgov.net; staff screen it, then the Environmentally Sensitive Lands Oversight Committee reviews it before the County Commission votes.

trackers.name: Volusia Forever — Volusia County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a dedicated 0.2-mill county tax approved by Volusia voters in 2000 and renewed for another 20 years in 2020, funding purchase of environmentally sensitive land, water-resource land, outdoor recreation land and now working forests and farmland — nearly 60,000 acres protected countywide with its predecessor programme. USE IT: the county accepts nominations “from any government entity, conservation organization, corporation or individual” for any property in the county, whether or not you own it (it is a willing-seller programme); the nine-member Volusia Forever Advisory Committee visits sites and recommends to the County Council. A separate Small Lot programme absorbs parcels in nine antiquated subdivisions with no survey or appraisal required.

trackers.name: Environmentally Endangered Lands (EEL) Program — Brevard County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a Brevard County referendum in 1990, reaffirmed in 2004 and extended again in 2022, EEL has protected more than 28,000 acres of scrub, wetland, woodland and lagoon-buffering habitat, buying from willing sellers and leveraging state and St. Johns River Water Management District money. Current acquisition focus: the Brevard Coastal Scrub Ecosystem and the North Indian River Lagoon Blueways projects. USE IT: parcels are nominated for public acquisition and reviewed by the eight-member volunteer EEL Selection & Management Committee — seven of them scientists — and only land the committee recommends can be bought with EEL funds, so that committee is where a campaign lands.

trackers.name: Conservation 20/20 — Lee County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Lee County voters in 1996, Conservation 20/20 has protected more than 31,000 acres of Southwest Florida wetlands, uplands and wildlife corridors, buying from willing sellers. Anyone can nominate a property; the citizen Conservation Land Acquisition and Stewardship Advisory Committee (CLASAC) ranks nominations into Tier I and Tier II priority lists in monthly public meetings, and purchases go to the County Commissioners for final approval. NOTE: county staff declined to replenish the acquisition fund in the 2025 budget round, so roughly $19 million remains against far more in nominated properties — tier ranking now decides what actually gets bought. USE IT: nominate the parcel anyway and turn out at CLASAC.

trackers.name: Preservation Project — City of Jacksonville
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: launched in 1999 as a $300m+ 'greenprint for growth' and the largest land acquisition programme in Florida's history, buying environmentally sensitive land across five priority corridors (St Johns River, the Southeast Greenbelt, the Intracoastal Waterway and others) explicitly to steer development away from them. Tens of thousands of acres protected; combined with National Park Service and state park land through a tri-governmental partnership it forms the largest urban park system in the contiguous US. USE IT: the city worked through the Trust for Public Land and a nonprofit intermediary to negotiate with landowners, and recovered millions via Florida Communities Trust grants — the model is city money plus a land trust doing the deals plus state grant reimbursement.

Record of stopping things: blocked expansion of nearly 20,000 acres of lime rock mines in the Everglades Agricultural Area; prevented a commercial airport between two national parks; defeated a proposal to deepen and widen the Lake Worth Inlet that would have destroyed corals and manatee seagrass beds; and successfully challenged numerous developments that violated Florida's growth-management laws. USE IT: they appear not only in court but before WATER MANAGEMENT DISTRICTS AND COUNTY COMMISSIONS — the bodies that actually approve most Florida development.

trackers.name: Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC)
trackers.desc: The Midwest’s leading public-interest environmental legal advocacy organization. WHO TO ENLIST against polluting facilities, pipelines, factory farms and dirty-energy projects across the region. You CAN: get legal and policy advocacy to challenge projects and permits. For activists: regional legal muscle and clean-energy expertise to fight harmful development. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Illinois OSLAD — Open Space Lands Acquisition & Development grant (IDNR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): IDNR's OSLAD program, funded by a dedicated share of the state Real Estate Transfer Tax, gives grants (up to 50%, or up to 100% for distressed communities) to local units of government to acquire land for public parks, open space and natural-resource preservation. USE IT: work through your municipality or park district to apply for an acquisition grant on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County — Cook County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Forest Preserves of Cook County — the largest forest preserve district in the U.S. (est. 1914, ~70,000 acres) — has a statutory mandate to acquire and permanently protect open space, prairies, woodlands and wetlands across metropolitan Chicago, funded by a county tax levy and bonds. USE IT: alert the District to a threatened natural parcel that fills a gap in its holdings, or partner with allied groups to push for its acquisition.

trackers.name: Lake County Forest Preserves — Lake County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Illinois's second-largest forest preserve district (est. 1958) protects nearly 31,000 acres in the county with the most threatened and endangered species in the state, and in November 2024 county voters approved a $155 million bond of which $65 million is earmarked specifically for buying more land. USE IT: bring a threatened natural parcel to the district's Planning and Land Preservation staff — all acquisitions are approved in public by the elected Board of Commissioners, so a community campaign can press the case there.

trackers.name: Forest Preserve District of DuPage County — DuPage County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established by referendum in 1915 and funded by a county property-tax levy and bonds, the district's statutory mission is to acquire and hold forests, prairies, wetlands and restorable land — nearly 26,000 acres, about 12 percent of DuPage County, in one of Illinois's most developed areas. It keeps buying: a $12 million, 35-acre purchase beside Danada Forest Preserve closed in 2024. USE IT: flag a threatened parcel that would fill a gap in or buffer an existing preserve; acquisitions are approved in public by the elected Board of Commissioners.

trackers.name: McHenry County Conservation District — McHenry County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established by countywide referendum in 1971 under the Illinois Conservation District Act — one of only five such districts in the state (with Boone, Macon, Putnam and Vermilion) — it protects roughly 25,800 acres including 17 dedicated State Nature Preserves, in a county holding some of Illinois's highest-quality remaining wetlands. Its statutory purpose is acquiring land by purchase, lease, gift or easement, funded by a dedicated tax levy plus referendum-approved bonds ($141.5 million across two open space referenda). USE IT: bring a parcel to the seven-member Board of Trustees.

trackers.name: Forest Preserve District of Kane County — Kane County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded in 1925 and now holding more than 23,000 acres of Fox Valley woodlands, wetlands and prairies, the district buys land only from willing sellers — either additions to existing preserves or entirely new sites — funded by successive voter referenda (1999, 2011, 2017, and a 2024 levy increase passed 125,219 to 87,811 to add up to 125 acres of new preserve a year). Its board is the Kane County Board sitting as forest preserve commissioners, with a standing Land Acquisition committee. USE IT: bring a threatened river-corridor or watershed parcel to that committee.

trackers.name: Greater Chicago Legal Clinic — Environmental Law Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a legal services provider for low-income Chicagoans whose Environmental Law Program exists specifically so that people confronting urban environmental problems have equal access to justice — free representation for residents and neighbourhood groups who would otherwise be unrepresented in matters affecting their family's health and safety. It runs the Chicago Environmental and Energy Law Clinic jointly with Chicago-Kent College of Law, appearing in rulemaking, permitting, remediation and enforcement cases at local, state and federal level under every major environmental statute. USE IT: the clinic states it does not impose an agenda on clients but responds to community-directed concerns — so bring your own objective, whether that is stopping a permit, forcing a cleanup or being heard in a rulemaking.

trackers.name: Conservation Law Foundation (CLF)
trackers.desc: New England’s flagship environmental advocacy and law organization. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, sprawl, dirty energy and water pollution across the region. You CAN: get legal advocacy, litigation and organizing support to fight projects and enforce environmental law. For activists: a regional powerhouse with the lawyers and track record to take on big projects. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Dept. of Environmental Protection (MassDEP)
trackers.desc: Massachusetts’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Massachusetts. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Massachusetts’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Massachusetts, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Massachusetts and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife
trackers.desc: Massachusetts’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 1 (Boston)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 1, Boston — the federal environmental regulator covering Massachusetts. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Massachusetts, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Northeast Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Northeast Region, Hadley MA — the federal wildlife authority covering Massachusetts. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Emmett Environmental Law and Policy Clinic — Harvard Law School
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Harvard Law School's environmental clinic, working on litigation, administrative, legislative and policy projects with scientists, medical professionals and public interest organisations at federal, state and local level. Output includes briefs, comment letters, model legislation and guidance documents written for NON-LAWYERS. WHO IT SUITS: be clear-eyed about the fit — this clinic leans policy, regulatory drafting and expert-facing work, and its clients include government bodies as well as NGOs. For a single contested application you likely want a plaintiff-side firm or a representation-focused clinic; for a rule, a permit programme or a technical comment that needs to withstand scrutiny, this is the stronger call.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Division of Conservation Services — land acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Massachusetts EEA Division of Conservation Services (DCS) runs several land-acquisition grant programs — the Conservation Partnership Grant reimburses nonprofit land trusts up to 50% (max ~$175k) to acquire land or conservation restrictions; the LAND grant funds municipal conservation-land purchases; and Landscape Partnership and Drinking Water Supply Protection grants fund larger acquisitions. USE IT: as a land trust or municipality, apply to fund the purchase or restriction of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Community Preservation Act (CPA) — local open space funds
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (town by town): a 2000 state law (MGL c.44B) letting any Massachusetts city or town vote in a property-tax surcharge of up to 3% to create a local Community Preservation Fund for open space protection, historic preservation, affordable housing and outdoor recreation — with an annual match from a statewide trust fund financed by Registry of Deeds fees. At least 10% of revenue each year must go to open space. Over 200 municipalities have adopted it and none has ever revoked it. USE IT: adoption is by ballot referendum, so this is the mechanism a community organises for where no county programme exists; spending is then decided each year by a local Community Preservation Committee and Town Meeting or council.

trackers.name: Nantucket Islands Land Bank
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the first land bank of its kind in the United States — recommended by Nantucket Town Meeting in 1983 by 446 votes to 1, authorised by special act of the Massachusetts legislature, and confirmed by the island's voters in 1984. It levies a 2% fee on most real estate transfers in Nantucket County, paid by the buyer, and uses it to buy and hold open space, farmland and recreation land. Over 3,475 acres owned plus 500 more under conservation restriction, more than $420 million spent, and with other conservation groups nearly half the island is now permanently protected. USE IT: five commissioners are directly ELECTED, so acquisition priorities are answerable at the ballot box; first-time homebuyers are exempt on a threshold raised annually (recently $1.2 million).

trackers.name: Martha's Vineyard Land Bank Commission
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created by island voters in 1986 after Nantucket's model, funded by a 2% surcharge on most real estate transfers across the Vineyard's six towns and charged with reversing the loss of farmland, trails and public access during a building boom. About 4,200 acres conserved. The commission is admirably blunt that this is only 7% of the island and that its revenue is modest against need. USE IT: the last item of business at every commission meeting (most Mondays at 3pm) is public input, letters are accepted any time, and a formal public input session runs every other autumn — the acquisition list is genuinely open to residents proposing land.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Massachusetts (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Attorney General
trackers.desc: Massachusetts’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Massachusetts. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Conservation Law Foundation — Massachusetts office, Boston
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: CLF has litigated for New England communities since 1966 and keeps a staffed office in every New England state, so the lawyer is local even though the organisation is regional. Massachusetts record includes cleaning up Boston Harbor, forcing coal plant closures, and current litigation holding polluters accountable for illegal stormwater discharge — a cause of action that applies to construction sites and paved development, not just factories. USE IT: stormwater and transit access are the two areas where it takes on local development directly.

trackers.name: Berkshire Natural Resources Council — Berkshire County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the county-wide land trust for Berkshire County (est. 1967), accredited, now caring for 27,000+ acres — it buys land outright and holds permanent conservation restrictions on farms, forests, ridgelines and stream corridors across the Berkshires, working alongside individual landowners, town land trusts and state agencies. USE IT: if land you are trying to save is in Berkshire County, bring BNRC in as the entity that can hold the easement or purchase the parcel; it also partners on projects too big for a single-town trust.

trackers.name: Greenbelt — Essex County's Land Trust — Essex County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Greenbelt (Essex County Greenbelt Association, est. 1961) is the land trust for all 34 cities and towns of Essex County, holding 8,200+ acres outright and 10,300+ acres under easement — farmland, salt marsh, wildlife habitat and scenic land north of Boston. It works directly with landowners and municipalities on conservation restrictions and purchases. USE IT: contact Greenbelt about conserving a threatened Essex County parcel, or ask it to partner with your town's conservation commission on an acquisition.

trackers.name: Franklin Land Trust — Franklin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a western-Massachusetts land trust (est. 1987) focused on Franklin County's working farms and woodlands — it holds 170+ conservation restrictions and agricultural preservation restrictions across 30+ towns, and has bought farms outright, sold the development rights into the state APR program, and resold the land to working farmers. USE IT: if development threatens farmland or forest in Franklin County, FLT will map the property free of charge and lay out the conservation options with no obligation.

trackers.name: Western Reserve Land Conservancy
trackers.desc: Western Reserve Land Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in Ohio. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation Program (OPWC)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation Program, a voter-approved state bond program administered by the Ohio Public Works Commission (OPWC) through 19 local Natural Resources Assistance Councils, provides grants for up to 75% of costs to acquire open space and easements — land for parks, forests, wetlands, natural areas and stream corridors — open to local governments, park districts and nonprofit conservation organizations. USE IT: apply through your district NRAC to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Cleveland Metroparks — Cuyahoga County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Cleveland Metropolitan Park District (est. 1917, now over 25,000 acres across 49 communities) has statutory power to acquire land inside or outside the district for conservation, and its Natural Resources Division evaluates tracts for protection by purchase, easement or other means — aggressively targeting the remaining major river valleys of Northeast Ohio, often alongside Western Reserve Land Conservancy and West Creek Conservancy. USE IT: flag a threatened stream corridor or woodland adjoining a reservation; donations of land, easements and life estates are accepted through the Land Protection Fund.

trackers.name: Columbus and Franklin County Metro Parks — Franklin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an independent political subdivision created in 1945 under Ohio Revised Code 1545 to conserve natural resources, now protecting over 28,000 acres across seven Central Ohio counties, funded primarily by a 10-year 0.95-mill levy Franklin County voters approved in 2018 that explicitly covers acquiring additional land for future preservation. Its parks were built river-corridor first, so stream and floodplain land is its core interest. USE IT: bring a threatened river or stream corridor parcel to the Board of Park Commissioners; the district has been assembling such land continuously since 1947.

trackers.name: Summit Metro Parks — Summit County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a levy-funded park district (est. 1921) managing roughly 14,000 acres in Summit County, including six conservation areas held purely for natural-resource protection rather than public recreation — stream corridors, kettle-hole bog, mature forest and rare-species habitat, some of it acquired specifically to stop subdivisions. It routinely partners with the Trust for Public Land, Western Reserve Land Conservancy and the Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District, stacking Clean Ohio Fund and Ohio EPA water-quality money against local levy dollars. USE IT: bring a threatened wetland or headwater parcel to the park district and to those land trusts together.

trackers.name: Five Rivers MetroParks — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Montgomery County park district protects more than 3,000 acres through conservation easements on privately owned land — headwater streams, large forest tracts and farmland adjoining its parks — alongside outright purchases, with roughly half its land-protection money coming from state and federal grants (chiefly the Clean Ohio Fund, plus LWCF, the Farm and Ranch Lands Protection Program and Ohio EPA's Water Resource Restoration Sponsor Program). Landowners keep ownership. USE IT: bring a stream-corridor or forest parcel to MetroParks' conservation staff; its three-member board approves all land acquisition in public.

trackers.name: Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services — Akron (nonprofit law firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the same nonprofit law firm serving Ohio from an Akron office, alongside Pennsylvania and West Virginia. It provides pro bono and sliding-scale representation to individuals, families, grassroots groups and nonprofits directly affected by environmental harm — oil and gas, zoning and land use, landfills, mine reclamation, water and air citizen suits, land conservation and nonprofit formation — and trains new lawyers specifically to serve modest-means environmental clients. USE IT: it is one of very few places in the Ohio River Valley where a community with no money can get an environmental lawyer, and it partners with regional nonprofits for workshops and legal clinics.

trackers.name: Delaware Wild Lands
trackers.desc: Delaware Wild Lands — a leading land trust/conservancy in Delaware. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Iowa's 99 county conservation boards — find yours (IACCB)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Iowa is the only state where every single county has a voter-established conservation board with statutory power to acquire and hold land — created by Chapter 350 of the Code of Iowa in 1955, the 99 boards now own or manage nearly 200,000 acres across more than 1,850 areas. trackers.name: Iowa Business Entity Search

trackers.name: Iowa Attorney General

trackers.name: Kansas Land Trust
trackers.desc: Kansas Land Trust — a leading land trust/conservancy in Kansas. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Kansas Dept. of Health & Environment (KDHE)

You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). trackers.name: Douglas County Natural and Cultural Heritage Grant Program — Douglas County

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Lexington-Fayette County

USE IT: farms of 20+ acres (or adjoining tracts totalling that) apply to the PDR office in the annual cycle; a Small Farm Program extends the same deal to smaller holdings.
