You CAN: tap their research, organizing, legal advocacy and lobbying to fight a specific project, and connect to local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your single best first call.

trackers.name: Conservation Law Foundation (CLF)
trackers.desc: New England’s flagship environmental advocacy and law organization. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, sprawl, dirty energy and water pollution across the region. You CAN: get legal advocacy, litigation and organizing support to fight projects and enforce environmental law. For activists: a regional powerhouse with the lawyers and track record to take on big projects. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Maine Dept. of Environmental Protection (DEP)
trackers.desc: Maine’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Maine. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Maine Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Maine’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Maine, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Maine and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Maine Inland Fisheries & Wildlife
trackers.desc: Maine’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 1 (Boston)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 1, Boston — the federal environmental regulator covering Maine. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Maine, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Northeast Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Northeast Region, Hadley MA — the federal wildlife authority covering Maine. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Land for Maine's Future (LMF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Land for Maine's Future is the state's primary land-conservation funding program — it provides land-acquisition funding to state agencies, municipalities and private land trusts to purchase land and easements of statewide, regional or local significance from willing sellers (farmland, water access, working waterfronts, wildlife habitat), and in 2026 gained ongoing dedicated funding. USE IT: partner with a Designated State Agency, or as a land trust or municipality, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Land for Maine's Future (LMF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): Maine's primary land conservation fund, created when voters approved a $35 million bond in 1987 and replenished by further bonds in 1999, 2005, 2007, 2010 and 2012, then appropriated $40 million in 2021 after nearly a decade without new money. Over 300 projects funded, protecting farmland, water access, working waterfront and recreation land — roughly 90% of Maine is privately owned, so public access depends on it. LAND TRUSTS AND MUNICIPALITIES can apply, not just state agencies. USE IT: awards go up to 50% of appraised value and you must secure matching funds at least equal to the award, so line up your other sources first — LMF publishes a partner-funding checklist showing which programmes stack with it.

trackers.name: Town conservation commissions — Maine Association of Conservation Commissions
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a municipal advisory board established by a Maine town, city or plantation through its legislative body, which advises planning and select boards, conducts natural resource surveys, develops open space plans, PROPOSES ORDINANCES, monitors development and stewards public land. The association exists to help citizens form new commissions as well as support existing ones. USE IT: in a state with weak county government this is the standing body a community can join or create to get conservation into the town plan and to watch permit applications — ring the association if your town has no commission and you want to start one.

trackers.name: Maine Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Maine (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Maine Attorney General
trackers.desc: Maine’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Maine. You CAN: file complaints and tips the office can investigate and prosecute; most have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: often the most powerful and reachable ally against a local corporate or official target.

trackers.name: Kennebec Land Trust — Kennebec County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the county land trust for Kennebec County (est. 1988), partnered with landowners in 21 communities to permanently protect thousands of acres of forest, shoreland and farm fields through donations, purchases and conservation easements, with 60+ miles of public trails. It co-founded the Kennebec Woodland Partnership with the Maine Forest Service. USE IT: contact KLT to place a permanent easement on threatened central-Maine land, or to have it hold land you want kept undeveloped.

trackers.name: Downeast Lakes Land Trust — Washington County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-founded land trust (est. 2001, Grand Lake Stream) created by interior Washington County residents when timber companies began heavily cutting and then selling land to developers — it now owns and sustainably manages the 57,703-acre Downeast Lakes Community Forest and has helped protect roughly 350,000 acres of forest, lakeshore and watershed. USE IT: the clearest US template for a community that wants to BUY the working forest around it rather than watch it be subdivided — contact DLLT about how the community-forest purchase was financed and structured.

trackers.name: Georges River Land Trust — Knox & Waldo Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: since 1987 this trust has conserved more than 3,600 acres along the 51-mile St. George River, from its headwaters at Frye Mountain in Waldo County to Muscongus Bay in Knox County, across ten towns — stewarding 60 properties, of which 43 are conservation easements and 17 are preserves it owns, plus the Georges Highland Path, a 45-mile watershed trail system running over privately owned land secured through handshake agreements. USE IT: it explicitly invites landowners to call and discuss permanently protecting their land, and works through donations, sales and easements.

trackers.name: Presumpscot Regional Land Trust — Cumberland County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-based trust serving Gorham, Gray, Standish, Westbrook and Windham in Cumberland County — 2,170 acres conserved with 18 free public-access preserves. It also runs the water-quality monitoring programme for the Presumpscot River watershed and coordinates the 28-mile Sebago to the Sea Trail from Standish to Portland. USE IT: the water-quality monitoring data is the useful part for a pollution dispute — an independent local record of river condition over time, held by a body with standing in the watershed.

trackers.name: Royal River Conservation Trust — Cumberland & Androscoggin Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established 1988, RRCT covers the seven Royal River watershed municipalities across Cumberland and Androscoggin counties — Yarmouth, North Yarmouth, Pownal, New Gloucester, Gray, Durham and Auburn. It owns preserves and trail networks and has helped create town-owned parks, state parks and state wildlife-management areas, including a fee acquisition at Thayer Brook Preserve in Gray funded through Land for Maine's Future. USE IT: a trust with a track record of converting private parcels into permanently public land through the state LMF programme.

trackers.name: Frenchman Bay Conservancy — Hancock County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the land trust for eastern and interior Hancock County, protecting the Frenchman Bay and Union River watersheds east to the county line — 25,000+ acres conserved and 40 miles of trails. Recent work shows the range of tools: it closed on the 405-acre Whitney Community Forest, the largest remaining undeveloped tract beside Ellsworth High School; took two easements in Aurora protecting 3,223 forever-wild acres; won a USD 1 million US Fish & Wildlife grant toward 216 acres of coastal wetlands at a former golf course; and permanently protected harvester access in Sullivan and Gouldsboro. USE IT: it is running a USD 10 million campaign for urgent Union River acquisitions, so a threatened parcel there has a funded buyer to approach.

trackers.name: Blue Hill Heritage Trust — Blue Hill Peninsula, Hancock County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-based trust conserving land and water resources in perpetuity across the Blue Hill Peninsula — it owns conserved land, monitors conservation easements on privately owned property, maintains low-impact trails including one to the summit of Blue Hill Mountain, and runs a Farmland Forever programme specifically for protecting local farmland. USE IT: if peninsula farmland is under development pressure, Farmland Forever is the named local route; the trust also monitors existing easements, so it can tell you whether a parcel is already restricted.

trackers.name: Midcoast Conservancy — Lincoln, Knox & Waldo Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an accredited trust covering 24 towns and 450 square miles across Lincoln, Knox and Waldo counties — the Damariscotta Lake, Medomak River and Sheepscot River watersheds — with 16,000+ acres conserved and 56 public preserves. It reopened 71 miles of river and 2,100 acres of pond for migratory fish through 3 dam or barrier projects, and drove the Damariscotta Lake hydrilla eradication from truckloads in 2009 to none found in 2018. USE IT: proof that river-barrier removal and invasive eradication are achievable locally — approach it for the project structure and funding path.

trackers.name: Kennebec Estuary Land Trust — Sagadahoc County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-based trust (est. 1989, formerly the Lower Kennebec Region Land Trust) covering Arrowsic, Bath, Bowdoinham, Dresden, West Bath, Georgetown, Westport Island and Woolwich — conserving and restoring land and water resources through conservation easements, property donation and outright purchase, and working within the Maine Wetlands Protection Coalition alongside state and federal agencies. USE IT: its first easement covered more than 80 acres and 2 miles of shoreline, so shoreline and wetland protection is its established territory.

trackers.name: York Land Trust — York County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a member-supported trust marking 40 years in 2026, conserving land of ecological, historic, scenic, agricultural and cultural significance in the greater York area of Maine's southernmost and second-most populous county — the part of the state under heaviest development pressure. It recently protected 181 acres of forest along the Josias River in Cape Neddick in perpetuity, and won an L.L.Bean Maine Land Trust grant for accessibility work at Near Point Preserve. USE IT: it runs about 90 free public programmes a year, which is an easy way to reach the people who would turn out for a local land fight.

trackers.name: Three Rivers Land Trust — inland York County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded in 2000 by a small group alarmed at the sale of thousands of local acres that were then developed into house lots — which makes it a direct precedent for a community organising against subdivision. It serves the inland York County towns of Acton, Alfred, Lebanon, Sanford/Springvale and Shapleigh, on the Little Ossipee, Salmon Falls and upper Mousam rivers, and has conserved almost 4,000 acres through easements and purchases with trails at 9 preserves, 2 of them wheelchair accessible. USE IT: it states plainly that conservation means bringing people in rather than keeping them out, and works with towns as well as landowners.

trackers.name: Western Foothills Land Trust — Oxford County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: conserves forests, farmland, wetlands and open space in the greater Oxford Hills area of western Maine, with miles of recreation trails for hiking, biking and Nordic skiing. Its Roberts Farm Preserve hosts school district afterschool and weekend ski programmes, and it has taken fee acquisitions such as Staples Woodlands in Oxford — 83.5 acres with about 1,140 feet of river frontage near schools and the downtown, funded through Land for Maine's Future. USE IT: a trust used to assembling LMF-funded purchases of parcels adjacent to schools and village centres.

trackers.name: Moosehead Regional Land Trust — Piscataquis & Somerset Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: conserves and protects the headwaters of the Kennebec and Penobscot watersheds and sustains the tradition of public access to land in the Moosehead region — the large, sparsely settled interior where most land is privately owned working forest and public access rests on custom rather than title. It works alongside the Forest Society of Maine and the Piscataquis County Soil and Water Conservation District. USE IT: where a landowner change threatens traditional access, this is the body that treats that access itself as the thing to be conserved.

trackers.name: Eastern Shore Land Conservancy
trackers.desc: Eastern Shore Land Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in Maryland. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). trackers.name: Maryland Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Maryland’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Maryland, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Maryland and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Maryland Wildlife & Heritage (DNR)
trackers.desc: Maryland’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). trackers.name: EPA Region 3 (Philadelphia)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 3, Philadelphia — the federal environmental regulator covering Maryland. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Maryland, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Northeast Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Northeast Region, Hadley MA — the federal wildlife authority covering Maryland. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Program Open Space (Maryland) — county-allocated land acquisition money
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Maryland's land programme since 1969, funded by a 0.5% STATE REAL ESTATE TRANSFER TAX — so it is not a budget line that competes each year, it flows with property sales. Over 7,100 projects and 422,700 acres. Two arms: STATESIDE buys large tracts by fee simple and conservation easement for State Parks, Forests and wildlife management areas; POS LOCAL funds county and municipal acquisition and development. WHO IT SUITS: the local arm is the one most communities can actually reach. HOW IT DIFFERS, AND THIS IS THE POINT: POS Local funds are ALLOCATED ANNUALLY TO ALL 23 COUNTIES AND BALTIMORE CITY BY FORMULA. Money is already earmarked for your county — what it gets spent on is decided locally, entered in the county's POS Local Annual Program and then sent to the Board of Public Works. So lobby the county, not the state. Separately, the Rural Legacy Program covers 36 locally designated areas where land trusts acquire easements over working landscapes.

trackers.name: Maryland Program Open Space (DNR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Maryland's Program Open Space, funded by the state real-estate transfer tax since 1969, funds land acquisition and conservation easements — its Stateside component acquires large tracts and easements for state parks, forests and wildlife areas, and its Local component and Rural Legacy program give grants to county and municipal governments and to land trusts to plan, acquire and protect recreational and conservation land (422,700+ acres protected). USE IT: work through your county or municipality, or a Rural Legacy land trust, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Montgomery County Agricultural Land Preservation — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Montgomery County has preserved more than 70,000 acres — the highest share of farmland under easement of any county in the nation — through seven stacked programs anchored on the 93,000-acre Agricultural Reserve: the county Agricultural Easement Program buys development rights outright, while Transferable Development Rights and Building Lot Termination easements permanently cap or extinguish residential density on a property. USE IT: landowners facing development pressure can apply to the county Agricultural Easement Program (typically 6–12 months, no state approval needed); communities can cite Ag Reserve zoning and recorded TDR easements when opposing a subdivision.

trackers.name: Baltimore County Land Preservation — Baltimore County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: with nearly 70,000 acres already under easement, Baltimore County's Planning Department runs a county Agricultural Protection Program alongside the state MALPF and Rural Legacy programs, and funds easements and outright purchases itself within five designated Rural Legacy Areas — targeting farm and forest land, stream valleys and reservoir watersheds. USE IT: landowners inside a Rural Legacy Area apply through the land trust that sponsors it (Land Preservation Trust for Piney Run, The Manor Conservancy for Manor, the county itself for the Coastal area); easements can be sold or donated.

trackers.name: Harford County Agricultural Preservation — Harford County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a nationally recognised farmland preservation leader since 1977 with more than 64,000 acres preserved, Harford County runs its own Agricultural Land Preservation Program (HALPP) buying development rights under Chapter 60 of the county code, alongside the state MALPF programme, the Maryland Environmental Trust and the Deer Creek Rural Legacy Area (nearly 67,000 acres of watershed) which the county administers. USE IT: landowners with agricultural or forest land, at least one spare development right and qualifying soils apply competitively through Planning and Zoning; easements are perpetual.

trackers.name: Installment Purchase Program — Frederick County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 2002 and funded by a dedicated share of the county's recordation tax, Frederick County's IPP buys permanent agricultural easements using installment purchase agreements — paying the farmer tax-free interest over 10 to 20 years with a lump-sum principal at the end, which for many families beats a single taxable payout. More than 24,000 acres preserved across 172 properties, alongside the county's MALPF and Critical Farms programmes. USE IT: apply through the Office of Agriculture; you need 50+ acres (or adjacency to protected land), qualifying soils and remaining development rights.

trackers.name: Agricultural & Woodland Preservation — Anne Arundel County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Anne Arundel runs a stack of easement programmes — its own local programme (from 1990, open to parcels of 50+ acres, 6,583 acres protected), the state MALPF programme (5,485 acres), and the Anne Arundel South Rural Legacy Area, a 37,381-acre corridor between the Patuxent and Rhode Rivers where the explicit goals include creating a greenway and extinguishing development rights. Recent easement offers have run $8,000–$10,000 per acre with cash at settlement. USE IT: deadlines differ by programme (MALPF 1 May; local 1 November and 1 April; Rural Legacy 1 December) — landowner interest drives the county's annual capital budget ask, so applying is itself the lobbying.

trackers.name: Rural Legacy Program — Maryland DNR
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): enacted in 1997 explicitly to discourage sprawl, Rural Legacy funds county governments and private land trusts — not the state directly — to buy conservation easements from willing owners inside locally designated Rural Legacy Areas, of which there is at least one in every Maryland county. Over 130,000 acres preserved, with annual awards recently running $15–35 million. USE IT: a local sponsor (your county or a land trust) applies each year to the Rural Legacy Board, and can also apply to expand an existing Rural Legacy Area or designate a brand-new one — so a community can get its landscape onto the map, not just individual parcels.

trackers.name: Maryland Business Entity Search

You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. trackers.name: Chesapeake Legal Alliance — pro bono environmental representation

trackers.name: Great Lakes Environmental Law Center
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Detroit-based environmental-justice law nonprofit providing legal services to frontline communities — disproportionately communities of colour and low-income neighbourhoods — across Wayne County, all of Michigan, and the wider Great Lakes region. Record includes helping shut the Detroit incinerator and challenging air permits (e.g. Stellantis, asphalt plants) alongside residents. For activists in Michigan: a local litigator that practises community lawyering against polluters.

trackers.name: Little Traverse Conservancy
trackers.desc: Little Traverse Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in Michigan. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC)
trackers.desc: The Midwest’s leading public-interest environmental legal advocacy organization. WHO TO ENLIST against polluting facilities, pipelines, factory farms and dirty-energy projects across the region. You CAN: get legal and policy advocacy to challenge projects and permits. For activists: regional legal muscle and clean-energy expertise to fight harmful development. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Michigan Dept. of Environment, Great Lakes & Energy (EGLE)
trackers.desc: Michigan’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Michigan. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Michigan Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)

You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Michigan and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Michigan DNR — Wildlife
trackers.desc: Michigan’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 5 (Chicago)

For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Midwest Region

trackers.name: Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund — DNR acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund, funded by state oil-and-gas mineral royalties, awards grants to local units of government (and the DNR) to acquire land for public recreation and for the protection of environmentally important or scenic land — by law at least 25% of annual funding goes to acquisition (over $1.3B granted since 1976). USE IT: work with your city, county or township to apply for an acquisition grant on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Ottawa County Parks & Open Space — Ottawa County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ottawa County Parks manages over 7,700 acres of parks, dunes, greenways and open space, bought and stewarded with a dedicated voter-approved Parks & Open Space millage renewed for ten years in 2026 — the money buys land and easements outright (the 353-acre Ottawa Sands dune purchase, ongoing Macatawa and Grand River Greenway acquisitions) and is routinely stacked with Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund grants. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel adjoining an existing park or greenway to Park Planning staff; acquisitions go before the Parks and Recreation Commission in public.

trackers.name: Natural Areas Preservation Program (NAPP) — Washtenaw County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 2000 by county ordinance and funded by a countywide quarter-mill NAPP millage (renewed by voters repeatedly), the programme buys natural areas outright for public nature preserves and, since 2010, also buys agricultural conservation easements — with 93% of millage revenue required by ordinance to go to land acquisition rather than overheads. It is run by the Washtenaw County Parks and Recreation Commission and has co-funded dozens of easements held by townships and land trusts. USE IT: landowners nominate their own land for purchase or for a purchase of development rights through the programme's application page.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Kent County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a voluntary county programme that pays farmland owners the difference between their land's unrestricted market value and its value as farmland, in exchange for a permanent deed restriction barring non-agricultural development — in one of Michigan's most agriculturally productive counties (over $231 million of annual output). Values are set by independent appraisal and negotiated farm by farm; the owner keeps title, can still sell the land as farmland, and can still borrow against it. USE IT: farmers facing development pressure apply to the county; the cash typically goes to debt reduction, expansion or generational transfer, which is what keeps the farm operating rather than selling out.

trackers.name: Greenbelt & Bluebelt Program — City of Ann Arbor
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ann Arbor voters passed a 30-year, 0.5-mill Open Space and Parkland Preservation millage in 2003 to buy development rights on farmland and natural areas — mostly OUTSIDE the city limits — protecting nearly 8,000 acres with Washtenaw County and surrounding townships, and in 2024 adding a second 'Bluebelt' boundary covering the Huron River watershed upstream of the city's drinking water intake. USE IT: two features are worth copying. Removing development rights lowers land price, which the city uses deliberately to get beginning farmers onto land; and its buy-protect-sell initiative buys a farm, attaches an easement, then resells it cheaply to income-qualified small farmers who own no land, recycling the proceeds back into the fund.

trackers.name: Mississippi Outdoor Stewardship Trust Fund (MOSTF)

trackers.name: Mississippi Center for Justice
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a nonprofit public interest law centre working statewide on racial and economic justice, with environmental among its listed practice areas alongside civil rights, community development, disaster assistance and housing. It provides free legal representation to low-income Mississippians and communities of color, and combines it with community education — workshops, clinics and presentations — aimed at helping people understand their rights, hold officials accountable and demand transparency. It works through a pro bono network of volunteer lawyers as well as staff attorneys, taking on impact litigation, class actions, policy advocacy and direct representation. USE IT: Mississippi has no dedicated environmental public interest firm, so this is the main route to free counsel for a community facing a polluting or unwanted facility.

trackers.name: County Soil & Water Conservation Districts — Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: under Mississippi's 1938 Soil and Water Conservation Law every county could organise a district, and today THERE IS ONE IN EVERY MISSISSIPPI COUNTY, overseen by the state Soil and Water Conservation Commission. Districts implement conservation practices on farm and forest land, work on erosion and water quality, and coordinate technical assistance from federal, state and local sources. USE IT: Mississippi has no dedicated environmental public interest law firm and few county land programmes, so the conservation district is often the only public body in the county with natural-resource expertise — use it for technical grounding, and pair it with the Mississippi Center for Justice for legal help.

trackers.name: Great Rivers Environmental Law Center (Missouri)

trackers.name: Great Rivers Greenway — St. Louis City, St. Louis County & St. Charles County

trackers.name: Western Environmental Law Center (WELC)

trackers.name: Nebraska's 23 Natural Resources Districts — find yours (NARD)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Nebraska has no county conservation boards — instead it has 23 Natural Resources Districts drawn on river-basin rather than county lines, each run by a locally elected board of directors and charged under state law with twelve areas of responsibility including flood control, soil erosion, groundwater quality and quantity, and recreation. They hold land and water rights, build and manage projects, and are the primary local contact on natural-resource decisions. USE IT: use the interactive map to find the NRD covering your watershed, then take a water-quality, groundwater or floodplain fight to its elected board.

trackers.name: Bold Nebraska — eminent domain and landowner defence
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a citizen advocacy organisation founded in 2010 that builds alliances of farmers, ranchers, Tribal Nations and residents against pipelines and eminent domain taken for private gain — best known for the decade-long fight that helped stop Keystone XL, coordinating public comment drives, tribal resolutions and legal challenges over aquifer risk and easements. It organises landowners into collective bargaining blocs (the Nebraska Easement Action Team model), runs know-your-rights forums for landowners on carbon-pipeline routes across Nebraska, Iowa, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Kansas and Illinois, and points people to specialist condemnation counsel. USE IT honestly: Bold is an organiser, not a law firm, and it has at times negotiated community benefit agreements instead of opposing a project outright.

trackers.name: Natural Resources Districts (NRDs) — elected local resource government
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Nebraska is divided into 23 Natural Resources Districts — multi-purpose LOCAL UNITS OF GOVERNMENT, unique to Nebraska, established in 1972 with boundaries following major river basins rather than county lines, and governed by DIRECTLY ELECTED non-partisan boards. They conserve, protect, develop and manage natural resources, funded by a small share of local property tax (typically 1–2% of what a county collects), and partner with NRCS, state and federal agencies, municipalities and counties. USE IT: because the board is elected and the district follows your watershed, this is the most accessible and most watershed-relevant body of government in Nebraska — attend board meetings, stand for election, and raise land and water threats there.

trackers.name: New Mexico Land Conservancy
trackers.desc: New Mexico Land Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in New Mexico. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Open Space Program — Bernalillo County

trackers.name: Open Space Division — City of Albuquerque

USE IT: the citizen Open Space Advisory Board sets acquisition priorities and also reviews any proposal to sell, lease or build on open space — so it is the body to petition both to protect land and to stop its disposal.

THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC)
trackers.desc: The Southeast’s leading nonprofit environmental law organization. WHO TO ENLIST when a development, highway, pipeline, landfill or polluting plant threatens your area. You CAN: get expert legal representation and advocacy to challenge permits and projects in court — SELC takes major regional cases at no charge to communities. For activists: proven legal firepower that has stopped and reshaped countless Southeastern projects. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: North Carolina Land and Water Fund (NCLWF) — acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the NC Land and Water Fund makes grants to local governments, state agencies and nonprofit conservation organizations — land trusts and watershed groups — to acquire land and easements that protect water quality, ecological diversity, natural areas and historic or military-buffer lands (no match strictly required, though matched projects rank better). USE IT: as a land trust, nonprofit or local government, apply (annual March 1 deadline) to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Wake County Open Space Program — Wake County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by successive voter-approved general obligation bonds, Wake County buys land and conservation easements in targeted conservation areas set out in its Consolidated Open Space Plan, using a voluntary reverse-auction 'Solicitation of Interest' in which landowners offer to sell, donate, or place an easement. Recommendations run through the Open Space and Parks Advisory Committee to the Board of Commissioners. USE IT: landowners can offer a parcel in the annual solicitation; recent projects stacked county open-space and farmland-preservation money with Triangle Land Conservancy easements.

trackers.name: Lands Legacy Program — Orange County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: enacted in 2000 and backed by $10 million in bond money county voters have approved since 1997, Lands Legacy buys land outright for parks and nature preserves and buys or accepts donated conservation easements — over 3,000 acres protected, including 28 working farms and “Forever Wild” easements on stream corridors in the Jordan Lake watershed. Local money has pulled in over $5 million in state and federal grants, and projects run with Triangle Land Conservancy, the Eno River Association and the NC Land and Water Fund. USE IT: every two years the County Commissioners adopt an Action Plan setting acquisition priorities — that adoption is the public moment to get a threatened parcel named.

trackers.name: Floodplain Buyout Program — Mecklenburg County (Charlotte-Mecklenburg Storm Water Services)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a joint county-and-municipal stormwater utility funded by impervious-area fees, which since 1999 has voluntarily bought and demolished more than 450 flood-prone properties, returning 185 acres to undeveloped public open space and greenway — over $67 million invested, an estimated $25 million in damage already avoided and $300 million in future losses prevented. Crucially it sets its own eligibility criteria and can make offers within months of a flood using local fee money, instead of waiting years for FEMA. USE IT: it identifies high-risk properties before floods happen, so ask to be on the priority list early; leaseback arrangements are available case by case.

trackers.name: Mountain Revolving Loan Fund — Conservation Trust for North Carolina
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (bridge finance and the costs nobody funds): CTNC runs revolving loan funds holding several million dollars, lending at minimal interest to North Carolina land trusts so they can buy conservation land and easements in the mountains before their own fundraising closes — and as loans are repaid the money is lent again. A share of the fund is given away each year as grants of up to $25,000 that do NOT have to be repaid, deliberately aimed at the hardest money to raise: surveys, appraisals, attorney fees, project administration and long-term stewardship. USE IT: transaction costs are the usual reason a landowner's intended donation or bargain sale collapses — this is the fund that covers them.

trackers.name: Soil Conservation Districts — elected local political subdivisions

USE IT: the downstream-standards argument it established is useful anywhere a permit is issued upstream or across a state line from the community that will bear the harm.

USE IT: with three seats elected locally and turnout in these races usually tiny, this is one of the most winnable public offices in the state — and a district board is a standing local body that can put soil, water and erosion evidence in front of county decision-makers.

Acquisition services are contracted through the Beaufort County Open Land Trust, and projects are often stacked with South Carolina Conservation Bank grants. USE IT: landowners and communities can bring a parcel to the Rural and Critical Lands Preservation Board, which meets monthly in public.

trackers.name: Charleston County Greenbelt Program — Charleston County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): created when Charleston County voters approved a half-cent transportation sales tax in 2004 (renewed 2016), the Greenbelt Program awards grants through separate Rural and Urban rounds — $134 million awarded so far, protecting well over 24,000 acres, and leveraging more than $200 million in matching public and private money. USE IT: eligible applicants are the county, any municipality in it, county or municipal agencies, federal agencies, and any 501(c)(3) land-conservation or historic-preservation charity empowered to hold land — so a local land trust can carry a community's parcel into the grant round.

trackers.name: Center for Heirs' Property — clearing title to family land
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: heirs' property is land passed down without a will, owned in common by all the heirs with no clear title — roughly 15 million acres across the US, and in the SC Lowcountry mostly land bought or deeded to African American families after Emancipation. It is the single most fragile form of ownership: ANY heir can force a court sale of the whole property, or sell their fractional share to an outside buyer such as a developer, who can then do the same. The Center gives free and low-cost legal services across 22 SC counties (and now East Texas) — title searches, surveys, determination of heirs, quiet title actions, court representation — plus forestry help to make the land earn. USE IT: ring for a free one-hour consultation; they also run family meetings to help relatives reach agreement.

trackers.name: South Carolina Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in South Carolina (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: South Carolina Attorney General
trackers.desc: South Carolina’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in South Carolina. You CAN: file complaints and tips the office can investigate and prosecute; most have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: often the most powerful and reachable ally against a local corporate or official target.

trackers.name: Great Plains Tribal Water Alliance
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a tribal water-protection alliance defending water and sacred lands across the Great Plains — currently fighting uranium mining and in-situ leach mining in the Black Hills (Craven Canyon), presenting expert testimony in permitting hearings and protecting the Missouri River and Lakota cultural sites. For activists in the Dakotas/Black Hills: a frontline Indigenous-led ally on water and extraction fights.

You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. trackers.name: Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC)
trackers.desc: The Midwest’s leading public-interest environmental legal advocacy organization. WHO TO ENLIST against polluting facilities, pipelines, factory farms and dirty-energy projects across the region. You CAN: get legal and policy advocacy to challenge projects and permits. For activists: regional legal muscle and clean-energy expertise to fight harmful development. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: South Dakota Dept. of Agriculture & Natural Resources (DANR)
trackers.desc: South Dakota’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within South Dakota. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: South Dakota Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: South Dakota’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in South Dakota, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of South Dakota and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: South Dakota Game, Fish & Parks
trackers.desc: South Dakota’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 8 (Denver)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 8, Denver — the federal environmental regulator covering South Dakota. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles South Dakota, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Mountain-Prairie Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Mountain-Prairie Region, Lakewood CO — the federal wildlife authority covering South Dakota. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Northern Prairies Land Trust
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a nonprofit land trust (est. 1999) serving South Dakota and Nebraska that protects native prairie, grasslands and wetlands — holding conservation easements (7,000+ acres) that let ranchers keep working the land while permanently preventing its conversion. USE IT: contact them to place a conservation easement on your land, or partner with them to protect a threatened grassland.

trackers.name: South Dakota Agricultural Land Trust (SDALT)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST / WHAT IT DOES: a 501(c)(3) land trust whose mission is conserving South Dakota's agricultural heritage and working landscapes — holding conservation easements that keep ranch and farm land in production and out of subdivision. It has been awarded federal climate-smart agriculture money to fund easement payments on thousands of acres of ranchland near the Black Hills. USE IT honestly: that federal award was among $134 million of conservation money reported frozen or paused in South Dakota in 2025, and these programmes are typically receipt-based, meaning landowners spend their own money first and wait for reimbursement — so confirm what is actually flowing before committing. Listed alongside other state conservation partners on the Dakota Conservation Network.

trackers.name: Conservation districts directory — South Dakota DANR
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the state's directory of South Dakota's conservation districts, together with the State Conservation Commission and the South Dakota Association of Conservation Districts. Districts are the local units that coordinate technical, financial and educational assistance for soil, water and related resources, working with landowners and with NRCS. USE IT: South Dakota has few county land programmes and its state conservation money has been unreliable, so the district is the practical local point of contact — use the directory to find yours, then pair it with the SD Agricultural Land Trust for permanent easement work.

trackers.name: The Land Trust for Tennessee
trackers.desc: The Land Trust for Tennessee — a leading land trust/conservancy in Tennessee. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Tennessee Heritage Conservation Trust Fund (TDEC)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Tennessee's Heritage Conservation Trust Fund, an independent board attached to TDEC, makes grants (subject to appropriation, often matched several-to-one) to local governments, state agencies and nonprofit conservation organizations to acquire land of high conservation value and conservation easements, including urgent action on threatened tracts. USE IT: submit a pre-application, as a land trust, nonprofit or local government, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Local Parks and Recreation Fund (LPRF) — land acquisition grants to counties and cities
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (for your county or town to buy land): Tennessee's LPRF makes grants to local governments for parks, natural areas, greenways, trails and land acquisition, funded from the state real estate transfer tax. Over 70 counties and 90 municipalities have used it. A 50% local match is required BUT can be met with land, volunteer services, materials or equipment rather than cash — which is what puts it within reach of a small town. Counties and municipalities may also issue bonds, by council vote or referendum, to acquire land for parks, trails, watershed protection, floodplain management and farmland. USE IT: pair the in-kind match rule with donated land value or volunteer labour to make a project viable.

trackers.name: Utah LeRay McAllister Working Farm & Ranch Fund (UDAF)

trackers.name: Summit County Open Space & Agricultural Conservation — Summit County

USE IT: any landowner can file a Notice of Interest (no fee) to have a property evaluated against the criteria set by the county's open space advisory committees; the county never asks for payment during the process.

trackers.name: Open Space Trust Fund — Salt Lake County

USE IT: contact the district for technical assistance and for the funding routes available to Franklin County landowners.

USE IT: it publishes board agendas, minutes and requests for bids, so its meetings are a public place to raise a local land or water concern early.

USE IT: the published assessment and action plan are usable evidence about what local natural resources matter and why, when you are contesting a proposal.

trackers.name: Orleans County Natural Resources Conservation District — Orleans County

USE IT: the lakeshore permitting assistance and watershed action plans are the practical entry points for shoreline and water-quality disputes.

trackers.name: Lamoille County Natural Resources Conservation District — Lamoille County
