trackers.name: Industrial Emissions Portal — what the facility actually releases
trackers.desc: IT ANSWERS ‘WHAT IS THIS FACILITY RELEASING, AND HOW MUCH’ — with named sites and quantities, not a description of a regulator. The Industrial Emissions Portal gives public access to environmental data from industrial facilities across EU Member States, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and the UK. The Industrial Emissions Portal Regulation (IEPR) replaces the earlier E-PRTR Regulation and implements the Kyiv Protocol on Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers — binding since 8 October 2009, the only legally binding international instrument on PRTRs, and a protocol to the Aarhus Convention. THE MECHANISM IS REPUTATIONAL, AND THE UNECE SAYS SO OPENLY: though it regulates information about pollution rather than pollution directly, it is expected to exert downward pressure ‘as no company will want to be identified as among the biggest polluters’. That is the campaign use — the register produces a ranked, official, quotable list. THE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT, AND IT PREVENTS A FALSE CONCLUSION: an installation not shown on a PRTR is either not an industrial activity covered by it, OR has not reached the stated pollutant-specific thresholds. Absence from the register is NOT evidence of no pollution — check the activity list and thresholds before relying on an absence. TWO DEFINITIONS THAT HELP: ‘the public’ includes natural or legal persons and their associations, organizations or groups, so an unincorporated community group qualifies; and a ‘facility’ is installations on the same site OR ON ADJOINING SITES under one operator — which matters where a plant has been split across parcels. As a scale example the UK register covers 91 pollutants back to 2007. IF YOU NEED ANOTHER COUNTRY: prtr.unece.org keeps a PRTR Global list of national registers, maintained by the OECD Working Party on PRTRs with UNECE, alongside CEC Taking Stock for North America and the NGO-built Blue Map Database in China — where a government has not built a register, that is the precedent for one built anyway.

trackers.name: INECE — not where you report, but how you find who enforces
trackers.desc: READ THIS BEFORE YOU WRITE TO THEM: INECE IS NOT A COMPLAINT ROUTE. Its members are inspectors, prosecutors, regulators, parliamentarians and judges — a community cannot report a violation to INECE. It is worth an entry for three other reasons. FIRST, THE REGIONAL NETWORKS ARE A ROUTING DEVICE: INECE names AECEN (Asian Environmental Compliance and Enforcement Network), AELERT (Australasian Environmental Law Enforcement and Regulators network) and RedLaFiCA (Red Latinoamericana de Fiscalización y Cumplimiento Ambiental) as part of the network — if you do not know which body enforces in your country, the regional network is a shorter list to search than the world. SECOND, ITS CITIZEN-SCIENCE POSITION IS LEVERAGE: INECE runs an ongoing webinar series on ‘how can citizen and community science contribute to environmental compliance and enforcement?’ — that the global network of enforcers is itself asking that question is citable when an agency dismisses community-gathered evidence. THIRD, IT SHOWS WHAT KIND OF BODY TO LOOK FOR: its named members include a superintendency, a protection agency, a ministry and a supreme court — which is why searching for ‘EPA’ by name fails outside the US. The Secretariat is the Environmental Law Institute, not a government; it keeps an online library of compliance and enforcement resources and runs training — a recent series on environmental and social impact assessment drew 161 people from 31 countries. Founded 1989, covering administrative, civil, criminal and judicial enforcement, with support from UNEP, the World Bank, the European Commission and the OECD. BE AWARE OF THE MEMBERSHIP WALL: members have exclusive access to INECE materials and capacity-building programmes. IN THIS COUNTRY: The Scottish Environment Protection Agency is named as a current member — note the enforcement body is devolved, not UK-wide.

trackers.name: Aarhus costs caps — £5,000 is a starting point, not a ceiling
trackers.desc: THE NUMBERS DECIDE WHETHER A CHALLENGE IS POSSIBLE. Under the environmental costs protection regime in CPR Part 46, the maximum an unsuccessful claimant can be ordered to pay is capped by default at £5,000 for an individual and £10,000 for an organisation, with the defendant's liability for your costs capped at £35,000. CPR 46.24(2) defines an Aarhus Convention claim as one by members of the public, by judicial or statutory review, against a body exercising public functions, within article 9(1), 9(2) or 9(3). ADD CLAIMANTS RATHER THAN AVOID THEM: under CPR 46.26(4) the protection applies to each claimant individually and may not be exceeded irrespective of the number of receiving parties — though a ‘shared claimant’ cap has been under consideration, so check the current rule. THE TRAP: THE CAP IS NOT FIXED. A hybrid regime lets the defendant apply to vary it using financial information you provide, and interested parties may apply too — applications that have almost universally served to increase it. £5,000 is a starting point, not a ceiling, and your own disclosure is the material used to raise it; the court will have regard to any financial support any person has provided or is likely to provide, so crowdfunding is visible to the court. CITE NORTHERN IRELAND when resisting an increase: there the claimant's cap can only be varied downwards and the defendant's only upwards. THE PROVISION ALMOST NOBODY KNOWS: where the court is satisfied an injunction is necessary to prevent significant environmental damage and to preserve the factual basis of the proceedings, that weighs in whether to require a cross-undertaking in damages from a member of the public — the cross-undertaking is normally what makes an injunction impossible for a community, so this is the most valuable provision here. Cite it when seeking interim relief. SCOPE: protection covers the whole claim, not just the qualifying part — White v Plymouth City Council [2024] EWHC, contempt proceedings over tree felling, so held; the same conclusion as Heather Hill in Ireland, reached separately. But private claims are outside it — CPR 46.24 covers review only, and SSCLG v Venn [2014] EWCA Civ 1539 records that the court cannot remedy that flaw by discretion, so private nuisance gets no protection. AND THERE ARE NO SEPARATE CAPS FOR THE PERMISSION AND SUBSTANTIVE STAGES (R (CPRE Kent) v SSCLG [2019] EWCA Civ 1230) — losing early can cost much the same as losing late. Planning JR must be brought promptly and within six weeks.

trackers.name: Aarhus Compliance Committee — one person may bring the State itself
trackers.desc: THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS MAP BY WHICH ONE PERSON CAN BRING A STATE ITSELF BEFORE AN INTERNATIONAL BODY over environmental decision-making. Under Decision I/7 (2002), paragraphs 18–24, communications may be brought by one or more members of the public concerning any Party's compliance — no organisation, no accreditation, no minimum number. The ACCC is a quasi-judicial body reporting to the Meeting of the Parties. THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD PART: YOU DO NOT HAVE TO EXHAUST DOMESTIC REMEDIES. Paragraph 21 says the Committee takes account of any available domestic remedy unless its application is unreasonably prolonged or obviously ineffective. What you must do is state whether steps have been taken and, if not, why not — a section of the form, not a bar to entry. WHAT MAKES IT INADMISSIBLE: anonymity, abuse of the right, being manifestly unreasonable including de minimis, incompatibility, or concerning a non-Party or a State that opted out — and no State has opted out. The only one most people risk is ‘de minimis’: frame it as a systemic failure of information, participation or access to justice, not a complaint about one permit. PRACTICALITIES THAT DECIDE WHETHER IT LANDS: there is a required format, and cut-off dates tied to meetings — as a worked example, communications received by 4 May 2026 were for the 15 and 18 June 2026 meeting, provided they were complete, in format, and needed no translation. Check the current cut-off; missing it costs a cycle. Submit in English, French or Russian — the secretariat translates, but needing translation can push you past a cut-off. Send copies, not originals. AND KNOW THIS BEFORE YOU FILE: once preliminary admissibility is determined the case gets a number and BECOMES PUBLIC — there is a confidentiality section on the form. The process runs receipt → admissibility → response by the Party → draft findings → public hearing → final findings and recommendations. Address: Aarhus Convention Secretariat, UNECE, Palais des Nations, Geneva. CONFIRM YOUR STATE IS A PARTY before relying on this — this entry is recorded here on the basis that the state is bound by the Kyiv Protocol to the Convention, which implies but does not prove Party status.

trackers.name: Espoo points of contact — a named official, and ‘were you notified?’
trackers.desc: A NAMED OFFICIAL, A DIRECT EMAIL, AND A QUESTION WITH A DOCUMENTARY ANSWER. The UNECE publishes the points of contact regarding notification under article 3 of the Espoo Convention on EIA in a transboundary context: notifications of activities likely to cause significant adverse transboundary impact shall be transmitted to the relevant points of contact. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR AN ORDINARY LAND CASE: if a project sits near a border, the affected country's point of contact should have been notified — so ask both points of contact whether notification was given. It is a cheap, precise question, and failure to notify is a procedural defect in the consent. The list gives each Party's named official, department, postal address, telephone and email: Czechia's sits in the Department of EIA and Integrated Prevention at the Ministry of the Environment; Denmark's is the Agency for Green Transition and Aquatic Environment using the functional address espoo@sgav.dk; Croatia's is a Director at the Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development; Canada's is the President of the Impact Assessment Agency. PREFER A FUNCTIONAL ADDRESS WHERE ONE IS LISTED — named officials move. AND NOTE A ROUTING PATTERN: some Parties route notification through their Ministry for Foreign Affairs c/o their Permanent Mission in Geneva rather than an environment ministry — where that is so, the environment ministry may not hold the file and the foreign-ministry route is the correct one. A SECOND DIRECTORY, AND A SECOND ROUTE TO THE SAME DOCUMENT: the EEA publishes a list of Eionet national focal points covering 32 member countries and 8 cooperating countries (Albania, Bosnia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine). Data are reported upwards — from stakeholder, to competent authority, to the EEA, to the Commission — so if your national authority has reported something, the EEA holds it too. Where a national body is unresponsive or its figures look wrong, the same data sits one level up in a body with no stake in the local decision. CONFIRM YOUR COUNTRY APPEARS ON THE LIST before relying on it. SCOPE: Espoo governs transboundary notification and Eionet governs data reporting — for the domestic EIA procedure itself, see the EIA Directive entry recorded separately.

trackers.name: The Architectural Heritage Fund — lends the money to buy the building (UK)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a registered charity founded in 1976, and by its own account the UK's only specialist lender for charities and social enterprises working on historic buildings. It has put £135 million of loan offers and £40 million of grants into community-led regeneration of historic buildings and places. 3 Spital Yard, London E1 6AQ. USE IT: it funds the whole arc, and the early stages are the ones nobody realises are fundable. Project Viability Grants cover testing whether reuse is possible at all — condition surveys, valuation, even help setting your organisation up. Project Development Grants cover architects' drawings, fundraising, business planning and acquiring the building itself. Then loans for the capital works once you own it or hold a long lease. Its Heritage Development Trust programme funds charities and social enterprises specifically to acquire and repurpose vacant or at-risk historic buildings, with twelve new trusts across the UK receiving £55,000 to £70,000 a year each. A worked example from its own pages: Tyne & Wear Building Preservation Trust turned a row of Georgian merchants' houses once threatened with demolition into a music venue, coffee shop and bar. THE ELIGIBILITY TRAP, AND IT IS THE WHOLE GAME: grants go to not-for-private-profit organisations or the lowest tiers of local government, and loans go to formally constituted incorporated charities, community businesses or social enterprises whose members have limited liability. An unincorporated residents' group cannot apply. If your building is at risk and you have not yet constituted, that is the first task, not the last — and the viability grant will help pay for it. The building should be listed or in a conservation area, though it will consider unlisted buildings outside one where you can show special significance to the community. ALSO USEFUL: it publishes its grant and loan data openly through 360Giving, so you can see what it has actually funded near you before you write.

trackers.name: SAVE Britain's Heritage — takes casework against demolition (UK)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a campaigning charity formed in 1975 by architectural historians and writers, which does casework rather than only publishing. It co-ordinates responses to major planning applications affecting historic buildings and places, and where it identifies a case it can actively intervene in, it writes in support of listing applications, opposes demolition plans, and contacts conservation officers to raise concerns or propose solutions. It has asked the Secretary of State to call in applications for public inquiry — the Liverpool Welsh Streets inquiry, where 440 homes faced demolition, is the case it counts among its biggest wins. 0207 253 3500, office@savebritainsheritage.org. THE TACTIC IT TEACHES, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES DEMOLITION CASES: a developer will produce viability figures showing restoration is impossibly expensive, and engineers' or surveyors' reports saying the building is structurally unsound. SAVE's position is blunt — very few old buildings are so unsound they cannot be saved, and many so-called expert reports simply provide the answer the commissioner wanted. You must obtain an independent architect, engineer or surveyor experienced with old buildings, and SAVE says the national amenity societies can often suggest local professionals willing to help, sometimes voluntarily. That is the request to make in your first call. IT ALSO BACKS ALTERNATIVES, NOT JUST OBJECTIONS: with the Victorian Society it submitted its own rival planning application for Smithfield General Market, built on a business plan from the firm behind Camden Lock and Spitalfields. A credible counter-scheme beats an objection. ONE CAVEAT IT STATES ITSELF: its Buildings at Risk register is compiled from public sources and from local residents, and SAVE does not independently verify the entries. Check details before relying on them — and note that you can put a building onto it.

trackers.name: Environmental Law Foundation — free counsel and technical experts (UK)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a national charity, registered 1045918 and founded in 1992, whose whole purpose is securing free legal help for ordinary people and communities facing environmental threats. It has an in-house team and a national network of more than 150 pro bono barristers, solicitors and technical experts, and it answers over 350 requests for legal support a year — help it describes as otherwise inaccessible or unaffordable. It also runs a clinical network with around twenty UK university law schools whose students work on its casework under supervision. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A LAW FIRM HERE: the network includes technical experts, not only lawyers. A community facing a 1,200-page environmental statement needs someone who can read the ecology before it needs anyone who can read the law, and this is one of the few places in the UK where both come through one door and neither sends an invoice. It also helps groups engage with consultations and negotiations with regulators, corporations and government, not only with litigation. WHAT TO EXPECT: it secures free initial advice and support — treat that as the shape of it rather than open-ended representation, and expect the pro bono professional to define what they will take on. Roughly 350 requests a year across the whole United Kingdom is the throughput, so approach early with the documents rather than late with the anger. Its chair since 2022 is a silk practising in environmental, planning and public law, which tells you the calibre available and also why the queue exists.

trackers.name: Planning Aid England — free planners for community groups (England only)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Royal Town Planning Institute's volunteer service, staffed by chartered planners. Two things are on offer and they are different sizes. A free email advice service for anyone, at planningaid.co.uk, where a qualified planner answers an enquiry — treat it as roughly a quarter of an hour of a professional's attention, which is enough to tell you whether your objection is aimed at the right thing. And, for eligible groups, bespoke casework passed to a chartered volunteer, plus free training: a half-day overview of the planning system, and specific help with representations on the Local Plan, responding to a planning application, or appealing a decision. THE ELIGIBILITY BAR: the casework and training are aimed at communities in areas of high multiple deprivation and groups not traditionally engaged with the planning system, and the RTPI reserves the right to decline or limit what it offers. The route in is the email service first — if you qualify for more, the case is passed on from there. TWO WARNINGS WORTH THE SPACE. It is England only. Planning Aid Scotland, Planning Aid Wales and Planning Aid for London are separate charities, and in Northern Ireland the not-for-profit Community Places provides free planning advice; contacting the wrong one costs weeks. And the service has two hats: alongside community advice, it supplies neutral facilitator support to local planning authorities. The advice line is for you; that other line is for the council. Ask which one you are speaking to.

trackers.name: Joint Committee of the National Amenity Societies — six bodies already notified of your demolition
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: six national organisations which local planning authorities in England and Wales must notify of any application to demolish a listed building, or to alter one where the works include demolishing any part of it. They are already being told about your case, whether or not anyone in the community has contacted them. The six are the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (pre-1720 buildings, repair methods and craft technique), Historic Buildings & Places (formerly the Ancient Monuments Society, founded 1924, buildings of all types and periods including undesignated ones), the Council for British Archaeology (particularly the archaeology of standing and buried structures), the Georgian Group (1700–1840), the Victorian Society (1840–1914 including Edwardian) and the Twentieth Century Society (1914 onwards). The Gardens Trust is the equivalent statutory consultee for designed historic landscapes. WHAT A COMMUNITY DOES WITH THIS: send the case to casework@jcnas.org.uk, which routes it to all six, and then check the public casework database to see which of them was notified and whether a conservation adviser has picked it up. The Council for British Archaeology runs that database on the Joint Committee's behalf and it links through to the local authority's own pages. You can see, without asking anyone, whether the society covering your building's period has your application in front of it. MANAGE THE EXPECTATION: the societies say plainly that they have limited resources and cannot take up every case. The Georgian Group alone is notified of many thousands a year. Being notified is not being represented. What moves a case up the list is a specific account of why the fabric of an important historic building is threatened, sent directly to the relevant society as well as through the portal. Note also the deliberate overlaps in their date ranges: a building altered across periods can legitimately interest more than one of them, and two societies objecting is stronger than one.

trackers.name: The Georgian Group — casework on 1700–1840 buildings and landscapes (England and Wales)
trackers.desc: WHO TO CALL: a conservation organisation founded in 1937 and a statutory consultee in the planning process in England and Wales since 1971, on proposals to alter or demolish listed buildings dating wholly or partly from between 1700 and 1840, and on planned landscapes of that period. Local planning authorities are required to consult it, and it is notified of many thousands of applications a year. TWO PRACTICAL THINGS IT PUBLISHES. It offers pre-application advice, which means a community that knows a scheme is coming can get an expert view before the application lands rather than after — request it through casework@jcnas.org.uk. And you can check the public database yourself: open your case, and a green tick beside the Georgian Group under notified organisations means it has reached a conservation adviser. Allow a few days for logging. WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ITS LIMITS, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART: it has limited resources and cannot take up all cases. The way in is to write to it directly at its consult address if you believe the fabric of an important historic building is threatened by neglect or by significant alteration — neglect included, which is worth knowing where an owner is running a building down towards a demolition case. Its casework is part-funded by Historic England and by Cadw, which is also why it covers Wales.

trackers.name: Scottish Land Fund — grants of £5,000 to £1 million to buy the land itself
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: grants of between £5,000 and £1 million to community-led organisations to buy land or land assets, funded by the Scottish Government and delivered in partnership by The National Lottery Community Fund and Highlands and Islands Enterprise. It also funds the planning and development work before a purchase. Between 2015 and 2024 it awarded over £50 million to more than 300 community organisations; in 2002 it helped fund the community buyout of the Isle of Gigha towards a £4 million purchase. Across 121 candidates in this file, nothing else pays a community a seven-figure sum to become the owner. WHO CAN APPLY: organisations in urban and rural Scotland that are community-led, community-controlled and defined by a geographic area, and non-profit distributing — voluntary organisations, social enterprises, community councils among them. Two-stage application. You work with a named Scottish Land Fund Adviser at Highlands and Islands Enterprise to shape the project before applying, and that advice is free. Enquiries to The National Lottery Community Fund on 0300 123 7110 or advicescotland@tnlcommunityfund.org.uk. WHAT IT WANTS TO SEE: that ownership will give the community a stronger role in and control over its own development, and that it will end up owning well managed, financially sustainable land or buildings. Applications showing significant benefit for the community as a whole are prioritised. So the case is economic and social, not conservation — the same reframing the community foundations and the community land trusts in this file require. TIMING IS THE RISK: the fund pauses. Applications were paused as a parliamentary term ended, with uncertainty over the following year, and it has run heavily oversubscribed with an estimated 150 projects waiting. Check whether it is open before building a plan around it. AND THE CONTEXT A SCOTTISH GROUP SHOULD KNOW: the Scottish Land Commission has reported wealthy corporations and forestry companies competing for land as a main driver of sharp price rises, making it harder for younger farmers, environmental groups and communities to afford land. You are bidding in that market. The main organisation promoting and supporting community ownership is Community Land Scotland, and Development Trusts Association Scotland runs a free Scotland-wide adviser-led support service for groups taking on assets.

trackers.name: Community Ownership Support Service (COSS) — free adviser at every stage (Scotland)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: an adviser-led service covering the whole of Scotland, established 2011, funded by the Scottish Government and run by the Development Trusts Association Scotland. It supports community groups to manage, lease or own publicly owned land and buildings — through the Community Asset Transfer process, and it also supports groups pursuing Community Right to Buy. One-to-one adviser support at every stage of the asset transfer process, access to expert help, network and training opportunities, comprehensive online resources — free, and you do not need to be a member of DTAS to use it. WHY THAT LAST CLAUSE MATTERS: almost every support body in this file requires a community to join something, incorporate, or find a member organisation to sponsor it. This one does not. A group that formed last month can pick up the phone. IT ALSO TRAINS: courses for community groups on business planning, governance and facilities management — which is what a group needs before it owns anything, and it delivers CPD to councils and other relevant authorities on asset transfer, so it is trusted on both sides of the table. ONE SPECIFIC PROGRAMME WORTH KNOWING: New Futures – Former Places of Worship, funded by Historic Environment Scotland and the National Lottery Heritage Fund, helps community groups consider taking ownership of former places of worship, in response to the unprecedented number due for disposal over the coming years. If the threatened building in your village is a church, there is a named programme for exactly that. AND THE ADVICE FROM A GROUP THAT DID IT: the Action Porty case records that the community offered to buy at market value first, took about five months from initial plans to completion, and its own advice to others is to be aware of the lengthy timescales and the level of work, and to register an interest in the land early — or at least minute it.

trackers.name: Community Land Scotland — 140 community landowners you can ask what it cost them
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: the national representative body for community landowners in Scotland, bringing together over 140 member organisations — from community-owned estates in the Highlands and Islands to urban community hubs. Its stated work is supporting communities to take control of land and assets, and shaping national policy on community ownership. WHY A COMMUNITY ANYWHERE SHOULD CARE, NOT ONLY IN SCOTLAND: this is a membership of 140 groups that have already bought the land. They know what it cost, how long it took, what the valuation fight was like, what the lawyer charged and what went wrong afterwards. Across 123 candidates in this file, that is the largest concentration of communities that have actually completed a purchase, and the representative body is the way to reach them. IT ALSO WORKS ON WHAT COMES AFTER: its Natural Capital Community Partnerships work is about how natural capital can support local priorities — which is the question a community faces once it owns land and has to pay for its upkeep, and which almost nothing else in this file addresses. USE IT WITH THE OTHER TWO SCOTTISH ENTRIES: the Scottish Land Fund pays for the purchase, COSS advises through the process, and this is the body of people who have been through it.

trackers.name: Plunkett UK — advisers who get rural communities to owning the asset
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: a national charity supporting rural community businesses across the UK, promoting the community ownership model for over a hundred years, based at The Quadrangle, Woodstock, Oxfordshire. It provides specialist business advice at every stage — from the initial idea and start-up to long after opening — and receives around 500 new enquiries a year. It has had over 250 community groups working with it to secure their local pub and a further 200 businesses at various stages of transferring to community ownership. THE NUMBER THAT SHOULD SHAPE YOUR PLAN, AND IT IS ITS OWN: of those 500 annual enquiries, only one in eight reaches trading status, with lack of premises a common challenge. No other entry in this file publishes its own failure rate. Take it as calibration rather than discouragement: the groups that succeed are the ones that get advice early and solve the premises question first. WHAT IT CAN FUND AS WELL AS ADVISE: under programme funding it has offered step-by-step adviser support plus grants covering the things a community cannot otherwise pay for at the start — surveying or consulting the community to assess support for the idea, funding a valuation of a building or site, setting up a legal structure, or paying for a professional consultant. A valuation and a legal structure are exactly what stand between a village and a credible offer. WHERE IT WORKS: UK-wide, with tailored support for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland including delivery in Welsh, and regional programmes funded by combined authorities and trusts. Contact its Community Business Team. WHAT IT IS NOT: rural community business is its subject — pubs, shops, cafes, community spaces. It is not a conservation body and not a law firm. If the threatened asset is a building or a business that anchors a village, this is the right door; if it is a field, use the land entries in this file instead.

trackers.name: Shared Assets — helps a community find the land, approach the owner and negotiate the deal
trackers.desc: WHAT IT WILL ACTUALLY DO, IN ITS OWN WORDS: help groups identify land, engage with landowners, identify appropriate tenure — ownership, lease or licence — and negotiate the sale or rent, including supporting community asset transfer processes. That sequence is the whole transaction, and across 125 candidates in this file almost nothing else offers to sit on a community's side of a land negotiation. It also does land access options with location and mapping, business plans, governance and legal structures, and support with incorporation. WHO IT WORKS WITH: it uses the phrase Common Good Land User for any community group managing land for public benefit — growing food or timber, health and wellbeing activities, woodlands, parks, sports facilities. A community interest company, distributed across the UK, surplus reinvested. Contact addresses for individual staff are published on its site. TRACK RECORD WORTH KNOWING: since 2017 it has supported Big Local areas taking on ownership or management of land, buildings and green spaces — a programme that gave 150 underserved communities in England £1 million each over ten years to spend as residents decide. It ran Making Local Woods Work for woodland social enterprises, and it provided support to groups applying to the Community Ownership Fund alongside Locality. READ ITS OWN WARNING BEFORE YOU START: it states plainly that we live in a system treating land as a commodity and a store of wealth, driving up prices of housing and agricultural land, and that however innovative the community-led models it works with are, they will always be disadvantaged by that system. That is an unusually honest thing for an advisory body to publish, and a community should plan around it rather than be surprised by it. ONE CONFLICT TO CHECK: it also sells services to landowners, local authorities and developers, and names previous clients including county and London borough councils, a major property group, a development corporation and the National Trust. Name the site and the other side in your first email.

trackers.name: Ecological Land Cooperative — buys farmland and holds it in perpetuity for farming
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a not-for-profit community benefit cooperative that purchases agricultural land, plans a cluster of usually three ecological smallholdings on it, wins the planning permission, and then sells on a 150-year lease or rents to new entrants at an affordable rate — holding the land in perpetuity for ecological agriculture and monitoring each holding against a binding whole-site ecological management plan. Sites established since 2013 across England and Wales: Greenham Reach in Mid Devon, Arlington in East Sussex on a former maize field, and a third on the Gower. It describes itself as the only organisation in England offering affordable residential smallholdings for ecological land users. WHY THE CLUSTER MODEL MATTERS TO A COMMUNITY: buying a larger site gives a lower price per acre, and the cost of infrastructure, the planning application and the ecological monitoring is spread across several holdings. That is how the numbers work at all — and it is a model a community facing the sale of a farm could propose rather than simply oppose. TWO ROUTES IN THAT ARE NOT MONEY. It invites landowners to gift land to it, with a named coordinator and a published FAQ on how that works — so an owner who wants a field kept in farming forever has somewhere to send it. And it raises capital through community share offers; one round brought its investor count to 111 with £326,350 between equity and loans. THE FIGURES IT PUBLISHES, WHICH ARE THE ARGUMENT: between 2000 and 2010 new entrants accounted for just 4% of agricultural land purchasers; the ratio of farm purchase price to average agricultural income exceeds twenty to one; the average age of the British farmer is now around 59; and County Farms have declined as councils sell them off. A community arguing that a farm should stay a farm has its case in those four numbers. WHAT IT IS NOT: it works on agricultural land in England and Wales, for agroecological livelihoods. Not a conservation buyer, not a funder for campaigns, not a law firm.

trackers.name: Development Trusts Association Wales — the Welsh route to taking on land and buildings
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an independent practitioner-based membership organisation supporting development trusts across Wales, and one of its three core areas is community ownership of assets — supporting communities considering taking on land and buildings across Wales, or developing those already in community ownership. It says plainly that although it is a membership body for development trusts it does not only serve members, and runs programmes benefiting the wider third sector in Wales. WHAT IT WILL DO: support for community asset transfer and for community asset development and ownership; feasibility studies; peer-to-peer learning and action learning sets; and support to consider and access grants, social investment and loans, community share issues and crowdfunding, plus investment-readiness support and risk analysis before a group takes an asset on. That last item is what stops a community acquiring something it cannot afford to keep. IT REACHES BEYOND WALES: it draws on its development trust association partners in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, describing a combined pool of more than 800 practitioners. So a Welsh group gets the Scottish and English experience through one door — and Northern Ireland has its own association in that same family, which is the route for a group there. THE CONTEXT A WELSH COMMUNITY SHOULD KNOW: the Welsh Government has identified community asset transfer as something public bodies in Wales should support, and links it to the well-being goals of the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 — useful language when writing to a council. But a Senedd committee report and two 2022 studies found Welsh communities among the least empowered on this island for community ownership, and Welsh Government research records lengthy transfer processes, poor communication during them, and post-transfer difficulty sustaining assets that generate no income. Plan for the running costs before the handover, not after. ALSO IN WALES: Cwmpas, the country's community-led housing hub, has argued for community ownership of land and assets as a route to affordable housing and proposed a commission on it, which the Welsh Government accepted in principle.

trackers.name: Development Trusts NI — asks public bodies for the land on your behalf (Northern Ireland)
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: established 2010, member-led, with over 100 member organisations — community development bodies, local enterprise agencies, arts and culture organisations, sports clubs and individuals. Locality's sister network in Northern Ireland, and the third sector partner to the Department for Communities in delivering its Community Asset Transfer policy, which is the formal position that makes the rest of this work. WHAT IT WILL DO THAT ALMOST NOTHING ELSE HERE DOES: it works with community and voluntary organisations to identify buildings and land that could meet their needs, and it proactively issues open calls to public bodies for surplus and under-utilised assets. A community does not have to wait for a public body to advertise something — there is an organisation whose job is to go and ask on the sector's behalf. If your group has a proposal or an identified need, that is the approach to make. IT IS HONEST ABOUT WHAT DECIDES SUCCESS: its own account names finance, capacity building and negotiation skills as the three things that determine whether a transfer completes, and it notes Northern Ireland's particular difficulty of divided and disadvantaged communities. It runs training, including facilities management courses, and a Department-funded Community Wealth Building programme. WHAT IT IS CURRENTLY ASKING FOR, which tells a group what does not yet exist: a £70 million Northern Ireland Community Ownership Fund — £57m capital for community-owned buildings and land, £10m revenue for sustaining projects, £3m for early-stage work — and a Community Rights and Empowerment Bill giving rights to buy, own, participate and challenge. Northern Ireland has no community right to buy at present. A group there should plan on negotiation and asset transfer rather than on a statutory route. WHAT IT IS NOT: not a land buyer itself, not a funder, not a law firm. It represents, advises and advocates, and it is the door for Northern Ireland, which had nothing in this file before.

trackers.name: Locality — 2,000 community organisations, and the new Community Right to Buy (England)
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: the national membership network for community organisations in England, with 2,000 members, providing specialist advice, peer learning, resources and campaigns. It has worked with over 80 local authorities. Its own description of itself is the national experts in community ownership and community asset transfer, and its consultancy list is precise about what that means: negotiating community asset transfer from local authorities and others; helping organisations exercise Community Rights to Bid over Assets of Community Value; business planning for community assets covering both capital and revenue phases; and access to blended finance including grant, loan, community share capital and discounted land and property through asset transfers. THE CHANGE A COMMUNITY IN ENGLAND NEEDS TO KNOW ABOUT: following its campaigning, the government has introduced a Community Right to Buy and a Community Right to Buy Fund as part of the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act, replacing the Right to Bid from the Localism Act 2011. The new power gives communities a right of first refusal when important local buildings and spaces come up for sale — but only if the asset has already been registered as an Asset of Community Value. Register the asset before it is for sale, not after. That single sequencing point decides whether the right is available at all. AND THE ROUTE THAT COSTS NOTHING: if the asset is owned by your local authority, talk to them first — they may transfer it to a community organisation at a discount, and many councils publish a community asset transfer policy. Locality notes that with local government reorganisation and funding pressure many authorities are considering selling assets, which cuts both ways: more is coming to market, and more councils are open to transferring rather than selling. WHAT IT IS NOT: membership and paid consultancy, not free legal aid and not a buyer. It also advises local authorities, so name the council and the asset in your first contact.

trackers.name: Common grazings committees and the Scottish Crofting Federation — 550,000 hectares
trackers.desc: WHAT THE COMMON GRAZINGS ARE: land over which one or more crofters hold a legal right to graze livestock, and often other rights — cutting peat and thatching material for domestic use, gathering seaweed for the croft, planting trees. There are around 900 common grazings covering roughly 500,000 to 550,000 hectares in the Highlands and Islands — about two thirds of all croft land. Each has its own regulations administered by a grazings committee and approved by the Crofting Commission, with a clerk who keeps the records, calls meetings and handles shareholders' money. WHY A CROFTING COMMUNITY IS ALREADY ORGANISED: the committee manages the rights of all crofters in the common grazing, can create or amend regulations, carries out maintenance or replaces fixed equipment with the ability to apply for financial assistance, manages the grazings finances, allocates unused shares seasonally, and reports to the Commission every five years. If your ground is a common grazing there is an existing statutory body with money, regulations and standing — and if it is out of office, that is the first thing to fix. THE CONSENT ROUTE WORTH KNOWING: for new uses, shareholders develop a proposal, the grazings committee puts it to the landlord, who consents — possibly with reasonable conditions — or refuses; the matter then goes to the Crofting Commission for decision, appealable to the Scottish Land Court. Guidance also notes that an owner's refusal of consent may be challenged in the Land Court, and that if consent is not forthcoming within six weeks of an application it is treated accordingly. WHO TO JOIN: the Scottish Crofting Federation, set up in 1985 as the Scottish Crofters Union, established and run by crofters themselves, working through advocacy, training, representation and support, and engaging with government at local, national and international level. Individual membership starts at £38 a year. AND THE LAW HAS JUST MOVED: the Crofting and Scottish Land Court Bill passed at Holyrood on 24 March 2026 — strengthening the role of grazings committees, restricting the separation of crofts from their associated grazing rights without approval, giving crofters more influence over how their land is used, updating the Commission's powers to safeguard croft land from neglect, and merging the Scottish Land Court and the Lands Tribunal for Scotland into a single body.

trackers.name: Foundation for Common Land and the Open Spaces Society — registered commons in England and Wales
trackers.desc: TWO BODIES, TWO JOBS. The Foundation for Common Land, a registered charity since 2013, helps communities better manage common land, represents commoners to policy-makers and runs training; its supporters include commoners' associations and federations. It publishes a common land toolkit covering, among other things, setting up and running an Association and identifying and recording public goods such as biodiversity and archaeology — which is the practical manual for a community that has rights and no organisation. The Open Spaces Society describes itself as the guardian of all common land in England and Wales and, crucially, states that it is notified of all applications for works on, and exchanges of, common land. An organisation that automatically sees every application affecting a common is the nearest thing in this file to an early warning system, and it campaigns on individual commons. WHY THE GROUND IS OFTEN ALREADY PROTECTED, and these are the figures to quote: over 34% of British commons are designated Sites of Special Scientific Interest, and in England over 59% of common land is SSSI. Over 28% of English common land is in an AONB; some 45% of common land in Wales and 48% in England lies within National Parks. Registered common land in Wales alone is around 175,000 hectares, about 8.5% of the country. WHAT THE PUBLIC ALREADY HAS: the Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000 extends public access rights to all registered common land in England and Wales — walking, sightseeing, birdwatching, climbing — though not cycling, riding, driving or camping, and many commons carry additional higher rights. WHERE TO CHECK: ownership and rights are listed in the Commons Register, held by the commons registration authority — in Wales each of the 22 local authorities, which also offer support and advice and are the first point of contact for most common land queries. Rights and land had to be registered under the Commons Registration Act 1965; the Commons Act 2006 now governs. Note the exceptions: Part I of the 2006 Act applies to all common land in England other than Epping Forest and the Forest of Dean.

trackers.name: Local Environmental Records Centres — where your wildlife sighting becomes planning evidence
trackers.desc: THE ROUTE, STEP BY STEP: if you submit a biological record to an app like iRecord or iNaturalist, it will be made available to your Local Environmental Records Centre. Records reaching 'research grade' on iNaturalist are shared with iRecord first and then made available to LERCs in turn. Verification is done by recognised species experts — county recorders, recording schemes and the local records centres themselves — using tools such as Recorder 6, NBN Record Cleaner and iRecord. WHY IT MATTERS FOR A PLANNING FIGHT, and these are the named uses: biological records inform Local Nature Recovery Strategies, the spatial strategies being developed by each local authority, which are heavily informed by records to create evidence-based maps for improving biodiversity; Biodiversity Net Gain calculations, where records inform what habitats should be created or enhanced; and green infrastructure planning. Your sighting, verified and lodged, becomes part of the evidence base your council uses. PRACTICAL POINTS THAT DECIDE WHETHER IT COUNTS: sightings without photographs cannot reach research grade and so will not be shared onward to GBIF, though they may still be useful to other organisations. Update your licence setting on your sightings to maximise the chance they can be used by recording schemes and records centres. Verification can take time, and once an observation is verified in iRecord no further updates flow through, so get the location and identification right first. WHO HOLDS IT: iNaturalistUK is managed by the National Biodiversity Network Trust with the Marine Biological Association and the Biological Records Centre, who are better placed than a global body to handle precise locations of protected species responsibly. Records go on to the NBN Atlas as the central store of UK biodiversity data, and research-grade records go to GBIF. IF YOU ARE OUTSIDE THE UK: the same architecture exists more widely — iNaturalist shares openly available data with GBIF and with national living atlases, and partner organisations curate national portals and engage with local governments on the platform's behalf. Ask what your country's equivalent of a records centre is.

trackers.name: CPRE, the countryside charity — find your local group
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: England's countryside charity (founded 1926, ~40,000 members, around 1,200 volunteers) with more than 200 local groups AND A BRANCH IN EVERY ENGLISH COUNTY. Local groups exist specifically to SHAPE PLANNING DECISIONS, combining local knowledge with national campaigning weight. WHO IT SUITS: anyone facing development on green field, Green Belt or valued landscape in England — this is the nearest thing to an off-the-shelf local ally, and unlike most national bodies you do not need to persuade head office to take an interest. Their track record is the planning system itself: campaigning that led to the Town and Country Planning Act 1947, the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949, the designation of AONBs, and the Green Belt circular. Current campaigns cover Green Belt, hedgerows, dark skies and rural affordable housing — useful if you need to frame an objection in policy terms rather than local feeling.

trackers.name: The Wildlife Trusts — find your county Wildlife Trust
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a federation of 46–47 INDEPENDENT COUNTY-BASED charities covering the UK, Isle of Man and Alderney — each one its own registered charity for its county, not a branch. Between them they own and manage more than 2,600 nature reserves over roughly 112,000 hectares plus 10,120 km of watercourse, with over 945,000 members. USE IT: the map finds the trust for your county. The reason they matter against development is ownership — almost all are significant landowners and COLLECTIVELY THE THIRD LARGEST VOLUNTARY-SECTOR LANDOWNER IN THE UK — so a county trust can take land on, hold a reserve adjoining your site, or object as an affected neighbouring landowner rather than merely as a consultee. Being independent charities, they can also campaign locally without waiting for national sign-off.

trackers.name: Fields in Trust — protect a green space in perpetuity
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a charity founded in 1925 that protects parks and recreational green space in perpetuity — a legal protection that survives a change of council or landowner, which a planning designation does not. THE LEVER MOST CAMPAIGNERS MISS: Fields in Trust sits on the UK Government's School Playing Fields Advisory Panel, convened by the Department for Education to scrutinise the disposal or change of use of playing fields and school land, so a threatened school field has a national body already inside the review. It also maintains the recreational space standard — originally 5 acres of public open space per 1,000 people, of which at least 4 for games and playgrounds — which is the benchmark to quote at a proposal that removes open space.

trackers.name: Planning Aid England — free advice on the planning process
trackers.desc: WHO TO CONTACT: a development is won or lost inside the planning process, not in general environmental argument, and Planning Aid provides free resources and advice on planning in England. This link is the wider advice-centre list that names it alongside the other free routes worth knowing: the Environmental Law Foundation, Advocate (pro bono barristers for those who cannot afford advice or get legal aid, England and Wales), LawWorks (the solicitors' equivalent), Lawyers For Nature, the Public Law Project and Kent Law Clinic. USE IT: work down that list before paying for advice — several of these will take a planning case at no cost.

trackers.name: Environmental Law Foundation — London planning inquiries
trackers.desc: USE THE PRECEDENT: ELF instructed counsel who appeared pro bono for The Isleworth Society at a 5-day planning inquiry over 80 flats proposed on a west London site used as allotments for over 100 years. The Planning Inspector dismissed the appeal, finding the proposal an unacceptable loss of local open space — and the landowner was Northumberland Estates. A residents' society with no budget beat an estate at inquiry, which is the template for a London green-space fight. HOW IT WORKS: communities call or write to ELF's helpline; it follows up every enquiry, assesses how the law can be used, then draws on a network of over 150 pro bono barristers, solicitors and technical experts, answering over 350 requests for legal support a year. It exists primarily for communities that lack the resources to get access to justice otherwise.

trackers.name: The Langholm Initiative — community buyout (worked example)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (worked example): the development trust behind south Scotland's largest community buyout — roughly £6 million raised across TWO buyouts to purchase a 4,249 ha former grouse moor from Buccleuch Estates, stacking a public crowdfunder, a £1m Scottish Land Fund award, philanthropic donors and charities including John Muir Trust, Woodland Trust, RSPB Scotland and Rewilding Britain. WHO IT SUITS: a community that wants to BUY the land rather than object to what happens to it. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is a template, not a funder — study how the funding stack was assembled.

trackers.name: Scottish Land Fund
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a grant fund established under Scotland's land reform legislation that supports COMMUNITY PURCHASES of land and assets — it awarded £1 million toward the Langholm buyout. WHO IT SUITS: Scottish communities where the answer to a threatened site is for the community to own it. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is public money with a statutory basis, not philanthropy — usually the anchor of a buyout funding stack.org.uk and rewild.scot. Grants of GBP 5,000 to GBP 1 million to community-led, community-controlled, non-profit-distributing organisations in urban and rural Scotland to buy land and buildings, with no cost to apply. It is a 2-stage process taking at least about 4 months, and grants are set by an independent market valuation. NOTE: the Fund has no website of its own — it is funded by the Scottish Government and delivered by The National Lottery Community Fund with Highlands and Islands Enterprise, so the link is the delivery partner's programme page. Contact The National Lottery Community Fund Scotland on 0300 123 7110 before applying; you are then assigned an adviser at HIE. DOMAIN NOW VERIFIED on gov.scot and tnlcommunityfund.org.uk. Grants run £5,000 to £1 million to buy land or assets, funded by the Scottish Government and delivered with the National Lottery Community Fund and Highlands and Islands Enterprise. Open to urban and rural organisations that are community-led, community-controlled and defined by a geographic area; applicants must be non-profit distributing; there is no cost to apply. THE TIMING FACT THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS IS USABLE: a two-stage process where the minimum time from application to decision is usually around four months, with grants based on an independent market valuation. Four months minimum means this is not a route for a site already at auction — start before the sale is live. YOU GET A NAMED ADVISER at Highlands and Islands Enterprise to shape the project before applying; contact advicescotland@tnlcommunityfund.org.uk or 0300 123 7110 and, if eligible, they issue the form. WHAT IT BUYS: £619,122 to Islay Development Initiative for Sgiba Forest; £162,130 to Balmacara Community Trust to buy a site from Forestry and Land Scotland which will remain natural woodland — note that a public landowner disposing of a site is a purchase opportunity, not only a threat. Recent rounds: 11 grants totalling £2,381,927; 10 totalling £1,975,563. Also ask about the Empowering Communities Fund where you are using land reform legislation.

trackers.name: Borders Forest Trust
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Scottish land-owning conservation charity — took ownership of the 655 ha Carrifran valley and has planted close to a million trees there, and backed the Langholm community buyout. USE IT: a southern-Scotland acquirer and restoration partner for degraded upland. NOTE: canonical domain not yet verified; named as a partner on rewildingbritain.org.uk. It bought the 1,600-acre Carrifran valley on 1 January 2000 for nearly GBP 400,000 raised without any public money — about 80 percent from private individuals, with 600 Founders giving at least GBP 250 each and more than 800 smaller donors — and has since added Talla & Gameshope (1,832 ha) and Corehead (640 ha). USE IT as a documented template for buying a valley outright by public subscription rather than waiting for a grant.

trackers.name: Environmental Rights Centre for Scotland (ERCS)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Scottish charity (SCIO SC050257) running SCOTLAND'S ONLY FREE ADVICE SERVICE on environmental and planning law — over 325 enquiries answered — and using public interest litigation to hold public bodies to account when advice is not enough. It is in the process of establishing its own law firm to become Scotland's first law centre for environmental justice. WHO IT SUITS: anyone in Scotland facing a worrying planning application, loss of greenspace, pollution, or a refused request for environmental information — Scots law and the Scottish planning system differ from England's, so this is the correct first call north of the border, not an English body.

trackers.name: Friends of the Earth Scotland
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Scottish campaigning organisation working on environmental rights and access to justice, which has taken big polluters to court — including defending Scotland's fracking ban when INEOS sought to overturn it — and campaigns for full Scottish compliance with the Aarhus Convention on participation, information and access to justice. WHO IT SUITS: communities wanting campaign support and rights expertise alongside legal help; for the legal advice itself, go to ERCS.

trackers.name: Wildlife Trusts Wales — planning and development in Wales
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Welsh federation of Wildlife Trusts, which works on development in the wrong place and publishes a plain guide to the Welsh planning system. USE THE GUIDE FIRST: planning is DEVOLVED, so Wales has its own primary legislation (Planning (Wales) Act 2015) and its own policy stack — Planning Policy Wales (PPW11), Future Wales: The National Plan 2040, and Technical Advice Note 5 on nature conservation — which local planning authorities must comply with. English planning guidance does not apply here, and citing it will weaken your objection. Their key argument: all development in Wales must now deliver a NET BENEFIT FOR BIODIVERSITY.

trackers.name: Future Generations Commissioner for Wales
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a politically independent statutory Commissioner created by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, which requires Welsh PUBLIC BODIES to act in pursuit of long-term well-being in accordance with the sustainable development principle. The Commissioner may advise and assist those bodies and advise the Auditor General for Wales on sustainable development. USE IT: this duty has no equivalent in England or Scotland — if a Welsh council, Natural Resources Wales or another public body is backing a damaging project, the Act gives you a distinct line of attack on HOW the decision was reached, and a Commissioner whose remit is to press them on exactly that.

trackers.name: Welsh Government — environmental regulators in Wales (signposting guide)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Welsh Government's own directory of who regulates what in Wales — Natural Resources Wales for air, land, water and intensive farming; Cadw for the historic environment and scheduled monument consent; the Agricultural Land Tribunal for Wales for tenancy, drainage and land-improvement disputes; plus animal, plant and fish health bodies. USE IT: to work out which body you actually complain to or request records from before you spend effort on the wrong one.

trackers.name: Local Places for Nature Capital Fund (Wales)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a Welsh Government and Heritage Fund priority programme for nature recovery, aimed specifically at nature 'FROM YOUR DOORSTEP' — where people live, work, access services and spend leisure time, rather than remote landscapes. WHO IT SUITS: not-for-profit organisations, statutory and third sector, with a bank account and a constitution; pre-application advice is available by email before you commit. HOW IT DIFFERS: 85% of the scheme is CAPITAL funding, and there is a hard catch — capital money MAY NOT BE USED TO LEASE LAND, so any proposal built around a lease is likely ineligible. You must also show you can maintain the asset long term. For grants between £100,000 and £250,000, contact them by email before proceeding.

trackers.name: Environmental Justice Network Ireland (EJNI)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a network working on environmental justice across the ISLAND OF IRELAND — both Northern Ireland and the Republic — publishing joint legal and policy submissions with Community Law & Mediation's Centre for Environmental Justice. WHO IT SUITS: anyone in Northern Ireland, where environmental enforcement has historically been weak and Brexit removed the European Commission's enforcement route, leaving a recognised accountability gap. Cross-border sites are its natural fit, since it works to both jurisdictions rather than only one.

trackers.name: FragDenStaat
trackers.desc: German freedom-of-information portal letting anyone request documents from 40,000+ public bodies and publishing what they hide. — Holds to account: officials handling public money & power — find FOI requests and released government documents.

trackers.name: Bundestag Lobbyregister
trackers.desc: Germany's mandatory lobbying register (since 2022, strengthened 2024) listing who lobbies the Bundestag and federal government. — Holds to account: lobbyists of the Bundestag and federal government — find the mandatory register of who lobbies, for whom, and with what budget.

trackers.name: Bundesbeauftragte für Informationsfreiheit (BfDI)
trackers.desc: Germany's federal commissioner for freedom of information and data protection. — Holds to account: German federal public bodies — find the commissioner's activity reports and rulings on freedom-of-information and data protection.

trackers.name: Rechtsprechung im Internet
trackers.desc: Official federal portal publishing decisions of Germany's highest federal courts. · Find here: selected decisions of Germany's federal supreme courts (Rechtsprechung im Internet).

trackers.name: Bundesverfassungsgericht
trackers.desc: Official decisions of the Federal Constitutional Court. · Find here: the decisions of Germany's Federal Constitutional Court.

trackers.name: openJur
trackers.desc: Free, open database of German court decisions. · Find here: a free German case-law database (openJur).

trackers.name: UVP-Verbund — federal/state EIA portal network
trackers.desc: Germany's joint federal-state portal for environmental impact assessments (UVP): the official publication point for assessment procedures, documents, and decisions across the Bund and Länder. You CAN get: which projects are undergoing UVP near you, the application documents and decisions, and the consultation timelines that set your objection (Einwendung) deadlines. You CAN'T get: a machine-readable API — it's built for reading, not harvesting. For activists: German participation rights hinge on filing objections within the consultation window; this portal is where the clock and the documents live, and recognized environmental associations gain litigation standing (Verbandsklage) from participating.

trackers.name: NABU-Stiftung Nationales Naturerbe — Naturschutz durch Landkauf
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a German foundation (established 2002, seat in Berlin) whose central method is BUYING conservation land — over 16,200 hectares now in its care, plus around 8,800 hectares across 157 protected areas taken over from the federal Nationales Naturerbe pool. It builds endowment capital (Stiftungskapital) alongside the land so running costs are met from investment income, making the holdings independent of year-to-year donations. USE IT: two routes. Propose a threatened site for purchase; or check whether the land is federally owned, because since 2005 the Bund no longer commercially privatises nationally significant conservation land and instead transfers it FREE OF CHARGE to Länder and conservation bodies — roughly 220,000 ha since 2003. If your site sits in that pool, the fight is about designation, not price.

trackers.name: UfU — Unabhängiges Institut für Umweltfragen (Umweltrecht & Partizipation)
trackers.desc: Germany's independent environmental-science institute and citizens' organisation, founded in East Berlin in 1990, with a standing department for environmental law and public participation. WHO TO ENLIST for the mechanics of getting heard: access to courts in environmental matters and Öffentlichkeitsbeteiligung are core profile areas, and it runs a dedicated participation portal alongside its studies. You CAN: draw on applied research written for citizens rather than for ministries, on how participation rights actually work in German procedures. For activists: the evidence base and the procedural map — this is a research institute, so expect analysis and training, not representation in your case.

trackers.name: Bewegungsstiftung — Förderung für Kampagnen und Bewegungsarbeit
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a German community foundation that funds protest itself — campaigns, not charity — across four programmes running from about €3,000 to €100,000, plus up to €3,000 towards paid external advice on facilitation, fundraising or press work. Around €6M to social movements since 2002, including anti-coal campaigning and resistance to villages being demolished for lignite mining. WHO IT SUITS: an initiative with a medium- or long-term campaign strategy, not a one-off event. For tax reasons most programmes require recognised gemeinnützig status — but an unincorporated initiative group CAN apply jointly with a registered gemeinnütziger Verein, which becomes the formal recipient, so lacking legal form is not a bar. HOW IT DIFFERS: funders that exclude political and awareness campaigning are the norm; this one exists for exactly that.

trackers.name: Justice and Environment — European green-law network
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the European network of environmental-law NGOs, whose national member here is UfU, the Independent Institute for Environmental Issues. Its fifteen members act as the environmental-law service point in their own countries, taking cases and intervening in legislative processes, while the network defends communities and nature in court and lodges infringement complaints against member-state governments. Its standing themes are access to justice under the Aarhus Convention, environmental assessment and pollution control. WHO IT SUITS: anyone who does not yet know which lawyer to call — knock on UfU, the Independent Institute for Environmental Issues's door first, and use the network only if your problem crosses a border. The network itself does not take individual cases; its members do. YOUR NATIONAL MEMBER IS Unabhängiges Institut für Umweltfragen (UfU) (ufu.de) — go to them, not to the network. J&E members serve as environmental law ‘service points’ in their countries, handling cases, participating in legislative processes and sometimes providing legal analyses and consultations for national governments. The network has 11 full and 4 associate members, and can launch infringement proceedings against faulty governments — a route a national body alone does not have. CURRENT SCOPE: access to justice under the Aarhus Convention, climate, environmental assessments, and the Environmental Liability Directive. It previously worked on waste, transport, health and Natura 2000, so an older document may overstate what it covers today.
