trackers.name: Lesoochranárske zoskupenie VLK — buys forest with small donations (Slovakia)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Slovak forest-protection association which buys threatened forest outright using small public donations, through a standing campaign called Kúp si svoj strom — buy your own tree. It began in 1997 with an effort to save fir and beech forest in the Čergov range in eastern Slovakia. The first block, 21.24 hectares, was bought from its owner with 1,822 separate contributions from donors in nineteen countries, and it is now the association's own property. Across Čergov it has since bought close to 138 hectares. WHAT HAPPENS TO THE LAND AFTERWARDS, WHICH IS THE PART TO UNDERSTAND: in 2004 the whole of that first block was declared the private nature reserve Vlčia, carrying the fifth and highest degree of protection under Slovak law. A community here does not need the state to own the ground to get the strongest protection on it — a private association holding the title can reach the same level. AND IT PUBLISHES THE TITLE: the parcels making up Vlčia are listed on deed number 510, cadastral area Olejníkov, district Sabinov. Very few organisations anywhere in this file give the land-registry reference for what they hold. It means a donor, a journalist or a sceptical neighbour can verify the ownership in the cadastre rather than take the claim on trust, and it is the answer to the accusation that a conservation body is not really buying anything. USE IT: bring it a specific block with a willing seller in the Slovak forest belt, and expect the money to be raised from many small donors rather than found in a fund. That is how every purchase here has worked.

trackers.name: Nadácia Ekopolis — Slovak Environmental Partnership Foundation
trackers.desc: WHAT THE CONSORTIUM IS: the Environmental Partnership Association, headquartered in Brno, is a consortium of six independent national foundations in central and eastern Europe that give grants to community projects protecting the environment. It grew out of a programme begun in 1990 by the C.S. Mott Foundation, the German Marshall Fund and the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, and the national foundations were established as independent bodies in the early 1990s. Alongside grants they run education programmes, provide professional services and build the capacity of civic initiatives — which is the part a new local group needs most. THE SLOVAK MEMBER: Nadácia Ekopolis, founded 1991, at ekopolis.sk. Slovakia already has a forest buyer and two legal allies in this file but no funder; this is the gap it fills. Approach it for the money to do the survey, the campaign or the site work that a case needs, and ask specifically about capacity building if your group has just formed. SOURCING: the consortium and its six national foundations are documented on the Environmental Partnership Association's own site; the national figures and founding dates come from consortium and partner material rather than each foundation's own pages. Confirm current grant rounds with the national foundation directly.

trackers.name: Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données (CNPD)
trackers.desc: Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données (CNPD) — Luxembourg’s independent data-protection / information commissioner, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Justice.lu
trackers.desc: Official Luxembourg justice portal with court information and selected case law. · Find here: Luxembourg's official justice portal — courts, procedures and selected case-law.

trackers.name: Fondation Hëllef fir d'Natur (natur&ëmwelt)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: buys land. Created in 1982 as a public-utility body within natur&ëmwelt, its two stated core activities are the acquisition and the management of nature reserves — specifically the purchase of ground of high ecological value — and its reserves now cover roughly 1,650 hectares spread across the whole country, with the explicit aim of acquiring more. In a country this small that is a substantial share of the protected network. USE IT: if a wetland, orchard or grassland near you is coming up for sale, this is the body that can hold it permanently, and it takes donations and partnerships earmarked to specific acquisitions — so a community can fund a purchase it could not make itself. The wider natur&ëmwelt association alongside it runs a nature advisory service and carries the political and campaigning side, so approach the foundation for the land and the association for the fight.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Luxembourg, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Superior Court of Justice of the Grand-Duchy of Luxembourg
trackers.desc: Superior Court of Justice of the Grand-Duchy of Luxembourg — supreme court (Luxembourg).

trackers.name: Marchés Publics
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Luxembourg, and for how much.

trackers.name: STATEC
trackers.desc: Luxembourg's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Luxembourg.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes
trackers.desc: National — Court of Audit of Luxembourg. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Luxembourg.

trackers.name: RCS (Registre de Commerce)
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Beneficial Ownership Register (RBE)
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.name: European Union Civil Service Tribunal
trackers.desc: European Union Civil Service Tribunal — tribunal in Luxembourg (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Agrément article 72 — one status unlocks both money and the courtroom
trackers.desc: GET APPROVED FIRST; EVERYTHING ELSE FOLLOWS. Article 72 of the loi modifiée du 18 juillet 2018 on protection of nature governs the agrément of environmental associations — and that one status appears on both sides of this map's needs. FUNDING: the appel à projets for the 3rd Plan national concernant la Protection de la Nature lists eligible beneficiaries as syndicats de communes for nature protection, syndicats de parcs naturels, public establishments with environmental attributions, and ‘les associations et les organisations agréées conformément à l'article 72’, with selected projects funded from the Fonds pour la protection de l'environnement. COURT ACCESS: the reform package guarantees the right of access to a judge for approved environmental associations, in conformity with international and European law. A PROCEDURAL UPGRADE WORTH KNOWING: the recours en annulation is replaced by a recours en réformation, aligning with the ‘eau’ and ‘commodo’ laws — annulment lets a court quash and send back; reformation lets the court substitute its own decision, so the administration cannot simply re-take the same decision with better reasoning. THE COUNTERWEIGHT, STATED HONESTLY: the same package enlarges the list of construction types needing no authorisation — access improves and the permitting net loosens together. Avant-projet 8308, approved 28 July 2023.

trackers.name: Pacte Nature — 84 of 102 communes already signed, and the catalogue is public
trackers.desc: YOUR COMMUNE HAS PROBABLY ALREADY COMMITTED. Voted 14 July 2021 and running to 31 December 2030, the Pacte Nature gives communes a legislative, financial, technical and advisory framework — and more than 80 percent have signed, 84 of 102. That changes the conversation from persuading your commune to care into holding it to a commitment it has already made. HOW IT WORKS: a public catalogue of 79 concrete measures in six categories covering urban, open, aquatic and forest environments plus communication and cooperation. Certification comes at 4 levels — 40, 50, 60 and 70 percent of catalogue points — the subsidy depends on the level, and communes must improve by a set number of points each year. THE STATE PAYS FOR THE ADVISERS: communes receive funds covering the cost of Pacte Nature conseillers who help plan and implement, as well as for measures on the ground. THE LEVER FOR A RESIDENT: the catalogue is public and the scoring is transparent, so identify which of the 79 measures your commune has not taken and press for the ones that protect your site — with the state already funding the adviser to deliver them. RELATED TOOLS: the cadastre des biotopes, environmental incidence evaluation of communal PAG plans, arbres remarquables, and the zone verte / Bauperimeter distinction.

trackers.name: Industrial Emissions Portal — what the facility actually releases
trackers.desc: IT ANSWERS ‘WHAT IS THIS FACILITY RELEASING, AND HOW MUCH’ — with named sites and quantities, not a description of a regulator. The Industrial Emissions Portal gives public access to environmental data from industrial facilities across EU Member States, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and the UK. The Industrial Emissions Portal Regulation (IEPR) replaces the earlier E-PRTR Regulation and implements the Kyiv Protocol on Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers — binding since 8 October 2009, the only legally binding international instrument on PRTRs, and a protocol to the Aarhus Convention. THE MECHANISM IS REPUTATIONAL, AND THE UNECE SAYS SO OPENLY: though it regulates information about pollution rather than pollution directly, it is expected to exert downward pressure ‘as no company will want to be identified as among the biggest polluters’. That is the campaign use — the register produces a ranked, official, quotable list. THE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT, AND IT PREVENTS A FALSE CONCLUSION: an installation not shown on a PRTR is either not an industrial activity covered by it, OR has not reached the stated pollutant-specific thresholds. Absence from the register is NOT evidence of no pollution — check the activity list and thresholds before relying on an absence. TWO DEFINITIONS THAT HELP: ‘the public’ includes natural or legal persons and their associations, organizations or groups, so an unincorporated community group qualifies; and a ‘facility’ is installations on the same site OR ON ADJOINING SITES under one operator — which matters where a plant has been split across parcels. As a scale example the UK register covers 91 pollutants back to 2007. IF YOU NEED ANOTHER COUNTRY: prtr.unece.org keeps a PRTR Global list of national registers, maintained by the OECD Working Party on PRTRs with UNECE, alongside CEC Taking Stock for North America and the NGO-built Blue Map Database in China — where a government has not built a register, that is the precedent for one built anyway.

trackers.name: Aarhus Compliance Committee — one person may bring the State itself
trackers.desc: THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS MAP BY WHICH ONE PERSON CAN BRING A STATE ITSELF BEFORE AN INTERNATIONAL BODY over environmental decision-making. Under Decision I/7 (2002), paragraphs 18–24, communications may be brought by one or more members of the public concerning any Party's compliance — no organisation, no accreditation, no minimum number. The ACCC is a quasi-judicial body reporting to the Meeting of the Parties. THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD PART: YOU DO NOT HAVE TO EXHAUST DOMESTIC REMEDIES. Paragraph 21 says the Committee takes account of any available domestic remedy unless its application is unreasonably prolonged or obviously ineffective. What you must do is state whether steps have been taken and, if not, why not — a section of the form, not a bar to entry. WHAT MAKES IT INADMISSIBLE: anonymity, abuse of the right, being manifestly unreasonable including de minimis, incompatibility, or concerning a non-Party or a State that opted out — and no State has opted out. The only one most people risk is ‘de minimis’: frame it as a systemic failure of information, participation or access to justice, not a complaint about one permit. PRACTICALITIES THAT DECIDE WHETHER IT LANDS: there is a required format, and cut-off dates tied to meetings — as a worked example, communications received by 4 May 2026 were for the 15 and 18 June 2026 meeting, provided they were complete, in format, and needed no translation. Check the current cut-off; missing it costs a cycle. Submit in English, French or Russian — the secretariat translates, but needing translation can push you past a cut-off. Send copies, not originals. AND KNOW THIS BEFORE YOU FILE: once preliminary admissibility is determined the case gets a number and BECOMES PUBLIC — there is a confidentiality section on the form. The process runs receipt → admissibility → response by the Party → draft findings → public hearing → final findings and recommendations. Address: Aarhus Convention Secretariat, UNECE, Palais des Nations, Geneva. CONFIRM YOUR STATE IS A PARTY before relying on this — this entry is recorded here on the basis that the state is bound by the Kyiv Protocol to the Convention, which implies but does not prove Party status.

trackers.name: EIA Directive — ask for the screening determination
trackers.desc: IF A PROJECT NEAR YOU IS PROCEEDING WITHOUT AN EIA, THERE IS A PUBLISHED, REASONED DOCUMENT EXPLAINING WHY — AND ALMOST NOBODY ASKS FOR IT. Annex I projects get mandatory EIA; Annex II projects — the far larger category — go through a screening procedure using the Annex III criteria. Under Directive 2014/52/EU the developer supplies specified Annex IIA information, and that determination SHALL be made available to the public and must be duly motivated. Ask for the screening determination: it is the most useful document in the procedure and the one people do not know exists. TIMING: determinations must be made within 90 days of complete information, unless the authority extends the period giving reasons in exceptional cases and informs the developer. BUT BE REALISTIC ABOUT THE LIMIT: proposals to require public participation during screening were dropped from the 2014 text as impractical — you have a right to the determination, not a right to be heard before it is made. THREE MORE THINGS THE 2014 AMENDMENT GIVES YOU: reports must be more understandable to the public, especially on the current state of the environment and alternatives; competent authorities must prove their objectivity to avoid conflicts of interest — making a conflict a ground of challenge, not a complaint; and the grounds for consent decisions must be clear and transparent. ASK ALSO WHETHER A SCOPING OPINION HAS BEEN REQUESTED — it fixes what the assessment is required to look at. Reports must carry a non-technical summary (Annex IV), and information must be provided as early as possible, electronically, by public notice or bill posting, or in local newspapers. THE DIRECTIVE IS A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING: Member States may lay down more stringent conditions and fix penalties — check the national transposition before assuming the EU minimum applies. The regime is Directive 2011/92/EU (applying since 17 February 2012) as amended by 2014/52/EU, codifying rules in force since 1988 and aligned to the Espoo and Aarhus Conventions. ONE PATTERN TO WATCH: the legislative history records concern that formal screening could become a ‘mini-EIA’ before the full EIA — an unusually detailed screening determination is itself an argument that full assessment was warranted.

trackers.name: Espoo points of contact — a named official, and ‘were you notified?’
trackers.desc: A NAMED OFFICIAL, A DIRECT EMAIL, AND A QUESTION WITH A DOCUMENTARY ANSWER. The UNECE publishes the points of contact regarding notification under article 3 of the Espoo Convention on EIA in a transboundary context: notifications of activities likely to cause significant adverse transboundary impact shall be transmitted to the relevant points of contact. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR AN ORDINARY LAND CASE: if a project sits near a border, the affected country's point of contact should have been notified — so ask both points of contact whether notification was given. It is a cheap, precise question, and failure to notify is a procedural defect in the consent. The list gives each Party's named official, department, postal address, telephone and email: Czechia's sits in the Department of EIA and Integrated Prevention at the Ministry of the Environment; Denmark's is the Agency for Green Transition and Aquatic Environment using the functional address espoo@sgav.dk; Croatia's is a Director at the Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development; Canada's is the President of the Impact Assessment Agency. PREFER A FUNCTIONAL ADDRESS WHERE ONE IS LISTED — named officials move. AND NOTE A ROUTING PATTERN: some Parties route notification through their Ministry for Foreign Affairs c/o their Permanent Mission in Geneva rather than an environment ministry — where that is so, the environment ministry may not hold the file and the foreign-ministry route is the correct one. A SECOND DIRECTORY, AND A SECOND ROUTE TO THE SAME DOCUMENT: the EEA publishes a list of Eionet national focal points covering 32 member countries and 8 cooperating countries (Albania, Bosnia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine). Data are reported upwards — from stakeholder, to competent authority, to the EEA, to the Commission — so if your national authority has reported something, the EEA holds it too. Where a national body is unresponsive or its figures look wrong, the same data sits one level up in a body with no stake in the local decision. CONFIRM YOUR COUNTRY APPEARS ON THE LIST before relying on it. SCOPE: Espoo governs transboundary notification and Eionet governs data reporting — for the domestic EIA procedure itself, see the EIA Directive entry recorded separately.

trackers.name: Fondation Hëllef fir d'Natur — acquisition is named first in what it does
trackers.desc: ‘The principal areas of activity of the Fondation Hëllef fir d'Natur are the ACQUISITION and management of nature reserves’ — acquisition is named first in its own description of itself. Its reserves cover about 1,400 hectares in Luxembourg and keep growing, with the stated objective of strengthening the national and European network of protected areas. Working for 30 years, it describes itself as the largest Luxembourgish environmental organisation, with specialists, geographers, biologists and engineers who draw up the management plan for each reserve — which is the technical capacity a community needs and cannot hire. APPROACH THE RIGHT DEPARTMENT: there are three — the a.s.b.l. (the association), the Foundation, which is the one that holds the land, and a wildlife care centre that takes in sick, injured and orphaned animals and animals seized or confiscated. For an acquisition, go to the Foundation, not the association. AND THERE IS A FUNDED BUYER ACTIVELY LOOKING RIGHT NOW: LIFE ArdennEislek (January 2025 to 2031), led by Natagora with the Fondation Hëllef fir d'Natur and natur&ëmwelt, will restore over 450 hectares in the Belgian and Luxembourg Ardenne — including 110 hectares of NEW ACQUISITIONS. If your site is in that area and is meadow, heath or biodiversity-rich forest, there is an EU-funded budget running now with land still to buy. A second project, LIFE ToadAlly, coordinated by Natuurpunt Beheer, covers Limburg and Liège.

trackers.name: Mouvement Écologique — the Grénge Telefon, and seven regional sections (Luxembourg)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Luxembourg's main independent environmental association, an asbl at 6 rue Vauban, L-2663 Luxembourg, +352 439030-1, meco@oeko.lu. It runs the Grénge Telefon — a green telephone line where a member of the public can ask what the law says about an environmental question and get an answer. Its own examples are exactly the everyday kind: what ecological rules must a business follow, how do I make a natural pond, what does the law say. For a country with almost nothing else in this file, that is a free first call. AND THE REGIONAL SECTIONS ARE THE POINT: it has seven — Miersch an Emgéigend, Echternach-Mullerthal, Luxembourg-Ville, Sud, Nordstad, Syrdall, Uelzechtdall — each with its own committee and named contacts, and it says that where no regional section covers your area you should write to the national office. Its stated view is that many of its goals are achieved by citizens working in the local and regional sections. WHAT IT DOES ON DEVELOPMENT: spatial planning and urbanism is one of its standing subjects, and it has published detailed case-by-case criticism of specific schemes — a filling station in open green belt beside a motorway, a housing development at Huncherange that would take a village of about 800 people to some 2,500, major residential projects at Leudelange, a shopping centre at Livange and a mixed project at Wickrange, an activity zone at Differdange/Niederkorn, and a bypass and oil reserve at Bascharage/Sanem cutting through a European-level protected area. Its argument in each case is that the scheme contradicts the government's own spatial planning guidelines. That is the frame to bring it: not that a project is undesirable, but that it departs from the state's own stated policy. IT ESCALATES TO BRUSSELS: with natur&ëmwelt — already in this file as Luxembourg's land-owning foundation — it has jointly filed complaints against the Luxembourg government with the European Commission over loss of protected habitats and species. The two organisations work together, and a Luxembourg community should treat them as a pair. WHAT IT IS NOT: not a law firm and not a land buyer. Advice, positions, complaints and local sections.

trackers.name: Œuvre Nationale — lottery-funded, with Environment as a standing field (Luxembourg)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a public establishment under the tutelage of the Ministry of State, financed almost entirely by the Loterie Nationale, created at Christmas 1944 by Grande-Duchess Charlotte to help victims of the Second World War and now the central philanthropic actor in Luxembourg. It organises and finances projects of general interest in five standing fields: Social, Culture, Environnement, Sport & Santé, and Mémoire & Patrimoine. Luxembourg had no funder in this file. THE ROUTE THAT FITS A LAND CASE: the demande d'aide ponctuelle — a one-off support request, addressed to any organisation wishing to finance or co-finance a concrete project limited in time. Any asbl, foundation or société d'impact sociétal operating at national level can request financing for a concrete, time-limited project with social impact in those five fields. Legal form is required — an unincorporated residents' group must incorporate or find a partner. THE EVIDENCE THAT IT PAYS FOR LAND, which is why it is filed here rather than as a general charity funder: it supported the Koulbich valley work of Luxembourg's land-buying foundation, where 2024 saw 18.5 additional hectares acquired, including a large tract of deciduous forest and several ponds for restoration, toward a target of 30 hectares to complete the reserve. A Luxembourgish community that has found a willing seller has, in this body, a funder with a demonstrated record of paying for the parcels. HOW IT WORKS BESIDES GIVING MONEY: it describes itself as a facilitator and intermediary, launching appels à projets and supporting initiatives coming directly from the ground, and it convenes the sector through exchanges, conferences, thematic days and training. Its impartial position lets it coordinate between stakeholders, and the guidelines for its initiatives come out of those exchanges. Telling it what is missing is part of how its calls get written. SCALE, FOR CALIBRATION: its themed calls have carried envelopes such as €250,000 for one programme and €2,000,000 for another, with individual funds capped at figures like €25,000. Watch the appels à projets page for an Environment-facing call.

trackers.name: Commissioner for Right to Information & Data Protection (IDP)
trackers.desc: Commissioner for Right to Information & Data Protection (IDP) — Albania’s national data-protection / information authority, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Albania
trackers.desc: Official site of Albania's highest court with published decisions. · Find here: information and judgments of the Supreme Court of Albania.

trackers.name: Commissioner for the Right to Information & Data Protection (IDP)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority (dual-mandate); Albania’s IDP Commissioner enforces the Law 119/2014 on the Right to Information — examining complaints, investigating and imposing administrative measures, Albania.

trackers.name: EcoAlbania (Qendra EcoAlbania)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Tirana organisation that brought the first environmental lawsuit ever heard in Albania's Administrative Court — and won it twice. In December 2016 it went to court against the Poçem hydropower plant on the Vjosa together with RiverWatch, EuroNatur and 38 affected residents as co-plaintiffs, arguing the environmental impact assessment was inadequate and the affected community had not been consulted, in breach of Albanian law and international conventions. The court struck the project down in 2017 and recognised the residents' standing; the Administrative Court of Appeal confirmed the annulment in 2024. Its own account calls that the case that opened the door for every environmental claim brought since. WHO IT SUITS: communities facing hydropower, and anyone whose project's paperwork is thin — the winning grounds were procedural. Worth copying its other habit too: when the government announced Vjosa protection in 2020, EcoAlbania read the actual public documents and found the designation was a protected landscape, not a national park. Always check which status was really granted.

trackers.name: Public Procurement Agency
trackers.desc: Albania's electronic public-procurement platform. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Albania, and for how much.

trackers.name: Albania Register of Beneficiary Owners (RBO)
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: HIDAACI
trackers.desc: Albania's High Inspectorate for the Declaration and Audit of Assets and Conflicts of Interest.

trackers.name: INSTAT
trackers.desc: Albania's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Albania.

trackers.name: Supreme State Audit (KLSH)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Albania, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: National Business Center (QKB)
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Park natyror bashkiak and Kurora e gjelbër — the municipal routes
trackers.desc: TWO ROUTES THAT DO NOT REQUIRE A COUNCIL OF MINISTERS DECISION. Under Ligj 81/2017, a park natyror bashkiak is declared by decision of the municipal council — an environmental protected area equated with category IV — within one or more municipalities, after preliminary approval by the responsible minister; its purpose is activities suited to the area and related exclusively to the needs of the community, management plans are approved by ministerial order and sent to municipalities for implementation immediately, and such parks join the national network. AND THE SECOND ROUTE IS AN OBLIGATION, NOT A REQUEST: a Kurorë e gjelbër (green crown) is declared by the Këshilli Kombëtar i Territorit as a forest protected area inside a municipality — and the law states it is an obligation for every municipality. If your municipality has not declared its green crown it is in default of a statutory duty, which is a stronger argument than asking a favour. FOR NATIONAL DECLARATIONS, the opinion of academic institutions, the municipality, civil society, field experts and the community of the area must be obtained first, and the declaring decision must fix permitted and prohibited activities per sub-zone and the use of revenues generated.

trackers.name: The Vjosa precedent — unsigned contracts do not survive a declaration
trackers.desc: WHAT A DECLARATION CAN DO TO A PROJECT ALREADY IN THE PIPELINE. VKM No. 155 of 13.03.2023 declared the Vjosa river ecosystem a National Park (category II), 12,727 hectares of water, bank, forest and pasture, upgrading it from Park Natyror to Park Kombëtar, with the boundary map and coordinate table forming part of the decision. THE OPERATIVE CLAUSE: activities for which the relevant contract had not been signed — regardless of procedures under way — and contracts which on the day the decision entered into force had not fulfilled their relevant conditions, are not permitted inside the Park where they come openly into conflict with article 16 of law 81/2017. So an unsigned concession, or a signed one whose conditions were unmet on the day of declaration, does not survive it — if a project is mid-procedure, the declaration is the race. A management plan was to follow within 2 years. TWO THINGS FROM THE 2024 AMENDMENTS: a proposal to change the area of a protected zone must be consulted in advance with the local community, with owners whose properties are included or removed, with scientific institutions and local government, and must argue the need — so boundary reduction has a consultation trigger to hold them to. But watch the carve-outs: activities in 5-star and agrotourism accommodation structures and their supporting infrastructure are listed as permitted regardless of whether the declaring VKM says so.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Energy Community — private bodies may complain, and refusal is appealable
trackers.desc: A COMPLAINT MECHANISM WHERE REFUSAL BY THE GATEKEEPER CAN BE TAKEN OVER ITS HEAD — which is rare, and is the reason to know about this. Under Article 90 of the Energy Community Treaty, private bodies may approach the Secretariat with complaints about a Party's non-compliance, and under Article 12.2 of the Consolidated Rules the Secretariat initiates procedures in response to a complaint by a private body as well as on its own initiative. AND IF THE SECRETARIAT DECLINES: the revised Rules give the complainant the right to approach the Permanent High Level Group directly, which may hear the complaint directly or initiate a preliminary procedure — in most systems recorded in this map, a secretariat declining to act ends the matter. The PHLG can also take interim measures in matters of urgency under Article 47(c) — that is what matters when works are already under way, so ask for it expressly. THE ENVIRONMENTAL ACQUIS IS IN SCOPE, including the EIA Directive as amended by 2014/52, which was to be transposed by 1 January 2019. CHECK THE TRANSPOSITION DEADLINE FOR THE DIRECTIVE YOU RELY ON — failure to transpose by the stated date is itself the non-compliance, and is a far simpler case than arguing about how a rule was applied. THE REALISTIC WIN CONDITION: a case opens with an Opening Letter, escalates to a Reasoned Opinion giving two months to rectify, then to the Ministerial Council — but a case closes whenever the Party complies, and many are recorded as complied with before any decision was adopted. The opening of proceedings is the lever, not the final decision. YOU CAN ALSO JOIN AN EXISTING CASE: interested third parties may access the case file and submit written observations, provided they substantiate their legitimate interest. Case law from Opening Letters is published with dates and numbers, so precedent is visible. Write to the Energy Community Secretariat, Am Hof 4, 1010 Vienna. ONE MORE ROUTE: the amended Rules provide for cooperation with national authorities and courts, giving concrete assistance to national courts on the interpretation of Energy Community law — a domestic judge unsure how an EU-derived rule applies can be pointed at it.

trackers.name: Espoo points of contact — a named official, and ‘were you notified?’
trackers.desc: A NAMED OFFICIAL, A DIRECT EMAIL, AND A QUESTION WITH A DOCUMENTARY ANSWER. The UNECE publishes the points of contact regarding notification under article 3 of the Espoo Convention on EIA in a transboundary context: notifications of activities likely to cause significant adverse transboundary impact shall be transmitted to the relevant points of contact. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR AN ORDINARY LAND CASE: if a project sits near a border, the affected country's point of contact should have been notified — so ask both points of contact whether notification was given. It is a cheap, precise question, and failure to notify is a procedural defect in the consent. The list gives each Party's named official, department, postal address, telephone and email: Czechia's sits in the Department of EIA and Integrated Prevention at the Ministry of the Environment; Denmark's is the Agency for Green Transition and Aquatic Environment using the functional address espoo@sgav.dk; Croatia's is a Director at the Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development; Canada's is the President of the Impact Assessment Agency. PREFER A FUNCTIONAL ADDRESS WHERE ONE IS LISTED — named officials move. AND NOTE A ROUTING PATTERN: some Parties route notification through their Ministry for Foreign Affairs c/o their Permanent Mission in Geneva rather than an environment ministry — where that is so, the environment ministry may not hold the file and the foreign-ministry route is the correct one. A SECOND DIRECTORY, AND A SECOND ROUTE TO THE SAME DOCUMENT: the EEA publishes a list of Eionet national focal points covering 32 member countries and 8 cooperating countries (Albania, Bosnia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine). Data are reported upwards — from stakeholder, to competent authority, to the EEA, to the Commission — so if your national authority has reported something, the EEA holds it too. Where a national body is unresponsive or its figures look wrong, the same data sits one level up in a body with no stake in the local decision. CONFIRM YOUR COUNTRY APPEARS ON THE LIST before relying on it. SCOPE: Espoo governs transboundary notification and Eionet governs data reporting — for the domestic EIA procedure itself, see the EIA Directive entry recorded separately.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Eurosite / ELCN — who already holds land near you, and the easement route
trackers.desc: A DIRECTORY OF THE PEOPLE WHO ALREADY HOLD AND MANAGE LAND IN YOUR COUNTRY — which is who you need when the answer to a development is getting the land into protective hands. Eurosite, established 1989, is one of the largest pan-European organisations bringing together NGOs, governmental organisations and private bodies, with members from the Atlantic islands to the Black Sea and from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. ITS ELCN STRAND IS ABOUT PRIVATE LAND SPECIFICALLY: the European Land Conservation Network was built to support private landowners — non-public bodies or individuals — willing to engage in conservation ON AT LEAST PART OF THEIR LAND. That last phrase is the opening: a landowner who will not sell may still protect a portion, and there is a European network built to make that happen. The three tools it promotes are conservation easements, privately protected areas, and land stewardship agreements. AND A FUNDING ROUTE IS ATTACHED: ELCN and the ILCN have run sessions on using EU LIFE funding for private land conservation, aimed at landowners and conservationists preparing a LIFE project proposal; in November 2025 Eurosite-ELCN launched a working group on nature finance and land stewardship focused on finance mechanisms that mobilise private investment, co-chaired by the former head of the EU LIFE Programme. IF YOUR FIGHT IS A QUARRY, ASK FOR THIS BY NAME: Eurosite and partners published work on project selection criteria for conservation easements to protect nature in European quarries — a published European method for putting an easement over one. The network also co-hosts meetings of the Commission's Expert Group on the Nature Directives (NADEG) on tools and incentives for private land conservation — the most important working-level platform between the Commission, member states and interest groups. IF EUROSITE DOES NOT REACH YOUR COUNTRY, the International Land Conservation Network (founded 2014, the first global network of private land conservation practitioners) is the wider net, active from Canada to Australia to Latin America. BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT THESE ARE: networks of practitioners — they connect you to the organisation that can act; they do not buy land themselves. Ask the network who operates in your country; membership is not asserted here.

trackers.name: EcoAlbania — goes to court alongside the village, not instead of it (Albania)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an Albanian environmental organisation created in December 2014 by biology professors from the University of Tirana together with the Save the Blue Heart of Europe team. Its method is to bring the case jointly with the affected residents as named co-plaintiffs, not on their behalf. Poçem: with 38 residents of Kutë village, plus EuroNatur and Riverwatch. Kalivac: with 39 members of the affected local community. Shushica: with 28 residents of Brataj. That is the offer — the villagers stay parties to their own case and the organisation brings the lawyers, the science and the international partners. WHAT IT HAS ACTUALLY WON: the Poçem concession was struck down in 2017 because the company had held no public hearing with the affected Mallakastër communities, having consulted 50 residents of Fier instead, and the Court of Appeal confirmed the annulment. The Tirana Administrative Court dismissed the Kalivac developer's challenge to the ministry's negative environmental declaration. In December 2024 the same court annulled the acts behind four hydropower plants on the Shushica. THE TIMELINE, WHICH IS THE THING TO BE HONEST ABOUT: the Poçem action began in December 2016 and the appeal was confirmed in 2024. Shushica took close to three years. A village considering this route should plan in years, not seasons, and should note that the organisation and its partners carried the cost across that span rather than the residents. THE ARGUMENT THAT KEEPS WORKING: in the Poçem case the fatal defect was the consultation — the wrong people were consulted, in the wrong place. Whatever else a community gathers, gather who was invited to the hearing, who attended, and where they lived.

trackers.name: PPNEA — Albania's oldest environmental organisation, and its science
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the first environmental organisation in Albania, established 5 June 1991 by decree of the Albanian Academy of Sciences, based in Tirana, with somewhere between eleven and fifty staff and the national BirdLife partner. It works across effectively all of Albania's protected areas and in the transboundary areas with Kosovo, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Greece. Its stated method is rigorous scientific research, community involvement, strategic partnerships and continuous interaction with decision-making institutions — which is the combination a community needs when it has to prove a site matters. WHAT IT CAN ACTUALLY SUPPLY: monitoring schemes run jointly with government agencies, training delivered to law enforcement bodies, and long-running species programmes — Balkan lynx since 2006, brown bear, Dalmatian pelican, Egyptian vulture, Mediterranean monk seal. If your site holds any of those, there is an existing monitoring record and an organisation with standing to speak about it. It also states a deep working relationship with investigative media, which is a different and sometimes faster route than a consultation response. AND IT SUPPORTS OTHER GROUPS: institutional development of environmental civil society organisations is one of its stated strands, so a new Albanian committee can ask for help becoming an organisation rather than only for help with its case. USE IT WITH THE OTHER TWO ALBANIAN ROUTES: EcoAlbania, already in this file, litigates alongside named village residents as co-plaintiffs; PONT, also in this file, funds environmental actors in exactly this region including operating costs. Science from PPNEA, the case from EcoAlbania, the money from PONT. Albania now has all three. WHAT IT IS NOT: not a land buyer and not a law firm. On its own account it works with government agencies rather than against them, which makes it strong on evidence and weaker as a confrontation partner — ask it for the record, not for the fight.

trackers.name: GreenAL — grants to environmental organisations across Albania, and a roster of them
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a grants programme to strengthen environmental organisations across Albania, administered through Co-PLAN, the Institute for Habitat Development. Albania had no funder of its own in this file — only the regional Balkan trust. THE MOST USEFUL THING HERE IS THE GRANTEE LIST, because it is effectively a directory of Albania's working environmental sector. Its second call funded, among others, the Albanian Ornithological Society (AOS), the Institute for Environment and Territory Management (ETMI), Qendra Res Publica, the association ILIRIA on environmental and social protection and development, PPNEA — already filed here — and Shtëpia e Gjelbër. Its smaller initiative grants went to a long list of local bodies including ADAD Malore, North Green Association, Agro-Eko Dibra, the EPER Center, DARC, SEEP, the Albanian Regional Environmental Board, Qendresa Qytetare, and the Cukali association of users of natural, forest and pasture resources. WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE MONEY: an Albanian community looking for an ally near its own valley now has around twenty named organisations to choose from, several of them explicitly regional — Dibra, the mountains, the north — and one of them an association of people who actually use forest and pasture. Nothing else in the Albanian bucket lists the sector. TWO OTHER ALBANIAN ROUTES SURFACED ALONGSIDE, both worth knowing: LëvizAlbania, a Swiss Development Cooperation project run by a consortium of the Open Society Foundation for Albania, Partners Albania and Co-PLAN, which supports civil society actors, informal groups and individuals on local democracy — across two phases it ran nine calls, backed 362 individuals, informal groups and organisations, and reached more than 75,000 citizens, and one of its supported cases was an environmental organisation working on municipal noise. Its journey was described as concluding, so check its status. And the European Commission has run calls for Albanian civil society with a dedicated lot on environment, climate change and nature protection. WHAT IT IS NOT: a grants programme, not a permanent institution. Confirm whether a call is open before planning around it.

trackers.name: AMSHC — the Albanian state agency that funds NGOs, and spreads grants across the country
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the Agjencia për Mbështetjen e Shoqërisë Civile, Albania's state agency for supporting civil society, which runs numbered public calls (thirrje) inviting non-profit organisations to submit project proposals. GreenAL is already in this file as Albania's sector funder; this is the state's own money, on a separate track. THE FIELDS IT NAMES, and two of them fit a land case directly: environmental initiatives for the protection of the environment and sustainable development; encouraging local and regional development through improved cooperation and participation and the activation of development and community actors; encouraging community development and strengthening volunteering and local and regional cooperation; and developing civil society through better institutional instruments and mechanisms. Another call lists protection of the environment and raising citizens' environmental awareness among its objects. THE DETAIL THAT FAVOURS A VILLAGE OVER TIRANA: the agency states that a distribution of winning projects as wide as possible across the whole territory is part of its philosophy and mission, and it has published the territorial distribution of winning projects by administrative region for its calls. That is a funder that reports where its money landed, by region — so a group outside the capital can see whether its own qarku has been served, and say so. Fourth funder in this file to prefer the periphery, after Montenegro, Serbia and Cyprus. HOW TO WATCH IT: calls are numbered and published on the agency's own site with the fields listed each time; the fields change between calls, so read the current thirrje rather than assuming. A SECOND ALBANIAN TRACK, for context: LëvizAlbania has run Grante Strategjike supporting formal and informal civil society actors and citizen engagement for accountability and participatory governance at local level — and its calls have explicitly invited networking and thematic coalitions between actors.

trackers.name: TOKA — five years of litigation, a bailiff at the powerhouse, and a SLAPP survived
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: The Organization to Conserve the Albanian Alps, founded June 2016 in Tirana and Valbona Valley National Park, with founding members from the local community, biologists, tourism experts and other supporters. That composition is the Kruščica checklist again — residents plus the expert disciplines — assembled at the start rather than recruited under pressure. It is one of the leading groups opposing plans for fourteen hydropower projects along the Valbona river inside the national park. WHAT THEY WON, AND HOW LONG IT TOOK: a group of residents together with the association filed suit, and roughly five years later, in July 2021, Albania's High Court ruled that the work and operations of two plants must stop immediately pending the outcome of the administrative case, with reports that the court also suspended the concession contracts. The plants kept running anyway. Enforcement came separately: a bailiff visited the powerhouses and confirmed they had ceased operation, with TOKA's founder present. Its own warning afterwards was that if the company switched the plants on again, even for five minutes, it becomes a criminal offence they will prosecute. Winning the judgment and enforcing it were two separate fights. THE GROUNDS THEY RAN: lack of proper impact assessments; threats against those opposing construction; and that such construction should not take place in a national park. Residents also claimed in court that the names of dead relatives, and names used without permission, appeared on documents purporting to show local support — so check the consent signatures. AND THE COST, WHICH IS THE WARNING: the developer brought an indemnity claim against TOKA and against its director personally for approximately 150,000 euros over alleged denigration and reputational damage. The Tirana District Court dismissed it; the company appealed. Members and others reported constant pressure over their opposition. Expect the personal suit. CONTEXT WORTH KNOWING: Tropoja is one of Europe's poorest regions, remaining residents depend on agriculture and the promise of tourism, and Valbona is one of Albania's top outdoor and mountain tourism destinations — the tourism argument carried real weight here.

trackers.name: Personal Data Protection Service of Georgia
trackers.desc: Personal Data Protection Service of Georgia — Georgia’s national data-protection / information authority, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Georgia
trackers.desc: Official site of Georgia's highest (cassation) court with judgments and case information. · Find here: information and judgments of the Supreme Court of Georgia.

trackers.name: Ask Gov — FOI requests (GEO)
trackers.desc: Accountability source (FOI request platform); Ask Gov — civic Freedom-of-Information request platform (Alaveteli/mySociety network) — lets citizens file public-records requests and publishes the requests and the authorities’ responses in a public archive.

trackers.name: GYLA (Georgian Young Lawyers' Association)
trackers.desc: Georgian legal-watchdog NGO (since 1994) that monitors government activities and elections (15+ years of election observation), advocates legislative and institutional reform, and runs accountability projects on budget spending and freedom of information.

trackers.name: Green Alternative (Association Green Alternative)
trackers.desc: Georgia's leading environmental and social-justice organisation, formed out of the campaigners of Friends of the Earth Georgia and a member of the CEE Bankwatch Network. It targets large projects with severe environmental or social impacts — hydropower above all, plus transport schemes and privatisation deals — and its published case files are unusually detailed, documenting for instance a hydropower plant approved inside Kazbegi National Park despite an explicit statutory prohibition. WHO TO ENLIST when a dam, road or concession lands on your valley. You CAN: use its alternative report on Aarhus Convention implementation in Georgia to argue access to information and public participation, and reach the wider Georgian Green Network and the independent forest monitoring network, both of which it founded. For activists: it explicitly pairs campaign work with capacity building of local groups and getting them directly into the campaign, so approach it as a partner rather than a service — with around ten staff, it cannot take everything.

trackers.name: State Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Georgia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Anti-Corruption Bureau — Asset Declarations
trackers.desc: National asset-declaration registry; Georgia’s Anti-Corruption Bureau publishes ~60,000 searchable officials’ asset declarations online (monitoring moved here from the Civil Service Bureau; two-month review before publication), Georgia.

trackers.name: Georgia — public officials’ asset declarations
trackers.desc: Accountability source (official asset-declaration register); Georgia — public officials’ asset declarations — the Civil Service Bureau’s public database and monitoring system for Georgian officials’ asset declarations.

trackers.name: IDFI (Institute for Development of Freedom of Information)
trackers.desc: Georgian watchdog/think-tank (since 2009) promoting freedom of information, open governance and anti-corruption. Monitors public procurement, the state and municipal budgets, and proactive disclosure by public bodies; advances citizen participation in decision-making, budgeting and lawmaking at central and local levels; and publishes officials' asset-declaration data (including after access to the official portal was restricted).

trackers.name: NAPR
trackers.desc: Georgia's National Agency of Public Registry (company registry). — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Public Defender of Georgia — National Preventive Mechanism
trackers.desc: Public Defender of Georgia — National Preventive Mechanism — Georgia’s OPCAT National Preventive Mechanism — the Public Defender’s Special Preventive

trackers.name: State Procurement (Ge)
trackers.desc: Georgia's unified electronic state-procurement system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Georgia, and for how much.

trackers.name: National Statistics Office of Georgia (GeoStat)
trackers.desc: Georgia's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Georgia.

trackers.name: დაცული ლანდშაფტი — the category for a place where people live
trackers.desc: GEORGIA'S PROTECTED AREA LAW, adopted 1996, provides 5 categories — state reserve, national park, natural monument, managed reserve and protected landscape. THE LAST IS THE ONE THAT FITS AN INHABITED PLACE: დაცული ლანდშაფტი is created expressly for the harmonious coexistence of nature and people, development of recreation and tourism, and support for the region's economic potential and the population's living conditions — and different zones may be arranged within it. That zoning flexibility is what makes it usable where people live and work, and it is the same category Skopje used for Vodno. It may sit inside a biosphere reserve or World Heritage site, or itself contain a natural monument. For sustainable resource use, zones with different permissible ratios of conservation and multiple use may be delineated. The first official reserve on Georgian territory dates to 1912.

trackers.name: Caucasus Nature Fund — it matches your government, so lobby your government
trackers.desc: A FUNDING MODEL WITH A LEVERAGE ARGUMENT BUILT IN. CNF is a conservation trust fund founded in 2007 by Conservation International, Germany's development ministry and WWF, with offices in Tbilisi and Yerevan, supporting 18 protected areas across Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia. Its mission is long-term funding for operating costs — the hardest money to raise anywhere in this map — plus improved management. THE MECHANISM: it works through partnerships with the three governments by matching, but not exceeding, the state budgets. So CNF money rises and falls with what your own government commits, which means lobbying your government to raise its protected-area budget also raises the matched international money. Use that argument directly. WHAT ASSEMBLES AT SCALE: a five-year initiative for 12 Georgian protected areas totalled USD 10 million — USD 1.8m GEF, USD 4.8m from the environment ministry, USD 3.1m CNF and USD 200,000 from the Bank of Georgia. AND KNOW WHO MANAGES YOUR SITE: protected areas total 600,597 ha, about 8 percent of the country, but only 387,800 ha — 64 percent of them — is managed by the Agency of Protected Areas. More than a third sits elsewhere, so identify the manager before directing a complaint.

trackers.name: Vreau Info (Moldova)
trackers.desc: Moldova's civic freedom-of-information request platform, built on the Alaveteli/mySociety software: you file an access-to-information request to a public authority through the site, and both the request and the authority's response — or its silence — are published in a public archive. USE IT: the archive shows which authorities answer and which do not, which is evidence in itself.

trackers.name: Portal of the Courts of Moldova
trackers.desc: Official national portal publishing decisions and case files of the Moldovan courts. · Find here: the unified portal of the courts of Moldova — case search and decisions.

trackers.name: State Chancellery — Access to Information
trackers.desc: National right-to-information implementation body; Moldova’s State Chancellery implements the 2023 Access to Information of Public Interest Law (Tromsø-aligned), with Ombudsman oversight, Moldova.

trackers.name: Eco-TIRAS — Asociaţia Internaţională a Păstrătorilor Râului
trackers.desc: The association of more than fifty environmental organisations across Moldova, including Transnistria, and Ukraine, built around the transboundary Dniester basin and registered under Moldovan law. WHO TO ENLIST: use it as the switchboard — if there is a local group anywhere in the basin, it is probably a member, and reaching the network is faster than finding one cold. You CAN: draw on its compilation of Moldovan environmental legislation, published in volumes on its own site, and on its scientific capacity, which is unusual for an NGO here — it developed a methodology for assessing hydropower impacts on river ecosystems and has surveyed riverbank erosion. It sits on the Dniester river commission it helped create, so it has a seat where basin decisions are taken. For activists: it has form on access to information, having pursued a case internationally under the Aarhus Convention after a state service demanded a very large fee for environmental data — worth citing if you are quoted a price for records.

trackers.name: EcoContact — Centrul Aarhus Chișinău / free environmental legal aid
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the association that has hosted Moldova's Aarhus environmental consultancy and information centre since 2013, and whose stated strategic aim is increasing public access to justice on environmental interests. It gives free legal assistance on environmental matters and has supported court actions on access to information, public participation and the protection of natural resources — reportedly more than fifty consultations across 2024-2025 — and it does not wait to be visited: in 2024 its teams reached 182 of the 187 localities in its target districts to offer free legal help on the spot. WHO IT SUITS: rural communities above all, and local councils, since it also drafts local environmental regulations covering grazing, mowing, recording of offences and transparency in decision-making. Two things that improve your odds: it runs the environmental-cases programme for judges and prosecutors at the National Institute of Justice, so the bench has been trained on exactly these questions, and it moderates a platform of over 230 environmental organisations and experts if the expertise you need is not in-house.

trackers.name: Court of Accounts
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Moldova, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: RISE Moldova
trackers.desc: Moldovan investigative group (OCCRP sister) tracking cross-border corruption and illicit money.

trackers.name: data.gov.md
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Moldova.

trackers.name: MTender
trackers.desc: Moldova's open public-procurement system built on the Open Contracting Data Standard. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Moldova, and for how much.

trackers.name: MTender (Public e-Procurement System)
trackers.desc: Moldova's official digital public-procurement service (Ministry of Finance), publishing all public tenders and procurement decisions online in real time via a government portal and open-data database, so citizens can watch how state and local budgets are spent.

trackers.name: National Integrity Authority (ANI)
trackers.desc: Legislator / public-official financial interest & asset declarations.

trackers.name: Public Services Agency (ASP)
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Constitutional Court of Moldova
trackers.desc: Constitutional Court of Moldova — supreme court (Moldova).

trackers.name: National Bureau of Statistics
trackers.desc: Moldova's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Moldova.

trackers.name: Ziarul de Gardă
trackers.desc: Moldovan investigative newspaper exposing corruption and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Fondul Național pentru Mediu — the fund that replaced the one you will find first
trackers.desc: CHECK THE NAME BEFORE YOU APPLY. Searching for Moldovan environmental funding surfaces the Fondul Ecologic Național across many government pages — created by Government Decision 988 of 26.09.98 under Law 1515/1993 — but it has been superseded. Law 54/2022 and Government Decision 711/2022 established the Fondul Național pentru Mediu within the state budget, exclusively for projects in environmental protection, climate change and sustainable management of natural resources. Its size is set by the annual state budget law and its money runs through the single treasury account. It is administered by the supervisory committee of ONIPM, the National Office for Implementation of Environmental Projects, which now issues the calls. AN EXISTING COMMITMENT DID NOT LAPSE: programmes the old fund's administrative council had already decided to finance — including drinking water and sanitation projects — transferred to the new Fund's administrator. The stated reason for reform was that the old arrangement limited environmental activity, and that better management would bring more transparency, equality and equity.

trackers.name: ONIPM — where the calls are actually announced
trackers.desc: WATCH THIS, NOT A STANDING WINDOW. ONIPM announces numbered calls approved by its supervisory committee — for example Apel nr. 04/2025, aimed at selecting investment projects to develop, modernise and extend recycling infrastructure for plastic, paper and packaging waste. Each call targets a defined theme, so the question is not whether the fund is open but whether a call matching your work is live. ELIGIBILITY SHAPE, from the predecessor fund: local public administration bodies, institutions, enterprises and civil society organisations of Moldova could apply, with restrictions on organisations already holding a grant — check the current regulation for the equivalent rule before assuming a second application is possible. ANOTHER ROUTE: a UNDP-GEF project on conservation and sustainable management of wetlands, focused on high nature value areas in the Prut basin and working with the Prutul de Jos Biosphere Reserve — the kind of programme a local group partners with rather than applies to.

trackers.name: Energy Community — private bodies may complain, and refusal is appealable
trackers.desc: A COMPLAINT MECHANISM WHERE REFUSAL BY THE GATEKEEPER CAN BE TAKEN OVER ITS HEAD — which is rare, and is the reason to know about this. Under Article 90 of the Energy Community Treaty, private bodies may approach the Secretariat with complaints about a Party's non-compliance, and under Article 12.2 of the Consolidated Rules the Secretariat initiates procedures in response to a complaint by a private body as well as on its own initiative. AND IF THE SECRETARIAT DECLINES: the revised Rules give the complainant the right to approach the Permanent High Level Group directly, which may hear the complaint directly or initiate a preliminary procedure — in most systems recorded in this map, a secretariat declining to act ends the matter. The PHLG can also take interim measures in matters of urgency under Article 47(c) — that is what matters when works are already under way, so ask for it expressly. THE ENVIRONMENTAL ACQUIS IS IN SCOPE, including the EIA Directive as amended by 2014/52, which was to be transposed by 1 January 2019. CHECK THE TRANSPOSITION DEADLINE FOR THE DIRECTIVE YOU RELY ON — failure to transpose by the stated date is itself the non-compliance, and is a far simpler case than arguing about how a rule was applied. THE REALISTIC WIN CONDITION: a case opens with an Opening Letter, escalates to a Reasoned Opinion giving two months to rectify, then to the Ministerial Council — but a case closes whenever the Party complies, and many are recorded as complied with before any decision was adopted. The opening of proceedings is the lever, not the final decision. YOU CAN ALSO JOIN AN EXISTING CASE: interested third parties may access the case file and submit written observations, provided they substantiate their legitimate interest. Case law from Opening Letters is published with dates and numbers, so precedent is visible. Write to the Energy Community Secretariat, Am Hof 4, 1010 Vienna. ONE MORE ROUTE: the amended Rules provide for cooperation with national authorities and courts, giving concrete assistance to national courts on the interpretation of Energy Community law — a domestic judge unsure how an EU-derived rule applies can be pointed at it.

trackers.name: Espoo points of contact — a named official, and ‘were you notified?’
trackers.desc: A NAMED OFFICIAL, A DIRECT EMAIL, AND A QUESTION WITH A DOCUMENTARY ANSWER. The UNECE publishes the points of contact regarding notification under article 3 of the Espoo Convention on EIA in a transboundary context: notifications of activities likely to cause significant adverse transboundary impact shall be transmitted to the relevant points of contact. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR AN ORDINARY LAND CASE: if a project sits near a border, the affected country's point of contact should have been notified — so ask both points of contact whether notification was given. It is a cheap, precise question, and failure to notify is a procedural defect in the consent. trackers.name: EcoContact and its Aarhus Centre — free environmental legal help (Moldova)

trackers.name: Fundația Est-Europeană — Moldova's main grant-maker, and its rules (Moldova)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: registered 3 November 2009 as successor to the Eurasia Foundation in Moldova, which had worked in the country since 1994. Offices at Str. 31 August 1989 nr. 98, floor 3, Chișinău MD-2004, +373 22 235343, info@eef.md. Its mission is equipping Moldovan citizens with the capacity and means for sustainable development, through education, technical assistance and grant programmes. It has run the Cetățeni activi, comunități prospere programme — active citizens, prosperous communities — across successive phases with Swedish funding, and publishes a record of grants awarded since 2010. Moldova had no funder in this file. READ THESE TWO RULES BEFORE YOU PLAN ANYTHING AROUND IT. Only non-governmental organisations legally registered in the Republic of Moldova are eligible — unlike the Serbian, Montenegrin, Kosovar and Belgian funders elsewhere in this file, an informal village group cannot apply and must register first or find a registered partner. Watch for the calls; do not write in cold. WHAT IT FUNDS: its programmes have covered social enterprise creation and development by local civil society organisations, employment for young people outside education and work, access to social, legal and medical services for disadvantaged groups in partnership with local authorities, and civic monitoring of business, government and donors. trackers.name: Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina
trackers.desc: Official site of the state-level Court of BiH with verdicts and case information. · Find here: the judgments and case records of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina (including the war-crimes sections).

trackers.name: Centar za životnu sredinu (Center for Environment, Banja Luka)

trackers.name: Justice and Environment — European green-law network
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the European network of environmental-law NGOs, whose national member here is Center for Environment (Centar za životnu sredinu).
