trackers.desc: WHO TO INSTRUCT: Lawyers for Human Rights (LHR), an independent South African organisation with a track record spanning nearly four decades of public interest litigation, which provides FREE LEGAL SERVICES to vulnerable, marginalised and indigent individuals and communities whose constitutional rights have been unlawfully infringed, through six strategic programmes staffed by specialist practitioners. THE PROGRAMME THAT MATTERS HERE: its land and housing work was established in OCTOBER 1998 to protect and promote the rights of RURAL DWELLERS DIRECTLY THREATENED WITH EVICTION — defending farm workers facing eviction, and advocating for their tenure security through training workshops, a regular newsletter and networking. Alongside it sits a STRATEGIC LITIGATION UNIT based at the Pretoria Law Clinic, running since 2003, which focuses on just administrative action for indigent persons and communities and increasingly on land reform matters, and which also works to protect the rights of MINING-AFFECTED COMMUNITIES and to secure corporate compliance in the extractives space. Ask for the programme by name — land and housing, or strategic litigation — rather than making a general enquiry. AND THE THING TO KEEP EVEN IF YOU NEVER RING LHR: South Africa has a PUBLIC DIRECTORY OF FREE LEGAL SERVICES listing the Rental Housing Tribunal, Legal Aid centres, UNIVERSITY LAW CLINICS and Legal Practice Councils with their addresses and locations — the single most useful page for a household facing eviction, because it does not depend on any one organisation having capacity. WHO IT SUITS: South African farm dwellers, rural households and mining-affected communities facing eviction or seeking tenure security, and anyone who needs to find the nearest free legal office themselves. CAVEATS: a public interest organisation with finite capacity that takes cases of wider significance; the directory lists services, not guarantees of representation. For farm dwellers and labour tenant claims in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa's AFRA entry; for environmental litigation, CER; for the Xolobeni line of cases, CALS.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Centre (LRC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: South Africa's largest public-interest law centre. Its Land and Natural Resources work litigates for rural communities, small-scale fishers and farmers on access to land, mining and extractive projects, customary governance and, increasingly, environmental and climate justice, alongside a long housing-and-evictions practice. Offices in Johannesburg (with the Constitutional Litigation Unit), Cape Town, Durban and Makhanda. WHO IT SUITS: a community or a class of vulnerable clients rather than an individual dispute — the LRC is client-based but works on a strategic-impact model and selects matters through its focus areas, so approach the nearest office with a community-level problem.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Centre (LRC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: South Africa's largest public-interest law centre. Its Land and Natural Resources work litigates for rural communities, small-scale fishers and farmers on access to land, mining and extractive projects, customary governance and, increasingly, environmental and climate justice, alongside a long housing-and-evictions practice. Offices in Johannesburg (with the Constitutional Litigation Unit), Cape Town, Durban and Makhanda. WHO IT SUITS: a community or a class of vulnerable clients rather than an individual dispute — the LRC is client-based but works on a strategic-impact model and selects matters through its focus areas, so approach the nearest office with a community-level problem.

trackers.name: Conservation Outcomes
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a KwaZulu-Natal-based non-profit that walks private and communal landowners through biodiversity stewardship — planning, establishment and governance of conservation areas, the declaration process itself, and the post-declaration management support that declaration alone does not provide: annual plans of operation, veld and fire management, alien species control, and help applying for the tax deduction and rates exemptions. It also develops tourism, ethical hunting and natural-resource ventures so protected land can pay for itself. USE IT: when you have land worth protecting but need someone who has done the declaration paperwork before.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Centre (LRC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: South Africa's largest public-interest law centre. Its Land and Natural Resources work litigates for rural communities, small-scale fishers and farmers on access to land, mining and extractive projects, customary governance and, increasingly, environmental and climate justice, alongside a long housing-and-evictions practice. Offices in Johannesburg (with the Constitutional Litigation Unit), Cape Town, Durban and Makhanda. WHO IT SUITS: a community or a class of vulnerable clients rather than an individual dispute — the LRC is client-based but works on a strategic-impact model and selects matters through its focus areas, so approach the nearest office with a community-level problem.

trackers.name: CapeNature — Protected Areas and Stewardship
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Western Cape's conservation authority and the body that signs biodiversity stewardship contracts with landowners in the province, then takes the site through to declaration as a nature reserve by the provincial Minister — the Twee Rivieren Nature Reserve was established this way by seven landowners acting together. Intentions to declare are published for comment. USE IT: to start a stewardship application on Western Cape land, to check what the Minister has given notice of intent to declare, and to reach the conservation stewardship specialist who handles the programme.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Centre (LRC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: South Africa's largest public-interest law centre. Its Land and Natural Resources work litigates for rural communities, small-scale fishers and farmers on access to land, mining and extractive projects, customary governance and, increasingly, environmental and climate justice, alongside a long housing-and-evictions practice. Offices in Johannesburg (with the Constitutional Litigation Unit), Cape Town, Durban and Makhanda. WHO IT SUITS: a community or a class of vulnerable clients rather than an individual dispute — the LRC is client-based but works on a strategic-impact model and selects matters through its focus areas, so approach the nearest office with a community-level problem.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: iWatch Africa
trackers.desc: Ghanaian accountability project tracking corruption, illicit flows and public spending.

trackers.name: Ghana Audit Service
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Ghana, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Ghana — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Data Protection Commission (Ghana)
trackers.desc: Data Protection Commission (Ghana) — Ghana’s independent data-protection / information commissioner, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Ghana Central Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Ghana — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: GhanaLII
trackers.desc: Ghana Legal Information Institute: free case law and legislation. · Find here: free Ghanaian judgments and legislation (GhanaLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC)
trackers.desc: Ghana’s official company register under the Companies Act 2019 — incorporation records and name search.

trackers.name: Registrar General's Department
trackers.desc: registration authority

trackers.name: Right to Information Commission (Ghana)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority; Ghana’s RTI Commission is the sole body mandated by the Right to Information Act 2019 (Act 989) to promote, monitor, protect and enforce the right to information, Ghana.

trackers.name: GHANEPS
trackers.desc: Ghana's mandatory electronic public-procurement system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Ghana, and for how much.

trackers.name: Ghana Audit Service
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Ghana — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Ghana Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (GHEITI)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and company ownership in Ghana.

trackers.name: Ghana EITI Beneficial Ownership Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Ghana Statistical Service
trackers.desc: Ghana's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Ghana.

trackers.name: Legal Aid Commission — free representation, and what it costs you
trackers.desc: FREE ADVICE AND FREE REPRESENTATION for an indigent person with reasonable grounds to be party to a matter in court, after a means test. THE COMMISSION HANDLES ALL LEGAL MATTERS — its own FAQ answers yes — so a land or environmental case is not excluded. ONCE YOU QUALIFY, NO OFFICER MAY DEMAND ANYTHING FROM YOU: the Commission states plainly that this is against its code of ethics, which is worth knowing because informal demands are what stop people using free services. You may also choose your preferred lawyer or mediator, and once your documents are endorsed with the Commission's stamp, Legal Aid automatically becomes your legal representative even without a lawyer present. CHECK COVERAGE BEFORE TRAVELLING: the Commission says it is operative in the traditional 10 regions and had yet to create offices in the other 6. It also gives no guaranteed timescale for concluding a case. Head office at the former Prosecution Division Building, Ministry of Land & Natural Resources, Starlets 91 Rd, Accra — info@lac.gov.gh, 0302975749.

trackers.name: CREMA — a devolution certificate over land outside protected areas
trackers.desc: HOW A GHANAIAN COMMUNITY GETS AUTHORITY OVER ITS OWN RESOURCES. A group of communities agrees a common objective over a defined area, and the Community Resource Management Area is regulated by its own constitution, bylaws and natural resource management plan, drawn up by committees of elected community members working with the Wildlife Division and District Assemblies. On inauguration the CREMA receives a Certificate of Devolution from the Minister responsible for forests, signifying its autonomy and authority over the area — authority to manage the land, protect wildlife and curb illegal logging, mining and bushmeat hunting. It is the Wildlife Division's primary mechanism for resource management outside protected areas and forest reserves. BENEFIT-SHARING IS DEFINED INTERNALLY by the CREMA rather than imposed from outside, though national benefit-sharing and tax law may affect the formula, and there has been work toward vesting CREMAs with full or partial carbon rights. Over 30 CREMAs were at various phases by 2012; IUCN, Conservation Alliance and WAPCA provide technical support.

trackers.name: Three weaknesses to plan around before starting a CREMA
trackers.desc: SAID BY GHANA'S OWN OFFICIALS AND RESEARCHERS. 1. THE LEGAL BASIS IS WEAK. A Wildlife Division official states that CREMA policy has cabinet approval, which is not equivalent to legislative backing; the minister's power to issue devolution certificates comes from a window in the Wildlife Preservation Act 43 of 1961, with explicit provision sitting in a Wildlife bill long before parliament without passing — in his words, it is not that there is no legal basis, ‘except that it is weak’. 2. THE FUNDING CLIFF. Research records that once the Certificate of Devolution was granted and project funds ran out, communities were left entirely to their own devices, with executives dissatisfied at government's absence in resolving conflicts. Plan for the period after the supporting NGO leaves, and build it into the management plan. 3. OFFICIALS CANNOT BE REMOVED MID-TERM: because the constitution provides elected officials with 3-year terms whose office is legally binding through the minister's devolution, an executive who is not functioning properly cannot be removed before the term expires — so the founding election matters more than it looks. CONTEXT: the State has centralised control over forest and wildlife resources, which has also legitimised chiefs' claims to complete land ownership, sustaining arrangements where both draw royalties and rents from forested land often at the expense of local people and migrants.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: CREMA authority descends from game wardenship, not from land title — and without a gazetted district bye-law it binds nobody
trackers.desc: WHAT A CERTIFICATE OF DEVOLUTION GIVES YOU AND WHAT IT LEAVES WITH THE STATE. The Wildlife Division of the Forestry Commission devolves management authority over a defined area to a community body — Community Resource Management Committees at village level, a CREMA Executive Committee above them — and the Minister responsible for lands and natural resources signs the certificate once the area is established and inaugurated. The original legal hook is section 1 of the Wild Animal Preservation Act 1961, which empowers the Minister to confer game wardenship on ordinary people: the authority runs to the resource and the people policing it, not to ownership of the ground, and a Wildlife Division presentation of April 2025 places the comprehensive provisions at sections 16 to 18 of the Wildlife Resources Management Act 2023 (Act 1115). The CREMA constitution is an internal instrument; what makes the rules enforceable against an outsider is a bye-law passed and gazetted by the District Assembly, so a CREMA with a certificate and no gazetted bye-law has standing among its own members and little else. Compare The Gambia, where the equivalent process ends in permanent community ownership of the forest rather than devolved management of the resources on it. CAVEATS: this page describes CREMA promotion as a divisional strategy and publishes no application steps, no timetable and no named CREMA officer; and fcghana.org serves live mirrors at oldwebsite.fcghana.org and newsite.fcghana.org, both of which surface in search results with different navigation, so confirm the address bar before relying on a page.

trackers.name: Legal Aid Commission — civil land litigation is in scope here, unlike The Gambia, but no means threshold is published
trackers.desc: THE DIVISION THAT MATTERS FOR A LAND CASE IS THE CITIZENS ADVISORY DIVISION, AND IT IS THE ONE PEOPLE SKIP. The Commission runs three divisions under the Legal Aid Commission Act 2018 (Act 977): the Citizens Advisory Division, which is principally in charge of civil litigation on behalf of indigent clients; the Public Defenders' Division, which is criminal; and an Alternative Dispute Resolution Division, which mediates any dispute reported to the Commission that is amenable to mediation. Ghana therefore does what The Gambia does not — it will run a civil case, not merely advise on one. WHAT IS NOT PUBLISHED: no income threshold, no asset test, no application form and no timetable. The test is stated only as indigence, which means the assessment happens at the office rather than before you go — contrast South Africa, which publishes a separate and higher monthly threshold for land matters specifically. Head office correspondence goes to P. O. Box 18432, Accra; the published line is +233 (0) 302 975 749, email info@lac.gov.gh, office hours Monday to Friday 08:00 to 16:00, and a WhatsApp number is advertised in the site header. SITE FAULT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU HUNT FOR A FORM: the footer Quick Links on the live site point at http://localhost/LegalAidCommission/ addresses — a development build that was published without rewriting its own links, so Services, Acts, Reports and the RTI Manual are unreachable from the footer. Use the top navigation instead.

trackers.name: Land Valuation Division — the escrow account is the precondition nobody asks about, and the review clock is 30 days
trackers.desc: ASK WHETHER THE COMPENSATION MONEY IS ALREADY IN ESCROW BEFORE ARGUING ABOUT THE VALUATION. The Land Valuation Division of the Lands Commission assesses the compensation payable when the State acquires land, and also does stamp duty, rating valuation lists and valuations for the public at a fee. Under the Land Act 2020 (Act 1036), the Lands Commission is barred from facilitating a compulsory acquisition unless the intended user proves in writing that the compensation funds have been paid into an interest-yielding escrow account that the Commission then manages in trust, and the acquiring ministry or agency must have Cabinet approval and a budget line. A written enquiry about whether that has happened is a legitimate question to the Commission and a much earlier intervention point than a valuation dispute. If the assessment is what you dispute: apply to the Commission for a review, and the Commission must respond within 30 days. Still dissatisfied, the matter goes to resolution under the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act 2010 (Act 798), and none of that removes the right to go to the High Court. The Division is headed by a named director, Surv. Dr. Theodora Mantebea Mends, and the Commission has offices in all 16 regions plus limited district offices for valuation and survey. CAVEATS: the Act 1036 provisions summarised here were read from reproductions of the statute, not from the Commission's own site, which does not set out the review route or the escrow rule. The Commission also publishes serial statutory notices — applications for deed registration carry a fourteen-day window to lodge an objection at the regional office — but lc.gov.gh refuses automated access, so those notices cannot be monitored by any tool or alert; someone has to open the site in a browser.

trackers.name: A Rocha Ghana — sued its own government to stop a bauxite mine, and had never litigated before
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the organisation leading the fight to stop bauxite mining in the Atewa Range Forest, which in January 2020 filed a notice of civil action against the Government of Ghana and took the case to the High Court in Accra — joined by other civil society groups and by private citizens as co-plaintiffs, with networks numbering dozens of organisations behind them. THE DETAIL THAT SHOULD ENCOURAGE ANY COMMUNITY GROUP READING THIS: its national director says the organisation had never filed suit before — twenty years of conservation and campaigning work, then a first case against the state, with him as the first witness and two days of cross-examination by a state lawyer. Not litigating before is not a reason not to start. HOW THE CASE WAS BUILT, WHICH IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART: the claim rests on constitutional rights to life, dignity and a clean and healthy environment and on the state's own constitutional duty to protect natural resources, and it asks for orders restraining mining and its related activities and compelling protection — rather than asking for compensation. Alongside the court case they ran a 95km walk by Atewa's own communities carrying clean water from the forest to government in Accra, global petitions, letters from aluminium-buying companies, a motion at the international conservation union, and a costed alternative: upgrading Atewa from forest reserve to national park, with a tourism revenue estimate attached. A campaign that only says no is weaker than one that arrives with a number. WHO IT SUITS: Ghanaian communities facing extraction or clearance in or near a forest reserve. A Rocha Ghana works from four field bases with coastal mangrove communities, villages around Atewa, farmers and fishers at Lake Bosomtwe and communities around Mole National Park. CAVEATS: this is a campaign page, not an intake route — no case-selection criteria or legal-aid offer is published, and the organisation instructed a private Ghanaian lawyer rather than running an in-house legal service. The Atewa litigation was still running at last report; treat it as a live campaign to join rather than a precedent already won.

trackers.name: Wacam — mining-affected communities mandate it to negotiate their compensation, and it has won payouts, water and closures
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Wacam, formed in 1998 in Tarkwa in response to the harms of Ghana's third gold rush, now working in over ninety mining-affected communities. Its own description of what it does is the list a community needs: paralegal training, litigation support, policy submissions, and community organising. HOW COMMUNITIES ACTUALLY USE IT, from its published record: affected people aggrieved by the compensation and resettlement packages offered for their farmlands and houses PETITIONED AND MANDATED Wacam and the Centre for Public Interest Law to engage the company on their behalf — in that case AngloGold Ashanti's Iduapriem mine over Mankessim Ajopa and Teberebie. That is the model: the community formally mandates a named organisation to negotiate, rather than each household facing the company alone. WHAT HAS COME OUT OF IT: compensation paid to 35 community people in Teberebie and 21 in Obuasi after engagements over human rights violations; potable water and access roads obtained in Obuasi; negotiated compensation for victims of abuses at the Obuasi mine; a victims support programme covering medical care and education for people harmed; and companies held to account for cyanide spillages. THE ONE TO COPY ANYWHERE: a female activist from Teberebie and others from Obuasi GATHERED THE EVIDENCE ON FAULTY TAILINGS STORAGE FACILITIES THAT LED THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY TO CLOSE THE FACILITIES DOWN — community-collected evidence producing a regulator's shutdown order. Its women's committee has also put around ten activists into District Assembly and Unit Committee seats, which puts community voices inside the body that approves things. It argues publicly that Ghana's mining law lacks no-go zones, human rights audits and provisions on cyanide spillage. WHO IT SUITS: Ghanaian communities facing mining concessions, resettlement, compensation disputes or water contamination. CAVEATS: Wacam is an advocacy and organising body — the legal work runs with partner lawyers (CEPIL acts as counsel and has its own entry in this file); no intake route or fee information was published; and negotiated compensation is not the same as stopping a mine.

trackers.name: CEPIL — a Ghanaian public interest law firm that gives mining communities free courtroom representation, and sued over the acreage-versus-headcount compensation rule
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Centre for Public Interest Law, established 1999 in Accra and describing itself as a rights-based law firm that provides free legal representation. Its landmark record includes defending 30,000 squatters against eviction by the Accra city authorities, defending mining communities in the Wassa district, and introducing paralegalism into Ghanaian human rights advocacy. WHAT IT OFFERS A COMMUNITY DIRECTLY: free courtroom representation to mining-affected communities, delivered across the Eastern, Ashanti and Brong-Ahafo regions, together with human rights education and paralegal training inside those same communities — so the community keeps capacity after the case ends. THE CASE TO READ BEFORE ACCEPTING ANY CROP COMPENSATION OFFER: a mining company dumped rock waste on farms, destroying oil palm, cocoa, coconut, cassava, pineapple and cocoyam, and offered compensation calculated on the acreage system. The Teberebe Concerned Farmers Association refused it and insisted on the head count system — enumerating the actual crops destroyed — as the only fair measure, and CEPIL sued in the High Court at Tarkwa for adequate compensation and for declarations that the company had violated their constitutional rights. How the loss is COUNTED decides what you are paid, and the company chooses the method unless someone refuses it. That is a question any farmer facing destruction can ask on day one. CEPIL also trains community members on mining law, compensation and grievance mechanisms — in one 2025 workshop, 39 people in the Ahafo region, 25 of them women — works on right to information officers, and litigates housing and eviction cases. WHO IT SUITS: Ghanaian communities and households facing eviction, mining damage, or a compensation offer they suspect is calculated to be low. CAVEATS: a small organisation with a national caseload; no published intake criteria or means test was found, so approach early rather than on the eve of a deadline. It works alongside Wacam, whose entry covers the organising and negotiation side of the same fights.

trackers.name: People's Dialogue on Human Settlements and GHAFUP — counting Old Fadama is what stopped it being cleared, three times over
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Ghana Federation of the Urban Poor (GHAFUP), formed in 2003 out of the eviction crisis at Old Fadama and built from daily savings groups — by early 2005 present in six of Ghana's ten regions — with People's Dialogue on Human Settlements, a registered non-profit, providing documentation, technical support and advocacy. WHY IT IS FILED, AND THE LESSON IS IN THE RESEARCH TITLE — “IF IN DOUBT, COUNT”: Old Fadama occupies about 31.3 hectares along the Odaw River and Korle Lagoon in central Accra, established 1981, with a population reported around 80,000 and 30,000 under threat of eviction at the outset. Government estimates of who lived there conflicted with reality, so residents ran their own enumeration in December 2004 — mostly women administering questionnaires and counting every structure — supported by federation teams from South Africa and Zimbabwe who had done it before. Further enumerations followed in 2006–2007 and 2009, each timed to counter a NEW eviction threat from a new city government. The count established both the true population and the scale of economic activity, and the community has held its ground for years through enumeration, mapping and long negotiation with the city authority rather than through litigation. WHAT ELSE THE ALLIANCE PRODUCES: the federation negotiated over clearance around the lagoon ahead of a de-silting project rather than being cleared by it, and at Amui Djor in Ashaiman members contributing toward acquisition moved into completed housing — 26 of 31 families reported moved in, the rest to follow. WHO IT SUITS: Ghanaian urban communities facing eviction or relocation, and any community whose official population figures are wrong in the government's favour. CAVEATS: this is negotiation and documentation, not litigation — for courtroom representation Ghana's CEPIL entry is the route, and for mining-affected communities, Wacam. Enumeration buys standing and time; it does not confer title, and Old Fadama's threat has recurred with each change of city government.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Centre, Accra — walk in Monday to Thursday, 9am to 4:30pm, no appointment needed
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Legal Resources Centre, a Ghanaian NGO building human rights capacity within communities and linking community concerns to national policy institutions. WHAT MAKES IT USABLE, AND IT IS THE PLAINEST ACCESS STATEMENT IN THIS ENTIRE FILE: experienced lawyers offer legal aid to indigents; the clinics run MONDAY TO THURSDAY, 9:00am to 4:30pm, and CLIENTS CAN SIMPLY WALK IN WITHIN THOSE HOURS WITHOUT AN APPOINTMENT — or call or email to schedule one. It also offers alternative dispute resolution sessions to clients who prefer that route, and has taken up cases of PUBLIC INTEREST to advance rights under the 1992 Constitution, other legislation and the treaties Ghana has ratified. Its legal aid work is concentrated around the Nima/Mamobi community, and it runs five-day LEGAL MOBILE CLINICS that set up where people already are — documented at the Dome Market for Ga East and at the Tema Station lorry park for Accra Metropolis, 9am to 3pm daily, offering free advice and representation, with an emphasis on women's access. Offices at Dzorwulu, Accra. It works alongside the state Legal Aid Commission on paralegal coordination. WHO IT SUITS: Ghanaians in and around Accra who need free legal advice, mediation or representation and cannot navigate an appointment system — including tenants, families in land disputes and people facing eviction. CAVEATS: a general human rights and access-to-justice organisation, not a land or mining specialist, and its clinic footprint is largely Accra-centred with mobile clinics dependent on project funding. For mining communities Ghana's Wacam entry, for courtroom representation CEPIL, and for urban settlement enumeration, People's Dialogue.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants Programme, Ghana — grants straight to community organisations, up to about US$30,000, no intermediary NGO required
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the Global Environment Facility Small Grants Programme (SGP), delivered through UNDP with a national country programme in Ghana — the rare window that grants DIRECTLY to community-based organisations and small NGOs rather than through a large intermediary. A recent Ghana call funded community-driven initiatives along the Black Volta Basin, addressing environmental challenges alongside sustainable development and social inclusion, with a value up to about US$30,000 per grant. WHY THIS IS THE MOST REACHABLE MONEY IN THIS FILE: the endowments and conservation funds recorded elsewhere pay park agencies, protected-area partners or vetted professional organisations; SGP's design point is the village-level group with a bank account and a constitution. US$30,000 will not buy a parcel of land, but it WILL pay for the things that decide whether a community can hold ground — boundary mapping, a land-use plan, a legal-status application, meetings, travel to the district office, and the equipment to document what a project is doing to you. HOW TO APPROACH IT: SGP runs as a national country programme with its own coordinator and national steering committee, and calls are issued periodically with fixed deadlines rather than rolling — so the practical step is to find the current country call and its closing date before writing anything, and to have your organisation registered in advance because eligibility runs on legal status. WHO IT SUITS: Ghanaian community-based organisations, associations and small NGOs with a concrete environmental or land-related project and no access to large donors. CAVEATS: it funds ENVIRONMENTAL PROJECTS, not litigation, not land purchase and not campaigns against a named developer — frame the application around what you will build, restore, map or manage. Deadlines are real and calls are periodic; grant ceilings vary by country and cycle, so confirm the current Ghana figures. For emergency support to threatened defenders, the African Environmental Defenders Fund already recorded in this file; for courtroom representation in Ghana, CEPIL.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? NO — this is project-to-project country. Natural Justice's 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, with additional staff in Antananarivo, Botswana and Guinea; elsewhere it works across African countries on a project-to-project basis. So you are asking them to take on a project, not walking into an office — approach with a defined case and expect that answer to depend on their current programme. Its team page does list staff and fellows beyond the hub countries. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR)
trackers.desc: Nigerian center exposing corruption and public-fund abuse.

trackers.name: Nigeria EITI Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Persons with Significant Control Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: BudgIT
trackers.desc: Nigerian civic-tech organisation (est. 2011) that simplifies federal and state budgets and tracks public-project delivery through its Tracka and State of States tools. Here you can trace how Nigeria's federal and state budgets are spent, with project-level tracking of whether the money delivered.

trackers.name: Code of Conduct Bureau
trackers.desc: Legislator / public-official financial interest & asset declarations.

trackers.name: Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre (CISLAC / TI Nigeria)
trackers.desc: Nigerian chapter of Transparency International — civil-society advocacy on anti-corruption, public debt and budget accountability.

trackers.name: Independent Corrupt Practices Commission (ICPC)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Nigeria — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
trackers.desc: Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) — Nigeria’s independent data-protection / information commissioner, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues and (in Nigeria) beneficial-ownership data for Nigeria.

trackers.name: Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU)
trackers.desc: Nigeria's financial intelligence unit, collecting and analysing suspicious-transaction disclosures to combat money laundering and terrorist financing. Here you can trace how suspicious transactions are reported and money-laundering intelligence is produced in Nigeria.

trackers.name: NigeriaLII
trackers.desc: Free database of Nigerian case law and legislation, part of the AfricanLII network. · Find here: free Nigerian judgments and legislation (NigeriaLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: NOCOPO
trackers.desc: Nigeria's open-contracting portal run by the Bureau of Public Procurement. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Nigeria, and for how much.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Audits federal public accounts. Here you can trace public-audit findings on waste, irregularity and misspending in Nigeria.

trackers.name: Open Treasury Portal
trackers.desc: Nigeria's federal portal publishing daily payments and financial data. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Nigeria.

trackers.name: Publish What You Pay Nigeria
trackers.desc: National civil-society coalition of the global Publish What You Pay campaign — advocates for transparency in oil, gas and mining revenues in Nigeria.

trackers.name: Tracka (BudgIT Foundation)
trackers.desc: Grassroots platform run by the BudgIT Foundation enabling citizens to monitor the implementation of budgeted public projects in their own communities — sharing photos and reports on roads, schools, boreholes and health centres, and engaging elected representatives to demand completion.

trackers.name: Bureau of Public Procurement (NOCOPO)
trackers.desc: Federal procurement regulator and open-contracting portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Nigeria, and for how much.

trackers.name: Corporate Affairs Commission
trackers.desc: Nigeria's company registry with a searchable persons-with-significant-control (beneficial ownership) register. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find who really owns and controls them; their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Nigeria — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: High Court of the Federal Capital Territory
trackers.desc: High Court of the Federal Capital Territory — tribunal (Nigeria).

trackers.name: National Bureau of Statistics
trackers.desc: Nigeria's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Nigeria.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General for the Federation (Nigeria)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Nigeria — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Federal High Court of Nigeria
trackers.desc: Federal High Court of Nigeria — tribunal in Nigeria (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Limitation periods — the deadline that decides Nigerian environmental claims
trackers.desc: CHECK THE CLOCK BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: limitation periods set deadlines for commencing a claim in Nigeria, and a claim filed outside the applicable period may be refused without the court considering its merits — however strong the evidence. Environmental damage is especially exposed to this because harm often continues or emerges long after the original event, and whether a wrong is ongoing or merely has continuing consequences is a contested area of Nigerian law — that distinction decides whether the clock has already run. Which law applies depends on the activity, location and nature of the harm, across the 1999 Constitution as amended, the NESREA Act (No. 20 of 2007), the Environmental Impact Assessment Act, the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 and state regulations. USE IT: establish your limitation position first, because it governs whether any other route is still open.

trackers.name: Nigerian Conservation Foundation — land held against a city
trackers.desc: A DOCUMENTED CASE OF LAND ACQUIRED AND HELD AGAINST URBAN DEVELOPMENT. NCF acquired the site from Chevron Nigeria in 1989 and established the Lekki Conservation Centre in 1990, expressly to protect the wildlife and mangrove forests of the south-west coastline from the threat of urban development — 78 hectares of swamp, secondary forest and savannah holding one of the last mangrove patches in Lagos. IT WAS ESTABLISHED BEFORE LEKKI WAS BUILT, and the peninsula around it is now among the most intensively developed areas in West Africa. The reserve held. TWO TRANSFERABLE LESSONS: site selection was deliberate and documented — 3 candidate areas were surveyed in 1987 by an NCF technical team with the state agriculture ministry before Lekki was chosen, rather than taking whatever was offered; and the facility came with an annual funding stream for management from the outset, because acquisition without an endowed management income tends not to survive. NCF runs projects in 9 states, including Participatory Forest Management in Taraba and management of the Becheve Nature Reserve at Obudu, Cross River State; national secretariat at Lekki, regional office in Calabar; added to UNEP's Global 500 Roll of Honour in 1992.

trackers.name: Land Use Act — customary rights of occupancy, and who really owns the land
trackers.desc: START HERE, BECAUSE THE STARTING POSITION IS NOT FAVOURABLE. Section 1 vests all land in each state in the Governor, held in trust for all Nigerians — commentary records that on commencement previous holders effectively became tenants on their own land. Rights of occupancy are statutory (urban, granted by the Governor under s.5) or customary (non-urban, granted by the Local Government under s.6) — and a Local Government may grant a customary right of occupancy to a community, for residential, grazing or other purposes. DEEMED GRANTS EXIST: where land was vested in someone immediately before the Act, a grant arises by operation of law and a certificate may be issued on application. TWO MISCONCEPTIONS THAT LOSE LAND: customary land is not exempt from the Act — it remains under the Governor and holders must still obtain customary rights of occupancy; and a Certificate of Occupancy is not freehold — it is prima facie evidence of title, effectively a 99-year lease, and the presumption can be rebutted by a party with a better claim. Inherited or family land still requires the Governor's consent on transfer, without which the transaction is void.

trackers.name: Revocation and compensation — decide where the money goes before it arrives
trackers.desc: WHEN A PROJECT TAKES COMMUNITY LAND. Government may revoke a right of occupancy for public purposes under ss.28–29, with compensation payable, and the power of compulsory acquisition is constitutionally recognised — but revocation must be valid and compensation actually paid; courts have addressed failures to acquire land properly, as in the gas plant case at Obite community, Rivers State. THE PROVISION TO ACT ON EARLY: where the holder entitled to compensation is a community, the Governor may direct that it be paid either to the chief or leader of the community, to be disposed of for the community's benefit under customary law, or into a fund specified by the Governor to be applied for the community's benefit. The choice is the Governor's, not the community's — and money routed through a single leader is a well-known failure point. Decide which route your community wants, resolve it formally, and press for it before any award is made. Disputes over valuation and the fairness of compensation are recorded as common.

trackers.name: NESREA field offices — one page routes you to the enforcement office in your own state, with a state@nesrea.gov.ng address
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE ROUTER FOR NIGERIA: ONE VERIFIED PAGE INSTEAD OF THIRTY-SEVEN GUESSED STATE AGENCY DOMAINS. The Agency lists six zonal headquarters — North Central at Jos, North East at Gombe, North West at Kano, South South at Port Harcourt, South East at Owerri, South West at Ibadan — a Lagos liaison office, and state field offices with street addresses across the federation. Where an email is published it follows the pattern state@nesrea.gov.ng, and zonal addresses follow nczone@ and ss@; confirmed on the page for Plateau, Nasarawa, Kwara, Kaduna, Kebbi, Sokoto, Zamfara, Imo, Oyo, Ondo, Cross River, Edo and Lagos. Headquarters is No. 56 Lome Crescent, Wuse Zone 7, Abuja. The same navigation carries a Report A Violation route, an Environmental Violations page, a permits and audit portal at neims.nesrea.gov.ng and an import clearance portal at nics.nesrea.gov.ng. WHAT THE PAGE GETS WRONG, SO YOU DO NOT WASTE A JOURNEY: the Jigawa State Field Office is listed as a heading with no address at all, and the Oyo State Field Office address ends “Ibadan, Uyo State” — two different states in one line. The page also claims 22 state offices in its own preamble while listing more headings than that, and most field offices publish no email or telephone number, so the zonal headquarters is the more reliable first contact for a state whose office details are blank.

trackers.name: Accredited environmental consultants register — check the category the firm that signed your EIA is actually accredited for
trackers.desc: ACCREDITATION IN NIGERIA IS BY CATEGORY, AND A FIRM CAN BE ACCREDITED FOR ONE THING AND SIGNING ANOTHER. The register publishes, for each consultant, a user ID, the firm name, status, the certificate categories held — Environmental Audit, Environmental Studies, Environmental Management System, Environmental Technology, Laboratory Services, Waste Management — plus an email address and telephone number. A firm holding Environmental Audit alone and producing an environmental study is outside its accredited category, which is a documentary point you can make in writing without needing a technical rebuttal of the report. Roughly 379 rows are listed and that is not the number of firms: several user IDs repeat, one of them three times, and at least one repeated ID appears with two different certificate lists, so cite the row you relied on rather than the firm name alone. THE REGISTER'S OWN INTEGRITY IS THE CAVEAT: every row reads Active, with no lapsed, suspended or withdrawn state anywhere in it, so absence of a sanction here is not evidence that none was imposed. Several rows are plainly unscrubbed self-registrations — entries named as tests, an entry whose certificate field reads null, and entries carrying placeholder telephone numbers such as 9000000000 — which tells you the list is accepted at registration rather than curated. Read it as a claim register, not a vetted panel.

trackers.name: ERA / Friends of the Earth Nigeria — two toll-free green lines to call when a spill, flare or rupture starts, and field monitors who come out
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Nigeria's foremost environmental advocacy organisation, founded in 1993 and the Nigerian member of Friends of the Earth International. IT PUBLISHES TOLL-FREE GREEN LINES FOR EXACTLY THIS SITUATION — 08031230088 and 08031230089 — to call in the event of a spill, pipeline rupture, fire, gas flare, or water, land or air pollution, and to ask for help responding and preventing recurrence. That is a rare thing in this file: a number, not a form. WHAT THEY DO WHEN YOU CALL, taken from their own field reporting: they visit the spill site, follow up by telephone with community leaders, and document what the joint investigation visit concluded — including where the JIV was inconclusive because the parties disagreed on the volume spilled and the leak was left unstopped. Independent documentation of a JIV is often the only counterweight to the operator's own account, and it is what later cases are built from. ERA's work has fed litigation: it marked a Dutch court ruling against Shell for four Niger Delta fishermen after a thirteen-year battle. It coordinates Oilwatch International's Africa work, hosts Green Alliance Nigeria, and campaigns on forests and biodiversity, energy and extractives, food sovereignty and GMOs, and corporate accountability. WHO IT SUITS: Niger Delta and other oil-, gas- and pipeline-affected communities; also forest and agricultural communities facing extractive or agro-industrial projects. Headquarters: KM 9 Benin-Lagos Road, Isiohor, Benin City, Edo State. CAVEATS: ERA is an advocacy organisation, not a law firm — it documents, campaigns and connects to counsel rather than filing your case. Its own site warns that a separate group has been using ERA's headquarters address and mailbox without any connection to the organisation, so verify who you are dealing with. Two domains, eraction.org and erafoen.org, both carry its material.

trackers.name: CEHRD, Port Harcourt — rural-focused documentation that has repeatedly contradicted an oil company's claim to have cleaned a site
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Centre for Environment, Human Rights and Development, founded in 1999 in the Niger Delta by conservationists, environmentalists, activists and health workers, registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission, and deliberately rural-based and rural-focused. It monitors, documents and reports human rights violations across the region, and states that in some cases it provides legal advocacy to victims — it defended communities in the Bodo versus Shell litigation. WHAT MAKES ITS DOCUMENTATION WORTH MORE THAN A COMPLAINT: with an international human rights organisation it returned to sites the company said were remediated and found otherwise. At Bomu Well 11 the site was still visibly contaminated in 2015 despite the company's claims; a later excavation, more than fifty years after the original spill and a decade after the 2015 clean-up claim, revealed a thick layer of oil below the soil surface, with rainwater carrying it into a nearby creek. At the Bomu Manifold, an area declared remediated was still heavily contaminated; after the report the company sent staff back, and pollution was still visible in 2024. Go back and check what was signed off. A clean-up certificate is a claim, not a fact, and the way you beat it is a dated site visit with photographs. Its published work also includes a joint report calling for the company to accept responsibility for Niger Delta spills and make a substantial initial payment toward clean-up, socio-economic baseline studies of oil-impacted Ogoni communities used in restoration planning, and training in alternative livelihoods for people whose land was destroyed by spills — plus mangrove restoration work with communities at Bori and Rumuolumeni. Legacy Center, 6 Abuja Lane, D-Line, Port Harcourt, Rivers State. WHO IT SUITS: Niger Delta communities facing spills, failed remediation or a compensation claim that turns on whether a site was ever really cleaned. CAVEATS: primarily a documentation, research and advocacy organisation — legal advocacy is offered in some cases rather than as a general service, and no intake route or fee information was published; its focus is the Niger Delta, though it describes its scope as national. Nigeria's ERA entry covers the emergency reporting lines.

trackers.name: Justice & Empowerment Initiatives — community paralegals in over 100 informal settlements, and community-managed litigation funds the residents themselves control
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: JEI, a Nigerian non-profit with offices in Lagos and Port Harcourt, which trains and supports a network of community-based paralegals serving over 100 informal settlements across those cities, and is the supporting organisation for the Nigerian Slum / Informal Settlement Federation — a movement of thousands of residents from hundreds of settlements, organised around community savings groups and community-led profiling, mapping and enumeration. THE FINANCING MODEL IS THE PART TO COPY, and it answers the question this whole file keeps running into — who pays for the case: JEI works with paralegals and member communities to establish COMMUNITY-MANAGED STRATEGIC LITIGATION AND ADVOCACY FUNDS, and maintains a referral network of complementary organisations and pro bono lawyers. A fund the community controls, built from its own savings groups, does not disappear when a donor's programme ends and does not need anyone's permission to be spent. WHAT IT HAS DONE: litigation before Nigerian courts, regional and international human rights bodies, the National Human Rights Commission and the World Bank Inspection Panel — the last over the forced eviction of more than 9,000 residents of Badia East in Lagos. In January 2017 the Lagos High Court found waterfront evictions to be inhuman and degrading in violation of the Constitution. Community enumeration data produced by the Federation has been used to establish who lived where, and a Lagos state agency later opened dialogue with settlements organised under the Federation toward in-situ upgrading rather than eviction. WHO IT SUITS: residents of informal settlements in Nigerian cities facing demolition, and community groups wanting paralegals and enumeration capacity of their own. CAVEATS: the risk is real — Federation leaders and JEI community paralegals have been arrested during peaceful protest, and communities have been demolished at night despite a subsisting injunction. This is legal empowerment and strategic litigation, not compensation negotiation; for oil-spill and pollution work Nigeria's ERA and CEHRD entries are the routes.

trackers.name: LEDAP — 750 lawyers and 50+ paralegals taking more than 6,000 indigent clients pro bono a year, with offices in five zones
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Legal Defence and Assistance Project, a non-governmental organisation of lawyers founded in 1997 by pro bono lawyers who had themselves been detained without charge under military government, now with over a thousand members nationally. THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER WHEN YOU CANNOT PAY: it has enlisted 750 lawyers and more than 50 paralegals who assist over 6,000 indigent clients PRO BONO each year, and it provides free legal representation to poor and vulnerable victims of human rights violations — not merely advice. WHERE IT IS: national office in Lagos, with zonal coordinators and offices in Oshogbo, Jos, Kano, Awka and Port Harcourt — which puts a door within reach of the south-west, the middle belt, the north, the south-east and the Niger Delta rather than the commercial capital alone. It holds observer status with the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, so a case that exhausts domestic remedies has a route onward. Its work includes public interest litigation to improve the rule of law and governance, alongside its indigent defence, women's rights and criminal justice programmes. WHO IT SUITS: Nigerians who need representation and cannot afford a lawyer, including people detained or prosecuted in the course of a land or environmental dispute. CAVEATS: its published programme areas are rule of law, human security and women's rights — it is a general human rights and criminal justice organisation, NOT an environmental or land specialist, so approach it for representation rather than for technical land work. Demand plainly exceeds 6,000 clients a year. For urban eviction paralegals and community litigation funds, Nigeria's JEI entry; for oil-spill documentation, ERA and CEHRD.

trackers.name: Nigeria's Legal Aid Council — a statutory right to funded representation, and the documented reason almost nobody uses it
trackers.desc: WHAT YOU ARE ENTITLED TO: the Legal Aid Council of Nigeria, established by an Act of Parliament, which provides for rendering FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE to any indigent citizen of Nigeria whose right has been infringed, to enable them to ENGAGE THE SERVICES OF A LEGAL PRACTITIONER to prosecute their claim — subject to the Council satisfying itself that the alleged infringement is substantial and the need for financial or legal aid is real. That is a funded lawyer, not advice, and it is a statutory entitlement rather than a favour. THE BARRIER, DOCUMENTED RATHER THAN GUESSED: research on access to justice in Nigeria records that AWARENESS OF THE LEGAL AID COUNCIL IS LOW, and that the Council, the state courts and the National Human Rights Commission are all SITUATED IN THE STATE CAPITALS — so access remains a challenge for people in rural and remote areas and for those with low literacy. The entitlement is national; the offices are not. Budget for the journey to the state capital, and send someone who can read the forms. THE NON-JUDICIAL ROUTES BESIDE IT, worth knowing when a court case is impossible: the National Human Rights Commission, the Nigeria Police Force public complaints mechanism, and NGO pro bono services and human rights clinics. Nigeria's federal and state high courts, in Abuja and all 36 states, guarantee the right to complain and seek redress. WHO IT SUITS: indigent Nigerians whose rights have been infringed — including in a land, eviction or pollution matter — who need the state to pay for counsel. CAVEATS: A STATE BODY WITH A MEANS TEST AND A MERITS TEST, and the assessment of whether your claim is “substantial” is made by the Council itself; capacity and awareness are both documented as weak. For urban eviction paralegals and community litigation funds, Nigeria's JEI entry; for pro bono representation through a lawyers' network, LEDAP; for oil-spill documentation, ERA and CEHRD.

trackers.name: The Ekuri Initiative — two villages own 33,600 hectares, formed their own NGO to hold it, beat the loggers and stopped a 260-km superhighway; the state then copied the model into 33 communities
trackers.desc: HOW A COMMUNITY HOLDS AND DEFENDS ITS OWN FOREST: Old Ekuri and New Ekuri villages in Cross River State TOGETHER OWN 33,600 HECTARES of community forest — the LARGEST REMAINING COMMUNITY FOREST IN NIGERIA, held by about 6,200 Nkokoli people. THE VEHICLE, WHICH IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART: after watching neighbouring communities lose their forests to overexploitation and logging, in 1992 the community ESTABLISHED THE EKURI INITIATIVE AS A COMMUNITY-BASED NGO with a mandate in conservation, sustainable forest management, community development and poverty reduction, with PROCEEDS USED TO IMPROVE LIVELIHOODS AND BUILD INFRASTRUCTURE — a road, school, health centre, market and town hall; the Initiative took on the road project itself and built about four bridges and several culverts. Registering your own community NGO to hold and trade from the forest is what converts customary ownership into a body that can sign, sue, receive money and be replicated — and it is why Ekuri could act when the state would not. WHAT IT HAS SEEN OFF: the Initiative RESISTED THREATS FROM LOGGING COMPANIES and, more recently, ATTEMPTS BY STATE AUTHORITIES TO BUILD A 260-KM SUPERHIGHWAY that would have destroyed much of the community forest. THE REPLICATION, WHICH IS THE PROOF IT TRAVELS: the success inspired the CROSS RIVER STATE FORESTRY COMMISSION TO REWRITE ITS FORESTRY STRATEGY around community-based forest management; a donor supported the Commission to REPLICATE THE EKURI MODEL IN 33 FOREST COMMUNITIES, a British NGO in five more, and the NIGERIAN CONSERVATION FOUNDATION replicated it in Taraba State. Ekuri won the UNDP Equator Award in 2004; communities from Nigeria, Cameroon and beyond have visited to learn from it. Alongside, the Nigerian Conservation Foundation (ncfnigeria.org), founded 1980 and registered 1982 AS A CHARITABLE TRUST UNDER THE LAND (PERPETUAL SUCCESSION) ACT, holds and manages sites including the Lekki Conservation Centre and works in tripartite management with state governments and local communities. WHO IT SUITS: Nigerian forest communities wanting to hold, defend and earn from their own land, and anyone needing a domestic precedent to cite. CAVEATS: NIGERIAN FOREST ESTATES ARE CONTROLLED BY STATE GOVERNMENTS and community forest management is still building nationally; community leaders have warned that continued official disregard could make villagers doubt that conservation respects their survival rights. For statutory legal aid, Nigeria's Legal Aid Council entry; for urban eviction paralegals and community litigation funds, JEI; for oil-spill documentation, ERA and CEHRD.

trackers.name: LASEPA — Lagos State Environmental Protection Agency
trackers.desc: WHO INVESTIGATES IN LAGOS: LASEPA is the state's environmental regulator, and its published functions include investigating and resolving public complaints and disputes and mediating environmental disputes between complainants and respondents — a named mediation role between a resident and whoever is causing the harm, which few regulators state outright. USE WHAT IT MEASURES: it samples water, air and noise during industrial visits to establish compliance and inspects Environmental Management Plans at iron and steel facilities, so it generates exactly the evidence a complaint needs and that evidence can be requested. Its work is organised across the state's 57 local government areas and LCDAs — the tier a community actually sits in — and it runs sanitation inspections of industrial facilities and markets on the last Thursday of each month.

trackers.name: Complaints Desk — Lagos State Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources
trackers.desc: A SECOND ROUTE, AND A DIFFERENT ONE: the Lagos State Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources runs its own online complaint form to a Complaint Task Force, covering issues in your neighbourhood — and, separately, misconduct by an official that you witnessed. USE THAT SECOND LIMB: when the problem is the regulator or an inspector rather than the developer, a complaint to the agency itself goes nowhere, and this is the channel built for it.

trackers.name: Ifriqiya
trackers.desc: Ifriqiya is an association committed to Human Rights, the environment, and development. Founded in August 2019, it began its activities officially following the publication of the Official Gazette number 10 of the year 2020, dated February 4, 2020. The association aims to contribute to the achievement of sustainable development goals through a tripartite vision centered on 1) working for the defense of rights and freedoms and contributing to the promotion of a human rights culture based on universal principles, 2) advocating for environmental issues, and 3) contributing to enhancing the role of Tunisia and its civil society in the African integration process by supporting the development of a common continental policy, particularly in the association's areas of intervention, within the framework of the African Union. To achieve these objectives, the association strives to be a source of proposals and a center of expertise for players in these fields, with the aim of inspiring new ideas and strengthening the constructive participation of young people in decision-making processes at local, national and continental levels.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes de Tunisie
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Tunisia — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Instance Nationale d’Accès à l’Information (INAI)
trackers.desc: Tunisia's independent access-to-information authority under Organic Law 2016-22: it receives appeals, issues binding decisions, publishes its rulings, monitors compliance and reports annually. USE IT: appeal a refused request to INAI rather than back to the body that refused it — its decisions bind.

trackers.name: The Legal Agenda – Tunisia
trackers.desc: Tunisia bureau of the Legal Agenda, the Beirut-based research and advocacy nonprofit, monitoring and critically analysing the courts, judicial independence and legal policy in Tunisia through research, media and litigation.

trackers.name: INPDP — Instance Nationale de Protection des Données Personnelles
trackers.desc: INPDP — Instance Nationale de Protection des Données Personnelles — Tunisia’s national data-protection / information authority, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: I Watch (أنا يقظ)
trackers.desc: Tunisia's independent anti-corruption watchdog and Transparency International chapter — files access-to-information requests and corruption complaints, supports whistleblowers, and runs Chahed Meter, tracking the head of government's promises made before parliament.

trackers.name: Registre National des Entreprises
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: TUNEPS
trackers.desc: Tunisia's national e-procurement system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Tunisia, and for how much.

trackers.name: Conseil de gestion — your community is already a legal person
trackers.desc: YOU MAY NOT NEED TO FORM ANYTHING. Under loi n° 64-28 of 4 June 1964, each group possessing a collective land constitutes a legal person endowed with civil personality, represented by a conseil de gestion of members elected by the collectivity, plus members designated by the governor who have a consultative voice only. So the community already holds legal personality without forming an association, and the governor's appointees do not vote — establish who on your conseil is elected and who is designated. THE FRANCHISE: the decree of 2 July 1965 gave the vote to every member of the collectivity aged at least 20, where the 1938 rule recognised only heads of family — making women electors in their own right for the first time. The conseil is elected for 5 years, and the law of 14 January 1971 expanded its powers from mere management to very extensive powers. THE CONSENT TO INSIST ON: financial operations for the cession, lease or contribution to capital of collective lands require the approval of the conseil de gestion AND of the governor — the governor agreeing is not enough. The conseil is also empowered to arbitrate land disputes over collective lands.

trackers.name: Protected areas — the municipal route is closed, aim at the ministry
trackers.desc: THE STRUCTURAL FACT THAT SHOULD DIRECT YOUR EFFORT: local public collectivities hold no role in the creation, management or exploitation of terrestrial or maritime natural spaces in Tunisia. Unlike Albania, Montenegro or Luxembourg, where this map records municipal declaration routes, the commune is not a route here — aim at the ministry. WHICH MINISTRY DEPENDS ON THE SPACE: forest protected areas fall under agriculture, marine areas under environment, governed by the Code forestier 1988 and the marine protected areas law of 20 July 2009 — and each protected area needs its own special text to be applicable. National parks are the bulk of Tunisian protection, 237,000 of 250,000 hectares. HOW ONE IS CREATED: bodies act as localisateurs and submit opinions to the ministry responsible for forests; once localisation is done the administration begins the land operations — in principle purchase or expropriation of privately owned land. TWO BODIES THAT DO NOT YET FUNCTION, worth knowing before you address a complaint to them: a national nature body lacking the decree to organise it and name members, and the Commission des aires marines et côtières protégées foreseen by the 2009 law, which had not come into being. AND THE HONEST NOTE ON CONSEILS DE GESTION: Tunisian analysis records administrative tutelle, lack of means and competences, poor governance and non-participation undermining them in practice.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: FTDES environmental justice department — regional offices that take up local pollution fights, and have stopped projects
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Tunisian Forum for Economic and Social Rights runs a standing environmental justice department with paid staff, alongside its work on labour, women's and migrants' rights. THE REASON IT MATTERS MORE THAN A NATIONAL NGO IN TUNIS: it operates through regional sections — Kairouan, Monastir/Ksibet el Mediouni, Gafsa/Redeyef, Kasserine — that take up local fights directly. Its own reporting records dozens of local environmental movements accompanied and supported on water access, industrial pollution, waste and wastewater, with named outcomes: water supply obtained for particular communities, a new municipal waste arrangement negotiated, and the halting of environmentally destructive projects at Jbel Fadloum and Ain Draham. It has also assembled a case against the national water utility over cutoffs in the mining basin, and connects households to water — seven families and a rural school through one project cycle. It publishes a half-yearly environmental justice report and runs regional forums that put officials in a room with affected residents. THE HARD CASE IT IS CURRENTLY LOSING, WHICH YOU SHOULD KNOW BEFORE RELYING ON THE COURTS HERE: at Gabès, where the state chemical group's phosphate fertiliser plant is the country's heaviest pollution file, a summary application to suspend production was rejected in February 2026 for want of proof of harm — FTDES called the ruling a serious regression and said the absence-of-evidence argument ignored established, documented data. Expect the evidentiary burden to be the fight. WHO IT SUITS: Tunisian communities facing industrial pollution, water dispossession or waste siting, especially in the interior and the mining basin. CAVEATS: FTDES is a rights organisation that litigates through instructed lawyers, not a law firm; no published intake route or case-selection criteria were found; and it works in a political environment where social movements have been criminalised, which it says limits the visibility and credibility of environmental struggles.

trackers.name: Observatoire tunisien de l'eau — report a cut, a leak or bad water on watchwater.tn and it goes into a public map the utility has to answer
trackers.desc: WHERE TO REPORT: the Tunisian Water Observatory, an associative project created in 2016 by the association Nomad 08 of Redeyef to defend the right of access to water, running the alert platform watchwater.tn.
