HOW IT WORKS AND WHY IT IS A RESOURCE RATHER THAN A CAMPAIGN: citizens report unannounced cuts, poor supply, leaks, water quality problems and water-related protests; the database is fed mainly by citizens, plus trained alerters and observatory administrators who VERIFY each alert and ensure the information reaches the national water utility (SONEDE) and the municipalities. The output is a participatory map — the “Carte de la Soif” (Thirst Map) — published monthly. An individual complaint to a utility disappears; a verified entry on a public national map does not. THE RECORD SHOWS THE SCALE, and it is what makes the map hard to dismiss: 1,893 alerts in 2023, of which 1,592 were cuts, sparing no governorate; a reported record 608 citizen alerts in July 2026 — 549 of them unannounced cuts or disruptions, 34 protest movements demanding access to water, 13 network leaks and 12 quality alerts. Monthly maps name the worst-hit governorates, which have included Kef, Ben Arous, Gafsa, Kasserine, Sousse, Monastir, Gabès, Médenine, Bizerte and Tunis. The observatory has also run field monitoring of the government's own summer water plan. WHO IT SUITS: Tunisian households and neighbourhoods facing cuts, contamination or supply failure — and anyone needing dated, third-party-verified evidence that a shortage is real and recurring. CAVEATS: it records and publicises — it does not restore your supply or litigate; its own staff note that generalised cuts have continued despite years of protest. For labour, environmental justice and regional case support, Tunisia's FTDES entry.

trackers.name: Tunisia's bureau d'aide judiciaire — a legal aid office sitting inside each court of first instance, under law 2002-52
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY: under law n°2002-52 of 3 June 2002 on judicial aid, Tunisia operates a BUREAU DE L'AIDE JUDICIAIRE — a specialised office that rules on applications for judicial aid, with its SEAT AT THE COURT OF FIRST INSTANCE. Unlike Morocco, recorded in this file as having no framework law on legal aid, Tunisia has a statute and a standing office; the practical problem is that few people know where it sits or who decides. WHO DECIDES YOUR APPLICATION, because knowing the room matters: the bureau comprises the public prosecutor or a deputy as PRESIDENT; a representative of the finance ministry; a lawyer registered at the court of cassation, appointed by the justice minister on the proposal of the bar council; and a court clerk. Note that the state's prosecutor chairs the body deciding whether you get a lawyer, and the finance ministry sits on it — that is the room, and it is worth knowing before you assume the decision is purely technical. TWO RULES THAT DECIDE HOW FAR YOUR GRANT STRETCHES: judicial aid is granted to cover the costs of a SINGLE CASE — but where protecting the right, or the procedure itself, requires seizing more than one court or chamber at the same time, the competent bureau MAY decide that the aid covers all costs arising from the cases brought, with the clerk notifying the president of the bureau at the seized court so auxiliaries can be appointed. And on APPEAL, the beneficiary may keep the assigned lawyer or bailiff — PROVIDED THE BUREAU IS INFORMED. That notification is a small step that silently ends representation if missed. WHO IT SUITS: Tunisians who cannot pay court costs or lawyer's fees in a land, expropriation or environmental case, and anyone taking a case to appeal. CAVEATS: A STATE PROCEDURE, NOT AN ALLY — it decides whether the state pays, and published research has found Tunisian legal aid poorly known and unevenly delivered; the aid covers costs, not the outcome. For regional casework and environmental justice, Tunisia's FTDES entry; for water cuts and supply failures, the Water Observatory.

trackers.name: Tunisia's terres collectives and their elected conseils de gestion — the sole deciders over ~3 million hectares, and the 2026 bill that would convert them into individual sellable titles
trackers.desc: WHO DECIDES ON COLLECTIVE LAND: Tunisia's TERRES COLLECTIVES (tribal lands) cover almost A THIRD OF AGRICULTURAL LAND — about 3 MILLION HECTARES, 1.5 million agricultural and as much again pastoral, with collective rangelands alone near ONE MILLION HECTARES. THE BODY THAT DECIDES IS YOURS AND IT IS ELECTED: the CONSEILS DE GESTION (majalis al tasarrof) are COMMUNITY STRUCTURES ELECTED BY THE AYANTS DROIT — they replaced the traditional councils of notables (myaâd) whose members were APPOINTED BY TRIBAL CHIEFS — and the LAW OF 14 JANUARY 1971 DESIGNATES THEM AS THE SOLE DECIDERS ON THE ATTRIBUTION OF COLLECTIVE LANDS. Sole decider, elected by the rightholders — if you are an ayant droit, the council election is the most consequential vote you cast over your own land. Find out when yours is held and who is on the register. WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS THEY DID WITH THAT POWER, STATED PLAINLY: under the 1971 law the councils' competences shifted toward CARRYING OUT THE PRIVATISATION of agricultural collective land, and being extremely well fitted to the social structure they enabled a rapid and frictionless unwinding of collective tenure; researchers record the consequences as fragmentation of holdings and land concentration leading to the impoverishment of many peasants, plus excessive resource mobilisation — cereal expansion onto fragile ground, proliferating shallow wells, overgrazing of rangelands. A council that can allocate can also dissolve; the same elected body is the protection and the risk, which is exactly why the register of ayants droit matters. THE LIVE DEVELOPMENT ANYONE ON COLLECTIVE LAND SHOULD KNOW: the ministry has finalised a DRAFT DECREE-LAW GIVING THE TRIBUNAL IMMOBILIER EXCEPTIONAL PREROGATIVES AND SIMPLIFIED DEROGATORY PROCEDURES to settle collective-property disputes definitively AND CONVERT THESE LAND RESERVES INTO INDIVIDUAL, TRANSFERABLE, BANKABLE TITLES — with the stated reason that the legal complexity of collective property DETERS PRIVATE INVESTMENT AND THE SITING OF LARGE PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE, NOTABLY WIND, SOLAR AND INDUSTRIAL PROJECTS. The government has said out loud that collective title is what stands between southern land and large energy projects. If you hold rights on collective land in the south, register your name and watch the Tribunal Immobilier. WHO IT SUITS: Tunisian ayants droit, pastoral communities and southern governorate residents. CAVEATS: A MANAGEMENT AND ALLOCATION RIGHT, NOT INDIVIDUAL TITLE — and the direction of travel is toward conversion. For access to administrative documents, Tunisia's INAI entry; for state-funded representation, the aide judiciaire entry; for rapid-response money, Urgent Action Fund-Africa.

trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Morocco.

trackers.name: Court of Cassation (Morocco)
trackers.desc: Official digital platform of Morocco's Court of Cassation publishing its rulings (11,000+ decisions). · Find here: the judgments of Morocco's Court of Cassation.

trackers.name: Public Beneficial Ownership Register (RBE)
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Commission du Droit d’Accès à l’Information (CDAI)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority; Morocco’s CDAI ensures application of the right of access under Law 31-13 — investigating complaints and publishing annual reports, Morocco.

trackers.desc: Morocco's company registry via OMPIC. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Haut-Commissariat au Plan
trackers.desc: Morocco's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Morocco.

trackers.name: Marchés Publics
trackers.desc: Morocco's public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Morocco, and for how much.

trackers.name: Terres collectives — the opposition window is now 3 months, not 6
trackers.desc: A DEADLINE THAT WAS HALVED, AND IT IS THE THING TO DIARISE. Three laws promulgated 9 August 2019 replaced the dahir of 27 April 1919 governing collective lands: loi 62-17 (administrative tutelle over collectivités ethniques and management of their property), loi 63-17 (administrative delimitation) and loi 64-17 (collective lands in irrigation perimeters). Loi 63-17 reduced the period for presenting oppositions against the delimitation procedure from 6 months to 3 months. If a delimitation touches your community, the window to object is now half what it was. Delimitation is run by a Commission de délimitation administrative presided by the local authority. BUT THE PERIOD ITSELF FREEZES TRANSACTIONS: during the operation it is prohibited on pain of nullity to conclude any act relating to the lands under delimitation (save the cases in articles 16, 17, 19, 20 and 21 of loi 62-17), and no new réquisition d'immatriculation by a third party may be admitted unless it confirms an opposition already presented. STEP ONE IS TO CHECK YOU ARE LISTED: the list of collectivités ethniques for each prefecture or province is fixed by the governor. Note too that loi 62-17 limits recourse to custom and tradition in managing these lands, requiring conformity with legislation in force.

trackers.name: Loi 22-07 — protection does not extinguish subsistence use
trackers.desc: TWO THINGS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE OPPOSING OR SEEKING A DESIGNATION. Loi 22-07 (July 2010) defines an aire protégée as any terrestrial or marine space, geographically delimited, duly recognised and specially managed to protect and improve biological diversity, conserve natural and cultural heritage, and prevent its degradation. AND IT PRESERVES LOCAL USE: the law recognises the right of populations living inside or near the protected area to benefit from usage rights — prélèvements made on a non-commercial basis for their domestic and vital needs. Designation therefore does not extinguish subsistence use, and that is in the statute rather than left to practice — a direct answer to the objection that protection starves residents. THE STATUS TO ASK ABOUT: the loi-cadre 99-12 National Charter sets objectives at article 7 including preserving sites d'intérêt biologique et écologique (SIBE) — terrestrial, coastal and marine — and encouraging the creation of protected areas there. Morocco's first protected areas strategy, the Plan directeur des aires protégées, dates to 1996. READ THE POLITICAL CONTEXT HONESTLY: the 2019 collective-land reform followed a royal speech of 12 October 2018 calling for one million additional hectares of collective land to be mobilised for agricultural investment projects.

trackers.name: ADFM and the soulaliyate movement — the campaign that won women a share of collective tribal land, and the body that trained them to speak for themselves
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Association Démocratique des Femmes du Maroc, a feminist organisation founded in 1985 and based in Rabat, which has accompanied the soulaliyate movement since 2007 — women of the collective tribal lands who were excluded from the land and its proceeds. WHY THIS IS A LAND RESOURCE AND NOT ONLY A GENDER ONE: roughly 42 per cent of Morocco's land is held collectively by tribes — in the order of 15 million hectares — and it is those collective lands that get ceded for major works and for property development, with compensation paid to the members of the collectivity. If your name is not on the list, you get nothing when the land goes. The movement forced the state to act: interior ministry circulars extended equal rights of enjoyment to women, and in 2018 women in Kénitra received plots on the same footing as men following a cession of collective land — the first time. Laws 62.17, 63.17 and 64.17 then reformed the administrative tutelage over soulaliyate communities and their assets. THE ORGANISING PRINCIPLE ADFM STATES, WHICH IS WORTH COPYING: they amplify the women's voice but do not speak in their place — the women were trained to state their own claims. It also runs national meetings that put affected women, ministries and civil society in one room over draft legislation. WHO IT SUITS: members of a collective (soulaliyate) community facing a cession of tribal land, particularly women excluded from the beneficiary lists. CAVEATS: ADFM is an advocacy and capacity-building organisation, not a law firm. The reform is incomplete on its own account — the law as adopted has been read as granting access only to women resident on the land, and ADFM warned that a 2020 interior ministry circular on allocating soulaliyate farmland made no mention of the historic exclusion of women, risking a repeat. This entry points at an intergovernmental account of the movement because ADFM's own site was not verified; treat the organisation as the contact and the account as the record.

trackers.name: AOFEP and the RADDO oasis network — a local association at Tinjdad and the Maghreb-wide network of oasis communities it belongs to
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Association Oasis Ferkla pour l'Environnement et le Patrimoine (AOFEP), a Moroccan non-profit created in 2001 at Tinjdad in Errachidia province in the south-east, working on the environment and heritage of the Ferkla oasis — and, through it, RADDO, the associative network for the sustainable development of oases, which links oasis associations across the Maghreb and gives an isolated oasis community counterparts in Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania facing the same threats. WHY THE OASIS IS A DISTINCT CASE, and why the soulaliyate route in Morocco's other entry does not cover it: an oasis is destroyed not by a single expropriation but by water abstraction, upstream boreholes, drought and the abandonment of the collective irrigation systems that make cultivation possible — the land can remain legally yours and still become worthless. Network members' stated aims are instructive as a template: to constitute an independent structure that is the counterpart to public authorities on all environmental questions, and to create alternatives allowing sustainable development of the oasis — through public awareness, exchange of experience with partners, and advocacy for agroecology and responsible tourism. A permanent independent body that the administration has to deal with, established before a crisis, is worth more than a committee formed the week the drilling rig arrives. WHO IT SUITS: oasis and pre-Saharan communities in south-eastern Morocco facing water loss, land degradation or extractive projects, and associations wanting counterparts across the Maghreb. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED SITE OF ITS OWN WAS FOUND for AOFEP — this entry points at the RADDO network page documenting it; treat that as the route in. It is a local environment-and-heritage association, not a law firm or a fund, and for collective tribal land and the soulaliyate movement Morocco's other entry is the one.

trackers.name: Morocco's university legal clinics and ADALA — free first advice in a country with no framework law on legal aid
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET LEGAL HELP, AND THE STRUCTURAL FACT THAT EXPLAINS WHY IT IS HARD: there is as yet NO FRAMEWORK LAW in Moroccan law setting out the contours of legal aid; in practice judicial assistance services are not known to the general public, and legal aid provision is largely carried by CIVIL SOCIETY. So do not start by asking a court for assistance you have never heard described — start with the organisations that actually run the service. WHAT EXISTS: UNIVERSITY LEGAL CLINICS, developed by the Moroccan justice-focused association ADALA together with an international lawyers' organisation, explicitly to strengthen access to justice for women. The clinics provide reception, listening, FIRST LEGAL ADVICE AND ORIENTATION to people in situations of vulnerability, supervised and supported by law teachers and legal professionals — law students doing the intake under supervision, which is what makes the service free and repeatable. A university law faculty is the cheapest legal door in any country that has one; ask whether yours runs a clinique juridique and on which days. The same international organisation works across North Africa and has published on how colonial-era penal provisions on begging, vagrancy and informal trade still bring people before the police and courts in Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria — relevant to anyone whose land dispute becomes a public-order charge. WHO IT SUITS: Moroccan households, and especially women, who need first legal advice and orientation on a land, inheritance or expropriation problem and cannot pay a lawyer. CAVEATS: FIRST ADVICE AND ORIENTATION, NOT REPRESENTATION — a clinic will tell you where you stand and where to go, not argue your case; ADALA has no verified live site of its own, so this entry points at the international partner that documents the programme, and clinic availability depends on the university and the academic year. For collective tribal land and the soulaliyate movement, Morocco's ADFM entry; for oasis territories, the AOFEP/RADDO entry.

trackers.name: Ask Your Government Uganda
trackers.desc: Ask Your Government Uganda — Uganda’s civil-society FOI request portal (Africa Freedom of Information Centre) — citizens make requests under the 2005 Access to Information Act and responses are published publicly. — Holds to account: Uganda’s public authorities on disclosure — find public FOI requests, responses and non-responses.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Government Procurement Portal (PPDA)
trackers.desc: Uganda's central government-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Uganda, and for how much.

trackers.name: ULII
trackers.desc: Uganda Legal Information Institute: free case law and legislation (AfricanLII network). · Find here: free Ugandan judgments and legislation (ULII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Uganda Registration Services Bureau (URSB)
trackers.desc: Uganda’s official registry of companies and business entities — searchable incorporation records.

trackers.name: ACODE (Advocates Coalition for Development and Environment)
trackers.desc: Ugandan public-policy research and advocacy think tank. Runs the Local Government Councils Scorecard Initiative, assessing the performance of district councils, chairpersons, speakers and individual councillors across 35+ districts, and strengthens parliamentary and district oversight through budget tracking and Public Accounts Committee support.

trackers.name: Civil Society Budget Advocacy Group (CSBAG)
trackers.desc: Ugandan coalition (formed 2004) of CSOs influencing national and district budget processes — resource mobilisation, allocation and utilisation — and pushing for transparency and accountability in public spending. Here you can trace how Uganda's national and district budgets allocate resources, tracked by the CSBAG civil-society coalition.

trackers.name: Inspectorate of Government (IGG)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Uganda — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor General (Uganda)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Uganda — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: CCO and Communal Land Association — the vehicle and the instrument
trackers.desc: UGANDA STARTS FROM AN UNUSUALLY STRONG POSITION: Article 237 of the Constitution and section 2 of the Land Act vest land in the citizens of Uganda — the opposite of Nigeria, where all land vests in the Governor. TWO ROUTES THAT COMBINE. Section 4(1) lets any person, family or community holding under customary tenure apply for a Certificate of Customary Ownership; a Land Committee processes it under section 5 and the District Land Board decides under section 8. THE EFFECT IS THE POINT: the certificate shall be taken as conclusive evidence of the customary rights specified in it — conclusive, not merely prima facie, unlike Nigeria's rebuttable Certificate of Occupancy. Section 15 then allows a Communal Land Association to be formed by any group of persons for any purpose connected with communal ownership and management of land, whether under customary law or otherwise — and communal land may be held under a CCO or freehold title by the managing committee on behalf of the association. So the CLA is the vehicle and the CCO the instrument. Formation is controlled by the Registrar of Titles, and disputes are resolved by the Registrar under section 20 — an administrative route, not only the courts. WATCH section 22, individual holding created out of communal land, if fragmentation is your threat.

trackers.name: Record your boundary markers and witnesses before a dispute
trackers.desc: THE HONEST PICTURE, FROM UGANDAN LAND ORGANISATIONS. Registration of customary land is described as complex, tedious and unaffordable to the majority of communities, with the process marred by gaps in service delivery in land administration institutions — and the National Land Policy 2013 and the Land Act contradict each other on the type of registry and documentation intended. THE SMALLEST PROPORTION OF LAND IN UGANDA IS REGISTERED, so rights recognition relies on informal mechanisms and non-documentary evidence: boundaries demarcated by ant hills, streams, hill tops, trees, shrubs or stones, with ownership witnessed by the clan, council of elders or family head. THOSE WITNESSED MARKERS ARE YOUR EVIDENCE — photograph them, map them and record who witnessed them now, not after a dispute starts. WHAT COUNTS AS COMMUNAL LAND is wider than productive ground: grazing grounds, hunting grounds, forest, rock outcrops, spiritual sites, and rivers and wetlands. HELP THAT EXISTS: a published step-by-step guide covers the CCO, the Communal Land Association and establishing a Land Trust in three chapters, written for chiefdoms, clans and cultural leaders. And two state remedies are under way — SLAAC systematic adjudication and certification, and Zonal Land Offices decentralising services.

trackers.name: ECOTRUST Trees for Global Benefits — it pays landowners to keep land under trees, in instalments, against a 25-year lock-in
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a Ugandan conservation trust that pays smallholders and community groups to put and keep their land under trees, selling the resulting carbon credits to buyers on the voluntary market under the Plan Vivo standard. Running since 2003, it works across districts in the Albertine Rift, the Queen Elizabeth and Murchison landscapes and the Mount Elgon ecosystem. Through 2024 it reports having paid out US$8.78 million to 51,874 participating households across 34,286 hectares in 26 districts, and states that US$6 of every US$10 raised reaches the farmer. For a household under pressure to sell or clear land, this is one of the few routes in the region where keeping land wooded produces cash rather than only costing money. HOW THE MONEY ARRIVES, WHICH IS THE PART TO UNDERSTAND BEFORE SIGNING: payments are performance-based and staged — reported as falling in years 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, on verification that the trees are there — and they sit inside a 25-year carbon contract with a land use plan attached. WHO IT SUITS — AND THE TRAP: the payments stop around year 10 but the obligation to maintain the trees runs the full 25 years, so the last fifteen years are unpaid stewardship on land you can no longer convert. Independent analysts also find that minimum plot sizes and the opportunity cost of taking cropland out of production push participation toward households with larger holdings, disadvantaging the poorest, and that the trust answers in practice to credit buyers more than to the smallholders it contracts with. A newer northern Uganda programme is designed around free, prior and informed consent and grower-developed land use plans, which suggests the criticism has landed — ask which terms apply to your scheme. Treat this as a way to fund holding land against development, entered with the lock-in understood, rather than as a grant.

trackers.name: Greenwatch — 29 years of environmental public interest litigation in Uganda, and it is opening a legal aid clinic
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the organisation that built environmental public interest litigation in Uganda. It brought the cases the profession names — the chimpanzee case, the kaveera (plastic bags) case, the pangolin case — and in 2012 it went to court with four children suing through a next friend, on their own behalf and that of the born and unborn children of Uganda, against the Attorney General and the national environment authority over failure to act on climate change. It publishes handbooks on Ugandan environmental law and a casebook of the decisions, which is the cheapest preparation available to a community lawyer here. IT IS ALSO EXPANDING WHAT IT OFFERS: Greenwatch states it is opening a legal aid clinic to widen its environmental justice and litigation work, and is training young lawyers, journalists, and — the unusual one — science experts in how to write witness statements and present evidence for environmental court proceedings. If your fight will turn on technical evidence, that last programme is the one to ask about. THE LESSON ITS OWN CASEBOOK RECORDS, WHICH YOU SHOULD READ BEFORE CELEBRATING A WIN: in one successful action the applicants could not enforce the judgment because it was merely declaratory — the permit was revoked but the developer stayed on the forest land, which it had already cut and replanted. Ask what order you are actually seeking, and whether anyone can execute it. Greenwatch also publishes a community-based guide to monitoring the impacts of oil and gas activity. WHO IT SUITS: Ugandan communities facing forest loss, oil and gas displacement, or a permit granted without consultation. Plot 7/9 Second Street, Industrial Area, Kinyara House, Kampala; +256 41 4344613; environment@greenwatch.or.ug. CAVEATS: no published intake criteria or means test; the legal aid clinic was announced rather than described, so confirm it is running; and its own practitioners point to the difficulty of funding environmental litigation as the recurring constraint.

trackers.name: LEMU — helps northern Ugandan communities register their commons, and publishes the risks of the certificates it helps them get
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Land and Equity Movement in Uganda, working mainly in the north and east where land ownership is almost entirely customary, to secure family and community land rights. It is a legal aid service provider: its listed work includes legal representation, legal advice, mediation and community paralegal work, alongside research and advocacy. THE PROCESS IT RUNS WHEN A COMMUNITY ASKS IT TO PROTECT A COMMONS — grazing land or wetland — is a sequence worth copying: collectively envisioning past, present and future use of the land; publicly drafting, evaluating and agreeing rules for managing it; strengthening the local governance structure that will hold it; resolving disputes and documenting boundaries with boundary trees and maps; and then formally documenting it, by registering a Communal Land Association and/or applying for a Certificate of Customary Ownership or a freehold title. Note the order: the rules and the boundaries come before the paperwork. In northern Uganda the commons is not a luxury — grazing land is also where households get fuel, water, food, building materials and traditional medicines. THE REASON TO READ ITS PUBLICATIONS BEFORE APPLYING FOR ANYTHING: LEMU publishes a policy brief titled, in effect, that Certificates of Customary Ownership are not what they seem on the surface, setting out the risks of CCOs, and another with questions to ask the promoters of current titles and certificates. It has also documented the complexities and failures of Communal Land Associations in Karamoja and written on the tragedy of the owners of the commons. An organisation that hands you the case against its own instrument is the one to trust on which instrument you need. It has codified customary law in the Principles, Practices, Rights and Responsibilities papers for Lango, Acholi and Kumam/Teso, published in local languages, which courts and land managers can be pointed at. Plot 39A Namuwongo Bukasa Road, Kampala. WHO IT SUITS: customary landholding families and communities in northern and eastern Uganda, especially those defending communal grazing land or wetland, and women whose customary rights are being denied. CAVEATS: focused on the north and east, not nationwide; documenting land is not the same as winning a fight with a developer, and LEMU's own briefs warn that a certificate can create new exposure as well as protection.

trackers.name: ACTogether Uganda and the National Slum Dwellers Federation — communities that map their own settlements, and whose maps the city had to use
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the National Slum Dwellers Federation of Uganda (NSDFU), a movement of urban poor residents organised around savings groups — reported at 355 savings groups across cities including Kampala, Arua, Jinja, Kabale, Mbale and Mbarara, and operating in some 20 towns and cities — together with ACTogether Uganda, the support NGO founded in September 2006 that provides its technical assistance. WHAT THEY DO THAT NOBODY ELSE WILL DO FOR YOU: residents profile, enumerate and map their own settlements, gathering data on land tenure, services, housing and livelihoods, with questionnaires administered by slum dwellers themselves. In Kampala they identified and profiled 62 settlements and handed the mapped report to the city authority. THE MOMENT THAT PROVES WHY THIS IS WORTH DOING: the city's own most recent map showed 31 slums; the federation's showed 62. When international consultants were commissioned for a water and sanitation feasibility study, they found official population data twelve years old and seriously understating the scale of settlement — and asked the federation to share its map to overlay with the city's. The federation and ACTogether were invited onto the project steering committee as the only community representatives. Whoever holds the only current map of where people actually live has to be dealt with. Their own profiling found nearly 70 per cent of Kampala's settlements had faced eviction threat, and a federation organiser explains the database is updated precisely because the data government cites to justify evictions is out of date. WHO IT SUITS: Ugandan urban communities facing eviction, upgrading or resettlement, and any community that needs to prove who lives where before someone else counts them. CAVEATS: this is legal-empowerment-by-data and negotiation, not litigation — for court work Uganda's Greenwatch entry is the route, and for rural customary land, LEMU. ACTogether's own site did not resolve to a verified page; this entry points at the network affiliate record documenting the alliance.

trackers.name: Uganda Land Alliance — 60+ member consortium running Land Rights Information Centres you can walk into in district towns
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Uganda Land Alliance, a membership consortium of more than 60 national and international organisations and individuals working on land rights for poor and marginalised people, listed on Uganda's legal aid service providers' network. WHAT MAKES IT USABLE RATHER THAN JUST NATIONAL: it has established LAND RIGHTS INFORMATION CENTRES hosted WITH partner organisations in the regions — reported at Kibaale district (Kagadi) with a rural development and training programme for the west; Mbale with the Uganda Association of Women Lawyers (FIDA-Uganda); Kapchorwa and Luweero with a development organisation and a volunteer development body for the east; and a centre in Kampala with the Legal Aid Project of the Uganda Law Society. It also uses public meetings, radio and newspaper advertising to explain land law and policy to people who will never read a statute. A referral consortium is worth more than any single organisation when you do not yet know which kind of help you need — a household facing eviction, an inheritance dispute and a company survey all start at the same counter. WHERE IT HAS DONE THE FIELDWORK: studies on land tenure and livelihoods in the Albertine Graben oil districts of Hoima, Buliisa, Amuru and Nwoya, where international oil companies operate, and documentation across eight districts on women's progress in claiming land. Its stated standard is that no one should be deprived of the use and control of the land their well-being depends on — through eviction, expulsion or exclusion — and that compulsory changes to tenure happen only in line with international human rights standards, with explicit emphasis on women's ability to defend, inherit and bequeath land. Plot 54, Muwafu Road, Ntinda, Kampala. WHO IT SUITS: Ugandans anywhere in the country who need to find the right land-rights help locally, especially women, and communities in the oil districts. CAVEATS: a consortium and information network — the casework happens at member organisations, so expect a referral rather than direct representation; centre coverage is partial and partner-dependent. For customary certificates and their risks, Uganda's LEMU entry; for litigation, Greenwatch; for urban settlements, ACTogether.

trackers.name: Bwindi Mgahinga Conservation Trust — an endowment where the BULK of the income is legally earmarked for the communities, not the park
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: BMCT, a registered trust fund established in 1994 under the Uganda Trust Act to provide long-term funding for the biodiversity of Bwindi Impenetrable and Mgahinga Gorilla national parks in south-western Uganda. It is a registered NGO run by a Trust Management Board under a Trust Deed, and it does NOT manage the parks — the wildlife authority does — so it is not the body that excluded you from the forest; it is the body that disburses money to the people living beside it. HOW THE MONEY IS SPLIT, AND WHY THAT SPLIT IS THE POINT: its principal strategy is working with the communities close to the two parks through the PROVISION OF GRANTS, intended to reduce dependency on the protected areas; park management receives grants amounting to a reported 20 per cent of income, and the BULK of net annual income is LEGALLY EARMARKED for community development — from common-good projects such as primary school classrooms, health units and rural roads to individual income-generating activities. Ask of any conservation trust near you what share of its income the deed obliges it to spend on communities; an endowment whose deed says “bulk” is a different instrument from one that grants at the board's discretion. The operational arm, the Trust Administrative Unit, is based at Kabale, with a Kampala office at Plot 1 Katalima Crescent, Naguru. WHO IT SUITS: communities and households adjacent to Bwindi and Mgahinga — including those displaced or restricted by the parks — seeking grant funding for community projects or livelihoods. CAVEATS: STRICTLY GEOGRAPHIC — it funds only around those two parks, and it funds development and conservation, NOT litigation, land purchase or opposition to a project; it works in partnership with the wildlife authority, so it is not an independent champion against park policy. For payments to landowners for keeping land under trees, Uganda's ECOTRUST entry; for customary certificates, LEMU.

trackers.name: Justice Centres Uganda — a state one-stop legal aid service with a TOLL-FREE line, and the extractives lawyers to call alongside it
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET A FREE LAWYER: Justice Centres Uganda, a one-stop legal aid model within the justice sector, offering legal advice, LEGAL REPRESENTATION, alternative dispute resolution, counselling, legal awareness, referrals and a TOLL-FREE PHONE LINE. ELIGIBILITY IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK, because it is strict: to qualify you must be among the most indigent persons in Uganda. Districts served from the Lira centre are published — Amolatar, Pader, Apac, Kitgum, Oyam, Dokolo, Kaberamaido and Kotido — so northern Uganda is covered from a named base rather than only from Kampala. WHY IT MATTERS HERE: justice-needs research cited by the justice sector found 88 per cent of Ugandans had experienced difficulty accessing justice over four years, with LAND and family cases the top two most critical disputes; a later study found 45 per cent of legal problems unresolved — 29 per cent still ongoing and 16 per cent abandoned. Abandonment is the real outcome to guard against: most people do not lose their land case, they stop being able to pursue it. Alongside the state service, regional legal aid clinics run with the Uganda Law Society provide pro bono civil and criminal services including land disputes. AND FOR OIL, GAS AND MINERALS SPECIFICALLY: ANARDE (Advocates for Natural Resources and Development) is a Ugandan non-profit of researchers, organisers and LAWYERS working on environmental governance and corporate and government accountability, arguing that the environment and land rights of communities where oil, gas and minerals are located must be protected and that extractive revenues be disclosed — with explicit focus on women in the natural resource sector. WHO IT SUITS: indigent Ugandans with a land or family dispute, especially in the north; and communities in the oil and mineral districts needing lawyers who know the sector. CAVEATS: JUSTICE CENTRES HAS NO VERIFIED STANDALONE SITE — this entry points at the justice sector's published account, and the indigence test excludes many who still cannot afford a lawyer; coverage is by centre, so confirm which districts your nearest one serves. For land rights information centres, Uganda's ULA entry; for environmental litigation, Greenwatch; for customary certificates, LEMU.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Lawyers' Environmental Action Team (LEAT)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Tanzania's first public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1994 — legal and social-policy research, advocacy and selected public-interest litigation on mining and extractives, land, water, forests and wildlife. It supported Rufiji Delta residents in the constitutional petition that helped stop a 10,000-hectare prawn farm, and has acted for households facing demolition on utility way-leaves. A member of ELAW and of Friends of the Earth International. WHO IT SUITS: a Tanzanian community or residents' association fighting an extractive project, an eviction or a major land-use decision — LEAT litigates selectively, so expect a case-selection conversation rather than open legal aid.

trackers.name: Legal and Human Rights Centre (LHRC)
trackers.desc: Tanzania's largest human-rights NGO, running free legal-aid centres alongside public-interest litigation. WHO TO ENLIST: legal aid through the Kinondoni (Dar es Salaam), Arusha and Dodoma offices and the Haki Kiganjani mobile legal-aid service. You CAN: get free advice and representation, and draw on LHRC's annual human-rights reporting; it was a co-applicant in the 2026 East African Court of Justice judgment that struck down Tanzanian restrictions on who may bring public-interest litigation. For activists: the practical route to a lawyer when a land or environment dispute becomes a rights case.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Open Data Tanzania
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Tanzania.

trackers.name: BRELA
trackers.desc: Tanzania's Business Registrations and Licensing Agency. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Sikika (Public Finance Governance Programme)
trackers.desc: Tanzanian civil-society organisation whose Public Finance Governance programme researches budget transparency, public-expenditure management, auditing and oversight — including the Subnational Open Budget Survey and assessments of the Public Accounts and Local Authorities Accounts Committees — to drive accountability and policy change.

trackers.name: TanzLII
trackers.desc: Tanzania Legal Information Institute: free case law and legislation. · Find here: free Tanzanian judgments and legislation (TanzLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Business Registrations and Licensing Agency (BRELA)
trackers.desc: Tanzania’s official company, business-name and intellectual-property register.

trackers.name: National Audit Office (Tanzania)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Tanzania — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Prevention and Combating of Corruption Bureau (PCCB)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Tanzania — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: TANePS
trackers.desc: Tanzania's National e-Procurement System. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Tanzania, and for how much.

trackers.name: Tanzania Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (TEITI)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and company ownership in Tanzania.

trackers.name: WAJIBU – Institute of Public Accountability
trackers.desc: Tanzanian public-accountability think tank (founded 2015 by a former Controller & Auditor General) that analyses CAG audit reports and the work of parliamentary oversight committees (PAC, LAAC, PIC), publishes simplified accountability reports on central, local and public-authority spending, and mobilises citizens and elected representatives around public financial accountability.

trackers.name: CCRO — collective tenure over village land, including as forest reserve
trackers.desc: HOW A TANZANIAN COMMUNITY SECURES THE LAND IT ALREADY OCCUPIES. The Village Land Act 1999 provides for both individual and collective rights (sections 12 and 13), and village land may be used by a community as pastoral grazing land, as a forest reserve, for a water dam and so on. Village Councils issue Certificates of Customary Right of Occupancy on application; a group on customarily held land over 250 hectares applies to its Village Council with the Commissioner of Lands' approval, and once granted the CCRO gives permanent tenure with all the attributes of a granted right of occupancy. THE COLLECTIVE FORM IS ITSELF THE PROTECTION: transactions and subdivisions require the consent of the entire group, so individual members cannot be picked off one at a time. THE SEQUENCE: the council must define and approve community by-laws; the village must obtain a Certificate of Village Land by having its outer boundaries surveyed, demarcated and registered; and boundaries and land use plans must be agreed through district-level demarcation and zoning. Issuance depends on regularisation of the village land, so the village-level work comes first.

trackers.name: Four limits on CCROs — and what tenure unlocked for the Hadza
trackers.desc: KNOW THESE BEFORE STARTING. 1. ELIGIBILITY IS RESTRICTED to Tanzanian citizens of African descent, or communities of such citizens, occupying under customary law. 2. TRANSFER OUTSIDE THE VILLAGE NEEDS COUNCIL APPROVAL — which protects village land from passing to outsiders, but seriously reduces collateral value, since rural banks prefer General Land titles; that undercuts one of the CCRO's own stated purposes. 3. IT IS SLOW — the International Land Coalition records long waits leaving people in limbo, inadequate implementation, difficulty understanding the legal texts and overlapping roles between land institutions. 4. CUSTOMARY ARRANGEMENTS THE ACT ENCOURAGES CAN DISCRIMINATE AGAINST WOMEN — worth naming, because a community drafting its by-laws under this process can address that deliberately rather than inherit it. WHAT TENURE UNLOCKED: after the Hadza obtained their CCRO, recognised ownership let them enter conservation programmes paying community members from certified carbon offset credit revenue for managing forest conservation — part paid to local scouts enforcing the community's own land use plans — plus eco-tourism work. Tenure first, revenue second. AND THE ROUTE BY WHICH LAND LEAVES COMMUNITY CONTROL: village land can be converted to General Land, requiring survey, registration, gazetting with local and presidential approval, valuation and compensation — watch for it.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Rainforest Trust — will fund a local organisation to buy the land outright, as it did at Magombera, and warns you never to pay an intermediary to apply
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a funder that pays in-country organisations, Indigenous Peoples and communities to create or expand legally recognised protected areas — and that has financed outright land purchase in Tanzania: its chief executive is on record supporting the purchase and management of Magombera, the forest secured in 2018 and subsequently declared a nature reserve. It offers two grant types: Feasibility Awards, for working out whether protection is possible, and Protected or Conserved Area Creation Awards for doing it — which means a community that does not yet know what the route or the price would be can be funded to find out. Its stated targets are sites facing immediate and direct threats, typically from loggers, miners or ranchers, so an active development threat strengthens rather than weakens the application. One criterion is worth quoting in a proposal: substantial management authority over the area is to be led by Indigenous Peoples or local communities. THE WARNING IT PUBLISHES ITSELF, WHICH SAYS SOMETHING ABOUT WHO PREYS ON THESE APPLICATIONS: you never need to pay a consultant or an intermediary to apply, only applications submitted directly by eligible organisations are reviewed, and the funder will work with you to refine a proposal that fits. WHO IT SUITS: a registered local non-profit, or a community working through one, with a specific parcel and a conservation case — not an individual landowner and not a campaign without a legal vehicle. CAVEATS: it counts Biosphere Reserve, World Heritage and Ramsar status as NOT amounting to protection on their own, so a site already carrying one of those labels still qualifies as unprotected; its focus is the tropics and subtropics; and it is recorded here for Tanzania because Tanzania is where a source names a purchase it funded — it works in dozens of countries and its presence in yours has to be checked, not assumed.

trackers.name: Tanzania Forest Conservation Group — they do the legal work of turning your village forest into a reserve in the village's name
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an organisation with 37 years in Tanzania that walks villages through legally establishing a Village Land Forest Reserve — the step that converts forest anyone can be allocated into forest the village has reserved and manages, and keeps the revenue from. THE NUMBER THAT EXPLAINS THE URGENCY: more than 17.6 million hectares, about 80 per cent of the forest standing on village land in Tanzania, is not legally reserved at all, and roughly 469,000 hectares are cleared a year. Unreserved village forest is the cheapest thing in the country for an outsider to acquire. WHAT THEY ACTUALLY DELIVER, not what they advocate for: 8 villages helped to establish new reserves covering 19,000 hectares in a single year; 61 communities supported through community-based forest management and participatory village land use planning over five years; a coastal programme creating ten new reserves in Lindi region with the villages themselves deciding where the reserve boundaries fall; and 24 villages earning roughly US$200,000 in a year from forest enterprises — the income that makes conserving the forest survivable rather than merely virtuous. They also set up village savings and loan associations, and through their Forest Justice programme they support villages to take forest crimes through the legal system and back local community-based organisations across a hundred villages to run their own advocacy. WHO IT SUITS: a registered village with forest on village land and a village assembly willing to act — this is a route for communities that still hold the land, not for recovering land already taken. THE WARNING THEY PUBLISH THEMSELVES: a 2019 government notice recentralised approval of harvesting plans and of buyers of forest products from village reserves, which cuts the revenue that makes reserving worthwhile and, in their own assessment, disincentivises communities from reserving more forest. Reserve the forest anyway, but do not budget on the revenue arriving unimpeded.

trackers.name: UCRT — has obtained communal title deeds over more than a million hectares for pastoralists and hunter-gatherers, using group land certificates
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a registered Tanzanian NGO working since the 1990s with roughly 40 to 60 pastoralist, agro-pastoralist and hunter-gatherer communities in the northern rangelands, to secure their rights to land and natural resources. THE INSTRUMENT, WHICH IS THE CLOSEST THING TO BUYING YOUR LAND THAT TANZANIAN LAW OFFERS: a Certificate of Customary Right of Occupancy (CCRO) formally allocates a parcel of village land — and UCRT piloted the stronger version, a group or communal CCRO granting customary group title over a defined communal area, which on approval provides permanent tenure to the holder. Under the Village Land Act an individual or group living on customarily held land over 250 hectares may apply to their Village Council with the Commissioner of Lands' approval. THE PREPARATION IS THE WORK, and it is the same list everywhere: the council must define and approve community by-laws, hold a certificate of village land, and agree boundaries and land use plans through a district demarcation and zoning process. UCRT does exactly those steps with communities — demarcation and boundary reconciliation, mapping, village registration, land use planning, by-laws. WHAT IT HAS PRODUCED: reported figures range from 1.1 million hectares secured in one account to 1.7 million hectares covering more than 400,000 people in 120 communities in a later one; for the Hadzabe specifically it obtained title deeds for customary rights of occupancy over 20,000 hectares, and over 46,320 hectares by another account, and helped secure Mongo wa Mono, the only Hadzabe-majority village in Tanzania. WHY THIS BEATS A CONSERVATION AGREEMENT: a communal CCRO is title, not a contract with an NGO or a promise from a district — it is the answer to the question of what stops the land being allocated to an investor. UCRT also runs a Hadzabe cultural mapping project to demonstrate the relationship to land, and works with women's rights and land forums in the region. WHO IT SUITS: pastoralist, hunter-gatherer and agro-pastoralist communities in northern Tanzania holding land customarily and facing agricultural expansion, investor allocation or exclusion. CAVEATS: the process runs through the Village Council, the district and the Commissioner of Lands, so it needs functioning village institutions and takes time; UCRT's own area is the northern rangelands, not the whole country; reported hectare and community figures differ between sources and years, so treat them as orders of magnitude; and no intake route or fee information was published.

trackers.name: HakiArdhi — trains Land Rights Monitors who live in the village: 600 volunteers across 300 villages, there before any lawyer is
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Land Rights Research & Resources Institute (LARRRI/HAKIARDHI), founded 1994 in Dar es Salaam, working on the land rights of rural and peri-urban small producers. THE INSTRUMENT, AND IT IS THE CHEAPEST STANDING DEFENCE IN THIS FILE: since 2012 it has built and trained a network of about 600 male and female “Land Rights Monitors” operating in some 300 villages — volunteers ELECTED BY THEIR OWN COMMUNITIES after village-wide capacity-building, trained in the land law, with deliberate gender balance. What they do: train neighbours on their land rights, advise village leaders, facilitate negotiation and mediation in disputes, and report serious violations back to HakiArdhi for further action. Reported reach: around 15,000 villagers supported over three years. A trained monitor lives in the village; a lawyer arrives after the damage. That is why this class of resource matters most where large-scale land-based investments arrive with little warning — the monitors were built specifically around the impact of those investments. HakiArdhi also researches, publishes and runs national land rights advocacy jointly with other Tanzanian civil society, and the model has been documented in detail by legal-empowerment practitioners precisely so others can copy the process: community capacity-building first, then election, then training, then reporting lines back to a national body that can escalate. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanian villages and small producers facing investor acquisitions, boundary disputes or pressure on village land, and organisations elsewhere wanting a replicable village-monitor model. CAVEATS: monitors are trained volunteers, not lawyers — they mediate and refer rather than litigate; for public interest environmental litigation Tanzania's LEAT entry is the route, and for group certificates of customary right of occupancy, UCRT. A second HakiArdhi domain exists as a development mirror; the .or.tz site is the current one.

trackers.name: Simanjiro voluntary land easements — 23,000 hectares kept open by paid agreement, with the village keeping the land and the grazing
trackers.desc: WHAT TO SIGN INSTEAD OF SELLING: on the Simanjiro plains east of Tarangire National Park, a consortium of tourism companies began working with Terrat village in 2005 and Sukuro village in 2009 to protect wet-season grazing through two VOLUNTARY LAND EASEMENTS totalling 23,000 hectares. THE TERMS ARE THE INSTRUMENT, and they are simple enough to copy: under the agreement livestock AND wildlife may graze the land, while FARMING, PERMANENT SETTLEMENTS, CHARCOAL PRODUCTION AND ILLEGAL HUNTING ARE NOT PERMITTED — and the communities earn an income for maintaining the land-use practices they were already following, while the tourism companies get sustained wildlife on land they do not own. An easement is the middle instrument this file has been missing: you do not sell, you do not lease the parcel out, you keep using it — you are paid to accept written limits on what may be done to it. That makes it available to a village that would never sell and could not afford to buy, and it is enforceable because the restrictions are written rather than customary. It sits between the two Tanzanian routes already recorded here — certificates of customary right of occupancy, which document who holds the land, and Wildlife Management Areas, where villages set aside communal land and transfer management authority to a registered Authorized Association. ASK WHICH OF THE THREE YOU ARE BEING OFFERED, because they give away very different things. Reported as a cost-effective model that has held; related work in the same landscape has cut crop damage on farms next to conservation areas by up to 70 per cent through village game scouts and community volunteers. WHO IT SUITS: northern Tanzanian pastoralist villages under pressure to convert grazing land to farming or settlement, and communities seeking income without transferring rights. CAVEATS: the payer is the TOURISM INDUSTRY, so the money depends on visitors and on companies that benefit from your restraint — read the term, the renewal and the exit clauses, and check who enforces the restrictions against outsiders. This is not a title; for CCROs and group certificates see Tanzania's UCRT entry, and for village-level monitors, HakiArdhi.

trackers.name: Tanzania's Register of Legal Aid Providers — paralegals are recognised in national law, and the Registrar keeps the list you can ask for
trackers.desc: WHAT THE LAW GIVES YOU: the Legal Aid Act, signed and gazetted on 3 March 2017, which OFFICIALLY RECOGNISES PARALEGALS NATIONALLY for the first time, replaces the old criminal-proceedings-only statute and extends legal aid to CIVIL proceedings — which is what a land case is. It applies to Mainland Tanzania. THE LIST TO ASK FOR: the Act establishes a REGISTER OF LEGAL AID PROVIDERS kept by a REGISTRAR, with ASSISTANT REGISTRARS at REGION AND DISTRICT level — the public officers who register community-based organisations are eligible to serve as them. Every institution intending to provide legal aid must apply to the Registrar for registration, and registration certificates are issued WITHOUT COST (renewal attracts a fee). So there is a district-level official whose job is to know which organisations near you are lawfully providing free legal aid — ask the Assistant Registrar for the register rather than hunting organisation by organisation. WHAT AN “INDIGENT PERSON” MEANS HERE, since eligibility turns on it: a person whose means are insufficient to engage a private legal practitioner, AND other categories of persons where the interests of justice so require — the second limb is broader than a pure means test. Legal aid services expressly include legal education and information, legal advice and assistance. The Registrar also investigates complaints of malpractice, negligence or misconduct against legal aid providers and can suspend or cancel a registration, and inspects providers' offices to check the quality of what they offer. If a paralegal or provider mistreats you, there is a named official to complain to. The national board includes a High Court judge as chair and a representative from the paralegal umbrella body. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanians on Mainland who need free legal help with a land, boundary or civil matter, and communities wanting to verify that whoever is advising them is lawfully registered. CAVEATS: A STATUTORY FRAMEWORK, NOT AN ORGANISATION — it tells you who is authorised, not who has capacity; paralegals may NOT do work reserved for advocates; and it does not apply in Zanzibar. For village-level Land Rights Monitors, Tanzania's HakiArdhi entry; for public interest environmental litigation, LEAT; for group certificates of customary right of occupancy, UCRT.

trackers.name: Adam Teva V'Din — Israel Union for Environmental Defense
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Israel's first public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1990 — a combined staff of lawyers, scientists, urban planners and an environmental economist, which is what lets it fight at the planning-committee stage rather than only in court. It petitions the High Court against coastal privatisation, oil-shale projects and ministerial inaction; its legal action has forced the Ministry of Environmental Protection to publish new conditions on businesses, won a ruling that Dead Sea Works must pay for the water it uses, and helped save the Bat Yam cliff. WHO IT SUITS: residents and local environmental groups facing a planning decision or a polluting facility. It is membership-based and picks strategic cases, and its planning team is often more use early than its litigators are late.

trackers.name: EcoPeace Middle East
trackers.desc: Founded in 1994 as Friends of the Earth Middle East and still a member of Friends of the Earth International, EcoPeace is staffed and directed jointly by Jordanians, Palestinians and Israelis, with its own offices in Amman, Ramallah and Tel Aviv and a national director in each. WHO TO ENLIST: the office in your own country. Its Good Water Neighbors programme works with communities on either side of a shared water problem, pairing them across the border rather than treating each in isolation. You CAN get community-level organising support and technical and advocacy weight on water, sewage and Jordan Valley development. You CAN'T get a litigator — EcoPeace works by cross-border cooperation, research and advocacy, not by suing proponents, so a community that needs a permit or an approval challenged in court should look elsewhere. For activists: in Jordan and Palestine this was the only substantial environmental organisation with an office and a named national director that could be verified on its own domain.

trackers.name: SPNI — founded over a lost fight, and what came of it
trackers.desc: ISRAEL'S OLDEST AND LARGEST INDEPENDENT ENVIRONMENTAL NON-PROFIT, working to preserve species by protecting the lands and waters needed for their survival. ITS HISTORY IS THE REASON TO RECORD IT HONESTLY: SPNI was founded in 1953 by Azaria Alon and Amotz Zahavi in response to plans to drain the Hula Valley — and it lost that fight: the government and the JNF drained the majority of the wetlands. But after 40 years of campaigning, roughly 10 percent of the Hula wetlands were re-flooded in the early 1990s. Losing the immediate fight, building an institution, and recovering a fraction four decades later is a truer picture of this work than most success stories. WHAT IT DOES NOW: biodiversity protection, environmental education, bird protection, sustainable ecotourism, and work with policy makers, schools and communities — including producing an agricultural management plan for the Hula Valley, so it does technical planning, not only advocacy. It has a branch structure and is an IUCN member; it received the Israel Prize in 1980. THE STANDING CONTEXT it names for any Israeli land fight: a small country with a growing population whose remaining open spaces are increasingly under threat of development.

trackers.name: Nature Israel — the diaspora funding channel for Israeli conservation
trackers.desc: HOW THIS WORK GETS PAID FOR. Nature Israel — formerly the Canadian Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, founded in 2011 — exists to raise awareness and funds supporting SPNI's activities in Israel. It is a diaspora fundraising channel rather than a grant-making body, so the route for a local group is partnering with or working through SPNI rather than applying to Nature Israel directly. HONEST GAP, STATED SO IT IS NOT MISTAKEN FOR COVERAGE: what could be verified for this entry is an organisation and a fundraising channel, not a standing Israeli grant programme with published eligibility for local community groups. If such a programme exists it should be added alongside this rather than inferred from it.

trackers.name: SPNI — the body that will carry your objection, and the one that files them by the thousand
trackers.desc: THE PRACTICAL POINT IS NOT THAT SPNI OBJECTS TO PLANS — IT IS THAT IT COLLECTS AND SUBMITS OTHER PEOPLE'S OBJECTIONS AT SCALE. When the government moved in 2026 to dilute environmental impact assessment requirements for large projects, around 1,300 individuals lodged their opposition through SPNI, alongside appeals from SPNI itself, Adam Teva V'Din, Zalul, Green Course, 15 Minutes and the Israel Association of Public Health Physicians. In 2024 it published the Hebrew legal memorandum on the Gaza-border reconstruction bill and told the public how to register objections to the proposed planning committee. If you have a local plan and no organisation, this is the route that turns one letter into a filed mass objection. WHO TO ASK FOR: Iris Han leads its open-landscape and planning work — irish@spni.org.il; Dan Alon runs the Israeli Ornithological Center; Yoav Perlman is the BirdLife contact at yoavp@spni.org.il. Head office Ha Negev 2, Tel Aviv. THE LOCAL LAYER MATTERS AND IS OFTEN MISSED: SPNI runs locally managed community branches in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa, Beer Sheva and Modiin, each focused on its own city's fights, plus more than ten field schools — approach the branch for an urban plan rather than head office. Founded 1953 in direct response to the draining of the Hula Valley, roughly 800 employees, Israel Prize 1980, and the organisation behind the 2004 Coastal Law that bars new development within 300 metres of the shoreline — which means for any coastal site the first question is whether that 300-metre bar applies before anything else is argued. Pair it with Adam Teva V'Din, already in this file, which litigates; SPNI's strength is planning objections and open-space advocacy rather than the courtroom. VERIFICATION CAVEAT: the canonical domain spni.org.il is established from BirdLife International's partner record and from staff addresses published in conference proceedings; the specific landing page was not fetched during verification, and the organisation's main site is Hebrew-language.

trackers.name: Article 23 delegation — a voluntary society can hold ministerial powers
trackers.desc: THE ROUTE JORDAN ACTUALLY USES. Article 23 lets the Ministry, with Cabinet approval, delegate any of its tasks or powers to ministries, institutions and relevant voluntary societies in environmental protection — provided the delegation is in writing and specific. That is how the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature enforces wildlife law by delegation from the Ministry of Agriculture, works with the environmental police, and has issued hunting licences since 1973. SO THE QUESTION IS WHO HOLDS THE WRITTEN DELEGATION for your subject and area — ask for it by name, because the law requires it to be written and specific. BUT ARTICLE 24 IS A REAL GATE ON ORGANISING: licensing and renewal of licensing of non-governmental societies working in environmental protection happens only after prior approval of the Ministry. The renewal limb is the one groups forget — diary the date and start ministry approval early. A DEFINITION WORTH USING: degradation means reducing the environment's value, distorting its nature, depleting its resources or harming living organisms or antiquities — antiquities sit inside the environmental definition of harm.

trackers.name: Special protection area — the category for a threatened species, not a view
trackers.desc: PICK THE RIGHT CATEGORY BEFORE YOU ARGUE. The nature reserves and national parks regulation defines: national park — land, water, shores, oases, forests or heritage areas that the Council of Ministers decides is one, so a site need not be wilderness; protected land — deliberately broad, any land the Council decides is protected; and special protection area — an area hosting a distinctive ecosystem or wildlife threatened with extinction. That last is the category to seek when your argument is a specific threatened species or a distinctive ecosystem rather than scenic value. WHO DECIDES: the Council of Ministers, on the Minister's recommendation — so the recommendation is the step to influence. The competent body that establishes or manages a reserve is appointed the same way, which is how a non-state body can run one. Article 21 requires the specifications and conditions for any reserve to be set by regulation, so the standards are written and checkable. CONTEXT: RSCN founded 1966, first reserve Shaumari 1975, Dibbeen sixth in 2004 at around 1,200 km²; Fifa 2011; Burqu, Dhuheikeh and Dumaitha 2018. RSCN has an elected 11-member board, elected every 4 years — a membership you can join and a board you can stand for.

trackers.name: Environment Protection Fund — currently disbursing, chaired by the Minister
trackers.desc: AN ACTIVE GRANT WINDOW, NOT A DORMANT ONE. The Board of the Environment Protection Fund meets at the Ministry of Environment and is chaired by the Minister of Environment, and has approved financing for a package of environmental and development projects covering sustainable agriculture and green economy work — aimed at protecting the environment, ensuring sustainability of natural resources, and enhancing the participation of local communities in achieving sustainable environmental development. TWO THINGS FOLLOW: approvals are being reported currently, so the fund is disbursing; and local community participation is an express objective of what the board has just funded, so a community-participation framing matches its stated priorities rather than arguing against them. The board being chaired by the Minister tells you the level at which decisions are made — ministry relationships matter alongside a paper application. Approvals are announced through Petra, the Jordan News Agency, which is a way to track what has actually been funded before you draft. DO NOT CONFUSE IT with the Saudi صندوق البيئة (Environment Fund), a different country's body covering ‘environment and meteorology’ that surfaces on the same search terms.

trackers.name: GEF endorsement runs through Planning, not Environment
trackers.desc: APPROACHING THE WRONG MINISTRY LOSES TIME. Jordan's GEF Operational Focal Point sits in the Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation, not the environment ministry — the Secretary General, focal point since 17 March 2021 — and a working contact is published: Head of Division, World Bank Division, International Cooperation Department, Amman; tel +962 6 4644466 ext 644; email maher.abdelrahim@mop.gov.jo. A GEF project needs that focal point's endorsement. Jordan sits in a constituency with Afghanistan, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Syria and Yemen, and financing for national and regional projects is inclusive of all participating countries. UNDER GEF-8 STAR FULL FLEXIBILITY, funds may be drawn across biodiversity, climate change and land degradation, with the source focal area endorsed by the Operational Focal Point — so which envelope your project is charged to is that person's decision, and worth discussing before submission. Jordan is also a Green Climate Fund country with a National Designated Authority. OTHER BODIES: JOHUD (created by royal decree 1977) is the largest development NGO, with a network of 51 community centres and, since 1979, special legal status with administrative and financial independence — its mandate is poverty, women, youth and water scarcity, not primarily environmental, so approach it on a livelihood or water framing. EcoPeace Middle East works across Amman, Bethlehem and Tel Aviv.

trackers.name: Lebanon — Commercial Register (Ministry of Justice)
