trackers.name: ZEMA call for comments — the appeal window is reported as ten days, the shortest found anywhere in this region, and the route is disputed
trackers.desc: TEN DAYS. IF THAT IS RIGHT — AND IT IS THE FIGURE IN THE STANDARD REGIONAL REFERENCE — IT IS THE TIGHTEST OBJECTION CLOCK IN AFRICA, AND MOST PEOPLE WILL MISS IT WHILE DECIDING WHO TO WRITE TO. An aggrieved party appeals a decision of the environment agency in writing to the Minister responsible for the environment within ten days of receiving the decision, and the Minister should decide within fourteen days; from there the route runs to the High Court. BUT THE ROUTE ITSELF IS CONTESTED: the assessment regulations still in force date from 1997 and send the appeal straight to the Minister, while the Environmental Management Act of 2011 provides for review and appeal first to the Agency's own Board and only then to the Minister. Revised regulations were prepared and sent for approval years ago and had not been enacted when this was written. The safe course is to lodge in writing within ten days, address it to the Board, copy the Minister, and say in the letter that you are proceeding under both routes — cheaper than being told you used the wrong one after the time has run. WHERE TO WATCH FOR THE TRIGGER: the Agency publishes an EIA call-for-comments section and a downloadable repository of environmental impact statements, so the document you need to object to is usually obtainable without a request; it also offers an SMS subscription for updates, which matters where data is expensive. The Act separately obliges the Agency to maintain a central environmental information system and an environmental information registry open to public viewing. Plot 6975, corner of Church and Suez Roads, Lusaka; +260 211 254023 or 254059; info@zema.org.zm; open 08:00 to 17:00 on weekdays. CAVEATS: the ten-day and fourteen-day figures come from a development-bank regional handbook and an assessment-commission country profile, not from the Agency's own pages, which publish no appeal deadline at all — treat ten days as the working assumption and confirm at the counter. This URL is the call-for-comments section as listed in the Agency's own site navigation; the page verified for this entry was its parent.

trackers.name: Zambia Land Alliance — paralegal officers in district branches across all ten provinces, and they have got grabbed land returned
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a network of Zambian NGOs on land rights that works through a national secretariat in Lusaka and district branches across all ten provinces, plus District Land Alliances that are separate registered organisations in their own right — so the first contact is usually local, not national. WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE IN PRACTICE, from a documented case: a family in Solwezi whose land had been taken by a church was advised by a ZLA paralegal officer to start with the Area Development Committee, given a referral letter, and when the other side refused to attend the convened meeting, advised to bring civil proceedings — which they won, with an order to vacate. That is the whole sequence a household needs and cannot usually find: who to go to first, the letter that makes them act, and when to stop negotiating and sue. It also runs Community Land Advocacy Committees with traditional leaders in districts including Kafue, Mkushi, Serenje and Kalumbila, and uses participatory land use planning to turn communities into land use negotiators before an investor arrives. District alliances in the Copperbelt describe strengthened paralegal networks reaching thousands of people, funded through the Zambian Governance Foundation, OSISA and Global Greengrants. WHO IT SUITS: rural and peri-urban households and communities facing land grabbing, mining displacement or investor allocations on customary land — particularly women, whose land rights are an explicit focus. Plot 126E Kudu Road, Kabulonga, Lusaka. CAVEATS: ZLA is an advocacy network with paralegals, not a law firm — it refers and advises rather than litigating for you; the national website is thin and partly filled with unrelated template text, so the district alliances are the more reliable point of contact; and no intake criteria or fee information was published.

trackers.name: Zambia's district land alliances — customary land holding certificates issued with the chiefs, and the argument about whether they help
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Chipata and Petauke District Land Alliances, Zambian civil society organisations documenting the land rights of households in Eastern Province. Since 2014 the Chipata alliance has partnered with six customary chiefs to run low-cost participatory documentation using mobile mapping, working through the chiefs, their advisors, village headpersons and each household, and building Village Land Committees that carry the process locally. WHY THIS EXISTS AT ALL: Zambia's government recognises customary tenure but has not legislated to secure it — roughly 14.5 million people rely on undocumented customary land while only about 140,000 leasehold titles exist. Households want documentation to prevent arbitrary takings and to secure fair compensation if land is converted by government, headpersons or chiefs. WHAT THE CERTIFICATE IS AND IS NOT, which is the most important paragraph here: it carries a georeferenced map of the holding plus the identity of the right holder, any joint holders, and any “persons of interest” attached to the parcel — and the issuers deliberately never call it a land title. Conditions printed on the certificate, in English and the local language, state that it does not constitute consent to convert customary land to leasehold. That distinction is the protection: conversion to leasehold is how customary land is lost. THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT: researchers studying the Petauke certificates issued from 2010 concluded, from interviews with farmers, chiefs and the alliance, that the certificates reinforced rather than reversed the commodification of land and inequality of access. Communities have also worried that documentation is a precursor to taxation. Weigh that before starting. WHO IT SUITS: households and villages on customary land in Eastern Province wanting their holding mapped and recorded before someone else claims it. CAVEATS: NEITHER ALLIANCE HAS A VERIFIED SITE OF ITS OWN — this entry points at the tenure programme record that documents them; approach through Zambia Land Alliance, whose entry is also in this file and which pilots chief-issued certificates nationally. The work has been donor-funded and pilot-scale, chiefdom boundaries rest on an out-of-date 1958 map, and the certificate's legal weight is untested.

trackers.name: Zambia's mining-pollution coalitions and the foreign-court route — how Chingola and Kabwe residents got past a company that ignored them at home
trackers.desc: WHAT WORKED, AND WHO TO FIND: Zambian mining-affected communities have repeatedly failed to get remedy at home and succeeded by suing the foreign PARENT company in ITS OWN courts. 1,826 residents of Chingola, whose water and farmland were contaminated by run-off from a copper mine from 2004, won the right to bring their case in the United Kingdom against the parent of the mine's operator — and that case produced compensation. Separately, a class action was filed in South Africa on behalf of an estimated 140,000 women and children in Kabwe alleging lead poisoning from a mine within a British group from 1925 to 1974, closed in 1994 and never cleaned up — an estimated 6.4 million tonnes of lead-bearing waste, soil in places above 3,000 mg/kg against a common regulatory limit of 400. THE ORGANISATIONS AROUND IT: a national development organisation trained Shimulala residents in Chingola on their rights and put community activists on local radio; the Alliance for Lead-Free Kabwe coalesces Zambian and international groups pressing for a clean-up plan; the Zambia Environmental Justice Coalition responded to a later acid spill by demanding the government RENEGOTIATE ALL COMPENSATION AGREEMENTS with the full involvement of affected communities; and a “Zambia's Sacrifice Zone” campaign of young activists, journalists and NGOs uses storytelling and radio to carry community voices. After one spill, 47 households threatened suit in the Lusaka High Court unless compensation was paid. ASK EARLY WHO THE PARENT COMPANY IS AND WHERE IT IS INCORPORATED — that answer decides whether a foreign court is open to you. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian communities living with mine pollution, contaminated water or lead waste, and anyone facing a subsidiary of a foreign-listed mining group. CAVEATS: NO SINGLE VERIFIED SITE EXISTS FOR THESE COALITIONS — this entry points at the international documentation record that names them; foreign litigation took Chingola thirteen years, activists report promised compensation unpaid and weak enforcement, and this route needs foreign counsel. For paralegals, Zambia Land Alliance; for EIA comment, the ZEMA entry.

trackers.name: Mize Community Conservancy, Nyawa Chiefdom — 585 km² registered under the Wildlife Act in the name of the community itself
trackers.desc: WHAT TO REGISTER, AND THE PRECEDENT THAT SHOWS IT CAN BE DONE: the Mize Community Conservancy (MiCC) in the Nyawa Chiefdom, Kazungula District, Southern Province — successfully REGISTERED UNDER ZAMBIA'S WILDLIFE ACT, covering 585 km², in a degraded wildlife corridor connecting Kafue National Park to the neighbouring transfrontier protected areas. A community conservancy in this model is a legally recognised, geographically defined area formed by communities that have united to manage and benefit from wildlife and other natural resources — which is the difference between using land at someone's discretion and holding a registered area in your own name. WHAT THE REGISTRATION TOOK, because the sequence is the useful part: a review of 354 legal texts on wildlife and related sectors, published on a public legal hub, established the basis; a customary law analysis was then run across the chiefdom — 57 participants from 20 villages, including senior headmen, women and youth; and ten new community resource board members, three of them women, were elected, with governance strengthened through exchange visits and training. Legal groundwork, then customary mapping, then an elected board — in that order. The chiefdom encompasses a reported 500 villages. Alongside registration, the work covers habitat and game management, human-wildlife conflict, and livelihoods through fish farming, beekeeping and livestock. Sister conservancies exist at Simalaha in Zambia and Mucheni in Zimbabwe under the same regional model, so there are neighbours who have done it. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian chiefdoms and villages that want a registered conservancy rather than an informal arrangement, especially in wildlife corridors under pressure. CAVEATS: THE CONSERVANCY HAS NO SITE OF ITS OWN — this entry points at the programme record documenting the registration, and the work was donor-funded through a time-limited international programme, so ask what survives its end. Registration is under the WILDLIFE Act and confers management rights over wildlife and resources; it is NOT a land title, and Zambia's customary land questions remain — see the district land alliances entry for certificates, and Zambia Land Alliance for paralegals.

trackers.name: Zambia Legal Aid Board — land disputes are the FIRST case type it lists, and applications are processed in 48 hours
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY: the Legal Aid Board of Zambia, a statutory body operating under the Legal Aid Act No. 1 of 2021, which repealed and replaced the 1967 Act and now also provides for the regulation of LAW CLINICS and the registration of practitioners, legal assistants, PARALEGALS and legal aid service providers. WHY IT LEADS THIS ENTRY: the Board's own published list of case types it deals with BEGINS with “land dispute and related issues”, followed by compensation demands, conveyancing, change of ownership, breach of contract, probate, property settlement and drafting assistance. A legal aid body that names land first is unusual, and it means you do not have to argue that your case belongs. WHAT IT COSTS AND HOW LONG IT TAKES: legal aid is provided FREE OF CHARGE, though after a MEANS TEST a modest contribution may be requested case by case; APPLICATIONS ARE PROCESSED WITHIN 48 HOURS, and you are told if more time is needed — up to 30 days. A published turnaround is rare enough in this file to be worth citing back at them if you are left waiting. You may request a particular lawyer, but assignment depends on availability, expertise and caseload. SCALE AND REACH: in one year the Board received 12,071 applications, granting legal aid — assistance or representation — in 6,397 and giving information and advice to the remaining 5,674; it runs six Legal Services Units at Subordinate Court level across three provinces, and supervises ten legal desks in correctional facilities and police stations staffed by paralegals from civil society organisations. In civil cases it may also provide mediation. Alongside it, the National Legal Aid Clinic for Women (NLACW), established 1990 under the Law Association of Zambia, offers representation, mobile legal clinics and community-level paralegal desks; Plot 110a/150 Musonda Ngosa Road, Villa Elizabetha, Lusaka, +260 211 220595. WHO IT SUITS: Zambians with a land dispute, compensation claim or property matter who cannot pay a lawyer; women and children through NLACW. CAVEATS: A STATE BOARD with a means test, a nominal consultation contribution and a criminal-heavy caseload; it will not act against government policy for you. For paralegals in ten provinces, Zambia's ZLA entry; for EIA comment, ZEMA; for the foreign parent-company route, the mining-pollution entry.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Accountability State Authority
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Egypt, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Egypt e-Tenders
trackers.desc: Egypt's government e-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Egypt, and for how much.

trackers.name: CAPMAS
trackers.desc: Egypt's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Egypt.

trackers.name: Court of Cassation (Egypt)
trackers.desc: Egypt's highest ordinary court; publishes many civil and some criminal judgments online. · Find here: information and selected rulings of Egypt's Court of Cassation.

trackers.name: GAFI
trackers.desc: Egypt's General Authority for Investment company registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: Egyptian Center for Economic and Social Rights — has litigated expropriation for public utility, and keeps legal representatives in more than twenty governorates
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an Egyptian non-governmental legal institution founded in 2009 that works through strategic litigation rather than reporting alone, and whose landmark cases include the expropriation for public utility case and litigation over the privatisation of public property — the two ways land moves out of people's hands in Egypt. It also runs housing and eviction work. WHERE IT CAN REACH YOU: the main office is in downtown Cairo with branches in Alexandria, Daqahliya and Aswan, plus legal representatives in more than twenty governorates — which in a country where nearly every rights organisation is Cairo-only is the difference between a case and a press release. Its published record shows it filing urgent proceedings before the Administrative Court, pressing the government over non-implementation of a court ruling that banned Nile pollution at Aswan, and bringing a suit to protect the Pyramids from vibration and laser damage caused by concerts — evidence it will litigate a site-protection claim, not only a labour or welfare one. WHO IT SUITS: communities and households facing expropriation, eviction, or industrial pollution, and workers' groups. CAVEATS, AND THEY ARE SERIOUS: Egyptian civic space is heavily constrained — ECESR's offices have been raided by police and staff detained, its founder is a prominent opposition lawyer, and association with it carries risk that a community should weigh before approaching. Its site publishes case news rather than an intake procedure, much of the material is Arabic-first, and no fee or eligibility information was found.

trackers.name: EIPR — Cairo rights organisation with a standing right-to-housing file, legal aid and strategic litigation on evictions
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, an independent Cairo organisation established in 2002, working through research, documentation, legal aid, strategic litigation and advocacy on civil liberties, economic and social rights and criminal justice — with a declared focus on the rights closest to a person: body, privacy and house. WHY IT IS FILED HERE: it maintains a standing published Right to Housing file, which is the rare thing a resident can read BEFORE the demolition crew arrives. Its documentation includes the demolition of the homes of almost 1,000 families at Izbat al-Nakhl in February 2014, carried out with riot police, without prior notice or consultation — some residents rehoused, others left homeless — within a period in which more than twenty forced eviction operations were recorded without reparation or fair compensation. THE ARGUMENT TO USE: it grounds housing claims in Article 78 of the Egyptian constitution, and has analysed the state budget to show the government failed to adopt policies supporting the poor's right to adequate housing. It also works the tenancy side, proposing rent subsidy through the state housing and mortgage fund with a legal rent-to-income ratio capped at 20 per cent, and arguing that tenants who paid key money or financed unfinished units and infrastructure themselves have built a long-term usufructuary entitlement distinct from ordinary tenancy — a useful line for anyone whose own money went into the building they are being moved out of. WHO IT SUITS: Egyptian households facing demolition, eviction, resettlement or rent liberalisation, especially in Greater Cairo. CAVEATS: EGYPTIAN CIVIC SPACE IS SEVERELY CONSTRAINED AND EIPR'S OWN SENIOR STAFF HAVE BEEN DETAINED; approach with that in mind. It supports litigation rather than acting as a general legal aid office, and for expropriation cases and its regional branches, Egypt's ECESR entry is the other route.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? YES — Dakar (hub). Natural Justice keeps 3 hubs: Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar. A hub means staff on the ground rather than a project relationship. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes du Sénégal
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Senegal — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Senegal EITI Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Office National de Lutte contre la Fraude et la Corruption (OFNAC)
trackers.desc: Senegal’s national anti-fraud and anti-corruption office — investigates corruption and manages public-official asset declarations.

trackers.name: OHADA RCCM (regional company registry)
trackers.desc: Federated regional registry of companies and financial statements across all OHADA member states (based at the CCJA, Abidjan). Here you can trace companies, their directors and filings registered in Senegal.

trackers.name: Senegal — Bureau d’Appui à la Création d’Entreprise (APIX)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the APIX one-stop business office registers companies, issues the RCCM & tax ID and publishes legal announcements, Senegal. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Marchés Publics
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Senegal, and for how much.

trackers.name: Extraordinary African Chambers
trackers.desc: Extraordinary African Chambers — tribunal in Senegal (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Code forestier 2018 — a commune can create its own bois communal
trackers.desc: THE AUTHORITY MOVED DOWNWARD, SO ADDRESS THE COMMUNE. Loi 2018-25 of 12 November 2018 replaced the 1998 Code and was aligned with the Code général des Collectivités locales, which redistributed environment and natural resource competences formerly held by the region to the department and the commune. WHAT THAT ENABLES: a bois communal is a wooded space created by the commune, outside the classified forest domain, for conservation or recreation — the commune can simply create one. The domaine forestier protégé covers forêts de terroir, réserves communautaires, bois communaux and natural sites of local interest. And conventions locales let territorial collectivities agree conservation and sustainable management of forest resources — subject to the forest service's opinion and approval by the State representative. Transferred competences must be organised in a plan simple de gestion or plan d'aménagement forestier. TWO FUNDS CAME WITH THE REFORM: the FNI for conservation of forest patrimony, and the Fonds local d'Aménagement (FLA), whose object is supporting the participation of concerned actors in implementing management plans — ask your commune about it.

trackers.name: Défrichement thresholds — who signs depends on the hectares
trackers.desc: KNOW THE THRESHOLD, AND WATCH FOR SPLITTING. A municipal council deliberation authorising défrichement is not executory until approved — and who approves depends on area: up to 10 hectares, the Sous-préfet or the Préfet; between 10 and 50 hectares, only the Préfet of the department; above 50 hectares, only the Governor of the region, by registered regulatory act at the Secrétariat général du gouvernement. That tells you whose decision to scrutinise — and whether a clearance has been divided into sub-threshold parcels to avoid a higher approval. THE HONEST CRITIQUE, from Senegalese analysis: requiring management plans for any forest over 20 hectares, drawn up by the local collectivity, was found to limit from the outset the exercise of these councils' power; under participatory management projects, delivery of cutting authorisations passed from rural councils to newly created village committees; private actors leasing community forest for hunting and tourism need the opinion of the regional council as well, giving a level with no territory of its own access to resources and revenue; and forest agents sit on all regional and technical commissions. Decentralisation on paper is not control in practice — check who actually signs.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Lumière Synergie pour le Développement — files complaints against the banks funding the project, and has had them declared admissible
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Senegalese non-profit, constituted in 2008, that attacks a project through its financiers rather than through its permits — which is the route that exists when a national process is closed or already decided. It has filed, with the affected communities themselves as co-complainants: a complaint to the African Development Bank's accountability mechanism over the Sendou coal plant at Bargny, alongside the women fish processors whose livelihoods it affected; a complaint with the Collectif des Impactés de la Centrale Electrique de Malicounda against the AfDB over a 120 MW thermal plant; a complaint to the Turkish OECD National Contact Point against Tosyali Holding; and, with the artisanal fishers' association at the Langue de Barbarie, a complaint against BP and Kosmos Energy over the Grand Tortue Ahmeyim gas project, which the United Kingdom's OECD contact point ruled admissible in 2026 — the fishers called it historic. A Dutch development bank's independent complaints mechanism has sent repeated monitoring missions to Senegal on the Sendou case. WHY THIS MATTERS TO A COMMUNITY ELSEWHERE: every one of those routes exists because someone abroad lent the money, and none of them requires standing in a national court. The organisation also runs capacity-building workshops across Africa on the transparency, accountability and involuntary-resettlement rules of international financial institutions — including one for Ivorian journalists in Abidjan — so its expertise is deliberately exportable. WHO IT SUITS: communities affected by a project with a development bank, export credit agency or foreign multinational behind it, who can document the harm and are prepared for a process measured in years. CAVEATS: this is complaints work and advocacy, not litigation and not land purchase — the mechanisms produce findings, monitoring and negotiated remedy rather than injunctions, and the Sendou complaint has been running since the plant was built. Contact is by email to the executive director rather than through a published intake form.

trackers.name: Enda Pronat and the CRAFS land coalition — someone is on the ground within a day of a dispossession, and they have won 10,000 hectares back in court
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Enda Pronat, working in Senegal since the 1980s on agroecology and, for the last fifteen years, squarely on land grabbing — and a founding member of CRAFS, the Cadre de Réflexion et d'Action sur le Foncier au Sénégal, an alliance of farmers' organisations, scientists and NGOs. THE RAPID-RESPONSE SYSTEM IS THE PART WORTH COPYING ANYWHERE IN THE WORLD: CRAFS members each hold direct contacts in rural communities, share alerts internally by mailing list, and when farmers are dispossessed, at least one member organisation travels to the site THE SAME DAY OR THE NEXT, investigates, and reports back to the others. What follows is chosen case by case: informing residents of their rights, mediation, help organising marches, instructing lawyers, then press interviews, social media and formal approaches to the authorities. Speed is the scarce commodity in a land grab — boundaries and facts are established in the first week, and almost nothing in this file moves that fast. WHAT IT HAS WON: reported three judicial victories for local land rights, one of them over 10,000 hectares of farmland at Dodel, plus training for producers, elected officials and local authorities on land regularisation procedures in the Niayes, the groundnut basin and eastern Senegal. It works with the community at Ndiaël, dispossessed of more than 20,000 hectares of agro-pastoral land. It also helped rural communities set up local watch platforms (plateformes de veille) to defend their rights and mobilise when a grab starts — a standing structure, built before the threat arrives. Enda Pronat is Senegal's focal point for COPAGEN, the West African coalition on genetic resources, biopiracy and land grabbing across nine countries. WHO IT SUITS: Senegalese farming and pastoral communities losing land to agro-industrial or investor allocations. CAVEATS: a farmer-movement and advocacy organisation — it instructs lawyers rather than being one; CRAFS itself has no verified standalone contact point, so approach through a member such as Enda Pronat; and for pressure on a project's foreign financiers, Senegal's Lumière Synergie entry is the other route.

trackers.name: Océanium de Dakar and the Bamboung community marine protected area — 7,000 ha declared by the villages, guarded by villagers, paid for by its own eco-lodge
trackers.desc: WHAT A VILLAGE CAN DECLARE: Océanium, a Senegalese environmental association founded in 1984, working on mangrove replanting, coastal clean-up, and against overfishing, forest pillage and bush fires. It piloted the creation of the Bamboung community marine protected area (AMPC) in the Sine-Saloum delta — reported as the first functional community MPA in West Africa. THE SEQUENCE, WHICH IS THE PART TO COPY: work began in 2000; the artisanal FISHERS THEMSELVES proposed which bolon to protect, and the precise boundary was agreed jointly between Océanium, the Senegalese authorities and the fishers; the rural council of Toubacouta voted the creation UNANIMOUSLY by deliberation on 10 October 2002; conservation began in 2003; and a presidential decree in November 2004 gave official recognition to something that already existed on the water. The community acted first and the state ratified afterwards — the opposite order to almost every other route in this file. SCALE AND WHO GUARDS IT: 7,000 hectares with the support of 13 surrounding villages, 72 fish species recorded; the eco-guards are residents of the neighbouring villages, taking shifts in a watchtower at the river mouth, and most of the area's 23 employees began as eco-guards. HOW IT PAYS FOR ITSELF: the villagers OWN the Keur Bamboung eco-tourism lodge, and its takings fund the area's running costs and surveillance plus community projects — with visitor numbers deliberately capped. Océanium has since run the same process at Pointe Saint-Georges and in the Petit Kasa in Casamance, and advises on community MPAs elsewhere in the sub-region. WHO IT SUITS: Senegalese coastal and estuarine villages wanting a protected zone they control and finance, and communities elsewhere studying how to make protection pay its own way. CAVEATS: management sits in a partnership with the state marine directorate and the communal council, so it is CO-management, not sole community control; the model depends on tourism revenue and on continued village consensus across 13 villages. For land-grab response and litigation in Senegal, the Enda Pronat entry; for pressure on a project's financiers, Lumière Synergie.

trackers.name: Nébéday — works through the village committees that already exist, and will not plant on land people are using
trackers.desc: WHO WORKS WITH THE COMMITTEE YOU ALREADY HAVE: Nébéday (Wolof for the moringa, the “tree of life”), a Senegalese association for participatory management of natural resources, created in June 2011 by a former coordinator of Océanium projects, with the stated motto that the environment sits at the heart of development. Its work runs across the Sine-Saloum, Petite Côte, Thiès and Saint-Louis regions. THE METHOD, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH INSISTING ON WITH ANY OUTSIDE ORGANISATION: it works with inter-village forest management committees, marine protected area management committees and local artisanal fishing councils (CLPA) to decide WHERE to plant and WHICH species — explicitly so that the work respects existing uses and community dynamics, for example by NOT replanting an area people are already using. An organisation that asks your existing committee which ground is in use, instead of arriving with a map, is the kind to let onto your land. WHAT IT DELIVERS: reported at nearly 3 million trees planted since 2015, with 1,150,000 planted in 2020; in the classified forests of the Sine-Saloum, 56,156 trees planted with community participation — 15,222 in Djilor forest, 10,770 in Néma Bah and 30,164 in Sangako. In Sangako it supported a forest management plan, 55,574 seedlings raised in 15 VILLAGE NURSERIES, firebreaks cleared, 5 villages engaged and 14 village committees established. Since 2016 every planting is recorded by species, zone, date and GEOLOCATION in a public register — which is exactly the evidence a community needs if someone later claims the land was empty. It also supports income activities that make protection pay: mangrove beekeeping, improved cookstoves, straw-based biochar, and women's producer groups. WHO IT SUITS: Senegalese villages with a forest, mangrove or protected-area committee wanting restoration that strengthens rather than overrides local governance. CAVEATS: a restoration and livelihoods organisation — NOT a legal service, and not a route for contesting a concession or an expropriation; its geography is concentrated in the Saloum and the north. For land grabs, Senegal's Enda Pronat entry; for financier complaints, Lumière Synergie; for the community MPA model, Océanium.

trackers.name: AJS Boutiques de Droit — ten free legal-advice shops across Senegal with published addresses and phone numbers, and LAND is among the commonest questions
trackers.desc: WHERE TO WALK IN: the Association des Juristes Sénégalaises (AJS), founded 1974, runs BOUTIQUES DE DROIT — spaces of listening, accompaniment and orientation on legal and judicial matters, staffed by jurists trained in listening and counselling techniques, with consultations FREE whatever the nature of the problem. The name was deliberately not commercial: the point was to put law in a shop people already pass. TEN BOUTIQUES ARE OPERATIONAL ACROSS THE NATIONAL TERRITORY — three in the Dakar region (Médina, Pikine, Gueule Tapée-Fass-Colobane) plus Thiès, Kaolack, Kolda, Kébémer, Sédhiou and Kédougou, and the association publishes the street address, telephone number and e-mail of each one: Pikine at the Maison de la Femme, Icotaf Est, 76 555 65 92 / 33 834 24 30; Thiès at CEDAF on the two-lane road toward the Zac, 76 555 65 95; Kaolack in the old public works building facing the gendarmerie, 33 942 22 67; Kolda at CEDAF-Sare Kemo, 76 555 65 93; Kébémer, Quartier Galla facing the lycée, 33 969 12 07. Published addresses and phone numbers for ten offices is the single most actionable access record in this file — nothing else here lets a person in a regional town simply ring the nearest door. WHY IT BELONGS IN A LAND MAP: staff report that inheritance, LAND (foncier) and civil-status questions are the most recurrent, and the boutiques orient people to the tax and domains service (impôts et domaines) on land matters, conduct mediations, draft requests that go to court and write complaints. Reported volume: 6,367 legal consultations in 2024, 3,807 of them in family law. WHO IT SUITS: Senegalese households — especially women — with an inheritance, land or civil-status problem, in Dakar or in the regions. CAVEATS: ADVICE, MEDIATION AND DRAFTING RATHER THAN COURTROOM REPRESENTATION, with a women-and-children focus; several boutiques run on project funding, so confirm the nearest is open. For land grabs and the 24-hour rapid response, Senegal's Enda Pronat entry; for pressure on a project's financiers, Lumière Synergie; for the community marine protected area model, Océanium.

trackers.name: Senegal's réserves naturelles communautaires — the rural council creates it, the state recognises it, the mayors govern it, and a minister used one to stop a mine
trackers.desc: HOW A COMMUNITY TAKES A TERRITORY UNDER ITS OWN PROTECTION: Senegal's RÉSERVE NATURELLE COMMUNAUTAIRE (RNC) is created on the initiative of local populations and BY DECISION OF THE LOCAL COUNCIL, and is then LEGALLY RECOGNISED BY THE STATE — at DINDÉFELO (Kédougou) the Conseil Rural decided in 2010 to create the reserve after scientific studies, with a management plan and an inventory following. WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE AT SCALE: the RNC DU BOUNDOU, created 2009, covers 120,000 HECTARES of former hunting land across FOUR COMMUNES — Dougué, Sinthiou Fissa, Koussan and Toumboura — and is MANAGED BY THE COMMUNITIES THROUGH A CONSERVATOIRE (CORENA) DIRECTED BY THE MAYORS OF THOSE FOUR COMMUNES, supported by a manager seconded from the national parks directorate and a salaried warden-animator DRAWN FROM THE LOCAL COMMUNITIES. Four communes governing 120,000 hectares jointly is the answer to the boundary problem that stopped Eswatini's Sivule project dead — create the reserve across all the communes that share the land, and make the mayors the board. The RNC de Palmarin, created 15 May 2001 on local initiative, covers 10,430 hectares in the Saloum delta. THE DOCUMENTED WIN, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS AN ACQUIRE INSTRUMENT AND NOT A LABEL: on a visit to Dindéfelo the environment minister OPPOSED ANY POSSIBILITY OF DOLOMITE EXTRACTION INSIDE THE RESERVE, undertook to find a solution with local authorities to STOP that mining project, and committed to posting a water-and-forests agent on site and a mobile anti-bushfire unit. A community reserve gave a minister the ground to refuse a mine — that is the whole case for creating one before a project arrives rather than after. WHO IT SUITS: Senegalese rural communities wanting durable protection over a shared territory, especially where several communes share it. CAVEATS: THIS IS COMMUNITY MANAGEMENT UNDER STATE RECOGNITION, NOT PRIVATE OWNERSHIP — it depends on council decision and continuing state acceptance, and reserves have been sustained by external project funding. For land grabs and the 24-hour rapid response, Senegal's Enda Pronat entry; for the community marine protected area at Bamboung, Océanium; for free legal advice with published addresses, the AJS Boutiques de Droit.

trackers.name: Sobanukirwa (Rwanda)
trackers.desc: Sobanukirwa (Rwanda) — Rwanda’s Freedom of Information request portal (in English, Kinyarwanda and French) — helps citizens request information from public bodies and publishes the responses. — Holds to account: Rwanda’s public authorities on disclosure — find public FOI requests, responses and non-responses.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.desc: Rwanda’s official business register within the Rwanda Development Board — company incorporation records.

trackers.name: Transparency International Rwanda (TI-RW)
trackers.desc: Transparency International's Rwanda chapter. Publishes the Rwanda Bribery Index, analyses the Auditor General's reports on public financial management, runs a citizen complaints web portal (with the Supreme Court), and engages Parliament on anti-corruption.

trackers.name: Umucyo e-GP
trackers.desc: Rwanda's national e-procurement system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Rwanda, and for how much.

trackers.name: Expropriation Law 32/2015 — the deadlines, and no suspension on filing
trackers.desc: THERE IS NO CUSTOMARY LAND OWNERSHIP IN RWANDA — every holder has a title, and after tenure regularization most hold emphyteutic leases (up to 99 years for agriculture, 20 for residential; investors 49). The community-land and customary routes this map records elsewhere do not apply here; the question is always the lease and the expropriation against it. THE DEADLINES UNDER LAW 32/2015: within 15 days of the valuation report being submitted the expropriator must decide and publish it, posting a copy at the Cell office and communicating through at least one wide-audience radio station and one widely read newspaper — if that did not happen it is a documented procedural failure. The window for signing an approved compensation report may not be less than 7 days or more than 21, so a demand to sign immediately is outside the law. THE APPEAL LADDER: 30 days after the project approval decision to appeal; then to the immediate higher Land Commission within 15 working days, which must decide within 30 days; then the competent court. THE RULE THAT SHAPES STRATEGY: under article 26, filing in court does not stop the expropriation from being effected — no automatic suspension, unlike Belgium or Switzerland. So the early rungs and the publication requirements matter far more than they otherwise would.

trackers.name: Attack the valuation method — and check for a development bank behind it
trackers.desc: THREE ROUTES BEYOND THE NUMBER ITSELF. 1. VALUATION IS ITS OWN LEGAL FIELD: Law N° 17/2010 establishes the real property valuation profession and stipulates the valuation methods to be applied — so challenge the method against that law, not merely the figure, which is a legal argument rather than a dispute about opinion. 2. THERE IS A VILLAGE-LEVEL FORUM: the Cell Adjudication Committee comprises all 5 members of the cell land committee plus 5 members of the particular umudugudu where demarcation is taking place, with the cell Executive Secretary as secretary without voting rights — and it can be used to resolve resettlement conflict in a project area before the Land Commissions. 3. CHECK WHO IS FINANCING: where a project is funded by the World Bank or AfDB, the implementing agency must satisfy World Bank ESS5 (formerly OP 4.12) and AfDB OS 2 on involuntary resettlement in addition to Rwandan law — and analysts record that the Bank policy goes further than national law on property rights and human settlement. A development bank behind the project means a second, often stronger, set of obligations and its own grievance route. ALSO WORTH CITING: Law 32/2015 is expressly grounded in the ICCPR, the ICESCR and article 14 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights — the statute invokes them itself.

trackers.name: Abunzi mediation committees — you cannot choose a court for a small land claim, and the committee that hears it is unpaid and untrained
trackers.desc: RWANDA MAKES COMMUNITY MEDIATION COMPULSORY RATHER THAN OPTIONAL: FOR CLAIMS UNDER THE THRESHOLD THERE IS NO COURT TO GO TO, ONLY THE CELL COMMITTEE. Mediation committees sit at cell level, with an appeal committee at sector level, in every district. Each committee is seven residents of that cell or sector, elected by the cell or sector council for a renewable five-year term, at least thirty per cent of them women, and they serve as volunteers, unremunerated. THE COMPOSITION RULE IS THE ONE TO CHECK, BECAUSE IT IS CHECKABLE AND IT IS BREACHED: members must be elected from among people who are not staff of local administrative entities or of judicial organs. If the person mediating your dispute with a local official also works for that administration, the committee is not properly constituted, and that is an objection you can make in writing before the hearing rather than an argument about bias afterwards. WHAT TO EXPECT: the process is oral, public and participatory, the parties pick three committee members to preside over their session, and the decision binds — a conventional court sees the matter only if a party appeals. CAVEATS, AND THE THRESHOLD IS THE IMPORTANT ONE: secondary sources put mandatory jurisdiction at claims below 3,000,000 Rwandan francs for land and other immovable property and 1,000,000 for movable property, but the ministry's own page does not state a figure and the organic law has been amended more than once — confirm the current threshold at the cell office before assuming your claim is above or below it. The people deciding a binding land dispute are respected neighbours, not lawyers, which is the system's strength for boundary and inheritance quarrels and its weakness where a company or an arm of the state is on the other side; commentators have argued for exactly that reason that disputes against the state should have another route.

trackers.name: ARCOS Network — a Kigali-based conservation network that backs community organisations, including in places nobody else reaches
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Albertine Rift Conservation Society, founded 1995, headquartered in Kigali and registered as an international NGO in Rwanda and Uganda, with over a hundred staff across three countries. It is a network of NGOs, community-based organisations and governments rather than a single field operator, which is what makes it useful to a small local group: its stated priorities are capacity building, information sharing and empowering the organisations already on the ground. THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR AN ISOLATED COMMUNITY: ARCOS has specifically supported community-based organisations in remote areas of eastern DRC and in Burundi, and built a regional information and training centre in Kigali to reach organisations in places that are hard to get to. If your group is too small or too far out to be visible to national NGOs, this is a network that deliberately looks for you. It also launched a revolving fund in 2017 — the terms are not set out on its public pages, so ask — and runs restoration work at scale across mountains, wetlands and farmland, including a thirty-year landscape project around Mukura Forest and the Lake Kivu catchment in Rutsiro and Ngororero districts begun in 2023. It holds the MacArthur award for creative and effective institutions. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations and local NGOs in Rwanda and the wider Albertine Rift — Burundi, eastern DRC, Uganda, Tanzania, northern Zambia — that need technical capacity, data or a regional ally rather than a lawyer. CAVEATS: a conservation and development network, not a legal or advocacy defence organisation — nothing here confronts a state project directly, and Rwandan civic space rewards partnership with government rather than opposition to it. Membership and fund terms are not published; the entry is placed under Rwanda because that is where it is registered and based, not because its work stops at the border.

trackers.name: Legal Aid Forum — walk-in free legal advice in Kigali, and community paralegals in all 30 districts whose commonest civil work is land
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Legal Aid Forum, a membership network of around 38 Rwandan and international NGOs, professional bodies, universities, legal aid clinics, faith-based organisations and trade unions providing legal aid, established 2006 and registered as a national NGO network in 2009. THE THINGS IT OFFERS THAT ARE RARE ENOUGH TO NAME: you can walk in during business hours and speak to its lawyer free of charge at the Kigali office; it has deployed community-based paralegals in all 30 districts of Rwanda, through a National Paralegal Network it helped establish in 2013, with district representatives elected by the paralegals themselves; and it runs mobile legal aid clinics that take paralegals, legal officers and attorneys into neighbourhoods rather than waiting for people to travel. Four university legal aid clinics sit in the network. WHAT THE PARALEGALS ACTUALLY DO, and why this belongs in a land map: their services are legal education, legal advice, mediation, referral and accompaniment, and their civil caseload is mostly land-related issues, alongside succession and family matters. WHY COST IS THE POINT: LAF's director has put the problem plainly — in the suburbs of Kigali there are people who cannot afford an advocate when a case goes to court, where the minimum cost is around RWF 500,000 — and LAF has an arrangement with the Rwanda Bar Association for lawyers to take such cases, with advice, mediation and other routes offered where court can be avoided. Kimihurura, KN 14, KG 668 St, Kigali; info@legalaidrwanda.org. WHO IT SUITS: Rwandans facing land disputes, expropriation or succession problems who cannot pay a lawyer, anywhere in the country. CAVEATS: a legal aid network for individuals and families rather than a campaigning or environmental organisation — it is not a route for opposing a state project, and Rwandan civic space is narrow; its work runs alongside the state Abunzi mediation route already recorded here, and for technical and conservation support Rwanda's ARCOS entry is the other one. THE SCALE, AND IT SHOWS THIS IS NOT A TOKEN SERVICE: over two years LAF served 24,666 individuals, of whom 1,058 received LEGAL REPRESENTATION before the courts, the National Prosecution Authority and the Rwanda Investigation Bureau; 17,019 of those cases were CIVIL and 7,647 criminal, with 16,032 female clients against 8,634 male. It describes itself as Rwanda's largest legal aid and human rights organisation, bringing together 36 MEMBER ORGANISATIONS — national and international NGOs, professional associations, university legal aid clinics and faith-based institutions, and it runs a NATIONAL CALL CENTRE alongside in-court representation. WHAT DECIDES WHETHER YOU QUALIFY: the National Legal Aid Policy of October 2014 provides legal aid — advice, assistance, representation, education and alternative dispute resolution — to indigent persons, women, children, persons with disabilities and victims of gender-based violence, WITHOUT LIMITATION as to civil, criminal, administrative, children or asylum cases; and LAF works through UBUDEHE, Rwanda's government social categorisation system, which is how indigence is assessed in practice. Find out which Ubudehe category your household is in before you apply — that classification, not your account of your circumstances, is what the assessment turns on. Pro bono work in Kigali is delivered with named Rwandan organisations including a women's rights NGO, a human rights association and the Rwandan human rights defence association, in collaboration with the Rwanda Bar Association and university legal aid clinics.

trackers.name: Rwanda's contrat de cession gratuite — land granted to NGOs, churches and nonprofit associations WITH NO LIMIT ON DURATION, and the association that restored Gishwati with it
trackers.desc: THE INSTRUMENT THAT PUTS LAND IN A NONPROFIT BODY'S HANDS: Rwandan land tenure includes the CONTRAT DE CESSION GRATUITE, GRANTED TO NGOs, CHURCHES AND OTHER NONPROFIT ASSOCIATIONS for donated or sanctioned land — and it has NO LIMIT ON ITS DURATION. An unlimited-duration grant to a nonprofit association is the strongest hold available in a country where almost everything else is leasehold; if your community can form a registered association, that is the vehicle to ask about. Compare the other named forms: the ACTE DE NOTORIÉTÉ, an occupancy permit common in urban areas, issued by the district mayor, with no fixed term but ANNUAL RENT plus a 6% TAX ON LAND VALUE ON REGISTRATION, preliminary to a long-term lease and mostly NOT REGISTERED CENTRALLY; and PAYSANNAT LAND, allocated in the 1960s-70s on condition of a use such as tea, with rights continuing SO LONG AS THE CONDITIONS OF USE ARE MET. If you hold paysannat land, the condition is the vulnerability — document that you are meeting it. WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE IN PRACTICE: FOREST OF HOPE ASSOCIATION (fharwanda.org), a Rwandan association working at GISHWATI — a forest that lost 98% OF ITS COVER in the early 2000s — which through the Gishwati Area Conservation Programme from 2008 and then as Forest of Hope significantly restored it through ASSISTED NATURAL REGENERATION and reduction of unsustainable resource use, with LOCAL COMMUNITY SUPPORT, now recorded as a conservation success. Around Gishwati-Mukura and Volcanoes National Park, community agroforestry plots, TEA COOPERATIVES and WOMEN-LED BEEKEEPING GROUPS hold ground outside the park boundaries. WHO IT SUITS: Rwandan associations, cooperatives and community groups seeking a durable hold on land for restoration or conservation. CAVEATS: THE CESSION GRATUITE IS A STATE GRANT TO A REGISTERED BODY, not a purchase — you must be constituted and the land must be donated or sanctioned; land pressure in Rwanda is extreme and most disputes recorded are intra-family inheritance claims. For small land disputes you cannot take to court directly, Rwanda's Abunzi entry; for representation and the Ubudehe category test, the Legal Aid Forum entry.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: EWNHS — Ethiopia's oldest conservation society, and the national door to a continental taskforce that has stopped damaging developments at 35 sites
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a membership-based Ethiopian conservation society founded in 1966, licensed with the civil society authority under registry number 0720 — the oldest non-governmental conservation organisation in the country, and the one with standing to be heard. It runs the Important Bird Areas programme, which is how a specific place in Ethiopia gets formally identified, surveyed and put on a national conservation inventory: an unlisted site is far harder to defend than a listed one, and getting your area recognised is something you can start before a project is announced. WHY THIS IS THE ENTRY FOR ETHIOPIA RATHER THAN A BIRDWATCHING CLUB: EWNHS is the national partner of an international conservation federation whose African Site Casework on Emerging Threats taskforce has, over fifteen years, safeguarded 35 major sites from damaging developments across the continent. That casework is reachable through the national partner, not directly — which makes EWNHS the door for an Ethiopian site facing a dam, plantation, road or industrial scheme. It also works with local communities on site management and monitoring under a regional flyway programme, and produces the survey data that an objection has to be built on. WHO IT SUITS: communities beside a wetland, lake, forest or flyway site facing a development, and anyone who needs their place formally recognised and surveyed. CAVEATS, AND THEY MATTER IN ETHIOPIA: this is a conservation society that describes its role as supporting government conservation efforts with advice, data and best practice — it is not a litigator, not an opponent of the state, and civil society operating space is tightly regulated under the civil society proclamation. The argument that moves it is biodiversity, not injustice: bring the species, the wetland, the flyway. No intake route, case-selection criteria or fee information was published, and membership carries an annual subscription.

trackers.name: Ethiopia's legal aid providers and the woreda Land Administration Committee — who to ask, and who actually issues the certificate
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET HELP: three named providers of free legal assistance. The Ethiopian Women Lawyers Association (EWLA) runs a Legal Aid Program giving legal advice and counselling, writing court briefs and affidavits, AND REPRESENTING CLIENTS IN COURT, free of charge, and is credited with legal support to more than 100,000 women and with a central role in changing the Family Law; near Bulgaria Mikael Church, Mexico, Kirkos Subcity, Addis Ababa; +251 11 50 87 83. The Ethiopian Lawyers Association, a non-partisan professional body, provides legal aid to the economically and socially underprivileged. Bahir Dar University Legal Aid Center gives free counselling, prepares pleadings and represents people in court, with an emphasis on women, children, people with disabilities and prison inmates. WHO ISSUES THE PAPER, WHICH IS THE PART MOST PEOPLE GET WRONG: Ethiopian land administration is decentralised — the federal Rural Land Administration and Land Use Proclamation No. 456/2005 frames it, regional states legislate the detail, and the work runs down to woreda (district) and kebele (village) level. Regional councils must form district-level LAND ADMINISTRATION AND USE COMMITTEES (LACs), which oversee land administration, REGISTRATION and DISPUTE RESOLUTION, and are obliged to include elected women members. So the body that registers your holding and hears your boundary dispute is a committee in your own district — find out who sits on it before you need it. The Constitution recognises long-term unchallenged possession of state land and grants usufruct rights to collectives, peasant farmers, semi-pastoralists and pastoralists WITH NO TIME LIMIT. Women in Oromia and Tigray have described certification as giving proof of ownership, protection from boundary encroachment and the confidence to submit claims. WHO IT SUITS: Ethiopian smallholders, pastoralists and women needing certification, a boundary dispute heard, or free representation. CAVEATS: THESE ARE GENERAL LEGAL AID BODIES, NOT LAND OR ENVIRONMENTAL SPECIALISTS, and Ethiopian civic space for advocacy organisations has been constrained; certification programmes are donor-supported and uneven by region, and security conditions have halted work in some zones. For birdlife and site-level conservation casework, Ethiopia's EWNHS entry.

trackers.name: Guassa-Menz Community Conservation Area — the community stopped two commercial sheep ranches BEFORE it had legal status, then won designation in 2008
trackers.desc: HOW A COMMUNITY HELD ITS LAND AND STOPPED AN INVESTMENT: the Guassa area of Menz in the Amhara highlands — over 11,000 hectares of Afro-alpine moorland above 3,200m — was governed for OVER 400 YEARS under a communal system called QERO, in which ELECTED HEADMEN determined when and for how long people could harvest thatch grass and graze livestock, with closure periods enforced by the users themselves. After the 1974 revolution abolished communal tenure the system collapsed and the grassland degraded; from 2003 the initiative revived it, transferring control to a GUASSA CONSERVATION COUNCIL, mapping the area in workshops with local village associations, DRAWING UP BYLAWS governing use of its resources, and training COMMUNITY SCOUTS in local bylaw enforcement. Map it, write the bylaws, appoint your own scouts — that sequence is the reproducible part, and the community did it before any authority recognised them. THE STOPPED INVESTMENTS, WHICH ARE THE POINT: PRIOR TO DESIGNATION as a community conserved area, the initiative SUCCESSFULLY HALTED TWO ATTEMPTS to establish COMMERCIAL SHEEP-FARMING in the Guassa area — applications to the regional investment office proposing a 150-HECTARE ENCLOSURE as a commercial sheep ranch — OPPOSED ON THE BASIS THAT IT WOULD ESTABLISH A LEGAL PRECEDENT FOR PRIVATE LAND ENCLOSURES. That is the argument to borrow: do not fight the single enclosure on its own merits, fight it as the precedent that opens all the others. LEGAL RECOGNITION OF THE GUASSA COMMUNITY CONSERVED AREA FOLLOWED IN 2008. THE LEGAL FOOTING: under the Amhara Regional Rural Land Administration Proclamation No. 46/2000, COMMUNAL LANDS CAN BE MANAGED AND USED BY CUSTOMARY LAWS so long as they do not contradict the law — the provision under which the area continues to be managed by the residents of NINE FARMERS' ASSOCIATIONS. WHO IT SUITS: Ethiopian communities holding communal grazing, grassland or forest, particularly in Amhara and Oromia where joint community-forestry office management exists. CAVEATS: RECOGNITION IS REGIONAL AND CUSTOMARY-BASED, NOT A TITLE — it rests on a regional proclamation and continuing state acceptance; Ethiopia has very few gazetted conservation areas. For free legal advice and the woreda committees, Ethiopia's EWLA entry.

trackers.name: Environmental Defenders Office — Pasifika Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific region, whose Pasifika-led programme works on extractive industries, forestry, marine protection and climate across Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu. WHO IT SUITS: an in-country organisation rather than an individual — EDO works predominantly through partner organisations (CELCOR in PNG, the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association, the Fiji Environmental Law Association and the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association), supplying strategic legal capacity, co-authored law-reform papers and litigation support. Approach your national environmental law association first; its free advice hotline is for Australia only. YOUR NATIONAL PARTNER IS the Fiji Environmental Law Association. EDO is an Australian organisation based in Sydney, and its Pasifika Program is Pasifika-led — including diaspora Pasifika lawyers with cultural and spiritual links to the region — working predominantly through partner organisations. So the partner is the front door and EDO is the legal capacity behind it. Focus areas: climate change, threats to marine environments, forestry and mining. EDO is an accredited community legal service with a community advice hotline, the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific, and records a historic Solomon Islands bauxite mine case. REACH IS LIMITED AND STATED: EDO names PNG, Solomon Islands, Fiji and Vanuatu, plus Tuvalu — it does not cover the other Pacific states, so do not assume regional coverage.

trackers.name: Fiji Environmental Law Association (FELA)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Fiji's only dedicated environmental law body — a membership association of lawyers, conservationists and academics, registered as a company limited by guarantee since 2008, whose members provide legal advice and technical support to community groups and run training on the Environment Management Act, the EIA process, coastal fisheries, qoliqoli rights and gravel extraction. It has co-authored policy and law papers on marine protected areas and Fiji's coastal fisheries. WHO IT SUITS: a Fijian community or landowning unit facing a coastal development, extraction or fisheries decision — advice is given in matters that meet the association's casework guidelines, so it is a screened service rather than open legal aid.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Fiji, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. trackers.name: Fiji — Ministry of Finance

trackers.name: Fiji — Registrar of Companies Office
trackers.desc: National company registry; registers business names, companies, credit unions & money lenders and maintains entity records (online platform since 2019), Fiji. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: PacLII
trackers.desc: Pacific Islands Legal Information Institute: free case law for Fiji and other Pacific jurisdictions. · Find here: free legislation and case-law for around twenty Pacific Island jurisdictions (PacLII).

trackers.name: Fiji Bureau of Statistics
trackers.desc: Fiji's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt.
