trackers.name: Two permissions, not one — the registration and grant regime
trackers.desc: READ THIS BEFORE PLANNING ANY FUNDED WORK. Amendments adopted in February 2013 make it impossible for unregistered groups to legally receive grants and donations, and increased fivefold the fines for receiving funding without concluding a grant agreement and registering it with the Ministry of Justice. Registered organisations must seek Ministry of Justice approval for any grant — so there are two separate permissions: register the organisation once, then register each grant agreement. After the 2014 crackdown, registering independent NGOs is described as nearly impossible, foreign NGOs were expelled, and the reported result is a stark absence of registered independent environmental NGOs, with the space dominated by GONGOs. Groups operating independently often lack registration and cannot legally accept grants. AND THE MONEY IS SCARCE SEPARATELY FROM THE REPRESSION: a review of international grant policies found Azerbaijani civil society receives the least financial support for environmental issues in the South Caucasus, with donors allocating no or minimal funding to ecological work. THIS MAP THEREFORE RECORDS CONSTRAINTS RATHER THAN A DIRECTORY FOR AZERBAIJAN — naming active independent groups would expose people already at risk, and most cannot lawfully receive funding in any case.

trackers.name: Strasbourg case law — including an environmental society's dissolution
trackers.desc: THE DURABLE LEGAL REFERENCE, AND ONE CASE IS DIRECTLY ANALOGOUS. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled repeatedly on Azerbaijani NGO registration and dissolution: Tebieti Mühafize Cemiyyeti and Israfilov v. Azerbaijan, no. 37083/03, 8 October 2009 — arbitrary dissolution of what was an environmental society; Islam-Ittihad Association and Others, no. 5548/05, 13 November 2014; and Rasul Jafarov, no. 69981/14, 17 March 2016, where the Court observed that the legislative environment governing NGO registration, funding and reporting has grown increasingly harsh. ONE PATTERN WORTH KNOWING: several earlier registration cases were struck out after the NGOs concerned were registered — so filing at Strasbourg has sometimes produced registration before judgment. The Council of Europe's Venice Commission has made recommendations on revising the NGO law. WHAT EXISTS BY TREATY RATHER THAN PERMISSION: REC Caucasus, whose charter was signed in September 1999 by the governments of Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia and the EU, has a mandate covering free exchange of information in line with the Aarhus Convention, assistance to all environmental NGOs, and increasing public participation in decision-making — a body the government co-founded is a different proposition from an independent NGO. The Caucasus Nature Fund also covers Azerbaijan.

trackers.name: Aarhus Centre Baku — information only; do not expect help with participation or a court case
trackers.desc: READ THE SCOPE BEFORE YOU RELY ON IT: the OSCE records that Azerbaijan's Aarhus Centre in Baku focuses primarily on supporting public access to environmental information. The Aarhus Convention has three pillars — information, participation in decisions, and access to justice — and on the OSCE's own description this centre is built around the first. That is a real limit, not a quibble: it means the centre is the place to obtain the environmental data underlying a project, and not the place to expect help lodging an objection or reaching a court. Plan for it by using the centre to get documents and building the objection elsewhere. WHY THIS ENTRY AND NOT AN AZERBAIJANI ORGANISATION: Azerbaijan is a closed operating environment, and naming small domestic groups in a public map can expose the people in them, so this file records the intergovernmental instrument and stops there. A SECOND THING AZERBAIJANI READERS SHOULD KNOW, BECAUSE IT LOOKS LIKE A ROUTE AND IS NOT: the Caucasus Nature Fund names Azerbaijan in its mandate, but its published list of supported protected areas carries 16 Georgian and 5 Armenian sites and no Azerbaijani site, and its own parks filter offers only Armenia and Georgia. An Azerbaijani community reading about CNF's three-country remit should not assume the funding route exists there. Aarhus Centres across this region vary enormously in what they actually do and several have gone quiet; establish that the Baku centre is currently staffed and answering before building a timetable around it.

trackers.name: Rivers without Boundaries (RwB)
trackers.desc: An international coalition of NGOs and experts working to save transnational rivers across north-east Asia, with its own named Mongolia coordinator. WHO TO ENLIST: the place to start when the threat is a dam, a reservoir or placer gold mining in a river basin. It runs independent hydropower assessments, maps threatened basins including the Selenga, Kherlen, Onon and the Mongolian Great Lakes, and tracks where mining licences sit relative to water-protection zones. You CAN: draw on its river-by-river document files and on its record of backing Mongolian herder movements pressing for enforcement of the 2009 law restricting mining near rivers, headwaters and forests. For activists: its work extends into Russia and China too, but Mongolia is the country for which it names a coordinator on its own site, so that is where this entry sits — ask about elsewhere.

trackers.name: Nukhurlul — herder communities named themselves into the civil code
trackers.desc: AN ORIGIN WORTH KNOWING. Nukhurlul is the name the early herder communities in the Gobi gave themselves — and during the 2000–2004 legislative period, South Gobi members of parliament introduced community organisations into Mongolia's civil law under that chosen name, as rural civil society organisations. Communities self-organised, named themselves, and the legislature adopted both the institution and the name; elsewhere in this map communities apply into categories drawn up for them. WHAT RECOGNITION UNLOCKED: it allowed contracts on communal land management to be made between local government and the communities, giving them legal standing to contract with the soum — not a designation, but the capacity to hold an agreement. Community organisations now protect wetlands, local protected areas and prehistoric sites. THE ASSESSED OUTCOME, in respondents' words: through the process they learned to express opinions and talk to the governor, and learned to have a stronger voice — many active communities made the soum governor listen and influenced pasture management plans. EXPECT THIS QUESTION IN THE ROOM: the assessment literature asks whether donor support has built a parallel structure to the territorial administrative structure, and whether local government sees community organisations as a threat. WHERE TO ENGAGE: soum and bag levels, aimag and soum khurals, and buffer zone councils, whose head sits within the Soum Khural.

trackers.name: Eternal Mongolia and GEF — a third of the money is outside protected areas
trackers.desc: TWO ROUTES, AND THE LARGER ONE TARGETS COMMUNITIES DIRECTLY. Eternal Mongolia is a Project Finance for Permanence partnership between The Nature Conservancy and the Government of Mongolia toward the country's 30x30 goals, mobilising about USD 198 million over 15 years. Its three targets: safeguard an additional 14.4 million hectares; strengthen management of the protected area network; and extend sustainable community-managed practices to 34 million hectares OUTSIDE protected areas, with a 2040 goal of secure community-based natural resource management involving up to 24,000 herder households. So a herder community is a target participant, not a bystander — the largest single component is community-managed land beyond the park boundaries. WATCH THE LAW REVISION: the Mongolia Nature's Legacy Foundation supports revisions to the Protected Areas Law so the 30x30 goal has clear legal frameworks and stable financing, and Mongolia approved its first Climate Change Law in the State Great Khural. FOR SMALLER, FASTER MONEY: the GEF Small Projects Programme, implemented by UNDP, gives up to USD 50,000 over up to 18 months for biodiversity conservation and sustainable agriculture — open to NGOs, CSOs and local community groups.

trackers.name: Put 'environmental protection' in your charter — a court said so
trackers.desc: THE STANDING TRAP THAT LOST A CASE BEFORE IT WAS HEARD. CHRD challenged extraction licences in Khuvsgul aimag and the court rejected its standing to sue, emphasising the absence of the words ‘environmental protection’ in its charter. Across this map the wording of an organisation's own constitution decides funding eligibility in six European countries — in Mongolia it decides access to the court itself. If your organisation might ever litigate, put environmental protection in the charter before you need it; Mongolian civil society's own recommendation was to create a legal environment allowing NGOs to sue. THE SECOND OBSTACLE IS MONEY FOR EXPERTS: expert evidence is unavoidable in environmental cases, and although the court is authorised to pay for it, it is often reluctant — in an administrative case on cancelling a uranium licence the court appointed an expert on its own initiative and the expert refused to work because the court did not pay. Budget for your own expert rather than relying on the court. WHO LITIGATES: CHRD has run public interest litigation on mining since 2005, around 40 cases on illegal licences, inadequate environmental impact assessment, water law breaches, mines left without rehabilitation and toxic contamination — and won cancellation of two illegally issued licences on the Burenkhaan phosphate deposit in 2014.

trackers.name: The Munkhbayar precedent — and what the petition actually asked for
trackers.desc: A SUPREME COURT ORDER TO ENFORCE. On 20 October 2011 the Supreme Court ruled that the government must enforce its 2009 resolution restricting mining, in a case filed by the United Movement of Mongolian Rivers & Lakes. The statute behind it prohibits mining at headwaters of rivers, protected zones of water reservoirs and forested areas, and was designed to protect up to 25 percent of Mongolia's natural ecosystems. THE PETITION IS A TEMPLATE WORTH STUDYING: it asked for assessment of damage to named river basins within 2 months, public notification of that assessment, recovery of damages from the respondent, restoration carried out by the petitioner organisation itself under contract to the respondent, enforcement of the Law, and revocation of the licences of entities operating there. Asking to be contracted to do the restoration is an unusual and powerful ask. AFTERWARDS the government began real implementation — the first batch of licences was revoked, protection zones approved, damage evaluated — and UMMRL then helped delineate the protection zones and negotiate them with local populations. BUT WINNING DID NOT END IT: after Munkhbayar's Goldman Prize for pressuring 35 of 37 operations in the Onggi basin, new companies received new licences for the same protected areas. TWO DOCUMENTS TO OBTAIN: the EIA report, and the annual environmental management plan that licence holders must file with the ministry by 1 November each year, covering subcontractor activities — a dated, ministry-held document is the most checkable obligation in the regime.

trackers.name: Protected Areas Regulation 2018/R-78 — consultation is a stated objective
trackers.desc: QUOTE THE REGULATION'S OWN OBJECTIVES BACK. Regulation No. 2018/R-78 lists six objectives, and two are about community involvement in designation: to ensure the process of protected area declaration is consultative and transparent, and to enhance awareness and participation of community in protected area designation and management. Where a designation process has excluded a community, that departs from the regulation's own stated purpose — cite those two limbs. It also aims to enlist environmentally significant areas, and it covers areas already declared and areas protected before or after it came into force, so it applies to existing sites too. THE ACT BEHIND IT, Law 4/93 (ratified 19 April 1993): the ministry identifies protected areas and reserves (s.4); an impact assessment must be submitted before any development project that may have a potential impact on the environment (s.5) — note that low threshold, not ‘significant’ impact; and the ministry has authority to TERMINATE any project that has an undesirable impact. Termination, not conditions or fines — and the test is ‘undesirable’, not ‘unlawful’. The Act declares the natural environment a national heritage.

trackers.name: Farukolhu — designation used instead of an airport, and the paper-parks answer
trackers.desc: A PRECEDENT AND A REBUTTAL. Sh. Farukolhu was designated a protected area under Act 4/93 in 2018 — recorded as a major victory because the island had previously been considered for development of an airport to boost tourism infrastructure. Its reefs are nurseries for endangered hawksbill turtles and vulnerable sicklefin lemon sharks; its mangroves and wetlands are bird nesting grounds. Designation is a demonstrated alternative to an airport in this jurisdiction. AND THE ANSWER TO ‘IT WILL NEVER BE MANAGED ANYWAY’: 93 sites have been designated in recent years while management has not kept pace — but as a conservationist puts it, paper parks are not always a bad thing, because declaring them helps earmark and preserve them rather than allocating them for industrial or tourism development. A designated site is one not allocated to something else. WHERE MONEY IS COMING FROM: the CATENATE project, US$2 million from the GEF plus US$7.5 million co-funding from the ministry, Sh. Funadhoo Council and the earlier USAID-funded REGENERATE, to manage Farukolhu and 14 other protected areas in the same atoll. An island council is a named co-funder — local councils can put money into protected area management. A CANDID NOTE: a legal handbook records that the Maldivian judiciary ‘has not yet taken an activist role in environmental management’, so administrative and designation routes are likely to outperform litigation here.

trackers.name: EcoPeace Middle East
trackers.desc: Founded in 1994 as Friends of the Earth Middle East and still a member of Friends of the Earth International, EcoPeace is staffed and directed jointly by Jordanians, Palestinians and Israelis, with its own offices in Amman, Ramallah and Tel Aviv and a national director in each. WHO TO ENLIST: the office in your own country. Its Good Water Neighbors programme works with communities on either side of a shared water problem, pairing them across the border rather than treating each in isolation. You CAN get community-level organising support and technical and advocacy weight on water, sewage and Jordan Valley development. You CAN'T get a litigator — EcoPeace works by cross-border cooperation, research and advocacy, not by suing proponents, so a community that needs a permit or an approval challenged in court should look elsewhere. For activists: in Jordan and Palestine this was the only substantial environmental organisation with an office and a named national director that could be verified on its own domain.

trackers.name: Establish your area classification first — it decides who has authority
trackers.desc: THE QUESTION THAT COMES BEFORE EVERY OTHER ONE. Of the 18 protected areas transferred to the Palestinian Authority under the Oslo agreements, only 8 are under actual Palestinian control, totalling less than 15 km²; the remaining 10 lie within Area C or overlapped areas. So establish your site's area classification before approaching any authority — the answer differs site by site, not governorate by governorate, and approaching the wrong body costs months. THE BODY THAT MANAGES RESERVES: the Directorate of Forests, Rangelands and Wildlife in the Ministry of Agriculture, with 4 divisions — forestry, nature reserves, rangelands and nurseries — and offices in all governorates of the West Bank, plus 40 rangers patrolling protected areas and natural forests. A governorate office with a rangelands division is the practical door, and rangelands matters where grazing land rather than forest is at issue. The Environment Quality Authority is the separate regulator, established 10 December 1996. trackers.name: Inspect your land physically — the appeal window is 10 days

trackers.name: ООПТ местного значения — aim at the oblast akimat, not the ministry

trackers.name: Reserved zones, and the mining article to ask about
trackers.desc: TWO PROVISIONS THAT DECIDE HOW YOU ARGUE. 1. LAND CAN BE HELD BEFORE DESIGNATION: a государственная заповедная зона is a protected area with differentiated protection regimes, established to conserve and restore the nature reserve fund and biodiversity on land and waters reserved for future zapovedniks, national parks and reserves — a mechanism in place since 1976. DO NOT ASSERT A BAN THE CODE DOES NOT CONTAIN: the Экологический кодекс sets ecological requirements for siting within ООПТ of settlements, industrial, agricultural, energy, transport and defence objects not connected with the purposes and functioning of the ООПТ, and article 255 sets special ecological requirements for subsoil use operations on the territory of state reserved zones. Mining inside a заповедная зона is therefore subject to special requirements rather than simply prohibited — so ask which requirements were applied and how compliance was assessed, which is a question with a documentary answer, instead of claiming a blanket prohibition that can be rebutted in one line.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants Programme — up to US$50,000 direct to communities
trackers.desc: WHERE THE COMMUNITY MONEY ACTUALLY IS. trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.desc: DO NOT DRESS A SPECIES PROJECT UP AS A CLIMATE PROJECT HERE — which is the opposite of the advice that fits almost every other fund in this map. trackers.name: Local self-government can withdraw land from economic use — since 2018
trackers.desc: THE SHORTEST DESIGNATION ROUTE IN CENTRAL ASIA, AND IT IS RECENT. Law No. 58 of 2 June 2018 added a definition of protected natural territories of local significance: plots of land, water surface and airspace above them holding natural complexes of special conservation, scientific, cultural, recreational or health value, withdrawn wholly or partly from economic use by decision of local self-government bodies. The power to establish is expressly shared between the Government, executive bodies and local self-government. Governing statute: the Law on Specially Protected Natural Territories of 3 May 2011 No. 18, succeeding that of 28 May 1994.

So there is no operative procedure for the state cadastre of protected areas: obtain and keep the establishing decision itself, because it may be the only durable proof. The same review examined 110 active normative legal acts making up Kyrgyz environmental law, and was produced under a project aimed at expanding public participation in decision-making and building civil society capacity — the Aarhus Centre Kyrgyzstan is the body to approach on participation rights. A DEFINITIONAL POINT WORTH USING: protected territories may be natural or artificially created complexes, so a restored or planted site is not excluded by definition — useful where the argument is rehabilitation rather than pristineness.

trackers.name: CFUG handover — the operational plan is a contract, so write it carefully
trackers.desc: HOW A NEPALI COMMUNITY GETS FOREST HANDED OVER TO IT. Under the Forest Act 1993 and Forest Regulations 1995, a Community Forest User Group forms democratically from individuals representing households and registers at the forest office; writes a CFUG constitution defining the rights of users to a particular forest; elects an executive committee that by law must include 33 percent female members; and prepares an operational plan — a forest working plan based partly on a forest resource inventory, typically covering 5 years — for approval by the District Forest Officer. The forest is handed over once that plan is approved. THE PLAN IS THE INSTRUMENT THAT MATTERS: it forms part of the contract between the CFUG and the government, covering growing stock, block division, silvicultural operations, conservation measures and provisions for harvesting, utilisation and sale. A community wanting to prevent a use should get that use excluded in the plan — because the plan is contractual, not advisory. SCALE: about 1.23 million of Nepal's 5.5 million forest hectares is community forest, held by more than 14,000 CFUGs, with several thousand groups awaiting certification.

trackers.name: Read your own constitution — and budget for up to 90 percent tax
trackers.desc: THREE THINGS A NEPALI CFUG MEMBER SHOULD KNOW. 1. THE TAX STRESS IS SEVERE. The Local Government Operation Act 2017 requires community forests to contribute 10 percent of product sales to the local Reserved Fund, and with other enforced and proposed taxes across all three tiers of government the total is estimated at up to 90 percent of a CFUG's annual transactions — FECOFUN, the national federation of community forestry users, has been protesting it. Build any plan against that, not against gross revenue. 2. CHECK WHICH OFFICE IS YOURS. Under the 2015 constitution forest is in the concurrent list, with community forestry the responsibility of local and provincial government; the Divisional Forest Office under the province approves operational plans and transfers forest rights, across 528 forest sub-divisions and 753 local bodies — and who approves is politically live, with CFUGs and local governments favouring local control and forest officers resisting. 3. GET AND READ YOUR CONSTITUTION AND OPERATIONAL PLAN. Research finds elites exercising power because they are more aware of legislation and better able to access information, while many members are hardly aware of their own constitutions and operational plans and do not know their rights. NOTE ALSO a recognised structural flaw: the Department of Forest is both regulator and provider of technical services, which analysts identify as creating conditions for rent seeking — so delays or charges from the same body that approves your plan are a known problem, not bad luck.

trackers.name: Mother Nature Cambodia
trackers.desc: A youth-led Cambodian environmental rights movement, active since 2012, which stopped a Chinese-led hydroelectric dam threatening an Indigenous community in the Areng Valley and helped end the sand-export trade that was destroying the Koh Kong estuaries. Right Livelihood Award, 2023. It was deregistered as an NGO by the Ministry of Interior in 2017 and has continued without legal registration. CHECK YOU HAVE THE RIGHT ONE: a separate, government-aligned organisation using the same name was launched in 2025 — this entry is the original movement, at mothernaturecambodia.org. For activists: association carries real risk. Five members have been imprisoned since July 2024 on plotting and lese-majeste charges, bail refused by both the Appeal and Supreme Courts, and dozens more have been arrested since 2015.

trackers.name: National Audit Authority
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Cambodia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: MoC Business Registration
trackers.desc: National — Ministry of Commerce business / company register of Cambodia. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Constitutional Council (Cambodia)
trackers.desc: Constitutional Council (Cambodia) — supreme court (Cambodia).

trackers.name: Cambodia — Ministry of Economy & Finance (MEF)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; administers financial & economic policy and the distribution & allocation of the national budget, Kingdom of Cambodia. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Cambodia.

trackers.name: Community Forest agreement — a written request starts it, 15 years runs it
trackers.desc: ESTABLISH WHICH MINISTRY HOLDS YOUR FOREST FIRST — Cambodian forest is state owned and split between the Forestry Administration under MAFF and the Ministry of Environment for protected areas, and a March 2016 reshuffle moved protected areas and nature preserves to the Environment ministry, so older guidance may name the wrong body. ON FA LAND: Sub-decree 79 (2003) under the 2002 Forestry Law gives any Cambodian community the right to establish a Community Forest on state public property. IT STARTS WITH A WRITTEN REQUEST from the local communities to the Forestry Administration, which then assesses their requirements and problems with the involvement of local authorities. The management committee is formed with help from the Commune Council and elected by secret ballot with at least two-thirds of members present at a public meeting. TWO DOCUMENTS GIVE YOU HARVESTING RIGHTS: a Community Forestry Agreement and a Community Forest Management Plan, both approved by the FA Cantonment. TERM: not more than 15 years from approval, extendable on monitoring and evaluation reports. KNOW YOUR secondary users — non-members who may still access the forest consistent with the plan — and note that royalties and premiums should be set after consultation with the community.

trackers.name: Community Protected Areas — you get management rights but not exclusion rights
trackers.desc: THE GAP THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS ROUTE SOLVES YOUR PROBLEM. Inside Ministry of Environment protected areas, communities may agree to manage part of the area — but legal analysis finds CPA communities hold only partial land tenure: they can generally exercise access, use, withdrawal and management rights, but lack exclusion rights, the ability to keep outsiders from entering or using CPA land. So a CPA can manage a forest but cannot keep others out of it — if your threat is incursion by outsiders rather than your own community's use, this route does not by itself solve it. WATCH THE DROP-OFF: of 182 CPAs established across 31 protected areas, 141 hold a Prakas of recognition, only 39 have a signed management agreement and just 48 a completed management plan — recognition is common, real management authority is not. AND A 15-DAY DEADLINE: within 15 days of being elected the CPA committee must obtain a warrant of recognition from the Commune/Sangkat Chief to legitimise its leadership. OTHER VARIANTS EXIST: Community-Based Production Forest, Partnership Forestry where the commune council is the management body rather than a community committee, and Community Conservation Forestry with more limited use rights.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants — a concept paper, and only shortlists get a reply
trackers.desc: MONEY THAT GOES DIRECTLY TO COMMUNITY ORGANISATIONS. GEF SGP has financed projects in Cambodia since 2005 through the UNDP country office, supporting nearly 218 grant projects, with grants up to USD 50,000 awarded competitively to local NGOs and community-based organisations. WHAT YOU SUBMIT FIRST IS A CONCEPT PAPER, not a full proposal — and only shortlisted proposals are contacted, so the concept paper is your entire first impression and silence is the normal outcome otherwise. THE ENTRY POINT IS A PERSON: contact the GEF SGP National Coordinator at UNDP Cambodia, Corner Sothearos & Sihanouk Blvd, Tonle Bassac, Phnom Penh, for guidelines — verify the current post-holder on UNDP's page rather than relying on a name recorded here, since individual officials move. BUDGET FOR A MATCH: SGP expects applicants to match funding with equivalent contributions, so this is not full cost recovery. WHAT SATISFIES THE MATCH — AND IT IS NOT ONLY CASH: UNDP's own wording is that the remaining funding may come from the organisation, community contribution and/or other donors, either monetary or in kind and services. Labour and in-kind contribution count, so budget them deliberately rather than assuming the match must be found in money — for a community group with no cash this is the difference between eligible and not. AND THE CEILING MOVES BY PHASE: recorded calls show USD 20,000 in an earlier round and up to USD 75,000 under Operational Phase 8, so verify the live call rather than relying on a fixed figure. Note too that Indigenous Peoples' community groups are named as eligible applicants in their own right alongside NGOs and CBOs — which matters given that the Community Protected Area route leaves communities without exclusion rights.

trackers.name: Check which landscape the call names — and the sub-grant route
trackers.desc: GEOGRAPHY IS THE FILTER THAT DECIDES ELIGIBILITY. Cambodian SGP calls target specific landscapes rather than the whole country — recorded examples include villages and districts inside and nearby the Central Cardamom Mountain National Park and biodiversity hotspots; the Stung Siem Reap Watershed in Siem Reap province; and Mekong River, Tonle Sap and coastal provinces under a blue economy stream running since July 2019 on community-based use of ocean and coastal resources. A strong project outside the named landscape does not qualify, so check the live call before investing time — the same trap this map records for Sri Lanka. A DEDICATED INDIGENOUS PEOPLES STREAM EXISTS: since June 2023, under the UNDP Climate Promise initiative, IPOs, local NGOs and CBOs working directly with indigenous communities in the forest and land use sector may apply — including for indigenous community-based ecotourism as an option that does not rely heavily on forest and land resources. AND IF YOU CANNOT WIN A DIRECT GRANT: REDD+ programmes in Cambodia support organisations which in turn sub-contract grants and further funds to local NGOs and small local initiatives — so being a sub-grantee of a larger programme holder is a real route for a group too small to apply directly.

trackers.name: Timor-Leste — SERVE, I.P. (Serviço de Registo e Verificação Empresarial)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the one-stop SERVE maintains the Companies Register, issues unique company numbers & commercial-registration certificates and licenses business activity, Timor-Leste. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Timor-Leste — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares the state budget and publishes budget transparency & execution data, Timor-Leste. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Timor-Leste.

trackers.name: Ombudsman for Human Rights and Justice (Provedor) of Timor-Leste
trackers.desc: National institution of Timor-Leste that provides free legal representation and defends access to justice, fair-trial and due-process rights for people who cannot afford counsel.

trackers.name: Tara bandu — a customary law named in the statute's own definitions
trackers.desc: A CUSTOMARY PRACTICE DEFINED BY NAME IN NATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL LEGISLATION IS RARE. The Environmental Basic Law (Decree-Law No. 26/2012 of 4 July) defines tara bandu in Article 1 as ‘a custom that is part of the culture of Timor-Leste that regulates the relationship between humans and the environment’, recognising it as applicable under rituals-based local common law, intended to conserve and promote the environment. So a tara bandu is not an informal arrangement the state may choose to respect — it is an instrument the environmental law itself names. It is a ceremony enshrining customary law with state recognition, generally at the scale of the suco, the smallest administrative division, over several years, focused on forests and on relations among people — and it anchors participatory land use plans, including agreements on property boundaries, rules of engagement, and interdictions and sanctions. One ceremony can settle a boundary, set a rule and attach a sanction — three things most jurisdictions need three separate processes for. AND IT NOW REACHES THE SEA: coastal communities have applied tara bandu, traditionally terrestrial, to marine resource management, creating MPAs that often give seagrass and dugongs special protection.

trackers.name: Vila Maumeta — temporary closure by ceremony, and the statute that backs it
trackers.desc: A WORKED, DATED TEMPLATE. At Vila Maumeta on Ataúro Island, the community with the NGO Roman Luan and the government demarcated a Marine Protected Area by applying tara bandu rules for closures; the MPA was launched in September 2017. Communities set temporary closures of a marine or terrestrial area through a tara bandu ceremony — a periodic instrument renewed by ceremony, which is a different and often easier proposition than permanent designation. The same Ataúro communities went on to water conservation and permaculture. THE STATUTE THAT BACKS IT: Decree-Law No. 5/2016 establishing the National System of Protected Areas provides that classification of a protected area should take into account the uses and customs of Timor-Leste which do not contravene the Constitution — naming lisuk, ofatin lulik, lisane and tarabandu — with community leaders, traditional leaders and local communities in the involved and adjacent area engaged. Named customs, named participants. It also provides for communities participating actively in environmental impact evaluation carried out in or near the area and for programmes offering alternative income. Decree-Law No. 6/2020 adds the biodiversity framework, covering protection, rehabilitation and ex situ restoration and requiring active participation of all sectors of society. Regulation 2000/19 focuses on forests, coral reefs and mangroves.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants Programme — up to US$50,000 direct to communities
trackers.desc: THE COMMUNITY-SCALE ROUTE. The GEF Small Grants Programme, running since 1992 and implemented by UNDP, reached 135 countries of 144 eligible in GEF-8, which secured US$135 million for the core programme with nearly US$1 million allocated to each participating country — a per-country floor, so the money is not competed for across borders. Grants of up to US$50,000 go directly to local communities, community-based organisations and other non-governmental groups. Focal areas: biodiversity, climate change, land degradation and sustainable forest management, international waters and chemicals. READ THE COUNTRY PROGRAMME STRATEGY FIRST — each country writes its own, emphasising particular themes and geographies, so global eligibility does not mean your region or theme is in scope. Under SGP 2.0 the implementing agency may be FAO or Conservation International rather than UNDP, and the host may be a national host institution rather than the UNDP country office — confirm which applies before addressing an application.

trackers.name: Transparency International Zimbabwe (TI Z)
trackers.desc: Transparency International's Zimbabwe chapter (accredited since 1996). Knowledge-driven anti-corruption CSO — legal aid, community journalism and trial observation, and monitoring of policy and legislation, with focus areas including land and mining corruption.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: PRAZ
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Zimbabwe, and for how much.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: Johannesburg-based regional NGO that advances human rights, the rule of law and access to justice in Zimbabwe through strategic litigation, criminal-justice reform and capacity-strengthening of local lawyers and courts. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights (ZLHR)
trackers.desc: Harare-based membership organisation of lawyers upholding the rule of law, separation of powers and the unimpeded administration of justice in Zimbabwe through strategic and anti-impunity litigation, monitoring of judicial intimidation and public-interest advocacy.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission (ZACC)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Zimbabwe — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe — Registrar of Companies (DCIP / ZimConnect e-Services)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the Registrar of Companies under the Deeds, Companies & Intellectual Property (DCIP) office registers PLCs, PBCs & other entities under the Companies and Other Business Entities Act [24:31], via the official ZimConnect government e-services portal, Zimbabwe. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: ZimLII
trackers.desc: Zimbabwe Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Zimbabwean judgments and legislation (ZimLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association — public interest lawyers who litigate for communities against mining, with a rights-violation hotline
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a public interest environmental law organisation that publishes a hotline for people whose environmental, economic, social or cultural rights have been violated or are about to be — +263 777 195 006 and +263 719 556 893. Formed in 2000 and constituted as a trust in 2001, it does impact litigation, not only advocacy — it puts its own lawyers on cases for communities rather than referring them elsewhere. Its programmes are organised around mining and extractives, land and natural resources, responsible investment and business, and local service delivery, which is the right shape for a community facing a concession rather than a factory. It also does conflict resolution and civic education, and it convenes and trains — so a community that is not yet in a dispute can get its people trained before one starts. WHO IT SUITS: its published strength is extractives — mining, lithium, minerals, and access to information about investment contracts, including Chinese investment contracts, and it has run work on community development agreements and on mediation mechanisms for the mining industry. If your fight is a mine, a quarry or a concession, this is the strongest single door in Zimbabwe. It is a smaller organisation than the national scale of the problem, so treat the hotline as a triage line rather than a guarantee of representation. Offices at 26B Seke Road, Hatfield, Harare; info@zela.org; +263 8677 010060. CAVEAT: no published intake criteria, means test or case-selection policy was found — unlike South Africa's law clinic, ZELA does not say in advance who qualifies, so make the first call short and factual: what is proposed, where, who is behind it, what stage it has reached. WHICH DESK TO ASK FOR: ZELA was formed in 2000 and legally constituted as a Trust in November 2001, and runs five programmes — Extractive Industries and Mining; Climate Change and Energy; Local Service Delivery; Land and Natural Resources; and Responsible Investments. Naming the programme when you approach an organisation this size gets you to a lawyer who already knows your sector. Its stated methods are public interest environmental litigation, investigative and evidence-based research, advocacy, legal education, COMMUNITY ORGANISING AND MOBILISING, institutional strengthening and CONFLICT RESOLUTION — so it will mediate as well as litigate, which matters where a case would take years. THE INSTRUMENT TO ASK ABOUT IF A MINE IS NEAR YOU: ZELA has analysed COMMUNITY SHARE OWNERSHIP TRUSTS (CSOTs) — the Zimbabwean vehicle through which a mining company is expected to place a shareholding or payment in trust for the host community — alongside the indigenisation legislation and the minerals revenue transparency initiative. Ask whether a CSOT exists for your district, who its trustees are, what the company actually paid in, and where that money went; a trust that exists on paper and pays nothing is a common outcome. ZELA holds observer status with the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, so a case that exhausts domestic remedies has a route onward, and it is based in Harare.

trackers.name: CAMPFIRE Association — the route by which a Zimbabwean district holds legal authority over its own wildlife, and the money that comes with it
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY, AND WHY IT IS ALSO A WAY OF HOLDING LAND: under the Communal Areas Management Programme for Indigenous Resources, rural district councils are granted Appropriate Authority — legal devolution of the rights to manage, use and benefit from wildlife — and, acting for the communities on communal land, sell safari operators access to that wildlife. Land that earns is land that is defended. The association reports the programme operating in 58 districts, with 23 rural district councils contributing to it, covering about 50,000 km² or roughly 12.7 per cent of the country, and touching 2.4 million people in an estimated 800,000 households; income comes principally from levies on 33 hunting safari operators and eight photographic operators. The first two councils received Appropriate Authority status in 1988. WHAT TO DO WITH THIS IF YOUR AREA IS UNDER PRESSURE: find out whether your district council holds Appropriate Authority, and if it does not, whether it has applied — a district with devolved authority over its wildlife has a revenue interest in refusing a land use that destroys habitat, and that converts a conservation argument into a council budget argument. The association works with the parks and wildlife authority and the local government ministry. THE ARGUMENT AGAINST IT, WHICH YOU SHOULD KNOW BEFORE RELYING ON IT: authority was devolved only to district councils, not to wards or villages, and independent studies of southern lowveld districts found the direct household benefits small — with councils criticised for excessive retention of the revenue generated — though households valued the infrastructure built with it. WHO IT SUITS: communal-area communities in wildlife districts, and ward councillors who want the district's own money argument on their side. CAVEATS: this is a national programme association working with government, not an advocacy or legal body — for litigation Zimbabwe's entry for the Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association is the one to use. Revenue depends on safari hunting, which is exposed to import bans and market shifts, and no intake route for a community approach was published.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Homeless People's Federation and Dialogue on Shelter — savings collectives that turned into a fund, then into land and 5,000 built houses
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Zimbabwe Homeless People's Federation (ZHPF), constituted in December 1998 as a national network of women-based savings and credit collectives of the urban poor (men are not excluded), with Dialogue on Shelter for the Homeless in Zimbabwe Trust, registered April 1998, as its support NGO. It began among families in the holding camps people were dumped in after mass evictions from informal settlements. THE SEQUENCE IS WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER FEDERATION ENTRIES IN THIS FILE: savings first, then a collectively held Urban Poor Fund (Gungano), then negotiation with councils, then land allocated to the federation itself and houses built on it. Reported delivery is roughly 5,000 housing units — including 512 at Victoria Falls, 233 at Crowborough in Harare and 150 at Kariba — with reach reported at more than 12,000 families across 73 of Zimbabwe's 92 councils. The Harare Slum Upgrading Programme, 2010–2016, was co-led by the federation, Dialogue on Shelter and Harare City Council, piloted at Dzivarasekwa Extension, where the council contributed exemption of approval fees, equipment and technical supervision alongside community contributions. Enumerations and settlement profiles were produced by residents — Dzivarasekwa, Mbare, Chinotimba — and used to show how long people had actually lived where they lived. Money you saved collectively is the only money in this file that buys land on your own terms. WHO IT SUITS: Zimbabwean urban households facing eviction, living in holding camps or unserviced settlements, or wanting a route to serviced land and title through a savings collective. CAVEATS: this is a slow route — progress has been minimal against the scale of need, regularisation is politically sensitive, and settlements have been tolerated or evicted according to shifting political allegiances; large projects here depended on foreign foundation grants. It builds housing; it does not litigate — for that, Zimbabwe's ZELA entry.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Foundation — free lawyers and paralegals in 25 offices across 9 of Zimbabwe's 10 provinces, and legal pamphlets in Shona and Ndebele
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET FREE LEGAL HELP: the Legal Resources Foundation (LRF), which provides legal education and legal services so that disadvantaged people, particularly women, can assert their rights. THE COVERAGE IS THE POINT, and it is the widest recorded anywhere in this file: underprivileged people get FREE ADVICE AND HELP FROM LAWYERS AND PARALEGALS IN 25 OFFICES ACROSS 9 OF ZIMBABWE'S 10 PROVINCES, organised as provincial centres with district offices under them — a provincial centre manager coordinating four district offices is the documented pattern. Its practitioners list COMMUNITY AND CUSTOMARY LAND RIGHTS and ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE among their working areas, alongside inheritance, marriage and gender-based violence. THE PUBLICATIONS UNIT IS THE SECOND REASON IT IS HERE: LRF produces practical information on around 28 legal topics — including wills, the Declaration of Rights and birth certificates — in ENGLISH, SHONA AND NDEBELE, distributed through workshops, offices, partner networks and places people already go, such as HOSPITALS AND POLICE STATIONS; it also publishes law reports and textbooks for the profession. Putting plain-language rights pamphlets in the hospital waiting room reaches people who will never enter a law office — the same logic as Malawi siting its legal aid desks inside the agriculture building. Offices in Harare at 5th Floor Blue Ridge, Eastgate, Sam Nujoma Street/Robert Mugabe Road, and 16 Oxford Road, Avondale. It also trains community leaders, teachers and prison officers as multipliers. Alongside it, Zimbabwe's justice ministry runs a Legal Aid Directorate providing advice and representation to indigents in civil and criminal litigation, and the Midlands State University Legal Aid Clinic offers free civil litigation and consultations subject to a means test. WHO IT SUITS: Zimbabweans anywhere outside the capital who need free legal advice, including on customary land and inheritance. CAVEATS: LRF'S OWN SITE DID NOT RESOLVE TO A VERIFIED PAGE — this entry points at a directory record documenting it; it is a generalist legal aid and education body, not an environmental litigator. For mining and environmental cases, Zimbabwe's ZELA entry; for wildlife devolution, CAMPFIRE.

trackers.name: InfoLib (Liberia)
trackers.desc: InfoLib (Liberia) — Liberia’s Freedom of Information request portal (linked from the Independent Information Commission) — lets citizens file FOI requests to public bodies and publishes all requests and responses online. — Holds to account: Liberia’s public authorities on disclosure — find public FOI requests, responses and non-responses.

trackers.name: Green Advocates International
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Liberia's first and only public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1997 — legal representation for rural, urban-slum and squatter communities against concessions and corporate projects, alongside EIA monitoring, community GIS mapping to clarify property rights, and land-tenure and forest-governance work. Its litigation and campaigning helped win temporary protection of millions of acres of forest from oil-palm development. WHO IT SUITS: a Liberian community facing a logging, mining, oil-palm or rubber concession, or an eviction — legal aid to affected communities is part of the mandate, but this is a small office that takes cases selectively.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Independent Information Commission (Liberia)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority; Liberia’s Independent Information Commission is the final administrative arbiter of FOI complaints under the Freedom of Information Act 2010 (official commission site on iicliberia.info), Liberia.

trackers.name: General Auditing Commission
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Liberia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Liberia Business Registry (LBR)
trackers.desc: National — official company register, Liberia. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (LEITI)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues and (in Nigeria) beneficial-ownership data for Liberia.

trackers.name: Liberia — Ministry of Finance & Development Planning (MFDP)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares & manages the national budget and fiscal policy, Liberia. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Liberia.

trackers.name: Land Rights Act 2018 — customary land now includes forests and carbon credits
trackers.desc: THE SCOPE IS WIDER THAN MOST PEOPLE REALISE. Under the Land Rights Act 2018 — described by Liberian civil society as the most progressive pro-community land reform law on the continent — customary land now includes ownership of forests, carbon credits, water and other natural resources, except minerals beneath the land. A formalised community therefore owns the standing forest and the carbon rights over it. Note also that a maximum of 10 percent may be set aside as public land for infrastructure — check what has been set aside and against what stated need. THE VEHICLE: a Community Land Development and Management Committee (CLDMC), which must be representative in terms of gender balance and youth, with the community adopting proper land and resource by-laws. Article 36 gives communities authority to act collectively in establishing one; article 35 gives the CLDMC power to manage the land with the overall consent of the community. EVIDENCE ACCEPTED for a claim: oral testimonies, maps and signed agreements with neighbours — though analysts note that how oral testimony is formally recognised in practice remains to be seen. The Land Authority adopted registration and governance regulations in November 2022.

trackers.name: Start the boundary talks early — that is the step that stalls deeds
trackers.desc: THE ORDER OF STEPS, AND WHERE THEY STOP. Customary Land Formalization runs: self-identification → CLDMC formation and by-laws → boundary harmonization and conflict negotiation → participatory mapping → confirmatory survey → deed. Communities self-identify as customary land-owning and then request a Customary Community Statutory Deed under article 32. BE REALISTIC ABOUT THE TIME: the Fessibu community in Zorzor District, Lofa County received its deed in March 2024 after 5 years of consistent support — and the blocker was the neighbours: on 12 April 2023 Fessibu and neighbouring Zelemai reached agreement on 3 boundaries that had previously delayed the deed. Boundary agreement with neighbours is the common choke point, so open those conversations first, not last. Civil society describes the steps as tedious and costly. WHO CAN HELP, AND THE DOCUMENT TO GET: three Liberian CSOs — the Foundation for Community Initiatives, the Sustainable Development Institute and Parley Liberia — produced ‘A Guide to Customary Land Formalization: Making the Law Work for the People’, a 38-page manual giving step-by-step instruction on self-identification, written because lack of awareness of the law is a major impediment. Reported scale: 82 communities over 1.3 million hectares in 10 counties.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: FDA's community forestry pages are a shell — three county entries, no procedure, no form
trackers.desc: DO NOT PLAN THE CFMA ROUTE FROM THE AUTHORITY'S WEBSITE. The Forestry Development Authority's Community Forestry section renders navigation and no body text; its Community Forestry Management Agreement branch resolves to three county pages — Grand Cape Mount, Marbon and Sinoe — and the parent publishes no procedure, no application form, no fee and no named officer. The sequence that actually governs sits in the Community Forestry Regulation: identification, assessment and demarcation of the forest area and resolution of the conflicts that surface during it; then preliminary permission from the Authority for the community to organise itself as an Authorised Forest Community under Chapter 4 of the Community Rights Law of 2009; then a Community Forest Agreement contracted between the community and the Authority, followed by a management plan. The result is a contract with the Authority over a defined area, not a transfer of the land — the opposite end of the scale from The Gambia. The Regulation text used here is the copy in FAO's FAOLEX database; the Authority's own law database page is the place to check for a current version, and no linked copy was found on this page. Central office: Whein Town, Mount Barclay.

trackers.name: Forest Licenses and Permits — find out who holds the paper over the forest before arguing about the trees
trackers.desc: THE AUTHORITY PUBLISHES ITS LICENCES AND PERMITS AS A DOCUMENT LIBRARY, AND THREE NEIGHBOURING LIBRARIES ON THE SAME MENU ARE MORE USEFUL THAN THIS ONE ALONE. Social Agreements holds the written undertakings a concession holder gave the affected community — the document to hold a company to when it claims it promised nothing. SGS Liberia Reports carries the output of the legality-verification contractor, which is where a chain-of-custody failure appears if one has been recorded. EITI Reports carries payments to government. Read together they answer who holds the right, what they undertook, and whether anyone has checked. CAVEATS: this is a static document library, not a searchable cadastre — there is no map, no parcel lookup, no stated update cycle and no way to query by county from this page. The Authority also maintains a Liberia Forest Atlas and a Liberia law database under the same Publications menu, both of which were seen only as navigation entries and were not opened for this entry.

trackers.name: Liberia Land Authority — three things in its own mandate that a community can hold it to: the surveyor ban, the FOI duty, and who allocates concessions
trackers.desc: READ THE AUTHORITY'S OWN LIST OF FUNCTIONS BEFORE YOU DEAL WITH IT, BECAUSE THREE OF THEM ARE LEVERS AND ONE IS A WARNING. THE SURVEYOR BAN: the Authority regulates survey and mapping and states that under no condition shall a surveyor or other staff of the Authority engage in the survey of private land, or in the survey of communal land, in a private capacity. If the survey that fixed a boundary against your community was carried out privately by Authority staff, that is prohibited by the Authority's own published mandate and is a complaint you can make in those words. THE FOI DUTY: the Authority must provide information on land holdings and interests in land on request, and its mandate states that this is public information under the Freedom of Information Act of 2010, subject only to charges covering the cost of provision — so a refusal is contestable and a fee is not a refusal. THE ADJUDICATION DOOR: it adjudicates disputes arising in the course of systematic land registration where mediation under the Administrative Procedures Act has failed, which is an administrative route that does not require going to court first. AND THE WARNING: the same body allocates public land for concessions in coordination with the relevant ministries, holds all unallocated public land, and may sell or alienate it with the prior written approval of the President. Its own recent record includes leading land verification and survey for a World Bank-backed solar independent power producer project at Buchanan and touring a free-zone area with the Special Economic Zone Authority and foreign investors. The body that will register your community's claim is the body that allocates concessions over public land — not a reason to avoid it, a reason to put everything in writing. SEPARATELY, on customary land: under the Land Rights Act 2018 communities move through self-identification, by-laws, formation of a Community Land Development and Management Committee, boundary harmonisation, mapping, confirmatory survey and registration, ending in a Statutory Land Deed; deeds have been issued in Nimba, Sinoe, Maryland, Grand Cape Mount and Lofa counties. That deed is ownership of the land, whereas a Community Forest Management Agreement with the Forestry Development Authority is a contract over use of the forest — different instruments, and a community can hold one without the other. CAVEATS: this mandate page was last updated in April 2022; fees are set by Gazette notice rather than published here; and a staging mirror at sandbox.lla.gov.lr serves the same pages and surfaces in search results. Head office Ashmun and Gurley Streets, Monrovia; info@lla.gov.lr; +231-55 576-1013; County Land Offices across the fifteen counties.

trackers.name: LLA news feed — where a County Land Office announces it is reopening the deeds over your clan's land, and the only channel it uses
trackers.desc: THIS IS A NOTICE CHANNEL DISGUISED AS A PRESS PAGE, AND IT CARRIES ITEMS THAT DECIDE THINGS. County Land Offices publish public service announcements here: in April 2026 the Maryland County Land Office announced that it had commenced a comprehensive investigation into all land ownership records, including deeds, within the Gbolobo Clan — an item that appears nowhere else and that anyone holding a deed in that clan would need to know about. The page exposes an RSS feed, so it can be monitored rather than remembered: append &format=feed to the listing URL. The same feed is where the Surveyors Licensing and Registration Board publishes its annual list of registered and licensed surveyors — the 2026 list was announced in February 2026 — which is how you check whether the surveyor who demarcated a boundary against you was licensed at the time. The Authority's Downloadable Resources menu carries a policies, laws and regulations repository, consultants' reports and knowledge products, including its land rights implementation strategy. CAVEATS: the announcements are undated in the feed beyond a publication day, carry no closing date for objections and name no officer to write to, so treat an item as notice that a process has started, not as a deadline you can rely on; and the archive runs to only four pages, so older county notices are not retrievable here.

trackers.name: SDI — walks Liberian communities through customary land formalization, all the way to a statutory customary land deed
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Sustainable Development Institute, a Liberian organisation working on natural resource decision-making, which runs a Community Land Protection Programme taking customary communities through the process created by the 2018 Land Rights Act — the law that provides for recognition, protection and registration of community land rights. THE END POINT IS A DEED, NOT AN AGREEMENT: SDI and partners supported the Fessibu community to receive a Statutory Customary Land Deed issued by the Liberia Land Authority, with the community's own Community Land Development and Management Committee the body that made it possible — under article 35 of the Act the CLDMC manages the community's land with the overall consent of the community. THE STEPS, so you know what you are committing to: Community Self-Identification; agreeing the community land space, resources and boundaries; boundary negotiation and memoranda of understanding with neighbouring communities; developing community by-laws using the Land Authority's own template, built up from each town's traditional rules; forming the CLDMC; then confirmatory survey and registration. SDI trains community leaders and local authorities in each of these, including financial reporting, and has deliberately pushed women into land governance roles in places where it had been male-dominated. WHAT SDI ITSELF SAYS IS GOING WRONG, which you should hear before starting: its staff have publicly told the Land Authority that confirmatory survey and boundary harmonisation remain the bottleneck, that the Authority pleads lack of capacity and equipment, and that formalization is slow and expensive — and communities that have completed the requirements have had to press to be issued their deeds. A plain-language guide, A Guide to Customary Land Formalization, was produced with two partner organisations to widen the pool of people who can help. WHO IT SUITS: customary and forest-dependent communities in Liberia that want documented, deeded title before an investor arrives, and that want to negotiate with companies from a position of known boundaries. P.O. Box 5678, Duarzon Village, Monrovia; +231 (0)330 641355. CAVEATS: this is formalization support, not litigation and not purchase; the timetable depends on a state authority that is itself under-resourced; and much of the work runs inside donor-funded projects in named counties, so ask whether a project is live in yours.

trackers.name: Foundation for Community Initiatives — wrote the plain-language guide to getting a customary land deed, and works 24 communities across 500,000 hectares
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: FCI, a Liberian NGO advocating for women, youth and marginalised groups, which heads a consortium of three Liberian civil society organisations working to secure land tenure for rural communities — with the Sustainable Development Institute and Parley-Liberia, backed by an international tenure fund and the Norwegian government. WHAT IT PRODUCED THAT YOU CAN USE TODAY: a 38-page plain-language manual, “A Guide to Customary Land Formalization: Making the Law Work for the People” — described as the first detailed manual by Liberian CSOs on how to support communities seeking deeds for their land, and a simplified supplement to the national guide. Since the Land Rights Act 2018, lack of awareness of the law has been the main impediment to communities legally owning their customary land, which is why an explainer counts as a resource. THE STEPS THE GUIDE COVERS, and the order matters because each one is a gate: community SELF-IDENTIFICATION, adoption of land and resource BYLAWS, election of a Community Land Development and Management Committee (CLDMC), BOUNDARY HARMONISATION with neighbours, mapping, then confirmatory survey and deed registration. Reported scale: the three organisations working with 24 communities totalling 500,000 hectares across eight counties — Nimba, Lofa, Bassa, River Cess, Bong, Margibi, Maryland and River Gee. Related work elsewhere in Liberia records five clans, more than 41,000 people on over 54,000 hectares, receiving a Statutory Community Deed in 2024. WATCH THIS: analysts note the later stages — confirmatory survey, deed registration, and the provision reserving up to 10 per cent of unused community land as public land — are the least tested; ask early how that 10 per cent will be identified on your map. WHO IT SUITS: Liberian rural communities starting or stuck in customary land formalisation. CAVEATS: a facilitating and advocacy organisation, not a law firm — the survey and registration still run through the Liberia Land Authority, whose surveyor capacity is the recorded bottleneck. For the SDI route and the LLA itself, Liberia's other entries.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Malawi, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.
