trackers.desc: Malawi Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Malawi judgments and legislation (MalawiLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: MBRS / CRIPC Business Registry
trackers.desc: National — Malawi Business Registration System (Companies Registration & Intellectual Property Centre). — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Malawi — Ministry of Finance & Economic Affairs
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the Treasury’s Budget Division prepares the national budget and formulates fiscal & economic policy, Malawi. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Malawi.

trackers.name: Malawi Human Rights Commission (MHRC)
trackers.desc: Malawi Human Rights Commission (MHRC) — Malawi’s Human Rights Commission — the oversight body for the Access to Information Act, receiving complaints and monitoring compliance. — Holds to account: Malawi’s public bodies on disclosure — find access-to-information complaint handling, compliance monitoring and reports.

trackers.name: Platform for Investigative Journalism, Malawi
trackers.desc: Malawian nonprofit newsroom investigating corruption and the misuse of public money.

trackers.name: Legal Aid Bureau — district offices, land disputes included
trackers.desc: A FREE LAWYER IN YOUR DISTRICT, AND LAND DISPUTES ARE ON THE LIST. Established under Section 3 of the Legal Aid Act 2011, giving effect to section 41 of the Constitution, the Bureau serves anyone in need of legal assistance who cannot afford a private lawyer. The civil matters it handles expressly include land disputes, alongside maintenance, matrimonial, adoption and personal injury — so a land case is not carved out as it is under many legal aid schemes. It represents clients in all courts in Malawi, from the subordinate courts up to the Supreme Court. WHERE TO GO: offices sit inside District Commissioner's Office complexes, district council buildings and magistrates court complexes — Mulanje, Mangochi, Machinga at Liwonde, Phalombe, Balaka, Mwanza and Nsanje among them — with addresses, phone numbers and email published per district on this page.

trackers.name: Malawi CBNRM Forum — buffer zones held in trust by Traditional Authorities
trackers.desc: IF YOUR SITE IS NEAR A PROTECTED AREA, THIS NETWORK IS ALREADY ORGANISED AROUND THAT GEOGRAPHY. The CBNRM Forum and its members cater for 3.8 million people living within 15 km of Malawi's national parks, wildlife reserves and forests, collectively managing over 1.8 million hectares of forests on customary land and 0.5 million hectares of protected area buffer zones held in trust by Traditional Authorities. THE BUFFER-ZONE-IN-TRUST MODEL IS THE DISTINCTIVE PART: land adjoining a protected area, held by the Traditional Authority, is where community management is concentrated — so the Traditional Authority is the counterparty for land at the boundary of a reserve, not the parks department alone. Contrast Botswana, where community access rests on policy directives rather than legislation: here the holding is through customary trust, which is a different and more durable footing. The Forum is also the route to peers already managing comparable land.

trackers.name: Land clerk and customary land committee — 30 days from publication of the adjudication record, and the certificate goes to the chief, not to you
trackers.desc: TWO DIFFERENT PIECES OF PAPER EXIST AND PEOPLE CONFUSE THEM: the Commissioner issues a certificate of customary land in the name of the Traditional Authority for a whole Traditional Land Management Area, while an individual household holds a customary estate inside it. The chief's certificate is not your title and your estate is not the chief's to give away. To register a customary estate you wait for adjudication and demarcation of the parcels, then complete Form 2 of the First Schedule and submit it to the customary land committee; a land clerk issues the adjudication record on Form 1 and keeps the customary land register — the final adjudication record, the demarcation record and the registry maps. A registered customary estate is of indefinite duration, inheritable and transmissible by will. THE DEADLINE THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING: a person aggrieved by a determination of a land committee has thirty days from the publication of the adjudication record and demarcation map to appeal to the customary land tribunal for that area; from there the ladder runs to the district land tribunal and then to the Central Land Board. Thirty days from publication, not from when you heard — so ask the land clerk when publication happened and get the date in writing. TWO PROVISIONS WORTH QUOTING BACK: a land committee or adjudication officer must treat the rights of women and other vulnerable groups no less favourably than those of men, and a customary land tribunal is not quorate without at least four members, two of whom are women — a hearing held without them is defective on its face. WHERE THE PEOPLE ARE: the ministry has deployed land clerks at Traditional Authority level and district land registrars in the councils, reported at 319 and 34 respectively, so the clerk is the nearest office rather than the ministry. Ministry of Lands, Zowe House, City Centre, Lilongwe; lands@lands.gov.mw. CAVEATS: the forms, the thirty-day limit and the quorum were read from the Customary Land Act as published by the Malawi legal information institute and by FAO's legislative database, not from this ministry page, which describes the lease route rather than customary registration; and registration began as a pilot in a handful of districts, so coverage is uneven and the register may not yet exist for your area.

trackers.name: CEPA — founded by Malawi's environmental law practitioners, and the body that gets communities into the room over a draft mining EIA
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Centre for Environmental Policy and Advocacy, founded in 2002 by Malawi's environmental law practitioners as the country's first organisation dedicated to environmental policy and advocacy, registered as a Trust in 2022. Its stated work includes facilitating access to environmental information, access to justice and public participation — the three things a community needs before it can object to anything — alongside policy research on land and agrarian reform and programmes on minerals, land, water, fisheries and wildlife. WHAT IT HAS ACTUALLY PUT COMMUNITIES INTO: its published work records a Malingunde mining committee engaging directly with company officials over the draft Environmental Impact Assessment report, under a mining governance project — a community body reading the developer's own EIA and questioning it face to face is the single most useful thing a project-affected village can do, and this is an organisation that arranges it. It also works with artisanal salt and small-scale miners, and builds the capacity of civil society organisations across Malawi to take part in these processes. Its programme manager Gloria Majiga-Kamoto won the Goldman Environmental Prize for Africa in 2021 for the campaign that got Malawi's ban on single-use plastics enforced — evidence that the organisation's people litigate and campaign to an outcome, not just publish. It runs a resource centre inside its office, open to the public on weekdays. Globe House, Raynor Avenue, Plot CC 365, Limbe, Blantyre; +265 212 700 104; info@cepa.org.mw. WHO IT SUITS: Malawian communities facing mining, land conversion or water and fisheries loss, and local organisations that need the policy and legal groundwork done. CAVEATS: a think tank and advocacy institution rather than a legal aid service — it was founded by lawyers but does not advertise representation, and no intake route or fee information was published; a legacy website mirror also carries older content, so use the current domain.

trackers.name: CCODE and the Malawi federation — the Mchenga Fund bought land on the open market, then started land banking for future need
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY AND BUY LAND: the Centre for Community Organisation and Development (CCODE), a Lilongwe-based non-profit founded in 2003, working in alliance with the grassroots savings network known as the Malawi Homeless People's Federation, later the Federation of the Rural and Urban Poor — reported at over 50,000 members across 26 districts, about 80 per cent of them women. THE FUND: members established the Mchenga Fund, capitalised by community savings plus donor funding, with members originally contributing MK20 a month; since 2003 it has made group loans for house construction. The name is the argument — mchenga means sand: single savings are grains, uncountable alone, decisive together. It exists because commercial lenders will not touch these households, and because shelter microfinance cannot fund collective investment in upgrading or new build at all where tenure is insecure — which is precisely the situation most people in this file are in. THE TWO MOVES WORTH COPYING: when land access delayed a project, the federation and CCODE secured land through MARKET PURCHASE using Mchenga Fund resources; and, having been burned by those delays, the federation decided to invest in LAND BANKING in informal settlements — buying and holding land ahead of need so future community projects are not hostage to whoever controls allocation. Reported results include tenure and decent housing secured for over 1,000 households and improved sanitation for over 2,500. WHO IT SUITS: Malawian low-income urban and rural households wanting a route to land and housing outside the banks, and groups considering buying land collectively before they need it. CAVEATS: THE RESEARCH IS BLUNT ABOUT STRAIN — repayment rates on the first loans approached 100 per cent but declined over the years; demand far outstrips the fund and the land available (in one city 222 houses against demand for 600, in another 83 against 600); and one project site was itself subject to a land grab. CCODE's own site did not resolve to a verified page — this entry points at a housing-fund partner record. For mining and EIA work, Malawi's CEPA entry is the route.

trackers.name: LandNet Malawi — the national land network to route through, in a country where paralegals are recognised in the Legal Aid Act
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: LandNet Malawi, the national land network of Malawian civil society organisations working on land and natural resource management, and Malawi's member of the international land coalition. Its stated objectives are to strengthen the advocacy and lobbying capacity of Malawian organisations engaged in land and natural resources, and to strengthen coordination between them through networking and information sharing — so for a community that does not know which organisation handles its problem, this is the routing layer. Its vision is land policy and legislation responsive to the needs of poor, vulnerable and marginalised groups. Its constituency is its own network members. P.O. Box 31437, Lilongwe 3. THE FACT THAT MAKES MALAWI DIFFERENT, and it is worth knowing before you look for help: community paralegals are RECOGNISED IN MALAWI'S LEGAL AID ACT OF 2010 as “Legal Aid Assistants” — a statutory basis most countries in this file lack — while other grassroots legal advocates operate outside that scheme, deployed by civil society organisations and known simply as paralegals. Ask whether the person helping you is a statutory Legal Aid Assistant or an NGO paralegal, because it changes what they can do inside the formal system. The pledges its network signs include protection for land rights defenders and equal land rights for women, including the right to inherit and bequeath tenure rights. WHO IT SUITS: Malawians who need to find the right land organisation, and organisations wanting to join a national land advocacy platform. CAVEATS: a NETWORK AND ADVOCACY PLATFORM — casework happens at member organisations, so expect a referral; the entry points at the coalition's member record because that is the verified public listing. For mining and EIA review, Malawi's CEPA entry; for savings-based land purchase and land banking, the CCODE entry.

trackers.name: Malawi Legal Aid Bureau — takes LAND DISPUTES, represents you in every court up to the Supreme Court, and has district offices inside existing government buildings
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET A FREE LAWYER: the Legal Aid Bureau, established under section 3 of the Legal Aid Act 2011 with a statutory mandate to provide legal aid to indigent and vulnerable people, and described as THE ONLY SUCH INSTITUTION IN MALAWI. It gives effect to section 41 of the Constitution, and its stated priority groups are women, children, the elderly and the sick. WHY IT IS IN A LAND MAP: its published civil caseload expressly includes LAND DISPUTES, alongside deceased estates, labour matters, maintenance and matrimonial cases — and it REPRESENTS CLIENTS IN ALL COURTS IN MALAWI, from the subordinate courts up the hierarchy to the SUPREME COURT. That is representation through appeal, not first advice — the thing most entries in this file cannot offer. WHERE IT IS, and the pattern is worth copying: four regional offices — Lilongwe (headquarters, 1st Floor Shire Building off Paul Kagame Highway, +265 1 753 945), Blantyre (Government Office Building, Lower Victoria Avenue, +265 1 822 082), Mzuzu (1st Floor Osman Gani Building, +265 1 311 086) and Zomba (Old Parliament Building, +265 1 528 856) — plus DISTRICT OFFICES HOUSED INSIDE BUILDINGS PEOPLE ALREADY VISIT: the Mchinji District Assembly Hall, the District Education Manager's office in Kasungu, and the Ministry of Agriculture building in Salima. Putting the legal aid desk in the agriculture office is how a rural service reaches people who would never travel to a regional capital — ask whether your district has one before assuming the nearest office is hours away. info@legalaidbureau.org. It also runs public legal education. WHO IT SUITS: Malawians who cannot afford a private lawyer and face a land dispute, an estate or eviction — particularly women, the elderly and the sick. CAVEATS: A STATE BUREAU with a means test and finite counsel; it is not a campaigning body and will not oppose a government project on your behalf. For mining and EIA review, Malawi's CEPA entry; for savings-based land purchase and land banking, CCODE; for finding the right member organisation, LandNet.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: ITIE Moçambique
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and licences in Mozambique.

trackers.name: Mozambique — Serviço Nacional de Registo (SNR)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the SNR portal handles online company name reservation & registration via the Conservatória do Registo das Entidades Legais (with Balcão de Atendimento Único one-stops), Mozambique. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Mozambique — Ministério da Economia e Finanças (MEF)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; designs, formulates & executes economic & social development policy and the State budget, Mozambique. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Mozambique.

trackers.name: Constitutional Council (Mozambique)
trackers.desc: Constitutional Council (Mozambique) — supreme court in Mozambique (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: Centro Terra Viva — Mozambican environmental lawyers who sit with communities through consultation and resettlement, and train women paralegals
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Mozambican non-profit founded in 2002 — Estudos e Advocacia Ambiental, environmental studies and advocacy — with lawyers on staff, some of them registered with the Mozambican bar. Its published work is the exact sequence a community faces when a project arrives: legal advice to rural communities to secure their land tenure, land delimitation, accompanying community and public consultation processes when land use rights are being granted to private investors, and monitoring resettlement. It works on the licensing processes in Palma and Montepuez in Cabo Delgado — gas and rubies — and has done community land delimitation in Inhambane. WHY DELIMITATION IS THE THING TO ASK FOR FIRST: in Mozambique the land itself cannot be sold or mortgaged, and communities hold rights of use and benefit rather than title, so what protects you is a delimited, documented community right recorded before an investor's application, not a purchase — which is why the resource classes that work in Kenya do not transfer here. THE PART WORTH COPYING ANYWHERE: CTV builds associations of women paralegals — it has trained and organised one in Massingir district in Gaza, and works in Ile in Zambézia — so that the people in resettlement villages can press their own claims after the lawyers leave. It also publishes reports on resettlement, land delimitation, logging and artisanal mining, and runs environmental education programmes. WHO IT SUITS: rural and coastal communities facing extractive projects, concessions or resettlement, and local associations that want their own paralegals trained. CAVEATS: no published intake route, case-selection criteria or fee information; much of the fieldwork sits inside donor-funded projects in named districts, so whether CTV can reach your district depends on which project is running. It is an advocacy and legal-assistance organisation, not a litigation firm, and no land purchase capacity exists here — in Mozambican law there is nothing to buy.

trackers.name: Justiça Ambiental (JA!) — stands with Mozambican communities that refuse the compensation offered, and goes after the projects' financiers
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: JA! / Amigos da Terra Moçambique, a Mozambican civil society organisation based in Maputo that works directly with communities displaced by the gas and coal megaprojects. It visits and works regularly with named villages — Milamba, Senga and Quitupo in the Rovuma basin area — and its documentation of what happened there is the specific kind a reader needs: the project took people's farmland and gave compensatory land that is far from their homes and in many cases not arable. THE MOMENT IT MATTERS MOST: JA! has publicly reported that communities at Maganja affected by the gas project were called in by the police after refusing to accept monetary compensation for their land, and named that as intimidation. Refusing a compensation offer is a legitimate act, and a community that does it needs a national organisation willing to say so out loud on the day the police call. WHAT ELSE IT DOES: it has documented resettlement in the Tete coal province into areas without access to agriculture, with rising food insecurity; it questions operators directly at their own shareholder and public meetings; and with international partners it works the money — raising the responsibilities of the French operator over Mozambique LNG since 2019, and pressing financial institutions, including over a development bank loan to a floating LNG project that UN-appointed human rights experts had raised concerns about. That is the same financier-pressure route this file records in Senegal and Guinea, run from inside the affected country. WHO IT SUITS: Mozambican communities facing displacement, resettlement or compensation offers from gas, coal or hydropower projects, especially in Cabo Delgado and Tete. CAVEATS: an advocacy and campaigning organisation — not a law firm and not a compensation negotiator; for legal assistance, delimitation and paralegal training Mozambique's Centro Terra Viva entry is the one to use. Cabo Delgado is an active conflict zone, and JA!'s own reporting records intimidation of communities that resist.

trackers.name: Centro de Integridade Pública — publishes what the resettlement contracts and mining deals actually say, and names the irregularities
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Centro de Integridade Pública (CIP), a Mozambican non-profit association created in 2005, independent and non-party, working on transparency, anti-corruption and integrity — and, for a community, the organisation that goes after the CONTRACT and the MONEY behind a project rather than the project's fence line. WHAT IT HAS DONE ON RESETTLEMENT AND EXTRACTION: monitoring reports on mining activity in Moma, Moatize, Manica and Sussundenga; documentation of the conflict between resettled families and the coal company at Cateme in Tete; and published exposure of a heavy-sands company installation in Zambézia “laden with irregularities”, dangers to a forest reserve, and a problematic resettlement on Olinda island, Inhassunge district — including impositions and negotiations conducted in the name of the population rather than with it. It has also criticised mining companies' conduct toward host communities nationally, and analysed a parliamentary inquiry into hazardous chemical use in gold mining in Manica, noting mercury pollution, habitat destruction, lost livelihoods and public health harm. THE FIGHT IT PICKED THAT MATTERS MOST TO AN AFFECTED VILLAGE: it stated publicly that the government was seeking to keep the contracts SECRET. A resettlement is governed by documents — the concession contract, the resettlement plan, the environmental licence — and a community that cannot read them is negotiating blind; an organisation whose whole purpose is prising those documents loose is a resource, not a commentator. WHO IT SUITS: Mozambican communities facing resettlement by mining, gas or heavy-sands projects who need the terms, the licence conditions and the money flows made public. CAVEATS: a research, transparency and advocacy organisation — not a law firm, not a paralegal service and not a fund; it publishes, it does not represent you. For delimitation, DUAT documentation and paralegals, Mozambique's Centro Terra Viva entry; for contesting the project and its financiers, JA!.

trackers.name: ORAM — Mozambique's rural mutual-aid association, founded 1992, which walks communities through delimitation to a DUAT certificate
trackers.desc: WHO GETS YOU THE CERTIFICATE: the Associação Rural de Ajuda Mútua (ORAM), a non-profit Mozambican membership association founded in 1992 whose stated mission is to defend the rights and interests of peasants and rural communities and secure sustainable tenure and use of land and natural resources — with the working aim of turning rights of access to land into actual benefits for rural communities. It has PROVINCIAL DELEGATIONS, including a Nampula delegation created in 1996 that extended into Cabo Delgado from 2008, so this is not a capital-city-only organisation. Head office: Rua da Resistência 1518, Maputo; open Monday to Friday, 7:30 to 15:30. WHAT THE PROCESS PRODUCES, AND AT WHAT SCALE: once a delimitation application is authorised, the DUAT certificate is issued and handed to the community at a ceremony attended by the provincial land service, the district government, local authorities, ORAM, partners and community leaders — a public handover, which matters because everyone who might later dispute the boundary is standing there. Documented community delimitations in this work include Muirite and Muilo in Chapa administrative post, Mueda district, Cabo Delgado, at 35,702 and 47,488 hectares respectively. ORAM also works on the alternative to full titling — local mapping and declaration of acquired DUAT rights, producing LOCALLY REGISTERED DECLARATIONS instead of formal titles, which is faster where the cadastre cannot cope. ASK WHICH YOU ARE GETTING: a delimitation certificate for the community, a locally registered declaration, or an individual DUAT — they are not the same document. WHO IT SUITS: Mozambican rural communities and peasant associations seeking delimitation, a community DUAT, or documentation before an investor applies over their land. CAVEATS: an associative rural development organisation, not a law firm; researchers note that the share of forest fees returning to communities has tended to create small local elites and that local government has at times interfered in managing those funds — ask how the money will be governed before it arrives. For paralegals and resettlement monitoring, Mozambique's CTV entry; for contesting a project and its financiers, JA!; for the contracts behind it, CIP.

trackers.name: IPAJ — Mozambique's constitutional free-lawyer service, with provincial AND district delegations, itinerant assistance and new counters inside administrative posts
trackers.desc: WHAT THE CONSTITUTION GUARANTEES: the Instituto do Patrocínio e Assistência Jurídica (IPAJ), created in 1994 under the justice ministry to satisfy the constitutional requirement that the state provide legal assistance and representation — the guarantee sits in Article 62 of the Constitution. A SECOND ENTITLEMENT MOST PEOPLE NEVER INVOKE: the statutes of the Mozambican Bar Association (Ordem dos Advogados de Moçambique) say that members MUST provide free legal representation as one of their duties. So if IPAJ has no capacity, a private advocate still carries a professional obligation — ask the Ordem, not only the Institute. HOW IT IS STRUCTURED AND WHERE IT IS GOING: IPAJ operates through PROVINCIAL AND DISTRICT DELEGATIONS, with provincial delegates subordinated centrally while coordinating with the provincial government; it marked 30 years in 2025, emphasising ITINERANT legal assistance and international partnerships, with the government identifying support to displaced populations of CABO DELGADO as a priority area for it. Reported for one year: more than 300,000 people to benefit from free legal assistance. AND THE ACCESS PATTERN WORTH CHECKING LOCALLY: in Sofala, three new IPAJ service counters were planned for the administrative posts of Munhava, Manga and Inhamízua in Beira district, explicitly to make attendance easier for citizens in need. Ask whether a balcão has opened at your administrative post — the same pattern as Malawi placing legal aid desks inside existing government buildings, and it is how a service reaches people who cannot travel. WHO IT SUITS: Mozambicans without means who need representation — including in land, DUAT and resettlement disputes — and displaced people in Cabo Delgado. CAVEATS: A STATE INSTITUTE under the justice ministry, means-tested and heavily loaded with criminal work; it will not campaign against a licensed project. For delimitation and paralegals, Mozambique's CTV entry; for community DUAT certificates, ORAM; for contesting a project and its financiers, JA!; for the contracts behind it, CIP.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Sierra Leone.

trackers.name: Audit Service Sierra Leone

trackers.name: Customary Land Rights Act 2022 — 60 percent written consent, no sector exempt
trackers.desc: THE STRONGEST CONSENT PROVISION IN THIS MAP. Section 28: no investment shall take place on customary land unless the investor obtains the written, informed consent of at least 60 percent of the male and female adult members of the family or a fair representation of the community with rights to the land. Written consent, not consultation; a numerical threshold, not an undefined ‘community view’ a chief can assert on your behalf; and male and female adults expressly. Section 31 requires investors to sign lease agreements before the investment starts. AND NO SECTOR IS EXEMPT, INCLUDING MINING — where FPIC is codified elsewhere it is typically limited to Indigenous peoples, watered down to ‘consultation’, and usually excludes mining. OTHER OPERATIVE TERMS: industrial development — mining, plantations, farming, housing — is banned in protected, conserved or ecologically sensitive areas, naming wetlands, wildlife habitats, steep slopes and old-growth forests; leasehold may not exceed 50 years; citizens hold a 10 percent minimum share in all large-scale land-based investments; local land use committees must be at least 30 percent women; and all customary land must be registered before it can be acquired for investment. Discrimination in owning or using land by gender, tribe, religion, age, marital, social or economic status is prohibited.

trackers.name: Licence conditions become contract terms — and how the law was won
trackers.desc: THE PROVISION TO REACH FOR WHEN A LICENCE IS BREACHED. The Act incorporates public environmental licence conditions into binding legal agreements between communities and companies — so a licence condition becomes a term of the community's own contract, and breach is actionable by the community itself rather than only by the regulator. That converts a regulatory failure into a contractual claim you control. HOW THE LAW WAS WON, WHICH IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART: it grew from a decade of local fights against land grabs and pollution, with its provisions on consent, women's land rights and responsible investment each stemming from specific grassroots struggles. Communities that had shaped the bill's contents then led a nationwide movement to get it passed — organising regional consultations, submitting inputs, and writing to the President to ask that the laws be sent to Parliament. Both Acts passed unanimously in August 2022. THE CASES THAT DROVE IT: an oil palm company obtained over 74,000 acres from government between 2011 and 2013; and in 2012 an investor took over 30,000 hectares through a one-sided deal with traditional authorities behind closed doors — a holding the size of a chiefdom, including homes and communal spaces. THE HONEST NOTE: Sierra Leonean civil society has said explicitly it needs international support to monitor implementation. A strong statute is not self-executing.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Legal Aid Board — the statute promises a paralegal in every chiefdom; roughly two thirds of chiefdoms have none
trackers.desc: SIERRA LEONE IS THE ONE COUNTRY IN THIS GROUP WHERE FREE HELP WITH A LAND DISPUTE IS MEANT TO REACH THE VILLAGE RATHER THAN THE DISTRICT TOWN, AND THE GAP BETWEEN THE STATUTE AND THE STAFFING IS THE WHOLE STORY. Section 14(2) of the Legal Aid Act 2012 requires the Board to appoint at least one paralegal to each chiefdom. There are 190 chiefdoms. The Board has reported placing paralegals in about a third of them, with a complement in the order of 65 paralegals and volunteer paralegals, and offices in 29 towns — 16 in district headquarter towns and 13 in chiefdom headquarter towns. What makes it worth approaching anyway: the Act endorses paralegals, university law clinics, civil society organisations and NGOs alongside practising lawyers as legal aid providers, the service is free and open regardless of nationality, and mediation is offered as a service in its own right rather than only as a step before litigation — paralegals routinely handle land disputes and conflicts with authorities, and monitor local and informal courts, including checking that fines imposed by a Local Court do not exceed the statutory ceiling and that clients are refunded where they have. URL NOT VERIFIED: no canonical domain for the Board was located, and no page for it was found on a Sierra Leonean government domain; the figures above come from the Board's own country report as circulated through Harvard Law School's Access to Justice programme, from Sierra Leone's Open Government Partnership commitment record, and from HiiL's case study. Approach through a district office in person rather than online, and treat the chiefdom-level presence as something to confirm locally before relying on it.

trackers.name: EPA-SL environmental impact assessment — 14 days to comment, addressed to the Executive Chairman, counted from the last publication
trackers.desc: THE COMMENT WINDOW IS FOURTEEN DAYS AND IT DOES NOT START WHEN YOU HEAR ABOUT THE PROJECT. Under the Environment Protection Agency Act 2022, once an applicant files an environmental impact assessment the Agency publishes it on its website or in a newspaper for inspection and comment by the public, government ministries, professional bodies and NGOs, and comments must reach the Executive Chairman within 14 days of the last publication. Two consequences follow. First, publication in a Freetown newspaper starts the clock for a chiefdom that will never see that newspaper, so the practical protection is to ask the Agency in writing to be notified of filings in your district rather than to watch for a notice. Second, because the period runs from the last publication, establish which of the website posting and the newspaper notice came later before assuming you are out of time. The Executive Chairman then submits the assessment with an environmental public disclosure report to the Board, which considers it within 30 working days. An EIA licence is a statutory requirement for the activities listed in the schedule of the Agency's founding legislation, licences are monitored for deviation from their terms, and the Act provides an appeal against the Agency's decision. Head office is 38 Freetown Road, Wilberforce Village, Freetown; info@epa.gov.sl; +232-88-908-951; open 08:00 to 16:45, Fridays to 15:30. CAVEAT ON THE ADDRESS: at least one intergovernmental directory still lists the Agency at 20E Fifth Road, Juba Hill — use the Agency's own contact page. The section numbering and the two time limits above were read from the Act as published on SierraLII, the national legal information institute, not from the Agency's site, which does not set out the comment procedure.

trackers.name: Green Scenery — documents Sierra Leonean land deals from the field, backs the affected landowners' association, and has been sued twice for defamation for doing it
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Freetown-based environmental and human rights organisation that monitors land grabbing nationally and works alongside MALOA, the Malen Affected Landowners and Users Association, the community's own body in the country's best-documented land conflict. THE FACT THAT DECIDES MOST SIERRA LEONEAN LAND DISPUTES, and which Green Scenery's work turns on: outside Freetown land is owned by individual families, and a paramount chief has no right to sell it — yet the leases at issue were arranged between the chief, government officials and the company. More than 80 per cent of one chiefdom's arable land was leased for palm oil, over 18,000 hectares, on a 50-year term, without the free, prior and informed consent of the landowners. Ask who signed, and whether they had the right to. A High Court ruling elsewhere in the country ordered the restoration of 1,486 acres belonging to over 70 families sold to a company without the owners' informed consent — the principle is enforceable. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES: field fact-finding missions producing published reports — including a 13-page report corroborating the arrest of 57 citizens in the chiefdom — monitoring of arrests and intimidation of land rights defenders, and challenges to the sustainability certification granted to the company despite the conflict. AND THE RISK IT CARRIES SHOULD BE UNDERSTOOD BY ANYONE WHO PUBLISHES: the company filed defamation complaints against Green Scenery in 2013 and again in 2019 over its reports; the first was dropped, and in the second a default judgment was reportedly obtained that the organisation says was never served on it or its lawyer. Community members have fared worse — MALOA members were jailed after a protracted trial, and two people were shot dead in a 2019 escalation. WHO IT SUITS: Sierra Leonean families and communities facing agro-industrial leases, and anyone needing the land deal documented rather than argued about. CAVEATS: a research, documentation and advocacy organisation, not a law firm — Sierra Leone's Legal Aid Board entry covers paralegal coverage, though its civil-representation gate is narrow. MALOA, the community association itself, may merit its own entry.

trackers.name: Namati Sierra Leone — paralegals who renegotiate leases already signed, including a 21,000-hectare deal covering dozens of villages
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Sierra Leone country programme of the legal empowerment organisation Namati, staffed by Sierra Leonean paralegals and lawyers. WHY IT ANSWERS THE SITUATION MOST COMMUNITIES ARE ACTUALLY IN: it works with communities who have seen the entire land of their villages signed away by elders and chiefs who did not have the whole community's best interests at heart — and it renegotiates. In one case it worked to renegotiate an inequitable 21,000-hectare lease with a Swiss biofuels company that had taken control of all the land of dozens of villages, leaving them nothing to grow food on, and where necessary it litigates to strike down deals that are manifestly unjust. A signed lease is not the end of the matter. REPORTED RESULTS IN A SINGLE HARD YEAR: paralegals supported six communities to negotiate equitable land lease agreements and four others to harmonise their boundaries, and got a Dutch agricultural company to replant 2,600 trees it had cut down without community consent. Farming families in Nimiyama Chiefdom defended their land rights in a landmark case against local leaders and a foreign company with paralegal support. WHAT ELSE TO KNOW: the paralegal model here is written into law — Sierra Leone's 2012 legal aid act recognised community paralegals and called for them to operate in EVERY CHIEFDOM, though coverage has never matched what the law envisaged. Namati's Sierra Leone team leaders were later contracted by the Ministry of Lands, as independent lawyers, to draft two model land laws, and the resulting land bills were signed into law. WHO IT SUITS: Sierra Leonean communities whose land has been leased over their heads, who want a lease renegotiated, boundaries harmonised, or environmental damage remedied. CAVEATS: an international organisation running a national programme, not a Sierra Leonean NGO; paralegal coverage is uneven; and for local documentation of a land deal, Sierra Leone's Green Scenery entry, or the Legal Aid Board for the statutory service.

trackers.name: Conservation Society of Sierra Leone — the organisation that helped pass the 2022 land laws, fought the Lake Sonfon mining, and built Gola into a £10m benefit-sharing park
trackers.desc: WHAT THE LAW NOW GIVES YOUR COMMUNITY: on 7 September 2022 Sierra Leone enacted the CUSTOMARY LAND RIGHTS ACT and the NATIONAL LAND COMMISSION ACT, which GRANT ALL LOCAL COMMUNITIES THE RIGHT TO FREE PRIOR INFORMED CONSENT OVER ALL INDUSTRIAL PROJECTS ON THEIR LANDS, BAN INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT — INCLUDING MINING, TIMBER AND AGRIBUSINESS — IN OLD-GROWTH FORESTS AND OTHER ECOLOGICALLY SENSITIVE AREAS, INCORPORATE PUBLIC ENVIRONMENTAL LICENCE CONDITIONS INTO BINDING LEGAL AGREEMENTS between communities and companies, and ESTABLISH LOCAL LAND USE COMMITTEES, mandated to be AT LEAST 30% WOMEN. Two things make this the strongest community-land statute in this file: FPIC is granted to ALL communities rather than only those a state classifies as indigenous, and MINING IS NOT EXEMPTED — elsewhere governments claim the subsoil and carve mining out. Landowners can veto a project affecting their land. And the licence clause is the quiet weapon: environmental conditions written into a public permit become terms of a contract you can enforce yourself, instead of waiting for a regulator. WHO HELPED PASS IT AND CAN HELP YOU USE IT: the CONSERVATION SOCIETY OF SIERRA LEONE (cs-sl.org), which contributed evidence-gathering, public awareness and community engagement to the campaign, led work against mining pressure at LAKE SONFON and the Pampana River, and played a foundational role in establishing the GOLA RAINFOREST NATIONAL PARK — 71,070 hectares, enacted by Parliament in December 2010, now a UNESCO World Heritage site — whose REDD+ programme has generated over £10 MILLION with a BENEFIT-SHARING MODEL. WHAT COMMUNITIES HAD ALREADY WON BEFORE THE ACT: Tonkolili district communities won a court judgment against the nation's largest iron mine, with damages and flooding remedies partially paid; and in the Gola region communities INVALIDATED AN ILLEGITIMATE 30,000-HECTARE PALM OIL CONCESSION negotiated without community consent. WHO IT SUITS: Sierra Leonean landowning families and communities facing a mining, plantation or timber project. CAVEATS: A NEW STATUTE STILL BEDDING IN — implementation depends on the land committees actually being constituted, and research records that outcomes differ sharply depending on whether decisions sit with landowning families or the paramount chief. For the committee procedure and the statute text itself, this file's Sierra Leone community land committees entry; for paralegals who renegotiate leases already signed, the Namati entry.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? STAFF, NOT A HUB — Botswana. The 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar; here there are additional staff, so expect a smaller presence and a longer route into casework. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Companies and Intellectual Property Authority
trackers.desc: CIPA is Botswana's registrar of companies and a parastatal of Botswana Government.

trackers.name: Online Business Registration System (OBRS)
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Botswana — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; formulates financial & economic policy, administers the treasury, and publishes the national budget & budget speeches, Botswana. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Botswana.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Botswana, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: SAFLII – Botswana
trackers.desc: Free judgments of the High Court of Botswana (1999– ), the Court of Appeal (1981– ) and the Industrial Court, via the Southern African Legal Information Institute. · Find here: free Botswana and Southern-African case-law and legislation (SAFLII).

trackers.name: Botswana CBNRM — a policy directive, not a legal right
trackers.desc: KNOW WHAT YOUR RIGHT RESTS ON BEFORE YOU RELY ON IT. Comparative legal analysis sets Botswana against its neighbours: in Namibia law grants communities the right to set up conservancies and retain all income from game; in Mozambique the Forest and Wildlife Law 1999 gives communities rights to obtain logging licences and concessions, to participate in granting licences to logging companies and to receive a share of public revenues. Those are rights granted through legislation — and, in the analysis's words, this contrasts with Botswana's CBNRM framework, where access to resources by local communities is only through policy directives. A policy directive can be revised by the department that issued it; a statutory right cannot. Treat CBNRM here as an administrative permission rather than a legal entitlement, and document everything, because there is no statutory floor beneath it. THE VEHICLE is a registered community trust with a board of trustees as supreme governing body — 105 registered trusts operate as viable entities generating and distributing revenue, and at its recorded peak CBNRM covered 150 villages in ten districts and more than 135,000 people, about 10 percent of the population.

trackers.name: Two documented failure modes — agree the trust's purpose in writing
trackers.desc: RECORDED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER, because both are avoidable if anticipated. 1. ELITE CAPTURE: an evaluation of Botswana's CBNRM framework found governance gaps, elite capture and limited capacity undermining equitable benefit sharing — so the trust's constitution and benefit-distribution rules are where the real fight is, not the wildlife quota. 2. MISMATCHED EXPECTATIONS: a study of communities next to Chobe National Park found general incongruence between community perceptions and expectations of the purpose and roles of Community Trusts and those of the wildlife authorities — after 2 decades, significant confusion translating into unfulfilled expectations and frustration. AGREE IN WRITING, WITH THE AUTHORITY, WHAT THE TRUST IS FOR AT THE OUTSET, including what revenue is expected and who decides its use. A CBNRM policy drafted for the Department of Wildlife and National Parks was intended to set specific objectives and implementation guidelines and to include a section on relations between protected areas and neighbouring communities — check whether it is in force, since that is the document that would govern a buffer-zone dispute.

trackers.name: Land Tribunal — it hears planning appeals as well as land board appeals, and a public body that ignores its ruling commits an offence
trackers.desc: MOST PEOPLE KNOW THIS AS THE PLACE YOU CHALLENGE A LAND BOARD. THE HALF THAT GETS MISSED IS THAT IT ALSO HEARS APPEALS FROM PLANNING AUTHORITIES — it is constituted under both the tribal land legislation and the town and country planning legislation, which makes it the forum for a planning permission you want to stop, not only for a plot allocation you want back. It is a court of law and equity, its judgments go on appeal to the High Court, and it sits in four divisions — Gaborone, Francistown, Palapye and Maun — with circuit sittings arranged for outlying areas. THE CLOCK: thirty days from the date you became aware of the land board's decision — awareness, not service, which cuts both ways and is worth pinning down in writing early. WHAT TO WALK IN WITH, because an incomplete filing is the common failure: the land board or planning authority resolution you are challenging; a notice and grounds of appeal lodged with the Clerk of Court giving full names, addresses and contacts of every party, the grounds, and the relief you want; a list of any witnesses; certified copies of your identity document or passport and of the certificate of customary land grant, lease or title deed; and a sketch plan showing the area in dispute. You then file an affidavit of service, and the respondent has one month from service to file a notice of intention to defend with its reasons. THE PROVISION NOBODY QUOTES: under the tribunal's own Act, a public body or party that without reasonable excuse fails to comply with or enforce a determination commits an offence, punishable by a fine of up to P10,000 or two years' imprisonment, and up to P20,000 for a body corporate — so a land board that simply ignores a ruling is not merely in breach, it is liable. CAVEAT: the thirty-day limit and the offence provision were read from the tribal land legislation and the tribunal's Act rather than from this services page, which sets out the filing steps but no deadline.

trackers.name: Land board allocation — demarcate within three months or the board can take the plot back through the tribunal, with no compensation
trackers.desc: THE GRANT IS STRONG AND THE FORFEITURE IS FAST, WHICH IS AN UNUSUAL COMBINATION AND THE REASON THIS ENTRY EXISTS. Tribal land is allocated by twelve main land boards and forty-one subordinate land boards; any citizen aged eighteen or over may apply for unallocated tribal land in any tribal territory, not only their own, on the ministry's customary land rights application form, submitted during the window stated in the allocation announcement — miss the announcement and you wait for the next one. A successful applicant receives a deed of customary land grant, and those rights are held in perpetuity and pass from one generation to the next. Allocation is to be completed within three months of the land becoming available. THEN THE TRAP: an allocated plot must be demarcated promptly, and a land board has publicly warned that failure to demarcate within three months of allocation can lead to cancellation — the board applies to the Land Tribunal to recover the land, and where it succeeds there is no compensation. Holders already occupying land under an older certificate were separately required to apply for a deed within six months of the 2018 Act commencing. ONE ACCESSIBILITY POINT WORTH KNOWING: an appeal from a subordinate land board to the main tribal land board may be lodged verbally or in writing with the clerk, and the clerk must then supply the board with the reasons for the decision and serve a copy of those reasons on you — ask for the written reasons, because they are what an appeal to the Land Tribunal is built on. Ministry of Land Management, Water and Sanitation Services toll free 0800 600 737; offices open 07:30 to 12:45 and 13:45 to 16:30 on weekdays. CAVEATS: the demarcation warning comes from the government news service reporting a land board briefing, not from a regulation quoted here, and the verbal-appeal provision from the subsidiary legislation rather than this page — confirm both at your land board, and treat three months as the working assumption rather than a certainty.

trackers.name: DITSHWANELO — Botswana's human rights centre, gives free advice on civil matters, and sat on the negotiating team the Kalahari communities mandated
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: DITSHWANELO — Setswana for “rights” — the Botswana Centre for Human Rights, founded in 1993 by Alice Mogwe, and the first non-state body in this country's entry list: everything else here is a tribunal, a land board or a registry. It offers free advice on civil judicial matters, supports San communities, and states that it deliberately takes the issues least supported by others. THE PRECEDENT THAT MATTERS FOR ANY COMMUNITY FACING RELOCATION: when the government moved to relocate residents of the Central Kalahari Game Reserve, the First People of the Kalahari mandated a negotiating team — community representatives, FPK, a regional indigenous peoples' network, DITSHWANELO and the church council — to deal with government on their behalf, from 1996. That is the same instrument Ghana's mining communities used: a written community mandate naming who speaks for you. AND THE LESSON IS WHAT HAPPENED NEXT: the negotiations collapsed when government refused to move, and the residents then went to court — 244 former CKGR residents mounted a legal challenge in 2002, and in 2006 the High Court at Lobatse ruled the eviction from their ancestral land unlawful, and the refusal of permits to return unconstitutional. Negotiation and litigation are sequential, not alternative; the negotiating record is what makes the later case. DITSHWANELO is the secretariat of the CKGR NGO Coalition and of the UPR NGO working group, so it is also the route into Botswana's reporting to international human rights bodies — useful when domestic remedies stall. Private Bag 00416, Gaborone. WHO IT SUITS: Botswana communities facing relocation, loss of land access or discrimination in access to justice; San communities in particular. CAVEATS: a human rights advocacy organisation offering free civil advice, not a dedicated environmental or land law firm; its published priorities are broad; and the CKGR litigation itself was carried by outside counsel and an international campaigning organisation, not by DITSHWANELO. FIRST PEOPLE OF THE KALAHARI, the community's own body that mandated the negotiating team, was founded in 1991, registered in 1992, officially recognised in 1993, received an international award in 2005 — and had dissolved as an organisation by 2013, so it is not a door that can be knocked on today. WHAT IT ACTUALLY PROVIDES, LISTED: free PARALEGAL COUNSELLING; a Domestic Workers Association giving legal and mediation assistance in labour matters; awareness-raising through workshops, school lectures and an annual human rights film festival in Gaborone; and accountability work that includes monitoring state actions and submitting SHADOW REPORTS to the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and to UN Special Procedures and the Universal Periodic Review. A shadow report is a route a community can feed into without a lawyer or a filing fee — ask DITSHWANELO when the next Botswana review cycle is and what evidence it needs. It states that it deliberately focuses on issues least supported by others, including ex-Botswana miners who worked in apartheid-era gold mines and domestic workers, and it works in partnership with Botswanan organisations on gender equality, freedom of expression and information, children and youth, and indigenous peoples. It is the secretariat of the Central Kalahari Game Reserve NGO Coalition, the UPR NGO Working Group, and a southern African civil society solidarity coalition covering Zimbabwe, Eswatini, human rights defenders and migration. For regional strategic litigation, the Southern Africa Litigation Centre is already recorded in this file.

trackers.name: Mauritian Wildlife Foundation (MWF)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the only Mauritian NGO working solely on conservation of the island's endemic plants and animals, founded in 1984 and operating under a memorandum of agreement with government since 1994. Beyond species work it holds and manages land: it runs hands-on restoration on the Mauritian mainland, the offshore islets and Rodrigues, and manages nature reserves including Île aux Aigrettes and Grande Montagne. An IUCN member and BirdLife International partner. USE IT: as the body in Mauritius with the standing and the field capacity to take on a site and actually manage it, and as a partner if land you are trying to protect needs an institution behind it. Note what it is not: MWF is a conservation manager working closely with government, not a campaigning or litigating organisation, so it is the wrong door for opposing a project and the right one for securing what survives.

trackers.name: Companies & Business Registration (CBRD)
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Data Protection Office (Mauritius)
trackers.desc: Data Protection Office (Mauritius) — Mauritius’s independent data-protection / information commissioner, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Mauritius e-Procurement
trackers.desc: Mauritius' public e-procurement system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Mauritius, and for how much.

trackers.name: National Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Mauritius, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Mauritius
trackers.desc: Official judgment search of the Supreme Court of Mauritius, browsable by year. · Find here: the judgment search of the Supreme Court of Mauritius.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: Environment and Land Use Appeal Tribunal — one forum for six Acts
trackers.desc: A SINGLE SPECIALIST TRIBUNAL COVERS MOST OF WHAT A DEVELOPMENT TOUCHES. The Environment and Land Use Appeal Tribunal hears appeals under the Act's listed relevant Acts: the Building Act, the Environment Protection Act, the Local Government Act, the Morcellement Act (land subdivision), the Town and Country Planning Act, and any other Act prescribed. A development is usually challengeable under more than one of those, and they all go to the same forum — so identify every relevant Act before choosing a ground. The Tribunal comprises a Chairperson, Vice-chairperson and members, may include an appointed expert under section 3(4), and may sit in divisions. ‘Party’ in proceedings before it expressly includes the State. THE HONEST PICTURE, from the Tribunal's own chair at an Aarhus Convention task force: after the AHRIM judgment, in practice the only recourse objectors have is judicial review of the local authority's decision — a long and costly process — with objectors, often immediate neighbours or environmental NGOs, constrained by the technicality of judicial review. Plan for that, and see the Eco-Sud entry for the standing position.

trackers.name: Eco-Sud (JCPC 2023-0070) — Privy Council authority for liberal standing
trackers.desc: THE CASE TO CITE ON STANDING. The Minister granted an EIA licence under section 23 of the Environment Protection Act 2002 for a residential development on two plots close to a designated Ramsar wetland. The NGO Eco-Sud appealed, and the Tribunal held it lacked standing under section 54(2) — not aggrieved, no undue prejudice. The Supreme Court of Mauritius allowed Eco-Sud's appeal, holding that test too restrictive and that environmental appeals require a more liberal approach to standing, following Walton v The Scottish Ministers [2012] UKSC 44 — and the Privy Council firmly rejected the Minister's appeal, taking a purposive approach to statutory construction. THE REASONING TO QUOTE: the Board accepted the purpose of the standing rule was to stop ‘busybodies interfering in things which do not concern them’, but held it ‘is to be understood within the larger purpose of the EPA 2002 which remains the protection of the environment’. A restrictive standing provision read in light of the statute's protective purpose — now Privy Council authority, binding in Mauritius and persuasive across other JCPC jurisdictions, several of which appear in this map. Note section 2 of the EPA, a general duty of care on the citizens of Mauritius, in force without amendment. BUT CHECK THE CURRENT TEXT: Act No. 7 of 2020 added further criteria qualifying who may appeal against the Minister — older commentary may be out of date. Mauritius has been a Ramsar party since 2002; appeals reach the JCPC under section 81 of the Constitution.

trackers.name: Eco-Sud — won the Privy Council case that lets Mauritian citizens challenge an EIA licence without proving personal injury
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Mauritian environmental NGO whose 2018 challenge to an EIA licence granted for a hotel in a sensitive zone produced the single most useful precedent on this island. THE POINT OF LAW, WHICH DECIDES WHETHER YOU CAN FIGHT AT ALL: the Environment Tribunal applied a locus standi test — requiring the challenger to show it was personally injured and would suffer undue personal prejudice — and rejected the case on that basis. The Supreme Court held that the interpretation of standing must be widened because the environment is everyone's concern, and the Privy Council confirmed it: you cannot be required to claim a personal impact when challenging a matter concerning the environment and the benefits nature provides to all living things. If someone tells your group it has no standing to contest a licence in Mauritius, that is now wrong, and this is the case to cite. WHO IT SUITS: Mauritian residents, associations and collectives wanting to challenge an environmental clearance or EIA licence, especially in coastal and wetland zones. CAVEATS: winning standing is not winning the case — it opens the door to the Environment and Land Use Appeal Tribunal, and campaigners note that legislation has been repeatedly amended since 2016 to make legal contestation harder; Eco-Sud is an NGO, not a law firm, and litigation there required years and instructed counsel.

trackers.name: Platform Moris Lanvironnman — a coalition of about fifteen Mauritian NGOs that takes apart developers' EIA reports in public, at length
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: PML, created in December 2009, bringing together around fifteen Mauritian NGOs and committed individuals around an environmental charter, formed so that separate campaigns could coordinate, share information and back each other. WHAT IT ACTUALLY PRODUCES, and it is the most transferable habit in this entry: detailed public commentary on developers' Environmental Impact Assessment reports, filed with the environment ministry and then published — in one case a 150-page critique, including preliminary expert opinions, of an EIA that had been written in six very short weeks, together with a French-language summary so residents could read it. It has done the same for oil bunkering EIAs in the port and for an industrial battery anode facility near an estuary, arguing that report did not comply with the relevant environmental legislation. THE ARGUMENTS IT MAKES ARE THE ONES TO REUSE: that a project claiming only a small share of buildings will be “green” is masking that over 80 per cent of a site's terrestrial area — forest and other ecosystems — would be destroyed; that a 30-metre buffer around wetlands is derisory relative to their function; and that calling a forest “unusable” reveals ignorance of its ecological, economic and social role. ITS OWN STRATEGIC ADVICE, from a spokesperson: civil society must mobilise experts AND a legal team from the start — contestations fail either because the odds are legally stacked or because the objectors' files are not well enough built, or both. It also notes a win: the contestation of one project was successful despite the promoters and government having a head start. WHO IT SUITS: Mauritian communities and collectives facing smart-city, hotel, marina or industrial projects, especially on the coast. CAVEATS: a coalition and information-sharing platform, not a legal service or a fund; its site is a modest association page and much of its output appears via national press; and for the standing point that makes contestation possible, the Eco-Sud entry is the companion.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? NO — this is project-to-project country. Natural Justice's 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, with additional staff in Antananarivo, Botswana and Guinea; elsewhere it works across African countries on a project-to-project basis. So you are asking them to take on a project, not walking into an office — approach with a defined case and expect that answer to depend on their current programme. Its team page does list staff and fellows beyond the hub countries. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs.
