HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. trackers.name: Cour des comptes
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Burkina Faso, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: data.gov.bf
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Burkina Faso.

trackers.name: Burkina Faso — Maison de l’Entreprise (eCreation / CEFORE)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the MEBF one-stop CEFORE & eCreation online platform handle company creation, modification & RCCM registration, Burkina Faso. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: Groupement de Gestion Forestière — the only village-level concessionaire
trackers.desc: THERE IS NO ALTERNATIVE VEHICLE. FAO's account of the Projet Aménagement des Forêts Naturelles states that the Groupement Villageois de Gestion Forestière (GGF), sponsored by a Commission villageoise de gestion de terroir or not, is the only concessionaire considered by the State at village scale for forest management — and that groupements can in some cases cover several villages, so a multi-village grouping is expressly possible. The model rests on three stated foundations: participation of the populations (erected as the base principle), economic sustainability and ecological sustainability. THE FUND BEHIND IT: the Fonds d'Aménagement Forestier, established 1987 to relay external financing with a permanent domestic system. Government texts later officially recognised the forest fund and extended it to all forest products across the whole territory — recorded as reducing unfair competition between products from managed and unmanaged zones. That competition problem is the one to understand: without the extension, wood from unmanaged forest undercut wood from managed forest, penalising exactly the communities doing the management work.

trackers.name: Five recognised access routes — and hunting zones put you on equal footing
trackers.desc: THE NATIONAL PROSPECTIVE DOCUMENT LISTS FIVE WAYS COMMUNITIES LAWFULLY ACCESS FOREST RESOURCES: (1) droits d'usage — traditional gathering rights, in both classed and protected forest; (2) concessions to groupements de gestion forestière through management plans, authorising commercial valorisation; (3) partnership agreements between neighbouring populations and hunting-zone concessionaires; (4) village management of hunting zones, which makes rural communities concessionaires on the same footing as private operators; and (5) commercial exploitation in unmanaged zones. Route 4 is the strongest — equal legal footing with commercial operators is rare. HOW A chantier d'aménagement forestier is built, per its cahier des charges: a social component (the UGGF), a conseil de gestion, a comité de contrôle interne, a commission de contrôle, a direction technique and the Fonds d'Aménagement Forestier. NOTE THERE ARE TWO SEPARATE CONTROL BODIES — internal committee and control commission — so where a CAF is failing, those are the named internal remedies before anything external. DOCUMENTS YOU CAN ASK FOR: an annual work plan based on expected receipts and quarterly physical and financial progress reports. BUT CHECK IT EXISTS: newer CAFs in the Centre-Nord were recorded as having neither a technical direction nor monitors yet — the structure on paper is not always the structure on the ground. A noted tension: foresters sometimes repress herders in the forests.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: ORCADE — the first Burkinabè NGO to take on the mining sector, and it explains the mining code to the councillors who have to apply it
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an organisation created in 2001 after a rights-based advocacy workshop in Ghana persuaded participants to set up bodies at home to accompany communities through rights-based advocacy against mining companies. It was the first NGO in Burkina Faso to work on the mining sector and is generally treated as the lead one. WHAT IT DOES THAT A VILLAGE CAN USE: it investigates the causes of conflict between mining companies and neighbouring communities, and its programme staff report that compensation for people who lost the assets and livelihoods taken for mining operations is the recurring grievance — so its research is the documentary base for a compensation claim. It has published a state-of-play study on artisanal and small-scale mining and an assessment of how the new mining code is being implemented. AND THE PART THAT IS UNUSUAL AND WORTH ASKING FOR: ORCADE runs workshops for local elected officials on the mining code and its implementing decrees, including the fund financed by levies on mining companies and placed at the disposal of communes — because a mayor who does not know the fund exists cannot claim it for your village. If your council is the body that should be defending you and does not understand the instrument, this is who trains it. ORCADE sits on the steering committee of the extractive industries transparency initiative in Burkina Faso, leads its civil society capacity-building working group, and has held the national chair of Publish What You Pay. 09 BP 675 Ouagadougou 09; secretariat@orcade.org. WHO IT SUITS: communities beside industrial or artisanal gold operations, and local councils in mining communes. CAVEATS: advocacy, research and training — not litigation, and no legal service or intake route was found; the security situation across much of Burkina Faso constrains field access, and published contact numbers vary between listings.

trackers.name: MBDHP — free legal clinics run by a human rights movement with sections in all 45 provinces and committees down to village level
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Mouvement Burkinabè des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples, founded in February 1989, and structurally the most far-reaching organisation in this country's entry list: sections in all 45 provinces, around a hundred sub-sections at department level, and sectoral and VILLAGE committees as a third tier. That structure is the point — in a country where the practical barriers to justice are ignorance, poverty, social and cultural obstacles and an under-resourced justice ministry, an organisation with a committee in the village is reachable in a way a Ouagadougou office is not. WHAT IT PROVIDES: it operates boutiques de droit — legal clinics — in a number of localities including Ouagadougou, Kongoussi, Tenkodogo, Dédougou, Banfora and Yako, and it is the UN refugee agency's partner for legal assistance in the country. ITS SERVICES ARE STATED TO BE FREE. WHAT TO KNOW BEFORE YOU GO: the documented legal-aid partnership is framed around deprivation of liberty and the situation of displaced and stateless people rather than land or environmental cases, so ask directly whether the local section will take a land dispute or a compensation claim — the structure is there, the mandate is broad (promoting and protecting citizens' rights and freedoms), but the advertised specialism is not land. Burkina Faso also maintains a state fonds d'aide juridique for the poor, which civil society including MBDHP has pressed to make accessible; ask about it if a case needs filing fees. WHO IT SUITS: Burkinabè households and communities — including in mining and displacement-affected areas — who need a lawyer and cannot pay for one. CAVEATS: a general human rights movement, not an environmental or land law specialist — for mining-sector work Burkina Faso's ORCADE entry is the complement; and the security situation across much of the country constrains what any organisation can reach.

trackers.name: FIAN Burkina Faso — took the failures of the rural land law to the UN review, and documents the attestation route smallholders are supposed to use
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Burkinabè section of the international right-to-food organisation, working on land and food rights, which has submitted evidence to the United Nations Universal Periodic Review on the difficulties of securing rural land possession in Burkina Faso — taking a domestic implementation failure to an international forum is a route most communities do not know exists, and this is an organisation that has used it. THE INSTRUMENT IT DOCUMENTS, WHICH ANY BURKINABÈ FARMER SHOULD ASK ABOUT: under the rural land law of 2009 customary rights are officially recognised and can be formalised through an Attestation de Possession Foncière Rurale (APFR), issued by the rural land service of your own commune, land management having been transferred to the rural communes. Any rural landholder may request recognition of their possession, individually OR COLLECTIVELY; the attestation passes by inheritance and may be transferred, with transfers entered in the commune's rural land transactions register. Loans of land can also be registered — a verbal loan is declared to the village land commission and written down on a form supplied by the commune, which is the protection for someone farming land they do not own. Communities may also adopt local land charters, validated by deliberation of the municipal council. WHAT FIAN SAYS IS WRONG, and it is what to check before relying on any of it: implementation requires rural land services staffed and equipped in every commune, and the material, financial and human means committed have been very weak, so the law is only partly applied. Reporting from communes near the capital bears that out — one had issued no attestations at all and was instead selling amicable transfer deeds by the hectare, another applied the law in only nine of its 26 villages. Ask whether your commune has a functioning rural land service before assuming the route is open. WHO IT SUITS: Burkinabè smallholders, women and collective landholders seeking documented possession, and communities losing land to real-estate expansion. CAVEATS: an advocacy and documentation organisation, not a law firm or a land agency; the security situation constrains fieldwork across much of the country; for mining-affected communities Burkina's ORCADE entry is the other route, and for free legal help its MBDHP entry.

trackers.name: NATUDEV and Burkina Faso's APACs — 53,858 community-conserved sites identified, 951 documented, and the documentation is the defence
trackers.desc: WHAT TO DOCUMENT, AND WHY IT COSTS ALMOST NOTHING: an APAC — aire ou territoire du patrimoine autochtone et communautaire, a “territory of life” — is land a community ALREADY conserves by custom: village forests, sacred woods, sacred water points, pastoral areas. You are not buying, leasing or transferring anything; you are getting what you already protect INVENTORIED, MAPPED AND WRITTEN DOWN so it can be defended when someone else wants it. THE ORGANISATION: Association Nature et Développement (NATUDEV) started the APAC dynamic in Burkina Faso in 2016 and is described as the reference NGO for it; the Burkina section of the global APAC consortium supports communities through inventories, mapping, studies, and the installation of boundary signage and PERIMETER FIREBREAK TRACKS to reduce bush-fire risk. THE SCALE, WHICH IS THE ARGUMENT TO PUT IN FRONT OF ANY AUTHORITY: 53,858 sites identified covering 721,527.98 hectares, of which 951 are documented — 69 village forests, 89 communal pastoral spaces, 121 sacred water points and 672 sacred woods. Named examples include the Kalwaka sacred wood (82 ha) in Centre-Ouest and the village conservation zones of Sadpenga (226 ha) and Saro (861 ha). THE THREATS IT IS AGAINST are the ones this file records everywhere: artisanal gold mining, real-estate promotion, extensive agriculture, charcoal burning, poaching and bush fires. NATUDEV has also commissioned a LEGAL STUDY on APACs to support advocacy for their formal legal recognition — which is the honest state of play. WHO IT SUITS: Burkinabè villages with a sacred wood, pasture or water point under pressure, and communities anywhere wanting a no-cost first step toward defending customary conservation. CAVEATS: APAC STATUS IS NOT YET A LEGAL TITLE IN BURKINA FASO — recognition is being advocated for, so documentation gives you evidence and visibility rather than enforceable ownership; and the security situation limits fieldwork in much of the country. For an attestation of possession, Burkina's FIAN entry; for mining communities, ORCADE; for free legal help, MBDHP.

trackers.name: Burkina Faso's Fonds d'Assistance Judiciaire — 27 commissions in the high courts, an UNSTAMPED written request, and you may apply before, during OR AFTER the trial
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY: under décret n°2016-185/PRES/PM/MJDHPC/MINEFID of 11 April 2016, assistance judiciaire is the benefit granted to people who, because their resources are insufficient, cannot exercise their rights in court — EITHER AS CLAIMANT OR AS DEFENDANT; the FONDS D'ASSISTANCE JUDICIAIRE (FAJ), a public establishment created in 2016, pays. Burkinabè law makes justice itself free — what costs money is the advocate, the bailiff and the expert, and that is exactly what the FAJ covers. THE PROCEDURE, STATED EXACTLY, AND IT IS THE CLEAREST IN THIS FILE: address a WRITTEN, UNSTAMPED request (demande écrite non timbrée) to the president of the commission d'assistance judiciaire installed at the Tribunal de Grande Instance OF YOUR PLACE OF RESIDENCE. Unstamped means you do not need to buy a fiscal stamp to ask for help — the commonest way a poor applicant is turned back at a counter. AND THE TIMING RULE IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE HERE: the request may be made BEFORE, DURING OR AFTER the trial — the last covering enforcement measures. So a judgment you cannot afford to ENFORCE is still within reach; most people assume the moment has passed. WHAT YOU GET: if TOTAL, all costs occasioned by the trial are covered, including the entirety of advocate's fees; if PARTIAL, the decision fixes the state's contributory share. WHO QUALIFIES: physical persons of Burkinabè OR FOREIGN nationality (subject to reciprocity), with certain categories entitled as of right on request — including children who are victims of trafficking or in conflict with the law, unassisted children and children of indigent parents, and victims of attacks on life or bodily integrity including acts of torture by state agents in the exercise of their functions. COVERAGE: the Fund is operational through 27 commissions d'assistance judiciaire sitting at the seats of the Tribunaux de Grande Instance across the territory, and it trains civil society organisations on the mechanism precisely because they are in direct contact with people on the ground. WHO IT SUITS: Burkinabè and foreign residents who cannot pay an advocate, bailiff or expert in a land, compensation or mining dispute. CAVEATS: A STATE FUND with an indigence assessment, and the security situation restricts access to several regions. For mining communities, Burkina's ORCADE entry; for free legal clinics, MBDHP; for attestations of rural possession, FIAN; for community-conserved areas, NATUDEV.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? STAFF, NOT A HUB — Antananarivo. The 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar; here there are additional staff, so expect a smaller presence and a longer route into casework. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: High Constitutional Court of Madagascar
trackers.desc: High Constitutional Court of Madagascar — supreme court (Madagascar).

trackers.name: EDBM – Guichet Unique
trackers.desc: National — company registration one-stop (RCS); publishes company constitution notices, Madagascar. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Madagascar — Ministère de l’Économie et des Finances
trackers.desc: National budget authority; coordinates the preparation & execution of the State budget and publishes public-finance information, Madagascar. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Madagascar.

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: Madagasikara Voakajy — a Malagasy organisation that is now the legal manager of seven protected areas, with communities in the governance
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Malagasy conservation organisation, founded 2005, that creates protected areas with communities and then holds the legal mandate to manage them. In 2025 the environment ministry formally entrusted it with seven protected areas — Mangabe-Ranomena-Sahasarotra, Mahialambo, Ampanangandehibe-Behasina, Analalava, Analabe-Betanatanana, Ambatofotsy and Ampotaka — signed by the Director General of Environmental Governance with the organisation's executive director. Sixteen protected area managers had their mandates renewed at the same ceremony after seven years without official recognition, which tells you how long the paperwork can stall and why an established delegate matters. WHY THIS IS THE MALAGASY VERSION OF BUYING LAND: nobody purchases forest here — protection runs through management transfer to a community body, the Vondron'Olona Ifotony or VOI, with an organisation like this one holding the delegated management contract and building the VOI's capacity to govern the resource. Its stated programme is strengthening VOI governance, restoration inside protected areas and management transfer zones through agroforestry and native species, five village nurseries producing about 15,000 seedlings each a year run with ten VOI in the Moramanga district, and income-generating activities so that conservation pays. WHO IT SUITS: communities in or beside forest who want a management transfer secured and defended, particularly around Moramanga, Bobaomby and the named protected areas. CAVEATS: this is a species-led conservation organisation — the case that wins its attention is endemic biodiversity, not the injustice of a project; it names degradation of the Mangabe protected area and damage to restoration sites by incomers among its own challenges; and no intake route, application form or fee information was found.

trackers.name: Fondation Tany Meva — a Malagasy foundation whose entire purpose is funding community environmental projects, about 1,850 of them so far
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: created in 1996 and recognised as being of public utility, Tany Meva is the first Malagasy environmental foundation and one built specifically for communities — its stated mission is to mobilise and manage funds for local initiatives to protect and sustainably manage natural resources, with communities at the centre of its financing. WHAT IT HAS ACTUALLY PAID OUT: by its thirtieth anniversary it reported more than US$20 million in grants across roughly 1,850 local projects throughout Madagascar, reaching over 415,000 households, with supported projects covering more than a million hectares of land and over 200,000 hectares of marine area managed or conserved, more than 10,000 hectares reforested or restored, and 20,000 hectares of forest under community management through natural resource management transfers (TGRN) — the Malagasy instrument by which a community takes over management of forest, which this file records elsewhere. WHAT IT FUNDS: biodiversity conservation and natural resource management, forest restoration and reforestation, ecotourism, climate adaptation, renewable energy and energy efficiency, environmental education, and income-generating activities that take the pressure off the resource — the last is the category most community groups underuse. HOW THE MONEY REACHES YOU NOW: under its 2023-2027 strategic plan it works through landscape partnerships, selecting established support organisations to work alongside local community organisations, prepare them for autonomy and keep the project running after the grant ends — for example four community projects around the Ankarafantsika protected area and three around Anjozorobe funded for three to five years. It has also signed agreements covering mangrove degradation in Boeny and the management of REDD+ carbon revenues with the environment ministry. WHO IT SUITS: Malagasy community organisations — including VOI holding a management transfer — that need money for the work rather than a lawyer for the fight. CAVEATS: a grant-maker for conservation and livelihoods, not a defence fund — nothing here pays for litigation or for opposing a project; financing now flows through selected landscape partners in named regions rather than by open national application, so ask which partner covers your area; and its stated alignment is with public policy, though it says it decides autonomously.

trackers.name: Collectif TANY — raises money specifically to pay for the legal defence of Malagasy farmers facing land grabs and prosecution
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Collectif pour la Défense des Terres Malgaches (TANY), a non-profit of Malagasy-origin members formed to oppose the dispossession of Malagasy citizens and farmers. Its stated activities are precise and unusual: collecting information on land-grab cases; sending missions into the field to conduct investigations and interviews; and the LEGAL DEFENCE of farmers or activists imprisoned or prosecuted. It runs public fundraising campaigns for named struggles — including one to fund legal assistance to communities in the Ihorombe region affected by land grabbing by a foreign agri-company. Money raised abroad to pay a specific community's lawyer is a resource almost nothing else in this file provides. THE FACT IT KEEPS PUTTING IN FRONT OF GOVERNMENT, which every Malagasy household should know: the great majority of Malagasy live on their land WITHOUT a land title, and more than 1,000 of Madagascar's 1,693 communes have no guichet foncier — the communal land desk that alone can issue a certificat foncier. Obtaining a title takes much time and much money. So TANY argues for strengthening in law the recognition of the legitimate rights of local communities EVEN WHERE THEY HOLD NEITHER TITLE NOR CERTIFICATE, legalising the rights of occupants of land with obsolete status, and halting allocations to investors by long lease or concession. It has also opposed provisions allowing foreigners to own titled land and criticised the state investment board for accelerating investors' paperwork while ordinary families queue. WHO IT SUITS: Malagasy farming communities facing land grabs, long leases or prosecution for defending their land. CAVEATS: ITS MEMBERS AND OFFICERS ARE BASED IN FRANCE — this is an advocacy and support collective working with partner farmer associations in Madagascar, not a walk-in office or a law firm; it funds and accompanies defence rather than conducting it. For protected-area management transfers, Madagascar's Voakajy entry; for community grants, Tany Meva.

trackers.name: Buying hectares by the acre — the fund that paid for 200 ha at Ankarabolava-Agnakatrika, and how a local partner gets it
trackers.desc: WHERE THE PURCHASE MONEY COMES FROM: a UK-based land-purchase trust runs a “Buy an Acre” programme that funds LAND ACQUISITION by LOCAL partner organisations — it does not buy or hold land itself — the in-country partner buys, and the partner holds the title. WHAT IT HAS PAID FOR IN MADAGASCAR: the expansion of the Ankarabolava-Agnakatrika forest by 200 hectares, reported as home to over 50 threatened species including a critically endangered lemur, secured by a botanical garden's Madagascar programme. A SECOND WORKED EXAMPLE, because it shows how long this takes: in South Africa a renosterveld conservation trust secured a 497-hectare property — the culmination of SIXTEEN YEARS OF NEGOTIATIONS — with the fund paying for 150 hectares of that purchase. Note what that means in practice: the fund covered under a third of the parcel, so the local organisation had to raise the rest — external purchase money is usually a CONTRIBUTION toward a deal you are already assembling, not the whole price. Reported programme-wide output includes protection of 152,205 hectares of priority land in a single reporting period, nearly half of it solely funded by the trust. HOW TO USE THIS: identify the parcel, get a local organisation with legal personality to be the buyer and future titleholder, price it, then approach acre-based funders for a share — and expect the negotiation with the seller to outlast the fundraising. WHO IT SUITS: Malagasy conservation organisations and community partners with a specific parcel in view and no capital, and organisations elsewhere studying how purchase money is actually assembled. CAVEATS: THIS IS A FOREIGN FUNDER WITH ITS OWN PRIORITIES — it funds land of high biodiversity value, so it will not pay for a parcel that matters to you for other reasons; it works through vetted partner organisations rather than with individuals or unregistered groups; and title rests with the partner, not automatically with neighbouring communities. For Malagasy community grants see the Tany Meva entry, for protected-area management transfers Voakajy, and for legal defence funding Collectif TANY.

trackers.name: Madagascar's land-law clinics — five cliniques de droit foncier in five regions, run with four Malagasy NGOs, plus Trano Aro Zo at Ihosy since 2011
trackers.desc: WHERE TO WALK IN: FIVE CLINIQUES DE DROIT FONCIER — land-law clinics — have been set up in five regions, IN COLLABORATION WITH FOUR MALAGASY NGOs, under a justice-governance programme supported by the UN development programme and USAID. Their stated purpose is prevention of land conflicts, awareness-raising on land legislation, civic education of the population, and DECONGESTING THE CIVIL COURTS — that is, resolving land disputes before they become cases. A SECOND, OLDER CLINIC WITH A NAME TO ASK FOR: at IHOSY the clinic Trano Aro Zo, established with European Union support in 2011 and run by a Malagasy NGO, provides advice, orientation, CONCILIATION and accompaniment of vulnerable people in protecting their rights. Conciliation and accompaniment are the two words to listen for: someone who will sit with you through the procedure is worth more in Madagascar than advice alone, because the file this country records elsewhere is that most communes have no land desk at all. WHAT ELSE THE SAME PROGRAMME PUT IN PLACE, because it changes what a court visit looks like: standardised JUSTICE INFORMATION KIOSKS at first-instance courts, equipment for the courts of five regions, renovation of eight first-instance courts in the south, and civil and commercial training for 51 magistrates and 141 court clerks. A judge quoted in that work describes the current context as marked by RECURRENT LAND DISPUTES, and notes the difficulty caused by texts issued without implementing decrees — the same gap this file records across the region. Madagascar has also launched a free online case-law platform at the justice ministry. WHO IT SUITS: Malagasy households and communities with a land dispute, boundary problem or inheritance claim, especially in the five programme regions and around Ihosy. CAVEATS: NO STANDALONE SITE FOR THE CLINICS — this entry points at the programme's published account; the clinics are donor-funded and programme-bound, so ask whether yours is still operating and which NGO runs it. They conciliate and orient rather than litigate. For legal-defence fundraising, Madagascar's Collectif TANY entry; for community grants, Tany Meva; for protected-area transfers, Voakajy.

trackers.name: Action des Chrétiens Activistes des Droits de l'Homme à Shabunda (ACADHOSHA)
trackers.desc: Action des Chrétiens Activistes des Droits de L’Homme a Shabunda (ACADHOSHA) is a Congolese civil society organisation specialising in human rights, justice, and the governance of natural resources. For over ten years, ACADHOSHA has been providing administrative and legal support to local communities and indigenous peoples who are often victims of the exploitation of natural resources.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes
trackers.desc: National — supreme audit institution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in DRC (Congo).

trackers.name: DR Congo — Guichet Unique de Création d’Entreprise (GUCE)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the GUCE one-stop window in Kinshasa centralises company name verification, registration & payment, Democratic Republic of the Congo. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: ITIE-RDC (EITI DR Congo)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and licences in DR Congo.

trackers.name: DRC EITI Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: Réseau CREF — has secured perpetual community forest titles over 223,000 hectares in North Kivu, and will walk a community through the same process
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a platform of about thirty environmental NGOs working in North Kivu since 2003, whose measurable output is the thing itself — more than 223,000 hectares secured for communities under perpetual community forest concession titles, with further applications sitting on the Governor's desk for signature. IN CONGOLESE LAW THIS IS THE CLOSEST THING TO BUYING YOUR LAND: article 22 of the 2002 forest code lets a forest community apply for a concession over forest it already holds by custom, and the resulting Concession Forestière des Communautés Locales is granted free of charge and in perpetuity by provincial decree. It is not a purchase and not a lease; it is recognition, and it converts customary forest into a title an outsider cannot be allocated over. WHY YOU NEED AN ORGANISATION AND NOT JUST THE LAW: the application requires a participatory map of the forest terroir agreed with neighbouring communities, proof of who is customarily entitled to act for the community, a local administrative enquiry on the ground, and afterwards a simple management plan approved locally — which is why every concession granted in the country so far has been supported by an NGO or civil society partner, communities lacking the money and technical knowledge to complete it alone. Réseau CREF works inside the Forêts d'Avenir consortium with Rainforest Foundation UK and Congolese partners including PREPPYG, APEM, CAGDFT and GASHE; two Lubero communities it supported began in 2021, received their titles in early 2024 and had their management plans approved in March 2025 despite an extremely precarious security situation. WHO IT SUITS: forest communities and indigenous peoples in North Kivu, and — through the consortium partners — Équateur, Mai-Ndombe, Maniema, Tshopo, Tshuapa and Kwilu. CAVEATS: the process is slow, intermediary-heavy and, as researchers warn, can be captured — without supervision a community concession can exclude vulnerable groups or sharpen local tensions, so insist on who is named as customarily entitled before the file is lodged. Areas are capped and land hunger in North Kivu means the forest available per person can be a fraction of a hectare. THE INSTRUMENT'S NATIONAL TERMS, WHICH ARE THE BEST IN THE REGION AND WORTH QUOTING BACK AT ANY OFFICIAL: community forestry in DR Congo is governed by the Forest Code and decree n°14/018 of 2 August 2014, which sets the conditions and procedure by which a LOCAL COMMUNITY acquires a forest concession over forests it regularly possesses BY CUSTOM — and the defining features are that the concession is MULTI-USE, granted FREE OF CHARGE, and PERPETUAL. Free and perpetual is a combination no other route in this file offers: there is no fee to find and no renewal date at which someone can decline. Since 2016 the DRC has adopted a National Strategy on Community Forestry. WHAT THAT HAS PRODUCED IN PRACTICE, and the numbers are the argument for starting a file: one programme reports 17 community forests created across Equateur, Maniema and North-Kivu provinces, covering 154,000 hectares and serving over 25,000 people; an earlier phase set up nine pilot sites in Equateur and North-Kivu. A NAMED WORKED EXAMPLE TO POINT AT: in September 2018 the community of Ilinga in Equateur — whose name means “Unity” — received its official community forest title over 3,393 hectares it had traditionally owned and managed for generations, granted in perpetuity, supported by a local Congolese NGO within a consortium of Congolese and international organisations. Ask which consortium organisation covers your province before assembling a file — the work is organised by province and by partner, not nationally. THE CEILING AND THE PROTECTION, THE TWO NUMBERS THIS ENTRY LACKED: a concession forestière des communautés locales may be granted UP TO 50,000 HECTARES per local community — ten times the Cameroonian community-forest ceiling recorded in this file — and it is attributed FREE OF CHARGE AND IN PERPETUITY, which together make it the strongest community land hold in the Congo Basin. If you are choosing between instruments across a border, the CFCL is the one that does not expire and does not have to be renewed. WHAT TO PUT IN THE APPLICATION FILE, BECAUSE THE FILE IS WHERE THESE FAIL: the request goes through the customary chief on behalf of the community, with the community's boundaries and its neighbours' agreement established BEFORE submission — the same boundary-first rule this file records for Cameroon, Senegal and Eswatini. Settle the boundary with your neighbours first; a contested edge is what stalls a file for years.

trackers.name: IBGDH, Kolwezi — the lawyers who cite Annexe XVIII at mining relocations, and the text every displaced Congolese household should quote
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Initiative pour la Bonne Gouvernance et les Droits Humains (IBGDH), an ASBL based at Kolwezi in Lualaba — the centre of the world's cobalt supply — led by a practising lawyer, working across Lualaba in particular and DR Congo generally on mining-related displacement and pollution. THE INSTRUMENT IT USES, AND THE ONE TO NAME IN ANY LETTER: Annexe XVIII of the Mining Regulation, which sets out the stages of relocation, the rights of each party and the obligations of the institutions involved. IBGDH's reading of its article 18 is the sentence to quote: whatever criteria and scale are agreed, the loss of housing, of community infrastructure and of rights must be covered. It publicly held that a Chinese-owned mining company breached Annexe XVIII and the provincial relocation edict in moving residents of a Kolwezi neighbourhood and a nearby village, and that the provincial government took part in forced evictions without guaranteeing communities their right of access to remedies, to dignified resettlement and to just and equitable compensation. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DELIVERS FOR RESIDENTS: public open days bringing affected communities together with the provincial land, planning and housing officials; documented demands to halt operations — including a call to stop a company's works at Kolwezi over air, water, soil and noise pollution affecting named neighbourhoods; and a joint report with an international human rights organisation on forced evictions in industrial cobalt and copper mines, presented at the national mining week, backed by reportedly more than 70,000 signatures against the evictions. It has demanded a presidential moratorium on all mining-related relocations and an independent inquiry. WHO IT SUITS: households and villages in the Congolese copper-cobalt belt facing relocation, house damage from blasting, loss of farmland or mine pollution. CAVEATS: an advocacy, documentation and legal-support organisation, not a compensation agent — note the province's own position that it is the CONCESSION HOLDER, not the state, that relocates, with the state only accompanying; for community forest concessions in the east, DR Congo's Réseau CREF entry is the other route.

trackers.name: DR Congo's Bureaux de Consultations Gratuites — free legal consultation at each bar, Monday to Friday 9h-16h, on production of an attestation d'indigence
trackers.desc: WHERE TO WALK IN: the BUREAUX DE CONSULTATIONS GRATUITES (BCG), run by the bar associations, which provide judicial assistance and legal advice to indigent people ON PRODUCTION OF AN ATTESTATION D'INDIGENCE. In Kinshasa two bars operate them and their coverage is published by commune: the Gombe BCG serves 14 communes — Gombe, Ngiri-Ngiri, Kasa-Vubu, Kalamu, Barumbu, Kinshasa, Selembao, Bumbu, Makala, Lingwala, Mont-Ngafula, Ngaliema, Bandalungwa and Kintambo — at avenue Kasa-Vubu n°87 at the Birmanie junction, Ngiri-Ngiri; the Matete BCG at n°1392 avenue Bakali, commune of Lemba. Consultations run every day MONDAY TO FRIDAY, 9h to 16h. Get the attestation d'indigence FIRST — as in Côte d'Ivoire, the poverty certificate is the document that opens the door, and turning up without it wastes the trip. Reported traffic gives a realistic sense of scale: one bureau received 85 people in a single month, 28 women and 57 men. THE INDEPENDENT ASSESSMENT, RECORDED BECAUSE IT SETS EXPECTATIONS: an evaluation for the EU justice reform programme found the BCG system globally EMBRYONIC, particularly in the western provinces — often a single bureau in the provincial capital, attached to the bar — too strictly built on mobilising TRAINEE ADVOCATES who are insufficiently supervised and supported, with no proactive strategy toward litigants. So expect a junior lawyer, expect the capital, and bring your own documents in order. WHO IT SUITS: Congolese city residents — above all in Kinshasa — needing free advice on an eviction, land or family matter. CAVEATS: ADVICE AND ASSISTANCE THROUGH THE BAR, NOT A CAMPAIGNING BODY, donor-supported and thin outside the main cities. For community forest concessions and the free perpetual CFCL route, DR Congo's Réseau CREF entry; for mining relocation in the copper-cobalt belt and Annexe XVIII, IBGDH.

trackers.name: South Sudan — Business Registry (Ministry of Justice / eServices)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the Business Registry under the Ministry of Justice & Constitutional Affairs registers companies & business names — with an official online Business Registration eServices portal for name search, application & certificates, South Sudan. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: South Sudan — Ministry of Finance & Planning (MoFP)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the MoFP prepares & executes the national budget, publishes budget speeches, execution & quarterly outturn reports and manages public financial management, South Sudan. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in South Sudan.

trackers.name: South Sudan — National Audit Chamber (NAC)
trackers.desc: National public-finance watchdog; the National Audit Chamber (headed by the Auditor General) audits the accounts of all public-sector institutions and reports to the Legislative Assembly, South Sudan.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: East African Court of Justice — it stopped a road across the Serengeti
trackers.desc: THIS COURT STOPPED A GOVERNMENT FROM BUILDING A ROAD. In African Network for Animal Welfare v Attorney General of the United Republic of Tanzania (Reference No. 9 of 2010, judgment 20 June 2014), the East African Court of Justice held Tanzania's proposed highway across the Serengeti National Park unlawful and issued an injunction restraining Tanzania from operationalising it. THE TREATY ARTICLES THAT DID THE WORK: article 5(3)(c) of the EAC Treaty — promotion of sustainable utilisation of natural resources and measures that would effectively protect the natural environment of the Partner States — and article 114(1)(a), which enjoins partner states to conserve, protect and manage the environment. THE HARMS PLEADED ARE A REUSABLE CHECKLIST: disrupted animal migration, fragmentation of habitats, loss of scenic and visual quality, deterioration of air quality, increased poaching, and surface water and soil pollution. NOTE THE SHAPE OF THE RELIEF: at para 78 the Court said its orders must be preventative, and that roads in the Serengeti should be used by wildlife, tourists and Park administrators and not the general public — a restriction on who may use a road is a narrower and more grantable order than an outright ban. The government's own report had conceded grave negative impacts. THREE THINGS MAKE THIS ROUTE UNUSUAL: (1) standing survived a full challenge — the objection on jurisdiction, limitation and form was overruled on 26 August 2011 and the appeal dismissed on 15 March 2012; (2) the applicant was not from the respondent state — ANAW is a pan-African charity that sued Tanzania without being Tanzanian, so an NGO based in one partner state can challenge another's project; and (3) this is a trade-and-integration court, not a specialist environmental one — the claim runs through treaty obligations between states. CONFIRM PARTNER-STATE STATUS BEFORE FILING: this state's EAC accession is relatively recent, and the Court's jurisdiction follows partner-state status. This entry does not assert current standing to file — verify it first.

trackers.name: SSHRDN — in South Sudan the resource is protection first: legal aid, medical and psycho-social support for people at risk for defending land
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST, AND WHY IT IS THIS RATHER THAN A CONSERVATION BODY: in South Sudan the binding problem is not that no one knows the land is being poisoned — it is that documenting it gets you arrested. The South Sudan Human Rights Defenders Network, registered with the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission under number 2284, is a coalition of organisations and individuals that provides rapid support to defenders at risk: legal aid, medical care and psycho-social services, plus training in risk assessment, security management and digital safety. It works with the Pan African Human Rights Defenders Network and other regional bodies. It published a report documenting at least 114 cases of censorship, harassment and arbitrary arrest of civil society actors and journalists over a three-year period, in a country whose 2024 national security law permits arrest without warrant. WHAT DOES EXIST ON THE ENVIRONMENT, so you know who to look for: the Sudd Environment Agency, formed in 2019 to work on oil pollution in Unity and Upper Nile states, which runs field assessments and community workshops and has led a consortium, the Environment and Climate Change Network, with three other South Sudanese organisations; and the Sudd Institute, which has published research on the health impacts of oil pollution. The Sudd Environment Agency's own account is that state security does not allow civil society or individuals to reach oil waste dumping sites or photograph them — which is exactly why the protection network comes first. WHO IT SUITS: South Sudanese community members, activists and journalists exposed to risk for challenging oil pollution, land allocation or displacement. CAVEATS: this is protection and legal aid for individuals at risk, NOT an organisation that will stop a project, and no land-defence or litigation service was found in this country. The environmental bodies named above had no verified public intake route, which is why they are described here rather than listed separately.

trackers.name: South Sudan Law Society and the Juba paralegal network — legal aid, paralegal training, and their own warning about institutional land grabbing
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the South Sudan Law Society (SSLS), a civil society organisation based in Juba running legal aid, community paralegal training, human rights awareness and capacity-building for legal professionals, and the author of a study on housing, land and property disputes in the country; alongside the community paralegal networks operating in Juba, including a Grassroots Women Network that mentors paralegals drawn mostly from community leaders, backed by a Norwegian aid organisation, and the South Sudan Land Alliance. WHAT THE PARALEGALS ARE TRAINED IN, which tells you what to ask for: alternative dispute resolution, the provisions of the 2009 Land Act, and evidence-gathering techniques to support lawyers handling land registration and dispute cases. WHY THE COUNTRY'S SITUATION MAKES THIS THE FIGHT: land grabs and expropriation typically increase after conflict, while land governance is in disarray and a new administration is still passing and implementing laws — and people who have not yet physically returned to stake their claim, especially widows, divorced women and orphans, are the ones who lose land in their absence. Returnees are often unaware of their rights inside and outside the customary system. IF YOU ARE DISPLACED, SOMEONE HAS TO STAND ON YOUR CLAIM OR RECORD IT WHILE YOU CANNOT. THE WARNING THE PARALEGALS THEMSELVES GIVE, and it belongs here rather than in a footnote: they describe “institutional” land grabbing — well coordinated and facilitated by networks of powerful individuals — and say that as paralegals they are at the centre of that problem and exposed when they challenge such cases; they also report working without offices, files or computers. WHO IT SUITS: South Sudanese households and returnees facing land disputes, occupation of their land in their absence, or registration problems — particularly women. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED LIVE SITE FOR SSLS WAS FOUND — this entry points at the NGO forum's document record; capacity is severely limited and donor-dependent, the security situation is volatile, and challenging coordinated land grabbing carries personal risk. For threats against defenders specifically, South Sudan's SSHRDN entry.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants in South Sudan — the country was added by name in the eighth cycle, so community environmental grants exist here for the first time
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the GEF SMALL GRANTS PROGRAMME expanded country coverage in its eighth replenishment from 124 to 135 countries, ADDING SOUTH SUDAN BY NAME — alongside Somalia, Libya, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Príncipe. South Sudan was outside this window and is now inside it; if you were told there were no community environmental grants here, that answer is out of date. THE ALLOCATION RULE: the eighth cycle secured USD 135 million for the core programme and ensures EQUAL ALLOCATION OF NEARLY USD 1 MILLION IN CORE FINANCING TO EACH of the 135 participating countries — regardless of size or previous participation, with STAR allocations raised over 30 per cent. A newly added country is not competing against large established programmes for the core money, which is the argument for applying in the FIRST cycle rather than waiting to see how it goes. The programme's stated objective is to catalyse and mobilise CIVIL SOCIETY actors and LOCAL ACTIONS addressing the major drivers of environmental degradation, and it has funded community-level environmental projects since 1992. WHY IT MATTERS PARTICULARLY HERE: South Sudan's recorded land problem is people losing land while displaced, and paralegals working without offices, files or computers. Grant money that buys a registered organisation an office, a filing system and a motorbike is not a side benefit in that setting — it is the capacity that makes claim-keeping possible. WHO IT SUITS: South Sudanese community organisations and associations with an environmental, land restoration, water or resilience project. CAVEATS: A DONOR CYCLE WITH FIXED CALLS — confirm the country programme is operational before counting on it; it funds environmental action, NOT litigation, land purchase or compensation claims, and the security situation constrains everything. For land disputes, paralegals and the 2009 Land Act, South Sudan's Law Society entry.

trackers.name: South Sudan's Land Act 2009 — customary rights held IN COMMON have EQUAL FORCE with freehold, community land can be registered, and mining is prohibited on community land
trackers.desc: WHAT THE LAW SAYS YOUR CUSTOMARY LAND IS WORTH — THE STRONGEST SENTENCE OF ITS KIND IN THIS FILE: under the LAND ACT 2009, section 8(6), CUSTOMARY LAND RIGHTS INCLUDING THOSE HELD IN COMMON SHALL HAVE EQUAL FORCE AND EFFECT IN LAW WITH FREEHOLD OR LEASEHOLD RIGHTS. Not a lesser right, not a right pending formalisation — equal. That is the sentence to put at the top of any letter about your land. The Act classifies land as PUBLIC, COMMUNITY or PRIVATE, provides that rights under customary tenure are AN ASSURED SECURITY OF OCCUPANCY whether held individually or in association with others, and states that customary land SHALL BE DEMARCATED AND REGISTERED — with a COMMUNITY LAND REGISTRATION procedure and a COMMUNITY LAND ENQUIRY in the Act itself. WHO ALLOCATES: section 15 — the TRADITIONAL AUTHORITY within a specific community may allocate customary land rights for RESIDENTIAL, AGRICULTURAL, FORESTRY AND GRAZING purposes, subject to consultation with the community; allocations over 250 FEDDANS must be verified by the state ministry as to purpose and compliance. Rights cannot be denied on the basis of SEX, ETHNICITY OR RELIGION, and WOMEN have the right to own and inherit land. THREE PROTECTIONS WORTH QUOTING AT AN INVESTOR: investment in land must reflect an important interest for the community and contribute economically and socially to local development; any community affected by activities in an investment area SHALL BE COMPENSATED; and MINING IS PROHIBITED ON PRIVATE OR COMMUNITY LAND except under the terms of a granted licence, with the Act carrying express sections on PROTECTION OF PASTORAL LANDS and COMMUNAL GRAZING LAND. WHO CAN HELP YOU USE IT: a South Sudanese land alliance has since 2015 run PILOT PROJECTS ON REGISTRATION OF COMMUNITY LAND in Central Equatoria State and legal support for rural communities' land rights in Western Equatoria, with LAND COMMITTEES inside local government councils responsible for mediating consultation on land leases between communities and investors. Ask whether a community land registration pilot has reached your county, and who sits on your land committee. WHO IT SUITS: South Sudanese communities, traditional authorities and displaced families whose land was taken while they were away. CAVEATS: THE LAW IS STRONG AND ITS MACHINERY IS WEAK — commentary records considerable ambiguity, customary ownership not yet fully established in practice, and concern over long foreign leases; registration capacity is thin and the security situation constrains everything. For paralegals and representation, South Sudan's Law Society entry; for protection first, SSHRDN; for community funding, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? NO — this is project-to-project country. Natural Justice's 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, with additional staff in Antananarivo, Botswana and Guinea; elsewhere it works across African countries on a project-to-project basis. So you are asking them to take on a project, not walking into an office — approach with a defined case and expect that answer to depend on their current programme. Its team page does list staff and fellows beyond the hub countries. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Namibia e-Procurement
trackers.desc: Namibia's government e-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Namibia, and for how much.

trackers.name: NamibLII
trackers.desc: Namibia Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Namibian judgments and legislation (NamibLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Namibia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Business and Intellectual Property Authority (BIPA)
trackers.desc: Namibia’s official registry of businesses and intellectual property — company incorporation and registration numbers.

trackers.name: BIPA Beneficial Ownership Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Namibia
trackers.desc: Supreme Court of Namibia — supreme court in Namibia (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: High Court of Namibia
trackers.desc: High Court of Namibia — supreme court in Namibia (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Communal conservancies — the community defines the area
trackers.desc: THE STRONGEST COMMUNITY LAND MODEL IN THIS MAP, AND THE REASONS ARE STRUCTURAL. A communal conservancy holds conditional rights to use the wildlife within a self-defined area, with fixed boundaries agreed with adjacent conservancies, communities or landowners — negotiated laterally with neighbours, not drawn by a ministry and handed down. It is a self-governing, democratic entity run by members through an elected committee, and it is recognised by the ministry but not governed by it: MEFT facilitates registration and monitors compliance, and may de-register a non-complying conservancy, but does not run it. AND IT REVERSED A CRIMINAL STATUS: before independence, residents on communal land who hunted game were treated as poachers; as legal entities with wildlife utilisation plans, conservancies were allowed to hunt under quotas based on annual game counts carried out by the ministry and the conservancies together. TO ESTABLISH ONE: an elected committee meets the requirements set under the 1996 amendment of the 1975 Nature Conservation Ordinance, then the Minister declares it in the Government Gazette. Obligations: wildlife management plans, annual general meetings and financial reports. SCALE: from 4 gazetted in 1998 to 86 conservancies and 43 community forests over 180,083 km² — community conservation areas now cover 20 percent of Namibia.

trackers.name: CCFN — a conservation fund that pays your legal costs
trackers.desc: THE WINDOW ALMOST NOTHING ELSE IN THIS MAP OFFERS. Alongside Minimum Support Packages and Payments for Ecosystem Services, CCFN provides financial aid to communities to meet their legal costs in pursuing their contract liberties and realising their benefits from contracts relating to their rights over their natural resources — expressly for conservancies that have been disadvantaged and/or shortchanged in contractual or other legally recognised arrangements. A conservation fund paying a community's legal fees to enforce a bad joint-venture contract is rare anywhere. Separate application forms exist for Conservancy Grants and JV Grants; check the Project Guidelines under Resources. There is also a human-wildlife conflict window — Germany through KfW announced a N$72.5 million HWC grant for communal conservancies, with the 43 worst-affected registered conservancies qualifying plus the Kyaramacan Association in Bwabwata National Park. LONG-TERM: ‘Namibia for Life’ secured N$1 billion in long-term financing with CCFN, NACSO, WWF and Enduring Earth. BUT KNOW THE TRANSITION: the movement is described as moving from a largely donor-funded development phase to a longer-term maintenance phase, with conservancy numbers expected to plateau around 90–100 — so new registrations are nearing a ceiling and the money is shifting toward sustaining what exists.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally.
