trackers.name: Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court (ECSC)
trackers.desc: A SUPERIOR COURT OF RECORD SERVING NINE EASTERN CARIBBEAN JURISDICTIONS, and the practical point is that you file at home. Established 27 February 1967 under the West Indies Associated States Supreme Court Order, the ECSC serves 6 independent states — Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines — and 3 British Overseas Territories — Anguilla, the Virgin Islands and Montserrat. It has unlimited jurisdiction in each member state and territory, and High Court operations are decentralised through registries in each participating territory, headed by trained registrars, allowing local filing, case management and initial hearings by resident or assigned judges. It exists so that very small jurisdictions can reach specialised judicial expertise without funding a standalone supreme court. THE BENCH HAS BEEN BRIEFED ON ESCAZÚ: ECLAC and the Government of Saint Lucia ran a consultation with ECSC judicial officers on the Regional Agreement on access to information, public participation and justice in environmental matters — so an environmental access-to-justice argument goes to judges who have had that agreement formally explained. Headquarters: Heraldine Rock Building, Castries, Saint Lucia; tel 758-457-3600; an e-Litigation Portal is available. CHECK YOUR FINAL COURT BEFORE PLANNING AN APPEAL — appeals from the ECSC go to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council or the Caribbean Court of Justice depending on the territory, and this is not uniform across the nine. For St Kitts and Nevis the final court is recorded as the Privy Council.

trackers.name: Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ)
trackers.desc: YOUR FINAL COURT OF APPEAL — this is one of only 5 states that have acceded to the CCJ's Appellate Jurisdiction, replacing the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for civil and criminal appeals: Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Guyana and Saint Lucia. Everywhere else in the Eastern Caribbean the final court remains the Privy Council, so do not assume the CCJ is your appeal route from a neighbouring jurisdiction's practice. BE CLEAR WHAT THE OTHER JURISDICTION DOES NOT COVER: in its Original Jurisdiction the CCJ interprets the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas on freedom of movement of people, goods, services, capital and the right of establishment — it does not extend to human rights generally, and it is not an environmental forum. A land-defence claim does not fit there unless it has a cross-border economic dimension, such as a project licensed to a company from another CARICOM state. WHERE IT DOES FIT, INDIVIDUALS CAN GET IN: under Article 222 a natural or juridical person may seek special leave, granted where the Treaty intended the right to enure to the benefit of individuals, the applicant has been prejudiced, and the member state entitled to espouse the claim omitted or declined to. 35 such cases have been brought, so the route is used rather than theoretical — Trinidad Cement Ltd v Republic of Guyana [2009] CCJ 1 (OJ) established that individuals and companies can use the Treaty to make their own state comply. The Court sits as a court of first instance there, its rulings immediately binding in international law, and hearings are broadcast live.

trackers.name: Forestry, Wildlife & Parks Division — its reach extends beyond the parks
trackers.desc: THE RIGHT BODY EVEN IF YOUR SITE IS NOT IN A NATIONAL PARK. The Division — whose Forest Service dates to 1949 — has jurisdiction over sites within the National Parks System (Morne Diablotin, Morne Trois Pitons, Cabrits) and over several other nature sites which are not within the established national parks, expressly including Soufriere Sulphur Springs, Indian River and Trafalgar Falls. Its National Park Unit is the largest section in the Division. A FUNDING MODEL WORTH COPYING: the Eco-tourist Site User Fee programme, running since June 1997, collects entry fees from non-residents only at 12 eco-tourism sites, including the Morne Trois Pitons World Heritage sites — Emerald Pool, Boiling Lake, Freshwater Lake, Boeri Lake and Middleham Falls. A non-resident fee at named sites, sustained for nearly three decades, is durable domestic revenue for park management that does not tax local users — a directly transferable design. CONTEXT: Morne Diablotin was established January 2000 at 3,335.3 ha, 4.4 percent of the nation; Morne Trois Pitons became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1998; each of the three parks has a management plan and continuous monitoring; and EIAs are recorded as mandatory for all developments.

trackers.name: DNCTF — it only adopted its governing policies in 2024
trackers.desc: TIME YOUR APPROACH. The Dominica National Conservation Trust Fund exists to provide a sustainable source of funding for effective management, conservation and restoration of Dominica's biodiversity — but it approved its foundational governance documents and internal policies only in 2024, aligning with the international Standards of Practice for Conservation Trust Funds. A fund that has just adopted its governing policies is at the start of its grantmaking life: expect procedures to be new and expect them to be applied strictly. IT IS ALSO A REGIONAL HUB — it hosted a USAID Sustainable Financing workshop building capacity among peer national funds from St Vincent and the Grenadines, St Kitts and Nevis and Suriname, engaged volunteers through the CORE project with CBF and CUSO International, and joined a regional capital-raising strategy led by the Bahamas Protected Areas Fund. MIRROR ITS OWN THREAT LIST IN AN APPLICATION: deforestation, overexploitation of wildlife, encroachment, land degradation, unregulated development, invasive species, loss of agrobiodiversity, climate impacts, pollution, hurricanes and seismic activity, land mining, gradual loss of traditional knowledge — and inappropriate legal and institutional frameworks. A national conservation fund naming the legal framework itself as a threat is quotable. ALSO ON THE ISLAND: Wild Dominica Conservancy, which invites people to join as member, trustee or sponsor — note it is a US 501(c)(3), so a US-registered charity operating on Dominica rather than a Dominican body.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional technical non-profit founded in 1989 and headquartered in Trinidad, working with grassroots and community-based organisations across the Caribbean on participatory natural resource governance. It supplies capacity rather than representation: coaching, mentoring, training of trainers, facilitated dialogues for planning and policymaking, and practical evidence tools including participatory GIS mapping, three-dimensional modelling and participatory video. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations that need to be equipped for a planning or policy fight. COVERAGE NOTE: CANARI is not registered as a non-profit in this country, but has delivered sub-grants to communities here under its Caribbean ecosystem-restoration work, so it does operate here — ask what is currently running. It is not a litigator and its re-granting is tied to donor projects. IS YOUR SITE A KBA? CHECK BEFORE YOU WRITE ANYTHING. CANARI publishes the CEPF Caribbean Islands Biodiversity Hotspot Ecosystem Profile, which identifies 45 Key Biodiversity Areas and 6 conservation corridors covering 28 KBAs as priorities for funding support, with maps — formulated through a process engaging over 200 stakeholders from more than 160 organisations. A campaign whose site is a KBA, or sits in one of the six corridors, has a materially stronger funding case and should say so explicitly. CORRECTED — AND THIS STREAM IS CLOSING. CEPF returned for a Phase II running August 2021 to July 2027, and CANARI is once again the Regional Implementation Team, managing US$11.8 million. THE ELEVENTH AND FINAL SMALL-GRANT CALL offers USD 5,000–50,000 for projects of up to 12 months between April 2026 and March 2027, and the tenth call was the final open call for large grants in the region — so treat the current call as the last scheduled opportunity, not one of many, though targeted solicitations may still fill portfolio gaps. ELIGIBILITY NARROWED IN PHASE II: the Phase I list of 11 countries no longer applies; Phase II calls name Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines, with CEPF stating 7 countries initially eligible. BUT THE SITE TEST CAN OUTRANK THE COUNTRY TEST: applicants based outside the eligible countries may submit provided activities focus on a conservation need within a priority corridor or site. THREE RULES: applicants must not be a government agency (government-owned bodies qualify only with independent legal personality and authority to receive private funds); joint projects are eligible with one lead organisation; and NGOs, community groups, universities and private enterprises may all apply. ASK BEFORE YOU DRAFT: RIT Manager Nicole Brown, caribbeanrit@canari.org — applicants uncertain about eligibility are expressly encouraged to make contact first. A Grievance Redress Mechanism exists for concerns about a funded project. WHAT CANARI ITSELF IS: a non-profit technical institute of thirty years' standing that acts as a conduit, channelling funding, information and technical support to CSOs — not a standing grant fund. Its project pattern is small grants plus technical coaching for partner CSOs to run participatory community vulnerability assessments and then design a project from the results.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund — regional conservation finance
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional umbrella environmental fund providing continuous finance for conservation, through an Endowment Fund and a Climate Change Program whose Ecosystem-based Adaptation Facility runs competitive calls for proposals — around 100 projects funded. WHO IT SUITS: Caribbean community and conservation groups. HOW IT DIFFERS: mostly you do NOT apply to CBF directly — partner National Conservation Trust Funds lead the grantmaking in each country, so find your national trust fund first. CBF states it works across 14 Caribbean countries; check its 'Where We Work' map for yours. APPLY TO YOUR NATIONAL FUND, NOT TO CBF — for most of the money. CBF is a regional umbrella: at national level the partner National Conservation Trust Funds (NCTFs) lead the grantmaking process, with endowment proceeds held in country-based subaccounts and channelled through them. So for the Conservation Finance stream, the regional body is the wrong door — find your NCTF. THE EXCEPTION IS THE EbA FACILITY, which awards through competitive calls for proposals and is a direct route. THE NUMBERS: EbA medium grants USD 250,000–1 million, large grants up to USD 2 million — large by the standards of most funds here, and not aimed at a small unincorporated group acting alone. Eligible recipients expressly include NCTFs, NGOs, community-based organisations, government agencies, universities and the private sector. SCOPE CHECK: the EbA Facility covers the marine and coastal zone of the insular Caribbean, so an inland project must show its connection to marine and coastal ecosystems. IF YOU ARE TOO SMALL FOR EbA: CBF partners with GEF SGP across 12 shared countries — that is the sibling route for community-scale grants, and it is recorded separately in this map. Endowment disbursements go to NCTFs that have signed agreements with CBF, the first in 2016 with Fondo MARENA in the Dominican Republic.

trackers.name: Grenada National Trust — and its WhatsApp number is the fastest way in
trackers.desc: A NAMED BODY WITH CONTACTS THAT ACTUALLY GET ANSWERED. The Grenada National Trust aims to protect Grenada's cultural, architectural and natural heritage. CONTACTS: P.O. Box 636, St George's; Kirani James Boulevard, corner Glean's Road, HiTech Building; WhatsApp +1 (473) 407-1212; admin@grenadanationaltrust.org. A WhatsApp number as an official channel is worth using — for a small-island body that is usually faster and more likely answered than post. Recorded work includes ‘Proud of my Heritage’, a national project officially approved and funded by UNESCO to identify, register and promote living heritage across the tri-island state through inventorying and education. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE BEFORE YOU RELY ON IT: the Trust's documented activity leans toward cultural and intangible heritage. Its stated aim expressly includes natural heritage, but this entry does not assert that it holds or acquires land — unlike the Saint Lucia National Trust, recorded separately here, whose statute carries an express acquisition power. If land-holding is what you need, ask them directly what they hold.

trackers.name: Grenada Sustainable Development Trust Fund — 6 projects, so expect competition
trackers.desc: THE NATIONAL CONSERVATION TRUST FUND FOR GRENADA, and one of the CBF partner funds that lead grantmaking at national level — so this, not the regional body, is your door for the endowment stream. It supports conservation and effective management of coastal, marine and terrestrial ecosystems. THE TRACK RECORD TELLS YOU WHAT IT BACKS AND HOW BIG IT IS: as at 31 December 2022 it had financed 6 projects — education and training for sustainable livelihoods, restoration of nature reserves, and protected area management. Six projects is a small portfolio: treat this as a fund still building capacity, and expect competition for a handful of awards. THREATS IT NAMES, worth mirroring in an application: climate change, invasive alien species, habitat degradation and fragmentation particularly in lowland forests, and pollution of freshwater and coastal environments. Grenada's ecosystems include mangroves, reefs, seagrass beds, lagoons, dry woodlands and cactus shrub. CONTEXT ON EXISTING PROTECTION: the Grand Etang and Annandale Forest Reserves, managed together, are the largest declared terrestrial protected area, followed by Mount St Catherine. PRACTICAL NOTE: the Caribbean Challenge Initiative directory lists the GSDTF with no website yet, so approach may need to go through CBF rather than a national page.

trackers.name: Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF)
trackers.desc: A FUND WHOSE SMALL-GRANT APPLICATION IS A SINGLE LETTER. CEPF (founded 2000; a joint initiative of the French Development Agency, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, the Government of Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank) has funded more than 2,500 grantees. FOR SMALL GRANTS THE LETTER OF INQUIRY IS THE ENTIRE APPLICATION — no longer project proposal is required — reviewed by the hotspot's Regional Implementation Team, with an offline template provided in the call's languages. Large grants go through the ConservationGrants portal and only then invite a full proposal. Reported averages: small grants around US$15,000, large around US$150,000; the small/large threshold varies by call (US$20,000 and US$50,000 both recorded), so read it. TIMING: calls run 6–8 weeks and notification comes several months after closing — but CEPF stops accepting letters once the designated funds are committed, so an open call can close early. WHO IS DISQUALIFIED: individuals cannot apply — you need a legally registered organisation with its own bank account — and government cannot apply. Community groups, farmers' cooperatives, Indigenous Peoples' organisations and women's groups all can, and CEPF welcomes first-time applicants. TWO RULES THAT SINK GOOD APPLICATIONS: your letter must aim at one single strategic direction; and site-based directions are geographically bound — community management work must be in a listed priority KBA, corridor work in a named corridor, while civil-society strengthening can be anywhere in the hotspot. THE STEP MOST PEOPLE SKIP: CEPF encourages you to contact RIT staff to discuss the idea before submitting — free, and the cheapest way to learn whether it fits.

trackers.name: Saint Lucia National Trust — can acquire land, and you can stand for its Council
trackers.desc: A STATUTORY BODY WHOSE OBJECTS INCLUDE ACQUIRING LAND. Established 1975 under the Saint Lucia National Trust Act, Chapter 6.02, as a body corporate, with objects that include to acquire property for the benefit of the State and to conserve areas of beauty including submarine and subterranean areas — so a cave system or reef is within its express statutory remit. Under section 16 it may make by-laws to protect and maintain property it holds: a body that can make its own rules over land it holds is stronger than one that merely owns it. YOU CAN JOIN AND YOU CAN STAND: it is a membership organisation with an 11-member Council, 7 elected annually by the membership at the AGM, the other four representing the Archaeological and Historical Society and the Government. HOW LAND REACHES IT: properties have been vested in, or donated and bequeathed by individuals for conservation — bequest is an established route here, not a theory. It manages national landmarks, historical sites, environmental protection areas and nature reserves whether owned or vested in it, including Pigeon Island, Maria Islands Nature Reserve (declared 1982), Anse La Liberte and the Pointe Sable Environmental Protection Area. ASK WHICH LEVEL APPLIES TO YOUR SITE: in the Trust's own words, some sites are protected areas by law and others are deemed for protection by nature of their biological components — two very different levels of security.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional technical non-profit founded in 1989, headquartered in Trinidad and legally registered as a non-profit in this country, working with grassroots and community-based organisations directly involved in natural resource management. What it actually supplies is capacity rather than representation: coaching, mentoring and training of trainers, facilitated multi-stakeholder dialogues for planning and policymaking, participatory research, and unusual practical tools — participatory GIS mapping, three-dimensional modelling, participatory video and photojournaling — for communities that need to evidence their own case. It also channels funding and technical support to civil society organisations. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations and CSOs that need to be equipped to hold their ground in a planning or policy process. It is not a litigator, and its re-granting runs through time-limited donor projects rather than a standing open call — ask what is currently running. IS YOUR SITE A KBA? CHECK BEFORE YOU WRITE ANYTHING. CANARI publishes the CEPF Caribbean Islands Biodiversity Hotspot Ecosystem Profile, which identifies 45 Key Biodiversity Areas and 6 conservation corridors covering 28 KBAs as priorities for funding support, with maps — formulated through a process engaging over 200 stakeholders from more than 160 organisations. A campaign whose site is a KBA, or sits in one of the six corridors, has a materially stronger funding case and should say so explicitly. CORRECTED — AND THIS STREAM IS CLOSING. CEPF returned for a Phase II running August 2021 to July 2027, and CANARI is once again the Regional Implementation Team, managing US$11.8 million. THE ELEVENTH AND FINAL SMALL-GRANT CALL offers USD 5,000–50,000 for projects of up to 12 months between April 2026 and March 2027, and the tenth call was the final open call for large grants in the region — so treat the current call as the last scheduled opportunity, not one of many, though targeted solicitations may still fill portfolio gaps. ELIGIBILITY NARROWED IN PHASE II: the Phase I list of 11 countries no longer applies; Phase II calls name Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines, with CEPF stating 7 countries initially eligible. BUT THE SITE TEST CAN OUTRANK THE COUNTRY TEST: applicants based outside the eligible countries may submit provided activities focus on a conservation need within a priority corridor or site. THREE RULES: applicants must not be a government agency (government-owned bodies qualify only with independent legal personality and authority to receive private funds); joint projects are eligible with one lead organisation; and NGOs, community groups, universities and private enterprises may all apply. ASK BEFORE YOU DRAFT: RIT Manager Nicole Brown, caribbeanrit@canari.org — applicants uncertain about eligibility are expressly encouraged to make contact first. A Grievance Redress Mechanism exists for concerns about a funded project. WHAT CANARI ITSELF IS: a non-profit technical institute of thirty years' standing that acts as a conduit, channelling funding, information and technical support to CSOs — not a standing grant fund. Its project pattern is small grants plus technical coaching for partner CSOs to run participatory community vulnerability assessments and then design a project from the results.

trackers.name: Office of the Director of Audit
trackers.desc: National — supreme audit institution of St. Vincent and the Grenadines. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in St Vincent and the Grenadines.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund — regional conservation finance
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional umbrella environmental fund providing continuous finance for conservation, through an Endowment Fund and a Climate Change Program whose Ecosystem-based Adaptation Facility runs competitive calls for proposals — around 100 projects funded. WHO IT SUITS: Caribbean community and conservation groups. HOW IT DIFFERS: mostly you do NOT apply to CBF directly — partner National Conservation Trust Funds lead the grantmaking in each country, so find your national trust fund first. CBF states it works across 14 Caribbean countries; check its 'Where We Work' map for yours. APPLY TO YOUR NATIONAL FUND, NOT TO CBF — for most of the money. CBF is a regional umbrella: at national level the partner National Conservation Trust Funds (NCTFs) lead the grantmaking process, with endowment proceeds held in country-based subaccounts and channelled through them. So for the Conservation Finance stream, the regional body is the wrong door — find your NCTF. THE EXCEPTION IS THE EbA FACILITY, which awards through competitive calls for proposals and is a direct route. THE NUMBERS: EbA medium grants USD 250,000–1 million, large grants up to USD 2 million — large by the standards of most funds here, and not aimed at a small unincorporated group acting alone. Eligible recipients expressly include NCTFs, NGOs, community-based organisations, government agencies, universities and the private sector. SCOPE CHECK: the EbA Facility covers the marine and coastal zone of the insular Caribbean, so an inland project must show its connection to marine and coastal ecosystems. IF YOU ARE TOO SMALL FOR EbA: CBF partners with GEF SGP across 12 shared countries — that is the sibling route for community-scale grants, and it is recorded separately in this map. Endowment disbursements go to NCTFs that have signed agreements with CBF, the first in 2016 with Fondo MARENA in the Dominican Republic.

trackers.name: St Vincent & the Grenadines — Commerce & Intellectual Property Office (CIPO)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Commerce & Intellectual Property Office registers companies & business names and administers IP, Saint Vincent & the Grenadines. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court (ECSC)
trackers.desc: A SUPERIOR COURT OF RECORD SERVING NINE EASTERN CARIBBEAN JURISDICTIONS, and the practical point is that you file at home. Established 27 February 1967 under the West Indies Associated States Supreme Court Order, the ECSC serves 6 independent states — Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines — and 3 British Overseas Territories — Anguilla, the Virgin Islands and Montserrat. It has unlimited jurisdiction in each member state and territory, and High Court operations are decentralised through registries in each participating territory, headed by trained registrars, allowing local filing, case management and initial hearings by resident or assigned judges. It exists so that very small jurisdictions can reach specialised judicial expertise without funding a standalone supreme court. THE BENCH HAS BEEN BRIEFED ON ESCAZÚ: ECLAC and the Government of Saint Lucia ran a consultation with ECSC judicial officers on the Regional Agreement on access to information, public participation and justice in environmental matters — so an environmental access-to-justice argument goes to judges who have had that agreement formally explained. Headquarters: Heraldine Rock Building, Castries, Saint Lucia; tel 758-457-3600; an e-Litigation Portal is available. CHECK YOUR FINAL COURT BEFORE PLANNING AN APPEAL — appeals from the ECSC go to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council or the Caribbean Court of Justice depending on the territory, and this is not uniform across the nine. For St Kitts and Nevis the final court is recorded as the Privy Council.

trackers.name: NPRBA — its own mission commits it to full community involvement
trackers.desc: A STATUTORY BODY THAT HAS WRITTEN YOUR STANDARD FOR YOU. The National Parks, Rivers and Beaches Authority was established by Act No. 33 of 2002 for the preservation, protection, management and development of natural, physical and ecological resources and historical and cultural heritage — and its mission is to protect those resources ‘by fully involving all relevant community groups and stakeholders in promoting and managing their use’. Quote that back. ITS DEFINITION OF A PROTECTED AREA IS BROAD: an area of land or water managed for ecological systems, biological diversity and/or specific natural, cultural and aesthetic resources — aesthetic resources are named, so a site can qualify on landscape value alone. AND ONE SYSTEM OBJECTIVE IS UNUSUALLY CONCRETE: protection of ecosystem function, expressly water, electricity and soil conservation. Where a development threatens a watershed feeding hydro generation or water supply, that is already a stated objective of the managing authority, not an argument you must construct. Other objectives include wilderness protection and landscape maintenance, maintenance of environmental services, maintenance of cultural and traditional attributes, and meeting obligations under international conventions. Contact: Jaycee's Building, corner Leeward Highway and Stoney Ground Road, Kingstown. Resource context: about 12,700 ha of tropical forest including palm brakes and elfin woodland, habitat of the St Vincent parrot.

trackers.name: SVG National Trust — it went dormant, and Cabinet revived it
trackers.desc: A LESSON ABOUT ANY BODY YOU FIND IN LEGISLATION. The Trust was established in 1969 to assist with the preservation and management of historical monuments and sites and to safeguard cultural patrimony — but the official history records that ‘interest waned and the Trust remained dormant for some time’. Cabinet then appointed a Board of Trustees to spearhead its revitalisation, with the Ministry of Tourism and Culture as parent ministry, and it now holds meetings of both the Board and the general membership — so it can be joined. TWO PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES: first, do not assume a body named in legislation is currently active — check for recent meetings before building a plan around it; second, where a useful statutory body has lapsed, revival by Cabinet appointment is a documented route in this jurisdiction rather than a novel request. FOR SCALE ON WHAT IS AT STAKE: the Tobago Cays marine park is a 1,400-acre lagoon encompassing five cays, the inhabited island of Mayreau and the 4 km Horseshoe Reef, listed as a regionally significant ecosystem under the SPAW Protocol in December 2014 — with an estimated 3,000 yachts anchoring in the lagoon each year and 10,000 cruise visitors reaching the cays.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: Algeria's public inquiry register — the one opening a resident has, and it closes in fifteen days
trackers.desc: WHERE TO FILE, AND WHY THIS ENTRY IS WRITTEN AS AN ABSENCE: no Algerian civil society organisation providing land defence, environmental litigation or community legal support could be verified for this file. What a resident does have is the enquête publique attached to environmental impact assessment, run by the environment ministry's procedure. THE MECHANICS, WHICH ARE THE WHOLE POINT: the order opening the public inquiry must be made known by posting at the wilaya headquarters, at the communes concerned and at the project site, and by insertion in two national daily newspapers AT THE PROMOTER'S EXPENSE; it must state the detailed object of the inquiry, its duration, and the hours and place where the public may record observations in a numbered and initialled register opened for that purpose. THE DURATION MUST NOT EXCEED FIFTEEN DAYS FROM THE DATE OF POSTING — so the window can open and close inside a fortnight, and a village that hears about it late has lost it. Requests to consult the impact study or notice are addressed to the wali, who must invite the person to read it at a place he designates and give them fifteen days to formulate their views and observations. For the inquiry the wali appoints a commissaire enquêteur responsible for ensuring the posting and publication rules are respected. The governing texts are the executive decree of 19 May 2007 on the scope, content and approval of impact studies and notices, with the lists of installations subject to a full study or a lighter notice set out in annexes. WATCH THE NOTICEBOARD AT THE COMMUNE, AND WRITE IN THE REGISTER — an entry in a numbered, initialled register is a dated record that the project file must carry. WHO IT SUITS: Algerian residents near a proposed installation who want a formal, dated objection on the record. CAVEATS: THIS IS A STATE PROCEDURE, NOT AN ALLY, and no independent Algerian organisation is recorded here to help you use it — Algeria was researched twice for this file without a qualifying civil society body being found. The publicity requirement depends on the promoter paying for it and on the wali's administration; fifteen days is the maximum, not a guarantee.

trackers.name: Algeria — under loi 13-07 an advocate designated by the bâtonnier MUST act for you, and when commis d'office must defend you before ALL jurisdictions, free
trackers.desc: WHO OWES YOU A LAWYER, AND THIS CORRECTS THIS FILE'S OWN EARLIER RECORD FOR ALGERIA: under loi n°13-07 organising the profession of advocate, Article 11 — THE ADVOCATE DESIGNATED BY THE BÂTONNIER OR HIS DELEGATE IN THE FRAMEWORK OF ASSISTANCE JUDICIAIRE MUST LEND HIS CONCOURS TO ANY LITIGANT WHO BENEFITS FROM IT; and when COMMIS D'OFFICE by the bâtonnier or his delegate, he is BOUND TO ENSURE THE DEFENCE OF THE INTERESTS OF ANY LITIGANT, BEFORE ALL JURISDICTIONS, gratuitously. So the person to approach in Algeria is THE BÂTONNIER OF THE TERRITORIALLY COMPETENT BAR — designation is his to make, and once made the advocate has no discretion to refuse. WHAT AN ADVOCATE'S ROLE COVERS, per the same law: representation, assistance and defence of the parties, and the provision of advice and LEGAL CONSULTATIONS (Art. 5), with power to take any measure and intervene in any act of procedure (Art. 6). Advocates must open a cabinet within the jurisdiction of a court and may have only one. WHERE THE BARS ARE: the BARREAU D'ALGER, seated at the Palais de Justice, Algiers, is described as the largest bar in Algeria and on the continent, with close to 7,000 registered advocates, appearing before the Cour d'Alger and the tribunals of Sidi M'Hamed, Bab El Oued, El Harrach, Hussein Dey, Bir Mourad Raïs, Dar El Beïda and Rouiba; other bars sit at each cour, including Blida. Seven thousand advocates in one bar means the constraint in Algeria is not supply but designation — get the bâtonnier to designate, and use the environment and immovable-property categories when asking for one who practises in your matter. WHO IT SUITS: Algerians without means facing expropriation, an immovable-property dispute or an environmental harm, anywhere a cour sits. CAVEATS: DESIGNATION RUNS THROUGH THE BÂTONNIER and the conditions of assistance judiciaire are set by separate legislation and regulations — confirm them; no independent Algerian civil society organisation providing land or environmental support could be verified for this file, across three searches. For the fifteen-day public inquiry window and the register to write in, Algeria's enquête publique entry.

trackers.name: Algeria's loi 11-02 — a protected area can be created by decision of the WALI or of your COMMUNAL POPULAR ASSEMBLY PRESIDENT, with a wilaya commission giving the opinion
trackers.desc: WHO CAN CREATE A PROTECTED AREA, AND THE ANSWER IS CLOSER TO HOME THAN MOST PEOPLE ASSUME: under LOI N°11-02 OF 17 FEBRUARY 2011 on protected areas, AN AIRE PROTÉGÉE MAY BE CREATED BY VIRTUE OF A DECISION OF THE WALI OR OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMMUNAL POPULAR ASSEMBLY, with A COMMISSION DE WILAYA comprising the sectors concerned charged with giving an OPINION ON THE PROPOSAL AND OBJECTIVE OF CLASSIFICATION and approving the classification studies (décret exécutif 16-259 of 10 October 2016 fixes the composition and functioning of the national and wilaya commissions). Your own APC president can create one. That makes classification a local political question you can actually reach — take the proposal to the commune first, and the wilaya commission is who must then be persuaded. WHAT THE PAPERWORK CONSISTS OF, so you know what you are asking a commune to commission: a SCHÉMA DIRECTEUR setting long-term objectives for biodiversity conservation, sustainable use of natural AND CULTURAL heritage, ecotourism and ecosystem restoration — drawn up IN CONCERTATION WITH THE SECTORS CONCERNED AND LOCAL ACTORS, and revised every FIFTEEN YEARS — and a PLAN DE GESTION (décret of 13 August 2019, under article 37 of loi 11-02) described as A TECHNICAL AND DYNAMIC DOCUMENT containing the heritage evaluation, strategic and operational objectives, protection means, short and medium-term intervention programme, research programme, an exhaustive state of the area highlighting PROBLEMS, STAKES AND OPPORTUNITIES, a YEAR-BY-YEAR, ZONE-BY-ZONE WORK PLAN with localisation AND FINANCIAL EVALUATION of operations, and mapping. Ask to see the plan de gestion for any Algerian protected area near you: the annual work plan carries costed, located operations, which is the most checkable document in this entire national system. The plan is approved by the managing establishment's orientation council after the scientific council's opinion. Practitioners writing on Algeria's parks have named the standing agenda as settling disputes arising after park creation — aggregate quarry concessions, public dumps, polluting industrial units, uncontrolled urbanisation — and associating neighbouring populations with rural development through local projects. WHO IT SUITS: Algerian communes, associations and residents seeking classification of ground, or scrutiny of an existing park's plan. CAVEATS: CLASSIFICATION AND MANAGEMENT SIT WITH PUBLIC ESTABLISHMENTS, not communities; no independent Algerian land or environmental civil-society organisation could be verified for this file. For the fifteen-day inquiry register, Algeria's enquête publique entry; for a designated advocate, the loi 13-07 entry.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: SOS Habitat — the Angolan association that documents demolitions, and the sequence a lawful eviction is supposed to follow
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an Angolan civic association working on the right to housing, which has spent two decades documenting forced evictions and demolitions in Luanda and beyond — its research with an international human rights organisation established that at least 18 mass evictions involving violence and excessive force took place in a four-year period, and it has continued through the demolitions at Zango, Areia Branca, Quiçama and Vida Pacífica, and the 2023 destruction of more than 300 houses at Zango 3. THE MOST USEFUL THING IT PUBLISHES IS A SEQUENCE, because in Angola the demolition usually comes first: its coordinator sets out that demolition should be the last step, after notification of the families, registration of the affected households, and provision of a housing alternative — and that what happens instead is demolition for the benefit of a private party with no legal procedure and no follow-up. Quote that order back at whoever arrives, and ask which step has been completed. THE OTHER GAP IT DOCUMENTS IS THE ONE TO ATTACK FIRST: investigations found the state did not tell residents which body issued the eviction order, on what legal basis, or which authority to appeal to. Those three questions, in writing, are where a defence starts. WHAT IT DOES BESIDES DOCUMENT: it supports affected residents' marches and negotiations — in one Luanda case the threat of a march it backed produced a government commitment to house more than 460 people demolished years earlier — and it has convened affected communities from Luanda, Benguela, Kwanza Sul, Huíla and Lunda Sul in a national gathering, the first of its kind. WHO IT SUITS: households in informal settlements without formal title — which is most of Luanda — facing demolition for a state or private project. CAVEATS: NO CANONICAL WEBSITE FOR SOS HABITAT WAS FOUND, so this entry carries no URL rather than pointing at a third party; contact is through Angolan civil society networks. It is a documentation and advocacy association, not a law firm. And the risk is real: its activists have themselves been subjected to state force, and residents who refused to leave or protested peacefully have been beaten and detained.

trackers.name: ADRA Angola — assembles the paperwork rural communities need to legalise their land, including the free perpetual community title
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Acção para o Desenvolvimento Rural e Ambiente, an Angolan NGO working on democratic and sustainable rural development, with provincial presence including Huambo. What it does that matters here: it works with the provincial government to assemble the documentation required to legalise the land of agricultural cooperatives and rural communities, because those communities cannot complete the paperwork alone — and it convenes provincial land security conferences bringing together family farmers, traditional authorities, civil society and government. THE INSTRUMENT TO ASK FOR BY NAME: under the Angolan land law, rural community land is defined as land used by a rural community according to custom — including the complementary areas for shifting cultivation, the corridors giving cattle access to water, pastures and the customary rights of way — and the state issues a Título de Reconhecimento, a title recognising the community's right of use and enjoyment of defined land, of PERPETUAL duration, and ISSUED FREE OF CHARGE. The law also requires that, when delimiting community areas, the competent authority hear the administrative authorities, the institutions of traditional power and the families of the rural community concerned. Custom alone constitutes the customary useful domain — but a title makes it visible to everyone else. WHAT ADRA AND ITS ALLIES SAY IS WRONG WITH IT: with the peasant confederation and the agrarian professionals' association it has publicly demanded urgent revision of the land law, arguing it obstructs family farming and communities' legal security, with farmers waiting ten years for legalisation. Ask what stage your file is at, and who is holding it. WHO IT SUITS: Angolan rural communities, cooperatives and family farmers seeking to document and legalise land before it is allocated to someone else. CAVEATS: a rural development organisation, not a law firm and not a fund; its provincial reach is partial; and demarcation is handled by the national geographic and cadastral institute, so the timetable is not ADRA's to control. For urban demolition and forced eviction, Angola's SOS Habitat entry is the other one.

trackers.name: Ordem dos Advogados de Angola — the law puts free legal assistance in the BAR's hands, not a public defender's, and the constitution says poverty cannot deny you justice
trackers.desc: WHO OWES YOU A LAWYER: in Angola the law assigns to the ORDEM DOS ADVOGADOS DE ANGOLA (OAA) the competence to grant legal assistance, access to law and FORENSIC SPONSORSHIP (patrocínio forense) at every stage — there is no separate public defender institute of the kind Mozambique operates, so the bar association is the door. THE TWO CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS TO QUOTE: Article 29 guarantees everyone access to law and to the courts to defend their rights and legally protected interests, and provides that JUSTICE CANNOT BE DENIED FOR INSUFFICIENCY OF ECONOMIC MEANS; and Article 195(2) requires the law to regulate legal assistance, access to law and forensic sponsorship, WITH THE STATE OBLIGED TO ESTABLISH THE FINANCIAL MEANS for it. If you are told you cannot proceed because you cannot pay, those two articles are the answer, and the OAA is who you address it to. WHAT THE BAR'S OWN STATUTES REQUIRE OF ITS MEMBERS: advocates have a duty to collaborate in access to law and to ACCEPT OFFICIAL APPOINTMENTS (nomeações oficiosas) on the conditions fixed by law and by the Ordem, and to protest against violations of human rights and combat arbitrary acts they learn of in practice. It also runs a DIREITO PARA TODOS programme taking groups of advocates — including the bastonário — into the provinces to give free legal assistance, documented in Kwanza Norte, Malange, Uíge, Namibe and Kuando Kubango, and free legal advice days in Luanda municipalities with dozens of advocates attending on civil, family, administrative and economic matters. THE CONSTRAINT, STATED BECAUSE IT DETERMINES WHAT YOU WILL ACTUALLY GET: advocates have publicly complained that the OAA pays for assistance and sponsorship only AFTER the work, never at the start, which hampers the steps a case requires; and in one budget year the state allocated a sum for assistance and judicial sponsorship of which the OAA received only about 45 per cent. WHO IT SUITS: Angolans without means who need representation — including in land, demolition and expropriation matters. CAVEATS: A PROFESSIONAL BODY, NOT A CAMPAIGNING ONE, chronically underfunded for this duty, and its provincial programmes are episodic rather than standing offices. For rural land title, Angola's ADRA entry; for urban demolitions and forced eviction, SOS Habitat.

trackers.name: Ligue Iteka
trackers.desc: Burundi’s oldest human-rights organization, founded in 1991 and forced into exile since the 2015 crisis — through a network of monitors inside the country it documents killings, torture, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrest and illegal detention, and catastrophic prison conditions (national prisons running at over 300% of capacity), publishing weekly ‘Iteka n’Ijambo’ bulletins and quarterly and annual human-rights reports even as the government brands it an ‘enemy of the nation’ and refuses to recognize its findings.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes du Burundi
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Burundi — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Burundi — Ministère des Finances, du Budget et de l’Économie Numérique
trackers.desc: National budget authority; designs & implements financial policy and prepares the State budget, Burundi. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Burundi.

trackers.name: Burundi — Agence de Développement du Burundi (Guichet Unique / Registre de Commerce)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the Agence de Développement du Burundi (ADB, successor to the API) runs the Guichet Unique de création d’entreprises — the single entry point hosting the Registre de Commerce et des Sociétés & business-creation formalities, Burundi. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: COMIFAC Treaty and Plan de Convergence — and its community protocol
trackers.desc: A TREATY BODY WITH A TEMPLATE YOU CAN COPY. The Traité relatif à la conservation et à la gestion durable des écosystèmes forestiers d'Afrique Centrale, signed by heads of state at their second summit on 5 February 2005 in Brazzaville, instituted the Commission des Forêts d'Afrique Centrale — described as the unique instance d'orientation, de décision et de coordination for subregional forest action, and the cadre politique et juridique global for cooperation in the field. Axis 7 covers capacity and participation des acteurs, expressly contemplating micro-projets générateurs de revenus pour les populations locales; axis 9 covers innovative financing mechanisms. THE DOCUMENT LIBRARY IS THE MOST USEFUL PART: COMIFAC publishes a worked Protocole Bioculturel Communautaire for a named village, a guide to inventorying genetic resources and traditional knowledge, a paper on les droits d'usage des peuples autochtones et communautés locales et les obligations qui en découlent, a subregional APA (access and benefit-sharing) strategy, and directives on forests and the SDGs built with FAO as 5 principles and 12 directives across 31 prioritised targets. A community biocultural protocol published by a treaty body is a template, not a theory. trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: ODEB — Burundi's first environmental civil society organisation, and the route by which local groups sign co-management memoranda over protected areas
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Organisation pour la Défense de l'Environnement au Burundi, created and legally recognised in 1992 — the first civil society organisation in the country working on environmental protection, with its own legal personality and working contacts among official decision-makers and international environmental bodies. Its stated mission includes supporting populations that take initiatives for ecologically sustainable development and conducting relentless advocacy, which is the closest thing Burundi has to a standing environmental defence body. WHAT THE ROUTE ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE HERE, and it is worth knowing before you approach anyone: protected areas are managed by the state environment office, which works with local associations and groupings — community protection support committees have been set up at protected areas, and memoranda of collaboration have been signed between the state office and four local groupings at one forest reserve, under a project run by a consortium of Burundian environmental associations with international small-grants funding. So a village grouping can hold a written co-management relationship over a reserve; the documented path to it runs through an established national association acting as intermediary. Address: 18 avenue des États-Unis, Rohero 2, Bujumbura. WHO IT SUITS: local groupings and associations near forests, wetlands and protected areas in Burundi that want recognition as a management partner rather than to be treated as encroachers. CAVEATS: NO LIVE CANONICAL WEBSITE FOR ODEB WAS VERIFIED — this entry points at the national biodiversity clearing-house record for the organisation, and a domain seen on its social media was not confirmed; treat the organisation as the contact and this as the record. It is an awareness, advocacy and support organisation, not a law firm; no intake route or fee information exists, and Burundian civic space is narrow.

trackers.name: ABO Burundi and the site support groups around Kibira — and the reason an EIA objection in Burundi may have nothing behind it
trackers.desc: WHO WORKS WITH PARK-EDGE COMMUNITIES: the Association Burundaise pour la protection des Oiseaux (ABO), created by ministerial ordinance n°530/231 of 8 April 2000 to protect the natural environment through the study and safeguarding of biodiversity, and working on the preservation and rehabilitation of ecosystems and natural habitats. Around the Kibira National Park it works with the neighbouring population on forestry and fruit-tree activities on the Mutana and Rukoma hills in Kayanza province, and runs awareness work aimed at the environmental police, the local administration and forest guards. THE STRUCTURE TO ASK FOR BY NAME: with an international birds partner it has set up income-generating projects for park-edge residents — goat rearing among them — organised through SITE SUPPORT GROUPS: standing local groups attached to a particular site, which give park-edge residents a recognised collective identity in dealings with the park administration. If you live beside a protected area and have no committee, this is the cheapest structure to form — it exists in law nowhere, but it gives you one name and one voice at the park gate. THE LEGAL PICTURE, STATED HONESTLY BECAUSE IT CHANGES WHAT IS WORTH ATTEMPTING: Burundi's environment code sets out the fundamental rules for protecting and managing the environment, BUT NO DECREE HAS BEEN ISSUED TO APPLY ITS PROVISIONS, INCLUDING ON ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT; and the land code contains no provision favouring conservation of natural areas and conflicts with the forest code on the cession or concession of wooded land. So an EIA objection in Burundi may have no implementing decree behind it — ask what instrument the decision is actually being made under before you build a case on the code. Protected areas themselves are administered by the national environment and nature conservation institute. WHO IT SUITS: Burundian communities living beside Kibira or other protected areas, seeking a recognised group and livelihood support rather than confrontation. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED SITE OF ITS OWN — this entry points at the international partner's Burundi page; ABO is a conservation association, NOT a legal service, a fund or an advocate against a project, and Burundian civic space is tightly constrained. For the country's first environmental civil society organisation, Burundi's ODEB entry.

trackers.name: Burundi's legal clinics — free advice AND representation for people who could otherwise never reach a court, in a country where land conflicts are the common case
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET FREE LEGAL HELP: legal clinics established in Burundi over recent years to bring justice closer to citizens, which provide FREE LEGAL ADVICE AND REPRESENTATION to people who would otherwise have no means of accessing the courts — a documented clinic operates at RUYIGI, in the east. WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT RESOURCE FOR BURUNDI SPECIFICALLY, in the reporting's own terms: access to justice remains fraught with obstacles despite progress; CONFLICTS OVER LAND ARE COMMON; and EVEN EDUCATED BURUNDIANS OFTEN LACK UNDERSTANDING OF LEGAL PROCEDURES and the requirements involved. That last point is the one to take seriously — if literate, schooled people cannot navigate the procedure, the barrier is the procedure, and what you need first is somebody who has done it before, not a better argument. The documented case is exactly the kind this file exists for: a woman in her seventies whose struggle to reclaim her late parents' land was long and painful, and who reached the clinic when nothing else was open to her. Inheritance is how most Burundian land disputes begin, and a widow or daughter contesting a family claim is the commonest client — go early, before the parcel is re-occupied. WHO IT SUITS: Burundians with a land, inheritance or succession dispute and no money for a lawyer, particularly older women and returnees. CAVEATS: THE CLINICS HAVE NO STANDALONE SITE — this entry points at the supporting organisation's published account, which names Ruyigi; coverage is by clinic rather than national, so confirm the nearest one and its days. Burundian civic space is tightly constrained and the national land commission recorded elsewhere in this file withdrew from at least one province, so do not count on it. For conservation and park-edge community structures, Burundi's ODEB and ABO entries.

trackers.name: Burundi's GEF small grants programme — 21 civil society organisations funded in the eighth cycle, with an ICCA window for community-conserved territories
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the Programme de Microfinancements du FEM (PMF/FEM) — the Global Environment Facility Small Grants Programme — run in Burundi with the UN development programme. Its EIGHTH OPERATIONAL PHASE was launched on 5 August 2026 in Bujumbura, and TWENTY-ONE CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS received financing agreements for projects on environmental protection, biodiversity conservation and climate adaptation. Twenty-one grants to civil society organisations in one cycle is the largest documented number of community-level environmental grants in any country in this file — this is a real window, not a notional one. WHAT THE NEW CYCLE ADDED, AND IT IS THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR LAND: selection was described as particularly competitive, the retained projects now integrate REINFORCED COMMUNITY RESILIENCE CRITERIA, and the cycle carries unprecedented co-financing under the second phase of the GLOBAL INITIATIVE ON INDIGENOUS AND COMMUNITY CONSERVED TERRITORIES AND AREAS (ICCA-GSI). An ICCA window is money specifically for territories communities already conserve — the same instrument recorded in Burkina Faso's APAC entry, and it is open in Burundi now. THE THREE FINANCING STREAMS BEHIND IT, so you ask for the right one: the global environment facility itself, funding climate, biodiversity, land restoration, international waters and waste; STAR funds mobilised through the environment, agriculture and livestock ministry, promoting sustainable agriculture and HILLSIDE COLLECTIVE IRRIGATION; and the ICCA co-financing. Note also the constraint the national environment office states openly: it lacked the expertise and data to fill in climate-fund application dossiers, and needed training to write concept notes — if the state office found the forms hard, budget for help with yours. WHO IT SUITS: Burundian community organisations and associations with a conservation, restoration, agriculture or climate project — especially one on land the community already protects. CAVEATS: A DONOR-CYCLE PROGRAMME with competitive selection and fixed calls — confirm whether the current phase is open; it funds environmental projects, NOT litigation or land purchase. For park-edge site support groups, Burundi's ABO entry; for the first environmental civil society organisation, ODEB; for free legal advice and representation, the legal clinics entry.

trackers.name: Burundi's forest code — a planted woodlot belongs to whoever made it, if you hold real rights over the land; plus the state woodlots handed to communities to co-manage
trackers.desc: PLANT IT AND IT IS YOURS — WITH ONE CONDITION THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING: Burundi's forest code provides that BOISEMENTS BELONG TO THE NATURAL OR LEGAL PERSONS WHO MADE THEM OR HAD THEM MADE, SUBJECT TO THOSE PERSONS HOLDING REAL RIGHTS OVER THE LAND SO REFORESTED. Establish your right to the ground FIRST, then plant — in that order. Trees planted on land you cannot show a real right to belong to whoever can, and Burundi's forest domain is otherwise included in the PUBLIC DOMAIN of the state and the collectivities. The forest code was REVISED BY LOI N°1/07 OF 15 JANUARY 2016, whose objects include ending the reduction of forest cover, sustainable management, and significantly increasing the area of PROTECTED forest and of sustainably managed forest; protected areas are governed separately by loi n°1/10 of 30 May 2011 on the creation and management of protected areas. WHAT CATEGORY YOUR TREES FALL IN: Burundian forest formations are classed as NATURAL FORMATIONS, and BOISEMENTS that are DOMANIAL (state), COMMUNAL, or PRIVATE — the last including MICRO-BOISEMENTS; agroforestry covers roughly 60,000 ha, and most forest products people actually use come from plantations, wooded islets and agroforestry systems rather than natural forest, of which only about 6.6% of the territory remains. A micro-boisement or a family woodlot is a recognised legal category in Burundi, not an informality — which makes tree-planting one of the cheapest tenure acts available to a household. THE COMMUNITY ROUTE, DOCUMENTED AS A PILOT: the forests minister launched an experimental COMMUNITY MANAGEMENT approach over TWO PILOT STATE WOODLOTS in the north — 65 HA in Gashikanwa commune, Ngozi province, and 30 HA on Ntamba hill — under an instrument establishing PARTICIPATORY MANAGEMENT (AMÉNAGEMENT PARTICIPATIF) OF STATE WOODLOTS to reconcile poverty reduction with sustainable management, requiring the forest administration to RESPONSABILISER local populations in managing forest resources. Ask whether a state boisement near you has been placed under participatory management — the pilots are small and named, so the precedent is concrete. Note that exploitation of state AND COMMUNAL forests requires MANAGEMENT PLANS APPROVED by the forest administration. WHO IT SUITS: Burundian households, hills and communes planting or holding woodlots. CAVEATS: OWNERSHIP OF TREES FOLLOWS RIGHTS IN LAND, and land pressure and inheritance disputes are Burundi's dominant land problem; the code was under revision alongside the land code. For free advice and representation, Burundi's legal clinics entry; for 21 civil-society grants and the ICCA window, the GEF Small Grants entry; for park-edge groups, ABO.
