trackers.name: GRAMPTC — took a complaint against the World Bank's lender on behalf of 25,220 farmers in the Doba oil zone, and got it declared admissible
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Groupe de Recherches Alternatives et de Monitoring du Projet Pétrole Tchad-Cameroun, a non-profit founded in 2001 and registered in December 2001 under folio 1226, working on the environmental, social and economic impacts of oil production. WHAT IT DID, WHICH IS THE LARGEST COMMUNITY COMPLAINT IN THIS FILE: with six other organisations it filed a complaint in October 2011 on behalf of 25,220 farmers from 25 villages of the Doba oil zone against the World Bank Group's private-sector lender, over the land take of the oil installations, pollution damage to crops and livestock, inadequate compensation, restricted movement between villages under a de facto night curfew, and the absence of monitoring. The complaints office found it eligible in January 2012 and held 115 individual and 25 community complaints admissible, then sent a mission to meet the affected people. WHY YOU SHOULD READ ITS RESEARCH BEFORE ACCEPTING ANY COMPENSATION OFFER: GRAMPTC's field studies found that compensation for crops was still being paid at the prices used in the 1995 environmental impact study while market prices had risen sharply, that goods to be destroyed were miscounted or misidentified, and that on the sites it surveyed the restored topsoil was a fraction of the required depth, with some 76 hectares of farmland effectively lost. Compensation frozen at the price list in the original impact study is a pattern worth checking anywhere. It publishes a monthly bulletin, La Lettre de Transparence, and has continued to press on newer operators. B.P. 4021, N'Djaména Moursal. WHO IT SUITS: farming communities in Chad's oil zone facing land take, pollution or a compensation offer. CAVEATS: NO LIVE ORGANISATIONAL WEBSITE WAS VERIFIED, so this entry carries no URL rather than pointing at a third party — its bulletins are mirrored on Chadian research-centre sites. It is a research and monitoring body, not a law firm; the complaint route produced assessment and negotiation, not an order; and much of the published record dates from the 2011-2013 period.

trackers.name: Chad's three legal assistance services — APLFT, the women lawyers' association and the public interest law centre
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: three Chadian organisations that offer legal advice and judicial assistance, from providing information through to assistance BEFORE THE COURTS — the Association pour la Promotion des Libertés Fondamentales au Tchad (APLFT), the Association des Femmes Juristes du Tchad (AFJT), and the Public Interest Law Center (PILC). They were supported together under a two-year access-to-justice programme for people in vulnerable situations, funded by the European Union and run with an international lawyers' organisation. APLFT was founded on 9 June 1991 and recognised in June 1992; it works through standing commissions including “assistance et conseil juridiques” and one on women's and children's rights, publishes a monthly bulletin on fundamental freedoms, and has hundreds of active members in Chadian towns beyond the capital. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR LAND IN CHAD SPECIFICALLY: pressure on land in the far south is severe — farmland expanding onto traditional grazing areas, herders migrating in from neighbouring countries, and agropastoral conflicts that reached unprecedented levels between 2021 and 2024, with more than a thousand people killed and over two thousand injured, in provinces where a majority live below the poverty line. Most Chadian land disputes are not company-versus-village but neighbour-versus-neighbour under demographic pressure, and the resource that fits is a legal advice service, not a campaign. WHO IT SUITS: Chadians facing land disputes, farmer-herder conflict, expropriation or any matter needing advice or representation, especially women. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED LIVE SITE WAS FOUND FOR ANY OF THE THREE — this entry points at the international lawyers' organisation's published record of the joint programme; some details date from the programme period and should be confirmed locally. These are general legal-aid and human rights services, not land specialists. For the oil zone and the complaint route to a project's financier, Chad's GRAMPTC entry.

trackers.name: Chad's Fonds Spécial en faveur de l'Environnement — calls for proposals open to associations, with training workshops held in the provinces, at a published N'Djamena address
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the Fonds Spécial en faveur de l'Environnement (FSE), created by loi n°014/PR/98 of 17 August 1998 setting the general principles of environmental protection, and made operational in 2012 by décret n°168/PR/PM/MERH/2012, under the environment ministry. Its mission is to mobilise, manage and allocate finance for concrete projects of protection, restoration and valorisation of the environment across the whole national territory, and it expressly supports initiatives carried by LOCAL AUTHORITIES, CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS, public services and technical partners. Address: Avenue Ngarta Tombalbaye, Klemat, rue de 40m, opposite the two water towers, N'Djamena. HOW THE MONEY IS ACTUALLY OFFERED, AND IT IS THE PART TO WATCH FOR: the FSE runs APPELS À PROPOSITIONS — numbered calls — and holds INFORMATION AND TRAINING WORKSHOPS IN THE PROVINCES before the deadline, explaining the guidelines and the application form to local organisations and associations; a third call was worked through in Moyen-Chari, and it has run workshops in Batha and Ouaddaï to help local actors capture climate financing. If a call is open, the FSE will come and teach you how to fill in the form — attend that workshop; it is the cheapest application training a Chadian association will ever get. WHERE ITS MONEY COMES FROM: state and local-authority subsidies, ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION TAXES, AND FINES COLLECTED FOR DAMAGE CAUSED TO THE ENVIRONMENT — so polluter penalties are meant to fund community projects. THE FUND'S OWN ADMISSION, RECORDED BECAUSE IT SETS EXPECTATIONS: its director general has publicly identified the NON-DISBURSEMENT of FSE money held at the public treasury in recent years as delaying both its activities and its international accreditation. A fund that cannot draw its own money will be slow; ask what has actually been disbursed in the last cycle, not what was allocated. WHO IT SUITS: Chadian associations, local authorities and community organisations with an environmental restoration, desertification or climate project. CAVEATS: A STATE FUND under the environment ministry — it finances environmental action, NOT litigation or land purchase, and its own disbursement record is the constraint. For legal advice and court assistance, Chad's APLFT/AFJT/PILC entry.

trackers.name: Chad's loi 14/PR/2008 — community forests are CLASSED on the Conseil Rural's advice, and a classed forest is inalienable, imprescriptible and unseizable
trackers.desc: THE LAW THAT MAKES YOUR FOREST UNSEIZABLE: loi n°14/PR/2008 of 10 June 2008 on the regime of forests, wildlife and fisheries resources — 336 ARTICLES, and THE FIRST LAW OF ITS KIND IN CHAD SINCE INDEPENDENCE IN 1960. THE TWO PROVISIONS THAT MATTER: COMMUNITY FORESTS ARE CLASSED BY DECISION OF THE MINISTER IN CHARGE OF FORESTS, AFTER THE OPINION OF THE CONSEIL RURAL CONCERNED or the groupement d'intérêt — so the route runs through your rural council, not around it; and CLASSED FORESTS ARE INALIENABLE, IMPRESCRIPTIBLE AND UNSEIZABLE, AND THEY KEEP THEIR NATURE AS CLASSED FOREST EVEN WHEN THEY NO LONGER CARRY FOREST. Cannot be sold, cannot be lost by lapse of time, cannot be seized — and clearing it does not release it. That last clause defeats the commonest tactic in this file: destroy the trees, then argue there is nothing left to protect. Classing does not block buildings, tracks and infrastructure needed for the forest's own management, nor associated forestry activities consistent with the forest's vocation. THE SECOND INSTRUMENT, FOR WILDLIFE COUNTRY: the law introduces many notions of natural-resource management BY COMMUNITIES and expressly provides for RECLASSIFYING CERTAIN CATEGORIES OF PROTECTED AREA — particularly THOSE CURRENTLY PERFORMING BADLY — INTO A ZONE DE GESTION CONCERTÉE DE LA FAUNE, MANAGED BY LOCAL COMMUNITIES in partnership with state services and the private sector; it also allows a protected area to be organised as A CENTRAL CORE surrounded by PERIPHERAL ZONES MANAGED BY THE COMMUNITIES. A failing protected area next to you is an opportunity, not only a burden — the statute names underperformance as a ground for handing management to communities. Ask for reclassification by name. The law's stated policy options include the effective participation and responsabilisation of the population and poverty reduction through local employment and revenue. WHO IT SUITS: Chadian villages and rural councils near forest or a weak protected area. CAVEATS: CLASSING IS A MINISTERIAL DECISION and the recorded field pressures are severe — chronic insecurity, pastoral pressure, organised poaching; note also that Chad banned wood-cutting and charcoal production outright in 2008, which criminalises common village activity. For environmental project money and the provincial training workshops, Chad's Fonds Spécial en faveur de l'Environnement entry; for legal advice, the APLFT entry.

trackers.name: AFPAT, N'Djamena — Mbororo women's organisation working land-conflict resolution and 3D participatory mapping, with parity governance and a published address
trackers.desc: WHO MAPS AND WHO SETTLES LAND CONFLICTS: the ASSOCIATION DES FEMMES PEULES ET PEUPLES AUTOCHTONES DU TCHAD (AFPAT), a Chadian COMMUNITY ORGANISATION OF INDIGENOUS FULANI (MBORORO) WOMEN, CREATED 1999 WITH OFFICIAL AUTHORISATION TO OPERATE FROM 2005, based at Rue de Bouta, N'Djamena (afpat.net). ITS STATED WORKING METHODS ARE THE REASON IT IS IN THIS FILE: AFPAT works on THE DEFENCE OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS, the creation of economic activities, and THE PROTECTION AND MANAGEMENT OF THE NATURAL RESOURCES ON WHICH NOMADIC HERDING COMMUNITIES DEPEND, using innovative methods for THE RESOLUTION OF LAND CONFLICTS, THREE-DIMENSIONAL PARTICIPATORY MAPPING OF NATURAL RESOURCES, and work against climate change, desertification and biodiversity loss. Land-conflict resolution and 3D participatory mapping in one Chadian organisation is the exact pairing that has won cases elsewhere in this file — Brainforest in Gabon, Action Mines in Guinea. In Chad it is held by a herders' women's association, which means it is reachable by pastoralists rather than only by villages with fixed fields. HOW IT IS GOVERNED, AND THIS IS WORTH COPYING: AFPAT is A STRUCTURE OF PARITY GOVERNANCE — the bureau and the team respect STRICT PARITY — with governance and all projects resting on the participation of women. Parity written into the statutes rather than promised in a proposal is what makes a women's mandate survive a change of leadership. WHERE ITS REACH EXTENDS: AFPAT is a member of the Congo Basin indigenous peoples' network (REPALEAC) and took part in a REGIONAL WORKSHOP ON LAND RIGHTS under a Community of Practice on land tenure in the Congo Basin (October 2025); it is registered in the UN civil-society database; and its coordinator sits as president of an international forest-certification body's Indigenous Peoples council. Its field campaigns run across Logone Occidental, Mayo Kebbi-Ouest and Mayo Kebbi-Est, with a green-entrepreneurship and climate-adaptation training workshop for women trainers held in N'Djamena with the environment ministry. WHO IT SUITS: Chadian pastoralist and Mbororo communities facing land conflict, and anyone needing a terroir mapped or a regional land-rights channel. CAVEATS: AN ADVOCACY AND MAPPING ORGANISATION, NOT A FUNDER OR A LAW FIRM. For the law that makes a classed forest inalienable and unseizable, Chad's loi 14/PR/2008 entry; for environment project money and the provincial calls, the Fonds Spécial en faveur de l'Environnement entry; for legal advice, APLFT.

trackers.name: Dahari
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the only IUCN member in the Comoros, founded in 2013, with around sixty staff working alongside communities on Anjouan and Grande Comore. Its central instrument is the INDIVIDUAL CONSERVATION AGREEMENT: a farmer contracts with Dahari for a fixed term not to clear forest or cut native trees on their plot, and receives payments calculated by the area preserved, checked by periodic inspection of the parcel. Management of the Moya forest zone has been delegated to Dahari by the national protected-areas network, and it has supported fishers in establishing the country's first permanent community-managed marine reserve. USE IT: if you hold or farm land carrying native forest, the conservation agreement is a way to make leaving it standing pay; if you fish, the marine programme is the route to a community-managed no-take zone.

trackers.name: Comoros — Ministry of Finance & Budget
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the Ministry of Finance, Budget & Banking Sector prepares & implements the state finance laws (lois de finances) and budget, and oversees public-spending control via the General Inspection of Finance, Comoros. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in the Comoros.

trackers.name: Comoros — Agence Nationale pour la Promotion des Investissements (ANPI)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the ANPI (est. 2008, under the Ministry of Investment) operates the guichet unique for company creation & permits and maintains a public directory of officially registered Comorian companies, Comoros. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: Parcs nationaux des Comores — check which law governs your site
trackers.desc: TWO REGIMES EXIST AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME. The Comoros has had a loi-cadre relative à l'environnement since 1994, and the first protected area was classified under article 46 of it — a participatory process from January 1999 leading to the 2001 décret creating the Parc marin de Mohéli. Then Loi n° 18-005/AU of 5 December 2018 on the système national des aires protégées, promulgated 26 November 2019, replaced the framework, and on 23 May the head of state signed décrets formally establishing 5 new protected areas. Establish whether your site sits under article 46 of the 1994 loi-cadre or under the 2018 system law — older classifications predate the newer statute. NOTE THE STATUS: the Parc marin de Mohéli is an établissement public à caractère administratif under the environment minister's tutelle — a state body, whatever its community origins. And its founding decree prohibits industrial or commercial activities in the park outright, regulates ecotourism planning and provides for strict application of penalties — a flat prohibition is stronger than a permitting regime, so check whether your area carries the same term. Since 2016 the strategic vision, with UNDP and GEF support, has been a system managing 27 percent of national territory with a community approach.

trackers.name: Mohéli — the two questions the model never answered
trackers.desc: IF YOU ARE OFFERED THE MOHÉLI MODEL, ASK WHAT IT LEFT OUT. The park began as a community effort to protect turtles at Mohéli's south-eastern tip — one of the Indian Ocean's largest green turtle nesting sites — and became the country's first protected area in 2001, winning the Equator Initiative prize at the 2002 Johannesburg Earth Summit. UNDP called it a ‘méthode de cogestion couronnée de succès’ and the state is replicating it across Ngazidja, Ndzuani and Mohéli. BUT SEVERAL UN REPORTS AND SOURCES INTERVIEWED BY MONGABAY RECORD THAT IT IS FAR FROM A TOTAL SUCCESS: it produced no defined plan either for supporting the communities whose traditional rights were restricted by the protected areas, or for sustainable financing of the network. So ask those two questions — what is the defined plan to support people whose traditional rights are restricted, and what is the financing plan? Both gaps are documented in UN reporting, so the questions are evidenced rather than adversarial. AND KNOW THE MISUNDERSTANDING THAT RECURS EVERYWHERE: Hachime Abdéremane of the Comorian NGO Ulanga-Ngazidja, who helped create the park, put it exactly — ‘at the start, officials thought we were going to create a park, install barriers and charge outsiders entry. Whereas for us it was a park at community scale, which meant we were going to work with the residents.’ Principal activities are fishing, agriculture and livestock; dynamite fishing was the practice that first alerted conservationists.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Comoros' FADC — the national community development fund, which finances labour-intensive village works
trackers.desc: WHERE COMMUNITY MONEY COMES FROM: the Fonds d'Appui au Développement Communautaire (FADC), the Comorian national vehicle through which community development money is channelled. A documented transfer shows how it is fed and what it buys: 500 million Comorian francs, part of a budget-support package released by France, were retroceded to the FADC to finance HIGH LABOUR-INTENSITY WORKS (travaux à haute intensité de main d'oeuvre). Labour-intensive works are the form of community money most useful to a village under pressure — the budget is spent on local wages and a physical asset in your own commune, not on a consultancy. WHY THIS ENTRY EXISTS AT ALL, AND IT IS AN HONEST CORRECTION: the Comoros was researched TWICE in this file for a civil-society organisation to stand beside communities — in both cases nothing met the bar, and the country was left with a single conservation entry. The answer turned out not to be an NGO but the fund itself: in a small island state with a thin associative sector, the realistic lever is the national community fund and the commune that applies to it. Ask which FADC-financed works are planned in your commune, who selected them, and whether the labour is being hired locally — those three questions are the whole of community oversight here. WHO IT SUITS: Comorian villages and communal authorities seeking financing for local infrastructure and work programmes, on any of the islands. CAVEATS: SOURCING FOR THIS ENTRY IS THIN — the verified facts are the fund's existence, its purpose and one documented transfer; NO CLAIM is made here about current windows, ceilings or application routes, so confirm those locally before relying on them. The FADC is a state channel, not an advocate, and it will not oppose a project. For community conservation and agriculture agreements, Comoros' Dahari entry.

trackers.name: Comoros — a published attorney list with street addresses, free Supreme Court case law, and the CADI courts that decide village land disputes first
trackers.desc: WHERE TO FIND A LAWYER AND WHICH COURT DECIDES: no Comorian legal aid organisation could be verified for this file, so the practical route is three published things. (1) AN ATTORNEY LIST WITH STREET ADDRESSES IS PUBLISHED for Moroni — including practitioners on the Route de la Corniche, at Immeuble Ridjal, and on Boulevard Karthala facing the Comoros Museum and the Palais de Justice — which in a country with one multi-advocate firm is how you find counsel at all. (2) COMORIAN SUPREME COURT JUDGMENTS ARE PUBLISHED FREE on a francophone case-law database, searchable by chamber — judicial, administrative, social. Free access to your own supreme court's reasoning is not a small thing where government printers charge per page; take the citation of a comparable case with you. (3) THE COURT STRUCTURE A LAND DISPUTE ACTUALLY RUNS THROUGH, and this is the substantive point: the Supreme Court record shows a judgment of the TRIBUNAL DE CADI at Foumbouni — a traditional court — concerning THE VILLAGERS of a named locality being PARTIALLY OVERTURNED by the Moroni Court of Appeal. So a village land case may start before a cadi and be reopened on appeal in the formal courts — losing at the cadi stage is not the end, and the appeal route is documented. A judge of the Moroni commercial court has separately written that the COEXISTENCE OF TRADITIONAL AND FORMAL JUDICIAL SYSTEMS harms efficiency and confidence in justice, and that DIFFICULTIES IN EXECUTING JUDGMENTS are a recognised national problem — plan for enforcement as a separate fight, as in Lesotho and Zambia. WHO IT SUITS: Comorians with a land, inheritance or village boundary dispute on any island, and anyone needing to instruct counsel or cite precedent. CAVEATS: THIN GROUND, STATED HONESTLY — what is recorded here is a directory, a database and a court structure, NOT a legal aid service; the attorney list is a foreign-mission compilation and should be checked as current. For community conservation and agriculture agreements, Comoros' Dahari entry; for community works funding, the FADC entry.

trackers.name: Comoros' accords de cogestion — article 60 of loi 18-105/AU, one agreement PER VILLAGE, village écogardes, and a village committee that handles breaches before any court
trackers.desc: A CO-MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT PER VILLAGE: the Comorian protected-areas system rests on LOI N°18-105/AU on the SYSTÈME NATIONAL DES AIRES PROTÉGÉES, whose ARTICLE 60 governs ACCORDS DE COGESTION — agreements that establish and organise co-management involving the responsibility and participation of named VILLAGE COMMUNITIES, and which are expected to EVOLVE FROM CONSULTATIVE co-management, state-led in its first learning phase, TOWARD COOPERATIVE co-management IN WHICH RESPONSIBILITIES ARE SHARED FOR BOTH TAKING AND APPLYING DECISIONS. Ask in writing which of the two types your agreement is, and what triggers the move from consultative to cooperative — that transition is where real authority passes, and the statute already names it as the direction of travel. HOW IT WORKS ON THE GROUND AT MOHÉLI, the country's first protected area (April 2001, renamed a national park in 2015, a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2021): EACH VILLAGE HAS ITS OWN SPECIFIC CO-MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT; ANY BREACH OF THE RULES IS DEALT WITH DIRECTLY BY A COMMITTEE OF VILLAGERS, and the case is transferred to the national judicial system ONLY WHERE LOCAL SOLUTIONS CANNOT BE FOUND; and local residents act as ÉCOGARDES responsible for awareness-raising and surveillance, trained with external technical support. One agreement per village and a village committee as the first instance is the strongest co-management design recorded in this file — it keeps enforcement local and cheap, and it means a neighbouring village's failure does not void your agreement. The park covers roughly 400 km2 marine and 200 km2 terrestrial, with 4,404 ha of marine area, protecting green and hawksbill turtle nesting; the model has been described as a successful co-management method and is being replicated across Ngazidja, Ndzuani and Mohéli. THE FAILURE, RECORDED SO YOU NEGOTIATE FOR IT: fourteen years after creation the park had NO DEDICATED OPERATING FINANCE and lived project to project, and THE ECONOMIC IMPACTS THE COMMUNITIES EXPECTED NEVER FOLLOWED; UN reporting found no defined plan either for SUPPORTING COMMUNITIES WHOSE TRADITIONAL RIGHTS WERE RESTRICTED by the protected areas, or for sustainably financing the network. If your traditional rights are being restricted, put the compensation and the funding line in the agreement itself — Mohéli shows that goodwill without a financing clause produces two decades of unmet expectation. WHO IT SUITS: Comorian coastal and forest villages inside or beside a protected area. CAVEATS: CO-MANAGEMENT OF STATE-DECLARED AREAS, NOT TENURE. For village-scale conservation agreements, Comoros' Dahari entry; for community works money, the FADC entry; for the cadi appeal route and the attorney list, the Comoros legal entry.

trackers.name: Ulanga-Ngazidja — the Grande Comore NGO that helped create a national park and signs partnership conventions with park conservators; its head defines what community-scale means
trackers.desc: THE NGO ON THE OTHER ISLAND: ULANGA-NGAZIDJA is a Comorian environmental NGO working on GRANDE COMORE (NGAZIDJA) — the island Dahari does not cover — which publishes its own environmental journal (Habari za Ulanga) and SIGNED A CONVENTION DE PARTENARIAT WITH THE CONSERVATOR OF THE PARC NATIONAL MITSAMIOULI-NDROUDÉ, at a ceremony gathering park members, LOCAL AUTHORITIES and the NGO. The convention fixes the terms of cooperation, both parties undertaking to cooperate on awareness-raising for environmental protection and valorisation, WITH THE STATED AIM OF CONTRIBUTING TO IMPROVING THE LIVING CONDITIONS OF THE COMMUNITIES LIVING IN THE PARK'S ZONES. A signed, publicly reported convention between a village NGO and a park conservator is a template you can ask for by name — it puts community living conditions into the text rather than leaving them to goodwill, which is exactly what Mohéli's twenty years of unmet expectation lacked. WHAT ITS HEAD SAYS, AND IT IS THE CLEAREST STATEMENT OF THE ARGUMENT IN THIS FILE: Hachime Abdéremane, head of Ulanga-Ngazidja, who took part in creating the park, recalls that AT THE START THE OFFICIALS THOUGHT WE WERE GOING TO CREATE A PARK, PUT UP BARRIERS AND CHARGE OUTSIDERS FOR ENTRY — WHEREAS FOR US IT WAS A PARK AT COMMUNITY SCALE, WHICH MEANT WE WERE GOING TO WORK WITH THE RESIDENTS. Say that sentence in your own first meeting. The difference between a fenced park and a community park is decided in the first conversation, not in the management plan. WHAT THE SITE HOLDS AND WHAT THREATENED IT: Ndroudé shelters the ÎLOT AUX TORTUES, a major GREEN TURTLE NESTING SITE unique on Ngazidja, whose reputation had been destroyed by POACHING, with recovery supported since 2011 by a Swiss marine-mammal conservation organisation. The other documented threat across the archipelago is DYNAMITE FISHING — pure dynamite thrown into the water to stun and kill fish en masse, with shockwaves capable of levelling coral reefs. WHO IT SUITS: Ngazidja villages and anyone on Grande Comore needing a domestic environmental partner or a park agreement precedent. CAVEATS: A VOLUNTEER-BASED NATIONAL NGO, not a funder or a legal service. For Anjouan and the village agreements, Comoros' Dahari entry; for the one-agreement-per-village co-management design, the accords de cogestion entry; for community works money, FADC.

trackers.name: Observatoire Congolais des Droits de l’Homme (OCDH)
trackers.desc: Leading independent human-rights organization in the Republic of Congo (Congo-Brazzaville), founded in 1994 — it monitors and documents the country’s catastrophic prison conditions and deaths in custody from starvation and neglect, torture and arbitrary detention, and the treatment of political prisoners, runs projects to prevent torture and arbitrary detention, and supports victims of human-rights violations in seeking justice; an ACHPR-observer NGO and member of FIDH and the World Organisation Against Torture, twice awarded the French Republic’s Human Rights Prize.

trackers.name: Association pour les Droits de l'Homme et l'Univers Carcéral (ADHUC)
trackers.desc: L’association pour les Droits de L’Homme et de L’Univers (ADHU) is concerned with the protection and promotion of human rights, in particular the rights of indigenous peoples such as the Pygmies. It is also concerned with respecting the rights of prisoners and improving conditions in Congolese detention facilities.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes et de discipline budgétaire
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Congo (Rep.), auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: ITIE Congo
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and licences in Republic of the Congo.

trackers.name: Republic of the Congo — Agence Congolaise pour la Création des Entreprises (ACPCE)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the ACPCE one-stop window centralises company-creation formalities, legal announcements & the business register, Republic of the Congo. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Republic of the Congo — Ministère des Finances, du Budget et du Portefeuille public
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares & executes the State budget and manages public finances & the public portfolio, Republic of the Congo (Brazzaville). Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in the Republic of the Congo.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: COMIFAC Treaty and Plan de Convergence — and its community protocol
trackers.desc: A TREATY BODY WITH A TEMPLATE YOU CAN COPY. The Traité relatif à la conservation et à la gestion durable des écosystèmes forestiers d'Afrique Centrale, signed by heads of state at their second summit on 5 February 2005 in Brazzaville, instituted the Commission des Forêts d'Afrique Centrale — described as the unique instance d'orientation, de décision et de coordination for subregional forest action, and the cadre politique et juridique global for cooperation in the field. A transboundary forest question belongs in that forum. The Plan de Convergence is the reference framework for all such interventions — first edition 2005–2014, revised in 2014 for 2015–2025 and restructured into 10 strategic axes, executed by a Secrétariat exécutif. CIVIL SOCIETY IS A NAMED STAKEHOLDER in implementing it, alongside state administrations, CEEAC and the private sector — so participation is built into the framework, not conceded case by case. Axis 7 covers capacity and participation des acteurs, expressly contemplating micro-projets générateurs de revenus pour les populations locales; axis 9 covers innovative financing mechanisms. THE DOCUMENT LIBRARY IS THE MOST USEFUL PART: COMIFAC publishes a worked Protocole Bioculturel Communautaire for a named village, a guide to inventorying genetic resources and traditional knowledge, a paper on les droits d'usage des peuples autochtones et communautés locales et les obligations qui en découlent, a subregional APA (access and benefit-sharing) strategy, and directives on forests and the SDGs built with FAO as 5 principles and 12 directives across 31 prioritised targets. A community biocultural protocol published by a treaty body is a template, not a theory. AND ITS OWN DIAGNOSIS IS QUOTABLE: the Plan records that participatory natural resource management and mediation of use conflicts, though already mapped out, are insufficiently developed.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Comptoir Juridique Junior — free legal clinics in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, staffed by young lawyers and supervised by magistrates
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Congolese association founded in 2000 by young jurists, which runs free legal clinics in neighbourhoods of Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire — open since 2002, staffed by young and unemployed lawyers, supervised by professional magistrates. The premise is the one that matters where courts feel unreachable: people have no money for an advocate and no confidence in the system, so the clinic is the relay that gets them into it. Its services are free legal advice, judicial accompaniment, and alternative dispute resolution — mediation and non-violent communication — alongside information campaigns and training. WHY IT BELONGS IN THIS MAP RATHER THAN A GENERAL LEGAL AID LIST: CJJ states that it fights continuously for the rights of indigenous peoples in the Republic of Congo through projects across the country, and it hosts the Congolese arm of the standardised external independent forest monitoring system, SNOIE-Congo — a certified process for documenting forest infractions and getting them to the authorities, run out of its Brazzaville office with a technical and ethics evaluation committee. A community with a logging or land problem therefore gets both the documentation route and the lawyers in one place. It also does citizen monitoring of public spending. B.P. 13700 Brazzaville. WHO IT SUITS: indigenous and rural communities and poor urban households in the Republic of Congo; the clinics take general civil matters too, which is how most people first walk in. CAVEATS: a small, lightly structured association run substantially on volunteers, and the reported caseload is heavy across many subjects, so expect queues; published email addresses are personal or generic, and older material sits on a legacy Google Sites page as well as the current domain.

trackers.name: RPDH, Pointe-Noire — works the cahier des charges, the schedule of obligations a company owes your village, and why it goes unrespected
trackers.desc: WHO ENFORCES WHAT THE COMPANY OWES YOU: Rencontre pour la Paix et les Droits de l'Homme (RPDH), a Congolese organisation working on natural resource governance, which publishes on what prevents respect of the CAHIER DES CHARGES in the Kouilou department — the schedule of social obligations a forestry or mining company signs up to for the communities around its permit. If a company promised your village a school, a road or a water point, that promise lives in the cahier des charges; the document exists whether or not anyone has shown it to you, and the first move is to obtain it and read what was actually signed. RPDH also anchors the national chapter of the extractives transparency coalition, whose published monitoring has covered 179 public investment projects in health, energy and water across a budget year, and it convenes national multi-actor forums on climate initiatives and sustainable forest management jointly with the Congolese human rights observatory. THE LAW THAT CHANGED IN 2020, AND THE GAP INSIDE IT: law n°33-2020 of 8 July 2020, the forest code, for the first time in Congo authorises forest management directly by LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND INDIGENOUS POPULATIONS (CLPA) — community forestry. Communities affected by logging also hold a right to benefit-sharing under a specific cahier des charges, and management plans must be adopted by a commission including civil society, local authorities and the communities and indigenous peoples concerned. BUT the code does NOT set out the attribution procedure: it defers to a ministerial order for how a community forest is allocated and delimited, how the monitoring body works, and what the simple management plan must contain — so ask whether that order has been issued before relying on the right. Community representatives have separately demanded that government and extractive companies guarantee their involvement in drawing up those particular cahiers de charges. WHO IT SUITS: Congolese villages beside a logging or mining permit, especially in Kouilou and the south-west, and communities pursuing benefit-sharing or the new community forestry route. CAVEATS: a governance, monitoring and advocacy organisation — not a law firm and not a fund; the community forestry route depends on implementing texts that may not yet exist. For free legal clinics in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, Congo's Comptoir Juridique Junior entry; for indigenous rights monitoring, OCDH.

trackers.name: Congo's Fonds de Développement Local — each forest unit's fund has its own published arrêté fixing the project/running-cost SPLIT and the payment dates
trackers.desc: THE MONEY OWED TO YOUR VILLAGE: in Congo-Brazzaville each unité forestière d'aménagement (UFA) has a SÉRIE DE DÉVELOPPEMENT COMMUNAUTAIRE with its own FONDS DE DÉVELOPPEMENT LOCAL, fed by a redevance paid by the logging company, and each fund is governed by its OWN ARRÊTÉ PUBLISHED IN THE JOURNAL OFFICIEL — Ngombé, Missa, Ipendja, Loundoungou-Toukoulaka, Djua-Ikié among them. Find the arrêté for the UFA next to your village: it is a public document and it states the rules of your fund by name. WHAT THOSE ARRÊTÉS ACTUALLY FIX, and this is the number to check first: the SPLIT between projects and administration — at Ngombé and Missa, 85% to the activities in the annual programme and 15% to running costs; at Djua-Ikié, 70% to activities and 30% to running costs INCLUDING PAYING A TECHNICAL ASSISTANT. Compare that with Gabon, where monitors found a company charging committee running costs against the fund with no ceiling at all — a published percentage is the defence. Djua-Ikié further splits the investment share 60% to microprojects of the communities DIRECTLY IMPACTED in or near the annual cutting block, 40% to the others. WHEN THE MONEY MUST ARRIVE: the arrêtés set the instalments — 50% of the annual redevance on delivery of the annual cutting authorisation, 25% in the first half of June, and 25% on completion of the annual cut AFTER the exploited volume has been readjusted. That last clause matters: the final instalment is recalculated on the volume actually cut, so ask for the readjustment figure. TWO PROTECTIONS WORTH KNOWING: cheques for disbursement must be countersigned by the president, the second vice-president of the conseil de concertation and the fund's accountant; and unused funds at year-end are automatically returned IN FULL to the local development fund rather than lapsing. WHO IT SUITS: Congolese villages inside or beside a forest management unit. CAVEATS: A CONTRACTUAL AND REGULATORY ENTITLEMENT, NOT A GRANT — it exists only where a UFA operates, and reporting from Louvakou records expropriation without compensation where land was sold to companies without the village committee's agreement. For the cahier des charges and mining, Congo's RPDH entry; for free legal clinics, Comptoir Juridique Junior; for indigenous rights, OCDH.

trackers.name: Réserve Communautaire du Lac Télé — 438,960 hectares and the ONLY community protected area in Congo; the precedent to cite when asking for a second
trackers.desc: THE ONE COMMUNITY-HELD AREA IN THE COUNTRY: the RÉSERVE COMMUNAUTAIRE DU LAC TÉLÉ-LIKOUALA-AUX-HERBES (RCLT), 438,960 HECTARES in the Likouala department, is recorded as THE ONLY CONGOLESE PROTECTED AREA DESCRIBED AS COMMUNAUTAIRE, and THE FIRST OF ITS TYPE TO BE INSCRIBED ON THE RAMSAR LIST as a wetland of international importance — swamp forest, seasonally flooded forest, savanna and marsh. One precedent is enough to argue from: a community reserve of that size already exists in Congolese law and practice, so the answer to a request for a second one cannot be that the category does not exist. WHAT THE LAW PROVIDES AND WHAT IT STILL LACKS, STATED TOGETHER: Congo's protected-areas law lists COMMUNITY RESERVES alongside special reserves, wildlife sanctuaries and zones of interest and is the central legal instrument for protected-area management — BUT its implementing texts were recorded as STILL BEING VALIDATED, so it is NOT YET EQUIPPED WITH THE DECREES that would let it operate fully. Ask which implementing decree governs the category you are applying under, and whether it has been published — this is the fifth Congolese instrument in this file where the statute exists and the machinery lags. A SECOND ROUTE IN THE SAME LEGAL FAMILY: the forest code does not mention protected areas explicitly but defines FORÊTS DE CONSERVATION NATURELLE (article 10), part of the state domain, whose mission is to secure the permanence of forest species, protect wildlife and flora habitats and preserve landscapes — and it sets the management rules for their peripheral zones, which is where villages sit. WHO IT SUITS: Congolese communities seeking recognised protection over a large shared territory, especially wetland or swamp-forest, and anyone needing a domestic precedent. CAVEATS: A STATE-RECOGNISED COMMUNITY RESERVE, NOT COMMUNITY OWNERSHIP — management is co-run and the enabling decrees were incomplete at the time recorded; verify the current position. For the logging fund your villages are owed and its published percentages, Congo's Fonds de Développement Local entry; for the cahier des charges and mining, RPDH; for free consultation, the bureaux de consultations gratuites.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Djibouti, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Djibouti — Ministère de l’Économie et des Finances (MEFIP)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; manages public finances & the economy and prepares the State budget, Djibouti. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Djibouti.

trackers.name: Djibouti — Guichet Unique (ANPI)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the ANPI’s Guichet Unique registers company constitution acts and (with the ODPIC) handles RCCM immatriculation & fiscal/social registration, Djibouti. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: Djibouti Nature — the country's oldest conservation association, and the civil society relay on the marine protected areas
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an independent, membership-based, non-profit grassroots association established in December 1999 (formerly the Wildlife Protection Organization) — the oldest and most experienced civil society organisation working on nature conservation in Djibouti. It is small, and it is effectively the only such body with a public record. WHY IT MATTERS WHERE YOU LIVE: Djibouti's marine protected areas are drawn around inhabited places — Khor Angar, Godoria, Ras Siyan, the Seven Brothers islands, Douda-Haramous, the Musha and Maskali islands and Arta — and the national programme has involved those communities in marine biodiversity protection, with training delivered locally in tourism and coastguard work. The government's own stated aim has been to expand the protected marine area substantially. That means the designation is the lever: a community inside or beside a protected area has a standing that a community on unprotected coast does not, and Djibouti Nature is named in national biodiversity reporting as one of the associations that acts as the relay between those programmes and the public. Note the honest complication, because it cuts both ways: analysts have observed that the siting of Djibouti's marine areas serves territorial control as well as ecology — the designations are not purely environmental, and a community should understand which interest it is aligning with. Its own published work is species and site documentation across the Goda mountains, Day forest, Bankouale, Assamo, the mangroves at Godoria and Douda, and the islands. WHO IT SUITS: coastal, island and mountain communities needing baseline documentation, membership of a recognised association, or a national counterpart. CAVEATS: a small scientific and conservation association — no legal capacity, no intake route, no fee information; civic space in Djibouti is narrow and the organisation works with rather than against the state.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants in Djibouti — an open call to community groups, 24 months maximum, and a 50% CO-FINANCING requirement half of which may be in kind
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the GEF Small Grants Programme (SGP), eighth operational phase, in DJIBOUTI, implemented with the UN development programme, inviting proposals FROM CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS AND GRASSROOTS COMMUNITY GROUPS for community-led projects on biodiversity conservation, climate mitigation and adaptation, SUSTAINABLE LAND MANAGEMENT, international waters, and reduction of harmful chemicals and waste. THE TWO TERMS THAT DECIDE WHETHER YOU CAN APPLY, and they are published: projects may run a MAXIMUM OF 24 MONTHS, and are required to provide AT LEAST 50% CO-FINANCING, DIVIDED EQUALLY BETWEEN CASH CONTRIBUTIONS AND IN-KIND SUPPORT. That means half the co-financing can be labour, land, materials or premises rather than money — count what your community already contributes before deciding you cannot meet the match, because in-kind is where a village's real contribution lives. Eligible proposals must align with national frameworks including the National Action Plan for Sustainable Environment (NAPE), show strategic relevance and clear environmental and social impact, and be DESIGNED COLLABORATIVELY WITH THE LOCAL COMMUNITY. Priorities include local climate resilience, affordable sustainable energy for household and economic use, and environmentally responsible livelihoods including agricultural production, processing and marketing. WHY THIS ENTRY EXISTS: Djibouti was searched THREE TIMES in this file for a local land or legal organisation and nothing verifiable was found beyond its conservation association. As in the Comoros, the realistic route in a small state with a thin associative sector is not an NGO to enlist but a CALL TO ANSWER — and this one is addressed to grassroots community groups by name. WHO IT SUITS: Djiboutian community groups and associations with a land management, water, energy or livelihoods project. CAVEATS: A DONOR CYCLE WITH FIXED DEADLINES and a real co-financing requirement — confirm the current call before counting on it; it funds environmental action, NOT litigation, land purchase or opposition to a project. For the country's conservation association, Djibouti's Djibouti Nature entry.

trackers.name: Djibouti's audiences foraines — the court travels to your commune and the calendar MUST be posted on the mairie door; there are only about 12 advocates, all in the capital
trackers.desc: WHERE JUSTICE PHYSICALLY HAPPENS, AND WHY THAT IS THE WHOLE QUESTION HERE: under Djibouti's Code de procédure civile (loi n°004/AN/18/8), Article L.111-12, the seat of the TRIBUNAL DE PREMIÈRE INSTANCE is in Djibouti city and its jurisdiction covers the ENTIRE territory — BUT AUDIENCES FORAINES (travelling hearings) MAY BE HELD at the seat of the communes of Djibouti city and Balbala AND AT THE SEAT OF EACH REGIONAL COUNCIL. AND THE PUBLICITY RULE IS THE PART TO USE: the CALENDAR OF THE AUDIENCES FORAINES IS MADE PUBLIC BY POSTING ON THE DOOR OF THE MAIRIES OR REGIONAL COUNCILS CONCERNED, and by any other appropriate means. Watch the door of your mairie — that posted calendar is how a person outside the capital learns when a court will physically be within reach, and it is required, not discretionary. A second provision: a DETACHED JUDGE of the personal status tribunal sits in each commune and region of the interior and must RESIDE at the regional or communal chief town, with the number and days of hearings fixed at the start of the judicial year. THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES EVERYTHING, STATED PLAINLY: an official account records about TWELVE ADVOCATES registered at the Djiboutian bar, ALL PRACTISING IN THE CAPITAL — for the simple reason that there are no tribunals in the other districts; fees are agreed freely between advocate and client under the profession's governing law. Twelve advocates for a whole country means the binding constraint is availability, not eligibility — secure counsel before you time anything else. New civil and civil procedure codes were adopted to replace the inherited colonial codes, with the second book of the civil code covering PROPERTY and patrimony. WHO IT SUITS: Djiboutians outside the capital needing to reach a court, and anyone timing a land or property claim. CAVEATS: NO LEGAL AID ORGANISATION OR CLINIC COULD BE VERIFIED for Djibouti — this entry records a procedural right and a bar of about twelve practitioners, not a service; foreign missions publish attorney lists that should be checked as current. For community environmental funding, Djibouti's GEF Small Grants entry; for the conservation association, Djibouti Nature.

trackers.name: Djibouti's loi 16/AN/23 on protected areas — the LOCAL COMMUNITY is named as a possible gestionnaire, and DECAN got two areas classified on its own initiative
trackers.desc: THE LAW THAT NAMES YOUR COMMUNITY AS MANAGER: LOI N°16/AN/23/9ème L on protected areas defines a GESTIONNAIRE D'UNE AIRE PROTÉGÉE as ANY PUBLIC OR PRIVATE PERSON, MIXED GROUPING, LEGALLY CONSTITUTED GROUPING OR THE LOCAL COMMUNITY assuring the management of the protected area in collaboration with the stakeholders concerned. The local community is written into the statute as a category of manager, not as a consultee — that single definition is what a Djiboutian community should quote when asking to manage the ground it lives on. The law also defines ÉCOTOURISME as responsible and sustainable tourism based on conserving Djibouti's natural heritage, RESPECTING THE ENVIRONMENT AND THE POPULATIONS WHILE ENSURING AN EQUITABLE REDISTRIBUTION OF THE ECONOMIC BENEFITS, and requires a PLAN D'AMÉNAGEMENT ET DE GESTION for each area, with areas linked in a RÉSEAU. Equitable redistribution is in the definition of the activity itself — so a tourism operation inside a protected area that returns nothing locally is failing the statutory definition, not merely being ungenerous. Behind it, the CODE DE L'ENVIRONNEMENT (loi 51/AN/09) guarantees EVERY PERSON RESIDING IN DJIBOUTI THE RIGHT TO A HEALTHY ENVIRONMENT, and places environmental policy on the state IN CLOSE COLLABORATION WITH LOCAL AUTHORITIES, CITIZENS AND CIVIL SOCIETY ACTORS. WHO HAS ACTUALLY DONE IT: DECAN, a Djiboutian association for the protection of the country's fauna and flora, IDENTIFIED AND DEFINED TWO PROTECTED AREAS — the DJALÉLO valley (45 km2, Arta region, 40 km from the capital) and the ASSAMO massif (15 km2, Ali-Sabieh region) — and it was ON THAT ASSOCIATION'S INITIATIVE, with ministry support, THAT THE GOVERNMENT CLASSIFIED BOTH SITES, creating a particular legal status of aire naturelle protégée for them; DECAN built an eco-camp on each area, and THE TOTALITY OF THE FUNDS RECEIVED IS REUSED DIRECTLY FOR PROTECTING THE SITES IT MANAGES. A local association identified the land, defined the boundary and the state then classified it — in Djibouti the initiative can come from below, and there are two named precedents. The context is stark: the Day forest, Djibouti's only forest and one of the continent's last primary forests, has fallen from about 7,500 ha two centuries ago to 1,500 ha in 1984 and under 900 ha today, with a law voted to give it protected-area status. WHO IT SUITS: Djiboutian communities and associations seeking to have ground classified and to manage it. CAVEATS: CLASSIFICATION IS A STATE ACT AND MANAGEMENT IS BY DESIGNATION — not tenure; the Day forest case shows protection status arriving without secured finance. For the posted travelling-court calendar and the twelve-advocate bar, Djibouti's audiences foraines entry; for community project money, the GEF Small Grants entry; for the conservation association, Djibouti Nature.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: COMIFAC Treaty and Plan de Convergence — and its community protocol
trackers.desc: A TREATY BODY WITH A TEMPLATE YOU CAN COPY. The Traité relatif à la conservation et à la gestion durable des écosystèmes forestiers d'Afrique Centrale, signed by heads of state at their second summit on 5 February 2005 in Brazzaville, instituted the Commission des Forêts d'Afrique Centrale — described as the unique instance d'orientation, de décision et de coordination for subregional forest action, and the cadre politique et juridique global for cooperation in the field. A transboundary forest question belongs in that forum. The Plan de Convergence is the reference framework for all such interventions — first edition 2005–2014, revised in 2014 for 2015–2025 and restructured into 10 strategic axes, executed by a Secrétariat exécutif. CIVIL SOCIETY IS A NAMED STAKEHOLDER in implementing it, alongside state administrations, CEEAC and the private sector — so participation is built into the framework, not conceded case by case. Axis 7 covers capacity and participation des acteurs, expressly contemplating micro-projets générateurs de revenus pour les populations locales; axis 9 covers innovative financing mechanisms. THE DOCUMENT LIBRARY IS THE MOST USEFUL PART: COMIFAC publishes a worked Protocole Bioculturel Communautaire for a named village, a guide to inventorying genetic resources and traditional knowledge, a paper on les droits d'usage des peuples autochtones et communautés locales et les obligations qui en découlent, a subregional APA (access and benefit-sharing) strategy, and directives on forests and the SDGs built with FAO as 5 principles and 12 directives across 31 prioritised targets. A community biocultural protocol published by a treaty body is a template, not a theory. AND ITS OWN DIAGNOSIS IS QUOTABLE: the Plan records that participatory natural resource management and mediation of use conflicts, though already mapped out, are insufficiently developed.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Brainforest — mapped Gabonese communities' forests with them, and documented seventeen communities standing up to logging companies
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Gabonese NGO of more than twenty years, working on forests and the environment with a deliberate double footing — support on the ground and monitoring of policy — and with the protection and promotion of the rights of forest communities and in particular of indigenous peoples as a stated purpose. It works across Haut-Ogooué, Ogooué-Ivindo, Nyanga, la Ngounié, Woleu-Ntem and the Estuaire. WHAT IT PUTS IN A COMMUNITY'S HANDS: participatory mapping of community forest resources, supported by satellite imagery — the same combination that won the Guinean bauxite mediation — plus independent external observation of forests and of non-forest investments, for which it publishes a simplified field guide, and work on getting the contractual obligations in logging concession specifications (cahiers de charges) actually implemented in a named concession. Those specifications are where a company's promises to a village are written down, and Brainforest's work is checking whether they were kept. IT ALSO PUBLISHES THE PRECEDENT ITSELF: its report titled, in translation, impunity is not what it was — seventeen communities stand up to logging companies, which is the document to put in front of a village that thinks nobody has ever won here. It runs analyses of forest conversion by large investments, and a programme on protecting environmental defenders in Gabon. Boulevard Rue Ndoukouet, Ambowé, Libreville; B.P. 23749; +241 011 73 08 86. WHO IT SUITS: forest villages and indigenous communities facing logging concessions, land conversion or non-forest investment. CAVEATS: this is advocacy, mapping and monitoring, not litigation — no legal service or intake route was found, and some published project material is old; a second domain, brainforestgabon.org, also carries its material.

trackers.name: Muyissi Environnement, Mouila — based inside the plantation belt, investigates for villages that cannot pay for a laboratory
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Muyissi Environnement, a Gabonese NGO founded in 2008 with its seat at Mouila in Ngounié province — inside the palm-oil belt rather than in the capital — working with villages that since 2012 have contested land-taking by an industrial oil palm company. WHAT IT DOES THAT NOBODY ELSE THERE WILL: its members carry out investigations in the affected villages, and the reason that matters is stated by a young farmer with skin irritation from the river water: communities have no means to contact laboratories and verify the degree of pollution. Villagers report dead fish in the watercourses, destruction of areas where they gathered fruit and medicinal plants, habitat fragmentation increasing conflict with elephants, and contamination of water sources by plantation agrochemicals. It has toured Ngounié villages to record the impact of the plantations on women specifically, and paired that with income-generating activities and a sale-exhibition of women's products, in villages where hunger had set in. THE ORGANISING ADVICE GIVEN AT ITS WORKSHOPS is worth carrying: communities were urged to invoke the Gabonese code against the company's violations, and to constitute themselves as COOPERATIVES OR ASSOCIATIONS so they speak with one voice — and were brought together with community delegations from Cameroon and Congo-Brazzaville facing the same company model, so that experience crossed borders. THE RISK IS DOCUMENTED: after one such workshop bringing affected communities together, a local NGO director and community leaders were intimidated by local authorities and told to stop organising such events. WHO IT SUITS: Gabonese villages inside or beside industrial plantations, especially in Ngounié, and women's groups losing gathering grounds and clean water. CAVEATS: no verified site of its own was found — this entry points at a land-grab archive record of its village work; it investigates and organises rather than litigating, and the certification label the plantations carry has not prevented the impacts communities report. For participatory mapping and national-level forest work, Gabon's Brainforest entry.

trackers.name: Gabon's environment charter for civil society — the protocol that makes a local association a recognised counterpart, and ACOSAH in Ogooué-Ivindo
trackers.desc: WHAT TO SIGN TO BE RECOGNISED: Gabon operates a CHARTE POUR LA PROTECTION DE L'ENVIRONNEMENT ET LA PRÉSERVATION DE LA NATURE — a protocol of understanding governing relations between the Direction Générale de l'Environnement et de la Protection de la Nature and the civil society organisations working in that field. An organisation signs it at the Directorate General's office, within the Ministry of Water and Forests. WHY A SMALL ASSOCIATION SHOULD CARE, in the words of one signatory's president: the signature “legitimises our actions as a CSO and auxiliary of the public authorities”, and from the Directorate's side the charter is intended to give the sector visibility through regular reporting of CSO activities, making that engagement visible to government and creating institutional synergies for MOBILISING RESOURCES. A signed protocol with the ministry converts a village association from a nuisance into a counterpart, and puts it on the list when money is allocated — ask whether your country has an equivalent instrument, because it is cheap and almost never mentioned. THE SIGNATORY THIS ENTRY RECORDS: ACOSAH (Association des Communicateurs Ogivins pour la Santé et l'Action Humanitaire), which signed on 25 October 2024 and states it has been active since 2019 in the protection of the environment in OGOOUÉ-IVINDO, alongside local communities, and against transnational environmental crime in the Congo Basin forests — which puts a community-facing organisation in Gabon's north-eastern forest province, away from the coastal and Ngounié work already recorded here. WHO IT SUITS: Gabonese local associations wanting formal standing with the environment administration, and communities in Ogooué-Ivindo facing logging, poaching networks or environmental crime. CAVEATS: THE CHARTER IS RECOGNITION, NOT FUNDING OR PROTECTION — it comes with a reporting expectation to the administration, which cuts both ways for an organisation that may later need to criticise that administration; ACOSAH is a communicators' and humanitarian association rather than a legal or land specialist. For participatory mapping, Gabon's Brainforest entry; for the plantation belt, Muyissi Environnement.

trackers.name: Gabon's Fonds de Développement Local — the concessionaire owes your villages 800 FCFA per cubic metre logged, and you can compute what you are owed
trackers.desc: THE MONEY OWED TO YOUR VILLAGE: under Gabon's forest framework, the CAHIER DES CHARGES CONTRACTUELLES is a contract signed between the FOREST CONCESSIONAIRE, the village communities, the local authorities and the forest administration, fixing how benefits from logging are shared and what each side commits to. It establishes a COMITÉ DE GESTION ET DE SUIVI DES PROJETS (CGSP), which must negotiate between villages to draw the map of their finage (customary land envelope), then set how the FONDS DE DÉVELOPPEMENT LOCAL (FDL) is divided, and meets regularly to choose which projects the money funds. THE RATE IS PUBLISHED AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT: the concessionaire feeds the FDL at 800 FCFA PER CUBIC METRE logged during the previous year. Volume times 800 is what your villages are owed — the only funding stream in this entire file a community can calculate for itself rather than apply for. Ask the administration for the declared annual production, do the arithmetic, and compare it with what reached the fund. THE DOCUMENTED ABUSE, RECORDED SO YOU KNOW WHAT TO LOOK FOR: monitoring in the Ngounié province (Douya-Onoye, Ndolou, Tsamba-Magotsi) found companies not respecting their social obligations; the Mokabo village grouping, which signed a cahier des charges in May 2017, denounced the lack of transparency in FDL management; communities did not even know the amount of the FDL; and one company's contract stipulated that the CGSP's OPERATING COSTS would be taken OUT OF the local development fund — 500,000 FCFA in the first year — while the annual production was not known, which the monitors called a clear breach. Watch for running costs being charged against your fund, and for production figures being withheld: without the volume, the rate is unenforceable. Nationally, the committee's own legal basis has been recognised as poorly defined, with reform proposed. WHO IT SUITS: Gabonese village groupings inside or beside a logging concession. CAVEATS: THIS IS A CONTRACTUAL ENTITLEMENT, NOT A GRANT YOU APPLY FOR — it exists only where a concession operates near you; the committee framework is legally weak and the administration under-resourced. For participatory mapping, Gabon's Brainforest entry; for the plantation belt, Muyissi; for formal standing with the environment administration, the charter entry.

trackers.name: RIAG and the Barreau du Gabon — a searchable directory of Gabonese lawyers, and free consultation days documented in Port-Gentil
trackers.desc: WHERE TO FIND A LAWYER: the Réseau International des Avocats Gabonais (RIAG), which runs RIAGCONNECT — a searchable directory for people looking for an advocate — and, with Gabonese diplomatic missions, organises FREE LEGAL CONSULTATIONS (consultations juridiques gratuites) aimed at the Gabonese community, to promote access to justice. A searchable public directory of practising advocates is the first thing to reach for in a country with no legal aid organisation; the second is a free consultation day. AND THE BAR ITSELF RUNS THEM DOMESTICALLY: the BARREAU DU GABON organised free legal consultations in PORT-GENTIL — the oil city, and the closest thing in this file to a scheduled walk-in service for Gabonese outside the capital. Ask the Barreau when the next consultation day is and which town it covers, and ask RIAG for a named advocate in your field — land, mining and environment are practised in Libreville. THE INSTABILITY TO PLAN AROUND, RECORDED BECAUSE IT DETERMINES WHAT YOU WILL FIND WHEN YOU CALL: Gabon's legal sector has passed through open turbulence — a crisis in the ordre des avocats following the ANNULMENT BY THE CONSEIL D'ÉTAT of a bar election, and an unlimited strike by magistrates over their working conditions — alongside a National Assembly-adopted judicial reform. A bar in crisis and striking magistrates mean delays that are institutional rather than personal; build your timetable around that rather than assuming your file has been forgotten. WHO IT SUITS: Gabonese needing to identify and instruct an advocate on a land, forest, plantation or mining matter, in Libreville, Port-Gentil or the provinces. CAVEATS: THIS IS A PROFESSIONAL DIRECTORY AND EPISODIC FREE CONSULTATIONS, NOT A LEGAL AID SCHEME — no Gabonese legal aid organisation could be verified for this file, and private practice in Libreville is oriented to business clients. For participatory mapping that stopped a plantation, Gabon's Brainforest entry; for the Ngounié plantation belt, Muyissi; for the logging fund your villages are owed, the FDL entry.

trackers.name: Gabon's forêts communautaires — the village forms an Entité Juridique de Gestion, cuts its own boundary layons, and signs a convention; 85 definitive conventions and 750,000 ha so far
trackers.desc: HOW A GABONESE VILLAGE GETS A FOREST: under articles 156-162 of loi n°016/01 of 31 December 2001 (code forestier) a forêt communautaire is a portion of the RURAL forest domain affected to a village community for sustainable natural-resource management on the basis of a CONVENTION DE GESTION between the water and forests administration and a village community ORGANISED AS AN ENTITÉ JURIDIQUE DE GESTION (EJG) — in practice a village association. Article 157 lets the request come from A VILLAGE, A GROUPING OF VILLAGES OR A CANTON, and the process is expressly volontariste — it happens only on the community's own demand.
