THE STEPS, IN ORDER: the village creates the legal entity, files the creation request with the LOCAL FOREST AUTHORITIES, holds information meetings INCLUDING PARTICIPATORY MAPPING of the territory concerned — with the WHOLE population, expressly INCLUDING WOMEN, YOUNG PEOPLE AND MINORITY ETHNIC GROUPS, required to understand the process — then a CONVENTION PROVISOIRE is signed, a PLAN SIMPLE DE GESTION prepared, and the definitive convention follows. TWO RULES WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE TELLS YOU OTHERWISE: (1) the 2022 arrêté states that the AREA OF A FC VARIES ACCORDING TO THE SIZE OF THE VILLAGE ASSOCIATION AND THE FOREST AVAILABLE — while sector guidance records a 5,000 ha working limit, the arrêté itself sets no fixed national ceiling; and (2) CREATION CANNOT BE THE ACT OF AN INDIVIDUAL, A FAMILY OR A CLAN. That second rule is protection, not obstruction — it is what stops one powerful family converting the village forest into a private holding, the exact failure recorded in Cameroon. AND THE BOUNDARY IS YOURS TO CUT: delimitation of the FC perimeter is carried out BY THE VILLAGE COMMUNITIES THEMSELVES, with support from the administration or a competent provider, by OPENING AND MAINTAINING TWO-METRE LAYONS around the whole perimeter WITH THE BOUNDARY TREES MARKED IN PAINT. A physically cut and painted boundary is worth more than a line on a map when a concession arrives — and it is work your own people can do. SCALE: launched 2013 in Ogooué-Ivindo, interrupted for TEN YEARS and relaunched in 2022; the country now counts 85 forests under definitive convention, 39 provisional and 45 reservation decisions — over 750,000 HECTARES. WHO IT SUITS: Gabonese villages, village groupings and cantons in the rural forest domain. CAVEATS: A MANAGEMENT CONVENTION WITH THE STATE, NOT OWNERSHIP, requiring a simple management plan and supply contracts to exploit; the ten-year interruption shows the queue can stop entirely. For participatory mapping to prepare the file, Gabon's Brainforest entry; for the logging fund your villages are owed, the FDL entry; for finding an advocate, RIAG.

trackers.name: Les Mêmes Droits Pour Tous (MDT)
trackers.desc: Guinea’s leading prisoner legal-aid organisation (“Same Rights For All”), founded in 2005 and specialising in criminal justice. Under a standing agreement with the Ministry of Justice it has unrestricted access to all of Guinea’s prisons — where the great majority of detainees are held in prolonged pretrial detention — and provides free legal and judicial assistance to people deprived of liberty, having won the release of hundreds who were illegally or unlawfully detained. It documents prison conditions, assists victims of torture and gender-based violence and communities affected by mining projects, and works from its Conakry headquarters and regional offices in N’Zérékoré and Kankan; it holds ECOSOC observer status.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? STAFF, NOT A HUB — Guinea. The 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar; here there are additional staff, so expect a smaller presence and a longer route into casework. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Guinea, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Guinea — Ministère du Budget
trackers.desc: National budget authority; optimises budget policy, prepares the finance law (loi de finances), and oversees fiscal & customs administration, Republic of Guinea. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Guinea.

trackers.name: Guinea — APIP-Guinée (Guichet Unique de Création d’Entreprise)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the APIP one-stop window handles company creation, online name reservation & RCCM formalities and promotes private investment, Republic of Guinea. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Association Guinéenne pour la Transparence (AGT)
trackers.desc: Transparency International's national contact in Guinea (since 2000). Anti-corruption advocacy that monitors public procurement and asset declarations and pushes UNCAC implementation. Its primary online presence is its Facebook page.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: Commission de classement — ask at the prefecture, and use the right words
trackers.desc: DO NOT ASK FOR A ‘FORÊT COMMUNAUTAIRE’ IN GUINEA. IUCN's review records that the forest code does not speak of community forests — but it does provide for classing the forest domain to the benefit of local collectivities. Ask for classement au bénéfice de la collectivité; the wrong term gets a request refused as unknown to the law. WHO CAN HOLD ONE: the Code names a commune urbaine, a Communauté Rurale de Développement, a district, A VILLAGE, or a groupement forestier — a village is named in its own right, so it need not federate first. NOTE THE INSTRUMENT: the State's forest domain is classed by décret; a collectivity's by arrêté — the lower and faster instrument. Land not yet subject to either is simply non-classé, so classement is the act that changes its status. WHERE IT IS DECIDED: a Commission de classement des forêts is instituted in each prefecture — this is decided locally, not in Conakry, so direct the request there and ask who sits on it. A DOCUMENT YOU CAN REQUEST: for each Plan Forestier Préfectoral the Préfet must produce an annual report on execution, submitted to the Ministry. Article 1: Guinean forests are a good of national interest. Codes in force: forest 1999, environment 1989, wildlife 1998.

trackers.name: The 1959 Dalaba status — sacred woods and spring heads, named
trackers.desc: A DOCUMENTED GUINEAN PRECEDENT FOR RECOGNISING COMMUNITY-PROTECTED SITES. Guinea's forest policy records a status adopted at Dalaba in 1959 for the Fouta Djallon whose objective was to guarantee customary collectivities the exclusive enjoyment of the forests they effectively protect for historical, cultural or religious reasons — expressly covering village groves, sacred woods (bois sacrés), spring heads (têtes de sources) and reserves. The counterpart was an undertaking by the collectivity to continue protecting them. Exclusive enjoyment in exchange for continued protection, with sacred woods and spring heads named as qualifying — precisely the kind of site that has no other category. CO-MANAGEMENT THAT EXISTS NOW: Zones de Chasse Communautaire are managed and controlled jointly by a Comité de gestion and state administration guards, with activities permitted, prohibited or regulated both in the zones and in the terroirs of surrounding villages; and Conseils Communautaires Environnementaux exist to sensitise users and serve as an interface between the collectivities and external actors. WHO IS ACTIVE: Guinée Écologie, with the Centre forestier de N'Zérékoré and BirdLife International, has run restoration in the Mont Béro classed forest since April 2023, funded by the Fondation L'OCCITANE, reaching 9,597 community members across five communities. Mont Béro covers about 26,850 ha, and more than 111,584 people in N'Zérékoré, Beyla and Lola depend on the forest.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: CECIDE — represented thirteen villages against the World Bank's bauxite lender, and built the evidence that made the mediation work
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Guinean NGO founded in 2000, working on mining and community rights through its natural resources programme, which represented thirteen villages around the Sangarédi bauxite mine in a complaint against the International Finance Corporation's client — filed in 2019 with the sister organisation ADREMGUI and the US group Inclusive Development International, on behalf of some 540 community members. The complaint went to the IFC's Compliance Advisor Ombudsman over lack of compensation for land loss and displacement, damage to livelihoods, safety risks and air and water pollution, and produced a dispute-resolution process and, eventually, an interim agreement with the company. HOW THEY WON THE ARGUMENT IS THE PART TO COPY, BECAUSE IT IS EVIDENCE WORK RATHER THAN LEGAL WORK: the communities elected their own representatives, were trained in negotiation, and then armed with proof — cartographers analysing forty years of satellite imagery, community members trained to map their own customary land and productive resources, and an expert hydrologist brought in to establish what the mine had done to local water. Against a company's consultants, that is what a community needs and almost never has. CECIDE also publicly challenged an aluminium industry certification scheme for downplaying the mine's harms, and works on artisanal mining, women's rights in mining areas and dam-affected communities at Souapiti. It anchors a Mano River Union civil society network with counterparts in Sierra Leone, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, so a cross-border problem is within reach. Kipé Dadya, Ratoma, Conakry; executive director Aboubacar Diallo, +224 622 110 113; contact.cecide@cecide.net. CAVEATS: this is community representation and advocacy, not litigation — the forum was a lender's complaints office, and its output was mediation and an interim agreement rather than an order. Resettlement went ahead at Hamdallaye during the Covid lockdown before mediation began, which is what that route cannot prevent. Two domains carry CECIDE material, cecide.net and an older cecide.org, and published email addresses differ between listings.

trackers.name: Action Mines Guinée — helps communities write their own protocol and negotiate the local development convention with the mining company
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Action Mines Guinée (AMINES), a Guinean organisation working on governance of the extractive sector. THE SERVICE THAT MATTERS MOST, stated in its own terms: it supports local authorities and communities in drawing up COMMUNITY PROTOCOLS and in NEGOTIATING THE LOCAL DEVELOPMENT CONVENTIONS with the companies, and in putting a monitoring system behind them. In Guinea the convention de développement local is the document that fixes what a mine owes the villages around it — a community that arrives at that negotiation without its own written protocol is negotiating on the company's paper. It also works to make communities aware of the legal and regulatory texts and the CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATIONS of mining projects, on the view that impacted people knowing the rights and duties of each party is what keeps local peace; it monitors whether the state and companies honour those obligations, including the payment and management of mining revenue. WHERE THE MONEY QUESTION BITES: it has run community dialogue workshops in Boké and Kindia on the use of LOCAL MINING ROYALTIES — bringing together civil society, communal councillors and women's and youth associations — because the royalty exists whether or not the community knows how it is being spent. Guinea holds the world's second-largest bauxite output and reserves above 40 billion tonnes, with 23 billion in the Boké region, and communities there report little local investment. AMINES has worked alongside Mêmes Droits pour Tous on community consultation missions at Siguirini, Kintinian, Moribadou and Lola, and has published research with an international partner on the consequences of bauxite mining. It also runs work with women on their rights in the face of extractive impacts. WHO IT SUITS: Guinean communities inside or beside mining permits, especially in Boké and the bauxite belt, and communal councillors handling mining revenue. CAVEATS: an advocacy, training and governance organisation — not a law firm and not a fund; some of its programme work has been donor-funded through state-linked mining governance programmes, so check whose money is behind a given workshop. For legal aid Guinea's MDT entry, and for the evidence-and-financier route, CECIDE's.

trackers.name: CGLTE-OA — the West African land-and-water convergence: 300+ member organisations, 15 national platforms, and a focal point in your country
trackers.desc: WHAT TO JOIN: the Convergence Globale des Luttes pour la Terre et l'Eau — Ouest Africaine (CGLTE-OA), a sub-regional platform created in June 2015 at Nyéléni in Mali, out of the African Social Forum in Dakar in 2014 and the World Social Forum in Tunis. IT IS A MEMBERSHIP ROUTE, NOT A SERVICE: it brings together more than 300 organisations — farmers, herders, pastoralists, fishers, foresters, organisations representing VICTIMS OF LAND AND WATER GRABBING in rural, peri-urban and urban settings, people evicted from popular neighbourhoods, youth, women and NGOs — across the 15 countries of the ECOWAS and UEMOA space, with Mauritania also taking part. Its 15 NATIONAL PLATFORMS each have a named FOCAL POINT: that person is the entry point for a community that wants to stop being alone with its case. Its secretariat sits at the office of Mali's land-grab convergence, which shares premises with the Malian farmers' coordination — both already recorded in this file. WHAT IT PRODUCES THAT YOU CAN USE: a “LIVRET VERT” (green booklet) setting out the movement's collective demands, a declaration, and a 2016–2030 action plan; and the CARAVANE OUEST-AFRICAINE, a travelling mobilisation that in its third edition drew more than 300 caravaners from ECOWAS countries and Mauritania and obtained audiences with the presidents of Guinea-Bissau and Guinea. Its demands centre on recognition and securing of customary rights and secure access to land for women and young people, and it has lobbied ECOWAS for recognition of family farms' land rights. THE MOVEMENT'S OWN REVIEW OF ITS WEAKNESSES, recorded because it tells you what to check before relying on it: weak functioning of its commissions, weak dynamism and anchoring of SOME national platforms, planning that did not account for context, logistical failures and mixed commitment from participants. WHO IT SUITS: West African communities and farmer organisations facing land or water grabbing who want sub-regional solidarity, visibility and a route to ECOWAS-level advocacy. CAVEATS: A SOCIAL MOVEMENT PLATFORM — it does not litigate, fund or buy land, and platform strength varies sharply by country; ask whether your national platform is actually active before counting on it. Guinea's own entries — CECIDE, MDT and Action Mines — are the service providers.

trackers.name: Guinea — there is NO free state legal aid; the routes are NGOs and the bar's own volunteer defence weeks
trackers.desc: WHAT DOES NOT EXIST, AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE FINDING TO EVERY OTHER FRANCOPHONE COUNTRY IN THIS FILE: human rights reporting on Guinea records that FOR WANT OF FREE AIDE JURIDICTIONNELLE for people who cannot pay an advocate, ONLY NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATIONS CAN PROVIDE THAT HELP. Do not go looking for a bureau d'assistance judiciaire in Guinea the way you would in Niger, Burkina or Côte d'Ivoire — go to the organisations. WHAT DOES EXIST: advocates of the Guinean bar organise VOLUNTEER FREE-DEFENCE PERIODS — women advocates have run a March initiative for successive years, defending accused people without means before the Conakry jurisdictions, with nine accused at the Mafanco first-instance tribunal assisted in one such month. Their own explanation of why it matters names the harm precisely: where a person cannot pay and no counsel is assigned of office, they can remain in detention a long time WITHOUT THEIR FILE BEING DEFENDED. If a family member is detained after a land protest, the bar's volunteer scheme and the NGOs are the whole of the answer — ask the barreau de Guinée when the next initiative runs and which tribunals it covers. Reporting also notes multi-service centres offering care and legal support, and that although a medico-legal report is not legally required to lodge a complaint, in practice it is often demanded — so obtain any medical documentation early, because its absence later becomes an obstacle to conviction. WHO IT SUITS: Guineans without means facing prosecution or detention, including after protests over mining and land, and anyone needing to know that the state route is absent. CAVEATS: VOLUNTEER AND EPISODIC — a month-long bar initiative is not a standing service, and NGO capacity is concentrated in Conakry. For legal aid and human rights casework, Guinea's MDT entry; for evidence and the financier route, CECIDE; for community protocols and mining royalties, Action Mines; for sub-regional solidarity, CGLTE-OA.

trackers.name: Guinea's code forestier L/2017/060 and the Direction Nationale des Eaux et Forêts — the law to cite, the office that runs village nurseries, and the permit-overlap trap in a bauxite country
trackers.desc: THE LAW TO CITE AND THE OFFICE TO ASK: Guinea's forest code is LOI ORDINAIRE L/2017/060/AN OF 12 DECEMBER 2017, adopted in plenary on 24 April 2017. Its opening definitions are the ones to quote in a letter: an AIRE PROTÉGÉE is a clearly defined geographic space, RECOGNISED ACCORDING TO INTERNATIONAL CRITERIA, dedicated and managed BY LEGAL OR OTHER MEANS to favour the LONG-TERM conservation of nature, ecosystem services AND THE CULTURAL VALUES ATTACHED TO THEM; and AMÉNAGEMENT FORESTIER covers technical AND SOCIO-ECONOMIC operations together with legal and administrative measures. Two phrases are worth carrying: BY LEGAL OR OTHER MEANS — which is the opening for a customary arrangement — and CULTURAL VALUES, which puts sacred groves and burial forests inside the statutory definition rather than outside it. THE OFFICE AND WHAT IT ALREADY DOES WITH VILLAGES: the DIRECTION NATIONALE DES EAUX ET FORÊTS, under the environment ministry, runs the ANNUAL NATIONAL REFORESTATION CAMPAIGN across the whole territory through its DECONCENTRATED SERVICES — prefectural and communal sections and the CANTONNEMENTS FORESTIERS — with strong grassroots community involvement; documented activity includes COMMUNITY REFORESTATION with teak in a village of Coyah with technical support from forestry agents, awareness sessions with village communities of the Mambiyah rural commune, Kindia, ON THE IMPORTANCE OF CREATING COMMUNITY FORESTS, and installing a VILLAGE NURSERY at Gogota in Guinée Forestière. The cantonnement forestier is the office to walk into: it already has agents assigned to villages, and a nursery is the cheapest way to start a claim that is visibly yours. THE TRAP, DOCUMENTED FOR THE REGION AND ACUTE HERE: research on community forests in neighbouring Gabon records the SUPERPOSITION of MINING AND LOGGING PERMITS over the space traditionally used by communities applying for a community forest, and calls for territorial planning that ranks land allocation and sets the conditions for coexistence. In a bauxite country, check the mining cadastre over your area BEFORE you invest in a forest application — an overlapping permit is the thing that defeats these files. WHO IT SUITS: Guinean villages and rural communes seeking forest recognition, reforestation support or a nursery. CAVEATS: THE CODE IS THE FRAME, NOT A GRANT — confirm which implementing texts are in force and what the cantonnement requires; state forestry involvement does not by itself secure tenure. For evidence and the financier route, Guinea's CECIDE entry; for community protocols and mining royalties, Action Mines; for legal aid, the no-state-scheme entry.

trackers.name: Tribunal de Contas
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Guinea-Bissau, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Guinea-Bissau — Ministério da Economia e Finanças
trackers.desc: National budget authority; formulates, executes & evaluates financial policy and prepares the State budget, Guinea-Bissau. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Guinea-Bissau.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: ECOWAS Court of Justice — file directly, but sue the State
trackers.desc: A COURT YOU CAN REACH WITHOUT EXHAUSTING DOMESTIC REMEDIES. The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has held human rights jurisdiction since 2005 and has broad access and standing rules permitting individuals and NGOs to bypass national courts and file directly. THE PRECEDENT: in SERAP v Federal Republic of Nigeria (ECW/CCJ/APP/08/09) the Court dismissed all three preliminary objections — no locus standi, no jurisdiction, statute-barred — and rejected the government's attempt to exclude an Amnesty International report from the evidence. NGO research was admitted as evidence, which matters when no state data exists. It found violations of articles 1 and 24 of the African Charter — article 24: ‘all peoples shall have the right to a general satisfactory environment favourable to their development’ — and of article 21, the right to natural wealth and resources. THE FAULT WAS AN OMISSION: the state ‘defaulted in its duties in terms of vigilance and diligence’, and ‘the omission to act and to prevent damage to the environment characterises the violation’. It ordered restoration within the shortest possible time and measures to prevent further damage, citing the ICJ that the environment ‘is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn’. THE LIMIT THAT DECIDES WHO YOU SUE: the Court held it had no jurisdiction over the private oil corporations, which were struck from the suit. You sue the State for failing to regulate; you cannot sue the company here — naming one as respondent loses that part of the case. AND PLAN FOR ENFORCEMENT: commentary records the Court did not identify a means for Nigeria to implement the ruling, and the ICJ later wrote to the President pressing for enforcement — judgment is the start of an enforcement campaign, not a self-executing remedy. Proposals to require exhaustion of domestic remedies were rejected by ECOWAS experts and Heads of Government, so the direct-access rule has been tested and held.

trackers.name: ORFAO — comparative land-law tables, and a directive in draft
trackers.desc: COMPARATIVE LEGAL TABLES FOR YOUR COUNTRY AND ITS NEIGHBOURS, IN ONE DOCUMENT. The Observatoire Régional du Foncier Rural en Afrique de l'Ouest (ORFAO), hosted by UEMOA, publishes a regional study on rural land markets containing side-by-side ‘cadre légal comparé’ tables — one covering Bénin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire and Sénégal, another Guinée-Bissau, Mali, Niger and Togo — plus typologies of direct and indirect interventions in land markets and a table of regulatory issues and families of instruments. If you need to know what instrument exists in your country and whether a neighbour has a stronger one, that is the document — comparative tables let a campaign point to a neighbour's provision as an achievable ask rather than a novelty. A WINDOW IS OPENING: on 26 June 2026 in Ouagadougou the UEMOA ministers for urbanisme, habitat, domaines et cadastre approved a draft directive to harmonise rules on immatriculation foncière, accès au titre de propriété and a système d'information foncière, aiming at a common framework of land governance. BE PRECISE ABOUT STATUS: that was a DRAFT directive approved by ministers, not an adopted and transposed instrument — check adoption and transposition before relying on it. But transposition is the moment domestic land law is reopened in each state, and that is when community provisions can be argued for. FOR A GRAZING OR TRANSHUMANCE DISPUTE: a regional pastoral situation bulletin covers 11 West African countries with the support of decentralised technical services — an evidence source drawing on the same services you would otherwise approach one by one. RECORDED PLAINLY: cattle theft is documented as a driver of conflict and instability in the Sahel, so a land dispute here may sit inside a security context that changes what is safe to do. And confirm your state's current ECOWAS standing — several members are recorded as suspended.

trackers.name: IBAP, Bissau — the protected-areas institute has a real address and a switchboard, and its website is carrying injected spam
trackers.desc: THE INSTITUTE IS GENUINE AND ITS WEBSITE IS PARTLY COMPROMISED; BOTH FACTS MATTER BEFORE YOU SEND ANYTHING. The Institute for Biodiversity and Protected Areas was created in 2005 by decree-law and holds administrative, financial and asset autonomy under the minister responsible for the environment, which means it can set conservation policy rather than only implement it. It administers the national protected areas system — around 470,000 hectares, roughly 15 per cent of the territory, of which two-thirds is marine or estuarine — with staff based at the Bissau headquarters and in the protected areas themselves, and an expansion toward 26.3 per cent of national territory is under way. For a coastal or island community this is the body with jurisdiction over the mangrove, the fishing ground and the park boundary. Headquarters: Avenida Dom Settimio Arturo Ferrazzetta, Caixa Postal 70, Bissau; switchboard (245) 320 71 06 and 320 71 07, taken from the institute's own reporting to the biodiversity convention. WARNINGS: the institute's home page currently carries injected spam articles on unrelated medical subjects in German and Portuguese, which means the site has been compromised at some point — the institutional pages and the annual reports still read as authentic, but do not download binaries from it and do not trust anything that asks for credentials. Its supervising ministry is stated differently in different places — the institute's own page says the minister responsible for the environment, while an international conservation union listing puts it under rural development, agriculture, forests and hunting — so confirm the ministry before addressing correspondence. No environmental complaint form, impact-assessment register or objection deadline was located for Guinea-Bissau, and the institute's own annual reporting records that it has operated largely on donor funds rather than budget allocations.

trackers.name: Tiniguena — the Bissau-Guinean NGO the island elders called in, which turned traditional rules into a legally decreed community marine protected area
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Bissau-Guinean NGO founded in 1991 promoting participatory and durable development. THE SEQUENCE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THIS ENTRY, because it is the order most communities get wrong: the traditional authorities of three Bijagós islands went to Tiniguena and asked for help; Tiniguena united the groups from the three islands, proposed turning the area into a community marine protected area, and built a management plan drawn from the Bijagó people's own traditional rules of access to and use of land, sea and resources. The plan was then approved at the same time as the government decree creating the area in 2005 — so the custom became the legal management regime rather than being overridden by one. WHAT IT PRODUCED: the Urok community marine protected area, about 54,500 hectares across Formosa, Nago and Chediã, including over 3,000 hectares of mangrove, governed by a management council made up of representatives of every tabanca on the islands, representatives from the wider archipelago, the state biodiversity and protected areas institute, and Tiniguena. The communities set fisheries management plans, reserved marine resources for local subsistence, and patrol their own waters against illegal fishing. In 2019 that council won the UN Development Programme's Equator Prize — the first time a Guinea-Bissau initiative had done so. Tiniguena also works on recognition of community and ancestral heritage areas on the coast, including sacred forests, and on climate-adapted family farming in Urok. WHO IT SUITS: coastal and island communities with living customary rules over their waters and land who want those rules made enforceable. CAVEATS: an NGO and facilitator, not a legal service — no litigation, no intake route, no fee information; the model depends on functioning traditional authority and took years, and Guinea-Bissau's political instability affects everything built through the state. THE ZONING RULE, WHICH IS THE PART ANOTHER COMMUNITY CAN COPY WORD FOR WORD: the area was built on THREE ZONES — a CENTRAL ZONE, essentially mangrove, RESERVED TO RESIDENTS for SUBSISTENCE AND CEREMONIAL fishing; a BUFFER ZONE reserved to residents for COMMERCIAL fishing; and a PERIPHERAL ZONE OPEN TO NON-RESIDENT FISHERS ON CONDITION THEY RESPECT THE RULES IN USE IN THE RESERVE. Naming a zone where outsiders may fish on your terms is what makes the whole scheme defensible — a total exclusion invites the argument that you are privatising a common, while a conditional opening turns every outside fisher into someone bound by your rules. WHAT CO-MANAGEMENT AND PARTICIPATORY SURVEILLANCE PRODUCED: a restoration of biodiversity, particularly MANATEE populations and migratory waterbirds; and the community's SEED GUARDIANS conserve 17 DIFFERENT RICE VARIETIES plus endemic bean and groundnut varieties. The co-management effort has since turned to protecting forests THREATENED BY THE EXPANSION OF CASHEW CULTIVATION, with measures written into the SECOND MANAGEMENT PLAN and the traditional role of the CAMABIS — the Bijagó age class responsible for forest surveillance — revived to carry it. Give the enforcement job to the customary body that already held it; a revived traditional role costs nothing and carries authority a hired guard does not.

trackers.name: Liga Guineense dos Direitos Humanos — the body that went to Varela and wrote down what the heavy-sands mining did there
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Liga Guineense dos Direitos Humanos (LGDH), Guinea-Bissau's human rights league, whose field report on the heavy-sands mining at Varela, in the north-west near the Senegalese border, is the documentation the affected villages had and would otherwise have lacked. WHAT ITS REPORT ESTABLISHED, and why documentation is the whole of the resource here: the communities “have nowhere to take their children and resettle their lives”; the concession over parcel 12 of the Varela sands at Nhinquin ran to 2028 and had passed from a Russian company that held it from 2015 to a company of unknown capital, presumed to originate in a free zone. The mineral at issue is ilmenite, the source of titanium dioxide — demand driven by the same industries that market themselves as sustainable. WHAT THE COMMUNITIES SAY IS WRONG, as set out in a public campaign: the environmental and social impact study was delivered AFTER the concession was granted, contrary to law; the consultancy that produced it was owned by a direct relative of the minister who approved the project; and the promised schools, health centres and roads were never built. The harms listed are forest, dune, mangrove and farmland destruction, salinisation of groundwater making water unfit to drink or irrigate with, coastal erosion, and loss of traditional livelihoods. ASK WHEN THE IMPACT STUDY WAS DATED RELATIVE TO THE CONCESSION, AND WHO OWNED THE CONSULTANCY — in this case both answers were the case. WHAT HAPPENED, STATED PLAINLY: protests led by women of Nhinquin in January halted the activity; more than 100 women protested peacefully and the area was militarised, with arbitrary detentions reported; in April villagers burned the company's installations and 16 people were detained and taken to a military barracks. WHO IT SUITS: Bissau-Guinean coastal communities facing mining concessions, and anyone needing a national human rights body to visit and record what is happening. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED LIVE SITE FOR LGDH WAS FOUND — this entry points at the newspaper record quoting its report. It documents and reports; it is not counsel and not a fund. This entry records the confrontation and the arrests as reported; it does not recommend them — the transferable move here is the dated, written field report. For the Urok islands model and community management, Guinea-Bissau's Tiniguena entry.

trackers.name: Guinea-Bissau's Centros de Acesso à Justiça — walk in, get a lawyer appointed at no cost and court fees waived; PROPERTY is the commonest problem they see
trackers.desc: WHERE TO WALK IN: the Centros de Acesso à Justiça (CAJ), created in 2011 under Decreto-lei 11/2010 (the legal-aid framework) and Decreto 11/2011, which also set up the justice ministry's Gabinete de Informação e Consulta Jurídica (GICJU) that coordinates them. WHAT A CENTRE ACTUALLY DOES FOR YOU, from a documented case: staff explain the options, then help you REQUEST THE APPOINTMENT OF A LAWYER AT NO COST THROUGH A PARTNERSHIP WITH THE ORDEM DOS ADVOGADOS, and file a request for EXEMPTION FROM COURT FEES. Two separate applications — counsel and fee waiver — and most people know about neither; the centre exists to make both for you. WHY THIS BELONGS IN A LAND MAP: the head of the Bissau Velho centre lists the commonest problems as PROPERTY first, then thefts, physical assault, debts, labour questions, family problems and illegal detention. COVERAGE AND REACH: centres were planned for nine regions; as of February 2018 seven were installed — two in Bissau and five in the regions, and by 2019 the network had assisted about 13,000 people. Rural reach runs through PAS — community-level activists who act as intermediaries between communities and the CAJ, reporting incidents and directing victims to the centres, with named posts in villages across Cacheu region; regional centres schedule meetings with local communities, and urban centres work directly through police stations and courts. THE HONEST LIMIT, RECORDED IN THE SAME EVALUATIONS: the UNDP-bar association partnership FAILED to secure legal representation in the regions because most advocates are concentrated in Bissau and visit the regions only sporadically. Expect the centre to open the door and the fee waiver to work; do not assume a lawyer will physically appear outside the capital. WHO IT SUITS: Bissau-Guineans with a property, inheritance or detention problem and no money, especially outside Bissau. CAVEATS: donor-dependent and unevenly staffed; traditional authorities still resolve many community disputes in practice. For the Varela mining documentation, Guinea-Bissau's LGDH entry; for the Urok islands community-management model, Tiniguena.

trackers.name: BioGuiné Foundation — a national biodiversity endowment whose stated purpose includes EMPOWERING the communities inside and around the protected areas
trackers.desc: WHERE THE LONG MONEY IS: the Fundação BioGuiné (BioGuinea Foundation, FBG), conceived as a DURABLE FINANCING STRATEGY to consolidate conservation work in Guinea-Bissau — and, in its own words, the EMPOWERMENT of the communities resident inside and in the surroundings of the country's PROTECTED AREAS, through appropriation, accountability and capacity-building of the different actors. A conservation endowment that names community empowerment as half its purpose is worth approaching differently from one that funds park management — quote that purpose back at it. The foundation was envisaged from the creation of the protected-areas institute in 2004 and is a pillar of the national protected-areas and biodiversity strategy. HOW THE MONEY REACHES THE GROUND, WHICH DETERMINES WHO YOU TALK TO: FBG funding is CHANNELLED THROUGH IBAP, the public institute responsible for the country's protected areas — so IBAP, already recorded in this file with its Bissau address, is the door, not the foundation directly. It has supported Orango National Park, a marine protected area in the Bijagós Archipelago — 88 islands, 21 inhabited by some 30,000 people, mostly of the Bijagó ethnicity, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1996. CAPITALISATION, BECAUSE AN ENDOWMENT ONLY MATTERS IF IT IS FUNDED: the government committed a minimum of ONE MILLION EUROS to the seed capital, witnessed by a joint co-financing letter signed by the finance minister and the state secretary for fisheries in December 2014, alongside contributions recorded from a French environment facility and REDD/carbon market sources. Protected areas cover a reported 12.2% of national territory, rising to 33.3% counting the Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve. WHO IT SUITS: Bissau-Guinean communities inside or bordering protected areas, especially in the Bijagós, seeking long-term financing for management and livelihoods. CAVEATS: AN ENDOWMENT CHANNELLED THROUGH A STATE INSTITUTE — you apply through IBAP, not to the foundation; it funds conservation and community capacity, NOT litigation, land purchase or opposition to a licensed project, and its reach is protected-area geography only. For the Varela mining documentation, Guinea-Bissau's LGDH entry; for community management at Urok, Tiniguena; for a free lawyer and fee waiver, the Centros de Acesso à Justiça.

trackers.name: Seinoli Legal Centre (SLC)
trackers.desc: Lesotho’s first public-interest legal centre (est. 2010) — provides free legal services and strategic litigation for communities affected by large development projects (the Lesotho Highlands Water Project dams, mining, agribusiness), operates a toll-free grievance line, and combines litigation, advocacy and community capacity-building to secure compensation, relocation and access to justice.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor General
trackers.desc: National — supreme audit institution of Lesotho. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Lesotho.

trackers.name: Lesotho — One-Stop Business Facilitation Centre (Registrar of Companies)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Registrar of Companies (Ministry of Trade & Industry) runs an online companies register with free public company search, Lesotho. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Lesotho, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: MNN Centre for Investigative Journalism
trackers.desc: Lesotho's investigative newsroom exposing corruption and misuse of public resources.

trackers.name: LesothoLII
trackers.desc: Lesotho Legal Information Institute: free case law and legislation (AfricanLII network). · Find here: free Lesotho judgments and legislation (LesothoLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Directorate on Corruption and Economic Offences (DCEO)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Lesotho — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Compensation over 50 years when the Land Act gives 99 — the argument to make
trackers.desc: THE STRONGEST FORM OF COMPENSATION CHALLENGE, AND IT TURNS ON A PERIOD RATHER THAN AN AMOUNT. Communities affected by the Lesotho Highlands Water Project rejected their scheme because compensation was calculated over 50 years while the Land Act 2010 gives a right to use the land for 99 years — on that basis they called the 50-year plan baseless. Not ‘the amount is too low’ but ‘the period used to calculate it is shorter than the tenure the statute gives me’. The rate was attacked the same way: 86 cents per square metre, described as arbitrarily decided with no basis compared to the actual harvest from the fields. AND LATE PAYMENT IS A BREACH, NOT A DELAY: the LHDA Order of 1986 imposes the primary duty to ensure the standard of living of affected communities does not deteriorate but is maintained or improved, and read with the Land Act it provides for prompt compensation even before entry into the property. ‘Before entry’ is the test — so record the date the project entered and the date any money arrived.

trackers.name: One appeal opened a queue — check whether your second tranche was ever paid
trackers.desc: A PRECEDENT THAT OTHERS IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWED. After a landmark Court of Appeal ruling, the LHDA missed a court-set deadline to pay compensation to communities affected by the Katse Dam — and 21 community associations lodged fresh compensation demands on the back of it. THE STRUCTURE OF THE CLAIM IS THE LESSON: 22 associations downstream of Katse were affected by Phase I; they received initial compensation in 2003 covering a 10-year pilot phase, with a second tranche due in 2013 covering the remaining 40 years of a 50-year lease period — and LHDA failed to pay, triggering over a decade of disputes. If your compensation was structured as a pilot tranche with a later instalment, check whether that instalment was ever paid: a decade-old unpaid tranche proved recoverable, and others in the same position followed. Sums ranged from M500,000 to M3 million, the winning society having received about M2.7 million initially. TWO MORE LEVERS: Phase II rates are adjusted annually by the Lesotho CPI, dwellings compensated at replacement cost, urban valuations certified by the LAA, and a land-for-land option exists; and financing involves the African Development Bank with Standard Bank as an Equator Principles institution, so bank-level grievance mechanisms are a second route. RECORDED HONESTLY: communities report formal complaints unanswered, grievance systems inaccessible, and defenders facing threats and intimidation. NOTE ALSO section 16 of the Land Act: rural landowners may apply for a lease but are not required to register, and Community Councils keep allocation records manually and in silos — get a certified copy of your council's allocation record now, because it may be the only proof and it exists in one place.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: Transformation Resource Centre — field workers living with the dam-affected communities, and it is already working the Polihali phase
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Lesotho NGO that has worked the country's biggest displacement file — the Lesotho Highlands Water Project — for decades, and stations field workers in the affected areas rather than visiting from Maseru: two were posted at Mohale and Ratau to follow resettlement, compensation and development day to day. It helped affected residents put their complaints to the development authority, supported the marches that followed, and worked alongside the community's own body, the Survivors of the Lesotho Dams. Outcomes attributed to that pressure include the compensation period being extended to fifty years and delayed communal compensation being released. IT IS ALREADY ON THE NEXT DAM, WHICH IS THE POINT FOR ANYONE FACING ONE: its Polihali Liaison Community Participation programme works with communities affected by Phase 2 construction, on compensation and resettlement, and investigates whether the social impact assessments the developers commissioned are actually being fulfilled — comparing the promises in the assessment against what is delivered is a documentary exercise a community can start immediately. WHAT ITS RECORD TEACHES ABOUT COMPENSATION, and it is the lesson to carry into any negotiation: TRC's finding was that cash compensation arrives late and only covers debts, that people had been feeding themselves from land before resettlement, and that no land-for-land was offered — so argue for replacement land and for water supply in the resettlement site, not for a figure. TRC publishes its documentation, including a book-length account of the lessons of the project. WHO IT SUITS: Basotho communities facing dam construction, resettlement or downstream flow loss. CAVEATS: TRC is a research, documentation and community-organising body — for litigation Lesotho already has the Seinoli Legal Centre, which acts for dam-affected communities. Its published contact detail is dated, and reported intimidation of people attending dam-affected peoples' meetings is part of the context.

trackers.name: Lesotho's Legal Aid department — 17 lawyers for the whole country, travelling to district courts on scheduled dates, now opening decentralised offices
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET A FREE LAWYER, AND THE CONSTRAINT STATED FIRST: the Legal Aid department, established by the Legal Aid Act of 1978 and mandated to provide legal REPRESENTATION to indigent Basotho, is one of four departments in the justice ministry. It has A TOTAL OF 17 LAWYERS, and the office is based only in MASERU. THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE IS THE THING TO PLAN AROUND: the department's lawyers TRAVEL TO THE DISTRICTS ON SCHEDULED DATES to represent clients in the district courts — so the question is not whether legal aid exists near you, it is WHEN THE CIRCUIT NEXT REACHES YOUR DISTRICT. Find that date and build your case around it. WHAT IS CHANGING: government has begun launching DECENTRALISED LEGAL AID OFFICES in the districts, with one opened at Melele Ground in Qacha's Nek with European Union support, aimed explicitly at vulnerable and remote communities — the elderly, children, people with disabilities and unemployed people in remote areas. The ministry frames this as a constitutional obligation: Lesotho's Bill of Rights covers access to justice, fair hearing and legal representation, and the state says it has a responsibility to provide legal aid nationally. Civil society was present at the launch through WILSA (Women and Law in Southern Africa), whose representative described the office as restoring hope to people who had felt forgotten. Ask whether a decentralised office has opened in your district before assuming you must reach Maseru. WHO IT SUITS: indigent Basotho needing representation in a district court, including in land, inheritance and eviction matters. CAVEATS: SEVERELY UNDER-RESOURCED — 17 lawyers nationally, a Maseru base and a travelling circuit mean delay is structural, not personal; it is a state department and will not act against government policy. For dam-affected communities and the financier-complaint route, Lesotho's TRC entry; for litigation, Seinoli Legal Centre.

trackers.name: Lesotho's dam community associations — the Court of Appeal ordered the second compensation tranche paid, and 21 more associations then filed
trackers.desc: THE MONEY A COURT HAS ORDERED, AND THE VEHICLE THAT CLAIMED IT: villages downstream of the Katse Dam are organised as REGISTERED COMMUNITY ASSOCIATIONS, and one of them — the Ukhopo-Maliba-Matšo Society at Bobete, Thaba-Tseka — took the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority to court and won. On 7 November the Court of Appeal dismissed the LHDA's challenge and upheld a High Court order compelling payment to MORE THAN 600 VILLAGERS, giving the authority 90 DAYS to pay. THE RULING IS THE PART TO CARRY ANYWHERE: the Chief Justice held that the authority CANNOT RELY ON INTERNAL POLICIES OR CONSULTANTS’ TECHNICAL REPORTS TO OVERRIDE ITS CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY DUTY TO COMPENSATE, that the duty arises from the Constitution, the Treaty and the LHDA Order, and IS NOT A MATTER OF BUREAUCRATIC DISCRETION — and it condemned the failure to consult villagers before unilaterally stopping payment in 2013. If an authority tells you its own policy or a consultant's report has ended your entitlement, that is the finding to put in front of it. THE ARITHMETIC, WHICH EVERY AFFECTED ASSOCIATION SHOULD DO: compensation is based on a 50-YEAR LEASE; associations received an initial tranche in 2003/4 covering a ten-year pilot period, and A SECOND TRANCHE WAS DUE IN 2013 TO COVER THE REMAINING 40 YEARS. Bobete's society had received about M2.7 million for the initial period; other associations were paid between M500,000 and M3 million. WHAT FOLLOWED, AND WHY YOU SHOULD NOT WAIT: after the ruling, 21 further community associations lodged fresh compensation demands, out of 22 representing villages downstream of Katse; separately more than 3,000 individuals and 889 registered businesses have brought a constitutional case alleging unpaid compensation, sums as low as 78 cents per square metre paid years after expropriation, and the failure ever to establish the promised community development fund. The LHDA missed the Court-set deadline. WHO IT SUITS: Basotho villages affected by Katse, Mohale or Polihali, and communities anywhere whose second-tranche or long-term compensation has quietly stopped. CAVEATS: THIS IS LITIGATION, NOT A GRANT WINDOW — it required an advocate and years; the promised community development fund was never established, so do not count on it. For litigation, Lesotho's Seinoli Legal Centre entry; for field-level accompaniment, the TRC entry; for the free-lawyer circuit, the Legal Aid department.

trackers.name: Lesotho's community councils and grazing associations — the council allocates land and controls grazing; only 20% of households hold a registered lease and 39% hold nothing
trackers.desc: WHO ALLOCATES YOUR LAND AND WHAT YOU HOLD: in Lesotho the COMMUNITY COUNCIL is the allocating authority, and its statutory functions include LAND ALLOCATION, GRAZING CONTROL, NATURAL RESOURCE CONTROL, POLLUTION AND ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION, BURIAL GROUNDS and AREA ECONOMIC PLANNING. One elected body near you holds allocation, grazing and natural-resource control together — which means a single council decision can open or close a piece of ground, and the council is therefore the first door, not the ministry. WHAT YOU PROBABLY HOLD, IN NUMBERS: the 2016 census records 20% of households with REGISTERED LEASEHOLDS, 41% with only UNREGISTERED CERTIFICATES OF ALLOCATION, and 39% WITH NEITHER; registered and unregistered parcels alike are predominantly non-agricultural, so extensive cropland and COMMUNAL PASTURE is not formally registered at all. Find out which of the three you are in before a project arrives: a certificate of allocation is not a lease, and 39% of households have no paper whatsoever. Under section 16 of the LAND ACT 2010 an allottee of residential land in a rural area MAY APPLY TO THE COMMISSIONER FOR A LEASE — the lease being the strongest form of title, issued by the national land administration authority — but for non-commercial rural land registration is OPTIONAL, which is why so few register. Councils record allocations MANUALLY and work in silos, with no integration between allocating authorities and the national registry. If your allocation exists only in a council ledger, get a certified copy now; that ledger is the only evidence you have. THE VEHICLE FOR PASTURE, AND THE LIMIT ON IT: Lesotho has a documented history of GRAZING ASSOCIATIONS as the community form for range management — but note that PRINCIPAL CHIEFS, NOT COMMUNITY COUNCILS, are in charge of range management and CATTLE POSTS, and that ALL NATURAL RESOURCES BELONG TO THE STATE and a MINING LEASE DOES NOT REQUIRE A LAND LEASE FIRST. That last rule is the one to plan around: a mining lease can be granted over ground you hold without your lease being touched — so registration protects your occupation, not the minerals under it. WHO IT SUITS: Basotho households and villages wanting to know what they hold, register it, or organise pasture. CAVEATS: ALLOCATION AND LEASEHOLD, NOT FREEHOLD — and the council-to-registry gap is a real risk of loss. For dam-affected communities and the second compensation tranche, Lesotho's community associations entry; for litigation, Seinoli; for the travelling legal-aid circuit, the Legal Aid department entry.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: Environment General Authority — the only environmental body a Libyan community can address, and an honest account of what does not exist
trackers.desc: WHO TO APPROACH, AND WHY THIS ENTRY IS WRITTEN AS AN ABSENCE: no verified Libyan civil society organisation providing land defence, environmental litigation or community legal support could be found. What exists is the Environment General Authority (EGA), established in 2000, a scientific, regulatory and advisory body responsible for conservation of biological resources, environmental pollution and integrated planning. The single legal hook worth knowing: the Environment Law of 2003 gives the environment ministry and the EGA under it the right to monitor pollution levels and to require emission permits for facilities covered by the regulation. If a facility near you is emitting, the permit and the monitoring duty are what to ask about, in writing, naming the law. WHAT YOU SHOULD EXPECT, STATED PLAINLY: the EGA long operated as an independent autonomous institution but now reports directly to the environment ministry; Libya has had no national development plan since 2011, its institutions were deeply divided and fragmented, and the authority itself is described as still needing international partnership to articulate environmental management measures and mobilise resources. Libya has ratified the main environmental conventions and the Paris Agreement but had not submitted a nationally determined contribution. There are branch offices in regional cities, including at Tobruk. WHO IT SUITS: Libyan residents facing industrial pollution or a facility operating without permits — as the only formal address available. CAVEATS: THIS IS A STATE REGULATOR, NOT AN ALLY: it is part of the government that licenses the projects, there is no independent civil society counterpart recorded here, and no intake or complaints procedure was found. NO VERIFIED LIVE SITE FOR THE EGA EXISTS — this entry points at an intergovernmental network's record of the organisation. In a fragmented state, confirm which authority is actually functioning in your region before relying on any of this.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants in Libya — added by name in the eighth cycle, and the first thing in this file a Libyan community can actually apply to
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the GEF SMALL GRANTS PROGRAMME expanded country coverage in its eighth replenishment from 124 to 135 countries, ADDING LIBYA BY NAME — alongside Somalia, South Sudan, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Príncipe. This file's Libya entry has until now recorded only a state regulator and the ABSENCE of civil society support; this is the first thing here a Libyan community group can actually apply to. THE ALLOCATION RULE: the eighth cycle secured USD 135 million for the core programme and ensures EQUAL ALLOCATION OF NEARLY USD 1 MILLION IN CORE FINANCING TO EACH of the 135 participating countries — regardless of size or previous participation, with STAR allocations raised over 30 per cent. A newly added country is not competing against large established programmes for the core money, which is the argument for applying in the FIRST cycle rather than waiting to see how it goes. The programme's stated objective is to catalyse and mobilise CIVIL SOCIETY actors and LOCAL ACTIONS addressing the major drivers of environmental degradation, and it has funded community-level environmental projects since 1992. WHO IT SUITS: Libyan community groups and associations with an environmental, water, waste or land degradation project. CAVEATS: A DONOR CYCLE WITH FIXED CALLS, AND A COUNTRY WHERE CIVIL SOCIETY OPERATES UNDER SEVERE CONSTRAINT — confirm the country programme is actually operational and what registration it requires before counting on it; it funds environmental action, NOT litigation or land purchase. For the state environmental regulator and the honest record of what does not exist, Libya's EGA entry.

trackers.name: Libya — the Bar Association does referrals, a Libyan legal aid organisation exists, and LFJL runs strategic litigation from the diaspora
trackers.desc: WHO TO ASK FOR A LAWYER, IN A COUNTRY THIS FILE HAS UNTIL NOW RECORDED ONLY AS AN ABSENCE: LAWYERS FOR JUSTICE IN LIBYA (LFJL), established in response to the February 2011 uprising BY A NETWORK OF LIBYAN LAWYERS, works through transitional justice, LEGAL REFORM, human rights education, STRATEGIC LITIGATION and advocacy, and is a member of the international legal-empowerment network. A strategic litigation organisation founded by Libyan lawyers is the closest thing to public interest counsel recorded for Libya — approach it for a case of wider significance, not an individual dispute. TWO OTHER NAMED BODIES: the LIBYAN BAR ASSOCIATION, which maintains A DIRECTORY OF PRACTISING LAWYERS and provides REFERRALS to law firms and lawyers — and which is also where you report a lawyer's misconduct — with a Tripoli bar named separately; and the LIBYAN ORGANIZATION FOR LEGAL AID. Legal-directory material also names the Libyan Center for Civil Liberties and Human Rights (lcclhr.org.ly). Start with the Bar Association referral: in a country where no walk-in legal aid desk could be verified, a referral from the professional body is how you reach a named practitioner rather than guessing. The justice ministry is cited as the second point for information on legal services and procedures. WHO IT SUITS: Libyans needing to identify counsel for a property, expropriation or rights matter, and anyone with a case of wider public significance. CAVEATS: SOURCING IS INDIRECT AND THE ENTRY SAYS SO — LFJL is verified through a legal-empowerment network profile; the bar association and the legal aid organisation are named in legal-directory material rather than through their own verified sites, so confirm contacts before relying on them. Libya is divided and insecure, civil society operates under severe constraint, and none of these bodies is a walk-in service. For the state environmental regulator and the record of what does not exist, Libya's EGA entry; for community environmental funding newly opened to Libya, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: The Libyan Nature Platform's reserve register — named reserves with hectares, dates and candid failure notes, plus the laws that already protect pastures and forests
trackers.desc: WHAT IS ALREADY PROTECTED AND WHO KEEPS THE LIST: a Libyan platform publishes a REGISTER OF THE COUNTRY'S NATURE RESERVES AND NATIONAL PARKS with names, areas, dates and honest condition notes — for example BIR AYAD NATURE RESERVE, 12,000 HECTARES in the Nafusa Mountains, 120 km southwest of Tripoli, INITIALLY AN AGRICULTURAL PROJECT AND DECLARED A RESERVE IN 1992, holding around 300 species of trees, shrubs and herbs; and KOUF, established 1975, one of seven national parks. An existing register with named areas and dates is what you cite when a project is proposed near you — and Bir Ayad shows the most useful precedent in Libya: an AGRICULTURAL PROJECT WAS CONVERTED INTO A DECLARED RESERVE, so the conversion runs in the direction you want. THE FAILURE NOTE WORTH MORE THAN THE SUCCESSES, PUBLISHED BY LIBYANS ABOUT LIBYA: ELNAGGAZA NATIONAL PARK, established 1992, 4,000 HECTARES with 600 STRICTLY PROTECTED, whose PINE FORESTS WERE CREATED BY SEASONAL REFORESTATION CARRIED OUT BY STUDENTS AND SCOUTS — but LACK OF MANAGEMENT HAS LED TO WILDFIRES AND LOCAL ENCROACHMENT, ESPECIALLY IN COASTAL AREAS. Volunteers can create a forest; only a funded management body keeps it. If you plant, negotiate who patrols and who pays before the first season ends — the same gap that emptied Mohéli's park of finance for fourteen years. THE LAWS THAT ALREADY EXIST TO CITE: LAW NO. 15 OF 2003 on the Protection and Improvement of the Environment covering pollution, natural resource management and wildlife conservation; LAW NO. 5 OF 1982 ON THE PROTECTION OF PASTURES AND FORESTS; LAW NO. 3 OF 1982 on the exploitation of water resources; the 1970 Law for the Protection of Agricultural Land; and Council of Ministers Decree No. 6 of 1997 PROHIBITING HUNTING IN ALL REGIONS, with Decree No. 183 of 2006 establishing the NATIONAL PARKS PROJECT to create new parks and upgrade existing ones. A pasture-and-forest protection law from 1982 and a national hunting ban are old, broad and still on the books — in a country with a weak central state, an existing statute you can name is worth more than a new one you must lobby for. Protected areas fall under national parks, protected reserves, protected areas and wetlands, managed through a technical committee for wildlife and national parks; an international conservation union report has called for improvements to the legal and institutional framework and identified 24 NEW MARINE AND COASTAL AREAS for protection. WHO IT SUITS: Libyan communities near an existing or proposed reserve, and anyone needing to name the statute that already covers their ground. CAVEATS: STATE-MANAGED AREAS IN A DIVIDED COUNTRY — management capacity is the documented weak point, not the legal categories. For the regulator and what does not exist, Libya's EGA entry; for a lawyer, the Bar Association and LFJL entry; for community funding newly opened to Libya, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Libyan Wildlife Trust and five other named Libyan conservation organisations — founded 2011, restoring named forests with hectare targets, and funded through a North African small-grants programme
trackers.desc: WHO TO CALL IN LIBYA — AND THIS CORRECTS THE THIN PICTURE THIS FILE HELD: the LIBYAN WILDLIFE TRUST (LWT), FOUNDED 9 NOVEMBER 2011 by a group of nature lovers and wildlife defenders, is a Libyan environmental NGO and a member of the international conservation union, described as the most active civil society association in the protection of wildlife in Libya, working year by year under unstable national conditions. A Libyan-founded organisation that has kept working through fourteen years of instability is a more reliable contact than any ministry in this file's Libya record — and it is reachable. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES, WITH THE NUMBERS: restoration of the JODAYEM FOREST, a coastal ecosystem east of AL-ZAWIYA and west of Tripoli, 110 HECTARES including 11 hectares of rocky terrain between the forest and the sea, degraded by plastic waste accumulation, erosion and LACK OF MANAGEMENT PLANS — with LWT introducing a comprehensive system of PLANNING, MONITORING AND COMMUNITY MANAGEMENT, working with local institutions and civil society, publishing scientific evaluations of the restoration, and restoring 45 HECTARES through planting. It also rehabilitated the NASSER FOREST, whose biodiversity had deteriorated from excessive water salinity, by RESTORING THE WATER INFRASTRUCTURE. Naming the hectares, publishing the evaluation and fixing the water before planting is the sequence — Libya's own record shows volunteer planting without management ends in wildfire and encroachment. IT ALSO SPEAKS PUBLICLY: LWT has warned that Libyan tortoise species are heading toward extinction through smuggling out of the country, and green activists have raised the increasing axing of acacia in the southwestern Al-Widyan region. WHERE ITS MONEY COMES FROM, WHICH IS THE REPLICABLE PART: LWT is supported by a SMALL INITIATIVES PROGRAMME FOR NORTH AFRICAN CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS, coordinated in Libya by a regional conservation union office and co-funded by three foundations. A small-grants programme with a named in-country coordinator is how a Libyan association gets funded at all — ask the coordinator, not the donors. FIVE MORE NAMED LIBYAN BODIES active in conservation: the LIBYAN SOCIETY FOR BIRDS, the LIBYAN ORGANISATION FOR CONSERVATION OF NATURE, ALHAYA ORGANIZATION FOR THE PROTECTION OF WILDLIFE AND MARINE ORGANISMS, and THE NEW LIBYA. LWT's own stated message: Libya is an open protected area for everyone. WHO IT SUITS: Libyan communities facing coastal degradation, forest loss or wildlife trafficking, and anyone needing a named domestic partner. CAVEATS: A VOLUNTEER-ROOTED NGO IN A DIVIDED COUNTRY, dependent on external small grants; contacts should be confirmed. For the reserve register with hectares and failure notes, Libya's Nature Platform entry; for the regulator, EGA; for a lawyer, the Bar Association and LFJL entry.

trackers.name: Guamina (Friends of the Earth Mali)
trackers.desc: The Malian member of Friends of the Earth International, based in Bamako. Its work covers desertification, mining, sustainable agriculture, food security and ecological debt, alongside training and literacy courses delivered in local languages and a particular focus on the status of women. WHO TO ENLIST: one of very few points of contact in Mali for a community facing a mining or land-use problem, and a route into the wider Friends of the Earth Africa network. Domain unverified: Guamina appears in Friends of the Earth International's own member directory at foei.org with a Bamako postal address and telephone number but no website listed, so reach it through that entry. Guamina has no website of its own, so the link is Friends of the Earth International's member-group page for Mali, which publishes its address and telephone numbers: Hamdallaye près du pont Diafarana, Rue 42 porte 232, 2744 Bamako, on +223 20 80 01 16 or +223 76 11 83 38. It takes part in FoEI's campaigns on desertification and mining as well as sustainable agriculture, food security and ecological debt, and separately runs training and literacy courses in local languages — which is why it can reach communities a capital-city organisation cannot.
