UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. trackers.name: ECOWAS Court of Justice — file directly, but sue the State
trackers.desc: A COURT YOU CAN REACH WITHOUT EXHAUSTING DOMESTIC REMEDIES. The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has held human rights jurisdiction since 2005 and has broad access and standing rules permitting individuals and NGOs to bypass national courts and file directly. THE PRECEDENT: in SERAP v Federal Republic of Nigeria (ECW/CCJ/APP/08/09) the Court dismissed all three preliminary objections — no locus standi, no jurisdiction, statute-barred — and rejected the government's attempt to exclude an Amnesty International report from the evidence. NGO research was admitted as evidence, which matters when no state data exists. It found violations of articles 1 and 24 of the African Charter — article 24: ‘all peoples shall have the right to a general satisfactory environment favourable to their development’ — and of article 21, the right to natural wealth and resources. THE FAULT WAS AN OMISSION: the state ‘defaulted in its duties in terms of vigilance and diligence’, and ‘the omission to act and to prevent damage to the environment characterises the violation’. It ordered restoration within the shortest possible time and measures to prevent further damage, citing the ICJ that the environment ‘is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn’. THE LIMIT THAT DECIDES WHO YOU SUE: the Court held it had no jurisdiction over the private oil corporations, which were struck from the suit. You sue the State for failing to regulate; you cannot sue the company here — naming one as respondent loses that part of the case. AND PLAN FOR ENFORCEMENT: commentary records the Court did not identify a means for Nigeria to implement the ruling, and the ICJ later wrote to the President pressing for enforcement — judgment is the start of an enforcement campaign, not a self-executing remedy. Proposals to require exhaustion of domestic remedies were rejected by ECOWAS experts and Heads of Government, so the direct-access rule has been tested and held. VERIFY MEMBERSHIP BEFORE FILING: this state has been reported as withdrawing from ECOWAS. This entry does not resolve that question — confirm current membership and the Court's jurisdiction over your state before relying on this route, because withdrawal, if effective, would remove it.

trackers.name: ORFAO — comparative land-law tables, and a directive in draft
trackers.desc: COMPARATIVE LEGAL TABLES FOR YOUR COUNTRY AND ITS NEIGHBOURS, IN ONE DOCUMENT. The Observatoire Régional du Foncier Rural en Afrique de l'Ouest (ORFAO), hosted by UEMOA, publishes a regional study on rural land markets containing side-by-side ‘cadre légal comparé’ tables — one covering Bénin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire and Sénégal, another Guinée-Bissau, Mali, Niger and Togo — plus typologies of direct and indirect interventions in land markets and a table of regulatory issues and families of instruments. If you need to know what instrument exists in your country and whether a neighbour has a stronger one, that is the document — comparative tables let a campaign point to a neighbour's provision as an achievable ask rather than a novelty. A WINDOW IS OPENING: on 26 June 2026 in Ouagadougou the UEMOA ministers for urbanisme, habitat, domaines et cadastre approved a draft directive to harmonise rules on immatriculation foncière, accès au titre de propriété and a système d'information foncière, aiming at a common framework of land governance. BE PRECISE ABOUT STATUS: that was a DRAFT directive approved by ministers, not an adopted and transposed instrument — check adoption and transposition before relying on it. But transposition is the moment domestic land law is reopened in each state, and that is when community provisions can be argued for. FOR A GRAZING OR TRANSHUMANCE DISPUTE: a regional pastoral situation bulletin covers 11 West African countries with the support of decentralised technical services — an evidence source drawing on the same services you would otherwise approach one by one. RECORDED PLAINLY: cattle theft is documented as a driver of conflict and instability in the Sahel, so a land dispute here may sit inside a security context that changes what is safe to do. And confirm your state's current ECOWAS standing — several members are recorded as suspended.

trackers.name: CMAT — five farmer and jurist organisations in one convergence against land grabbing, running a legal clinic for the dispossessed
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Convergence Malienne contre les Accaparements de Terres, formed in 2012 and formalised in 2013, which joins five umbrella organisations — the farmers' professional associations (AOPP), the Coalition des Alternatives Africaines (CAD-Mali), the national peasant coordination (CNOP), the association of the dispossessed (UACDDDD), and the Ligue des Jeunes Juristes pour le Développement Humain. That last member is the point: the convergence has lawyers inside it, and one of its stated objectives is to run a legal clinic for victims of expropriation, eviction and land grabbing. ITS STATED AIMS ARE UNUSUALLY OPERATIONAL: enable victims of expropriation and eviction to know and assert their rights; stop evictions and expropriations legally and legitimately; and demand reparation for both material and immaterial damage. It supports named village communities through their disputes, and its own estimate is that more than a million hectares have been grabbed in a country where the agricultural land law it pressed for was finally passed in 2017. It has also run training for communities on the UN declaration on peasants' rights, and published a comparative analysis of Mali's various natural resource codes — useful because, as its own briefing puts it, Mali has no single legal instrument covering agricultural land: the provisions are scattered across many texts, and that vagueness is what makes customary holders easy to dispossess. WHO IT SUITS: villages and urban neighbourhoods facing expropriation, eviction or an investor allocation. CAVEATS: a coalition rather than a service provider — approach is through a member organisation, and no intake route, fee or clinic timetable was published; its own account records severe repression of protesting communities, including arrests and long arbitrary detention, which is context a community should weigh.

trackers.name: CNOP-Mali — supports the village land commissions that let a village delimit its own terroir under the 2017 agricultural land law
trackers.desc: WHO GETS YOUR VILLAGE COMMISSION WORKING: the Coordination Nationale des Organisations Paysannes du Mali (CNOP), created in May 2002 as a framework for exchange and joint action between Malian farmers' organisations, active in policy dialogue with the state and in denouncing land-grab cases, notably in the Office du Niger zone; it hosted the international peasant conference against land grabbing at Nyéléni in November 2011. WHAT IT IS DOING NOW THAT A VILLAGE CAN USE: in February 2025 it convened the first steering committee of a project on SUPPORTING THE LAND AND FOREST SECURITY OF COMMUNITIES THROUGH THE LAND COMMISSIONS (COFO), bringing civil society, ministries and technical services together on the commissions' role in preventing and resolving land conflicts and protecting community land and natural resources. THE INSTRUMENT BEHIND IT: the agricultural land law of April 2017 recognises the land rights of rural communities and puts VILLAGE LAND COMMISSIONS at the centre — for the first time letting villages DELIMIT THEIR OWN TERROIR; a CNOP staffer's diagnosis of why this was needed is exact — the state had never put in place any mechanism for getting customary rights recognised. Implementing decrees were adopted in late March. ASK WHETHER YOUR VILLAGE HAS A COMMISSION FONCIÈRE VILLAGEOISE AND WHETHER IT HAS DELIMITED THE TERROIR — that delimitation is the document that answers an investor's map. THE HONEST WARNING FROM THE MOVEMENT ITSELF: campaigners record that the bill went from 180 articles to 49 during adoption, losing coherence and clarity precisely on the application of customary rights and the roles of the village land commissions — so expect the text to be thinner than the promise, and press for the implementing detail. WHO IT SUITS: Malian villages and farmers' organisations wanting their terroir delimited and their customary rights recognised, especially in the Office du Niger zone. CAVEATS: a farmers' movement and policy organisation, not a law firm — for legal advice and aid it works alongside the jurists' league inside the CMAT convergence, whose entry is also in this file; Mali's security situation constrains fieldwork in much of the country. WHY THIS IS A LAND-HOLDING INSTRUMENT AND NOT ONLY AN ADVISORY ONE: THE DELIMITED TERROIR IS THE ASSET. Once a village has delimited its terroir through the commission, it holds a bounded, officially acknowledged area attached to the village rather than to individuals — which is what an investor, a neighbouring village or a state service must then negotiate against. Delimit before you are approached, not after: every instrument in this file that works — Senegal's reserves, Cameroon's convention, the Congolese CFCL, Ethiopia's Guassa — was in place BEFORE the project arrived, and the ones that failed were attempted after.

trackers.name: ANICT and the FNACT — Mali's national fund for local-authority investment, five windows, 37.9 billion FCFA in one year, and your commune is the applicant
trackers.desc: WHERE THE MONEY FOR LOCAL PROJECTS SITS: the Agence Nationale d'Investissement des Collectivités Territoriales (ANICT), a public administrative establishment created by loi n°0042 of 7 July 2000 to manage the subsidies allocated to local investments carried out UNDER THE PROJECT OWNERSHIP OF THE TERRITORIAL COLLECTIVITIES, and to guarantee certain loans they contract. It runs the FONDS NATIONAL D'APPUI AUX COLLECTIVITÉS TERRITORIALES (FNACT), which has FIVE WINDOWS covering investment, training and support to the collectivities' functioning. THE APPLICANT IS YOUR COMMUNE, NOT YOU — which is exactly why a village should know this exists: the money for a borehole, a road or a market is already allocated to your local authority, and the lever is the mayor and the communal council, not a donor. One window worth naming: the Dotation d'Investissement affectée au Financement du Développement Économique Régional (DIN-DER), placed at the disposal of Regional Councils expressly for projects of economic interest that valorise THE PROTECTION AND VALORISATION OF NATURAL RESOURCES and improve access to goods and services. THE SCALE, PUBLISHED IN ITS OWN ANNUAL REPORT: in 2024 the FNACT was funded to 37,905,274,755 FCFA — the Malian state providing the largest share (22.6 billion for the regions' FNACT budget plus 6.6 billion via the special investment budget), with KfW, Denmark, the World Bank and UNCDF completing it — financing 140 PROJECTS across all regions, with emphasis on Koulikoro, Ménaka and Nioro. Performance-linked grants of 230 to 256 million FCFA per commune have been awarded under a conditional performance programme, and ANICT publishes which dossiers were judged compliant — in one regional round, 32 of 40 submitted. Ask your commune what it submitted, and whether it was judged compliant; the list is public. WHO IT SUITS: Malian villages and communal councillors seeking financing for local infrastructure or natural-resource projects. CAVEATS: THE COLLECTIVITY IS THE BENEFICIARY, NOT THE COMMUNITY DIRECTLY, so this is a lever over your mayor rather than a grant you can win; security conditions restrict verification visits in several regions. For village land commissions and terroir delimitation, Mali's CNOP entry; for the land-grab convergence and its lawyers, CMAT.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes de Mauritanie
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Mauritania — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: CN-ITIE Mauritanie
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and licences in Mauritania.

trackers.name: Mauritania — Agence pour la Promotion des Investissements (APIM, Guichet Unique)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; APIM’s One-Stop Shop (Guichet Unique, Khidmaty platform) handles company registration — Commercial Registry, tax & social-security registration — for SARLs, SAs, branches & GIEs within 48 hours, Mauritania. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Mauritania — Ministère des Finances
trackers.desc: National budget authority; governs & manages public finances and prepares the national budget, Islamic Republic of Mauritania. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Mauritania.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: Nature Mauritanie — the national wetlands and waterbird association, and the technical counterweight on the coast where the projects land
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Association Mauritanienne de protection de la nature, founded in 2000 by experts concerned with wetlands and officially recognised by the Mauritanian authorities in 2004 under receipt number 0216. Its work is conservation and sustainable use of Mauritania's wetland biodiversity, waterbirds and their habitats, and fragile ecosystems, and it takes part in the international waterbird censuses on national territory — which is the point for a community, because a census is a dated, comparable, independently collected number, and that is what an objection to a coastal or wetland project has to be built on. WHERE THE PRESSURE IS IN THIS COUNTRY: the wetlands it works in include the Banc d'Arguin national park, a Ramsar site since 1982 and World Heritage site since 1989, covering a third of the Mauritanian coast and inhabited by the Imraguen fishing communities, whose traditional fishery sits inside a protected area that is also a national economic asset — the classic setting for a fisheries, port or extractive dispute in which the residents are the ones treated as the problem. WHO IT SUITS: coastal and wetland communities, especially fishing communities in and around the Banc d'Arguin and the Diawling area, needing survey data, technical argument or a national ally. 6th district, Ilot 70, BP 2647, Nouakchott. CAVEATS: a scientific and conservation association, not a legal or advocacy defence body — no litigation capacity, intake route or fee information was found, and much of its published activity is bird monitoring and awareness rather than casework. Some site content is several years old; confirm current programmes before relying on it.

trackers.name: BACoMaB Trust Fund — a permanent endowment that pays the running costs of Mauritania's coastal protected areas, with a small grants window
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the Banc d'Arguin and Coastal and Marine Biodiversity Trust Fund, created in 2009 as a permanent endowment — capital invested on ethical and socially responsible markets, with the income used to fund conservation and management along the Mauritanian coast. A charitable foundation under English law with a headquarters agreement in Mauritania, recognised there as being of public utility since December 2010. WHY AN ENDOWMENT MATTERS MORE THAN A GRANT: it is designed to cover the RECURRENT costs that donors will not fund — surveillance, shared governance, community development, ecological monitoring, environmental education and capacity building — which is exactly what fails when a project ends. In one year it signed annual grant agreements totalling €860,000 with the Banc d'Arguin national park (€550,000), the Diawling national park, and a monk seal conservation programme (€120,000); its support to the Banc d'Arguin maritime and coastal surveillance system alone rose year on year from €69,000 to €176,500 across four years. THE DOOR FOR A COMMUNITY OR A SMALL ORGANISATION: alongside the park grants, BACoMaB runs a “Petites Subventions” (small grants) window to support other actors working in or for the sustainable management of the beneficiary zones, and its stated funding priorities include support to the livelihoods of people living in or near those zones, in ways compatible with the protection objectives, plus shared environmental governance arrangements. Note the origin of the money, because it is a precedent worth citing elsewhere: the government's initial contribution came from €1.5 million of revenues from the fisheries agreement with the European Union — the first time in Africa that fisheries-agreement money was directed to biodiversity protection. WHO IT SUITS: Mauritanian coastal communities and local organisations working in or beside the protected areas — principally the Banc d'Arguin and Diawling. CAVEATS: this funds conservation and compatible livelihoods, not opposition to a project; the main beneficiaries are the protected-area agencies themselves, and eligibility is tied to officially protected sites, so a community outside one has no claim on it; and it will not pay for legal costs.

trackers.name: Mauritania — aide juridique is provided for in the judicial organisation ordinance on proof of indigence, and the bar association in Nouakchott is who to ask
trackers.desc: WHAT THE LAW PROVIDES: Mauritania's ordinance on judicial organisation states that court fee tariffs are fixed by decree and that AIDE JURIDIQUE MAY BE GRANTED TO PARTIES WHO JUSTIFY THEIR INDIGENCE, in the conditions the law lays down. Proof of indigence is the gate here as in every francophone country in this file — ask which text fixes the criteria and what document is accepted before you assemble anything else. TWO OTHER PROVISIONS OF THAT ORDINANCE WORTH KNOWING IF YOU LIVE FAR FROM A COURT: courts and tribunals MAY HOLD AUDIENCES FORAINES — travelling hearings — within their jurisdiction, which is the same circuit principle recorded in Lesotho; and advocates exercise their ministry FREELY BEFORE ALL JURISDICTIONS, with the guarantee that no one may be removed from their natural judges. WHO TO ASK: the ORDRE NATIONAL DES AVOCATS DE MAURITANIE, the national bar, based in NOUAKCHOTT (+222 45 24 30 30 area; directory contacts +222 2245 47 74 and +222 31 10 00 06), whose own site publishes a list of members and copies of the laws regulating the legal profession, together with full texts of criminal, social, commercial and civil laws — the members list is how you find a named advocate in a country where no legal aid organisation could be verified for this file. Court infrastructure is being extended under a justice reform programme, with new tribunals delivered at Boutilimit, El Mina and Nouakchott-Sud. WHO IT SUITS: Mauritanians without means facing a land, inheritance or expropriation matter, and anyone needing to identify a practising advocate. CAVEATS: THIN GROUND, STATED HONESTLY — no Mauritanian legal aid organisation or clinic could be verified for this file; what is recorded here is a statutory provision and a bar association, not a service with an intake desk, and the bar's site is in Arabic. For the coastal endowment and its small grants window, Mauritania's BACoMaB entry.

trackers.name: Banc d'Arguin — only the resident Imraguen may fish in 1.2 million hectares, and only under sail; an exclusive use right rather than a title
trackers.desc: THE EXCLUSIVE RIGHT AND WHO HOLDS IT: the Parc National du Banc d'Arguin (PNBA), created 24 June 1976 by decree 76-147, covers 1,200,000 HECTARES — a third of the Mauritanian coast and the largest coastal and marine protected area in West Africa, Ramsar 1982 and UNESCO World Heritage 1989. THE PROVISION THAT MATTERS: THE POPULATIONS RESIDENT IN THE PARK ARE THE ONLY ONES AUTHORISED to practise controlled exploitation of the fish stocks, and MOTORISED BOATS ARE STRICTLY FORBIDDEN. About 1,200 Imraguen live permanently in EIGHT COASTAL VILLAGES, fishing from LANCHES — single-sail, engineless boats — which the park administration REGISTERS AND LIMITS IN NUMBER, around a hundred, USABLE ONLY BY THE IMRAGUEN. The park's missions under loi 2000-024 expressly include contributing to the development of those traditional fishing populations. Where a state has abolished collective land title — as Mauritanian land law did — an EXCLUSIVE USE RIGHT tied to residence and to a technology only you possess can hold ground that a deed cannot. The gear restriction IS the protection: it excludes industrial fleets by rule, not by argument. HOW IT CAME ABOUT, which is the transferable part: a conservation funder encouraged the government to BAN MOTORISED GEAR AND GUARANTEE EXCLUSIVE ACCESS TO THE PARK FOR THE IMRAGUEN PROVIDED THEY USED THEIR TRADITIONAL LANCHES — the community's own practice became the condition of its monopoly. From 1997 the park controlled Imraguen fishing activity; from 1998 it policed and repressed outside incursions. THE RECORDED WEAKNESS, so you do not copy the flaw: COMITÉS DE PLAGE (beach committees) were created in 2000 and can set a fishing rule, discipline, monitor and sanction — BUT their decisions bind ONLY THEIR OWN ACTIVE MEMBERS and not outsiders, BECAUSE no fishing terroirs were fixed within which each committee's authority would run. A committee without a defined territory can only govern its own members — fix the boundary of its authority when you create it. Analysts also warn that the gap between lanche-owning and non-owning families is the fault line to watch. WHO IT SUITS: Mauritanian coastal communities, and anyone whose state denies collective title but might grant an exclusive, gear-conditioned use right. CAVEATS: A USE RIGHT INSIDE A STATE PARK, NOT OWNERSHIP — revocable by the same authority that granted it, and dependent on continued enforcement against outside fleets. For the endowment that pays recurrent park costs, Mauritania's BACoMaB entry; for the wetlands association, Nature Mauritanie; for a lawyer, the aide juridique entry.

trackers.name: ROTAB-Niger / Publiez Ce Que Vous Payez
trackers.desc: Nigerien network of civil-society organisations for budget transparency and analysis, and the local Publish What You Pay coalition — scrutinises the national budget and revenues from the extractive (uranium, oil) sector.

trackers.name: Cour des Comptes
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Niger, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: ITIE Niger
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and licences in Niger.

trackers.name: Niger — Ministère des Finances
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares & executes the State budget and manages public debt & finances, Niger. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Niger.

trackers.name: Niger — Maison de l’Entreprise (CFE / Guichet Unique)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Maison de l’Entreprise (under the CCIN) runs the Centre de Formalités des Entreprises one-stop window for company creation, modification, radiation & RCCM registration, Niger. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: ECOWAS Court of Justice — file directly, but sue the State
trackers.desc: A COURT YOU CAN REACH WITHOUT EXHAUSTING DOMESTIC REMEDIES. The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has held human rights jurisdiction since 2005 and has broad access and standing rules permitting individuals and NGOs to bypass national courts and file directly. THE PRECEDENT: in SERAP v Federal Republic of Nigeria (ECW/CCJ/APP/08/09) the Court dismissed all three preliminary objections — no locus standi, no jurisdiction, statute-barred — and rejected the government's attempt to exclude an Amnesty International report from the evidence. NGO research was admitted as evidence, which matters when no state data exists. It found violations of articles 1 and 24 of the African Charter — article 24: ‘all peoples shall have the right to a general satisfactory environment favourable to their development’ — and of article 21, the right to natural wealth and resources. THE FAULT WAS AN OMISSION: the state ‘defaulted in its duties in terms of vigilance and diligence’, and ‘the omission to act and to prevent damage to the environment characterises the violation’. It ordered restoration within the shortest possible time and measures to prevent further damage, citing the ICJ that the environment ‘is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn’. THE LIMIT THAT DECIDES WHO YOU SUE: the Court held it had no jurisdiction over the private oil corporations, which were struck from the suit. You sue the State for failing to regulate; you cannot sue the company here — naming one as respondent loses that part of the case. AND PLAN FOR ENFORCEMENT: commentary records the Court did not identify a means for Nigeria to implement the ruling, and the ICJ later wrote to the President pressing for enforcement — judgment is the start of an enforcement campaign, not a self-executing remedy. Proposals to require exhaustion of domestic remedies were rejected by ECOWAS experts and Heads of Government, so the direct-access rule has been tested and held. VERIFY MEMBERSHIP BEFORE FILING: this state has been reported as withdrawing from ECOWAS. This entry does not resolve that question — confirm current membership and the Court's jurisdiction over your state before relying on this route, because withdrawal, if effective, would remove it.

trackers.name: ORFAO — comparative land-law tables, and a directive in draft
trackers.desc: COMPARATIVE LEGAL TABLES FOR YOUR COUNTRY AND ITS NEIGHBOURS, IN ONE DOCUMENT. The Observatoire Régional du Foncier Rural en Afrique de l'Ouest (ORFAO), hosted by UEMOA, publishes a regional study on rural land markets containing side-by-side ‘cadre légal comparé’ tables — one covering Bénin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire and Sénégal, another Guinée-Bissau, Mali, Niger and Togo — plus typologies of direct and indirect interventions in land markets and a table of regulatory issues and families of instruments. If you need to know what instrument exists in your country and whether a neighbour has a stronger one, that is the document — comparative tables let a campaign point to a neighbour's provision as an achievable ask rather than a novelty. A WINDOW IS OPENING: on 26 June 2026 in Ouagadougou the UEMOA ministers for urbanisme, habitat, domaines et cadastre approved a draft directive to harmonise rules on immatriculation foncière, accès au titre de propriété and a système d'information foncière, aiming at a common framework of land governance. BE PRECISE ABOUT STATUS: that was a DRAFT directive approved by ministers, not an adopted and transposed instrument — check adoption and transposition before relying on it. But transposition is the moment domestic land law is reopened in each state, and that is when community provisions can be argued for. FOR A GRAZING OR TRANSHUMANCE DISPUTE: a regional pastoral situation bulletin covers 11 West African countries with the support of decentralised technical services — an evidence source drawing on the same services you would otherwise approach one by one. RECORDED PLAINLY: cattle theft is documented as a driver of conflict and instability in the Sahel, so a land dispute here may sit inside a security context that changes what is safe to do. And confirm your state's current ECOWAS standing — several members are recorded as suspended.

trackers.name: Aghirin'man, Arlit — the mining-town association that got an independent laboratory in, and now owns a radiation meter of its own
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Nigerien association founded in 2002 in Arlit, in the uranium districts of the north, working on education, environmental protection and health in the face of uranium mining. HOW IT STARTED, WHICH IS THE PART EVERY COMPANY TOWN WILL RECOGNISE: it began by asking the operator why people were dying early. According to its president the company answered by threatening to close the mine, which frightened members who feared for their jobs — and then the miners' wives and other civil society organisations joined and carried it. WHAT IT DID NEXT IS THE MODEL: in December 2003 it invited an independent French radioactivity laboratory to come and measure, and the results are why the case exists at all — drinking-water wells at ten times the World Health Organization's uranium guideline while the operator's own communications denied any water contamination, and radioactive waste rock used as road fill outside a hospital reading a hundred times normal background, which was removed only eight months after the laboratory wrote to the company's chief executive, who never replied. AND THEN IT BOUGHT THE INSTRUMENT: with a scintillometer donated by an Austrian foundation, Aghirin'man now takes its own radiation measurements in the town — a community that owns the meter does not have to wait for anyone's permission to know. It also watches new projects, using the rule that Nigerien regulation requires an environmental impact study to be produced and made public BEFORE the public hearings at which residents can question the promoter, and it has written to operators demanding the radiological and bacteriological analyses of drinking-water boreholes. Its stated programme includes training local people in environmental rights and supporting income activities away from contaminated ground. WHO IT SUITS: communities in and around Arlit, Akokan and the newer uranium concessions; and, as a template, any community beside an extractive operation that needs its own measurements. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED SITE OF ITS OWN — this entry points at the French relay association that supports it and publishes its work; treat that as the route in, not as the organisation. It is a small local association operating under real pressure, its president has described an embargo imposed by the mining companies, and it has no legal service or intake procedure.

trackers.name: Niger's Commissions foncières and the farmers' chamber network — village-level offices that issue written land acts for a few thousand francs
trackers.desc: WHO TO APPROACH: the Commissions foncières (Cofo) — offices established under Niger's Code rural at village and tribe level (Cofob), commune level (Cofocom) and department level (Cofodep) — whose job is to verify people's land rights and issue written acts attesting to them, then archive a copy. Coverage reported: more than 3,000 of about 15,000 villages have a base commission, 145 of 265 communes, and all 36 departments, with a permanent regional secretariat of the Code rural in each of the 8 regions. The Réseau National des Chambres d'Agriculture (RECA) publishes plain-language notes on how to use them, which is why its page is the entry point here. WHAT YOU CAN GET AND WHY IT PROTECTS YOU: the commissions issue attestations of customary holding, of sale, of donation, and formalise contracts of rental, loan and customary pledge — and these acts count as WRITTEN PROOF, usable as evidence if a dispute reaches a court. Crucially, the acts are ADMINISTRATIVE acts, so they can only be challenged by hierarchical appeal or by an action for excess of power before an administrative tribunal — that is what gives them their protective force. In rural areas a full land title from the cadastre service is built on the basis of an attestation of customary holding issued by a Cofo, so the attestation is the first step, not a lesser alternative. Reported cost in one documented case: acts issued after enquiry for 2,500 to 3,000 FCFA, plus the commission members' travel costs, with fees set by each commission's internal rules. Commissions also identify and delimit pastoral areas, passage corridors and water points, and controlled a plateau to check that fields had not been created on land reserved for grazing. If the base commission in your village is not functioning, the commune or department commission can issue the act — and the act has the same legal value whichever level issues it. WHO IT SUITS: Nigerien farmers, herders and villages wanting written proof of a holding, a sale, an inheritance or a shared pastoral resource before a dispute or an allocation arrives. CAVEATS: these are STATE bodies with uneven coverage — the base commissions exist in only a fifth of villages, and the cadastre service may require the attestation to come from commune or department level; disputes between rural operators must first go through an attempt at customary conciliation before a judicial procedure. For the uranium zone and radiation monitoring, Niger's Aghirin'man entry.

trackers.name: ANAJJ Niger — ten legal-aid bureaux sitting inside the high courts, open to ANY person living in Niger, with a rights-NGO representative on each panel
trackers.desc: WHERE TO FILE: the Agence Nationale de l'Assistance Juridique et Judiciaire (ANAJJ), a public administrative establishment created by loi n°2011-42 of 14 December 2011, with statutes fixed by decree in 2012. Its mission is to make ASSISTANCE JURIDIQUE available FREE TO ANY APPLICANT, and ASSISTANCE JUDICIAIRE to vulnerable and indigent persons — the two limbs named in Benin's entry, split explicitly by who qualifies. WHERE THE OFFICES ARE, AND THIS IS THE BEST-DISTRIBUTED FRANCOPHONE NETWORK IN THIS FILE: TEN local bureaux (BAJJ) established INSIDE the Tribunaux de Grande Instance — Agadez, Arlit, Diffa, Dosso, Konni, Maradi, Niamey, Tahoua, Tillabéry and Zinder — so the counter is in the courthouse you would have to attend anyway, including at ARLIT, the uranium town whose community monitoring is recorded separately in this file. WHO SITS ON THE PANEL THAT DECIDES, published and worth knowing: the president of the high court chairs it; the chief clerk is secretary; and it includes a representative of the population ministry, A REPRESENTATIVE OF HUMAN RIGHTS DEFENCE ASSOCIATIONS, and a representative of the advocates or court-appointed defenders. A rights-NGO representative sits on the body deciding your application — if you know that organisation, they are already in the room. WHO CAN APPLY: the Director General states that ANAJJ may be seized for legal or judicial assistance by ANY PERSON LIVING ON NIGERIEN TERRITORY, the law making NO DISTINCTION BY NATIONALITY; detained persons apply through the head of the prison establishment. Note the limit she also draws: the agency can offer legal assistance on its own initiative through awareness sessions and open days, but in a DISPUTE it must be formally seized — nobody will come to you. WHO IT SUITS: anyone living in Niger — citizen or not — facing a land, compensation or pollution dispute and unable to pay. CAVEATS: A STATE AGENCY under the justice ministry, means-tested on the judicial limb, and Niger's security situation restricts movement in several regions. For attestations of customary possession at commune level, Niger's Commissions foncières entry; for uranium-zone radiation monitoring, Aghirin'man. HOW POVERTY IS PROVED, WHICH IS THE GATE EVERY FRANCOPHONE SCHEME IN THIS FILE TURNS ON: Niger is the country that publishes the rule. Décret n°2014-04/PRN/MJ of 3 January 2014 fixes THE CRITERIA AND THE MODES OF PROOF OF INDIGENCE for obtaining assistance judiciaire, made under the 2011 law and the 2012 ANAJJ statutes. Its article 2 defines what you are actually getting: assistance judiciaire subject to the indigence condition is a SET OF SERVICES for an indigent person during a judicial procedure, comprising THE DEFENCE OF THAT PERSON AND THE TAKING IN CHARGE OF ALL COSTS RELATING TO THE PROCEDURE. Defence plus all procedural costs — not advice, not a contribution — so ask for the decree by number if a bureau tries to narrow it. AND THE TRANSFERABLE MOVE: in every francophone country recorded here the application fails or succeeds on the indigence document, so ask your own bureau WHICH TEXT fixes the criteria and what proof it names, before you assemble anything else. Niger's answer is a decree; Côte d'Ivoire's is a certificat d'indigence from the police commissioner or district head; DR Congo's is an attestation d'indigence; Burkina's request is unstamped.

trackers.name: Fundação Príncipe
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an NGO working to conserve Príncipe Island with and for its people, with a team of nearly fifty, more than 90 per cent of them local, running marine conservation, terrestrial conservation and community-engagement programmes in partnership with the regional authorities and local communities. The whole island has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 2012. Its terrestrial work documents species and the threats to them, builds protection initiatives with communities, and trains technicians in local government institutions and guide associations. USE IT: for Príncipe specifically. This is an island-scale organisation in an autonomous region, not a national body, so it is the wrong contact for a problem on São Tomé island.

trackers.name: São Tomé & Príncipe — Guiché Único para Empresas (GUE)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the GUE (Ministry of Justice) one-stop handles company constitution, alteration & extinction with online registration in 1–5 days, São Tomé & Príncipe. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: São Tomé & Príncipe — Ministério do Planeamento, Finanças e Economia Azul

Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: Article 31 park fund, and the plans you can demand by date
trackers.desc: THREE INSTRUMENTS WITH NUMBERS ATTACHED. The Lei de Base do Ambiente (10/1999) and the Lei da Conservação da Fauna, Flora e das Áreas Protegidas (11/1999) were given effect by Lei n.º 6/2006 of 13 June creating the Parque Natural Obô de São Tomé (19,500 ha) and Lei n.º 7/2006 creating the Parque Natural Obô do Príncipe (8,500 ha). ‘Obô’ means virgin forest in forro. ARTICLE 31 OF LEI 11/1999 CREATES A FUNDO ESPECIAL DO PARQUE, funded by fines (coimas and multas) and fees — enforcement generates the management money, so ask whether the fund has been constituted and what has been paid in; documentation refers to the need to ‘create and consolidate’ it, so it may exist on paper first. DOCUMENTS YOU CAN DEMAND: the Plano de Manejo is the statutory management instrument on a 5-year cycle covering the park and its buffer zone — PNOST has had three (2009–2014, 2015–2020, 2021–2025); and the Plano de Gestão is annual, must coincide with the economic year, and is presented at the latest 30 days after approval. CHECK CONFFAP IS ACTUALLY CONVENING before addressing it: the coordinating Conselho was to function only from the first completed year of park services operating. NOTE THE BUFFER: on Príncipe the zona tampão is extensible to the entire remainder of the island. And delegated management is established practice — MARAPA and the Jalé Ecolodge have held management of part of PNOST under state supervision.

trackers.name: 21 Reservas Especiais — a live category, and HCV is the accepted method
trackers.desc: A DESIGNATION ROUTE THAT HAS JUST BEEN USED AT SCALE. With funding from the Rainforest Trust and the European Union, BirdLife International with academic institutions and national and international NGOs supported the Government in identifying and designating 21 new areas with the status of Reservas Especiais, totalling more than 12,300 hectares on São Tomé island, selected using High Conservation Value (HCV) criteria. THREE THINGS FOLLOW: Reserva Especial is a live, recently used category; HCV criteria are the accepted selection method, so frame a proposal in those terms; and the official rationale is directly quotable — the buffer zones, the lowland forests and the coastal and marine zones, also rich in biodiversity, have limited or non-existent protection. That is the state acknowledging the gaps lie outside the two parks, which is exactly where most sites are. THREATS NAMED IN THE PARKS' OWN DOCUMENTATION: disordered hunting, disordered and illegal felling, extraction of sand from beaches and palm planting for palm wine. Both parks are uninhabited, attributed to relief, high rainfall, difficult access and soils unsuited to agriculture — so a proposal covering inhabited land is a different and less-tested proposition here.

trackers.name: MARAPA — the São Toméan fishing NGO that co-manages the resource with fishers, and helped designate the country's marine protected areas
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a São Toméan non-governmental organisation founded in 1999 out of a French-funded artisanal fisheries programme, staffed by fisheries technicians, marine biologists and development workers, and treated as one of the country's leading NGOs. Its stated work is protecting marine and coastal habitats, co-managing fisheries resources, and supporting the people in the fishing chain — production, processing and marketing — including the palaiês, the women fish traders who are usually left out of any consultation. WHY IT IS THE ENTRY FOR THIS COUNTRY: on a small island state, the development that takes a community's livelihood is usually coastal or marine — a port, a resort, an industrial fishing licence, a mangrove cleared — and MARAPA is the organisation with the technical standing to contest it. It is one of three consortium members that delivered the national network of marine protected areas, alongside Fundação Príncipe and a development NGO, with international technical support; those designations were made with local communities and local conservation teams rather than over them, and the stated next problem is whether the protected areas are actually managed — which is where a community can insist on a role. Its longer-running programmes cover sea turtles and cetaceans, ecotourism around the Malanza mangrove and the Jalé beach camp near the Obô national park, and improving safety at sea for fishers. WHO IT SUITS: fishing communities and coastal villages in São Tomé and Príncipe facing a coastal project, a mangrove clearance or exclusion from a fishery. CAVEATS: a technical conservation and fisheries organisation, not a legal service — no litigation capacity, intake route or fee information was found; much of its work runs inside donor-funded projects, so what it can do in your area depends on which project is live. THE CONFLICT IT EXISTS TO HANDLE, AND WHY A COMMUNITY SHOULD CALL IT EARLY: the coastal zone of Caué district, the southern littoral from Angra Toldo to the bay of São Miguel, is described as having become a battleground of the artisanal fishing sector — it is where fish still remain, because the north of the island no longer has them — with coastal species still abundant near Ilhéu das Rolas, Sete Pedras, São Miguel and Porto Alegre. A MARAPA study found that 60 per cent of those fishing in the south come from the north of the country, and the resulting disputes, sometimes violent, have reached the port captaincy, the coast guard and the fisheries directorate. Resource exhaustion in one part of a country arrives in the next as a conflict between neighbours, not as a conservation problem — which is why the response MARAPA works on is SHARED MANAGEMENT of fishery resources: research on the species and the pressures on them first, then negotiated dialogue between the fishing groups. It was created in 1999 by fisheries technicians, marine biologists and development workers out of a French-funded artisanal fisheries project, and published in the Diário da República that December. It also supports the palaê women fish traders with training in handling and conservation of fish and with drying ovens supplied to a fishers' and palaê association, works alongside the national federation of fishers' and palaê associations, and developed an improved cookstove cutting fuelwood use by around 60 per cent.

trackers.name: São Tomé's legal assistance — provided for in law but NOT formally organised; the working route is the Ministério Público and the bar, district by district
trackers.desc: WHAT EXISTS AND WHAT DOES NOT, STATED FIRST BECAUSE IT SAVES A WASTED JOURNEY: in São Tomé and Príncipe judicial assistance and legal assistance ARE PROVIDED FOR BY LAW BUT ARE NOT FORMALLY ORGANISED. There is no legal aid institute to walk into here — do not spend a day looking for one. WHAT IS BEING BUILT INSTEAD, AND WHAT TO ASK FOR: a judicial modernisation programme working IN COLLABORATION WITH THE ORDEM DOS ADVOGADOS undertook to work immediately on DECENTRALISING LEGAL CONSULTATION AND PUBLIC ATTENDANCE BY THE MINISTÉRIO PÚBLICO IN EVERY DISTRICT OF THE COUNTRY, expressly so that citizens are not obliged to travel to the CAPITAL to bring a matter forward. So the two doors in São Tomé are the public prosecutor's public-attendance service in your own district and the bar association — ask for consulta jurídica by name. The same programme covers digitalisation of judicial procedures, aimed at removing the existing GEOGRAPHIC AND ECONOMIC BARRIERS to the justice system — the programme's own words, and the two barriers this whole file keeps recording. WHO IT SUITS: São Toméans with a land, inheritance or fishing-rights dispute who cannot travel to São Tomé city and cannot pay an advocate. CAVEATS: THIS IS A REFORM IN PROGRESS, NOT A STANDING SERVICE — confirm locally whether district attendance has actually begun before relying on it, and treat published dates as intentions; there is no organised legal aid scheme behind it. For the fishing sector and the Caué coastal conflict, São Tomé's MARAPA entry; for Príncipe, the Fundação Príncipe entry.

trackers.name: Obô natural parks — the Conselho de Gestão MUST include the communities resident in the buffer zones, and the buffer boundary is where the argument happens
trackers.desc: THE SEAT THE LAW RESERVES FOR YOU: São Tomé and Príncipe's protected-area system rests on the LEI DE BASES DO AMBIENTE (LEI Nº10/1999) and the LEI DE CONSERVAÇÃO DA FAUNA, FLORA E ÁREAS PROTEGIDAS (LEI Nº11/1999), under which LEI Nº6/2006 created the PARQUE NATURAL OBÔ DE SÃO TOMÉ and LEI Nº7/2006 the PARQUE NATURAL OBÔ DO PRÍNCIPE — together covering about 30% OF THE COUNTRY'S LAND AREA, with the Príncipe park incorporating ALL REMAINING NATIVE FOREST and occupying 45% of that island. THE PROVISION TO QUOTE IS ARTICLE 29 OF LEI 11/1999: the park's CONSELHO DE GESTÃO, a minimum of FIVE people, INTEGRATES REPRESENTATION OF THE LOCAL AUTHORITIES AND OF THE COMMUNITIES RESIDENT IN THE BUFFER ZONES. A statutory minimum of five with your community named among them is a seat, not a consultation — ask who currently sits for the buffer-zone communities and when the council next meets. The management plan is the park's principal tool, and the annual plan must be presented within 30 DAYS of the plano de manejo's approval, revised EVERY 12 MONTHS, and APPROVED BY THE CONSELHO DE GESTÃO. Twelve-month revision means a live document you can move each year rather than a settlement fixed once. WHY THE BUFFER ZONE IS WHERE THE ARGUMENT HAPPENS: the law provides a ZONA TAMPÃO surrounding the park limits WHERE HUMAN ACTIVITY IS MOST NOTABLE, serving simultaneously as A MODEL FOR SUSTAINABLE USE and as a BARRIER protecting the park's forests; the São Tomé park is uninhabited, with no permanent settlements, so the residents the law names are buffer-zone residents. AND THE RECORDED WEAKNESS, WHICH CUTS BOTH WAYS: park limits are well defined in the respective law WITH THE EXCEPTION OF THE ZONA TAMPÃO, WHOSE INTERPRETATION HAS REMAINED ARBITRARY. The one boundary the law left vague is the one your houses and fields sit inside — press for the buffer zone to be mapped, because an arbitrary boundary can be read against you as easily as for you. Documented pressures include unregulated hunting, sand extraction from beaches and palm planting for wine. WHO IT SUITS: São Toméan and Principense communities living beside or inside a buffer zone. CAVEATS: A STATE PARK WITH A STATUTORY COMMUNITY SEAT, NOT COMMUNITY TENURE. For fisheries co-management, São Tomé's MARAPA entry; for the concept-note test and HCV survey contracts, the Príncipe Foundation entry.

trackers.name: Nature Seychelles
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the oldest and largest environmental NGO in Seychelles, a registered association since 1998 with a board of trustees and around fifteen full-time staff including protected-area specialists. It manages Cousin Island Special Reserve and the Sanctuary at Roche Caiman, and through its Locally Empowered Area Protection project it has pioneered CO-MANAGEMENT under the country's nature reserve and conservancy legislation — the route by which local people take on protection and management of an area rather than leaving it to government. USE IT: start with LEAP if you want an area near you protected and locally run; use its protected-area staff if you need the technical case for why a site matters. It sits on government committees and taskforces and in the Citizen Engagement Platform Seychelles, so it has standing in consultations — but it works with government rather than against it, and will not fight a project for you.

trackers.desc: National company registry; the FSA registers & regulates companies, IBCs, foundations, trusts & securities and maintains the corporate register, Seychelles. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. trackers.name: Court of Appeal — the state must clean up, and may owe damages
trackers.desc: A CONSTITUTIONAL DUTY TO ACT AGAINST POLLUTION BY PRIVATE PARTIES. Seychelles' highest court held that Article 38 of the Constitution means the state must act to ensure ‘that private citizens do not pollute the environment’; that it is obliged to take steps to clean up pollution caused to public places like rivers and beaches; and that failure to act could lead to claims for damages. The case was brought by a landowner at Fairview estate against the Minister of Environment, the Minister of Health and the Attorney General over serious E. coli pollution of a river, with the state arguing it was not constitutionally obliged to act. THREE THINGS MAKE THIS UNUSUALLY USEFUL: the duty runs against state passivity, so where a regulator does nothing the inaction is itself the breach; it attaches to public places, rivers and beaches named; and it carries a damages remedy, not merely a declaration. The judgment was unanimous, written by Janak de Silva, a non-resident judge from Sri Lanka — the appellate bench includes non-resident judges, which is why its environmental reasoning draws on wider common-law authority and why the decision is described as potentially influential beyond Seychelles.

trackers.name: EPA 2016 Appeals Board — written procedure, but budget for the fee
trackers.desc: THE ROUTE BELOW THE COURTS. The Environment Protection Act 2016 (No. 18 of 2016), gazetted 5 September 2016, expressly establishes an Appeals Board, and dedicated Appeals Rules of Procedure Regulations exist — so the procedure is written down and obtainable. BUDGET FOR THE FEE: the statutory Memorandum of Appeal requires you to state the grounds of appeal and to certify that a fee in Seychelles Rupees has been paid, with receipt number and date — appeals are not free, so establish the current fee before the deadline, not after. WHAT ELSE THE ACT PROVIDES: the Minister may declare protected coastal zones and prepare an Integrated Coastal Zone Management Plan; may regulate petroleum and mineral exploration in territorial waters and the EEZ; EIA runs by prescribed classes, with an Environmental Appraisal Committee and registered EIA consultants — so a consultant's registration is checkable. THE ADMINISTRATOR MAY SERVE AN ENFORCEMENT NOTICE OR A PROHIBITION NOTICE — ask whether either has been served, because they are documents. Obstructing an inspection is punishable. The Act is live: plastic bag rules 2017, a tourism environmental sustainability levy, effluent standards and laboratory rules all 2023. WHO OPERATES: Nature Seychelles (BirdLife partner) manages the Cousin Special Island Reserve — 27 ha plus waters to 400 m from the high-water mark; Island Conservation Society staffs centres on 6 outer islands under a 2007 agreement with the parastatal Islands Development Company. DO NOT APPROACH the Nature Protection Trust of Seychelles — the first environmental NGO registered here (1992) — it ceased operating in 2011.

trackers.name: SeyCCAT Blue Grants Fund — grant money created by converting national debt, with the application form translated into Creole so locals could actually apply
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the Seychelles Conservation and Climate Adaptation Trust, created in 2015 as an independent, nationally based public-private trust fund to manage the proceeds of the world's first debt-for-nature swap for ocean conservation — US$21.6 million of national debt bought back at a discount, with the redirected debt service capitalising the trust — later joined by proceeds of a sovereign blue bond that raised US$15 million from investors. It runs the Blue Grants Fund. WHAT IT PAYS AND ON WHAT TERMS: reported disbursement rose from about US$286,500 in the first call to roughly US$889,000 across twenty-one projects in the third year, with US$700,000 a year available at that point and more than US$5.3 million distributed in total by 2025. Two windows are described: small-to-medium grants up to SCR 100,000, awarded on an approved concept note, maximum 12 months; and large grants between SCR 100,000 and SCR 1,000,000, shortlisted on a concept note then awarded on a full proposal, maximum 24 months. A concept note first, not a full proposal, is a low-cost way in for a small association. THE PART TO STEAL, BECAUSE IT IS AN ACCESS PROBLEM EVERY FUND IN THIS FILE HAS: the application form was originally in a standard European format that experienced NGOs could handle but local stakeholders could not, so in 2019 SeyCCAT translated the application form into Creole so people could apply in their own language, held public meetings across three islands, and did one-to-one visits with fishing communities, students and young women entrepreneurs. Ask any fund whether its form exists in the language its intended applicants speak. WHO IT SUITS: Seychellois NGOs, fishers' associations and community groups working on marine protection, sustainable fisheries and climate adaptation. CAVEATS: it funds ocean, fisheries and climate work — not litigation, not land purchase, and not opposition to a project; grants run to fixed short terms; and the model depends on debt-conversion and bond proceeds rather than open-ended income.

trackers.name: Seychelles legal aid — EVERY licensed lawyer must take legal aid cases as a condition of their licence, and you apply to the Judiciary
trackers.desc: WHO OWES YOU A LAWYER, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST RULE FOUND ANYWHERE IN THIS FILE: in Seychelles ALL LICENSED LEGAL PRACTITIONERS — UNLESS EXEMPT — MUST, AS A CONDITION OF THEIR LEGAL PRACTITIONER'S LICENCE, TAKE LEGAL AID CASES. Not a voluntary scheme, not a pro bono appeal to conscience: the obligation is attached to the licence itself, so the entire practising profession is the pool. Compare Mozambique and Angola, where the bar's statutes impose a duty, and every other country in this file where legal aid depends on who volunteers. HOW TO APPLY, AND WHERE: applications are filed WITH THE JUDICIARY, which reviews them, notifies the outcome, and ALLOCATES A LAWYER to your case if approved. THE MEANS TEST IS PUBLISHED AS A NUMBER: you must earn LESS THAN SCR 8,000 PER MONTH, and proof of your financial position is required. A published income threshold means you can determine your own eligibility before you go — rarer in this file than it should be. Scale: 784 legal aid applications were filed with the Judiciary in a single year in a country of under 100,000 people. The Registrar of the Supreme Court licenses practitioners under the Legal Practitioners Act, and publishes the roll of licensed lawyers — including suspensions, so you can check who is currently entitled to practise before instructing anyone. WHO IT SUITS: Seychellois who cannot afford a lawyer in a land, property, planning or environmental matter, on any island. CAVEATS: A MEANS-TESTED STATE SCHEME administered by the Judiciary — allocation is to an available practitioner rather than a specialist of your choosing, and the scheme does not fund campaigning; the threshold figure should be confirmed as current. For the coastal and marine conservation route and the Blue Grants Fund, Seychelles' SeyCCAT entry; for standing to litigate environmental matters, the Eco-Sud precedent recorded under Mauritius.
