trackers.name: East African Court of Justice — it stopped a road across the Serengeti
trackers.desc: THIS COURT STOPPED A GOVERNMENT FROM BUILDING A ROAD. In African Network for Animal Welfare v Attorney General of the United Republic of Tanzania (Reference No. 9 of 2010, judgment 20 June 2014), the East African Court of Justice held Tanzania's proposed highway across the Serengeti National Park unlawful and issued an injunction restraining Tanzania from operationalising it. THE TREATY ARTICLES THAT DID THE WORK: article 5(3)(c) of the EAC Treaty — promotion of sustainable utilisation of natural resources and measures that would effectively protect the natural environment of the Partner States — and article 114(1)(a), which enjoins partner states to conserve, protect and manage the environment. THE HARMS PLEADED ARE A REUSABLE CHECKLIST: disrupted animal migration, fragmentation of habitats, loss of scenic and visual quality, deterioration of air quality, increased poaching, and surface water and soil pollution. NOTE THE SHAPE OF THE RELIEF: at para 78 the Court said its orders must be preventative, and that roads in the Serengeti should be used by wildlife, tourists and Park administrators and not the general public — a restriction on who may use a road is a narrower and more grantable order than an outright ban. The government's own report had conceded grave negative impacts. THREE THINGS MAKE THIS ROUTE UNUSUAL: (1) standing survived a full challenge — the objection on jurisdiction, limitation and form was overruled on 26 August 2011 and the appeal dismissed on 15 March 2012; (2) the applicant was not from the respondent state — ANAW is a pan-African charity that sued Tanzania without being Tanzanian, so an NGO based in one partner state can challenge another's project; and (3) this is a trade-and-integration court, not a specialist environmental one — the claim runs through treaty obligations between states. CONFIRM PARTNER-STATE STATUS BEFORE FILING: this state's EAC accession is relatively recent, and the Court's jurisdiction follows partner-state status. This entry does not assert current standing to file — verify it first.

trackers.name: Candlelight — a Somaliland organisation with eighty staff and four offices that restores communal grazing land with the communities that hold it
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Candlelight for Environment, Education and Health, founded in 1995 in the wreckage of the civil war, now working across all six regions of Somaliland with more than eighty staff, a head office in Hargeisa and sub-offices in Sheikh, Burao and Erigavo, and stated work in Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya as well. Environmental restoration and protection is its first stated priority. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES ON LAND, which is the part that transfers: it works on the restoration of communal grazing areas — its documented case being the Dulcad plain — using crescent-shaped soil bunds built to a standard section, roughly 80 centimetres high on a one-metre base, in runs of thirty metres and up, which is a technique a village can be trained in and can build itself. In a pastoral economy where the land is held in common and the threat is degradation, enclosure and charcoal cutting rather than a permit, rehabilitating and re-establishing the commons is how you hold it. It runs community environmental awareness in named villages, trains community animal health workers, and researches the invasive mesquite that is taking over degraded land — including testing whether it can be turned into charcoal so the pressure comes off the native Acacia. It sits in the Resource Management Somali Network, which brings together thirteen organisations and teams from Somalia and Somaliland working on environment, and works with the pastoral development and environment ministry. WHO IT SUITS: pastoral and rural communities in Somaliland facing loss of communal grazing, enclosure or deforestation. Sha'ab Road, Hargeisa. CAVEATS: THIS IS A SOMALILAND ORGANISATION and its reach into south-central Somalia should not be assumed — it is filed under Somalia because this map has no separate key. It is a development and environment NGO, not a legal or advocacy defence body: no litigation, no intake route, no fee information, and published contact addresses vary between its own pages.

trackers.name: SOLLA and Somalia's land-dispute routes — the bar association whose members must give free legal aid, and the collective land purchase that worked
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: SOLLA, Somaliland's bar association, whose members are OBLIGED to provide free legal aid — with lawyers representing female clients at all stages of proceedings and paralegals working in the Hargeisa region; a legal aid clinic operates at the University of Hargeisa. That obligation is the single most useful fact for anyone in Somaliland who cannot pay. THE TWO COMMUNITY ROUTES THAT RESEARCH RECORDS AS HAVING WORKED, and both are things a group can organise itself: MINORITY GROUPS COLLECTIVELY PURCHASING LAND to improve their negotiating power, which has secured tenure; and grassroots MEDIATION COMMITTEES, in regions such as Kismayo, resolving disputes outside the formal courts. In Puntland, community elders are reported to resolve between 90 and 95 per cent of land disputes — so the forum that decides your case is probably not a court, and the elders' process is the one to prepare for. WHAT THE DISPUTES ACTUALLY ARE: most people buy and sell land outside the formal system; very few hold registered ownership and most are squatters or tenants. Disputes involve land grabbing and illegal occupation by clan leaders, businessmen, corporations, returnees and members of the diaspora, abuses by IDP camp gatekeepers, conflicts between international NGOs and private landowners, and returning refugees claiming the same plot. Officials have been reported abusing their positions for land grabbing and forced eviction, particularly against displaced returnees. Women are structurally exposed — excluded from inheritance and holding unequal negotiating power in customary dispute resolution — which is why the free representation of female clients matters. Somalia has National Eviction Guidelines (2019) and an IDP policy; campaigners note the guidelines still need enabling legislation to sue under. WHO IT SUITS: Somalis and Somalilanders facing eviction, occupation of their plot, or a land dispute headed to elders rather than a court — especially women and displaced returnees. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED LIVE SITE FOR SOLLA WAS FOUND — this entry points at the housing, land and property mapping that records it, and some details date from that research; provision is concentrated in Somaliland and Hargeisa. For environment and communal grazing restoration, Somalia's Candlelight entry.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants in Somalia — the eighth cycle added Somalia by name, with nearly USD 1 million allocated equally to every participating country
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the GEF SMALL GRANTS PROGRAMME, running since 1992 to fund CIVIL SOCIETY and LOCAL ACTION on environmental degradation. THE FACT THAT MATTERS HERE, AND IT IS RECENT: the eighth replenishment EXPANDED COUNTRY COVERAGE FROM 124 TO 135 COUNTRIES, ADDING SOMALIA BY NAME — alongside SOUTH SUDAN, LIBYA, EQUATORIAL GUINEA, SÃO TOMÉ AND PRÍNCIPE and Angola. Somalia was outside this window and now is inside it; if you were told years ago that no environmental small grants existed here, that answer is out of date. THE ALLOCATION RULE IS THE UNUSUAL PART: the cycle secured USD 135 million for the core programme and ensures EQUAL ALLOCATION OF NEARLY USD 1 MILLION IN CORE FINANCING TO EACH OF THE 135 COUNTRIES — regardless of size or previous participation levels, with STAR allocations to the programme raised over 30 per cent. Equal allocation regardless of size means a small or newly-added country is not competing against large established programmes for the core money — that is the argument for applying early in a first cycle. Its stated objective is to catalyse and mobilise civil society actors and LOCAL ACTIONS addressing the major drivers of environmental degradation. ALSO OPEN TO SOMALI ORGANISATIONS, recorded together because the search is the same: UN-administered LOW-VALUE GRANTS of USD 30,000 to USD 80,000 per project for Somali civil society organisations, and larger community-resilience grants of up to USD 1,000,000 over 24 to 36 months requiring legal registration BOTH in the target federal member state AND with the federal government. Registration in both places is the gate on the large grants — check yours before drafting. WHO IT SUITS: Somali and Somaliland community organisations with an environmental, rangeland, water or resilience project. CAVEATS: DONOR CYCLES WITH FIXED DEADLINES — confirm the country programme is operational before counting on it, and note it funds environmental and resilience action, NOT litigation or land purchase. For land disputes, free legal aid and the collective-purchase route, Somalia's SOLLA entry; for environment and communal grazing, Candlelight.

trackers.name: Community rangeland enclosures and grazing reserves — the Balaanbal sequence that worked, and the difference between a community reserve and a private land grab
trackers.desc: HOW A COMMUNITY HOLDS GRAZING GROUND: the working instrument in Somaliland and Puntland is the COMMUNITY RANGELAND ENCLOSURE or GRAZING RESERVE — land fenced and closed by a village so pasture regenerates and is held in reserve for drought. THE DOCUMENTED SEQUENCE, WHICH IS THE PART TO COPY, from BALAANBAL in the TOGDHEER region: residents were asked to LIST THEIR NATURAL RESOURCES and then IDENTIFY THE AREA to be fenced; a NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE was set up; the committee DEVELOPED A NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT PLAN, STOPPED ALL ONGOING CHARCOAL PRODUCTION on community land, SET UP A COMMUNITY PATROL, and then RAISED EXTENSIVE COMMUNITY AWARENESS about the reserve. List, choose, commit a plan, stop the extraction already happening, patrol, then tell everyone — in that order. Stopping your own charcoal cutting before you ask anyone else to respect the boundary is what makes the claim defensible. WHAT IT PRODUCED: the project was HANDED OVER TO THE GOVERNMENT on completion, and during the 2025 drought the government OPENED THE ENCLOSED AREAS for livestock — officials reported 20,000 ANIMALS GRAZING in the enclosure when there was no pasture in the open rangelands. Research on the AROORI GRAZING RESERVE, re-established 2016, records reserves as fodder refuges in prolonged drought and as tools to maintain indigenous grass biodiversity, and identifies the emerging form as VILLAGE GRAZING LOTS established through JOINT LAND-USE PLANNING. THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDES WHETHER YOURS IS LEGITIMATE, RECORDED HONESTLY: conflict research finds unregulated enclosures PREDOMINANT in rural Somaliland, often built to produce CHARCOAL FOR CASH from the trees inside, with the state too weak to regulate land — and attempts to dismantle them in Balligubadle FAILED because people simply re-established them when no alternative livelihood was offered. A private enclosure that harvests what is inside it is a land grab; a community reserve that closes an area, bans charcoal and opens in drought is the opposite — the paperwork looks identical, so make the ban, the patrol and the drought rule explicit and public from the start. WHO IT SUITS: Somali and Somaliland pastoral communities and village committees. CAVEATS: CUSTOMARY AND PROJECT-BASED, NOT TITLE — the Balaanbal reserve was handed to government and opened by government decision; land regulation is weak and enclosure is itself a live source of conflict. For land disputes and collective purchase, Somalia's SOLLA entry; for environment and communal grazing work, Candlelight; for community funding, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Sudan — Commercial Registration Department (Registrar General)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the Commercial Registration Department (Registrar General) under the Ministry of Justice maintains the commercial register under the Companies Act 1925 & Registration Law 1971, with an online registered-company-name search, Sudan. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Sudan — Ministry of Finance & Economic Planning (MoFEP)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the MoFEP oversees Sudan’s public finances — budgeting, fiscal policy & economic planning — and publishes the national budget, Sudan. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Sudan.

trackers.name: National Audit Chamber (Sudan)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Sudan — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: SECS — Sudan's pioneer environmental society, registered in 1975, with a branch network reaching far past Khartoum
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Sudanese Environment Conservation Society, officially registered in 1975 as the country's pioneer national environmental NGO — national, voluntary and independent, and by its own account grown into a network of more than 113 branches across Sudan, run largely by volunteers. In a country where almost every organisation is Khartoum-bound, a branch network of that reach is the point: the nearest branch, not the capital office, is the realistic contact. WHAT IT DOES FOR PEOPLE ON THE LAND: environmental rehabilitation and conservation work at community level; water, sanitation and health work with farmers and pastoralists specifically; lobbying and advocacy for environmental rights; and capacity building for grassroots communities. It campaigned for the creation of the higher council for environment and natural resources at national and state level, and has pressed for environmental provisions in Sudan's constitution and for enforcement of environmental law — which is unusual: this is an organisation that has argued about the shape of the law, not only about trees. Deforestation is its long-running specific focus. It runs a centre for environmental research and studies. Str. 57 Extension, PO Box 44266, Khartoum. WHO IT SUITS: farming and pastoral communities facing land degradation, deforestation, or loss of water access. CAVEATS, AND THEY ARE OVERRIDING: SUDAN IS IN A FULL-SCALE WAR. Institutional capacity, staffing and reachability cannot be assumed, published contact details predate the current conflict, and much of the descriptive record is several years old. SECS is a voluntary conservation and advocacy society, not a law firm: no litigation capacity, no intake route, no fee information.

trackers.name: Darfur Bar Association — 535 volunteer lawyers who represent people the state is prosecuting, and the reason land records now matter more than ever
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Darfur Bar Association, a Sudanese lawyers' organisation created in 1995 to protect and defend victims of violence, with a reported membership of 535 lawyers across Sudan volunteering as human rights defenders and providing legal aid to citizens, with an emphasis on activists. It participates in consultations at the African Commission and UN bodies, and received an international democracy award in 2020 for supporting marginalised people to advocate for their rights. A client's account of what it is worth is blunt: if the DBA has not supported you, you will be hurt and you will be in court. During the 2019 revolution it represented hundreds of arbitrarily detained people. THE LAND FACT THAT MAKES THIS URGENT, and it is the reason a bar association appears in a land map: reporting on Sudan's judicial system records that across Khartoum, the Darfur states, Kordofan and Gezira the civilian judicial infrastructure has collapsed, courts have been bombed or looted, and there has been DELIBERATE BURNING OF JUDICIAL RECORDS AND LAND REGISTRIES. If the registry that held proof of your family's land has been destroyed, the copy in your own hands — and any dated statement a lawyer takes from you now — becomes the record. Separately, an Emergency Lawyers group provides legal assistance and documents war-related abuses including attacks on civilian areas. WHO IT SUITS: Sudanese households and displaced families needing representation, documentation of what happened to their property, or help reconstructing lost land proof. CAVEATS: SUDAN IS AT WAR AND THIS IS DANGEROUS WORK — lawyers have been forced into exile, arrested and tortured, Darfuri rights monitors have been killed, and legal representation itself has been criminalised; the elected national bar council was dissolved by decree in 2023. Contact details and capacity may have changed. For the environmental branch network, Sudan's SECS entry.

trackers.name: Sudan's mutual aid funding route — money going DIRECTLY to Emergency Response Rooms and local coordination councils, not through international intermediaries
trackers.desc: WHERE MONEY REACHES COMMUNITIES: with Sudan at war and formal institutions collapsed, the funding route that works is DIRECT AND FLEXIBLE EMERGENCY GRANTS TO VETTED MUTUAL AID GROUPS. A funder coalition expanded its commitment to AT LEAST USD 16 MILLION in such grants by the end of 2026, having exceeded an earlier commitment to channel at least USD 2 million by end-2024. THE STRUCTURES THAT RECEIVE IT ARE THE POINT, because they are things communities already are rather than organisations to approach: EMERGENCY RESPONSE ROOMS, LOCAL COORDINATION COUNCILS and other community groups — the coalition works with partners on the ground to MAP them, conduct due diligence and determine transfer options, delivering through transfer services, HAWALA, digital cash and other pathways. If your neighbourhood runs an emergency response room, it is already the kind of body this money is designed for — the task is being mapped and vetted, not being founded. A separate route: a migration agency Rapid Response Fund makes SMALL GRANTS to local partners, and identifies MENTOR ORGANISATIONS so funds can be channelled in support of informal networks including the Emergency Response Rooms — explicitly recognising that front-line response runs through informal structures. Ask which registered organisation is acting as mentor for your area; that is how an unregistered neighbourhood group gets funded without registering. Funders state the case plainly: mutual aid networks and local leadership are the most viable and cost-effective mechanism to reach at-risk communities. WHO IT SUITS: Sudanese neighbourhood committees, emergency response rooms and community groups — including those trying to hold ground, keep records and support displaced families. CAVEATS: THIS IS HUMANITARIAN MUTUAL AID FUNDING, NOT LAND OR ENVIRONMENTAL GRANT-MAKING — it will not buy land or fund litigation, and vetting and transfer mechanics are the practical obstacles; nothing here is safe to publicise carelessly in a war. For representation, documentation of what happened to your property, and the burned land registries, Sudan's Darfur Bar Association entry; for the environmental branch network, SECS.

trackers.name: Forests National Corporation — the body that has registered and coordinated Sudanese forests since 1989, and the extension route that reaches village women directly
trackers.desc: WHO REGISTERS A FOREST IN SUDAN: the FORESTS NATIONAL CORPORATION (FNC) has coordinated forestry development in Sudan SINCE 1989, standing at the end of a statutory line that runs back to the WOODS AND FORESTS ORDINANCE OF 1901, the FIRST FOREST ACT OF 1908 which replaced it, and a century of successive legislation. An institution with a continuous mandate since 1989 and a legal lineage since 1901 is the body that holds the forest register — in a country where most other records have been destroyed or displaced, ask the FNC what is recorded for your area and get a copy of it. THE ROUTE THAT REACHES ORDINARY PEOPLE, DOCUMENTED: the FNC has run FORESTRY EXTENSION ACTIVITIES built on explicit recognition of the role of WOMEN in natural resource management AS PRODUCERS, USERS AND CONSUMERS OF TREES AND FORESTS, with extension work concentrated in the EASTERN AND CENTRAL REGIONS and reviews specifically examining women's participation. Extension officers are the cheapest formal contact with the forest authority a village has — and where the programme is already built around women's use of trees, a women's group is a recognised interlocutor rather than a petitioner. The record notes what any claim must account for: Sudan is large and diverse, with significant REGIONAL AND CULTURAL VARIATION in agricultural production systems, LAND TENURE, and the exploitation of forest products — so the tenure position in Kassala is not the tenure position in Darfur, and a national rule will not settle a local claim. WHO IT SUITS: Sudanese villages, women's producer groups and displaced communities seeking to establish or recover a record of forest rights. CAVEATS: STATED PLAINLY — this is a state forestry institution, not a community-tenure grant, and the sources verified for this file predate the current war; FNC capacity, records and field presence in an active conflict cannot be assumed. Confirm before relying on it. For USD 16M in mutual-aid funding, the mentor-organisation route for unregistered groups and hawala transfer, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms entry; for 535 volunteer lawyers, the Darfur Bar Association entry.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.desc: National — supreme audit institution of Eswatini. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Eswatini.

trackers.name: Anti-Corruption Commission (Eswatini)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Eswatini — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.desc: Eswatini Legal Information Institute: free case law and legislation. · Find here: free Eswatini judgments and legislation (EswatiniLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Registrar of Companies (online.gov.sz)
trackers.desc: National — online company name search & registration, Registrar of Companies, Eswatini. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: Yonge Nawe — the Eswatini environmental justice group that sued a minister to the highest court and won civil society a seat on the environment regulator
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an environmental action group founded in 1987, the Friends of the Earth member in Eswatini, working on environmental justice and getting local voices into environmental decisions. THE PRECEDENT IT SET IS THE REASON TO KNOW IT EXISTS: when the environment law was amended in 2002 it required a representative of an environmental NGO to sit on the management board of the national environment authority. The responsible minister ignored that provision and excluded NGOs. Yonge Nawe, then led by the environmental attorney Thuli Brilliance Makama, pressed the point and, when the minister refused to comply, took the minister to the country's highest court rather than let the disobedience become the precedent for every future minister — work for which Makama received the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2010. WHAT THAT MEANS FOR YOU: in Eswatini a civil society seat on the regulator exists in law and had to be litigated into existence, so ask who currently occupies the NGO seat on the authority's board, and take your project to that person. The authority itself has the statutory power to halt developments that have not been properly assessed for environmental impact. Yonge Nawe also works on industrial pollution of rivers and on land rehabilitation projects in communities, and shares a national radio slot with the environment authority and the national trust commission. WHO IT SUITS: Swazi communities facing pollution, land degradation or a development approved without proper assessment. CAVEATS: LEADERSHIP AND CONTACT DETAILS HAVE CHANGED OVER TIME — Makama has long since moved to international work, published email addresses in directories are old, and the website was not verified as live; confirm before relying on it. Eswatini is an absolute monarchy with narrow civic space, and most rural land is held under the King in trust, which shapes what any organisation there can do.

trackers.name: Swaziland Justice Forum — documents Eswatini's evictions, and the communities it works with took their case to the African Commission
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Swazi civil society organisation that documents forced evictions and names those responsible — it alleged that the royal sugar corporation was complicit in the illegal eviction of 33 farmers and their dependents from Vuvulane, following plans to take over the land, vest it in the royal wealth fund and lease it on to the corporation, and argues that the sugar industry has benefited the King and multinationals while displacing Swazi people from plantation land. WHY DOCUMENTATION IS THE ONLY FOUNDATION HERE: most land is Swazi Nation Land held in trust by the King and allocated through chiefs, with no formal legal security of tenure and no uniform official written record of allocations — so a household has nothing to produce when the bulldozers arrive. Recorded evictions include 61 people, more than 30 of them children, made homeless when armed police and bulldozers demolished homes at Embetseni in 2018; over 100 people from at least 20 homesteads cleared at Nokwane, where a 159-hectare science and technology park now stands; and about 106 people served notice by the national provident fund at Madonsa. THE ROUTE THAT WAS ACTUALLY USED WHEN DOMESTIC REMEDIES CLOSED: Swazi participants submitted a report documenting forced evictions to the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and engaged it at its 63rd Ordinary Session in Banjul in October 2018 — and then invited an ACHPR Commissioner to attend their own community meeting in Manzini in 2019. Bringing a regional Commissioner into the affected village is a move worth copying. The legal standard they invoke is that forced evictions may happen only as a last resort, under a court order, once all feasible alternatives are exhausted and procedural protections are in place. WHO IT SUITS: Swazi households and communities facing eviction from Swazi Nation Land, title-deed farms or plantation land. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED WEBSITE FOR SJF WAS FOUND, so this entry carries no URL rather than pointing at a third party — approach through Swazi civil society networks or Eswatini's Yonge Nawe entry. For pro bono counsel before the African Commission, the IHRDA entry filed under The Gambia is the counsel; Eswatini is an absolute monarchy and the risks of publicity should be weighed.

trackers.name: Eswatini Legal Aid — opened 2023 at RHUS Office, Mbabane; advice, referrals and mediation now, representation NOT yet
trackers.desc: WHAT EXISTS NOW: Eswatini Legal Aid, the country's FIRST legal aid office, set up following the National Legal Aid Policy adopted by Cabinet in September 2022 and established at the RHUS Office in Mbabane, with technical support from the UN development programme to the justice ministry. THE ONE THING TO KNOW BEFORE YOU GO, STATED BY THE MINISTER HERSELF: services are being rolled out across four thematic areas — legal information and awareness; advice and referrals; mediation; and legal assistance including REPRESENTATION — but because legal aid is at the inception stage, services are provided INCREMENTALLY STARTING WITH THE FIRST THREE, WHICH DO NOT INCLUDE LEGAL REPRESENTATION. So this office will inform you, advise you, refer you and mediate for you; it will not yet stand up in court for you. Ask whether representation has since been added before relying on it for a hearing. THE EVIDENCE BEHIND IT, which is also the argument for using it: a 2022 legal aid needs survey found that 58 per cent of emaSwati cannot afford the services of a lawyer, and 90 per cent said they would use legal support if it were made accessible. The ministry identifies the barriers precisely — lack of money, inadequate awareness of how to access services, insufficient command of legal language, and LONG DISTANCES to service providers. The Legal Aid Bill process began in 2012 and stalled; the policy route was taken instead, and the country has faced a case backlog in the absence of legal aid except where capital punishment was in play. A FREE SOURCE OF THE LAW ITSELF: EswatiniLII, operated by the Judiciary, publishes the country's judgments and legislation free online — which matters where government printers charge per page. WHO IT SUITS: emaSwati who need to understand a land, eviction or inheritance problem, get a referral, or attempt mediation. CAVEATS: NO VERIFIED STANDALONE SITE — this entry points at the UN account of the launch; NO COURT REPRESENTATION at inception; and Eswatini is an absolute monarchy where most land is held by the King in trust, so a state office will not challenge an allocation. For forced evictions and the African Commission route, Eswatini's Swaziland Justice Forum entry; for environmental precedent, Yonge Nawe.

trackers.name: Eswatini Environment Fund — grants up to E300,000, open to COMMUNITY GROUPS AND INDIVIDUALS, with 80% required to go to direct environmental action
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the Eswatini Environment Fund (EEF), established under the ENVIRONMENT MANAGEMENT ACT 2002, administered by the Eswatini Environment Authority and approved by a Board of Trustees on the recommendation of a technical proposal selection committee, through an OPEN NATIONAL CALL FOR PROPOSALS covering all four administrative regions. THE TERMS, WHICH ARE UNUSUALLY OPEN: grants of UP TO E300,000; eligibility runs to community groups, non-governmental organisations, environmental organisations, INDIVIDUALS, and educational or research institutions based in Eswatini; and AT LEAST 80% OF THE FUNDING MUST GO TO DIRECT ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIONS. An 80% floor on direct action is the exact protection missing from the Gabonese and Congolese forest funds recorded in this file, where running costs were charged against the community's share — if your country's fund has no such rule, this is the clause to ask for. Priority areas: climate change adaptation, sustainable water and land management, waste management, and biodiversity conservation, with weight given to community participation and long-term impact. WHAT IT HAS ACTUALLY FUNDED, AND THE FAILURE THE AUTHORITY PUBLISHES ITSELF: the Luve wetland and donga rehabilitation project, run through a local NGO under a signed contract, with a corporate partner completing the fencing and adding E30,000; a waste project at Lobamba Inkhundla; and the first-ever grant in 2009 to the Langa project, where the earth dam was successfully protected but the spring later dried up. And the Sivule wetland protection project — 12 ha spanning the boundaries of THREE CHIEFDOMS — could not start despite several meetings, because of conflicts between the chiefdoms. Money does not resolve a boundary dispute between traditional authorities; settle who speaks for the land before you apply, or the grant will sit unspent. WHO IT SUITS: Eswatini community groups, individuals and NGOs with a wetland, land-degradation, water or biodiversity project. CAVEATS: A STATE-ADMINISTERED FUND under the environment authority — it funds environmental action, NOT litigation against a development or land purchase; calls are periodic with fixed deadlines, so confirm the current cycle. For litigation that stopped a mine, Eswatini's Yonge Nawe entry; for forced evictions and the African Commission route, the Swaziland Justice Forum; for advice and mediation, Eswatini Legal Aid.

trackers.name: Khonta on Swazi Nation Land and the Lubombo Conservancy — heritable family tenure through the chiefdom, and a community nature reserve sitting inside a 60,000 ha conservancy
trackers.desc: WHAT YOU HOLD ON SWAZI NATION LAND: access runs through KHONTA — individuals seeking Swazi Nation Land must obtain the approval of the structures associated with the LOCAL CHIEFTAINCY, and obtain USE RIGHTS to build on and cultivate; in exchange the household is expected to KUHLEHLA, render services to the chief's house and in his fields. THE TWO FACTS THAT MATTER MOST, AND THE SECOND IS BETTER NEWS THAN MOST OF THIS FILE: the land MAY PASS TO DESCENDANTS under Swazi customary law; and although chiefs retain powers to evict or re-allocate on evidence of crime or witchcraft, customary landholding rights and family tenure are described as STRONG AND SECURE, and IT IS RARE THAT A FAMILY IS EVICTED from a chiefdom. Heritable and rarely disturbed is a real tenure position — the risk in Eswatini is not usually the chief removing your family, it is a project arriving with authority above the chiefdom. WHAT THE CONTEST IS ACTUALLY ABOUT: research records the tension between chiefs and councils as NOT ONLY over allocation powers but over the REVENUE STREAMS attached — chiefs seeking KHONTA FEES, councils seeking plot and rates payments. Know which body is charging you for what; a demand for money is often a claim of jurisdiction in disguise. THE COLLECTIVE INSTRUMENT: the LUBOMBO CONSERVANCY joins FIVE areas totalling about 60,000 HECTARES — and it deliberately mixes tenure, comprising STATUTORILY PROCLAIMED PROTECTED AREAS, PRIVATE PROPERTY AND SWAZI NATION LAND together, including the SHEWULA COMMUNITY NATURE RESERVE alongside a royal national park, a private game reserve, a national trust reserve and a ranch. A conservancy that admits community land, private land and state reserves as equal members is the model to ask for: it lets a chiefdom sit at the same table as a private reserve without surrendering its land. Note also, as the neighbouring benchmark, that Eswatini's private reserves are PROCLAIMED AND GAZETTED IN LAW FOR PERPETUITY, carrying the highest levels of legal protection available, with land use PREDETERMINED BY LAW so it may not be used for anything but nature conservation. That perpetual gazettement is what a community should ask for over its own reserve — the instrument exists in Eswatini law and has been used for privately owned land. CAVEATS: USE RIGHTS UNDER A CHIEFDOM, NOT TITLE, in an absolute monarchy where most land is held by the King in trust; conservancy membership does not itself change tenure. For forced evictions and the African Commission route, Eswatini's Swaziland Justice Forum entry; for project grants up to E300,000, the Environment Fund entry; for litigation that stopped a mine, Yonge Nawe.

trackers.name: National Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Kiribati, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Kiribati — Business & Companies Regulatory Division (MCIC)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Business & Companies Regulatory Division of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry & Cooperatives manages the commercial register (company & business-name registration), Kiribati. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Kiribati — Ministry of Finance & Economic Development (MFED)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares the national budget & financial reports and manages fiscal & economic policy, Kiribati. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Kiribati.

trackers.name: A prohibition without a management duty is not protection
trackers.desc: KIRIBATI'S OWN RECORD SHOWS THREE MODELS THAT FAILED AND ONE THAT WORKED — check which your site sits under. Birnie, Kanton, Enderbury and Orona were ‘prohibited areas’ under the Prohibited Areas Ordinance 1957, which prohibited entry but did not require or contemplate active management measures. Parts of Kanton were protected under the Closed Districts Act 1990 — but the principal objective was to allow orderly development of the atoll, not conservation. Rawaki, Birnie and McKean were wildlife sanctuaries under the Wildlife Conservation Ordinance. And the only previous management plan, from 1983, was never effectively implemented. A prohibition without a management duty is not protection, and a designation made for another purpose will be administered for that purpose. WHAT WORKED: an environment conservation order under the Environment Act 1999 — the PIPA Regulations, 2006, formally extended by the PIPA Regulations 2008 to 408,250 km², or 11.7 percent of Kiribati's EEZ, closing it to extractive activity — and crucially providing for a management plan and clear permitting rules. The instrument is a regulation-level order, so the 1999 Act is the enabling power to cite.

trackers.name: Land sales need next-of-kin and High Court approval — and a needs test
trackers.desc: CUSTOMARY TENURE CONSTRAINS EVERYTHING ON INHABITED ISLANDS, AND ONE RULE PROTECTS FAMILIES DIRECTLY. Under the Gilbert and Phoenix Islands Land Code, which codifies custom, an owner may sell land, a pit or a fish pond only after the owner's next-of-kin AND the High Court approve — and approval turns on the capacity of the owner's remaining land to provide for their needs. A sale that would leave a family without enough land to live on is not approvable. That is a protection in itself, and also why acquisition-based conservation is largely unavailable here. NOTE TWO MORE FEATURES: the Code regulates lands, fish ponds and fish traps together — fish ponds and traps are land interests, which matters for any lagoon or coastal proposal; and joint ownership is provided for, with owners taking access in alternate years. The Native Lands Ordinance 1956 governs ownership and a decision of the Court is indefeasible. Environmental management, as the legislative review puts it, requires the co-operation of landowners. TWO PROCEDURAL HOOKS: the Environment Act 1999 requires any development proposal to be accompanied by an assessment, and General and Detailed Land Use Plans setting out development proposals are presented for public scrutiny. Local Government Councils exist under the Local Government Act 1984 with precise functions.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so an individual can apply, which is rare and matters where no registered body exists. Eligible places include Kiribati, Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu, Fiji, Palau, PNG, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Tokelau, the Marshall Islands, FSM, and the French and US Pacific territories. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest, which the Trustees consider; successful applicants are then invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. THE MOST USEFUL THING BEFORE YOU DRAFT: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25. Read the published record of what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries — that is better evidence than any guidance note. ONE DISTINCTION THAT AFFECTS HOW YOU REACH UNDP HERE: UNDP's Pacific Office provides country support to ten states — FSM, Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, Palau, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu — but only regional support to five, including Samoa, Cook Islands, Niue, PNG and Tokelau. Check which applies to you before expecting an in-country office.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN KIRIBATI: an RTI strategy was developed in 2014 and a draft FOI law is reported.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Micronesia Conservation Trust (MCT)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a conservation trust fund based in Kolonia, Pohnpei, running small-grant programmes across the five Micronesia Challenge jurisdictions and accredited as an entity of the Green Climate Fund. Its stated impact areas include coastal fisheries management plans and actions, forest stewardship, expansion and improvement of Protected Areas Networks, watershed and forest management for climate resilience, invasive species control, and livelihoods tied to conservation. Money moves by periodic calls for proposals, not on a rolling basis.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Marshall Islands, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. trackers.name: Marshall Islands — Ministry of Finance, Banking & Postal Services

trackers.name: Marshall Islands Corporate Registry (IRI)
trackers.desc: Accountability source (official company register); the Republic of the Marshall Islands corporate registry, administered by International Registries Inc. — the official register of RMI companies and legal entities.

trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers. THERE IS A SPREP PRESENCE IN YOUR COUNTRY: beyond Apia, host country agreements exist with the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu — so you need not approach Samoa first. YOUR STATE IS RECORDED AS A NOUMEA CONVENTION PARTY: it was among those represented at the 18th Conference of the Parties, Apia, 5 September 2025 — so the Convention's obligations and its Workplan apply here.

trackers.name: Micronesia Conservation Trust and your national society — who funds and who acts
trackers.desc: MONEY DESIGNED TO OUTLAST THE GOVERNMENT OF THE DAY. The Micronesia Conservation Trust, established 2002 as a charitable and IRREVOCABLE corporation, exists to support conservation ‘by providing long term sustained funding’ — an endowment, not a project grant cycle. It hosts a regional endowment that has secured US$14.8 million since 2007, with pledges from The Nature Conservancy, Conservation International and the GEF, aiming for a further $41 million. Its goals include strengthening the ability of communities and community organisations — named ahead of government agencies — to conserve biodiversity, and supporting conservation of priority natural biodiversity resource areas. Micronesians in Island Conservation is a peer network of the national societies with a member-nominated steering committee, offering members peers, mentors and experts, with MCT funding its annual retreats. trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. trackers.name: Micronesia Conservation Trust and your national society — who funds and who acts
trackers.desc: MONEY DESIGNED TO OUTLAST THE GOVERNMENT OF THE DAY. The Micronesia Conservation Trust, established 2002 as a charitable and IRREVOCABLE corporation, exists to support conservation ‘by providing long term sustained funding’ — an endowment, not a project grant cycle. It hosts a regional endowment that has secured US$14.8 million since 2007, with pledges from The Nature Conservancy, Conservation International and the GEF, aiming for a further $41 million. Its goals include strengthening the ability of communities and community organisations — named ahead of government agencies — to conserve biodiversity, and supporting conservation of priority natural biodiversity resource areas. THE REGIONAL PRECEDENT IS LARGE: the Micronesia Challenge has aided in strengthening or establishing over 150 protected areas, so comparable local examples exist. Also active and named in the partnership records: OneReef, Island Conservation, RARE, the Pacific Marine Resources Institute, and PIMPAC, which shares community and government approaches to enforcement of marine managed areas. Micronesians in Island Conservation is a peer network of the national societies with a member-nominated steering committee, offering members peers, mentors and experts, with MCT funding its annual retreats. IN MICRONESIA THE ORGANISATIONS ARE STATE-BY-STATE, NOT NATIONAL — approach the one for your state: the Conservation Society of Pohnpei, the Kosrae Conservation and Safety Organization, and the Chuuk Conservation Society are each named in the published partnership records.

trackers.name: Palau Conservation Society (PCS)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Palau's first environmental NGO, founded in 1994 during a period of rapid development and still the country's leading conservation organisation — community-based, a BirdLife partner, working across marine and terrestrial ecosystems from Koror. It supports STATES in preparing Protected Areas Network site plans and protected-area management plans, with the stated aim of building each state's own capacity rather than managing on its behalf, and runs a Private Lands Initiative extending conservation onto land outside the state system. USE IT: if your state or village wants a conservation area recognised and managed, PCS is the body that helps write and run the plan. It implements national policy rather than opposing it, and says openly that what it can take on is limited by staff and funding.

trackers.name: Palau Protected Areas Network Fund (PAN Fund)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the independent non-profit that acts as financial trustee for Palau's Protected Areas Network, holding and disbursing money raised from donations and from the arrival fee paid by visitors. Areas enter the network at the initiative of state governments, traditional leaders and individuals who have protected land or reef inside their own boundaries; the Fund then supports the running of those sites, including enforcement coordination and conservation training. WHO IT SUITS: states, traditional leaders and landholders whose area is a PAN site or could become one. This is money for managing a designated protected area, not a grant for campaigning against a project. HOW IT DIFFERS: it is financed by a visitor arrival fee rather than by donor cycles, which makes it far steadier than most conservation money in the region.

trackers.name: Micronesia Conservation Trust (MCT)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a conservation trust fund based in Kolonia, Pohnpei, running small-grant programmes across the five Micronesia Challenge jurisdictions and accredited as an entity of the Green Climate Fund. Its stated impact areas include coastal fisheries management plans and actions, forest stewardship, expansion and improvement of Protected Areas Networks, watershed and forest management for climate resilience, invasive species control, and livelihoods tied to conservation. WHO IT SUITS: legally recognised not-for-profits in those jurisdictions — NGOs, associations, schools and universities, church groups, women's groups, youth groups, research bodies — and, importantly, communities themselves: a chartered community can apply directly, and an unchartered one can too if its legitimacy is corroborated in writing by a state or municipal government. HOW IT DIFFERS: it gives priority to projects implementing an EXISTING management plan or Local Early Action Plan over projects that would write a new one, so an already-adopted plan is worth more here than a good idea. Money moves by periodic calls for proposals, not on a rolling basis.

trackers.name: Office of the Public Auditor
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Palau, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Palau — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; manages expenditures, revenues & financing and supports the national budget process, Republic of Palau. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Palau.

trackers.name: Palau — Bureau of Revenue & Taxation (Business Registration)
trackers.desc: National business registry; Palau has no separate companies registrar — all commercial entities must register with the Bureau of Revenue & Taxation (Ministry of Finance) and obtain a business license; foreign investment via the Foreign Investment Board. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: EQPB — earthmoving is regulated in its own right
trackers.desc: A SEPARATE, CHECKABLE PERMIT FOR CLEARING LAND. The Environmental Quality Protection Act, Title 24 of the Palau National Code Annotated (1981), created the Environmental Quality Protection Board, a semi-autonomous agency of the executive branch. Title 24 authorises it to promulgate and enforce regulations on 9 named topics, and the first is EARTHMOVING — alongside marine and fresh water quality, wastewater, solid waste, pesticides, public water supply, environmental impact statements, air pollution and ozone-depleting substances. Site clearance and grading is regulated in its own right, not merely as a component of an EIS — so an earthmoving permit is a separate document to ask for. EQPB issues permits for activities that may affect the environment, including industrial operations, land development and waste disposal. CONTACT: P.O. Box 8086, Bureau of Public Works Building, Koror 96940; tel (680) 488-1639 or 488-3600; fax (680) 488-2963; palaueqpb@gmail.com — recorded as the agency publishes it. The separate Bureau of Environment holds regulatory oversight and enforcement, aiming at a protected areas network defined by science and traditional knowledge.

trackers.name: PAN Act — designation runs upward, and joining unlocks the money
trackers.desc: THE STRUCTURE IS THE REVERSE OF MOST IN THIS MAP. Under the Protected Areas Network Act 2003, state governments, traditional leaders and individuals independently protect areas within their own boundaries, and the national government supports those efforts — designation runs upward. ALL SITES THAT JOIN THE PAN ARE ELIGIBLE TO APPLY FOR PAN FUNDS, used by each site to manage its own resources — so for an existing local protected area the question is whether it has joined, not whether it qualifies. Note that 35 MPAs exist but not all are part of the network. THE MONEY COMES FROM VISITORS: the green fee supports local communities with US$1.8 million annually — a long-running, directly transferable design. WHAT SITES DO: management plans and monitoring protocols built on biological, ecological, socio-economic, cultural and historical gap analyses, baseline data collected in parallel, record-keeping, and enforcement mechanisms including prosecution of illegal fishing or poaching. A DOCUMENTED OUTCOME WORTH CITING: it created jobs so that people returned to their villages, reducing urban drift — reverse migration as a conservation result. THE CUSTOMARY INSTRUMENT: chiefs of Ngarchelong and Kayangel jointly declared the first modern-day bul, a moratorium on fishing in their traditional grounds to protect spawning aggregations — a joint declaration by two communities' chiefs is the precedent for a shared resource. The 2015 National Marine Sanctuary Act closes 80 percent of the EEZ to commercial and extractive activity.

trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

THE WORKED ROUTE: PCS helped 15 states prepare five-year management plans so they could access PAN funds — the plan is what unlocks the money, and PCS is who helps you write it. It also connects communities to outside money: the KIWA Initiative provided over $400,000 to 10 Babeldaob states. STATED HONESTLY, IN ITS OWN WORDS: ‘we have a lot of requests or plans we want to do toward the different states, but it is limited by financing resources and also the number of staff.’ Its identified priority problems are sedimentation and sea pollution.

trackers.name: Samoa Conservation Society (Fa’asao Samoa)
trackers.desc: A Samoan NGO established in 2013, working with communities, government and NGO partners on the threats to Samoa's biodiversity and natural heritage — invasive species, over-harvesting, habitat degradation, pollution and climate change — through research, awareness raising and practical conservation carried out with communities. WHO TO ENLIST: SCS if you have a site or a species to protect rather than a project to fight. It states plainly that if you or your group want to run a project protecting Samoa's native species and habitats it wants to hear from you, which is an unusually open door for a country with few options. You CAN'T expect a campaigner or a litigator: it works collaboratively with government, and its strength is research, partnership and practical action rather than opposition.

trackers.name: Samoa — Audit Office (Controller & Auditor General)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution; independent public-sector auditor reporting to Parliament and promoting public-administration accountability, Samoa.

trackers.name: Online Samoa Company Registry
trackers.desc: National — Samoa company register (MCIL), searchable free. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Samoa — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares the national budget and publishes fiscal & budget documents, Samoa. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Samoa.

trackers.name: PacLII – Samoa
trackers.desc: Free case law and legislation for Samoa via the Pacific Islands Legal Information Institute. · Find here: free Samoa legislation and court decisions, hosted by PacLII.

trackers.name: The fono makes village law — and which chief controls your land
trackers.desc: IN SAMOA THE DECISION-MAKER FOR VILLAGE LAND IS THE VILLAGE COUNCIL. Under the Village Fono Act 1990, councils hold authority over village law and order and are given additional powers over the development and usage of village land for the betterment of the village, exercised in accordance with the traditional custom and usage of that village. Fono can impose fines, work or banishment, and appoint sub-committees for local matters as they see fit. So a conservation measure adopted by the fono is not a request to government — it is village law with sanctions, and a sub-committee can be created to run it. IDENTIFY YOUR LAND CATEGORY FIRST: customary land divides into village, plantation and settlement land — all village land is controlled by the village chiefs; residential and plantation land by the family chiefs. Get this wrong and you are negotiating with people who do not control the land. Matai are the chiefs, heads of extended families (aiga), in two kinds — tulafale (orator) and ali'i (high chief). FOR A COASTAL VILLAGE: under customary law the waters adjacent to a village were part of the land controlled by that village, and no-take zones were declared by imposing tabu, with fines in money or pigs — the customary precedent for a village-declared marine closure.

trackers.name: Land classification is a lever — and village by-laws may become justiciable
trackers.desc: TWO THINGS TO CHECK BEFORE ACTING. 1. THE CLASSIFICATION OF YOUR LAND IS ITSELF A LEVER. The Land, Surveys and Environment Act 1989 provides for establishing national parks and other protected areas, and classifies land as farm, urban, or commercial/industrial — with alienation, disposal or reservation determined on the basis of those classifications. So the classification decides what can lawfully happen to the land, and is worth establishing early. MNRE's functions include advising the Minister on all aspects of environmental management and ensuring and promoting conservation of Samoa's natural resources. 2. A CHANGE TO WATCH IN THE COURTS. The Land and Titles Court arbitrates disputes over customary land and matai titles — and under the 2020 reform package (Land and Titles Bill, Constitution Amendment Bill and Judicature Bill) it gains added powers to adjudicate on village laws passed by village councils, with its own appeal structure separate from the Supreme Court. If village laws become justiciable in a separate court, a fono conservation by-law becomes both more enforceable and more challengeable — check the current position before relying on either. ALSO: the Internal Affairs Division of the Ministry of Women, Community and Social Development oversees village authority. TARGET TO CITE: protected areas covered 5 percent of land in 2010; the government aims for 15 percent.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. trackers.name: Samoa Conservation Society — and a national carbon programme already running
