The network also co-hosts meetings of the Commission's Expert Group on the Nature Directives (NADEG) on tools and incentives for private land conservation — the most important working-level platform between the Commission, member states and interest groups. IF EUROSITE DOES NOT REACH YOUR COUNTRY, the International Land Conservation Network (founded 2014, the first global network of private land conservation practitioners) is the wider net, active from Canada to Australia to Latin America. BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT THESE ARE: networks of practitioners — they connect you to the organisation that can act; they do not buy land themselves. Ask the network who operates in your country; membership is not asserted here.

trackers.name: Faroese Parliamentary Ombudsman
trackers.desc: The Faroe Islands’ Parliamentary Ombudsman, investigating complaints against public administration.

trackers.name: Faroe Islands — Landsgrann­ skoðanin (National Audit)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution; Landsgrannskoðanin is the independent audit body under the Løgting (per Audit Act no. 25 of 21 April 1999) that audits the national accounts and publishes annual reports & appropriation-oversight findings, Faroe Islands.

trackers.name: Faroe Islands — Ministry of Finance (Fíggjarmálaráðið)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the Ministry of Finance coordinates the Faroese government’s budgetary, financial & economic matters, underpins taxation & fees legislation and oversees public-sector finances, Faroe Islands. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Faroe Islands.

trackers.name: Faroe Islands — Skráseting Føroya (Company Registration Authority)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Faroese Company Registration Authority registers & maintains records of companies & associations (and the national ship register), Faroe Islands. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Faroe Islands District Court
trackers.desc: Faroe Islands District Court — first instance court in Faroe Islands (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Jurisdiction is Faroese — and the conservation act dates from 1970
trackers.desc: DO NOT ADDRESS A DANISH MINISTRY. Under the Home Rule Act, environment and nature management are Faroese jurisdictions — the islands are responsible for the legislation protecting nature and regulating harmful activities, and the Løgting legislates on environmental matters. THE THREE INSTRUMENTS: the Act on Nature Conservation, 1970, which protects areas of natural beauty, wildlife and habitats and regulates the creation and management of protected areas such as national parks and nature reserves; the Act on Environmental Protection, 1988, on pollution of air, water and soil and vibrations; and the Act on the Protection of the Marine Environment, 2005. NOTE THE 1970 DATE: the conservation act predates the rapid development the islands have seen since the 1960s in infrastructure, energy consumption and tourism — a half-century-old designation statute is worth reading closely for what it does not anticipate. WHAT IS ALREADY PROTECTED: important bird areas as Ramsar sites, including Skúvoy, Nólsoy and Mykines. Over 300 bird species recorded, 50 breeding regularly, with endemic subspecies including the Faroe eider — and the Faroe charr, an endemic fish known only from Lake Leynavatn. A single-lake endemic is the strongest possible site-specific argument. PRESSURES IN THE BAYS: transportation, sand extraction and aquaculture, alongside 70,000 sheep on semi-natural pasture.

trackers.name: The tourism law puts environment first — in those words
trackers.desc: A STATUTORY PRIORITY ORDERING, STATED IN TERMS. The Løgting's law on sustainable tourism is explained by the Ministry's senior adviser as follows: ‘The aim is to achieve environmental, social, and economic sustainability, in that order.’ A government stating the priority sequence explicitly is unusual and directly quotable against any proposal that inverts it. AND COMMUNITIES CAN CAP VISITOR NUMBERS: the law makes it possible for local communities to restrict the number of tourists, to ensure these communities remain good places to live in — a community power exercised on liveability grounds, which is rare. The law is also to protect the natural environment, existing agricultural activities, and local ownership and participation; access may be restricted when collecting sheep, in lambing season, or in poor weather. Fee income is earmarked for hiking paths and tourism planning. WHY IT WAS NEEDED: the previous rule on walking traditional paths was the agriculture law from 1937, long before tourism was contemplated, and as tourism surged farmers and operators met it with various private unauthorised systems. RECORDED HONESTLY: reporting notes the hiking fee has in places been driven by private landowners rather than government, and that it is not yet clear who exactly benefits — treat the fee regime as unsettled rather than as a model.

trackers.name: Granskingarráðið — ‘significant in a Faroese context’ is an alternative limb
trackers.desc: RECORDED HONESTLY: THREE ROUNDS OF SEARCHING, IN ENGLISH AND FAROESE, FOUND NO COMMUNITY ENVIRONMENTAL GRANT SCHEME IN THE FAROE ISLANDS. What exists is research funding plus Horizon Europe access. The Research Council Faroe Islands is a public research funding body which also administers the islands' association agreement on participation in Horizon Europe. Funding opens once a year — the next deadline published as 15 February 2027, 12:00 noon local time — so missing the single date costs a year. ELIGIBILITY HAS THREE ALTERNATIVE LIMBS: research carried out by a Faroese researcher, OR in cooperation with a Faroese research institute, OR considered significant in a Faroese context. That third limb is an alternative, not an additional requirement — so a project need not be led by a Faroese researcher if its significance to the Faroes can be established. That is the limb to argue if you are a community or outside partner rather than an academic body. It funds PhD projects, postdoc or other projects of at least 6 months, and industrial R&D; criteria are scientific excellence, impact and implementation, with advantage to projects producing data and lasting knowledge and skills. THE PRACTICAL ROUTE: pair with a Faroese research institute and frame the work as producing data — baseline surveys, monitoring and inventories fit this funder in a way campaigning does not.

trackers.name: Umhvørvisstovan — conservation, the cadastre and land registration in one agency
trackers.desc: ONE ENQUIRY ESTABLISHES BOTH OWNERSHIP AND STATUS. The Faroese Environment Agency, under the Ministry of Environment and based at Argir, covers environmental protection, environmental research, nature conservation, energy and electricity supply supervision, woodlands and recreational areas, land and sea maps, the cadastre (matrikul), land registration (tinglýsing) and the national population register. Nature conservation, the cadastre and land registration sit in the same agency — so establishing who is registered against a parcel and its conservation status is a single-agency enquiry, which is unusual and makes early fact-finding far cheaper than in most jurisdictions in this map. IT ALSO CO-FUNDS APPLIED RESEARCH: it is recorded as a named financier of Faroese fjord benthic macrofauna classification work alongside the aquaculture association, and the environment and industry ministry has directly financed environmental monitoring in Faroese fjords — by arrangement rather than through an open call. SO THE THREE REALISTIC ROUTES HERE ARE: partnering with a research institute into the Research Council's annual call; a direct arrangement with Umhvørvisstovan; or Horizon Europe via the association agreement. None is an application form a village association can complete alone — plan for a partner.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Eurosite / ELCN — who already holds land near you, and the easement route
trackers.desc: A DIRECTORY OF THE PEOPLE WHO ALREADY HOLD AND MANAGE LAND IN YOUR COUNTRY — which is who you need when the answer to a development is getting the land into protective hands. Eurosite, established 1989, is one of the largest pan-European organisations bringing together NGOs, governmental organisations and private bodies, with members from the Atlantic islands to the Black Sea and from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. ITS ELCN STRAND IS ABOUT PRIVATE LAND SPECIFICALLY: the European Land Conservation Network was built to support private landowners — non-public bodies or individuals — willing to engage in conservation ON AT LEAST PART OF THEIR LAND. That last phrase is the opening: a landowner who will not sell may still protect a portion, and there is a European network built to make that happen. The three tools it promotes are conservation easements, privately protected areas, and land stewardship agreements. AND A FUNDING ROUTE IS ATTACHED: ELCN and the ILCN have run sessions on using EU LIFE funding for private land conservation, aimed at landowners and conservationists preparing a LIFE project proposal; in November 2025 Eurosite-ELCN launched a working group on nature finance and land stewardship focused on finance mechanisms that mobilise private investment, co-chaired by the former head of the EU LIFE Programme. IF YOUR FIGHT IS A QUARRY, ASK FOR THIS BY NAME: Eurosite and partners published work on project selection criteria for conservation easements to protect nature in European quarries — a published European method for putting an easement over one. The network also co-hosts meetings of the Commission's Expert Group on the Nature Directives (NADEG) on tools and incentives for private land conservation — the most important working-level platform between the Commission, member states and interest groups. IF EUROSITE DOES NOT REACH YOUR COUNTRY, the International Land Conservation Network (founded 2014, the first global network of private land conservation practitioners) is the wider net, active from Canada to Australia to Latin America. BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT THESE ARE: networks of practitioners — they connect you to the organisation that can act; they do not buy land themselves. Ask the network who operates in your country; membership is not asserted here.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants Programme (SGP) — Turkmenistan
trackers.desc: TURKMENISTAN WAS ADDED TO SGP PARTICIPATION IN GEF-8, and is named among the 11 new countries on the GEF's own page — so this is a newly available route, and older guidance will not list it. SGP is a GEF corporate programme running since 1992, implemented by UNDP and executed by UNOPS; GEF-8 raised participation from 124 countries to 135, out of 144 eligible. THE MONEY IS NOT COMPETED FOR ACROSS COUNTRIES: GEF-8 secured $135 million for the core programme with equal allocation of nearly $1 million in core financing to each of the 135 countries — a per-country floor, which is unusual. Grants of up to $50,000 go directly to local communities, including community-based organisations and other non-governmental groups. FOCAL AREAS: biodiversity, climate change, land degradation and sustainable forest management, international waters and chemicals. READ YOUR COUNTRY PROGRAMME STRATEGY BEFORE APPLYING: each country writes its own CPS which puts emphasis on certain thematic and geographic areas, so it may exclude your region or theme regardless of global eligibility. WHO DECIDES LOCALLY: a locally recruited National Coordinator and a voluntary National Steering Committee, described as the central element of SGP and the body providing substantive oversight. Note that under SGP 2.0 the implementing agency may be FAO or Conservation International rather than UNDP, and the host may be a national host institution rather than the UNDP country office — confirm which applies before addressing an application.

trackers.name: Law on Nature Protection — public associations' rights, and the emergency chapter
trackers.desc: CITE THE RIGHT INSTRUMENT — the statutes are dated and distinct. «Об охране природы» dates from 12 November 1991; «О государственных особо охраняемых природных территориях» from 19 May 1992; «О государственной экологической экспертизе» from 15 June 1995; «Об углеводородных ресурсах» from 1996. WHAT THE NATURE PROTECTION LAW GIVES YOU: it enshrines the rights and obligations of citizens and of public associations (общественных объединений) in nature protection, and establishes financing — a statutory recognition of public associations' rights in the founding law, not a subordinate act. Chapter IX (articles 42–45) covers forests, flora, fauna and specially protected territories, with article 45 on objects subject to special protection. Article 38 sets ecological requirements for activity in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea. AND WHERE DEGRADATION IS ALREADY SEVERE: Chapter XI covers чрезвычайные экологические ситуации and зоны экологического бедствия — emergency ecological situations and ecological disaster zones — with article 49 on the emergency situation. That is a named statutory category with its own chapter, distinct from ordinary protection. Violating the regime of a protected territory carries administrative, civil or criminal responsibility. ASK WHETHER A STATE ECOLOGICAL EXPERTIZA WAS CONDUCTED — it has its own 1995 statute and is a separate act from any permit.

trackers.name: Aarhus Compliance Committee — it takes communications from the public
trackers.desc: A ROUTE THAT DOES NOT DEPEND ON DOMESTIC STANDING. Turkmenistan is a Party to the Aarhus Convention, and UNECE hosts Turkmen environmental legislation within its compliance section under decisions of the Meeting of the Parties, including a country-specific MoP4 decision folder — so the mechanism has been engaged with Turkmenistan before. The Compliance Committee receives communications from members of the public concerning a Party's compliance with obligations on access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice. Where domestic routes are closed, this one does not turn on national standing rules — which is why it matters more here than in most jurisdictions in this map. BE REALISTIC ABOUT WHAT IT DELIVERS: the Committee's outputs are findings and recommendations adopted by the Meeting of the Parties, not orders enforceable in a national court. It is a compliance and publicity mechanism, not a remedy — useful for creating a documented international record and for pressure, and it should be planned as that rather than as litigation.

trackers.name: IMF — State of Eritrea
trackers.desc: IMF country page: Article IV assessments and the main public macro-fiscal data for Eritrea, whose national finances are otherwise largely undisclosed. Here you can trace how much Eritrea owes, to whom and on what terms.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: National Union of Eritrean Women — 200,000+ members, offices in all six zobas, and a group-loan credit programme where the group itself is the collateral
trackers.desc: THE ONE MEMBERSHIP BODY WITH OFFICES EVERYWHERE: the NATIONAL UNION OF ERITREAN WOMEN (NUEW), established 1979 as a mass organisation of the liberation front and describing itself today as AN AUTONOMOUS NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATION, operates from headquarters in ASMARA and REGIONAL OFFICES ACROSS ALL SIX ZONES OF ERITREA, with a MEMBERSHIP EXCEEDING 200,000 WOMEN and funding from membership fees, grants, development projects and member-led fundraising. Published contacts place it at AV Gureito, Asmara, P.O. Box 239, tel +291-1-119304 / +291-1-115172, nuew@nuew.org. In a country where this file could verify no independent civil society, an organisation with 200,000 members and an office in every zoba is the only body a village woman can walk into — and it is where a community group without legal personality can be heard. THE CREDIT TERMS, WHICH ARE THE ACTUAL RESOURCE: NUEW is named among the country's few micro-credit providers alongside the SAVING AND MICROCREDIT PROGRAM (SMCP) and the youth and war-disabled unions. Its published product is A GROUP LOAN — IF ONE MEMBER FAILS TO REPAY, THE OTHER MEMBERS ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE DEBT, AND THIS MECHANISM ACTS AS THE COLLATERAL — with a THREE-CYCLE CEILING of 3,000, then 8,000, then 10,000 NAKFA, repayment within TWO YEARS for agri-business and ONE YEAR for service business, at a 12% FLAT interest rate. A group loan collateralised by the group is how people without land title borrow at all — and in Eritrea, where all land belongs to the state and you can own only the trees you plant, that is the financing route that actually matches the tenure. Start at cycle one; the ceiling rises as the group repays. Access to finance is recorded as limited by the small number of financial institutions and civil society organisations providing credit. WHO IT SUITS: Eritrean women's groups and village associations needing working capital for agri-business, nurseries or restoration work. CAVEATS: NUEW ORIGINATED AS A LIBERATION-FRONT MASS ORGANISATION and this file records no independent Eritrean civil society — read its autonomy claim in that light; contacts should be confirmed. For the seed to plant, Eritrea's NARI and ERCOE entry; for the baito closures and tree tenure, the village closures entry; for community project grants through four phases, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Department of Environment, Ministry of Land, Water and Environment — the EIA guidelines exist, the framework law never did, and there is nobody else to ask
trackers.desc: WHO TO APPROACH, AND WHY THIS IS WRITTEN AS AN ABSENCE: no verified Eritrean civil society organisation providing land defence, environmental litigation or community support could be found. The formal address is the Department of Environment within the Ministry of Land, Water and Environment, responsible for implementing national environmental policy. THE TWO INSTRUMENTS THAT DO EXIST: in March 1999 the department launched National Environmental Impact Assessment Guidelines and Procedures setting out EIA licensing procedures — described as similar in content to World Bank operational policies — later developed into National Environmental Assessment Procedures and Guidelines; and land is governed by the Land Reform Proclamation of 1994, under which the state allots land and grants usufruct rights, including leases for investment and agro-industrial activity. If a project near you is large-scale, the EIA licensing procedure is the only formal hook, and the land you hold is held as usufruct from the state, not as property. THE FINDING THE STATE PUBLISHED ABOUT ITSELF, which is the most useful thing here: an assessment prepared for the ministry recorded that the legal framework for environmental management had yet to be formalised, that this had been identified repeatedly over the years as a serious impediment to the effective functioning of the Department of Environment, and that drafting and redrafting of the environmental proclamation continued without resolution — with the justice ministry indicating the draft would not be acceptable in its current form. An EIA procedure without a framework law behind it is guidance, not enforceable duty; ask which instrument any decision is actually made under. WHO IT SUITS: Eritrean residents facing a large-scale project, as the only formal address available. CAVEATS: THIS IS A GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT, NOT AN ALLY, in a country with no independent civil society sector recorded here, no complaints route and no free press. NO VERIFIED DEPARTMENTAL SITE EXISTS — this entry points at the state information service's account of the ministry. Published material is old; treat every detail as needing confirmation.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants in Eritrea — a country programme through FOUR operational phases, run with the Ministry of Land, Water and Environment, for community-based organisations
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the GEF SMALL GRANTS PROGRAMME in Eritrea, implemented by the UN development programme on behalf of the facility partnership and executed by the UN office for project services, TAILORED TO SUPPORT COMMUNITIES THROUGH COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANISATIONS AND LOCAL NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATIONS. THE FACT THAT MATTERS, GIVEN WHAT ELSE THIS FILE RECORDS ABOUT ERITREA: the country office has developed FOUR CONSECUTIVE COUNTRY PROGRAMME STRATEGIES across four operational phases, with the MINISTRY OF LAND, WATER AND ENVIRONMENT (MLWE) and the development programme holding significant roles in establishing and running it. Four completed phases means this is a functioning national window, not a paper one — which is more than can be said for the environmental framework law recorded elsewhere in Eritrea's file as never having been finalised. THE TERMS, PROGRAMME-WIDE: grants of UP TO USD 50,000 per project, averaging around USD 25,000, made DIRECTLY to local communities, community-based organisations and other non-governmental groups, for biodiversity, climate mitigation and adaptation, LAND DEGRADATION AND SUSTAINABLE FOREST MANAGEMENT, international waters and chemicals. Applications must show how the project meets the programme's criteria and how it aligns with the COUNTRY PROGRAMME STRATEGY (CPS) of your own country — read your national CPS before writing anything; it is the document your proposal is scored against. Eritrea's national adaptation programme names its own priorities as rangeland management in the lowlands, and community-based adaptation in pastoralism, forestry, water and agriculture — align to those. WHO IT SUITS: Eritrean community-based organisations and village groups with a land degradation, rangeland, forestry, water or agriculture project. CAVEATS: STATE THIS PLAINLY — Eritrea's civic space is among the most restricted on the continent, independent organising carries serious risk, and the programme runs WITH a government ministry; that shapes what can realistically be proposed. Grants fund environmental action, NOT litigation, land purchase or opposition to a state project. For the environmental framework and what does not exist, Eritrea's Department of Environment entry.

trackers.name: Eritrea — the expropriation DECISION cannot be challenged in court, but COMPENSATION goes to the High Court; community courts hear land disputes, and the only lawyers' association is in exile
trackers.desc: WHAT YOU CAN AND CANNOT TAKE TO COURT, AND KNOWING THE DIFFERENCE IS THE WHOLE OF IT HERE: under PROCLAMATION 58/1994, the Land Proclamation, ALL LAND IN ERITREA BELONGS TO THE STATE and a person may hold only USUFRUCTUARY RIGHTS on land allotted by the government. THE LIMIT: analysis of the proclamation records that THE GOVERNMENTAL DECISION TO EXPROPRIATE CANNOT BE CHALLENGED IN COURT. THE OPENING, IN THE SAME TEXT: Article 54 provides that where land is taken for national reconstruction or development projects, DISPUTES INVOLVING COMPENSATION SHALL BE ENTERTAINED BY THE HIGH COURT OF ERITREA — and the previous holder MAY PETITION THE HIGH COURT for compensation for any INSTALLATION OR IMPROVEMENT on the land. So do not spend your money contesting the taking; spend it on the compensation claim and on documenting every installation and improvement you built, because that is the half the law lets a court hear. WHERE A VILLAGE-LEVEL DISPUTE IS HEARD: village courts were established by Proclamation 25/1992 and COMMUNITY COURTS by Proclamation 132/2003, with first-instance jurisdiction over civil disputes including those involving IMMOVEABLE PROPERTY, appealable upward to the high courts and the Court of Final Appeal. WHO REPRESENTS YOU: there is NO BAR ASSOCIATION IN ERITREA — admission to practise is decided by the LEGAL COMMITTEE OF THE MINISTRY OF JUSTICE, CHAIRED BY THE MINISTER, which also handles discipline; practice comes in two layers, attorneys who may appear in Zoba courts only, and those who may also appear in the High Court and Appellate Court. Ask which layer your attorney holds before you plan an appeal. The ERITREAN LAW SOCIETY (erilaw.org) is the only professional association of Eritrean lawyers and states plainly that it was established in exile and operates from exile, because the political situation does not allow free and independent professional associations. WHO IT SUITS: Eritreans facing expropriation or a village land dispute, and anyone needing to know which grievance a court will hear. CAVEATS: STATE THIS PLAINLY — civic space is among the most restricted on the continent; the only lawyers' body is outside the country and there is no independent bar; nothing here is a legal aid service. For community environmental funding through four operational phases, Eritrea's GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Eritrea's village closures — the BAITOS close wooded hillsides for 5–10 years and reopen them; about 100,000 ha closed, and proclamation 155/2006 gives the trees to whoever plants them
trackers.desc: THE VILLAGE COUNCIL CLOSES THE HILLSIDE: from the late 1980s Eritrea has operated a system of CLOSURES of wooded hillsides and juniper forest, OPERATED BY LOCAL VILLAGE COUNCILS — THE BAITOS — IN PARTNERSHIP WITH GOVERNMENT. Such areas are CLOSED TO ACCESS for tree-cutting, grazing or agriculture for a number of years to allow forest regeneration, including some tree-planting, and to STABILISE SLOPES; after 5-10 YEARS THEY ARE REOPENED AND NEW CLOSURES ESTABLISHED ELSEWHERE. In total ABOUT 100,000 HECTARES have been closed in the Semenawi and Debubawi Bahri regions. The baito is the acquire instrument in a country with no land title — a village council decision, backed by government partnership, that takes ground out of use for a decade. And because the closure ROTATES rather than being permanent, it is negotiable ground rather than an expropriation, which is why it has survived where formal designation has not. THE TENURE RULE THAT GOES WITH IT: the FORESTRY AND WILDLIFE CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT PROCLAMATION NO. 155/2006 states that TREE TENURE RIGHTS BELONG TO THE PERSONS PLANTING THE TREES ON USER-RELATED LANDS, AND OPENS OPPORTUNITIES FOR INDIVIDUALS AND/OR COMMUNITIES TO ESTABLISH SUSTAINABLE-HARVEST WOODLOTS — the same principle recorded for Burundi in this file, and the practical answer where the 1994 Land Reform Proclamation vests ALL LAND IN THE STATE with citizens holding USER RIGHTS. You cannot own the land; you can own the trees you plant on land you have user rights to. Plant, and record who planted. WHAT IS PROPOSED AND WHAT IS NOT YET REAL, STATED HONESTLY: SEMENAWI BAHRI — the GREEN BELT, about 1,300 km2 of tropical montane forest — REMAINS A PROPOSED NATIONAL PARK UNDER DE FACTO MANAGEMENT WITH NO FORMAL GAZETTEMENT; the four priority areas identified for protection are Semenawi and Debubawi Bahri (106,000 ha), Buri-Irori-Hawakil (867,000 ha), the Berasole estuary (13,100 ha) and the Gash-Setit Elephant Sanctuary (44,000 ha), none officially gazetted. A de facto protected area with no gazettement is exactly where a village closure carries the most weight — the baito's decision is the operative protection on the ground. WHO IT SUITS: Eritrean villages on wooded or eroding hillsides, and anyone planting trees under user rights. CAVEATS: A ROTATING ADMINISTRATIVE CLOSURE IN PARTNERSHIP WITH GOVERNMENT, NOT TENURE; civic space is severely restricted. For which grievance a court will hear — the expropriation decision cannot be challenged but COMPENSATION goes to the High Court — Eritrea's Land Proclamation entry; for community project money through four phases, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: NARI's seed bank and ERCOE's environmental plan update — 6,300 seed accessions across 160 crop and tree species, and the body commissioned to rewrite the national environment plan
trackers.desc: WHERE THE SEED AND THE PLAN ARE KEPT: two Eritrean institutions are addressable by an ordinary person, and both matter to a village trying to hold ground. (1) THE NATIONAL AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH INSTITUTE (NARI), a department of the agriculture ministry whose ORIGINS DATE TO 1910, MAKING IT ONE OF AFRICA'S OLDEST SCIENTIFIC INSTITUTIONS, employing 270 STAFF, ABOUT 80% OF THEM RESEARCHERS AND TECHNICAL PROFESSIONALS, with divisions covering NATURAL RESOURCES MANAGEMENT RESEARCH alongside crops, livestock and agricultural engineering, and research conducted at NINE AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH STATIONS since 1997. ITS MOST USEFUL HOLDING: MORE THAN 6,300 SEED ACCESSIONS REPRESENTING ABOUT 160 SPECIES OF CROPS AND TREES. A national seed bank holding tree species is where you go when you must replant what a project or a drought removed — and in Eritrea, where tree tenure belongs to whoever plants, the seed is the first step in the only ownership claim available to you. (2) THE ERITREAN CENTER FOR ORGANIZATIONAL EXCELLENCE (ERCOE), established 10 August 2006, based in Asmara, which provides training, research and consultancy to ministries, REGIONAL ADMINISTRATIONS, parastatals, CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS and colleges — and which WAS COMMISSIONED BY THE MINISTRY OF LAND, WATER AND ENVIRONMENT to run a multi-sectoral project UPDATING THE NATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN FOR ERITREA (NEMP-E), first prepared in 1995. The NEMP-E is the plan that originally identified Semenawi Bahri for national park status — so the body rewriting it is the body deciding what gets named for protection next. If your area has a case, that update is where it belongs. WHAT THE STATE HAS BEEN COUNTING: institutions working over five years have DOCUMENTED MORE THAN 5,000 SPECIES, presented at a national conference on fauna and flora in Asmara under the theme that conserving Eritrea's fauna and flora safeguards its future. WHO IT SUITS: Eritrean villages replanting closures or woodlots, and anyone wanting a protection case recorded in the national plan. CAVEATS: BOTH ARE STATE BODIES — ERCOE operates directly under the Office of the President — and this file records no independent Eritrean civil society; approach accordingly. For the baito closures and tree tenure, Eritrea's village closures entry; for what a court will and will not hear, the Land Proclamation entry; for community project money, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: U.S. Treasury OFAC — North Korea Sanctions
trackers.desc: U.S. sanctions program targeting DPRK illicit finance and evasion — among the few public windows onto North Korean money flows. Here you can trace how suspicious transactions are reported and money-laundering intelligence is produced in North Korea.

trackers.name: PERAC Principles — protected zones when domestic machinery has stopped
trackers.desc: AN INSTRUMENT WRITTEN FOR EXACTLY THIS SITUATION, AND IT NAMES NO ONE. The Principles on Protection of the Environment in Relation to Armed Conflicts — 28 principles adopted by the International Law Commission on second reading on 27 May 2022 and welcomed by the UN General Assembly in A/RES/77/104 of 7 December 2022, adopted without vote — cover the whole arc: before, during and after armed conflict, and situations of occupation. BE HONEST ABOUT THEIR STATUS: they are nonbinding — but ILC documents are recorded as increasingly interpreted by tribunals, courts and governments as ‘reflections of customary international law’. Cite them as that, not as treaty obligations. PRINCIPLE 4 IS THE DESIGNATION ROUTE WHEN DOMESTIC MACHINERY HAS STOPPED: States should designate, by agreement or otherwise, areas of environmental importance as protected zones in the event of an armed conflict, including where those areas are of cultural importance — cultural importance is an express qualifying ground. PRINCIPLE 5 requires States, international organisations AND other relevant actors to protect the environment of the lands and territories that indigenous peoples inhabit or traditionally use, and where conflict has harmed it, to consult and cooperate with indigenous peoples on remedial measures — note that the addressees are not only States, which reaches bodies operating where a government cannot or will not act. PRINCIPLE 3 requires effective legislative, administrative, judicial and other measures. AND THE STRUCTURAL POINT: the ILC chose not to differentiate between international and non-international armed conflicts, so the environment-related conduct of non-state armed groups also comes within their purview — which matters where harm is done by armed groups rather than a state army. The distinctions sit in the commentaries, which should be read together with the principles. CITE ALONGSIDE: the 2020 ICRC Guidelines on protection of the natural environment in armed conflict, UNEA resolution 2/15 (27 May 2016), the 2019 Geneva List of Principles on the Protection of Water Infrastructure, and victim-assistance provisions in the Mine Ban Treaty and the Convention on Cluster Munitions.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: COMIFAC Treaty and Plan de Convergence — and its community protocol
trackers.desc: A TREATY BODY WITH A TEMPLATE YOU CAN COPY. The Traité relatif à la conservation et à la gestion durable des écosystèmes forestiers d'Afrique Centrale, signed by heads of state at their second summit on 5 February 2005 in Brazzaville, instituted the Commission des Forêts d'Afrique Centrale — described as the unique instance d'orientation, de décision et de coordination for subregional forest action, and the cadre politique et juridique global for cooperation in the field. A transboundary forest question belongs in that forum. The Plan de Convergence is the reference framework for all such interventions — first edition 2005–2014, revised in 2014 for 2015–2025 and restructured into 10 strategic axes, executed by a Secrétariat exécutif. CIVIL SOCIETY IS A NAMED STAKEHOLDER in implementing it, alongside state administrations, CEEAC and the private sector — so participation is built into the framework, not conceded case by case. Axis 7 covers capacity and participation des acteurs, expressly contemplating micro-projets générateurs de revenus pour les populations locales; axis 9 covers innovative financing mechanisms. THE DOCUMENT LIBRARY IS THE MOST USEFUL PART: COMIFAC publishes a worked Protocole Bioculturel Communautaire for a named village, a guide to inventorying genetic resources and traditional knowledge, a paper on les droits d'usage des peuples autochtones et communautés locales et les obligations qui en découlent, a subregional APA (access and benefit-sharing) strategy, and directives on forests and the SDGs built with FAO as 5 principles and 12 directives across 31 prioritised targets. A community biocultural protocol published by a treaty body is a template, not a theory. AND ITS OWN DIAGNOSIS IS QUOTABLE: the Plan records that participatory natural resource management and mediation of use conflicts, though already mapped out, are insufficiently developed.

trackers.name: Equatorial Guinea — published attorney lists and named firms with Malabo AND Bata offices, for a country where the bar cannot be used as a referral route
trackers.desc: WHERE TO FIND A NAMED LAWYER WHEN THE BAR IS NOT AN OPTION: this file records that the Equatoguinean Colegio de Abogados was dissolved by decree in 2002, its replacement's members reportedly appointed by and under the control of the justice minister, and that it SUSPENDS ADVOCATES FOR REPRESENTING CLIENTS — so the ordinary route used everywhere else in Africa, a bar referral, is closed here. What exists instead are PUBLISHED LISTS. A FOREIGN MISSION IN MALABO PUBLISHES AN ALPHABETICAL LIST OF LAWYERS AND FIRMS WILLING TO PROVIDE LEGAL SERVICES, stating plainly that it assumes no responsibility for their professional ability or integrity and cannot vouch for information the providers supplied themselves. An embassy attorney list is a starting point, not a recommendation — use it to get names, then ask each firm directly what it has actually done in your field. NAMED FIRMS WITH DOMESTIC REACH: NGOMO ASOCIADOS, operating NATIONALLY THROUGH OFFICES IN BOTH MALABO AND BATA, advising companies AND PARTICULARES — private individuals — across all branches of law, with professionals of more than 30 years' experience and a network of collaborating firms abroad (tel +240 551-109-500); CLARENCE ABOGADOS & ASOCIADOS, whose practice areas include ENERGY AND NATURAL RESOURCES and REAL ESTATE; ALOGO LAW FIRM, covering employment, energy and natural resources; and HELPEN ABOGADOS & CONSULTORES at Banapa, Malabo. A national business directory lists firms under a juridical category with addresses in Malabo and Bata. Offices in both Malabo AND Bata is the filter that matters — the mainland is where the forest, the plantations and the concessions are, and a Bioko-only firm cannot reach them. AND THE HONEST WARNING, REPEATED FROM THIS FILE'S OWN RECORD: the firms reachable this way are oriented to corporate and investor clients — the same firms that advise the companies. Ask directly whether a firm will act AGAINST a concession holder before you disclose your case, and remember that Equatoguinean advocates who represent activists have been detained and suspended. WHO IT SUITS: Equatoguineans needing to instruct counsel on land, expropriation, employment or a natural-resource matter. CAVEATS: COMMERCIAL FIRMS AND A FOREIGN-MISSION LIST, NOT LEGAL AID. For lawyers who defend lawyers and represented over 40 activists, Equatorial Guinea's Comisión Ecuatoguineana de Juristas entry; for constituting your own association first, the NGO registration entry.

trackers.name: INDEFOR-AP, Bata — the only reachable environmental body in the country, and the way in is a telephone number
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE FIRST ENTRY IN THE FILE FOR EQUATORIAL GUINEA, AND THE HONEST SUMMARY IS THAT ONE INSTITUTION PUBLISHES A CONTACT AND NOTHING PUBLISHES A COMPLAINT ROUTE. The National Institute for Forestry Development and Management of the Protected Areas System is a public body with administrative and financial autonomy, headquartered in Bata, responsible for sustainable use of the forests and for running the national protected areas system. It is organised in departments for protected-area management, the national herbarium, sustainable forestry, training and outreach, cartography and topography, and administration. The contact page names the Director General, Fidel Esono Mba Eyono, and gives one telephone number, +240 222 250 465; that name is corroborated by independent Equatoguinean press reporting of the institute's ecoguard training, which is why this entry exists at all. WHAT TO KNOW BEFORE YOU RELY ON IT: the published institutional email address is a personal Yahoo account, and the mail link on the same page resolves to an unrelated address left in by the site's developer — the contact form and the email cannot be relied on, so use the telephone or go to Bata. The site is on a .com domain; no government-domain page for the institute was located, and no ministry page listing it was found, so this is recorded as the institute's own site on the strength of its content and the corroborated director rather than because a state domain confirms it. THE ABSENCES, WHICH ARE THE FINDING: no environmental complaint route, no impact-assessment register, no published objection period, no legal aid scheme and no ombudsman were located for this country. Reporting on the protected areas — thirteen of them, with ecoguards deployed in five — comes from conservation NGOs working alongside the institute rather than from the state.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants in Equatorial Guinea — added by name in the eighth cycle; the only community-accessible money recorded for this country
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY FOR MONEY: the GEF SMALL GRANTS PROGRAMME expanded country coverage in its eighth replenishment from 124 to 135 countries, ADDING EQUATORIAL GUINEA BY NAME — alongside Somalia, South Sudan, Libya and São Tomé and Príncipe. THE ALLOCATION RULE: the eighth cycle secured USD 135 million for the core programme and ensures EQUAL ALLOCATION OF NEARLY USD 1 MILLION IN CORE FINANCING TO EACH of the 135 participating countries — regardless of size or previous participation, with STAR allocations raised over 30 per cent. A newly added country is not competing against large established programmes for the core money, which is the argument for applying in the FIRST cycle rather than waiting to see how it goes. The programme's stated objective is to catalyse and mobilise CIVIL SOCIETY actors and LOCAL ACTIONS addressing the major drivers of environmental degradation, and it has funded community-level environmental projects since 1992. WHY THIS ENTRY EXISTS: Equatorial Guinea has been the thinnest bucket in this entire file, carrying a single honest-absence entry recording that the state forestry and protected-areas institute is all that exists and no independent civil society counterpart could be verified. A funding window is not a substitute for that — but it is the first recorded route by which money could reach a local group, and it costs nothing to ask whether the country programme has opened. WHO IT SUITS: Equatoguinean community groups and associations with an environmental project, and anyone testing whether the window is live. CAVEATS: STATE THIS PLAINLY — civic space in Equatorial Guinea is severely restricted, independent organising carries real risk, and a grant programme does not change that; registration requirements may be the binding obstacle. It funds environmental action, NOT litigation or land purchase. For what does and does not exist institutionally, Equatorial Guinea's INDEFOR-AP entry.

trackers.name: Comisión Ecuatoguineana de Juristas and EG Justice — they defend the lawyers, because in Equatorial Guinea representing a client is what gets an advocate suspended
trackers.desc: WHO DEFENDS THE DEFENDERS, AND THE RISK COMES FIRST BECAUSE IT IS THE POINT: in Equatorial Guinea taking a client can cost an advocate the right to practise. Advocate Ángel Obama Obiang Eseng was ILLEGALLY DETAINED for 48 hours on 4 August and TEMPORARILY SUSPENDED FROM THE PROFESSION on 14 August 2024 by the Colegio de Abogados — the suspension arising BECAUSE HE REPRESENTED a detained activist; the wife and nephew of Doctor Ponciano Mbomio Nvo were arbitrarily detained; and Mbomio himself was earlier suspended for expressing opinions and criticisms of the government in his closing arguments, having already been suspended for a year in similar circumstances. Before you instruct anyone here, understand that you are asking them to accept professional and personal risk — that is the honest frame for this entire entry. WHY THE BAR IS NOT THE ANSWER HERE, UNLIKE EVERY OTHER COUNTRY IN THIS FILE: the original Colegio de Abogados was DISSOLVED BY GOVERNMENT DECREE in May 2002; the justice minister created a High Council of Lawyers chaired by himself and required all lawyers to seek ministry recognition; a new bar was formed in 2003 whose members were reportedly appointed by, and under the control of, the Minister of Justice. So a referral from the bar is not an independent route in Equatorial Guinea — it is the body that suspends advocates for defending clients. WHO TO GO TO INSTEAD: the COMISIÓN ECUATOGUINEANA DE JURISTAS (juristasge.org), working with EG JUSTICE — described as the only human rights organisation devoted solely to Equatorial Guinea, founded by an Equatoguinean exile — which together defend human rights advocates, represent prisoners of conscience, and have secured LEGAL REPRESENTATION FOR OVER 40 ACTIVISTS with humanitarian support for their families, brought legal action against the government in December 2022, and raised the persecution of lawyers at the UN Universal Periodic Review with the Paris bar. WHO IT SUITS: Equatoguineans facing detention, land seizure or reprisal who need counsel that will not be deterred, and families of detained people. CAVEATS: THESE ARE DIASPORA-BASED AND NETWORKED BODIES, not a walk-in service inside the country; contact carries risk for you and for them. For what does and does not exist institutionally, Equatorial Guinea's INDEFOR-AP entry; for the newly opened community funding window, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Ley 6/2025 on protected areas and ANDEGE — the law that finally replaced a statute repealed in 2003, and the national NGO that visits communities bordering Monte Alén
trackers.desc: THE NEW LAW, AND WHY THE GAP IT FILLS MATTERS MORE THAN THE LAW ITSELF: Equatorial Guinea has promulgated LEY 6/2025 ON PROTECTED AREAS, which the state's own account says responds to LEGAL NEEDS OUTSTANDING SINCE THE 2003 REPEAL OF THE EARLIER LEY 4/2000 — A REPEAL THAT LEFT NORMATIVE VOIDS ON THE DECLARATION, PROTECTION, MANAGEMENT AND FINANCING of the country's protected natural areas. For roughly two decades there was no operative rule on how an area gets declared or funded. If you were told in that period that nothing could be done for your forest, that was true and it is no longer — the new law is the reason to ask again. Its stated objects include conserving priority ecosystems AND FOREST CARBON RESERVES, protecting biodiversity, promoting ecotourism, and PROMOTING CARBON AND BIODIVERSITY CREDITS AS A SUSTAINABLE ECONOMIC ALTERNATIVE, aligned with the global biodiversity framework target of protecting at least 30% of terrestrial, marine and coastal areas by 2030; more than 80% of the country's surface is vegetation-covered. Carbon and biodiversity credits are named in the statute as an economic alternative — which means a community forest proposal can be argued in the government's own revenue terms rather than only conservation ones. WHAT ALREADY EXISTS TO ATTACH TO: the SISTEMA NACIONAL DE ÁREAS PROTEGIDAS (SNAP) comprises THIRTEEN protected areas, EXPRESSLY WITHOUT PREJUDICE TO FUTURE EXPANSION — including Monte Alén (2,000 km2), Los Altos de Nsork (700 km2), the Caldera de Luba scientific reserve and Annobón island — built under LEY 1/1997 on the use and management of forests and administered from Bata. Thirteen areas with expansion written into the founding purpose is an open door: the list was never meant to be closed. WHO GOES TO THE VILLAGES: ANDEGE (Amigos de la Naturaleza y del Medio Ambiente de Guinea Ecuatorial), a national NGO, has run awareness missions in the local communities of SENDJE, MISERGUE, TEGUETE and MIDJOBO — districts of Mbini, Evinayong and Kogo, all bordering MONTE ALÉN NATIONAL PARK, working with an international conservation partner. A named national NGO that has physically visited named villages is the most concrete civil-society contact recorded for Equatorial Guinea in this file. WHO IT SUITS: Equatoguinean communities bordering a park or holding forest, and anyone seeking declaration of new ground. CAVEATS: A NEW STATUTE NOT YET TESTED, in a country where the earlier one was repealed and left unreplaced for twenty years, and where an earlier national biodiversity strategy WENT UNIMPLEMENTED FOR LACK OF FINANCING. For the institute that manages the system and what does not exist around it, Equatorial Guinea's INDEFOR-AP entry; for lawyers who defend lawyers, the Comisión Ecuatoguineana de Juristas entry; for community money, the GEF Small Grants entry.

trackers.name: Bioko Biodiversity Protection Program — contracts about 50 LOCAL WORKERS as forest and beach patrol teams in the Gran Caldera protected area, and is building a centre at Moka
trackers.desc: WHO EMPLOYS LOCAL PEOPLE TO PATROL: the BIOKO BIODIVERSITY PROTECTION PROGRAM (BBPP), working across Bioko island in partnership with the NATIONAL UNIVERSITY OF EQUATORIAL GUINEA (UNGE), CONTRACTS APPROXIMATELY 50 LOCAL WORKERS in the GRAN CALDERA AND SOUTHERN HIGHLANDS PROTECTED AREA to serve in FOREST AND BEACH PATROL TEAMS, to deter hunting and collect data on wildlife. Fifty paid local patrol jobs is the most substantial community employment recorded for Equatorial Guinea in this file — in a country where the acquire and legal routes are thin, a conservation operation that pays wages is a real presence on the ground, and worth approaching for work as much as for protection. WHAT ELSE IT RUNS: an annual JANUARY CENSUS of primates in the remote Gran Caldera Volcánica de Luba, conducted by trained students and volunteers; an ONGOING SURVEY OF THE MALABO BUSHMEAT MARKET; a study-abroad programme based at UNGE involving both Equatoguinean and American students; and a wildlife research centre under development in the town of MOKA to host ecotourists and visiting scientists, with a GUEST HOUSE, WILDLIFE SANCTUARY AND A SYSTEM OF TRAILS. A market survey is documentation you can cite, and a named town with a guest house is a place you can physically go — both rarer in this country's record than they sound. THE GROUND IT COVERS AND WHY IT MATTERS: the RESERVA CIENTÍFICA DE LA GRAN CALDERA DE LUBA, created 2000, covers 51,000 HECTARES of dense rainforest on Bioko, much of it PRISTINE FOREST, with a high primate population including species endemic to the reserve, and it is one of the most important nesting areas in the Atlantic for FOUR SEA TURTLE SPECIES. THE THREAT NAMED PLAINLY IN THE RECORD: the primate population is endangered by growing bushmeat demand COUPLED WITH LACK OF ENFORCEMENT OF THE HUNTING BAN INSIDE THE RESERVE — a Spanish NGO had run conservation and ecotourism work there from 1995 focused on green turtles. An unenforced ban is the standing condition here; patrol teams paid to walk the forest are what substitutes for enforcement, which is why the employment matters more than the designation. WHO IT SUITS: Bioko communities, and Equatoguineans seeking conservation work, training or a named institution to approach. CAVEATS: A RESEARCH AND PATROL PROGRAMME WITH FOREIGN UNIVERSITY BACKING, NOT A COMMUNITY-OWNED BODY, and it operates in the severely restricted civic space this file records elsewhere. For the new protected-areas law and the NGO that visits villages, Equatorial Guinea's Ley 6/2025 and ANDEGE entry; for the institute that manages the system, INDEFOR-AP; for lawyers who defend lawyers, the Comisión Ecuatoguineana de Juristas entry.

trackers.name: Registering an NGO in Equatorial Guinea — the published requirements: notarised statutes, a favourable report from the provincial Governor AND from every ministry regulating your activity
trackers.desc: HOW TO BECOME A LEGAL PERSON, WHICH EVERY OTHER INSTRUMENT IN THIS FILE ASSUMES YOU ALREADY ARE: in Equatorial Guinea NGOs ARE DEFINED BY LAW AS ASSOCIATIONS OF AN APOLITICAL, NON-PROFIT AND SOCIAL-UTILITY NATURE WITH THEIR OWN LEGAL PERSONALITY; they HAVE THEIR OWN ASSETS AND MAY ENGAGE IN LUCRATIVE ACTIVITIES that enrich that patrimony for the better fulfilment of their purpose, provided financial contributions received ARE NOT DISTRIBUTED AMONG MEMBERS and are used solely for the purpose. An NGO here may hold assets and trade to fund itself — that is the vehicle a community needs to hold land, receive grant money and sign anything, and it is the step Cameroon, Gabon, Nigeria and Togo all require before their community-forest instruments will look at you. THE DOCUMENTS: a MEMORANDUM OF INCORPORATION AND ARTICLES OF ASSOCIATION reflecting the minimum requirements provided by law, LEGALISED BEFORE A PUBLIC NOTARY; the association must HAVE A SOCIAL PURPOSE AIMED AT BENEFITING A GENERIC GROUP AND NOT ADVOCATE THE PRIVATE INTERESTS OF ITS MEMBERS. Write the purpose as the benefit to the whole community, not to the founding families — the law makes that a condition of existence, and it is also the rule that protects your body from capture. THE GATE, STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT IS THE HARD PART: A FAVOURABLE REPORT IS REQUIRED FROM THE GOVERNOR OF THE PROVINCE where the NGO intends to operate, applied for by formal letter to the Governor's office with the legalised statutes and an affidavit attached; AND, to submit the registration application to the MINISTRY OF INTERIOR AND LOCAL CORPORATIONS, A FAVOURABLE REPORT IS ALSO REQUIRED FROM ALL MINISTERIAL DEPARTMENTS REGULATING THE ACTIVITIES OF THE NGO. Every ministry that touches your subject holds a veto. Count them before you start, approach the Governor first, and expect the environment ministry to be one of them — which is why the INDEFOR-AP and ANDEGE contacts in this file matter before you file, not after. The interior ministry has also publicly invited existing associations and NGOs to REGULARISE THEIR SITUATION. WHO IT SUITS: Equatoguinean communities and groups needing a body that can hold assets, receive funds and sign agreements. CAVEATS: SOURCED FROM A LAW-FIRM PRACTICE NOTE, not the statute text — confirm current requirements; and the apolitical condition is enforced in a state this file records as suspending advocates for defending clients. For the protected-areas law and the NGO that visits villages, Equatorial Guinea's Ley 6/2025 and ANDEGE entry; for 50 paid patrol jobs on Bioko, the BBPP entry; for counsel, the Comisión Ecuatoguineana de Juristas entry.

trackers.name: Syria — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the Ministry of Finance prepares the state budget & financial policies, collects public revenue, supervises state expenditure and manages public debt, Syria. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Syria.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Nauru — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; oversees public financial management and prepares the annual budget, Republic of Nauru. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Nauru.

trackers.name: SPREP — three conventions, and 26 members is not 12 parties
trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. SPREP is an independent intergovernmental organisation, autonomous since the Agreement Establishing SPREP was signed at Apia on 16 June 1993, with the Article 2 purpose of providing assistance to protect and improve the environment and ensure sustainable development for present and future generations. It has 26 members — 14 Pacific island countries, 7 territories and 5 metropolitan states — and is headquartered in Apia, Samoa. ESTABLISH WHICH CONVENTION FITS YOUR ISSUE: the Noumea Convention (1986, in force 1990), described by UNEP as the only comprehensive multilateral umbrella agreement for protection of natural resources and environment in the region; the Waigani Convention on hazardous and radioactive waste imports; and the Apia Convention on nature conservation. THE NOUMEA CONVENTION IS UNDER ACTIVE REVIEW — WHICH IS AN OPENING: a 2021 Review produced recommendations now being implemented through a Noumea Workplan and Budget whose stated aim is to elevate the work of the Convention and enhance awareness and implementation, with a Communications Plan and a Finance Strategy named as critical. BUT CHECK WHETHER YOUR STATE IS A PARTY: SPREP has 26 members while the Noumea Convention has only 12 contracting parties — membership and party status are different things, and this entry does not assert the latter. GOVERNANCE POINT WORTH KNOWING: the SPREP Meeting is the plenary decision-making body; the Executive Board (established 2015) is subordinate to it and has no power to make decisions requiring input of all Members — so a decision affecting all members must go to the Meeting. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers. YOUR STATE IS RECORDED AS A NOUMEA CONVENTION PARTY: it was among those represented at the 18th Conference of the Parties, Apia, 5 September 2025 — so the Convention's obligations and its Workplan apply here.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so no incorporated body is required, which removes the commonest barrier recorded across this map. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest; only successful applicants are invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted — wasted work, and expensive wasted work where drafting means travelling. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. READ THE PUBLISHED GRANT RECORD BEFORE DRAFTING: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25 — showing what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries. That is better evidence of what will succeed than any guidance note. UNDP SUPPORT HERE IS COUNTRY-LEVEL: UNDP's Pacific Office provides country support to this state, so an in-country office is a realistic second route alongside the Trust.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN NAURU: it was proposed in 2009 to appoint an Ombudsman to oversee development of an RTI regime.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — individuals can apply
trackers.desc: INDIVIDUALS CAN APPLY, NOT JUST ORGANISATIONS — the third fund in this file with that feature, and consistently the thing local groups do not realise. New Zealand's Pacific Development and Conservation Trust distributes up to $250,000 a year in grants to groups and individuals for conservation, cultural heritage, development and goodwill, prioritising community projects including those involving representative, endangered, threatened or unique habitats and species. Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu and Samoa are all expressly on its eligible list, alongside every other Pacific state and territory. TWO OF ITS FUNDING CRITERIA ARE UNUSUALLY USEFUL: it funds projects that ‘improve legal access to facilities or resources necessary for social, cultural and economic sufficiency’ — broad enough to cover securing a community's access to land and water, which is not how most conservation funds are written — and projects that develop local capacities, particularly for indigenous ecological knowledge development. So documenting customary knowledge of a threatened site is itself a fundable project, and that documentation is often exactly the evidence an objection needs. The Trust is committed to communities working in partnership with iwi, hapū, aiga and local indigenous people — a proposal led by a customary group is what it is looking for, not an exception it tolerates. Apply via New Zealand's communitymatters service. THE OTHER REGIONAL FUNDER, WITH ITS LIMITS STATED: the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund invested in the Polynesia-Micronesia hotspot — backed by AFD, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank, run through CI's team in Apia with SPREP support — funding over 90 projects in 13 countries, including 58 community-based projects. That five-year programme ran 2008–2013 and this entry does NOT assert an open window — check CEPF directly. A RESULT WORTH CITING: in Fiji the National Trust of Fiji, Pacific Invasives Initiative, BirdLife and the local community eradicated goats and rats on Monuriki, creating a haven for the Critically Endangered Fiji crested iguana. AND A FIGURE THAT STRENGTHENS ANY APPLICATION FROM HERE: only 21 percent of the region's original vegetation remains pristine, across a hotspot of 4,500 islands whose total land area is about the size of Switzerland.

trackers.name: Central African Republic — Ministère des Finances et du Budget
